The Pepper Programming Language

Introduction

Pepper is a compiled programming language for writing fast, native programs that are safe by default. Like Rust and Swift, it aims to rule out whole classes of memory bugs without asking you to manage memory by hand. It puts three things first:

  • Clarity. Code should say what it does. Pepper has a small, familiar syntax, one way to write most things, and error messages that point at the exact token you need to change.
  • Simplicity. There is no inheritance, no garbage collector to tune, and no ownership annotations to learn. Structs hold data, methods and extensions add behavior, and traits describe what a type can do.
  • Concurrent safety. Shared data should be safe to use from more than one thread. Only thread-safe values can be shared: numbers, async.Atomic<T>, and structs declared [Shared], whose fields the compiler checks.

Here is a complete Pepper program:

# Every program starts at main. Its return value is the process exit code.
main(): int {
    print("Hello, world!");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# Hello, world!

How Pepper manages memory

Every struct value in Pepper is a reference to an object on the heap, and the object is freed when the last reference to it goes away. The model is exactly C++'s std::shared_ptr<T> passed by value: storing a reference in a variable, a field, an array element or a parameter adds a reference, and that reference is released when the variable goes out of scope or is overwritten. There is no separate notion of a "borrowed" reference to learn. Numbers and other primitive values are copied, as in C.

Because the rules are the same everywhere, you can predict exactly when an object is freed and when its destructor runs. The chapter on memory and reference counting covers the model in detail.

How Pepper is built

The compiler is written in Pepper, and builds itself. It parses your program, checks it, and generates native code through LLVM, then links an executable with the system's C toolchain. The same compiler powers a language server, so editors such as VS Code show Pepper's errors as you type.

Pepper runs on Windows (x64), Linux (x64) and macOS (arm64), compiles to WebAssembly for WASI (--target wasm32-wasip1, see WebAssembly), and builds libraries that iOS and Android apps call (see iOS and Android). Each release is prebuilt for Windows (x64), Linux (x64, glibc 2.28 or newer) and macOS (arm64 and x64), and installs with one command: see Installing Pepper.

Current status

Pepper is young. The core language works and is tested, and so does a standard library large enough to write real programs, but expect gaps. In the order this book covers them:

  • Basics: variables, functions, tuples and multiple return values, enums (with cases that carry values, methods and computed properties) and match (as a statement or a value, on enums, integers, characters, strings and trait values, with is tests, nested and tuple patterns, guards, ranges and constants), Optional values, and Result-based error handling (Result is an enum, and ? propagates errors).
  • Collections and iteration: array and map literals, sortable, searchable arrays with read-only slices, hash maps and sets, sorted maps and sets (Map, Set) and an insertion-ordered OrderedMap, a BitSet of small integers, a double-ended Deque and a PriorityQueue, and iteration (with adapters such as map, filter, take and chain, and consumers such as fold, any and sum).
  • Types of your own: structs with constructors, destructors, methods and properties, value structs and enums ([Value]), derived == and hash ([Equatable]), a Comparable trait for ordered types, traits (with default methods, and usable as types that convert back with as?), generics (with type arguments inferred at calls, and generic methods), type aliases, and function types and closures.
  • Memory and resources: with blocks, and weak references (to structs and trait values).
  • Concurrency: atomics, threads, channels and mutexes, and tasks (green threads that take turns on a few worker threads, parking on sockets and timeouts).
  • Organizing a program: modules (with export * from re-exports), and unit tests: [Test] functions that pepper test runs in parallel, each in a process of its own.
  • Compile time, platforms and C: calling C (including C callbacks), and being called from C ([Export]ed functions in a static or shared library, with a generated header), and SIMD vectors (simd.Vector<T, N>).
  • Standard library: strings (with a StringBuilder, StringConstant for literals' constant bytes, to_string and a ToString trait, $"{a + b:>8}" interpolation with format specifications, and String.format), file-system access (with glob patterns and watching a directory for changes; see files), text encodings (UTF-16, ASCII; see text), TCP, UDP and Unix domain sockets, TLS, an HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 client and server (streamed bodies, redirects, connection reuse, ALPN), URI parsing and percent-encoding, base64, form data and UUIDs, regular expressions, JSON (parsing and writing JsonValues, JSONC documents that keep their comments, and converting structs with json.encode and json.decode), TOML (parsing, writing, editing a document in place, and converting structs), gzip and zlib compression, tar archives, cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, SHA-1 and BLAKE3, with HMAC and PBKDF2, in the digest module), random numbers (secure bytes from the operating system and a seedable generator), command-line arguments (main(args: String[]), parsed into options with the cli module), starting child processes, the os module (environment variables, monotonic and wall clocks with Duration, and machine and user information), the time module (dates, times of day, time zones from the system's database, and RFC 3339, HTTP and strftime text), the debug module (stack backtraces, which a panic also prints, and the debugger), and leveled, structured logging (the log module). YAML and zip archives come as packages.

pep-fmt, the code formatter, pep-profile, which profiles a program and draws a flame graph, pep-test, which runs unit tests, and pepper, the entry point that runs every tool, are themselves written in Pepper. A pep.toml project builds with pepper build alone and imports the packages it depends on by name, which pepper package fetches from GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg. Some things you will meet quickly:

  • Functions are values: a named function, an extern C function, a method (p.norm, Point.norm), a constructor (Point), a generic function's specialization (larger<int>) or a closure such as (x: int) => x * 2 can be stored, passed and called through a function type such as (int) => int (see function types and closures).
  • A constructor marked [Implicit] converts a value into its struct wherever the struct is expected, so io.Path parameters accept a String (see implicit conversions).
  • Free functions, methods, operators, constructors, extension methods and trait members can be overloaded.
  • A static block runs in the compiler: it can list a struct's fields and the attributes on them ([Attribute] structs of your own) and generate code for each, so one function can encode any struct (see reflection and attributes).
  • -D NAME=VALUE on the command line defines a build option, which [BuildOption("NAME")] and [Target(BuildOption(NAME) >= 2)] select code by and static blocks read (see build options).
  • A call can name its arguments, window("Editor", resizable = false), to skip defaulted parameters or pass them in any order (see named arguments).
  • Generic parameters can require traits (<T: Shape & Named>), checked wherever the generic is used and, inside the generic, against what the traits declare (see constraints). Numbers, bool and enums whose cases carry nothing can declare traits too, for constraints, but are never trait values.
  • Threads can share only thread-safe values, which the compiler checks, closure captures included. A channel hands over what it is sent without copying it (send(move(x)), or send(copy(x)) to keep x), a Select waits to receive from or send to several channels at once, and a Mutex holds any struct, with the compiler keeping each locked value apart from the rest of the program (see threads). An RwLock lets many threads read a thread-safe value at once, and Semaphore, Barrier and Latch coordinate groups of threads. A [ThreadLocal] module-scope var gives every thread its own copy, compiled to the platform's native thread-local storage (see thread-local variables).
  • Integer arithmetic that overflows panics instead of wrapping, at every optimization level; wrapping_add and its siblings wrap on purpose (see integer overflow). Bit counting, rotation, byte swapping and the floating-point functions are methods that compile to LLVM's intrinsics, and any other intrinsic can be declared as an extern (see LLVM intrinsics).
  • Reference counting does not reclaim cycles on its own: two objects that refer to each other are never freed. Break the cycle with a weak reference on one side.

Each chapter of this book says plainly what is and is not supported. When a chapter shows a feature, the example was compiled and run to check it.

How this book is organized

  • Tutorial. Getting started builds the compiler and runs your first program. A tour of Pepper then walks through the main features by building a small word-counting program.
  • Language guide. One chapter per part of the language, in an order to learn it by: the basics, from types and variables to error handling; collections and iteration; types of your own; memory; concurrency; organizing a program into modules and tests; and then compile time, platforms and C, starting at attributes. Read it in order, or jump to the topic you need.
  • Standard library guide. A chapter for each area of the library, from files to HTTP.
  • Tools. The pepper command, pep-new, pep-run, pep-fmt, pep-profile, pep-test and debugging.
  • Standard library reference. Every type and function in the runtime, generated from the runtime's own documentation comments. Start at the overview.
  • Contributing. Building this documentation.

Every complete program in this book lives in the repository's docs/examples/ folder and is compiled and run by the test suite, so what you read is what works.

Versions of this book

This documentation is versioned with the compiler. Use the version picker in the top-right corner of each page to switch between releases; dev follows the main branch. Read the version that matches the compiler you are using.

Getting started

This chapter installs Pepper on your machine, compiles and runs a first program, and sets up your editor.

Install Pepper

Each release has the Pepper toolchain prebuilt for Linux, macOS and Windows. One command installs it:

# Linux and macOS
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pep-lang/pepper/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pep-lang/pepper/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

It installs into ~/.pepper (%LOCALAPPDATA%\pepper on Windows), adds its bin folder to your PATH, and offers to install what linking a program needs when it is missing: clang on Linux, Xcode's command line tools on macOS, LLVM and the Visual Studio Build Tools on Windows. Open a new terminal afterwards. Installing Pepper covers the options, what it installs, and uninstalling.

Building from source

To work on Pepper itself, or on a platform with no prebuilt binaries, build the toolchain from source: see Building Pepper from source.

Your first program

Pepper source files end in .pep. Create a file named hello.pep:

# Every program starts at main. Its return value is the process exit code.
main(): int {
    print("Hello, world!");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# Hello, world!

Every program starts at main, which here takes no arguments and returns an int (it can also take the command-line arguments; see Functions): the process's exit code, where 0 means success. print writes a value's text to standard output, followed by a new line. Comments start with # and run to the end of the line.

Compile and run it

Pass the source file to pepper build. It compiles and links a native executable, but does not run it, so run the result yourself:

pepper build hello.pep -o hello
./hello

Hello, world!

On Windows, name the output with .exe (-o hello.exe), since Windows will not run a file without an extension, and run it as .\hello.exe. Without -o the executable is written to the current directory, named after the source file with no extension (hello for hello.pep).

Running a program

To build and run in one step, as python hello.py does, use pepper run. It keeps the executable out of your folder, and runs it again at once when nothing changed:

pepper run hello.pep

Arguments after the file go to the program's main; see Running a program: pep-run.

Starting a project

A program bigger than one file is a project: a folder with a pep.toml that names it and lists the packages it uses. pepper new starts one, with a main.pep and a test, so pepper build and pepper test work in it straight away:

pepper new hello
cd hello
pepper build     # builds ./hello
pepper test      # runs its [Test] function

pepper new geometry --lib starts a package instead, and pepper init starts either in the current folder; see Starting a project: pep-new and pep-init.

Where the compiler finds the standard library

Every program is compiled together with Pepper's standard library, the runtime/ folder of the repository. The compiler looks for it in this order:

  1. The directory named by the PEPPER_RUNTIME environment variable, if it is set. Nothing else is searched.
  2. Starting from the directory you run it from: runtime/, .pep/runtime/, then ../runtime/, ../../runtime/, and so on, up to five levels up.
  3. Starting from the directory that holds the compiler executable: runtime/ beside it, then in each parent directory, up to five levels up.

So an installed compiler, in ~/.pepper/bin, finds ~/.pepper/runtime, and one built in target/bin finds the runtime of the clone it was built from, wherever you run it. To use a different runtime, set PEPPER_RUNTIME or link the runtime into a project's .pep folder:

mkdir .pep
ln -s /path/to/pepper/runtime .pep/runtime

If the compiler cannot find the runtime, it stops with an error:

error: cannot find the Pepper runtime: no runtime directory near /home/me/project or the compiler; set PEPPER_RUNTIME to its path

The compiler also writes intermediate files to .pep/build/ under the directory you run it from, and keeps a build cache in .pep/cache/: each file of the program (and the standard library) is compiled to its own object, and on the next build a file whose sources did not change reuses its object without being compiled or checked again, as long as what its imports declare did not change either: editing a function's body recompiles that file alone, while changing a signature also recompiles the files that import it. A file that compiled with warnings is checked again, so its warnings print on every build. When nothing changed, nothing is checked or linked again. The cache also keeps the standard library checked, so a program's own files are the only ones checked on each build. Deleting .pep/cache/ is always safe.

When something is wrong

The compiler reports errors the way clang does: the file, line and column, a message, and the source line with a caret under the exact token to fix. Store the message in a variable first, then misspell its name:

main(): int {
    var greeting = "Hello, world!";
    print(greting);
    return 0;
}

The compiler reports:

main.pep:3:11: error: use of undeclared identifier 'greting'
    3 |     print(greting);
      |           ^~~~~~~

Errors are colored when the output is a terminal; set NO_COLOR to turn color off. The chapter on compiler errors covers them in more detail.

A failed assert or a panic at run time prints its message and stops the program abnormally. For example, value() on a failed Result prints Result.value on an Err value.

Useful compiler options

OptionWhat it does
-o <file>Name the output executable (or library, with --lib).
-O, -O<n>Optimize: -O0 (the default) through -O3; -O alone is -O2.
-gEmit debug info for gdb, lldb, Visual Studio and WinDbg. See debugging.
-I <dir>Add a directory to search for imported modules. See modules and imports.
-l <lib>, -L <dir>Link a C library, and add a folder to find it in. See linking.
-D <name>[=<value>]Define a build option.
--target <triple>Compile for another platform; see Cross-compiling.
--lib static, --lib sharedBuild a library for C code to link. See calling Pepper from C.
--helpList every option.

The compiler: pep-build describes every option and environment variable the compiler reads.

A program can span several files: pass the entry file, and the compiler finds the files it imports on its own.

Editor support

The VS Code extension adds syntax highlighting and a language server, which reports compiler errors as you type and provides hover information, completion, go to definition, and an outline of each file.

The packaged extension is published as a .vsix file on the pep-lang/vscode-pepper releases page. Download it and install it in VS Code with Extensions: Install from VSIX... from the command palette. It runs the language server of your Pepper toolchain, and offers to install the toolchain when there is none.

A few things are useful once it is installed:

  • Pepper: Restart Language Server restarts the server on demand.
  • Where a value is converted by an [Implicit] constructor, the editor shows the call it stands for as an inlay hint (Path( before "notes.txt" and ) after), and hovering the value says so. The pepper.inlayHints.implicitConversions setting turns the hints off.
  • A literal passed by position shows the name of its parameter as an inlay hint (resize(width: 800, height: 600)); the pepper.inlayHints.parameterNames setting turns these off. Inside a call's parentheses, completion offers the parameter names to name (width = ).
  • Hover and go to definition also work where the compiler has not checked the code yet: in a generic function or method nothing calls, on a match arm's case and the names it binds (Circle(r) => ...), and on the values an enum case declares.
  • The pepper.lspPath setting points the extension at a language server you built yourself (pep-build -O tools/pep-lsp/main.pep -o target/pep-lsp/pep-lsp in a checkout of the repository; see The language server: pep-lsp). The server restarts whenever that file changes.

To install the extension from the branch you have checked out instead of the release, see The VS Code extension.

A tour of Pepper

This chapter walks through the main features of Pepper by writing small programs, and ends with a word counter that reads a file and reports how often each word appears. It moves quickly and shows the common case of each feature; every section links to the chapter of the language guide that covers it fully.

Every program here is complete: save it to a file, compile it as shown in Getting started, and run it. Each one checks its own results with assert(condition, "message"), which stops the program with the message if the condition is false, so a program that runs to the end and returns 0 did what the comments say.

Variables and functions

# A function lists its parameters as `name: type` and gives its return
# type after the closing parenthesis.
square(x: int): int {
    return x * x;
}

# A parameter may have a default value, used when the caller leaves it out.
greet(name: String = "world"): String {
    return "Hello, " + name + "!";
}

# Adds up 1 + 2 + ... + n with a while loop.
sum_to(n: int): int {
    var total = 0;
    var i = 1;
    while i <= n {
        total += i;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

describe(n: int): String {
    if n > 100 {
        return "big";
    } else {
        if n > 10 {
            return "medium";
        }
    }
    return "small";
}

main(): int {
    var answer = 42;          # the type, int, comes from the value
    double ratio = 0.5;       # or write the type yourself
    var whole = (ratio * 10.0) as int;
    assert(whole == 5, "'as' converts between number types");

    assert(square(answer) == 1764, "square(42)");
    assert(greet() == "Hello, world!", "the default name");
    assert(greet("Pepper") == "Hello, Pepper!", "an explicit name");
    assert(sum_to(4) == 10, "1 + 2 + 3 + 4");

    assert(describe(answer) == "medium", "42 is medium");
    assert(describe(7) == "small", "7 is small");

    print(greet("Pepper"));
    print($"{sum_to(100)}");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# Hello, Pepper!
# 5050

A few things to notice:

  • var declares a variable whose type comes from its initial value: 42 is an int. You can also name the type yourself, as in double ratio = 0.5;. as converts between types, such as from double to int. See Types and variables.
  • A function is declared as name(parameters): return type, and each parameter as name: type. A parameter can have a default value, as name does in greet. A function that returns nothing leaves out the return type. See Functions.
  • if and while do not need parentheses around the condition, but the body always needs braces. Chain conditions with else if. See Control flow.
  • += updates a variable in place, and + joins two strings.
  • print writes one value's text on its own line. Interpolate to combine values: print($"total: {sum_to(100)}").

Structs

A struct groups related data with the methods that act on it:

struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;

    # `this.x = 0` as a parameter stores the argument straight into the field.
    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    length_squared(): int {
        return this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y;
    }

    move_by(dx: int, dy: int) {
        this.x = this.x + dx;
        this.y = this.y + dy;
    }
}

# An extension adds methods to a struct that is declared elsewhere.
extend Point {
    swapped(): Point {
        return Point(this.y, this.x);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point(3, 4);
    assert(p.length_squared() == 25, "3*3 + 4*4");

    var origin = Point();
    assert(origin.x == 0 && origin.y == 0, "defaults from the constructor");

    # Struct values are references: q and p name the same Point.
    var q = p;
    q.move_by(1, 1);
    assert(p.x == 4 && p.y == 5, "p sees the move made through q");

    var s = p.swapped();
    assert(s.x == 5 && s.y == 4, "swapped is a new Point");
    assert(p.x == 4, "p itself is unchanged");
    return 0;
}
  • Fields are declared like variables, with var name: type, and may have default values.
  • The constructor is named construct. A parameter written as this.x = 0 stores its argument straight into the field x, and = 0 makes it optional, so Point() and Point(3, 4) both work.
  • Methods are functions declared inside the struct. Inside a method, this is the object the method was called on.
  • extend Point { ... } adds methods to a struct from outside its declaration, even to a struct from the standard library.

Struct values are references. var q = p; does not copy the point: p and q refer to the same object, so moving q moves p. Pepper frees an object when the last reference to it goes away, so you never free memory yourself. See Structs and Memory and reference counting.

Collections

The standard library provides growable arrays, strings, and hash maps. You do not need to import them:

main(): int {
    # Array<T> is a growable list. int[] is another way to write Array<int>.
    var scores = [90, 72];
    scores.append(85);
    assert(scores.count == 3, "three scores");
    assert(scores[0] == 90, "indexing starts at 0");
    scores[1] = 75;
    assert(scores.contains(85), "contains");

    var total = 0;
    for (var score in scores) {
        total += score;
    }
    assert(total == 250, "90 + 75 + 85");

    # sort orders the elements by a comparison function.
    scores.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    assert(scores[0] == 75 && scores[2] == 90, "sorted ascending");

    int[] none = Array<int>();
    assert(none.is_empty, "a new array is empty");

    # String holds UTF-8 text.
    var name = "Pepper";
    var greeting = "Hello, " + name;
    greeting += "!";
    assert(greeting == "Hello, Pepper!", "+ and += join strings");
    assert(greeting.length == 14, "length counts characters");
    assert(greeting.starts_with("Hello"), "starts_with");
    assert(greeting.substr(7, 6) == "Pepper", "substr(start, count)");
    assert(greeting.find("Pepper") == 7, "find returns an offset, or -1");
    assert(greeting[0] == "H", "s[i] is a one-character String");

    # HashMap<K, V> maps keys to values.
    var ages = ["Ada": 36];
    ages.insert("Alan", 41);
    assert(ages.count == 2, "two entries");
    assert(ages["Ada"] == 36, "look up by key");
    assert(ages.contains("Alan"), "contains");
    assert(ages["Grace"] == 0, "a missing key reads as the default value");
    assert(!ages.contains("Grace"), "reading does not insert");
    ages.remove("Ada");
    assert(ages.count == 1, "removed");

    # HashSet<K> keeps each key once.
    var seen = HashSet<String>();
    seen.insert("apple");
    seen.insert("apple");
    assert(seen.count == 1, "duplicates are ignored");
    return 0;
}
  • [90, 72] and ["Ada": 36] are collection literals: a new array and a new map.
  • Array<T> is a list that grows as you append. int[] is a shorter way to write the type Array<int>. Indexing is checked: reading past the end stops the program with an error rather than reading stray memory. sort takes a function that compares two elements, such as the closure (a, b) => a - b.
  • String holds UTF-8 text. The length property counts characters (code points), and s[i] is the character at index i, as a one-character string. Strings compare by content with ==.
  • HashMap<K, V> maps keys to values. Reading a key that is not there gives the default value of V (0 for numbers) without adding it; use contains to tell the two apart. HashSet<K> keeps each key once.
  • for (var x in collection) visits each element of an array, or each character of a string, in order, and for (var i in 0..n) counts from 0 to n - 1. See Iteration.

Handling errors with Result

Pepper has no exceptions. A function that can fail returns a Result: either a value, or an error that explains what went wrong.

# Converts a string of decimal digits to an int, or explains why it cannot.
parse_number(text: String): Result<int> {
    if text.is_empty {
        return Result<int>.err(Error("expected a number, found nothing"));
    }
    var value = 0;
    for (var c in text) {
        var digit = "0123456789".find(c);
        if digit < 0 {
            return Result<int>.err(Error("'" + c + "' is not a digit"));
        }
        value = value * 10 + (digit as int);
    }
    return Result<int>.ok(value);
}

main(): int {
    var good = parse_number("2026");
    assert(good.is_ok(), "digits parse");
    assert(good.value() == 2026, "value() returns the value");

    var bad = parse_number("12x");
    assert(bad.is_err(), "x is not a digit");
    assert(bad.error().message == "'x' is not a digit", "the error explains why");
    print(bad.error().message);

    assert(parse_number("").ok_or(-1) == -1, "ok_or supplies a fallback");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# 'x' is not a digit
  • Result<int> holds either an int or an Error. Build one with Result<int>.ok(value) or Result<int>.err(Error("message")).
  • is_ok() and is_err() tell you which one you have. value() and error() return what it holds; error().message is the error's text.
  • value() returns the value, and stops the program if there is none. Use it only when an error would be a bug. ok_or(fallback) returns the value, or fallback if there is none.

See Error handling with Result.

Putting it together: a word counter

The last program combines everything above. It writes a short text file, reads it back, and counts how often each word appears. It is split into two files: counter.pep defines a WordCounter struct, and main.pep uses it.

counter.pep:

# Counts how often each word occurs in some text.
export struct WordCounter {
    var counts: HashMap<String, int>;
    var order: String[];    # each distinct word, in the order first seen
    var total: int;

    construct() {
        this.counts = HashMap<String, int>();
        this.order = Array<String>();
        this.total = 0;
    }

    add(word: String) {
        if !word.is_empty {
            if !this.counts.contains(word) {
                this.order.append(word);
            }
            this.counts[word] = this.counts[word] + 1;
            this.total = this.total + 1;
        }
    }

    # Splits `text` into words at spaces and counts each one. `add` skips
    # the empty pieces that runs of spaces leave.
    add_text(text: String) {
        for (var word in text.split(" ")) {
            this.add(word);
        }
    }

    count(word: String): int {
        return this.counts[word];
    }
}

main.pep:

import [File, Directory, Path] from io;
import "counter";

# Reads the file at `path` and counts its words.
count_file(path: Path): Result<WordCounter> {
    var text = File.read_to_string(path);
    if text.is_err() {
        return Result<WordCounter>.err(Error(text.error().message));
    }
    var counter = WordCounter();
    counter.add_text(text.value());
    return Result<WordCounter>.ok(counter);
}

main(): int {
    # Write a small file to read back.
    var dir = Directory.temp().join("pepper-word-count");
    Directory.create_all(dir);
    var path = dir.join("poem.txt");
    File.write_text(path, "the cat sat on the mat and the dog sat too");

    var result = count_file(path);
    assert(result.is_ok(), "the file we just wrote can be read");
    var counter = result.value();
    for (var word in counter.order) {
        print($"{word}: {counter.count(word)}");
    }
    assert(counter.total == 11, "eleven words");
    assert(counter.count("the") == 3, "'the' appears three times");
    assert(counter.count("sat") == 2, "'sat' appears twice");
    assert(counter.count("bird") == 0, "'bird' does not appear");

    var missing = count_file(dir.join("missing.txt"));
    assert(missing.is_err(), "a missing file is an error, not a crash");
    print(missing.error().message);

    Directory.remove_all(dir);
    return 0;
}

Compile it by passing the entry file; the compiler finds counter.pep from the import:

pepper build main.pep -o word-count
./word-count

It prints each word with its count, one word per line, and then the error message for the missing file (its exact text comes from the operating system):

the: 3
cat: 1
sat: 2
...
No such file or directory

What is new here:

  • Imports. import "counter"; makes the declarations that counter.pep marks with export available in main.pep. Anything not exported stays private to its file (or, in a module, to the module's files). import [File, Directory, Path] from io; brings three names in from the standard library's io module, which, unlike String or Array, must be imported. See Modules and imports and Visibility.
  • Files. Directory.temp() is the system's temporary directory, and join adds a name to a Path; the name can be a plain String, which converts to a Path implicitly. File has helpers that read or write a whole file at once: File.write_text and File.read_to_string.
  • I/O errors are Results. File.read_to_string returns a Result whose error is an IoError, so reading a missing file is an ordinary error value, not a crash. count_file turns it into its own Result<WordCounter>.
  • Splitting strings. add_text breaks the text into words with split(" "), which returns an Array<String> of the pieces between the spaces (see String).

Where to go next

You have now seen most of what you need to write everyday Pepper code. The language guide covers each topic in depth, including features this tour skipped: generics, function types and closures, traits and extensions, atomics, threads, and calling C.

Types and variables

This chapter covers the values every Pepper program is built from: numbers, booleans and strings, the variables that hold them, and the operators that combine them.

Built-in types

Integers

Pepper has signed and unsigned integers of 8, 16, 32 and 64 bits. Each width has a short name (i32) and a descriptive alias (int). The two names are the same type, so you can use whichever reads better and assign freely between them.

BitsSignedUnsigned
8i8, charu8, byte
16i16, shortu16, ushort
32i32, intu32, uint
64i64, longu64, ulong

int is 32 bits and long is 64 bits on every platform. sizeof<T>() gives the size of a type in bytes.

Integer literals are written in decimal (42) or hexadecimal (0xFF). A literal on its own is an int when its value fits in an int, and a long otherwise, so var big = 3000000000; is a long. It takes another type when you store it in a variable of that type (u64 huge = 9000000000000000000;). A hexadecimal literal is a 64-bit bit pattern: u64 all = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF; sets every bit.

A decimal literal larger than the largest long (9223372036854775807), up to the largest ulong (18446744073709551615), is a ulong: it is the same value as its hexadecimal spelling, and it fits only where a ulong (or a floating-point type) takes it. long's minimum is written with its sign, -9223372036854775808.

# Integer types: widths, signedness, wraparound and conversions.
main(): int {
    # Each width has a short name and a descriptive alias.
    i8 tiny = -100;       # same type as char
    u8 octet = 200;       # same type as byte
    i16 small = -30000;   # same type as short
    u16 port = 65000;     # same type as ushort
    i32 count = 2000000;  # same type as int
    u32 mask = 4000000000; # same type as uint
    i64 big = 9000000000; # same type as long
    u64 huge = 9000000000000000000;  # same type as ulong

    assert(sizeof<char>() == 1 && sizeof<short>() == 2, "8 and 16 bits");
    assert(sizeof<int>() == 4 && sizeof<long>() == 8, "32 and 64 bits");

    # An alias names the same type, so assigning between them is lossless.
    short s = small;
    assert(s == -30000, "short and i16 are one type");

    # Storing a value that does not fit wraps around, as in C.
    u16 wrap = 65535;
    wrap = wrap + 1;
    assert(wrap == 0, "u16 wraps from 65535 to 0");
    i16 overflow = 32767;
    overflow += 1;
    assert(overflow == -32768, "i16 wraps from 32767 to -32768");

    # Widening keeps the value: signed types sign-extend, unsigned zero-extend.
    long widened = small;
    assert(widened == -30000, "i16 widens to long");
    assert((tiny as u8) == 156, "-100 as u8 is 156");
    assert((octet as i8) == -56, "200 as i8 is -56");

    # Narrowing with 'as' keeps the low bits.
    assert((70000 as u16) == 4464, "70000 as u16 keeps the low 16 bits");

    # Hexadecimal literals.
    assert(0xFF == 255, "0xFF is 255");

    # A decimal literal past long's range is a ulong.
    u64 top = 18446744073709551615;
    assert(top == 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, "the largest ulong, in decimal");
    long lowest = -9223372036854775808;
    assert(lowest < 0, "long's minimum is written with its sign");
    assert(count + big > 0 && mask > 0 && huge > 0 && port > 0, "all in range");
    return 0;
}

Storing a value that does not fit in the destination keeps its low bits, as in C: a u16 holding 65535 becomes 0 when you add 1 and store the result, and 70000 as u16 is 4464. Arithmetic that overflows int or a wider type panics instead (see Integer overflow).

A decimal literal larger than the largest ulong, or a hexadecimal literal with more than 64 bits, is an error:

main.pep:2:13: error: integer literal is too large to be represented in a 64-bit integer
    2 |     var f = 99999999999999999999;
      |             ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

So is a decimal literal past long's range stored in an integer type other than ulong:

main.pep:2:14: error: integer literal is too large for type 'long'
    2 |     long g = 9223372036854775808;
      |              ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Floating point

float is a 32-bit and double a 64-bit IEEE 754 number (f32 and f64 are aliases). A literal with a decimal point or an exponent, such as 0.25 or 1e3, is a double.

Comparisons follow IEEE 754, as in C: against NaN (0.0 / 0.0), ==, <, <=, > and >= are false and != is true, so x != x is true only for a NaN. As a condition, a float is true unless it equals zero, NaN included.

Reading numbers from text

Every number type has a static parse that reads one from a String: int.parse("42") gives an int? (see optionals), empty when the text is not a number of that type: not digits, or too big or too small for it. The integer types take a base from 2 to 36 as a second argument ("ff" in base 16 is 255), and float and double read decimal notation ("2.5", ".5", "1e-3"). Neither accepts spaces, a 0x prefix, inf or nan. Each spelling of a type is the same type, so i32.parse is int.parse:

# Reading numbers from text with each number type's static parse.

main(): int {
    # An integer type takes an optional base from 2 to 36.
    assert(int.parse("-42").value() == -42, "decimal");
    assert(byte.parse("ff", 16).value() == 255, "hexadecimal");

    # The result is empty when the text is not a number of that type.
    assert(int.parse("4 2").is_empty(), "not an integer");
    assert(byte.parse("256").is_empty(), "too big for a byte");

    # float and double read decimal notation.
    var ratio = double.parse("2.5e-1");
    if (ratio.is_value()) {
        assert(ratio.value() == 0.25, "an exponent");
    }
    return 0;
}

Booleans

bool holds true or false. Comparisons and the logical operators produce a bool. In arithmetic a bool counts as 0 or 1, and its text is true or false ($"{flag}").

Characters

A character literal is one ASCII character between single quotes: 'a', '"', '#'. Its value is the character's code, and its type is byte (u8), the type of one byte of a UTF-8 string. Like any byte it widens to the other integer types, so it compares with, and stores into, an int or a char as well:

# Character literals are bytes.
is_lower(c: int): bool {
    return c >= 'a' and c <= 'z';
}

main(): int {
    var letter = 'a';   # a byte holding 97
    assert(letter == 97, "a character literal is its ASCII code");
    assert('"' == 34 and '\n' == 10 and '\'' == 39, "escapes work as in strings");

    # Compare the bytes of a String with character literals.
    var text = "x = 1";
    var bytes = text.c_str();
    assert(bytes[0] == 'x' and bytes[2] == '=', "compare raw bytes");
    assert(is_lower(bytes[0]), "a byte widens to int");

    # Arithmetic works as on any integer.
    int digit = bytes[4] - '0';
    assert(digit == 1, "the digit's value");

    print($"{letter}");   # 97
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# 97

The escapes are the same as a string's (see the table under Strings), plus \xHH for any byte, '\xFF' included. A character literal holds exactly one ASCII character; for anything else use a string:

main.pep:2:13: error: character literal may only contain one character; use a string for more
    2 |     var x = 'ab';
      |             ^~~~
main.pep:2:14: error: character literal must be a single ASCII character; use a string for other characters
    2 |     var x = 'é';
      |              ^

char is an 8-bit signed integer, the same type as i8, used mostly for C strings (__ptr<char>). The ASCII characters have the same value as a char and as a byte; '\xFF' is 255 as a byte but -1 read through a char. Text is a String, and a single character of it is a one-code-point String.

byte and char classify ASCII characters as C's ctype.h does in the "C" locale: is_digit, is_hex_digit, is_alphabetic, is_alphanumeric, is_upper, is_lower, is_whitespace, is_blank, is_punctuation, is_graphic, is_printable, is_control and is_ascii, plus to_upper, to_lower and digit_value(base). The names are spelled out (is_punctuation for C's ispunct). A byte above 127, which is a negative char, is never a letter, digit, space or punctuation. Unicode classification is not covered.

# Classify and convert ASCII characters, as C's ctype.h does.
main(): int {
    assert('7'.is_digit() and 'f'.is_hex_digit(), "digits");
    assert('q'.is_alphabetic() and 'Q'.is_upper() and 'q'.is_lower(), "letters");
    assert('\t'.is_whitespace() and '\t'.is_blank(), "whitespace");
    assert(';'.is_punctuation() and !'_'.is_alphanumeric(), "punctuation");
    assert('\n'.is_control() and !'\n'.is_printable(), "control");
    assert('a'.to_upper() == 'A' and '?'.to_upper() == '?', "case");

    # The digit's value in a base, or none when it is not a digit there.
    assert('F'.digit_value(16).value() == 15, "hexadecimal");
    assert('9'.digit_value(8).is_empty(), "not an octal digit");

    # Count the words and digits of a String, a byte at a time.
    var text = "Call 555-0100 at 9 a.m.";
    var words = 0;
    var digits = 0;
    var in_word = false;
    for (var b in text.bytes()) {
        if (b.is_digit()) {
            digits = digits + 1;
        }
        if (b.is_alphanumeric() and !in_word) {
            words = words + 1;
        }
        in_word = b.is_alphanumeric();
    }

    # A char answers the same, and bytes above 127 (negative as a char)
    # are never letters.
    char e_acute = -61;   # the first byte of "é" in UTF-8
    assert(!e_acute.is_alphabetic() and !e_acute.is_ascii(), "not ASCII");

    print($"{words} words, {digits} digits");   # 7 words, 8 digits
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# 7 words, 8 digits

Strings

String is a UTF-8 string. A string literal such as "hello" is a String value wherever a String is expected, and wherever nothing asks for another type (var s = "hello"; declares a String). Where it is stored or passed as a __ptr<char>, it is the literal's NUL-terminated bytes (see Passing strings), and where a StringConstant is expected, it is one. + joins two strings into a new one, == and != compare contents, the length property counts code points, size counts bytes, and s[i] gives the code point at index i as a one-code-point String.

# String literals are String values.
main(): int {
    var language = "Pepper";
    assert(language.length == 6, "6 code points");

    # + makes a new String; == compares contents.
    var message = "Hello, " + language;
    assert(message == "Hello, Pepper", "concatenation");
    assert(message != language, "different contents");

    # Strings are UTF-8. `length` counts code points, `size` counts bytes.
    var word = "héllo";
    assert(word.length == 5, "5 code points");
    assert(word.size == 6, "6 bytes: 'é' takes 2");
    assert(word[1] == "é", "indexing yields a one-code-point String");

    # A String is a reference: both names see an append.
    var alias = message;
    message.append("!");
    assert(alias == "Hello, Pepper!", "one object, two references");

    print(message);
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# Hello, Pepper!

A String is a reference type: var alias = message; makes a second reference to the same object rather than a copy, so a change made with append shows through both names. Memory and reference counting explains how references work, and the String reference lists every method.

Every place a literal is stored (a variable, a field, an array element, a function's result) gets a new String, so changing it never changes the literal: after var s = "a"; s.append("b"); the next "a" is still "a". Where a literal is only read, passed to a parameter that the function neither keeps nor changes (builder.append("x"), name.contains("x")), every evaluation shares one constant object and allocates nothing.

String constants

A literal's own type is StringConstant: a pointer to the literal's bytes, which never change and are never freed, with their size and length. It is a [Value] type, so copying one steps no reference count, any thread may read it, and a literal stored as one allocates nothing. Its bytes always end in a NUL byte, so c_str() passes it to C as it is (a String's c_str() does too, but a String built with no data has none).

A StringConstant has String's read API (length, size, find, split, trim, ==, <, the indexer, for loops and so on); the methods that make new text return a String. It converts to a String wherever a String is expected, as if String had an [Implicit] constructor taking it: the conversion (and String(text)) copies the bytes, so an API that takes a String takes a StringConstant too. Where C expects a char*, it passes its own bytes, as c_str() does. Among overloads, a literal picks a StringConstant parameter over a String one, and a StringConstant value picks a String parameter last, as an implicit conversion.

# A string literal's own type is StringConstant: its constant bytes, with no
# allocation and no reference count.
extern ulong strlen(char* text);

# A `const` initialized from a literal is a StringConstant.
const GREETING = "hello";

shout(text: String): String {
    return text.upper() + "!";
}

main(): int {
    StringConstant name = "pepper";
    assert(name.length == 6, "the read API of String");
    assert(name.starts_with("pep") && name.find("p", 1) == 2, "find counts bytes");

    # Always NUL-terminated: c_str() goes to C with no copy.
    assert(strlen(GREETING.c_str()) == 5, "C reads the literal's bytes");

    # A StringConstant converts to a String wherever one is expected.
    String copy = name;
    copy.append("!");
    assert(copy == "pepper!" && name == "pepper", "the copy has its own bytes");
    print(shout(GREETING));

    # Compared with a String either way round, with no copy.
    String typed = "pepper";
    assert(name == typed && typed == name && GREETING < typed, "mixed comparisons");

    # Copying a StringConstant copies a pointer.
    var also = name;
    assert(also == name, "same text");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# HELLO!
  • Where a literal is a StringConstant: a variable, field, parameter or return value of type StringConstant, a HashMap<StringConstant, V> key, and a const with no written type (const GREETING = "hello";), so a module-scope text constant allocates nothing and any thread may read it. Everywhere else, var s = "x" included, a literal is a String, as before.
  • Converting chains once: a literal reaches a type that converts from String (io.Path, Error) directly, but a StringConstant variable does not, since conversions never chain. Write String(text) or pass a literal.
  • Comparing: ==, !=, <, <=, > and >= compare a StringConstant with another StringConstant (a literal included) or with a String, either way round, and copy nothing.
  • A literal method call ("a,b".split(",")) calls the String method.

to_string turns any integer into its decimal text. For parsing and generating text, byte_at and substr_bytes work in bytes (the offsets find returns), compare and <, <=, >, >= order strings byte by byte (code-point order for UTF-8), lines() splits on "\n" or "\r\n", trim(), trim_start() and trim_end() drop whitespace, lower() and upper() change the case of ASCII letters, repeat(n) joins n copies, and bytes() copies the UTF-8 bytes into an array. A StringBuilder builds a long String from many pieces without recopying the text built so far on every append:

# Numbers to text, byte-level access, ordering, and building text in pieces.
main(): int {
    # to_string turns any integer into its decimal text.
    var line = 3;
    var where = to_string(line) + ":" + to_string(-7);
    assert(where == "3:-7", "to_string");

    # byte_at and substr_bytes count bytes, so they work with find's offsets.
    var setting = "indent=4";
    var eq = setting.find("=") as ulong;
    assert(setting.byte_at(eq) == '=', "byte_at compares with a character literal");
    assert(setting.substr_bytes(0, eq) == "indent", "the bytes before '='");

    # compare, <, <=, > and >= order strings byte by byte.
    assert("apple" < "banana", "ordering");
    assert("b".compare("a") > 0, "compare is negative, 0 or positive");

    # lines() splits on "\n" or "\r\n"; trim_end() drops trailing whitespace.
    var lines = "one  \r\ntwo\n".lines();
    assert(lines.count == 2, "no empty line after the final newline");
    assert(lines[0].trim_end() == "one", "trim_end");

    # trim() drops whitespace at both ends; lower() and upper() change ASCII case.
    var field = "  Content-Type ".trim();
    assert(field.lower() == "content-type", "lower");
    assert(field.upper() == "CONTENT-TYPE", "upper");

    # repeat joins copies; StringBuilder appends without recopying the text.
    var out = StringBuilder();
    for (var text in lines) {
        out.append(" ".repeat(4)).append(text.trim_end()).append("\n");
    }
    assert(out.to_string() == "    one\n    two\n", "StringBuilder");
    return 0;
}

To search and take text apart, find(needle, from) starts at a byte offset and rfind finds the last match, split(separator) cuts at every separator and split_once at the first (giving an optional pair), separator.join(parts) puts the parts back together, and replace(from, to) swaps every match (to read a number from text, see Reading numbers from text):

# Searching, splitting, joining and replacing text.

main(): int {
    # find takes a byte offset to start from; rfind finds the last match.
    var path = "src/lib/main.pep";
    var first = path.find("/");
    assert(path.find("/", (first as ulong) + 1) == 7, "the second slash");
    assert(path.rfind("/") == 7, "the last slash");

    # split cuts at every separator; split_once at the first, if any.
    var fields = "name,,age".split(",");
    assert(fields.count == 3 && fields[1] == "", "an empty field");
    var header = "Content-Type: text/plain".split_once(": ");
    if (header.is_value()) {
        var (name, value) = header.value();
        assert(name == "Content-Type" && value == "text/plain", "both halves");
    }

    # join puts the separator between the parts; replace swaps every match.
    assert(" | ".join(fields) == "name |  | age", "joined");
    assert("a\r\nb\r\n".replace("\r\n", "\n") == "a\nb\n", "line endings");
    return 0;
}

An interpolated string puts values' text into a string literal: $"line {line + 1}: {message}". String interpolation covers which values it accepts.

A backslash in a string literal starts an escape sequence, as in C and Rust:

EscapeCharacter
\nnewline
\ttab
\rcarriage return
\0the zero byte
\\a backslash
\"a double quote
\'a single quote
\xHHthe ASCII character with hexadecimal code HH, at most \x7F (any byte in a character literal); always two digits, so "\x4" is an error
\u{H...}the Unicode code point with hexadecimal code H... (1 to 6 digits)
print("name:\t\"Pepper\"");   # name:	"Pepper"
print("caf\u{e9}");            # café

Any other character after a backslash is an error:

main.pep:2:13: error: unknown escape sequence '\q'
    2 |     print("a\qb");
      |             ^~

Other built-in types

  • void means "no value". It is the return type of a function that returns nothing.
  • Array<T> is a growable array of T; int[] is shorthand for Array<int>, and int[][] for Array<Array<int>>. See Array.
  • Optional<T> is a value that may be missing; int? is shorthand for Optional<int>. See Optional values.
  • HashMap<K, V> and HashSet<K> are hash tables. See HashMap and HashSet.
  • Result<TValue, TError> and Error describe operations that can fail. See Error handling with Result.
  • async.Atomic<T> is a value that threads can update safely. See Atomics and Threads and shared data.

Raw pointers and __null

For talking to C, Pepper has raw pointers, written __ptr<T> (for example __ptr<char> or __ptr<void>), and the null pointer literal __null:

var p: __ptr<void> = __null;
assert(p == __null, "p is null");

Most programs never need them. Calling C covers pointers in full.

Naming conventions

Primitive types and keywords are lowercase: int, float, bool, var, while. Types, including the ones the runtime provides, are PascalCase: String, Array<T>, HashMap<K, V>, Result<TValue, TError>. Functions, variables and fields are snake_case, and constants are SCREAMING_CASE. Naming conventions has the full rules.

Identifiers are made of ASCII letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit. Avoid names that start with two underscores: the compiler and runtime use them for their own names, such as __ptr and __null.

Variables

Declare a variable with var and let Pepper infer its type from the initial value, or write the type yourself. Prefer var whenever the type is obvious from the value.

import async;

# Declaring variables: inferred, explicitly typed, constant, and module-level.

# Module-level variables (globals) live for the whole program. Any thread
# can reach them, so they are const and of a thread-safe type: a number, or
# an Atomic for state that changes.
const MAX_REQUESTS = 10;
const request_count = async.Atomic<int>(0);
const total_bytes = async.Atomic<long>(0);

record(bytes: int) {
    request_count.fetch_add(1);
    total_bytes.fetch_add(bytes);
}

main(): int {
    # 'var' infers the type from the initializer.
    var answer = 42;          # int: integer literals are int
    var ratio = 0.25;         # double: floating-point literals are double
    var ready = true;         # bool
    var name = "Pepper";      # String

    # Write the type first, C style...
    int width = 80;
    float scale = 1.5;
    (String, int)[] sizes = [("small", 1)];

    # ...or after the name with a colon.
    var height: int = 24;
    var offset: long = 5000000000;

    # A variable declared without a value starts at zero.
    var hits: int;
    assert(hits == 0, "numbers start at zero");

    # 'const' declares a name that should not be reassigned.
    const LIMIT = 3;

    record(100);
    record(250);
    assert(request_count.load() == 2, "two requests recorded");
    assert(total_bytes.load() == 350, "350 bytes in total");
    assert(request_count.load() < MAX_REQUESTS, "globals are visible in every function");

    assert(answer + width + height == 146, "sum of ints");
    assert(ratio * 4 == 1.0 && scale == 1.5, "floating point");
    assert(ready && name == "Pepper", "bool and String");
    assert(sizes[0].1 == 1, "a tuple type written first");
    assert(offset > 4000000000 && LIMIT == 3, "long and const");
    return 0;
}

The three forms are:

  • var name = value; infers the type from the value.
  • Type name = value; is the C style, with the type first. Any type can come first, a tuple type too: (String, int)[] sizes = [];.
  • var name: Type = value; puts the type after the name.

A variable declared without a value starts out as zero: 0 for numbers, false for bool, and null for a struct type such as String. Give struct variables a value before you use them.

When var infers the type of an arithmetic expression, it takes the type the arithmetic produces under C's rules (see Arithmetic follows C): var m = 1 + 0.5; is a double holding 1.5, and with u8 small = 250;, var s = small + 10; is an int holding 260.

Scope and shadowing

A variable is visible from its declaration to the end of the block that declares it. Declaring the same name twice in one block is an error (redefinition of 'x', with a note at the first). A function's or closure's parameters belong to its body's outermost block, so a local there may not repeat a parameter's name either, nor may two parameters share one, as in C++:

main.pep:2:9: error: redefinition of 'x'
    2 |     var x = 5;
      |         ^
main.pep:1:3: note: previous definition is here
    1 | f(x: bool): int {
      |   ^

An inner scope may reuse a name, hiding the outer one until it ends: a nested block, a for loop's variable, a match arm's or an is pattern's bindings, and a closure's parameters.

# Shadowing: a name declared in an inner scope hides the outer one until
# that scope ends. A function's parameters share its body's outermost
# scope, so `var count = 0;` there would be a redefinition of 'count'.

enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Square(side: int),
}

# A loop variable and a block's local live in scopes of their own.
sum_below(count: int): int {
    var total = 0;
    for (var count in 0..3) {
        total += count as int;
    }
    {
        var count = 100;
        total += count;
    }
    return total + count;
}

# A match arm binds its names in the arm's scope.
size(radius: int, shape: Shape): int {
    match (shape) {
        Circle(radius) => {
            return radius;
        }
        Square(side) => {
            return side + radius;
        }
    }
}

# So does an `is` pattern, in the block it guards.
first_or(value: int, found: int?): int {
    if (found is Value(value)) {
        return value;
    }
    return value;
}

# A closure's parameter hides a local of the function it is written in.
twice_plus(offset: int): int {
    var value = 4;
    var twice = (value: int) => value * 2;
    return twice(offset) + value;
}

main(): int {
    assert(sum_below(5) == 108, "0 + 1 + 2, the block's 100, and the parameter's 5");
    assert(size(1, Shape.Circle(7)) == 7, "the arm's radius hides the parameter");
    assert(size(1, Shape.Square(2)) == 3, "the parameter is visible in the other arm");
    assert(first_or(1, Optional<int>.Value(9)) == 9, "the pattern's value hides the parameter");
    assert(first_or(1, Optional<int>.Empty) == 1, "the parameter is back after the block");
    assert(twice_plus(3) == 10, "the closure's value is its argument; the local is still 4");
    return 0;
}

Constants

const declares a name that you do not intend to change:

const LIMIT = 3;
const RATIO: double = 0.5;

Assigning to a const, with =, a compound assignment, ++ or --, is an error:

main.pep:5:5: error: cannot assign to const variable 'LIMIT'
    5 |     LIMIT = 4;
      |     ^~~~~
main.pep:1:7: note: 'LIMIT' declared const here
    1 | const LIMIT = 3;
      |       ^~~~~

Module-level variables

A variable declared outside any function is a module-level (global) variable. It exists for the whole run of the program and every function in the file can read it. Its initializer can be any expression, including a function call, and runs before main. Like other top-level declarations, a global is private to its file (or module) unless you mark it export (see Visibility).

Any function can run on any thread, so every thread can reach a global. It must therefore be declared const and have a thread-safe type, such as a number, an Atomic<T>, a ThreadLocal<T>, or a [Shared] struct (see Module-scope variables). A global that changes is an Atomic<T>, or a [ThreadLocal] var, which every thread has its own copy of (see Thread-local variables):

const MAX_RETRIES = 3;
const requests = async.Atomic<long>(0);   # changed with requests.fetch_add(1)
[ThreadLocal]
var depth: int = 0;                       # one per thread

A global whose initializer is a literal (a number, a bool, __null, or a string literal) is set when the program loads, with no code run. So is a [Value] struct made of literals, when its constructor only stores its arguments and constants in its fields (const TABLE = Table("...", 4);); a constructor that does anything else runs at startup. One that nothing reads, like a function nothing calls, is left out of the executable, so a module's data tables cost only the programs that use them. A Windows build with -g keeps them all.

Casting with as

value as Type converts a value to another type explicitly, like static_cast in C++:

var ratio = 7.9;
var whole = ratio as int;   # 7
var wide = whole as long;
  • Floating point to integer truncates toward zero: -7.9 as int is -7.
  • Integer to a narrower integer keeps the low bits: 70000 as u16 is 4464.
  • Integer to a wider integer sign-extends a signed source and zero-extends an unsigned one: (-1 as i16) as long is -1, and (65535 as u16) as long is 65535.
  • bool and enums convert like integers: true as int is 1, and an enum converts to the integer it is stored as. An integer does not convert to an enum; name a case instead.
  • A struct converts to a trait it conforms to: dog as Named. The other way, from a trait value, may fail: shape as? Square gives a Square? (see Converting a trait value back).
  • A pointer converts to __ptr<void> and back: p as __ptr<void>, then v as __ptr<int>.
  • A value converts to its own type.

Anything else is a compile error at the as, since it would not be a value conversion but a reinterpretation of memory:

main.pep:3:15: error: cannot cast '__ptr<int>' to 'ulong' with 'as'; use 'unsafe_cast<ulong>(...)' to reinterpret
    3 |     var a = p as ulong;
      |               ^~

Casting between unrelated struct types, or between a struct and a number or pointer, is an error with no alternative (cannot cast 'P' to 'Q').

as binds more tightly than the arithmetic operators, so x * 10 as int means x * (10 as int). Put parentheses around the expression you want to convert: (x * 10) as int. C-style casts such as (int)x do not exist.

Many conversions also happen without as: assigning or passing a number to a variable or parameter of another numeric type converts it, as in C, including narrowing conversions (int n = 2.7; stores 2).

Reinterpreting with unsafe_cast

unsafe_cast<Type>(value) reinterprets a value's bits as another type, like reinterpret_cast in C++. It is for C interop and low-level code, and nothing checks that the result makes sense:

  • A pointer to a pointer of another type: unsafe_cast<__ptr<u8>>(text.c_str()).
  • A pointer to an integer, and an integer to a pointer: unsafe_cast<ulong>(p), unsafe_cast<__ptr<int>>(address).
  • A number to another number of the same width, keeping its bits: unsafe_cast<uint>(1.0 as float) is 0x3F800000, and unsafe_cast<double>(bits) turns a ulong back into a double.
# `as` converts values; `unsafe_cast<T>(value)` reinterprets bits.

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

main(): int {
    # A float's bits, and back: the same 32 bits seen as a uint.
    var one = 1.0 as float;
    var bits = unsafe_cast<uint>(one);
    assert(bits == 0x3F800000, "1.0 is 0x3F800000");
    assert(unsafe_cast<float>(bits) == one, "the bits convert back");

    # A double's sign bit is its top bit.
    var negative = unsafe_cast<ulong>(-2.0);
    assert((negative >> 63) == 1, "the sign bit is set");

    # `as` converts a pointer to and from `__ptr<void>`.
    var memory = malloc(8);
    var words = memory as __ptr<uint>;
    words[0] = 0x01020304;
    words[1] = 0;

    # Reading the same memory as bytes reinterprets it.
    var bytes = unsafe_cast<__ptr<u8>>(words);
    assert(bytes[0] == 4 || bytes[0] == 1, "the first byte is the low or the high one");

    # An address is an integer, and an integer is an address.
    var address = unsafe_cast<ulong>(words);
    assert(unsafe_cast<__ptr<uint>>(address + 4)[0] == 0, "the address four bytes on is the second word");

    free(memory as __ptr<void>);
    return 0;
}

It never converts a struct, trait or function value, so it cannot get around reference counting. A conversion as can make is not a reinterpretation, so unsafe_cast<long>(n) on an int is an error that says to use as:

main.pep:3:13: error: 'unsafe_cast' cannot convert 'int' to 'long': the sizes differ; use 'as' to convert the value
    3 |     var w = unsafe_cast<long>(n);
      |             ^~~~~~~~~~~

Arithmetic follows C

Arithmetic on numbers behaves exactly as it does in C (the "usual arithmetic conversions"), so code ported from C gives the same results:

  • Integer promotion. Types narrower than int (char, u8, short, u16, and bool) are converted to int before any arithmetic. The sum of two chars is an int, so 100 + 100 gives 200 rather than wrapping at 8 bits.
  • Mixed widths use the wider type: int + long is a long.
  • Signed and unsigned. When both operands have the same width and one is unsigned, the operation is unsigned: comparing int -1 with uint 1 treats -1 as 4294967295, so -1 < 1 is false for those types.
  • Integer and floating point gives floating point: 3 * 0.5 is 1.5.
  • Division of integers truncates toward zero (-7 / 2 is -3), and % takes the sign of the left operand (-7 % 3 is -1).
  • Conditionals. c ? a : b with numeric arms of different types has their common type by the same rules (c ? 0 : s.length is a ulong), and so does a match expression over its arms. The value converts from that type wherever it goes, and a var it initializes has that type (var n = c ? 0 : s.length is a ulong, not an int).
  • Shifts take the type of the (promoted) left operand. >> keeps the sign for signed types and fills with zeros for unsigned types.
  • Overflow is where Pepper leaves C: it panics, for signed and unsigned types alike (see Integer overflow).
# Arithmetic follows C's rules for promotion and conversion.
main(): int {
    # Integer division truncates toward zero; % takes the sign of the left side.
    assert(7 / 2 == 3, "7 / 2 is 3");
    assert(-7 / 2 == -3, "-7 / 2 is -3");
    assert(-7 % 3 == -1, "-7 % 3 is -1");

    # Types narrower than int are promoted to int before arithmetic,
    # so the sum of two chars does not wrap at 8 bits...
    char a = 100;
    char b = 100;
    int sum = a + b;
    assert(sum == 200, "char + char is computed as int");

    # ...but storing the result back into a char does.
    char c = a + b;
    assert(c == -56, "200 does not fit in a char");

    # Mixing signed and unsigned of the same width is unsigned, as in C.
    int minus_one = -1;
    uint one = 1;
    assert(!(minus_one < one), "-1 converts to 4294967295 when compared with a uint");
    uint zero = 0;
    assert(zero.wrapping_sub(1) == 4294967295, "zero - 1 would panic; wrapping_sub wraps");

    # Mixing an integer with a floating-point value gives floating point.
    int whole = 3;
    double half = 0.5;
    double product = whole * half;
    assert(product == 1.5, "3 * 0.5 is 1.5");

    # 'as' converts explicitly. Floating point to integer truncates toward zero.
    assert((7.9 as int) == 7, "7.9 as int is 7");
    assert((-7.9 as int) == -7, "-7.9 as int is -7");
    assert(((whole as double) / 2) == 1.5, "divide as double");

    # Assignment converts implicitly, including from double to int.
    int truncated = 2.7;
    assert(truncated == 2, "2.7 stored in an int is 2");

    # Shifts: >> is arithmetic for signed types and logical for unsigned types.
    assert(-8 >> 1 == -4, "signed shift keeps the sign");
    uint bits = 0x80000000;
    assert(bits >> 31 == 1, "unsigned shift fills with zeros");
    return 0;
}

Integer overflow

Integer arithmetic whose result does not fit its type stops the program, as in Swift (and Rust's debug builds), instead of wrapping around silently:

main.pep:3:16: panic: integer overflow in 'int' addition

The message names the operator's location and the type the operation ran at. These operations check:

  • +, -, * and **, unary -, ++ and --, and the compound assignments (+=, -=, *=). Negating the most negative value of a signed type overflows, and so does negating any nonzero unsigned value or subtracting past 0 (uint 0 - 1).
  • / and % by zero (division by zero), and the most negative value of a signed type divided by -1 (MIN / -1 and MIN % -1), whose result does not fit.
  • << and >> by a count of at least the type's width, or a negative one: shift count out of range for 'int': must be from 0 to 31.

Arithmetic on types narrower than int runs at int (see above), so it overflows only past int's range; storing the result back in the narrow type keeps its low bits, like any narrowing conversion. x++ on a u8 holding 255 leaves 0, as x += 1 does. Casts with as never check: 70000 as u16 is 4464.

When both operands are constants, an overflow is a compile error at the operator, and so is a division by a constant 0:

main.pep:2:28: error: integer overflow in 'int' multiplication
    2 |     var seconds = 100000 * 100000;
      |                          ^

Wrapping on purpose

Hashes, checksums and random number generators rely on wrapping. Each integer type has methods that say what to do on overflow instead of panicking:

MethodOn overflow
wrapping_add(x), wrapping_sub(x), wrapping_mul(x)Wraps around: the result modulo 2^bits.
checked_add(x), checked_sub(x), checked_mul(x)Returns Empty (the result is a T?).
saturating_add(x), saturating_sub(x), saturating_mul(x)Clamps to the type's highest or lowest value.
overflowing_add(x), overflowing_sub(x), overflowing_mul(x)Returns the wrapped result and true as a (T, bool).
# Arithmetic that overflows panics; these methods say what to do instead.
main(): int {
    int big = 2147483647;

    # big + 1 would stop the program: "integer overflow in 'int' addition".
    # wrapping_ wraps around, as C's unsigned arithmetic does.
    assert(big.wrapping_add(1) == -2147483648, "wraps to the lowest int");

    # checked_ returns none on overflow.
    assert(big.checked_add(1).is_empty(), "no int is big + 1");
    assert(big.checked_sub(1).value() == 2147483646, "big - 1 fits");

    # saturating_ clamps to the type's range.
    assert(big.saturating_mul(2) == 2147483647, "clamped to the highest int");
    byte level = 10;
    assert(level.saturating_sub(20) == 0, "a byte stops at 0");

    # overflowing_ returns the wrapped result and whether it overflowed.
    var (product, overflowed) = big.overflowing_mul(2);
    assert(product == -2 && overflowed, "wrapped, and overflowed");

    # A hash multiplies with wrapping on purpose (FNV-1a).
    ulong hash = 0xcbf29ce484222325;
    var text = "pepper";
    for (var i in 0..text.size) {
        hash = (hash ^ (text.byte_at(i) as ulong)).wrapping_mul(0x100000001b3);
    }
    assert(hash == 0xac11131d51a77079, "the FNV-1a hash of 'pepper'");
    return 0;
}

The methods work at their type's own width: byte 200.checked_add(100) is Empty, while 200 + 100 on two bytes is 300 at int.

Removing the checks

The checks stay on at every optimization level. A build that has measured their cost and accepts the risk can remove kinds of check with --no-runtime-checks, a comma-separated list:

NameRemovesThen
overflowThe overflow checks of +, -, *, **, unary -, ++, --Arithmetic wraps around (never undefined).
divideDivision and remainder by zero, and MIN / -1The result is undefined, as in C.
shiftThe shift count checkThe count is masked to the type's width (x << 33 on an int shifts by 1).
boundsArray and String index checks (a[i], byte_at)An index out of range reads or writes arbitrary memory.
nullCalls through null function and trait values, and match on a null referenceThe program crashes or misbehaves.
allEvery check above
pepper build -O main.pep --no-runtime-checks=overflow,shift

Removing bounds or null gives up Pepper's memory safety: an index out of range or a null reference then reads or writes arbitrary memory instead of panicking. The flag does nothing at -O0, the default, where every check stays on and the compiler warns warning: '--no-runtime-checks' has no effect at -O0. It applies from -O1 up, -g included. The setting is part of the build cache's key, like the optimization level.

To remove checks from one function instead of a whole build, mark it [Unsafe("...")] with the same names, comma-separated in one string: [Unsafe("overflow")], [Unsafe("overflow,bounds")] or [Unsafe("all")]. It removes them from that function's body only, at every optimization level (-O0 included), so the function behaves the same in every build. Closures written in it lose the same checks. Functions it calls keep theirs, with one exception: bounds also removes the index checks that Array and String make for it, since those run inside their indexers. [Unsafe] goes on a free function, a method or a constructor. An unknown name is an error at the string.

# `[Unsafe("...")]` removes runtime checks from one function's body.

# A hash that wraps on purpose: without the overflow check, `*` and `+`
# wrap around instead of panicking.
[Unsafe("overflow")]
hash(values: Array<int>): uint {
    uint result = 2166136261;
    for (var value in values) {
        result = (result ^ (value as uint)) * 16777619;
    }
    return result;
}

# A loop that already checked its range: the index checks of `a[i]`, made by
# `Array`'s indexer for this caller, are removed too.
[Unsafe("bounds")]
sum(values: Array<int>): long {
    long total = 0;
    ulong i = 0;
    while (i < values.count) {
        total = total + values[i];
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    var values = Array<int>();
    for (var i in 0..100) {
        values.append(i);
    }
    assert(hash(values) != 0, "a hash");
    assert(sum(values) == 4950, "0 + 1 + ... + 99");
    # Outside those functions every check stays: 2147483647 + 1 here would
    # still panic.
    return 0;
}

Bit operations and math functions

Each integer type has methods that compile to a single instruction on most CPUs, through LLVM's intrinsics, for code that would otherwise loop over bits:

MethodReturns
leading_zeros(), trailing_zeros()The zero bits above the highest set bit, or below the lowest; the type's width for zero.
count_ones(), count_zeros()How many bits are set, or clear.
swap_bytes()The value with its bytes reversed, to convert between little and big endian.
reverse_bits()The value with its bits reversed.
rotate_left(n), rotate_right(n)The bits rotated by n, modulo the width.
min(x), max(x)The smaller or the larger value.
abs()The value without its sign (signed types). Panics for the lowest value, whose negation does not fit.

Like the overflow methods, they work at their type's own width: byte 1.leading_zeros() is 7.

# Bit operations on integers: counting, reversing and rotating bits.
main(): int {
    uint mask = 0x00F0;
    assert(mask.trailing_zeros() == 4, "the lowest set bit is bit 4");
    assert(mask.leading_zeros() == 24, "the highest set bit is bit 7");
    assert(mask.count_ones() == 4, "four bits are set");

    # Zero has no set bit: its counts are the type's width.
    assert((0 as ulong).trailing_zeros() == 64, "no set bit");

    # The methods work at their type's own width.
    byte low = 1;
    assert(low.leading_zeros() == 7, "a byte has 8 bits");
    assert(low.rotate_right(1) == 0x80, "the bottom bit comes back at the top");

    # Byte order: swap_bytes converts between little and big endian.
    assert((0x12345678 as uint).swap_bytes() == 0x78563412, "bytes reversed");
    assert((1 as uint).reverse_bits() == 0x80000000, "bits reversed");

    # min, max and abs.
    assert((-7).abs() == 7, "without its sign");
    assert((3).min(5) == 3 && (3).max(5) == 5, "smaller and larger");
    return 0;
}

float and double have square_root(), floor(), ceiling(), truncate(), round() (halfway cases away from zero), abs(), copy_sign(sign), multiply_add(factor, addend) (this * factor + addend rounded once) and min(x) and max(x) (which ignore a NaN argument):

# Floating-point functions: square root, rounding, sign and fused
# multiply-add.
main(): int {
    var side = (2.0).square_root();
    assert(side * side > 1.999 && side * side < 2.001, "close to 2");

    assert((-1.5).floor() == -2.0, "toward negative infinity");
    assert((-1.5).ceiling() == -1.0, "toward positive infinity");
    assert((-1.5).truncate() == -1.0, "toward zero");
    assert((2.5).round() == 3.0, "halfway cases away from zero");

    assert((-4.0).abs() == 4.0, "without its sign");
    assert((4.0).copy_sign(-1.0) == -4.0, "the sign of the argument");
    assert((2.0).multiply_add(3.0, 1.0) == 7.0, "2 * 3 + 1, rounded once");
    assert((1.5).min(-2.0) == -2.0 && (1.5).max(-2.0) == 1.5, "smaller and larger");
    return 0;
}

They also have the functions of C's <math.h>, with their names spelled out. Angles are in radians. LLVM's intrinsics compute the ones it has, and the C math library the rest:

MethodsC's names
sine(), cosine(), tangent()sin, cos, tan
arc_sine(), arc_cosine(), arc_tangent(), y.arc_tangent2(x)asin, acos, atan, atan2(y, x)
hyperbolic_sine(), hyperbolic_cosine(), hyperbolic_tangent()sinh, cosh, tanh
arc_hyperbolic_sine(), arc_hyperbolic_cosine(), arc_hyperbolic_tangent()asinh, acosh, atanh
exponential(), exponential2(), exponential_minus_one()exp, exp2, expm1
logarithm(), logarithm2(), logarithm10(), logarithm_one_plus()log, log2, log10, log1p
cube_root(), hypotenuse(other)cbrt, hypot
remainder(divisor)remainder (the quotient rounded to nearest; % is fmod, rounded toward zero)
is_nan(), is_infinite(), is_finite(), sign_bit()isnan, isinf, isfinite, signbit

Powers are the ** operator: x ** 0.5, or x ** 3 with an integer exponent. The math module has the constants (math.PI, math.TAU, math.E, math.INFINITY, math.NAN, and the epsilon and limits of float and double) and math.gcd and math.lcm for integers:

# Floating-point math: trigonometry, logarithms, powers, classification,
# and the math module's constants and integer functions.
import math;

main(): int {
    var angle = math.PI / 6;
    assert((angle.sine() - 0.5).abs() < 1e-12, "sin 30 degrees is 1/2");
    assert(((1.0).arc_tangent2(1.0) - math.PI / 4).abs() < 1e-12, "45 degrees");

    assert((1024.0).logarithm2() == 10.0, "2 to the 10th is 1024");
    assert((1.0).exponential() == math.E, "e to the 1st");
    assert(2.0 ** 10 == 1024.0 && (-8.0).cube_root() == -2.0, "powers and roots");
    assert((3.0).hypotenuse(4.0) == 5.0, "a 3-4-5 triangle");

    assert(math.NAN.is_nan() && math.NAN != math.NAN, "NaN is not equal to itself");
    assert(math.INFINITY.is_infinite() && !math.INFINITY.is_finite(), "infinite");
    assert((-0.0).sign_bit() && !(-0.0 < 0), "negative zero");

    assert(math.gcd(12, 18) == 6 && math.lcm(4, 6) == 12, "integers");
    return 0;
}

Hints for the optimizer are [Likely] and [Unlikely] on a branch and the prefetches of the hint module. Any other LLVM intrinsic can be declared as an extern; see LLVM intrinsics.

Operators

# Operators on numbers and booleans.
main(): int {
    # Arithmetic.
    assert(2 + 3 * 4 == 14, "* binds tighter than +");
    assert((2 + 3) * 4 == 20, "parentheses group");
    assert(17 % 5 == 2, "remainder");
    assert(-(3) == -3, "negation");

    # Exponentiation is right-associative: 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** 9.
    assert(2 ** 10 == 1024, "power");
    assert(2 ** 3 ** 2 == 512, "right-associative");
    # With a floating-point operand, the result is floating point.
    assert(2.0 ** -2 == 0.25, "float power");
    assert(9 ** 0.5 == 3.0, "square root");

    # Comparison yields a bool.
    var small = 3 < 5;
    assert(small, "3 < 5");
    assert(5 >= 5 && 4 <= 5 && 6 > 5 && 5 == 5 && 5 != 6, "comparisons");
    # On numbers, `===` and `!==` are the same as `==` and `!=`.
    assert(5 === 5 && 5 !== 6, "identity on numbers");

    # Logical operators; 'and' and 'or' are spellings of && and ||.
    var t = true;
    var f = false;
    assert(t && !f, "and, not");
    assert(f || t, "or");
    assert(t and (f or t), "word forms");

    # Bitwise operators.
    assert((6 & 3) == 2, "and");
    assert((6 | 3) == 7, "or");
    assert((6 ^ 3) == 5, "exclusive or");
    assert(~0 == -1, "complement");
    assert(1 << 4 == 16 && 256 >> 2 == 64, "shifts");

    # Compound assignment and increment.
    var n = 5;
    n += 3;   # 8
    n -= 2;   # 6
    n *= 4;   # 24
    n /= 5;   # 4
    n %= 3;   # 1
    n <<= 3;  # 8
    n >>= 1;  # 4
    n &= 6;   # 4
    assert(n == 4, "compound assignment");
    n++;
    ++n;
    n--;
    assert(n == 5, "increment and decrement");

    # The conditional (ternary) operator.
    var sign = n > 0 ? "positive" : "not positive";
    assert(sign == "positive", "ternary");
    return 0;
}
KindOperators
Arithmetic+ - * / % **, unary - and +
Comparison== != < <= > >=
Identity=== !== (two references to the same object; plain equality for numbers and bool)
