Logical&& (or and), || (or or), !
Bitwise& | ^ ~ << >>
Assignment= += -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= |= ^=
Increment++ --, prefix or postfix
Conditionalcondition ? a : b

&& and || short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated only when the left one does not decide the result, so items.count > 0 && items[0] == 1 never reads items[0] from an empty array.

Unary operators nest: -~x is -(~x), and !!x is !(!x), which turns a number into a bool. A struct can define its own operators, the truth test !! included (see Operators).

** raises a number to a power, and is right-associative: 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 2 ** 9. On two integers the result is an integer, and the exponent can be any integer expression. A negative exponent gives the truncated real result: 1 for a base of 1, 1 or -1 for a base of -1, and 0 otherwise (2 ** -1 is 0).

When either operand is a float or double, the result is floating point, by the usual conversions above: 2.0 ** 0.5 is the square root of 2, 2.0 ** -2 is 0.25, and 4 ** 0.5 is the double 2.0. An integer exponent of at most 32 bits computes by repeated multiplication (LLVM's powi), which is fast but may differ from C's pow in the last bit; any other exponent calls pow itself. ** on anything but numbers or a struct that defines it is an error:

main.pep:3:15: error: invalid operands to binary expression ('__ptr<int>' and 'int')
    3 |     var q = p ** 2;
      |               ^~

Operators bind in this order, tightest first:

  1. Postfix: calls f(x), indexing a[i], member access a.b, x++, x--
  2. **
  3. as, as?
  4. Unary +, -, !, ~
  5. Prefix ++, --
  6. *, /, %
  7. +, -
  8. <<, >>
  9. .., ..> (ranges; not associative)
  10. is
  11. <, <=, >, >=
  12. ==, !=, ===, !==
  13. &
  14. |, ^
  15. &&, and
  16. ||, or
  17. ? :
  18. = and the compound assignments (right-associative)

As in C, & binds more loosely than ==, so write (flags & mask) == mask with the parentheses.

An expression can nest at most 256 levels deep, counting each operator of a chain as one level, so a sum of more than about 250 terms is a compile error (see Compiler errors).

Statements and semicolons

Every simple statement ends with a ;: a variable declaration, an expression, return, break and continue. So does every declaration that does not end in a block: a module variable, a struct field, a type alias, an import, a re-export and an extern function. A statement or declaration that ends in a block (if, while, for, with, a function, a struct) needs none.

Line breaks, spaces and comments mean nothing to the grammar. A statement can span as many lines as it needs, breaking anywhere between tokens, including before an operator or a ., and several statements can share a line.

# Every simple statement ends with a `;`; line breaks mean nothing.
is_small(n: int): bool {
    return n > 0 && n < 10;
}

main(): int {
    var width = 3;
    var height = 4; var depth = 5;

    # A statement may span several lines, breaking before or after an
    # operator.
    var volume = width * height
        * depth;
    assert(volume == 60, "3 * 4 * 5");

    var in_range = is_small(width)
        && is_small(height)
        && !is_small(volume);
    assert(in_range, "3 and 4 are small; 60 is not");

    var words = Array<String>();
    words.append("line");
    words.append("breaks");
    var long_words = 0;
    # A chain of calls may break before each `.`.
    for (var word in words
        .iterate()
        .filter((w) => w.length > 4)) {  # comments are fine anywhere
        long_words += 1;
    }
    assert(long_words == 1, "one word is longer than four characters");

    # So may a call's arguments.
    assert(volume + words[0].length == 64,
        "60 + 4");
    return 0;
}

A missing ; is an error

Leaving out a ; is an error, reported right after the statement it should end, with a fix that adds it. The language server offers the fix as a quick fix:

main.pep:2:18: error: expected ';'
    2 |     var total = 1
      |                  ^
      |                  ;

Because line breaks do not end anything, a statement missing its ; would otherwise run on into the next line whenever that line can continue it:

x = y
-z

reads as x = y - z; with its ; missing, not as two statements. The error says where the ; belongs when the parse cannot go on.

Control flow

Pepper has the familiar structured control flow of C-family languages: if and else to choose, while and for to repeat, and break, continue and return to leave early.

if and else

if runs a block when its condition is true, and the optional else block when it is false. The parentheses around the condition are optional; the braces around each block are required, even for a single statement.

# Branching with if and else.
classify(n: int): String {
    if n < 0 {
        return "negative";
    } else if n == 0 {
        return "zero";
    } else {
        return "positive";
    }
}

main(): int {
    var temperature = 25;

    # Parentheses around the condition are optional; braces are required.
    if temperature > 30 {
        print("hot");
    } else {
        print("not hot");
    }

    if (temperature > 20) {
        temperature = 20;
    }
    assert(temperature == 20, "clamped to 20");

    assert(classify(-5) == "negative", "negative");
    assert(classify(0) == "zero", "zero");
    assert(classify(7) == "positive", "positive");

    # For a choice between two values, the ternary operator is shorter.
    var parity = temperature % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd";
    assert(parity == "even", "20 is even");

    # && and || stop at the first operand that decides the result, so the
    # count check guards the index.
    var readings = Array<int>();
    var starts_high = false;
    if (readings.count > 0 && readings[0] > 100) {
        starts_high = true;
    }
    assert(!starts_high, "an empty array does not start high");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# not hot

The condition is usually a bool, but a number also works: any value other than zero counts as true, as in C. A raw pointer (__ptr<T>) or a function value counts as true when it is not null. A struct counts only if it declares the truth-test operator !!(): bool, which the condition calls; any other struct is an error, so write node !== __null to ask whether a reference is set (see Truth tests and conditions). The same holds for the condition of while and of ?:, the operands of &&, ||, and and or, and the operand of !.

Chains of conditions

else if tests another condition when the ones before it were false. The first true condition's block runs, and the final else block, if there is one, runs when none was true:

if x > 0 {
    return 1;
} else if x < 0 {
    return -1;
} else {
    return 0;
}

For a choice between two values, the conditional operator condition ? a : b is often shorter than an if.

Guarding a check

&& and || short-circuit, as in C: the right operand is evaluated only when the left one does not already decide the result. A guard can therefore come first in the same condition:

if items.count > 0 && items[0] > 100 {
    print("starts high");
}

When items is empty, items[0] is never read.

while

while repeats its block as long as the condition is true. The condition is checked before each iteration, so the body may run zero times. As with if, the parentheses are optional and the braces are required.

var countdown = 3;
while countdown > 0 {
    countdown -= 1;
}

for

for runs its block once for each element of an Array, each code point of a String, or each value of any type that follows the iterator protocol:

for (var score in scores) {
    total += score;
}

The loop variable can be declared with var or a type (for (int score in scores), for (var score: int in scores)), and the parentheses are optional. Iteration covers the protocol behind for and how to make your own types iterable.

Pepper has no C-style for (init; condition; step) loop. To count, loop over a range: for (var i in 0..count).

with

with enters a scope object for the length of a block and binds what it hands out. The object cleans up when it is destroyed, on every way out of the block:

with (var session = Session("grace")) {
    greet(session.user);
}

Scoped blocks with with covers the protocol and the optional else block.

match

match runs the arm for the case an enum value holds, and the compiler checks that every case is handled:

match (light) {
    Red, Amber => { stop(); }
    Green => { go(); }
}

Enums and match covers patterns and the else arm.

Branch hints: [Likely] and [Unlikely]

[Likely] or [Unlikely] on the line above an if, an else if's if or a match arm (the else arm too) says how often that branch runs. The optimizer keeps the likely path as straight-line code and moves the unlikely one, such as error handling, out of its way. A hint never changes what the program computes; a wrong one costs only speed.

# Branch hints: `[Likely]` and `[Unlikely]` say which way a branch usually
# goes, so the optimizer keeps the common path straight.
enum Reading {
    Value(celsius: double),
    Missing,
}

parse_digit(c: char): int {
    [Unlikely]
    if (c < '0' || c > '9') {
        return -1;
    } else [Likely] if (c != '0') {
        return c - '0';
    }
    return 0;
}

describe(reading: Reading): String {
    match (reading) {
        [Likely]
        Value(celsius) => {
            return $"{celsius}";
        }
        [Unlikely]
        Missing => {
            return "missing";
        }
    }
}

main(): int {
    assert(parse_digit('7') == 7, "a digit");
    assert(parse_digit('x') == -1, "not a digit");
    assert(describe(Reading.Missing) == "missing", "the rare arm still runs");
    return 0;
}

  • [Likely] above an if marks its block, so its else is the unlikely side; [Unlikely] marks the block as the rare one. To mark an else, mark the if the other way.

  • In an else if, the attribute goes between else and if: } else [Unlikely] if (x) {.

  • A hint is an LLVM branch weight (2000 to 1, as clang gives __builtin_expect), so it matters with optimization (-O1 and up).

  • Only one of them, with no arguments, can mark a branch, and no other attribute can:

    main.pep:3:5: error: 'Target' cannot mark an 'if'; only '[Likely]' or '[Unlikely]' can
    3 |     [Target(OS(Linux))]
      |     ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

while loops and the arms of a match expression take no hint yet.

break and continue

break leaves the innermost loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and goes on with the next one; in a while loop that means checking the condition again, so update the counter before any continue.

# Looping with while and for, and leaving early with break and continue.
main(): int {
    # while repeats as long as its condition is true.
    var countdown = 3;
    var launched = false;
    while countdown > 0 {
        countdown -= 1;
    }
    launched = countdown == 0;
    assert(launched, "counted down to zero");

    # for visits each element of an Array (or any other iterable).
    var scores = Array<int>();
    scores.append(70);
    scores.append(85);
    scores.append(92);
    var total = 0;
    for (var score in scores) {
        total += score;
    }
    assert(total == 247, "sum of the scores");

    # continue skips to the next iteration; break leaves the loop.
    var odd_sum = 0;
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 100) {
        i += 1;
        if (i % 2 == 0) { continue; }
        if (i > 9) { break; }
        odd_sum += i;
    }
    assert(odd_sum == 25, "1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9");

    # break and continue apply to the innermost loop.
    var pairs = 0;
    for (var a in scores) {
        for (var b in scores) {
            if (b == a) { break; }
            pairs += 1;
        }
    }
    assert(pairs == 3, "(85, 70), (92, 70), (92, 85)");
    return 0;
}

Both work in while and for loops and always apply to the innermost loop. There are no labeled breaks: to leave several loops at once, set a flag and test it, or move the loops into a function and return from it.

return

return value; leaves the current function and hands value back to the caller. It works from anywhere in the function, including from inside loops. See Functions.

In a function that returns nothing, a bare return; leaves the function early.

Functions

A function is a named block of code that takes parameters and can return a value. Functions declared at the top level of a file are free functions; functions declared inside a struct are methods, covered in Structs.

Declaring a function

Write the name, the parameters in parentheses as name: Type, and the return type after a colon:

area(width: int, height: int): int {
    return width * height;
}

Pepper also accepts a C-style form, with the return type first and each parameter's type before its name:

int perimeter(int width, int height) {
    return 2 * (width + height);
}

Both forms declare the same kind of function; pick one style and use it consistently. The first form is the one used throughout this book.

# Declaring and calling functions.

import async;

# Parameters are written 'name: Type'; the return type follows the ')'.
area(width: int, height: int): int {
    return width * height;
}

# The C-style form puts the return type first and the type before each name.
int perimeter(int width, int height) {
    return 2 * (width + height);
}

# A function that returns nothing leaves out the return type
# (or writes ': void', or 'void' in front).
# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const log_count = async.Atomic<int>(0);
log(message: String) {
    log_count.fetch_add(1);
    print("log: " + message);
}

# Functions can call themselves, and can be declared in any order.
factorial(n: int): long {
    if (n <= 1) { return 1; }
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

main(): int {
    assert(area(3, 4) == 12, "3 x 4");
    assert(perimeter(3, 4) == 14, "2 x (3 + 4)");
    assert(factorial(20) == 2432902008176640000, "20!");
    assert(is_even(10), "declared after main, still callable");
    # An argument converts to its parameter's type as assignment does:
    # a double passed to an int parameter truncates toward zero.
    assert(area(2.9, 3) == 6, "2.9 becomes 2");

    log("starting");
    log("done");
    assert(log_count.load() == 2, "logged twice");
    return 0;
}

is_even(n: int): bool {
    return n % 2 == 0;
}

# Output:
# log: starting
# log: done

  • Order does not matter. A function can call functions declared later in the file, and can call itself.

  • The program starts at main. main(): int returns the process's exit code; return 0 for success. To receive the command-line arguments, declare it main(args: String[]): int instead. See Command-line arguments and exit.

  • Calls must match the declaration. Passing the wrong number of arguments is a compile error:

    main.pep:3:12: error: too many arguments to 'add': expected 2, have 3
    3 |     return add(1, 2, 3);
      |            ^~~

Functions that return nothing

A function that returns no value leaves out the return type. You can also write : void, or void in front in the C-style form:

log(message: String) { print(message); }
log_line(message: String): void { print(message); }
void log_c(String message) { print(message); }

Such a function ends when it reaches the closing brace, or earlier at a bare return;:

log_positive(n: int) {
    if n <= 0 {
        return;
    }
    print($"{n}");
}

A call to such a function has no value, so it cannot be stored, passed, returned, or used as an operand or condition: var x = log("hi"); reports cannot use a value of type 'void' as variable 'x'.

In a function that returns a value, return; is an error:

main.pep:2:5: error: non-void function 'f' should return a value
    2 |     return;
      |     ^~~~~~

Inferred return types

A function without a return type gets one from its return statements. It returns void when no return has a value, and otherwise the type of the first return that has one, so half(x: double) { return x / 2; } returns a double. A generic function's return type is inferred for each specialization, so first<T>(a: T, b: T) { return a; } returns an int for first<int>. main with no return type returns an int, and reaching its closing brace exits with 0.

Writing the return type is still clearer for a function that returns a value, and it lets the compiler check each return against it.

Parameters

Parameters are passed by value. For numbers and bool, the function receives its own copy. For a String, an Array or any other struct, the value is a reference, so the function receives another reference to the same object: it can change the object's contents, and the caller sees the change. Assigning a new object to the parameter does not affect the caller's variable.

A parameter is a local of the function's body: a var in the body's outermost block may not reuse its name (see Scope and shadowing). Memory and reference counting describes exactly how references are counted when you pass them.

Arguments convert to the parameter's type the same way assignment does, so you can pass an int where a long or double is expected, a double where an int is expected (it truncates toward zero, like int n = 2.7;), and a String where a struct with an [Implicit] constructor from String (such as io.Path) is expected.

Default parameter values

A parameter can have a default value, written = value after its type. A call that leaves the argument out gets the default. Put parameters with defaults at the end of the list, since arguments are matched from the left.

# Default parameter values.

# Parameters with defaults come last; a call may leave them out.
greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hello", punctuation: String = "!"): String {
    return greeting + ", " + name + punctuation;
}

# Defaults work with the C-style form too.
int clamp(int value, int low = 0, int high = 100) {
    if (value < low) { return low; }
    if (value > high) { return high; }
    return value;
}

# A default can be any expression: an interpolated string, a literal.
labels(prefix: String = $"v{2}" + ".", sizes: int[] = [1, 2]): String {
    return $"{prefix}{sizes.count}";
}

main(): int {
    assert(labels() == "v2.2", "computed defaults");
    assert(greet("Ada") == "Hello, Ada!", "both defaults");
    assert(greet("Ada", "Hi") == "Hi, Ada!", "one default");
    assert(greet("Ada", "Hi", ".") == "Hi, Ada.", "no defaults");

    assert(clamp(150) == 100, "clamped to the default high");
    assert(clamp(-5) == 0, "clamped to the default low");
    assert(clamp(-5, -10) == -5, "low given");
    return 0;
}

A default can be an expression, not only a literal: strings joined with +, an interpolated string, an array, map or tuple literal, a range, or a call. Each call that leaves the argument out evaluates it again. The default converts to the parameter's type as an argument would, so a string literal can be the default of an io.Path parameter (path: io.Path = "out.txt").

Defaults work the same way for methods and constructors. To give a later parameter a value without passing every parameter before it, name it (see Named arguments).

Named arguments

A call can name its arguments, name = value, so it reads clearly and can set one defaulted parameter without passing the ones before it:

# Named arguments: `name = value` after the positional arguments.
window(title: String, width: int = 800, height: int = 600, resizable: bool = true): String {
    return $"{title} {width}x{height} resizable={resizable}";
}

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    moved(dx: int = 0, dy: int = 0): Point {
        return Point(x + dx, y + dy);
    }
}

# 'size = ...' works as well as 'count = ...'; 'n = ...' still works, with a
# deprecation warning.
[Alias("size", "count")]
[Rename("n", "count")]
repeat(text: String, count: int = 1): String {
    var result = "";
    for (var i in 0..count) {
        result = result + text;
    }
    return result;
}

main(): int {
    assert(window("Editor") == "Editor 800x600 resizable=true", "all defaults");
    # Skip width and height.
    assert(window("Editor", resizable = false) == "Editor 800x600 resizable=false", "skip");
    # Named arguments in any order.
    assert(window("Editor", height = 400, width = 1200) == "Editor 1200x400 resizable=true", "any order");
    # Every argument may be named.
    assert(window(title = "Editor", width = 1024) == "Editor 1024x600 resizable=true", "all named");

    # Constructors and methods take them too.
    var p = Point(y = 5);
    assert(p.moved(dy = 2).y == 7, "method");

    assert(repeat("ab", size = 3) == "ababab", "alias");
    return 0;
}
  • Positional first. Positional arguments come first and match parameters from the left; named arguments follow, in any order. A positional argument after a named one is an error: positional argument cannot follow a named argument.
  • Each parameter once. Naming a parameter that already has an argument is an error: argument for 'width' given twice.
  • Every required parameter. A parameter without a default must get an argument: missing argument for parameter 'title' in call to 'window'. A name the function does not have is an error, with a suggestion when one is close: no parameter named 'widht' in 'window'; did you mean 'width'?.
  • Order of evaluation. Arguments are evaluated in the order written, then passed to their parameters.
  • Everywhere a call is. Free functions, methods, static methods, constructors (a this.x parameter is named x), extension methods, enum methods, generic functions, and calls through a trait value, which use the trait's parameter names. A method that implements a trait should use the trait's names, so a call names the same arguments either way: a different name is a warning (parameter 'factor' of 'area' is named 'scale' in trait 'Shape') whose fix renames the parameter.
  • Overloads. A member of an overload set without a parameter of a given name is not a candidate, so names can pick between overloads.
  • Not through function values. A function type carries no parameter names, so a call through a function value is positional only: cannot name arguments in a call through a function value of type '(int, int) => int'.
  • Not to extern functions. Their parameter names are copied from C headers and stay free to change: cannot name arguments in a call to extern function 'CreateFileW'. Wrap the C function in a Pepper function to give it named arguments.

Other names for a parameter

Two attributes on a function give its parameters more names. In both, the declared parameter's name comes second:

  • [Alias("size", "count")] lets a call name parameter count as size too, permanently.
  • [Rename("n", "count")] keeps the former name n working after the parameter was renamed to count. Each use warns, like a deprecated declaration, with a fix that renames it.

The first name must not already be a parameter or another name, and the second must be a parameter of the function. A call that names one parameter by two of its names gets argument for 'count' given twice.

Returning several values

A function returns several values as a tuple, and the caller destructures it:

divide(a: int, b: int): (int, int) {
    return (a / b, a % b);
}

var (quotient, remainder) = divide(17, 5);

Overloading

Functions can share a name when their parameter lists differ, in one file, across a module's files, or across the modules a file imports, and each call picks the best fit for its arguments. See Overloading.

Generic functions

A function can take type parameters in angle brackets after its name, such as first<T>(items: T[]): T. Generics covers them.

Printing with print

print(value) writes a value's text and a line break to standard output: what interpolating it, $"{value}", would make. That covers a String, numbers, bool (true or false), tuples, and any type with a to_string(). To print several values on one line, interpolate them (print($"total: {n}")), or pass a format string and its arguments, which prints what String.format makes of them (print("{0} of {1}", done, total)).

# print writes a value's text and a line break.
main(): int {
    print("Hello, world!");
    print(42);                            # any value with a text form
    print((1.5, true));                   # (1.5, true)
    var name = "Pepper";
    var count = 42;
    print($"{name} has {count} items");   # interpolate other values
    print("{0} + {1} = {2}", 3, 4, 3 + 4); # or format them: "3 + 4 = 7"
    print("{braces} alone print as written");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# Hello, world!
# 42
# (1.5, true)
# Pepper has 42 items
# 3 + 4 = 7
# {braces} alone print as written
  • With a string literal and no other arguments, the text prints as written: its braces are not a format.
  • A value with no text form is an error at the argument:
main.pep:5:11: error: cannot print a value of type 'Foo': it has no 'to_string()' method and no 'to_string' overload
    5 |     print(f);
      |           ^

print writes each line out as it prints it, like Rust's println!, so the output appears as the program runs even when standard output is a pipe or a file. Text from print and from io.File.stdout() comes out in the order the program wrote it.

A float or double prints its shortest exact text (print(0.5) prints 0.5), and a tuple its elements in parentheses ((1, two)).

Assertions and panics

For checks in your programs, the runtime provides assert(condition, message), which stops the program with message when condition is false, and panic(message), which always stops it. Each is overloaded: the message may be a String, built at run time (assert(n > 0, name + " must be positive")), or a C string, which a string literal picks, so a literal message builds nothing when the assertion holds. See Built-in functions.

A panic flushes what the program printed, writes the location of the failing call and the message to standard error, and aborts:

main.pep:12:5: panic: count must be positive

In a build without -O, a backtrace of the calls that led there follows the message. PEPPER_BACKTRACE=1 turns it on in an optimized build and PEPPER_BACKTRACE=0 turns it off (see Backtraces and the debugger).

The checks the compiler adds report the same way, at the expression that failed: an overflowing operator, a null function value, a match on a null reference enum. So do the runtime's checking methods, which report their caller's line, not their own: indexing an Array or String out of range, Array.pop() on an empty array, Optional.value() on an Empty optional, Result.value() on an error, and the like.

They do it with an ordinary default parameter, location: __ptr<char> = __caller_location(). A call that leaves location out gets the place of that call, as file:line:col. Write the same parameter on a function of your own that checks its arguments, and pass location on to assert or panic, so a failure names the line that passed the bad value:

# Reporting the caller's location with `__caller_location()`.

# A check that names its caller's line when it fails, the way `assert`,
# `panic`, `Array` indexing and `Optional.value()` do: the default is the
# location of the call that leaves `location` out.
check_positive(value: int, location: __ptr<char> = __caller_location()): int {
    assert(value > 0, "expected a positive value", location);
    return value;
}

# The location is a C string, `file:line:col`.
here(location: __ptr<char> = __caller_location()): String {
    return String(location);
}

main(): int {
    assert(check_positive(3) == 3, "positive");
    var at = here();
    assert(at.ends_with("functions-caller-location.pep:18:14"), "this call");
    return 0;
}

Written anywhere else, __caller_location() is its own location. A compiler-generated check with no single place to report, such as a call through a null trait value, prints the message alone.

A stack overflow, from recursion that never ends for example, is reported the same way, on the main thread, a thread or a task:

panic: stack overflow

The stack has no room left to format anything, so the message has no location and no backtrace, the program's buffered output is not flushed, and the panic hook does not run. Any other memory fault goes to the handler installed before the program's own (or crashes the program, when there is none), and a debugger sees the overflow first. WebAssembly has no guard pages, so a WASI program gets no such report.

Panic hooks

set_panic_hook(hook) installs a function that every panic calls before it prints its message: a full-screen program uses it to restore the terminal, so the message lands where the user can read it. The hook is a shared (String, String) => void (the type alias PanicHook), called with the message and the location (file:line:col, or an empty string when the panic has none):

# A panic hook: code that runs before a panic prints its message.

import [File] from io;

# A full-screen program draws on the terminal's alternate screen, and must
# leave it before a panic's message prints, or the message goes with it.
leave_alternate_screen() {
    File.stdout().write_all("\x1B[?1049l");
}

main(): int {
    File.stdout().write_all("\x1B[?1049h");
    # Chain the hook installed before (none here) after this program's own.
    var previous = take_panic_hook();
    set_panic_hook((message, location) => {
        leave_alternate_screen();
        previous(message, location);
    });

    # ... draw, until the user quits; a panic here leaves the screen first.

    leave_alternate_screen();
    take_panic_hook();
    return 0;
}

  • There is one hook for the whole process. Set on any thread, it runs on the thread that panics, for every kind of panic: panic, a failed assert, an index out of range, an overflowing operator, and every other check. A stack overflow is the exception: it has no stack left to run the hook on, so it prints its message alone.

  • The hook cannot stop the panic: when it returns, the message and the backtrace print and the program aborts, as without one.

  • It runs in the middle of whatever the panicking thread was doing, and two threads that panic at once each run it, at the same time. Keep it short, and keep it from taking a lock the panicking code may hold (a Mutex it panicked inside): it would wait forever instead of letting the program end.

  • set_panic_hook replaces the hook installed before. take_panic_hook() removes it and returns it (or a hook that does nothing, when there was none), so a library can chain the one it found, as the example does.

  • A panic inside the hook does not run the hook again. It prints the message of the panic that ran the hook, then its own, and aborts:

    main.pep:9:5: panic: first
main.pep:4:28: panic in the panic hook: second

Command-line arguments and exit

main comes in two forms. main(): int takes nothing. main(args: String[]): int receives the program's command-line arguments: element 0 is the program as it was started, and the arguments typed after it follow in order. Declare the parameter only when the program reads it, as a Windows console program declares argc/argv only when it needs them. Any other parameter list on main is an error, and so is declaring both forms.

pepper build --entry <name> (and pepper run --entry <name>) starts the program in the top-level function name instead, which takes either form of parameter list, as main does. Every main is then left out of the program, so a file can hold several entry points, such as a benchmark beside the tool it measures.

Elsewhere, process.arguments() returns the same array, so code outside main can read the arguments without having them passed down. process.exit(code) ends the program at once with status code, from anywhere, after flushing what was printed. Both are in the process module, so the file needs import process.

import process;

# args holds the program name, then each command-line argument.
main(args: String[]): int {
    if (args.count > 2) {
        print("usage: greet [NAME]");
        process.exit(2);  # ends the program here, with status 2
    }
    var name = "world";
    if (args.count == 2) {
        name = args[1];
    }
    print("Hello, " + name + "!");
    return 0;
}

exit skips the Pepper code that would run on the way out of main: locals are not released and destructors do not run. What C runs at the end does run, as when main returns: the handlers a C library registered with atexit, then the flush of C's output streams. Prefer returning from main, and keep exit for ending from deep inside a call. See Processes.

Functions as values

A function's name used without a call is a value that you can store in a variable, pass to another function, or return, and a closure such as (x: int) => x * 2 is a function written where it is used. See Function types and closures.

String interpolation

An interpolated string is a string literal with a $ before its opening quote. Inside it, an expression in braces, {name} or {a + b}, is replaced by the text of its value:

# Interpolated strings: `$"..."` with expressions in braces.
main(): int {
    var name = "Pepper";
    var count = 3;
    var ready = true;

    # Each {name} is replaced by that variable's text.
    var line = $"{name} has {count} items, ready: {ready}";
    assert(line == "Pepper has 3 items, ready: true", "integers, bool and String");

    # Any expression fits between the braces, strings included.
    var sizes = [2, 5];
    assert($"total {sizes[0] + sizes[1]}" == "total 7", "arithmetic and index");
    assert($"{name.size} letters" == "6 letters", "call");
    assert($"{count > 1 ? "many" : "one"}" == "many", "ternary with strings");

    # Doubled braces are literal braces; escapes work as in any string.
    assert($"{{count}} = {count}" == "{count} = 3", "literal braces");
    assert($"tab\t{count}\n" == "tab\t3\n", "escapes");
    return 0;
}
  • {expression} holds an expression: a name (a local, a parameter, a global, or inside a method a field), a member access ({p.x}), a call ({f(x)}), an index ({items[0]}), arithmetic ({a + b}), or a ternary ({a > b ? a : b}). Spaces around it are ignored.
  • The expression changes no variable: an assignment (=, +=, ...), ++ or -- anywhere in it is an error, even inside a call's arguments ({f(a = 3)}). Only a closure's body, which does not run in place, may hold one. A function it calls may still have effects of its own.
  • String literals may appear inside the braces ({greet("you")}), and so may character literals and other interpolated strings. A } inside them, or inside brackets of the expression's own, does not end it.
  • The expression fits on one line and holds no comment: a line break or a # inside the braces is an error.
  • A format specification may follow the expression after a :, as in {n:>8} or {n:08x}: see below.
  • {{ and }} are a literal { and }.
  • Escapes (\n, \t, \", ...) work as in any string literal.
  • The result is a new String. An interpolated string with no braces is an ordinary string.

Which values can be interpolated

Each value is converted with to_string(value), so it can be:

  • an integer of any size, signed or unsigned, which gives its decimal text;
  • a float or double, which gives the shortest decimal text that reads back as the same number, as Swift prints one: 0.1, 3.0 (a whole number keeps its .0), -2.5, and an exponent outside 1e-4 to 1e16 (1e+16, 1.5e-05); nan, inf and -inf for the special values;
  • a bool, which gives true or false;
  • a tuple of up to eight values that can each be interpolated, which gives its elements' text in parentheses, (1, two) (a String element without quotes);
  • a String, which is used as it is;
  • a value whose type has a to_string(): String method, such as a struct that implements the runtime's ToString trait, or a value of type ToString itself;
  • a value whose type has a to_string<T> override. Like hash<Point> (see overriding a generic function), an override applies to the whole program, so it serves types that have no to_string() method of their own.
# A struct is interpolated through its to_string() method.
struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
}

extend Point with ToString {
    to_string(): String {
        # Inside a method, fields are names too.
        return $"({x}, {y})";
    }
}

# A type without the method gets a to_string<T> override instead.
struct Celsius {
    var degrees: int = 0;
    construct(this.degrees = 0) {}
}

to_string<Celsius>(value: Celsius): String {
    return $"{value.degrees} C";
}

main(): int {
    var start = Point(1, 2);
    var reading = Celsius(21);
    assert($"from {start}" == "from (1, 2)", "ToString");
    assert($"it is {reading}" == "it is 21 C", "override");

    # A trait value converts through the value's own method.
    var shown: ToString = start;
    assert($"{shown}" == "(1, 2)", "trait value");
    return 0;
}

Numbers and tuples, with the format specifications below:

# Floating-point numbers and tuples have text too.
main(): int {
    var price = 4.5;
    var ratio = 1.0 / 3.0;
    assert($"{price}" == "4.5", "the shortest text that reads back");
    assert($"{2.0}" == "2.0", "a whole number keeps its point");
    assert($"{1.0e20}" == "1e+20", "large numbers use an exponent");
    assert($"{ratio:.3}" == "0.333", "a precision rounds to that many digits");
    assert($"[{price:8.2}]" == "[    4.50]", "numbers align right");
    assert($"{price:+08.2}" == "+0004.50", "with a sign and zeros");

    var point = (3, "north");
    assert($"{point}" == "(3, north)", "a tuple's elements in parentheses");
    print("{0} at {1:.1}", point, price);   # (3, north) at 4.5
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# (3, north) at 4.5

Runtime types such as String, StringBuilder, io.Path, Uri and regex.Match implement ToString. An enum is interpolated through a to_string() method it declares (return name(); gives the case's name).

A plain overload such as to_string(p: Point) is not used: the runtime's code does not import your file, so it cannot see yours (see overloading). Write a to_string<Point> override or a method instead.

Format specifications

A : after the expression starts a format specification, which pads the value's text, writes an integer in another base, or rounds a floating-point number to a number of digits. Its parts, all optional, come in this order:

{value:[[fill]align][+][0][width][.precision][type]}
PartMeaning
align< left, ^ centered (leaning left), > right. Without one, numbers go to the right and everything else to the left.
fillThe character the padding is made of, written before align; a space by default. It can be any character but {, }, ", ' and #.
+Writes a + before a number that is not negative.
0Pads with zeros after the sign (-0042). It cannot be combined with align.
widthThe least number of characters the text takes; longer text is kept whole.
.precisionFor a float or double: the number of digits after the point, rounded to nearest, a tie to the even digit ({pi:.2} is 3.14, {0.125:.2} is 0.12; .0 leaves no point). At most 100.
typed decimal, x and X hexadecimal (lower and upper case), b binary, o octal.
# Format specifications: padding, signs and other bases after a `:`.
main(): int {
    var count = 42;
    var name = "Pepper";

    # Width and alignment pad any value; numbers go right by default.
    assert($"[{count:6}]" == "[    42]", "a number goes right");
    assert($"[{name:10}]" == "[Pepper    ]", "text goes left");
    assert($"[{name:>10}]" == "[    Pepper]", "right");
    assert($"[{name:*^10}]" == "[**Pepper**]", "centered with a fill");

    # Integers take a sign, zero padding and a base.
    assert($"{count:+}" == "+42", "a plus sign");
    assert($"{count:05}" == "00042", "zero padding");
    assert($"{255:x} {255:X} {5:b} {8:o}" == "ff FF 101 10", "bases");
    assert($"0x{255:08x}" == "0x000000ff", "padded hexadecimal");
    assert($"{-42:x}" == "-2a", "a negative number keeps its sign");

    # The `:` after the whole expression starts the specification.
    assert($"[{count > 1 ? "many" : "one":>5}]" == "[ many]", "a ternary");
    return 0;
}
  • Padding (fill, align and width) works for any value that can be interpolated: it pads the value's to_string text, counting characters, not bytes.
  • + and 0 need a number: an integer (of any size, signed or unsigned), or a float or double given a precision ({x:+08.2}). A type needs an integer, and a precision a float or double. Using one with any other value is an error at that character, and a precision cannot be combined with a type.
  • A negative number keeps its sign in every base: {-42:x} is -2a, not the bits of its two's complement.
  • The : that starts the specification is the one after the whole expression, so a ternary can be formatted as it is: {n > 1 ? "many" : "one":>5}.

Formatting by position: String.format

String.format takes a string literal whose braces name its other arguments by position, {0} for the first, each with an optional format specification, and returns the text:

# String.format: braces name the arguments by position.
main(): int {
    var a = 2;
    var b = 3;
    assert(String.format("{0} + {1} = {2}", a, b, a + b) == "2 + 3 = 5", "in order");

    # An index can repeat or come out of order, with its own specification.
    assert(String.format("{1} before {0}", "first", "second") == "second before first", "reordered");
    assert(String.format("{0} is {0:x} in hex", 255) == "255 is ff in hex", "repeated");
    assert(String.format("[{0:>4}] {{literal}}", a) == "[   2] {literal}", "padding and braces");
    return 0;
}
  • The format must be a string literal: the compiler reads it, so an index out of range, an argument no brace names, or a bad specification is an error at compile time. {{ and }} are literal braces, as in an interpolated string.
  • Each argument is evaluated once, from left to right, however many braces name it and in whatever order.
  • An index can repeat, to show one value twice or in two forms ("{0} is {0:x} in hex").
  • It is part of the compiler, not a function in the runtime: it cannot be stored in a variable or called through a function value.
  • print takes the same arguments: print("{0} of {1}", done, total) prints what String.format makes of them.

Errors

A value with no conversion is reported at its braces, with a note at its type:

main.pep:5:17: error: cannot interpolate a value of type 'Foo': it has no 'to_string()' method and no 'to_string' overload
    5 |     print($"f = {f}");
      |                 ^~~
main.pep:1:8: note: declare 'to_string(): String' in 'Foo', or implement 'ToString' with 'extend Foo with ToString'
    1 | struct Foo {}
      |        ^~~

A lone brace is an error, since doubling it is how to write one, and so is anything after the expression but its }:

main.pep:2:15: error: unmatched '}' in interpolated string; write '}}' for a literal '}'
    2 |     print($"a } b");
      |               ^
main.pep:3:18: error: expected '}'
    3 |     print($"a {x b");
      |                  ^
main.pep:3:15: note: to match this '{'
    3 |     print($"a {x b");
      |               ^

Empty braces are reported where the expression should start:

main.pep:2:16: error: expected an expression after '{' in interpolated string; write '{{' for a literal '{'
    2 |     print($"a {} b");
      |                ^

An error in the expression itself, such as a name that is not declared (use of undeclared identifier 'x') or a member its type lacks (no member named 'z' in 'Point'), is reported like any other, at the token inside the braces.

A format specification's errors are reported at the character in it that is wrong:

main.pep:5:16: error: unexpected 'q' in format specification; expected '[[fill]align][+][0][width][.precision][type]'
    5 |     print($"{n:q}");
      |                ^
main.pep:5:19: error: cannot format a value of type 'String' as an integer
    5 |     print($"{name:x}");
      |                   ^
main.pep:6:16: error: cannot format a value of type 'int' with a precision; only 'float' and 'double' take one
    6 |     print($"{n:.2}");
      |                ^

String.format reports an index with no argument at the index, and an argument with no index at the argument:

main.pep:5:31: error: argument index 2 is out of range for 2 arguments
    5 |     print(String.format("{0} {2}", n, n));
      |                               ^
main.pep:5:35: error: argument 1 of 'String.format' is not used by its format string
    5 |     print(String.format("{0}", n, n + 1));
      |                                   ^~~~~

Changing a variable inside the braces is reported at the operator:

main.pep:3:16: error: an assignment cannot appear in an interpolated string
    3 |     print($"{a += 1}");
      |                ^~

How it works

The compiler turns $"({x}, {y + 1})" into "(" + to_string(x) + ", " + to_string(y + 1) + ")", resolving to_string in the runtime rather than in your file. So a struct's own to_string() method can interpolate its fields without calling itself, and the result costs what the same + expression does. A value with a format specification goes through a runtime call that pads or converts its text instead. String.format becomes the same concatenation, with its arguments bound to hidden names first when the braces name them out of order or more than once.

Tuples and multiple return values

A tuple groups a fixed number of values, each of its own type, into one value. Its main use is returning several values from a function:

# A function returns several values as a tuple.
divide(a: int, b: int): (int, int) {
    return (a / b, a % b);
}

# Elements can be of any type, and a tuple can hold another tuple.
describe(n: int): (String, (bool, int)) {
    return ("number", (n % 2 == 0, n * n));
}

main(): int {
    # Read elements by position: t.0, t.1, ...
    var t = divide(17, 5);
    assert(t.0 == 3, "the quotient");
    assert(t.1 == 2, "the remainder");

    # Nested tuples chain: d.1.0 is element 0 of element 1.
    var d = describe(4);
    assert(d.0 == "number", "the name");
    assert(d.1.0 && d.1.1 == 16, "even, and its square");

    # A tuple type can be written out; the literal converts to it.
    var wide: (long, double) = (1, 2);
    assert(wide.0 == 1 && wide.1 == 2.0, "converted elements");
    return 0;
}

Tuple types and values

  • A tuple type lists its element types in parentheses: (int, String), (bool, (int, int)). A tuple has at least two elements.
  • A tuple value lists its elements the same way: (a / b, a % b). The compiler infers its type from the elements, so (1, "x") is an (int, String).
  • Where a tuple type is expected (a declared variable, a parameter, a return value), each element converts to its element type, as it would on its own: var wide: (long, double) = (1, 2);.
  • t.0, t.1, … read an element by position, counting from 0. t.1.0 is element 0 of element 1. An element that does not exist is a compile error.
  • Elements are read-only. t.0 = 3 is a compile error; build a new tuple instead: t = (3, t.1);.
  • Tuple<A, B> is another spelling of (A, B), for places where a type in angle brackets reads better.
  • (int, String)? is an optional tuple, Optional<(int, String)> (see Optional values), and (int, String)[] is an array of tuples, Array<(int, String)>.

Labels

A tuple type can name its elements: (line: int, column: int), and so can a tuple value: (line: 3, column: 7). A label is another name for a position, so p.line and p.0 read the same element:

# Labels name a tuple's elements.
position(): (line: int, column: int) {
    return (line: 3, column: 7);
}

# A generic function hands back the labels of its type argument.
first_of<T>(items: Array<T>): T {
    return items[0];
}

struct Token {
    var text: String = "";
    var at: (line: int, column: int);

    # So does a generic method.
    pick<T>(items: Array<T>): T {
        return items[0];
    }
}

main(): int {
    var p = position();
    assert(p.line == 3 && p.column == 7, "read by label");
    assert(p.0 == 3, "positions still work");

    # Labeled and unlabeled tuples convert to each other.
    var plain: (int, int) = p;
    assert(plain.1 == 7, "same elements");

    # A labeled value carries its labels into the variable's type.
    var end = (line: 4, column: 1);
    assert(end.line == p.line + 1, "labeled literal");

    var t = Token();
    t.at = (5, 6);
    assert(t.at.column == 6, "a labeled field");

    # Labels pass through a type argument.
    var counts = Array<(word: String, count: int)>();
    counts.append((word: "tuple", count: 2));
    assert(counts[0].count == 2, "a labeled element");
    var found = Optional<(line: int, column: int)>.Value(p);
    assert(found.value().column == 7, "through an enum case");
    assert(first_of(counts).count == 2, "through a generic function");
    assert(t.pick<(word: String, count: int)>(counts).count == 2, "through a generic method");
    return 0;
}
  • Labels belong to the type you write, not to the value. A labeled tuple and an unlabeled one with the same element types are the same type, so each converts to the other freely.
  • Either every element has a label or none does, and labels in one tuple must differ.
  • Labels pass through a type argument: an element of an Array<(word: String, count: int)>, a HashMap value or the value() of a (line: int, column: int)? answers to its labels, and so does what a static method or an enum case called on the labeled type gives (var p = Optional<(line: int, column: int)>.Value(at);), though Optional<(line: int, column: int)> is the same type as Optional<(int, int)>. A member takes back only the labels its declaration writes as a type parameter: a method of Box<(a: int, b: int)> declared to return (int, int) returns an unlabeled tuple. A generic function's or generic method's result takes back the labels of its type arguments, written or inferred, the same way: identity<(a: int, b: int)>(p).b, box.pass<(a: int, b: int)>(p).b and, for p: (a: int, b: int), identity(p).b read an element by its label.
  • var p = (line: 3, column: 7); gives p the labeled type (line: int, column: int). A labeled value takes at least two elements.
  • A labeled value initializing or returned as a labeled type must use its labels in order: (column: 7, line: 3) where a (line: int, column: int) is expected is an error, not a swap. An unlabeled value, or a labeled one going to an unlabeled type, converts by position.
  • A destructuring assignment lists places alone: (a, b) = (b, a);, never (x: a, y: b) = ....

Destructuring

var (a, b) = value; declares one variable for each element of a tuple:

struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
}

min_max(values: Array<int>): (int, int) {
    var low = values[0];
    var high = values[0];
    for (var v in values) {
        if (v < low) {
            low = v;
        }
        if (v > high) {
            high = v;
        }
    }
    return (low, high);
}

main(): int {
    var values = Array<int>();
    values.append(4);
    values.append(-2);
    values.append(9);

    # Destructure the result into new variables.
    var (low, high) = min_max(values);
    assert(low == -2 && high == 9, "both ends");

    # `_` skips an element; a binding may state its type.
    var (_, top: long) = min_max(values);
    assert(top == 9, "only the maximum");

    # `const` makes every binding constant.
    const (first, last) = (values[0], values[2]);
    assert(first == 4 && last == 9, "constants");

    # Assign to existing places. The right side is evaluated first,
    # so this swaps.
    var a = 1;
    var b = 2;
    (a, b) = (b, a);
    assert(a == 2 && b == 1, "swapped");

    var p = Point();
    (p.x, p.y) = min_max(values);
    assert(p.x == -2 && p.y == 9, "fields are places too");
    return 0;
}
  • The number of names must match the number of elements.
  • _ skips an element.
  • A name may state its type, var (_, top: long) = …; the element converts to it. Without one, the variable takes the element's type.
  • const (a, b) = … declares constants.
  • Patterns nest: var (id, (name, age)) = … takes an element that is itself a tuple apart.
  • A for loop destructures each element: for (var (name, count) in pairs).
  • (a, b) = value; assigns to places that already exist: variables, fields (p.x) and array elements. The whole right side is evaluated before any assignment, so (a, b) = (b, a) swaps.

Tuples and references

A tuple is a value, like a number. It is not an object on the heap, and copying it copies its elements. An element that is a reference is shared, not copied, exactly as if you had assigned it to a variable:

  • Building a tuple from a variable adds a reference to the object; building it from a function result takes over that result's reference.
  • A tuple holds its references until it goes out of scope or is replaced, then releases them.
  • Destructuring moves each element into its variable. After var (a, b) = pair();, a holds the only reference to its object, just as it would after var a = make();.

A tuple is thread-safe when all its elements are, so a module-scope const origin: (int, long) = (0, 0); is allowed.

Collections, comparing and printing

A tuple works anywhere a type does, including as a type argument: Array<(int, String)>, HashMap<(int, int), String>. Iterating a HashMap yields (key, value) tuples:

main(): int {
    # A tuple can be a key: here, a grid position.
    var grid = HashMap<(int, int), String>();
    grid[(0, 0)] = "start";
    grid[(2, 3)] = "goal";
    assert(grid[(2, 3)] == "goal", "looked up by value");

    # Tuples compare element by element.
    assert((1, "a") == (1, "a"), "equal");
    assert((1, "a") != (1, "b"), "different");

    # A HashMap yields (key, value) tuples; destructure them in the loop.
    var ages = HashMap<String, int>();
    ages["ada"] = 36;
    ages["grace"] = 85;
    var total = 0;
    for (var (name, age) in ages) {
        total += age;
    }
    assert(total == 121, "every entry");

    # An array of tuples: `(String, int)[]` is `Array<(String, int)>`.
    var pairs: (String, int)[] = [];
    pairs.append(("x", 1));
    pairs.append(("y", 2));
    for (var (name, count) in pairs) {
        print($"{name}: {count}");
    }
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# x: 1
# y: 2
  • == and != compare element by element. Each element compares the way it would on its own: a type with an == operator (such as String) uses it, and any other struct compares by identity (the same object).
  • A tuple can be a HashMap key or a HashSet member. Its hash combines the hashes of its elements, so equal tuples hash equally.
  • to_string((1, "two")) is (1, two), so a tuple of up to eight values that each have a to_string can be interpolated and printed: print($"{t}").
  • copy(t) (see Copying a value) copies each element: a struct element as copy would copy it on its own, anything thread-safe as is.

Matching tuples

A match over a tuple tests all of its elements at once. A tuple pattern lists a pattern for each element: (Rock, Scissors), (Number(v), 1), (4, column). Write the tuple in the match itself with double parentheses, match ((a, b)), or match a tuple value, match (at).

# `match` takes a tuple apart, testing every element at once.
enum Move {
    Rock,
    Paper,
    Scissors,
}

# Who wins: 1 for the first player, 2 for the second, 0 for a draw.
winner(first: Move, second: Move): int {
    match ((first, second)) {
        (Rock, Scissors), (Paper, Rock), (Scissors, Paper) => {
            return 1;
        }
        (Rock, Rock), (Paper, Paper), (Scissors, Scissors) => {
            return 0;
        }
        else => {
            return 2;
        }
    }
}

enum Token {
    Number(value: int),
    Word(text: String),
}

# Literals, cases with values, bound names and `_` mix in one pattern.
describe(token: Token, line: int): String {
    return match ((token, line)) {
        (Number(v), 1) => "a number on the first line",
        (Word(text), _) => text,
        (_, _) => "another number",
    };
}

main(): int {
    assert(winner(Move.Rock, Move.Scissors) == 1, "rock blunts scissors");
    assert(winner(Move.Paper, Move.Scissors) == 2, "scissors cut paper");
    assert(winner(Move.Paper, Move.Paper) == 0, "a draw");

    assert(describe(Token.Word("hi"), 3) == "hi", "a word binds its text");
    assert(describe(Token.Number(7), 1) == "a number on the first line", "a literal element");

    # A name binds its element; `is` tests one pattern.
    var at = (4, 2);
    if (at is (4, column)) {
        assert(column == 2, "bound by the pattern");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • Each element takes a case of its enum (Rock, Word(text)), a literal (1, "x", true), a range or a constant (0..9, LIMIT), another tuple pattern, _ for any value, or a name.
  • A name binds its element, unless it names a module-scope constant, which the element is compared with, or the element is an enum with a case of that name, which it then matches. So in (Circle, other) over two shapes, Circle is a case and other holds the second shape.
  • An arm's patterns bind the same names, each at the same element: (x, 0), (0, x) is an error, since x would mean a different element depending on which pattern matched.
  • The arms must handle every value unless there is an else. A missing value is named with an example: match on '(Shape, int)' does not handle '(Line, _)'. Only enum cases and true/false can be listed in full; other literals and ranges need a pattern with _ or a name at that element.
  • A pattern that the arms before it already cover is an error, and an else after arms that cover everything is a warning.
  • value is (4, column) tests one tuple pattern, and binds its names as the whole condition of an if or while, as for enums.

Enums and match

An enum is a type with a fixed set of named cases. A value of the enum holds exactly one of them. Use an enum where you would otherwise pass an integer code or a string, so the compiler checks that only the listed cases flow through, and that a match handles each one.

There are two kinds:

  • In an enum whose cases carry nothing (Red, Green), each case is an integer. Such an enum is a value type, like int.
  • When a case carries values (Circle(radius: int)), the enum is a reference type, like a struct. See Cases that carry values.
# An enum names a fixed set of cases; a slot of the enum type holds one.
enum Suit {
    Clubs,
    Diamonds,
    Hearts,
    Spades,
}

# A representation sets the stored integer type; a case may give its value.
enum Status: u8 {
    Ok,
    NotFound = 44,
    Failed,
}

struct Card {
    Suit suit;
    int rank = 1;
}

main(): int {
    var card = Card();
    assert(card.suit == Suit.Clubs, "a slot starts at the case whose value is 0");
    card.suit = Suit.Hearts;
    assert(card.suit != Suit.Spades, "cases compare with == and !=");

    # 'as' turns a case into its integer; the reverse is not allowed.
    assert((Suit.Hearts as int) == 2, "cases number from 0");
    assert((Status.Failed as int) == 45, "numbering continues after an explicit value");
    assert(sizeof<Status>() == 1, "Status is stored as a u8");
    return 0;
}

Declaring an enum

enum Name { ... } lists the cases, separated by commas; a comma after the last case is optional. Case names are PascalCase, like types (see naming conventions). A case may share a type's name (String(value: String)); a string literal in the enum's methods is still a String, and String(...) there calls the case.

Each case is an integer. The first case is 0 and each case after it is one more than the one before. A case can give its own value with = value, and numbering continues from there:

enum Status: u8 {
    Ok,             # 0
    NotFound = 44,  # 44
    Failed,         # 45
}

A value must be an integer constant: a literal such as -1 or 0x20, or a character such as 'y'. Two cases cannot have the same value.

The type after the colon is the representation, the integer type the enum is stored as. It can be any integer type (u8, short, int, long, and so on). Without one, the enum is stored as an int. Every case value must fit in the representation.

A case can carry a [Target] attribute, so a platform can have cases that others lack. A dropped case does not renumber the others.

Using enum values

This section is about enums whose cases carry nothing.

Name.Case is a value of the enum type. Such an enum is a value type, like int: it is copied, not reference counted, and it can be stored in locals, fields, arrays and module-scope constants, and passed to and returned from functions.

  • == and != compare two values of the same enum. Other operators apply only when the enum declares them (see Operators and indexers).
  • An enum does not mix with integers or with other enums: int x = Color.Red and Color c = 0 are errors, and so is comparing a Color with a Size.
  • value as int (or any integer type) gives a case's integer value. The reverse, 1 as Color, is an error, since the integer may not name a case; name the case, or use from_value.
  • A slot of an enum type that is not given a value (a field, or a local declared without one) holds the case whose value is 0, or the first case when no case is 0.
  • sizeof<Name>() is the size of the representation.
  • An enum works wherever an integer does: as a HashMap key or HashSet element, in an Atomic<Name>, and in an extern function's signature, where C sees the representation (an int unless the enum names another).

Cases that carry values

A case can carry values, declared like parameters: Circle(radius: int). An enum with such a case is a reference type: each value is an object, reference counted like a struct.

# Cases that carry values: each case is a constructor, and a `match`
# pattern binds the values of the case it matches.
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Square(side: int),
    Point,

    area(): int {
        match (this) {
            Circle(r) => { return 3 * r * r; }
            Rect(w, h) => { return w * h; }
            Square(s) => { return s * s; }
            Point => { return 0; }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

# A generic enum can name itself: a list is empty, or a value and the rest.
enum List<T> {
    Empty,
    Cons(head: T, tail: List<T>),
}

length(list: List<String>): int {
    match (list) {
        Empty => { return 0; }
        # `_` skips a value.
        Cons(_, tail) => { return 1 + length(tail); }
    }
    return 0;
}

main(): int {
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    shapes.append(Shape.Circle(2));
    shapes.append(Shape.Rect(3, 4));
    shapes.append(Shape.Point);
    var total = 0;
    for (var s in shapes) {
        total += s.area();
    }
    assert(total == 24, "12 + 12 + 0");

    # Several patterns in one arm bind the same names.
    var side = 0;
    match (Shape.Square(5)) {
        Rect(w, _), Square(w) => { side = w; }
        else => {}
    }
    assert(side == 5, "a square's side");

    var names = List<String>.Cons("a", List<String>.Cons("b", List<String>.Empty));
    assert(length(names) == 2, "two names");
    assert(names.name() == "Cons", "name() spells the case");
    return 0;
}
  • Name.Case(values...) makes a new value, like a constructor call, and Name.Case alone is a case that carries nothing. An enum's values are made only by its cases: Shape(...) is an error.
  • A case that carries values must be given them: Shape.Circle without (radius) is an error.
  • The values are fixed once made. There is no way to change them, so a value can be shared freely. To change one, make a new value.
  • Each case that carries nothing is a single object that every use shares. It is never freed and costs no allocation, however often it is used.
  • A slot of the enum type that is not given a value holds null, as a struct slot does. === and !== compare identity, and so does ==, unless the enum is [Equatable].
  • Mark the enum [Equatable] to derive == and hash from its cases: two values are equal when they hold the same case with equal values, so they work as HashMap and HashSet keys.
  • An enum can have type parameters (enum List<T>), and its cases can hold the enum itself, directly or through other types, so lists and trees are enums.
  • The enum can be [Shared] when every value its cases carry is thread-safe (see What threads can share). An enum whose cases carry nothing is stored as an integer and is always thread-safe. It can conform to a trait with extend Name with Trait, like a struct, and its methods can come from an extend block too.
  • Cases cannot have explicit values (= 3), and the enum has no representation type (: u8), since its values are not integers.

Value enums

An enum whose cases carry values can be marked [Value], like a value struct. Each value is then stored inline in whatever holds it, and copied when assigned, passed or returned, instead of being an object. Making one allocates nothing, which suits small enums that are made often, such as Optional and Result, which are both value enums.

[Value]
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Point,
}
  • Its cases share one storage: a value is as large as its largest case, plus the tag that says which case it holds (sizeof<Shape>() is 12: the tag, then room for Rect's two ints, which Circle's radius reuses).
  • A value enum is never null. A slot that is not given a value holds the first case, with every value it carries zero, false, or null: an unset Shape is Circle(0).
  • == compares the cases and their values; ===, !== and __null are errors.
  • Its cases cannot hold the enum itself, since the value would be infinitely large. Use a reference enum for lists and trees.
  • Everything else a value struct cannot do applies too, and so does boxing when it flows into a trait value.

Methods

An enum can declare methods after its cases. Inside a method, this is the value the method was called on, and a bare call of another method of the enum (next()) calls it on this. A static method is called on the enum itself (Light.first()). A method can be generic (choose<T>), with its type arguments inferred or written out (light.choose<String>(...)).

# An enum can declare methods after its cases; `this` is the value.
enum Light: u8 {
    Red,
    Amber,
    Green,

    may_go(): bool {
        return this == Light.Green;
    }

    next(): Light {
        match (this) {
            Red => { return Light.Green; }
            Amber => { return Light.Red; }
            Green => { return Light.Amber; }
        }
        return this;
    }

    # A bare call of another method acts on `this`.
    after_two(): Light {
        return next().next();
    }

    # A method can be generic, like any function.
    choose<T>(stop: T, go: T): T {
        return may_go() ? go : stop;
    }

    static first(): Light {
        return Light.Red;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var light = Light.first();
    assert(!light.may_go(), "red means stop");
    assert(light.next().may_go(), "green follows red");
    assert(light.after_two() == Light.Amber, "then amber");
    assert(light.choose("wait", "walk") == "wait" && Light.Green.choose(0, 1) == 1, "a generic method");

    # Every enum has name() and from_value().
    assert(light.name() == "Red", "name() spells the case");
    var found = Light.from_value(2);
    assert(found.is_ok() and found.value() == Light.Green, "2 is Green");
    assert(!Light.from_value(7).is_ok(), "no case has the value 7");

    # Enums key hash maps and fill atomics, like integers.
    var waits = HashMap<Light, int>();
    waits[Light.Red] = 30;
    assert(waits[Light.Red] == 30, "an enum is a hash key");
    return 0;
}

For an enum whose cases carry nothing, this is passed by value, like an int: a method cannot change the value it was called on. Return a new case instead, as next() does. Such an enum can also declare a trait with extend Light with Describe { ... }, which makes it meet the constraint T: Describe (see numbers, bool and enums); it is still never a trait value. For an enum whose cases carry values, this is the object, as in a struct's method; its values still cannot change.

Operators and indexers

An enum can declare operators and an indexer the way a struct does: a method named after the operator (<(other: Level): bool) or []. For an enum whose cases carry nothing, a < b calls Level.< with a as this.

# An enum can declare operators and an indexer, as a struct does.
enum Level: u8 {
    Low,
    Mid,
    High,

    # `a < b` calls `Level.<`: the cases rank in order.
    <(other: Level): bool {
        return (this as int) < (other as int);
    }

    # `level + 1` moves up a level, stopping at the top.
    +(steps: int): Level {
        var next = Level.from_value((this as int + steps) as u8);
        return next.is_ok() ? next.value() : Level.High;
    }

    # `-level` mirrors it.
    -(): Level {
        return match (this) {
            Low => Level.High,
            Mid => Level.Mid,
            High => Level.Low,
        };
    }

    # `level[i]` reads, like any indexer.
    [](bit: int): bool {
        return ((this as int) >> bit) & 1 == 1;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var level = Level.Low;
    assert(level < Level.Mid && !(Level.High < level), "cases rank in order");
    assert(level + 1 == Level.Mid && level + 5 == Level.High, "a step up");
    assert(-level == Level.High, "mirrored");
    assert(Level.Mid[0] && !Level.Mid[1] && Level.High[1], "bits");
    return 0;
}

Its values never change and it already compares with == and !=, so such an enum cannot declare ==, !=, a compound assignment (+=), an indexer that assigns ([](index, value)) or the truth test !!, and its operators are not static.

Properties

An enum can also declare computed properties after its cases, var name: T { get { ... } }, which are read like fields (size.ounces). Inside the enum, a bare property name reads it on this.

# An enum can declare computed properties after its cases, read like
# fields: `size.ounces`, not `size.ounces()`.
enum Size {
    Small,
    Medium,
    Large,

    var ounces: int {
        get {
            return match (this) {
                Small => 8,
                Medium => 12,
                Large => 16,
            };
        }
    }

    # Inside the enum, a bare property name reads it on `this`.
    var cups: int {
        get { return ounces / 8; }
    }
}

# The same works for an enum whose cases carry values.
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Square(side: int),

    var area: int {
        get {
            return match (this) {
                Circle(r) => 3 * r * r,
                Square(s) => s * s,
            };
        }
    }
}

main(): int {
    var size = Size.Medium;
    assert(size.ounces == 12 && Size.Large.cups == 2, "value enum properties");
    assert(Shape.Square(4).area == 16 && Shape.Circle(2).area == 12, "properties that read the payload");
    return 0;
}

An enum value has nowhere to keep anything and never changes, so an enum's property has a get with a body that does not use field, and no set:

main.pep:6:9: error: property 'n' of enum 'E' must be computed: give 'get' a body that does not use 'field'
main.pep:6:38: error: property 'n' of enum 'E' cannot have a 'set' accessor: enum values are immutable

Built-in methods

Every enum has these methods without declaring them, and cannot declare methods of the same names:

MethodWhat it does
value.name()Returns the case's name as written ("Red"), a String. Every enum has it.
Name.from_value(n)Returns a Result<Name>: Ok with the case whose value is n, or an Err when no case has it. n has the enum's representation type. Only enums whose cases carry nothing have it.

from_value is the checked way back from an integer (from a file, a C library or the network) to a case, since as only goes the other way.

match

match (value) { ... } runs the arm for the case that value holds:

# 'match' runs the arm of the case a value holds, and must handle every case.
enum Light {
    Red,
    Amber,
    Green,
}

next(light: Light): Light {
    match (light) {
        Red => { return Light.Green; }
        Amber => { return Light.Red; }
        Green => { return Light.Amber; }
    }
    return light;
}

may_go(light: Light): bool {
    match (light) {
        Green => { return true; }
        else => { return false; }
    }
    return false;
}

wait_seconds(light: Light): int {
    match (light) {
        Red, Amber => { return 30; }
        Light.Green => { return 0; }
    }
    return 0;
}

main(): int {
    var light = Light.Red;
    var changes = 0;
    while (!may_go(light)) {
        light = next(light);
        changes += 1;
    }
    assert(changes == 1, "red turns green");
    assert(wait_seconds(Light.Amber) == 30, "one arm handles two cases");
    assert(wait_seconds(light) == 0, "a pattern may name the enum");
    return 0;
}
  • Each arm is one or more patterns, separated by commas, then => and a block. A pattern is a case name (Red) or the case qualified by its enum (Light.Red).
  • A pattern for a case that carries values can bind them: Rect(w, h) declares w and h in its arm, holding the case's values in order. The bindings are const. _ skips a value. A pattern lists all of its case's values or, written without parentheses (Rect), none. Each value can also be a pattern of its own (see Nested patterns).
  • Patterns that share an arm must bind the same names, with the same types (Rect(w, _), Square(w)).
  • An else => { ... } arm, last, handles every case the other arms do not.
  • The arms must handle every case. A missing case is an error that names it, located at match; the language server offers a quick fix that adds an empty arm for each missing case. An else that can never run, because the other arms handle every case, is a warning.
  • Handling a case twice is an error.
  • In a match statement, break, continue and return inside an arm act on the enclosing loop or function, as they would inside an if.

The value is evaluated once, before any arm runs. A match on a null value of an enum whose cases carry values panics with match on a null 'Name'; a value enum is never null.

match expressions, is, and literal patterns

# `match` produces a value, `is` tests one case, and a `match` on an
# integer, character, `bool` or `String` compares with literals.
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Point,
}

enum List {
    Empty,
    Cons(head: int, tail: List),
}

area(s: Shape): int {
    return match (s) {
        Circle(r) => 3 * r * r,
        Rect(w, h) => w * h,
        Point => 0,
    };
}

keyword(word: String): int {
    return match (word) {
        "import" => 1,
        "export", "extern" => 2,
        else => 0,
    };
}

# The arms' values are numbers of different types (`0` is an `int`,
# `length` a `ulong`), so the `match` has their common type, `ulong`, and
# converts to the `int` this function returns.
length_of(word: String): int {
    return match (word) {
        "" => 0,
        else => word.length,
    };
}

main(): int {
    var total = area(Shape.Rect(2, 3)) + keyword("extern");

    # `is` binds only in the block of the `if` or `while` it is the
    # condition of.
    var s = Shape.Circle(1);
    if (s is Circle(r)) {
        total += r;
    }

    var list = List.Cons(1, List.Cons(2, List.Empty));
    while (list is Cons(head, tail)) {
        total += head;
        list = tail;
    }

    var point = Shape.Point is Point;
    if (point && !(s is Rect)) {
        total += 100;
    }

    # A `match` on an integer needs an `else`: literals cannot list every
    # value.
    var size = match (total) {
        0 => "none",
        1, 2, 3 => "few",
        else => "many",
    };
    assert(size == "many", "total is past three");
    assert(length_of("four") == 4 && length_of("") == 0, "lengths convert");
    assert(total == 6 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 100, "every step adds up");
    return 0;
}
  • A match that produces a value can go wherever a value can: after var x =, return, in an argument. Each arm is patterns => value, and arms are separated by commas (one after the last is allowed). It follows the rules above: a pattern binds names for its arm's value, and the arms must handle every case unless there is an else. The value has the first arm's type, and every other arm's value must convert to it. When the arms are numbers of different types, the value has their common type, as C's ? : does (int and long give long), and converts from it wherever it goes (0 or a ulong length, returned as an int). A closure in an arm's value cannot use a name the arm binds; use a match statement there.
  • value is Pattern is a bool: whether value holds that case (d is Line, !(d is Text)). It takes any one pattern. When it is the whole condition of an if or while, its bindings are declared in that block only: if (d is Text(t)) { ... } reads t inside the braces, and while (list is Cons(head, tail)) { ... } examines list again on every iteration. Anywhere else, is cannot bind names. is is a keyword only between a value and a pattern, so it stays usable as a name (token.is(text)).
  • A trait value is matched by type rather than by case: Circle(c) tests for the struct Circle and binds the value as one. See Converting a trait value back.
  • Literal patterns: a match on an integer, a character, a bool or a String compares with literals (1, -1, 'a', true, "import"), using ==. Literals cannot list every value, so such a match needs an else arm, except on a bool that handles both true and false. Matching the same literal twice is an error. A match on an enum takes its case names, not literals, and a match on int takes literals, not names (except constants).

Nested patterns

The values in a case's parentheses are patterns, as a tuple pattern's elements are, so patterns nest to any depth:

# Patterns nest: the values a case carries can be matched by patterns of
# their own, as tuple elements can.
enum Doc {
    Text(text: String),
    Line,
    Pair(left: Doc, right: Doc),
}

describe(found: Optional<Doc>): String {
    return match (found) {
        Empty => "nothing",
        # A literal compares the value: only an empty `Text`.
        Value(Text("")) => "empty text",
        # A case of the value's enum, binding its own values.
        Value(Text(t)) => t,
        Value(Line) => "a line",
        # Deeper still, with `_` for a value that does not matter.
        Value(Pair(Line, _)) => "a pair that starts with a line",
        Value(Pair) => "a pair",
    };
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe(Optional<Doc>.Empty) == "nothing", "no document");
    assert(describe(Optional<Doc>.Value(Doc.Text(""))) == "empty text", "a literal value");
    assert(describe(Optional<Doc>.Value(Doc.Text("hi"))) == "hi", "a bound value");
    assert(
        describe(Optional<Doc>.Value(Doc.Pair(Doc.Line, Doc.Text("x")))) == "a pair that starts with a line",
        "two levels deep"
    );

    # A bare name binds the value, unless the value's enum has a case of
    # that name: here `Empty` is `Optional<int>`'s case.
    var nested = Optional<Optional<int>>.Value(Optional<int>.Empty);
    var depth = match (nested) {
        Empty => 0,
        Value(Empty) => 1,
        Value(Value(n)) => 2 + n,
    };
    assert(depth == 1, "the inner Optional is empty");

    # Ranges and guards work inside too, and so does `is`.
    var count = Optional<int>.Value(7);
    var size = match (count) {
        Value(0) => "none",
        Value(1..10) => "a few",
        Value(n) if n < 0 => "negative",
        Value(_) => "many",
        Empty => "unknown",
    };
    assert(size == "a few", "a range inside a case");
