    var pair = Doc.Pair(Doc.Text("left"), Doc.Line);
    if (pair is Pair(Text(word), Line)) {
        assert(word == "left", "is binds nested names");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • Each value takes _, a name, a case of its enum (with patterns of its own values: Value(Pair(Line, _))), a literal, a range or constant, or a tuple pattern.
  • A bare name binds the value, unless the value's enum has a case of that name, which it then matches (Value(Empty)), or it names a module-scope constant. A name repeated in one pattern (Pair(x, x)) must be a case.
  • A nested pattern handles part of its case: the arms must still handle every value. A case that only nested patterns handle is reported with the value they miss (match on 'Optional<Doc>' does not handle 'Value(Line)'), and a pattern whose values the earlier arms already match is an error.
  • Patterns that share an arm bind the same names, each at the same place: Pair(Text(t), Line), Pair(Text(t), Pair) binds t from either, but Pair(Text(t), _), Pair(_, Text(t)) is an error.
  • A nested test reads a value only once the case around it matched, so the tests stop at the first part that does not match.

Ranges and constants

A match on an integer or a character can compare with a range of values, and a match on an integer, a character or a bool with a module-scope constant:

# Range and constant patterns: a `match` on an integer or a character
# compares with ranges (`1..9`, `'a'..>'z'`) and module-scope constants.
const LIMIT = 100;

size(n: int): String {
    return match (n) {
        0 => "none",
        # `1..10` stops before 10; `10..>99` includes 99.
        1..10 => "a few",
        10..>99 => "many",
        LIMIT => "the limit",
        else => "out of range",
    };
}

kind(c: char): String {
    return match (c) {
        'a'..>'z', 'A'..>'Z' => "letter",
        '0'..>'9' => "digit",
        else => "other",
    };
}

# Ranges that cover every value of the type need no `else`.
half(b: u8): int {
    return match (b) {
        0..128 => 0,
        128..>255 => 1,
    };
}

main(): int {
    assert(size(0) == "none" && size(9) == "a few" && size(10) == "many", "ranges");
    assert(size(100) == "the limit" && size(-1) == "out of range", "a constant, then else");
    assert(kind('q') == "letter" && kind('7') == "digit" && kind('!') == "other", "character ranges");
    u8 high = 200;
    assert(half(3) == 0 && half(high) == 1, "every u8 is handled");

    # In a tuple pattern, a range or a constant compares its element.
    var pair = (LIMIT, true);
    var which = match (pair) {
        (0..LIMIT, _) => 1,
        (LIMIT, true) => 2,
        (_, _) => 3,
    };
    assert(which == 2, "the constant matches the first element");
    return 0;
}
  • start..end matches from start up to but not including end, and start..>end includes end, as ranges do elsewhere. Each bound is a literal (-1, 'z') or a constant (MIN..MAX). Ranges match integers and characters only, not bool or String.
  • A name that is a module-scope constant (const LIMIT = 100;, declared in the file or imported, or limits.MAX through a module) compares the value with it, like a literal. A local variable is not a pattern; compare with it in a guard instead (n if n == limit).
  • Inside a tuple pattern, a range or a constant compares its element ((0..LIMIT, _)), and any other bare name binds it, as before.
  • When every bound is a literal, the compiler knows which values a pattern matches: a pattern whose values the earlier arms already match is an error (2..>5 after 1..9), and a match whose ranges and literals cover every value of its type (0..128 and 128..>255 for a u8) needs no else. A pattern with a constant bound covers nothing for this check.
  • A match on an enum takes its cases, not ranges or constants, even a constant holding one of its cases.

Guards

An arm can add a guard after its patterns, if condition: the arm runs only when one of its patterns matches and the condition holds. Otherwise the next arm is tried, as if this one had not matched.

# A guard (`if condition`) after an arm's patterns: the arm runs only when a
# pattern matches and the guard holds; otherwise the next arm is tried.
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Point,
}

describe(s: Shape): String {
    return match (s) {
        # The guard reads the names its patterns bind.
        Circle(r) if r > 10 => "a large circle",
        Circle => "a circle",
        Rect(w, h) if w == h => "a square",
        Rect => "a rectangle",
        Point => "a point",
    };
}

# A guarded arm handles nothing for the check that every value is handled,
# since its guard may fail: the `bool` match below still needs `false`.
toll(heavy: bool, axles: int): int {
    match (heavy) {
        true if axles > 4 => {
            return 30;
        }
        true => {
            return 20;
        }
        false => {
            return 10;
        }
    }
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe(Shape.Circle(20)) == "a large circle", "the guard holds");
    assert(describe(Shape.Circle(2)) == "a circle", "the guard fails, the next arm runs");
    assert(describe(Shape.Rect(3, 3)) == "a square", "equal sides");
    assert(describe(Shape.Rect(3, 4)) == "a rectangle", "unequal sides");
    assert(toll(true, 6) + toll(true, 2) + toll(false, 2) == 60, "each arm runs once");

    # Guards work on tuples too.
    var pair = (5, true);
    var kind = match (pair) {
        (n, true) if n > 3 => 1,
        (_, true) => 2,
        (_, false) => 3,
    };
    assert(kind == 1, "the first arm's guard holds");
    return 0;
}
  • The guard reads the names the arm's patterns bind (Circle(r) if r > 10). With several patterns (Word(s), Quoted(s) if s.length == 0), it applies to the arm, whichever pattern matched.
  • Guards work in match statements and match expressions, over enums, literals and tuples. is takes no guard: write x is P && condition, or test the condition inside the if.
  • A guarded arm handles nothing when the compiler checks that every case is handled, since its guard may fail: a match whose only arm for Circle has a guard does not handle Circle, and a later unguarded arm (or else) must. An else after guarded arms is not unreachable.
  • A guarded arm for a case an earlier unguarded arm already handles is an error, like any case handled twice. Two guarded arms may name the same case.
  • A closure in a guard cannot use a name the arm binds.

Current limits

  • An enum whose cases carry nothing cannot be generic, by design: its value is a plain integer, so a type parameter would have nothing to describe. An enum whose cases carry values can be (enum List<T>).
  • An enum whose cases carry values compares by identity with ==, as a struct does, unless it is a [Value] enum, is [Equatable], or declares == (with a matching hash<T> to be a key).
  • A constant is a pattern only when it is declared at module scope.
  • A match cannot examine floating-point values.
  • The methods of an enum whose cases carry nothing have no value form: c.name without the call is an error ("'name' is a method of 'Color': call it as 'name()'"), where a struct's p.norm is a bound method. Wrap the call in a closure instead, () => c.name().
  • An enum whose cases carry nothing is extended only with a trait (extend Color with Describe { ... }); declare its other methods inside it. It is never a trait value, since a trait value is a reference to an object, which such an enum's value is not.

Optional values

A value that may be missing has the type Optional<T>, written T? for short: either Value, holding a T, or Empty, holding nothing. It plays the role of Rust's Option<T> and Swift's Optional. Use it instead of a null reference or a sentinel such as -1 or "": the type tells the caller that the value can be absent, and reading it goes through a method that checks.

Optional is part of the runtime, so you can use it without an import. The Optional reference lists every member.

# A lookup that may find nothing returns an Optional instead of a sentinel.
struct Person {
    String name;
    int age;

    construct(this.name = "", this.age = 0) {}
}

find_adult(people: Array<Person>): Optional<Person> {
    for (var p in people) {
        if (p.age >= 18) { return Optional<Person>.Value(p); }
    }
    return Optional<Person>.Empty;
}

# `ulong?` is shorthand for `Optional<ulong>`.
index_of(text: String, wanted: String): ulong? {
    var i: ulong = 0;
    while (i < text.length) {
        if (text[i] == wanted) { return Optional<ulong>.Value(i); }
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return Optional<ulong>.Empty;
}

main(): int {
    var people = Array<Person>();
    people.append(Person("ada", 12));
    assert(find_adult(people).is_empty(), "no adult yet");

    people.append(Person("grace", 45));
    var adult = find_adult(people);
    assert(adult.is_value(), "grace is an adult");
    # An optional is a condition by itself: `if (adult)` tests is_some().
    if (!adult) { return 1; }
    assert(adult.value().name == "grace", "value() returns the Person");

    # Works for types that have no null, too.
    assert(index_of("pepper", "e").value() == 1, "first 'e' is at 1");
    assert(index_of("pepper", "z").is_empty(), "no 'z'");

    # value_or supplies a fallback instead of panicking.
    assert(index_of("pepper", "z").value_or(99) == 99, "fallback for Empty");

    # Optional is an enum with the cases Empty and Value(value).
    var nothing = Optional<int>.Empty;
    assert(nothing.is_empty(), "the Empty case is empty");
    var first_p = match (index_of("pepper", "p")) {
        Empty => -1,
        Value(at) => at as int,
    };
    assert(first_p == 0, "match on an optional");

    # An optional slot that is not given a value starts as Empty.
    var later: String?;
    assert(later.is_empty(), "unassigned optionals are Empty");
    return 0;
}

The T? shorthand

T? means Optional<T> wherever a type is written: x: int?, find(key: String): Node?, Array<Node?>, a field Token? leaf;. The ? applies to everything before it, so int[]? is an optional array, and Array<int?> is an array of optional values.

A C-style declaration inside a function body, such as Node? n = m;, is read as a declaration only when a name follows the ? and then =, ; or the end of the line; a ? b : c stays a conditional expression.

Returning early with ?

In a function that returns an optional, ? after an optional is its value, or, when it is Empty, returns Empty from the function at once, as ? does with an error for Result:

middle_name(person: Person): String? {
    var names = person.full_name?.split(" ");
    if (names.count < 3) {
        return Optional<String>.Empty;
    }
    return Optional<String>.Value(names[1]);
}

Using ? on an optional in a function that does not return an optional is an error ('?' requires the enclosing function to return an Optional).

Optional slots start as Empty

A variable or field of an optional type that is not given a value starts as Empty, not null:

struct Node {
    Token? leaf;   # Empty until assigned
}
var count: int?;   # Empty

Creating and checking optionals

MemberWhat it does
Optional<T>.Value(value)Creates a Value optional holding value.
Optional<T>.EmptyAn Empty optional.
is_value(), is_empty()Report which case the optional is.
!! (truth test)An optional is a condition by itself: if (found) is if (found.is_value()), and !found is found.is_empty().
value()Returns the value; panics with Optional.value on an Empty optional if the optional is Empty.
value_or(fallback)Returns the value, or fallback if the optional is Empty. Never panics.

Use value() when an Empty optional would be a bug in your program, since it stops the program. When a missing value is an expected outcome, test it first (if (found), is_value() or is_empty()), or supply a fallback with value_or. Testing the optional itself works because Optional declares the truth-test operator !! (see Truth tests).

Optional<T> works for every T, including types that have no null at all, such as int or ulong. For a struct type, a Value optional holds a reference to the object, like any other struct slot (see Memory and reference counting).

Optional<T> is an enum with the cases Empty and Value(value), so match and is work on it too:

var shown = match (name) {
    Empty => "nobody",
    Value(text) => text,
};
if (name is Value(text)) { print(text); }

An optional is a value enum: it lives inline in the variable, field or array element that holds it, so creating one allocates nothing, and copying one gives an independent optional. It is never null, and has no identity: compare two optionals with ==, which compares whether each holds a value and, if both do, their values; === on an optional is an error.

Optionals in the standard library

Standard library lookups that can come up empty return an optional rather than a sentinel value:

APIReturnsEmpty when
Array<T>.find(item)ulong?no element equals item
io.Path.parent()Path?the path is a root (/, C:\), a bare name with no root (a, ., ..), or empty
io.Path.file_name()String?the path is a root or empty, or its last component is . or ..
io.Path.file_stem()String?there is no file name
io.Path.extension()String?there is no file name, or the name has no dot after its first character (Makefile, .bashrc); foo. has the empty extension ""
io.Path.dot_index(name)ulong?name has no dot after its first character
http.Headers.get(name)String?no field has that name
HashMap<K, V>.try_get(key) (and Map, OrderedMap)V?key is absent
# Standard library lookups that may come up empty return an optional.
import io;

main(): int {
    # Array.find returns `ulong?`: the index, or none.
    var names = ["ada", "grace", "linus"];
    var at = names.find("grace");
    assert(at.value() == 1, "grace is at index 1");
    assert(names.find("ken").is_empty(), "ken is not in the array");

    # Path.parent, file_name, file_stem and extension return `Path?` or
    # `String?`: none when the path has no such part.
    var path = io.Path("docs").join("guide.md");
    assert(path.file_name().value() == "guide.md", "file name");
    assert(path.file_stem().value() == "guide", "stem");
    assert(path.extension().value() == "md", "extension");
    assert(path.parent().value() == io.Path("docs"), "parent");

    assert(io.Path("/").parent().is_empty(), "a root has no parent");
    assert(io.Path("notes").parent().is_empty(), "nor does a bare name");
    assert(io.Path("a/..").file_name().is_empty(), "'..' is not a file name");
    assert(io.Path("Makefile").extension().is_empty(), "no dot, no extension");

    # value_or supplies a default when none is an expected outcome.
    var ext = io.Path("Makefile").extension().value_or("txt");
    assert(ext == "txt", "fallback extension");
    return 0;
}

Breaking change. Array.find used to return a long that was -1 for "not found", and the Path methods above returned an empty Path or String (or name.size for dot_index). Code written against the old API must test the optional instead: a.find(x) >= 0 becomes a.find(x).is_value(), p.parent().is_empty becomes p.parent().is_empty(), and a value is read with value() or value_or. A comparison such as a.find(x) == -1 still compiles but compares the optional object rather than an index, so search for these and rewrite them. String.find is unchanged and still returns -1.

Optional or Result

An Optional<T> says only that a value is missing. When the caller needs to know why, return a Result instead, whose Err carries an error.

Current limits

  • Some runtime APIs still use null references, default values or sentinels for "missing": a HashMap's get (and indexer) returns the default value for a missing key (use try_get for an optional), and String.find returns -1, for example.

Error handling with Result

An operation that can fail returns a Result: either Ok, holding the value you asked for, or Err, holding an error that says what went wrong. The caller checks which one it got before using the value. Pepper has no exceptions, so Result is how a function reports a failure the caller is expected to handle. For a failure that should stop the program, such as a broken invariant, use assert or panic instead.

Result and Error are part of the runtime, so you can use them without an import. The Result reference lists every member.

Creating and checking results

Result<TValue, TError> works like Rust's Result<T, E>. It is an enum with two cases, Ok(value: TValue) and Err(error: TError). You build one with a case or with the static functions ok and err, and read it with match, is, or its methods:

# A function that can fail returns a Result instead of a plain value.
parse_digit(String s): Result<int> {
    if (s == "0") { return Result<int>.ok(0); }
    if (s == "1") { return Result<int>.ok(1); }
    if (s == "2") { return Result<int>.ok(2); }
    return Result<int>.err(Error("not a digit: " + s));
}

main(): int {
    var good = parse_digit("2");
    assert(good.is_ok(), "2 parses");
    assert(!good.is_err(), "is_err is the opposite of is_ok");
    assert(good.value() == 2, "value() returns the value");

    var bad = parse_digit("x");
    assert(bad.is_err(), "x does not parse");
    assert(bad.error().message == "not a digit: x", "the error explains why");

    # ok_or returns the value, or the fallback for an Err. It never panics.
    assert(good.ok_or(-1) == 2, "Ok gives its value");
    assert(bad.ok_or(-1) == -1, "Err gives the fallback");

    # Result<int> is short for Result<int, Error>.
    Result<int, Error> spelled_out = good;
    assert(spelled_out.value() == 2, "the same type");

    # Result is an enum: its cases build values too, and match reads them.
    var parsed = Result<int>.Ok(7);
    var doubled = match (parsed) { Ok(n) => n * 2, Err(e) => 0 };
    assert(doubled == 14, "match binds the value");
    if (bad is Err(e)) {
        assert(e.message.length > 0, "is binds the error");
    }

    # An operation with no value to return uses void.
    var done = Result<void>.ok();
    var failed = Result<void>.err(Error("disk full"));
    assert(done.is_ok() && failed.is_err(), "Result<void> works like any other");
    return 0;
}

The pieces:

MemberWhat it does
Result<T>.Ok(value), Result<T>.ok(value)Creates an Ok result holding value.
Result<T>.Err(error), Result<T>.err(error)Creates an Err result holding error.
is_ok(), is_err()Report which kind the result is.
value()Returns the value; panics with Result.value on an Err value if the result is an Err.
error()Returns the error; panics with Result.error on an Ok value if the result is Ok.
ok_or(fallback)Returns the value, or fallback if the result is an Err. Never panics.

TError defaults to Error, so Result<int> means Result<int, Error>, and values of the two spellings can be assigned to each other freely (the compiler does generate a separate specialization for each spelling). Error is a struct with one field, String message: Error("boom").message is "boom".

Use value() when an Err would be a bug in your program, since it stops the program. When an Err is an expected outcome, match on the result, test it with is (if (r is Err(e)) { ... }) or is_ok(), or supply a fallback with ok_or.

Check before you read

A Result holds either its value or its error, never both. A match or an is test reads the one it holds, so it cannot pick the wrong one. value() and error() panic on the wrong one, so call value() only after checking is_ok(), and error() only after checking is_err().

Result is a value enum: it is stored inline in whatever holds it, so making one allocates nothing, and it is never null. A slot of type Result that is never given a value holds its first case, Ok, carrying the zero value of TValue (0, or null for a struct), so give every result slot a value. Result<int>() is an error, since only the cases make values.

Results with no value

An operation that has nothing to return on success, such as deleting a file, uses void as its value type, like Result<(), E> in Rust. A void type argument erases what it types, so in Result<void> the case Ok carries nothing, ok() takes no argument, and value() returns nothing: calling it only checks that the result is Ok. Using that call as a value, as in var x = done.value();, is a compile error, as it is for any function that returns void.

var done = Result<void>.Ok;   # or Result<void>.ok()
var failed = Result<void>.err(Error("disk full"));
done.value();   # panics if `done` is an Err
match (failed) {
    Ok => {}
    Err(e) => { print(e.message); }
}

Custom error types and propagation

Any type can be the error type. A struct lets you carry details the caller can act on, not just a message. To pass an error up to your own caller, check the result and return early with its error; to change the error's type on the way, build a new error from the old one:

# A custom error type: any type can be the second type argument.
struct ParseError {
    String input;
    int position;

    construct(this.input = "", this.position = 0) {}
}

digit_value(String c): int {
    var digits = "0123456789";
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 10) {
        if (c == digits[i]) {
            return i;
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

parse_number(String s): Result<int, ParseError> {
    if (s.length == 0) {
        return Result<int, ParseError>.err(ParseError(s, 0));
    }
    var value = 0;
    var position = 0;
    for (var c in s) {
        var d = digit_value(c);
        if (d < 0) {
            return Result<int, ParseError>.err(ParseError(s, position));
        }
        value = value * 10 + d;
        position = position + 1;
    }
    return Result<int, ParseError>.ok(value);
}

# Propagate an error: check it, and return early with the same error.
add_numbers(String a, String b): Result<int, ParseError> {
    var x = parse_number(a);
    if (x.is_err()) {
        return Result<int, ParseError>.err(x.error());
    }
    var y = parse_number(b);
    if (y.is_err()) {
        return Result<int, ParseError>.err(y.error());
    }
    return Result<int, ParseError>.ok(x.value() + y.value());
}

# Convert an error into another type on the way out.
check_total(String a, String b, int limit): Result<void> {
    var sum = add_numbers(a, b);
    if (sum.is_err()) {
        var e = sum.error();
        return Result<void>.err(Error("bad number '" + e.input + "'"));
    }
    if (sum.value() > limit) {
        return Result<void>.err(Error("total is over the limit"));
    }
    return Result<void>.ok();
}

main(): int {
    var sum = add_numbers("40", "2");
    assert(sum.value() == 42, "40 + 2");

    var bad = add_numbers("40", "4x2");
    assert(bad.is_err(), "the second number is bad");
    assert(bad.error().input == "4x2", "the error names the input");
    assert(bad.error().position == 1, "and where it went wrong");

    assert(check_total("1", "2", 10).is_ok(), "3 is within the limit");
    var over = check_total("10", "20", 10);
    assert(over.error().message == "total is over the limit", "30 is not");
    var wrong = check_total("1", "", 10);
    assert(wrong.error().message == "bad number ''", "an empty number is an error");
    return 0;
}

The ? operator, below, writes each of these checks in one character.

Propagating errors with ?

? after a Result passes its error up, like Rust's ?: on an Ok result it is the value, and on an Err result it returns that error from the enclosing function at once. var x = parse(s)?; does what the if (x.is_err()) { return ...err(x.error()); } checks above do:

# `?` propagates a failure: on an Err it returns that error from the
# enclosing function, and on an Ok it is the value.
struct ParseError {
    String input;

    construct(this.input = "") {}
}

parse_number(text: String): Result<int, ParseError> {
    if (text.is_empty) {
        return Result<int, ParseError>.err(ParseError(text));
    }
    var value = 0;
    for (var c in text) {
        var digit = "0123456789".find(c);
        if (digit < 0) {
            return Result<int, ParseError>.err(ParseError(text));
        }
        value = value * 10 + (digit as int);
    }
    return Result<int, ParseError>.ok(value);
}

# Each `?` returns early with the error, so the sum is computed only when
# both numbers parse.
add_numbers(a: String, b: String): Result<int, ParseError> {
    return Result<int, ParseError>.ok(parse_number(a)? + parse_number(b)?);
}

# A function with a different error type: the `[Implicit]` constructor
# converts a ParseError on its way out.
struct ConfigError {
    String message;

    [Implicit]
    construct(e: ParseError) {
        this.message = "bad number '" + e.input + "'";
    }
}

read_limit(text: String): Result<int, ConfigError> {
    var limit = parse_number(text)?;
    if (limit == 0) {
        return Result<int, ConfigError>.err(ConfigError(ParseError(text)));
    }
    return Result<int, ConfigError>.ok(limit);
}

first_name(names: Array<String>): String? {
    if (names.is_empty) {
        return Optional<String>.Empty;
    }
    return Optional<String>.Value(names[0]);
}

# On an Optional, `?` returns an Empty optional from a function that returns
# one.
first_length(names: Array<String>): ulong? {
    return Optional<ulong>.Value(first_name(names)?.length);
}

main(): int {
    assert(add_numbers("40", "2").value() == 42, "40 + 2");
    assert(add_numbers("40", "4x2").error().input == "4x2", "the error is the second number's");

    assert(read_limit("10").value() == 10, "a limit");
    assert(read_limit("ten").error().message == "bad number 'ten'", "converted to a ConfigError");

    assert(first_length(["Ada", "Grace"]).value() == 3, "Ada");
    assert(first_length(Array<String>()).is_empty(), "no names");
    return 0;
}

The rules:

  • The enclosing function must declare that it returns a Result, or the compiler reports '?' requires the enclosing function to return a Result. A closure that uses ? writes its return type out: (s: String): Result<int> => Result<int>.ok(parse(s)? + 1).
  • The error type must be the function's error type, or convert to it through an [Implicit] constructor (see Implicit conversions), as ConfigError does above, like Rust's From. Otherwise the error is cannot convert error type 'ParseError' to 'ConfigError'.
  • On a Result<void>, ? yields nothing, so it stands as a statement: remove(path)?;.
  • On an Optional, ? works the same way in a function that returns an optional: an Empty optional returns Empty (see Optional values).
  • The early return is an ordinary return: locals are released and with blocks are exited as for any other.

Each ? in a statement runs before the rest of the statement, so two placements are errors:

  • After a call in the same statement, as in f() + g()?, where g() would run before f(): '?' cannot follow a call in the same statement. Call f() in a statement of its own first. Reading variables and fields before a ? is fine, and several ?s run in the order written: add(parse(a)?, parse(b)?).
  • Where it might not run: the right operand of && or ||, a branch of ?:, or a match arm. Use an if or match statement there.

A ? in a while condition runs on every iteration, before the condition is tested.

Results from the io module

The io module is a good model of a library built on Result. Every operation that can fail returns an IoResult<T>, a type alias for Result<T, IoError>, and operations with nothing to return use IoResult<void>. IoError holds the platform's error code and a message. To decide what to do about the failure, kind() returns the code's portable ErrorKind (NotFound, PermissionDenied, AlreadyExists, ..., Other), an enum to match on, and a predicate per kind, such as is_not_found() and is_permission_denied(), tests for one of them:

import [File, Directory, Path, IoResult, IoError, ErrorKind] from io;

# IoResult<T> is Result<T, IoError>: the same methods, a richer error.
read_setting(Path path): String {
    var text = File.read_to_string(path);
    if (text.is_err()) {
        if (text.error().is_not_found()) {
            return "default";
        }
        return "error: " + text.error().message;
    }
    return text.value();
}

# kind() sorts the platform's code into an ErrorKind, for a match.
describe(error: IoError): String {
    return match (error.kind()) {
        NotFound => "missing",
        PermissionDenied => "not allowed",
        else => error.message,
    };
}

main(): int {
    var dir = Directory.temp().join("pepper-results-io-example");
    var created = Directory.create_all(dir);
    assert(created.is_ok(), "created the folder");

    var path = dir.join("setting.txt");
    assert(read_setting(path) == "default", "a missing file gives the default");
    var missing = File.open(path);
    assert(missing.is_err() && missing.error().kind() == ErrorKind.NotFound, "the kind of the error");
    assert(describe(missing.error()) == "missing", "a match on the kind");

    IoResult<void> written = File.write_text(path, "blue");
    assert(written.is_ok(), "wrote the file");
    assert(read_setting(path) == "blue", "the file's contents");

    assert(Directory.remove_all(dir).is_ok(), "cleaned up");
    return 0;
}

See io: errors and platform types for the full list of kinds and the platform codes each one covers.

A library that reads a file format reports damaged data the same way: IoError.invalid_input(message) makes an error whose is_invalid_input() holds, as compress and archive return for corrupt input.

Reading a directory or a file line by line in a for loop yields one IoResult per element, so each error is handled where it happens; see Iteration.

Collection literals

A collection literal writes an array, a map or a set in one expression:

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

struct Square {
    int side;

    construct(side: int) {
        this.side = side;
    }
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }
}

total(values: long[]): long {
    long sum = 0;
    for (var value in values) {
        sum += value;
    }
    return sum;
}

main(): int {
    # An array literal is an Array of its elements' type.
    var primes = [2, 3, 5, 7];
    assert(primes.count == 4 && primes[3] == 7, "an Array<int>");

    # A trailing comma lets a long literal put one element per line.
    var operators = [
        "===",
        "!==",
        "=>",
    ];
    assert(operators[1] == "!==", "an Array<String>");

    # Where an Array type is expected, the elements convert to its element type.
    assert(total([1, 2, 3]) == 6, "an Array<long> argument");
    Shape[] shapes = [Square(2), Square(3)];
    assert(shapes[1].area() == 9, "elements convert to the trait type");

    # A map literal is a HashMap; a repeated key keeps its last value.
    var ages = ["Ada": 36, "Alan": 41];
    assert(ages["Alan"] == 41, "a HashMap<String, int>");

    # An array literal where a HashSet is expected makes a set.
    HashSet<String> keywords = ["if", "else", "if"];
    assert(keywords.count == 2, "duplicates are kept once");

    # [] and [:] are empty, where the type is declared.
    long[] none = [];
    HashMap<String, int> nobody = [:];
    assert(none.is_empty && nobody.count == 0, "empty collections");
    return 0;
}

Arrays

  • [a, b, c] is a new Array<T> holding the elements in order. A trailing comma is allowed: [a, b, c,].
  • With no other type to go by, T is the first element's type, and every later element converts to it the way an argument converts to a parameter: [1, 2] is an Array<int>, and [1, "a"] is an error.
  • Where an array type is expected (a declared variable, a parameter, a return value, an assignment), T is that type's element type instead, and every element converts to it: long[] a = [1, 2];, Shape[] s = [square, circle];.
  • Nested literals are typed the same way: long[][] grid = [[1], [2, 3]];.
  • [] is an empty array. It needs a declared type (long[] none = [];), since it has no element to take a type from:
main.pep:2:13: error: empty array literal has no element type; declare the variable's type or write 'Array<T>()'
    2 |     var a = [];
      |             ^~

Maps

  • [k1: v1, k2: v2] is a new HashMap<K, V> holding the entries. K and V come from the first entry, or from the HashMap<K, V> a declared variable, parameter or return type expects.
  • A key written twice keeps its last value, as two insert calls would.
  • [:] is an empty map, and needs a declared type: HashMap<String, int> none = [:];.

Sets

There is no separate set literal. An array literal where a HashSet<K> or a Set<K> is expected converts to one through the set's implicit constructor, which keeps each element once: HashSet<String> keywords = ["if", "else"];.

Types of specializations

A literal never changes a collection's type after it is built: Array<int> and Array<long> are different types, and neither converts to the other.

main.pep:2:21: error: cannot initialize variable 'a' of type 'Array<long>' with a value of type 'Array<int>'
    2 |     Array<long> a = Array<int>();
      |                     ^~~~~~~~~~

Arrays and slices

Array<T> is Pepper's growable list. Beyond append, indexing and sort, it has the everyday algorithms, and slice gives a function "some of the elements" without copying them:

total(values: ArrayView<int>): int {
    var sum = 0;
    for (var x in values) {
        sum = sum + x;
    }
    return sum;
}

main(): int {
    # Searching a sorted array.
    var sorted = [1, 3, 3, 5, 8];
    assert(sorted.is_sorted(), "sorted");
    assert(sorted.binary_search(5).value() == 3, "found at 3");
    assert(sorted.binary_search(4).is_empty(), "no 4");
    assert(sorted.upper_bound(3) - sorted.lower_bound(3) == 2, "two 3s");

    # Changing elements in place.
    var a = [4, 4, 1, 2, 2, 7];
    a.dedup();
    assert(a == [4, 1, 2, 7], "adjacent repeats removed");
    a.retain((x) => x % 2 == 0);
    assert(a == [4, 2], "odd elements removed");
    a.resize(4, 0);
    assert(a == [4, 2, 0, 0], "padded with 0");
    var tail = a.split_off(2);
    assert(a == [4, 2] && tail == [0, 0], "split in two");
    tail.fill(9);
    assert(tail == [9, 9], "filled");

    # Reshaping.
    var digits = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    digits.rotate(2);
    assert(digits == [3, 4, 5, 1, 2], "rotated");
    var drained = digits.drain(1, 3);
    assert(digits == [3, 1, 2] && drained == [4, 5], "drained");
    digits.remove_if((x) => x > 2);
    digits.extend_from(drained.slice(0, 1));
    assert(digits == [1, 2, 4], "filtered and extended");

    # Ordering without a full stable sort.
    var scores = [40, 95, 12, 77, 63, 8];
    scores.select_nth(2);
    assert(scores[2] == 40, "the third smallest");
    scores.partial_sort(2);
    assert(scores[0] == 8 && scores[1] == 12, "the two smallest, in order");
    scores.sort_unstable((x, y) => y - x);
    assert(scores == [95, 77, 63, 40, 12, 8], "descending");
    assert([1, 2, 3].compare([1, 3]) < 0, "lexicographic");

    # A slice views part of an array without copying it.
    var numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    var middle = numbers.slice(1, 4);
    assert(middle.count == 3 && middle[0] == 2, "views [2, 3, 4]");
    assert(total(middle) == 9, "passed to a function");
    assert(middle.to_array() == [2, 3, 4], "copied out");
    var (head, rest) = middle.split_at(1);
    assert(head.count == 1 && rest[0] == 3, "split in two");
    var pairs = 0;
    for (var pair in numbers.chunks(2)) {
        pairs = pairs + pair.count;   # [1, 2], [3, 4], [5]
    }
    assert(pairs == 5, "every element in some chunk");
    var rises = 0;
    for (var pair in numbers.windows(2)) {
        rises = rises + (pair[1] > pair[0] ? 1 : 0);
    }
    assert(rises == 4, "each neighbor is larger");
    assert(numbers.slice(0, 2) == [9, 1, 2].slice(1, 3), "equal elements");
    return 0;
}

Searching a sorted array

  • binary_search(item) returns the index of the first element equal to item as a ulong?, in O(log count). The element type must be Comparable (every number, char and String is), and the array sorted in its compare order.
  • binary_search_by(order) searches with a function that says whether an element sorts before (negative), at (0) or after (positive) the target.
  • lower_bound(item) and upper_bound(item) are the first and last places item could be inserted to keep the array sorted; the elements between them equal item.
  • is_sorted() reports whether the array is in that order.

Changing elements in place

  • fill(value) sets every element to value.
  • retain(keep) removes each element keep returns false for, keeping the order of the rest. keep must not change the array; if it does, retain panics with Array modified during retain.
  • dedup() removes each element equal (==) to the one before it; on a sorted array that removes every duplicate.
  • resize(count, value) shortens the array, or appends copies of value.
  • split_off(index) moves the elements from index on into a new array, and drain(start, end) moves out the elements in between.
  • remove_if(remove) is the opposite of retain.
  • rotate(count) moves the first count elements to the end.
  • extend_from(slice) appends the elements of a slice, which may be a slice of the same array.

Each counts as modifying the array, so a for loop over it panics on its next step.

Ordering

  • sort_unstable() sorts with pattern-defeating quicksort: no scratch buffer, and O(count) on input that is already sorted or all equal, but equal elements may change places. sort() is the stable sort.
  • select_nth(nth) puts the element a sort would put at nth there, with smaller elements before it and larger ones after (C++'s nth_element), in O(count) on average: the median without a full sort.
  • partial_sort(count) sorts only the count smallest elements into the front.
  • a.compare(b) orders two arrays lexicographically: by the first elements that differ, else the shorter first. == compares element by element.

Each takes a comparer too (sort_unstable((a, b) => b - a)) for an order other than the elements' own, or for elements that are not Comparable.

Slices

a.slice(start, end) is an ArrayView<T> (formerly ArraySlice<T>, a name that still works, with a deprecation warning): a read-only view of the elements from start up to but not including end. It has count, is_empty, indexing, for loops, slice, to_array, find, contains and the searches above, plus:

  • split_at(index), which returns two slices: the elements before index, and those from it on.
  • chunks(size), which visits runs of size elements side by side, as slices; the last run is shorter when size does not divide the count.
  • windows(size), which visits every run of size neighbors, each starting one element after the one before.
  • == and, for Comparable elements, the lexicographic compare, which compare the elements, not where they are.

Array has chunks and windows too, over all its elements. Neither copies an element: each run is a slice of the same array.

var rises = 0;
for (var pair in [1, 3, 2, 5].windows(2)) {
    if (pair[1] > pair[0]) {
        rises = rises + 1;   # 2 in all
    }
}

A slice is safe by construction:

  • It holds a reference to its array, so the array lives as long as the slice does.
  • It is fail-fast, like an iterator. Once the array changes (any store, append, remove_at, sort, ...), every later use of the slice panics with Array modified while a slice of it is in use, so it can never read an element that moved or a buffer that was freed. Make a new slice after changing the array.
  • It never holds a pointer into the array's buffer, only the array and a range, so even growing the array (which moves the buffer) cannot leave it pointing at freed memory. The runs chunks and windows give are slices too, and follow the same rules.

Not yet

  • Slices are read-only; there is no slice that writes through to its array, and no a[1..4] syntax: write a.slice(1, 4).
  • An Array is not itself Comparable (there are no conditional trait implementations yet), so < between arrays and sort() on an array of arrays need compare: rows.sort((a, b) => a.compare(b)).
  • String has no slice type; substr copies.

Maps and sets

The standard library has three kinds of map, which differ in the order they keep their keys in, and a compact set of small integers, BitSet:

TypeOrderLookup, insert, removeKeys need
HashMap<K, V>, HashSet<K>noneexpected O(1)hash<K> and == (Hashing and equality)
Map<K, V>, Set<K>sorted by keyO(log n)compare<K> (below)
OrderedMap<K, V>the order keys were first insertedexpected O(1)hash<K> and ==

All of them share one API: m[key] reads (a missing key reads as the default of V, and is not inserted) and m[key] = value writes; insert, get, try_get (an optional, Empty when the key is absent), contains, remove, count, is_empty and clear. A for loop visits a map's entries as (key, value) tuples and a set's members one by one. Adding or removing an entry while a loop iterates the map panics with the type's name ("Map modified during iteration", "Set modified during iteration", and so on), as it does for Array; changing the value of a key that is present is allowed.

Sorted: Map and Set

Map<K, V> keeps its entries sorted by key, on a red-black tree. Besides iterating in order, it answers questions about the order:

  • first() and last(): the entries with the smallest and largest key.
  • lower_bound(key): the first entry whose key is at least key; upper_bound(key): the first whose key is greater.
  • reversed(): iterates from the largest key down.
  • range(from, to): iterates the keys from from up to, not including, to.

Each of the four queries returns an optional (key, value) tuple, Empty when there is no such entry. Set<K> is the same tree without values, and its queries return an optional member. An array converts to a Set, so an array literal can initialize one.

main(): int {
    var scores = Map<String, int>();
    scores["carol"] = 91;
    scores["alice"] = 84;
    scores["bob"] = 77;

    # Entries come out sorted by key.
    var names = "";
    for (var (name, score) in scores) {
        names = names + name + " ";
    }
    assert(names == "alice bob carol ", "key order");

    # Order queries return an optional (key, value) tuple.
    assert(scores.first().value().0 == "alice", "smallest key");
    assert(scores.lower_bound("b").value().0 == "bob", "first key >= b");
    assert(scores.upper_bound("carol").is_empty(), "nothing after carol");

    # A key range: from "a" up to, not including, "c".
    var in_range = 0;
    for (var (name, score) in scores.range("a", "c")) {
        in_range += 1;
    }
    assert(in_range == 2, "alice and bob");

    # A Set keeps sorted members; an array converts to one.
    Set<int> primes = [7, 2, 5, 3];
    var digits = 0;
    for (var p in primes.reversed()) {
        digits = digits * 10 + p;
    }
    assert(digits == 7532, "descending");
    return 0;
}

How keys are ordered

Map and Set order keys with the generic function compare<K>(a, b), which returns a negative number, zero or a positive number as a sorts before, equal to or after b. Two keys that compare equal are the same key.

  • Numbers and char compare by value, and String by content (the same order as String.compare). A NaN float or double key sorts after every number (see Ordering with Comparable).
  • A Comparable struct, or one that declares a < operator, sorts by it: the generic compare asks a < b and b < a.
  • Any other struct declares Comparable, or overrides compare<T> for itself, as a hashed key overrides hash<T> (see Overriding a generic function for one type).
# A struct with a `<` operator sorts by it.
struct Version {
    int major;
    int minor;

    construct(this.major = 0, this.minor = 0) {}

    <(other: Version): bool {
        return major < other.major or (major == other.major and minor < other.minor);
    }
}

# A struct without one overrides `compare<T>` for itself.
struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
}

compare<Point>(a: Point, b: Point): int {
    return a.x != b.x ? a.x - b.x : a.y - b.y;
}

main(): int {
    var releases = Map<Version, String>();
    releases[Version(1, 10)] = "third";
    releases[Version(0, 9)] = "first";
    releases[Version(1, 2)] = "second";
    assert(releases.first().value().1 == "first", "0.9 sorts first");
    assert(releases.last().value().1 == "third", "1.10 sorts last");

    var points = Set<Point>();
    points.insert(Point(2, 1));
    points.insert(Point(1, 5));
    # An equal point (compare returns 0) is the same member.
    assert(!points.insert(Point(1, 5)), "already a member");
    assert(points.first().value().x == 1, "sorted by x");
    return 0;
}

The order must be consistent: the same two keys must always compare the same way, and if a sorts before b and b before c, a sorts before c. A struct key whose fields change while it is in a map breaks that promise.

Insertion order: OrderedMap

OrderedMap<K, V> hashes its keys like HashMap, and iterates its entries in the order their keys were first inserted, like a Python dict. Setting the value of a key that is present keeps its place; removing a key and inserting it again moves it to the end. The other entries keep their order when one is removed.

main(): int {
    var config = OrderedMap<String, String>();
    config["name"] = "pepper";
    config["version"] = "0.2";
    config["license"] = "MIT";

    # Setting a key that is present keeps its place.
    config["name"] = "Pepper";

    # Removing a key and adding it again moves it to the end.
    config.remove("version");
    config["version"] = "0.3";

    var keys = "";
    for (var (key, value) in config) {
        keys = keys + key + " ";
    }
    assert(keys == "name license version ", "insertion order");

    if (config.try_get("license") is Value(license)) {
        assert(license == "MIT", "found");
    }
    assert(config.try_get("author").is_empty(), "absent");
    return 0;
}

Use it where the order of the input matters, such as the keys of a configuration file that should be written back as they were read.

Small integers: BitSet

BitSet is a set of non-negative ints that stores one bit per possible member, so a set whose largest member is m takes about m / 8 bytes however many members it holds. It suits visited flags, masks, and sieve or liveness tables over small integers; for sparse or large integers, use a HashSet<int>.

It has the set API above (insert, contains, remove, count, is_empty, clear) and iterates its members in ascending order. insert grows the set as needed and reserve(n) makes room for 0 to n - 1 ahead of time; it never shrinks. Inserting a negative number panics, while contains and remove of one return false. Changing the set while a loop iterates it is allowed: the loop sees the members above its position as they are when it reaches them.

The set operations come in two forms: union, intersection, difference and symmetric_difference return a new set, and union_with, intersect_with, difference_with and symmetric_difference_with change the set in place. is_subset and is_disjoint compare two sets. Two sets are ==, and hash equally, when they hold the same members whatever their capacity, so a BitSet works as a HashMap or HashSet key. An array converts to a BitSet, so an array literal can initialize one.

main(): int {
    # A sieve: every number below 50 starts out as a candidate.
    var composite = BitSet(50);
    var primes = BitSet();
    for (var n in 2..50) {
        if (composite.contains(n)) {
            continue;
        }
        primes.insert(n);
        var multiple = n * n;
        while (multiple < 50) {
            composite.insert(multiple);
            multiple = multiple + n;
        }
    }
    assert(primes.count == 15, "15 primes below 50");

    # Members come out in ascending order.
    var first = "";
    for (var p in primes) {
        if (p > 11) {
            break;
        }
        first = $"{first}{p} ";
    }
    assert(first == "2 3 5 7 11 ", "ascending");

    # Set operations, by value or in place.
    BitSet odd = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11];
    var odd_primes = primes.intersection(odd);
    assert(odd_primes.count == 4, "3, 5, 7 and 11");
    assert(odd_primes.is_subset(primes), "a subset");
    odd.difference_with(primes);
    assert(odd == BitSet([1, 9]), "1 and 9 are odd but not prime");
    return 0;
}

Queues: Deque and PriorityQueue

Two collections take elements out in an order other than an Array's:

TypeTakes outPush, popElements need
Deque<T>either endamortized O(1) at both endsnothing
PriorityQueue<T>the greatest elementO(log n)compare<T>, or a comparer

An Array can stand in for either, but removing its first element takes O(n), and keeping it sorted takes O(n) per insert.

Deque

A Deque (a double-ended queue) is a ring buffer that grows when full: push_back, push_front, pop_back and pop_front add and remove at the two ends, front() and back() read them, and d[i] reads or writes the element i places from the front. It is the queue of a breadth-first search, a sliding window, or an undo history that drops its oldest entry.

# Breadth-first search: a Deque is the queue of nodes to visit.
main(): int {
    # Each node's neighbors: 0 - 1 - 2 - 4 and 0 - 3 - 4.
    int[][] edges = [[1, 3], [0, 2], [1, 4], [0, 4], [2, 3]];
    int[] hops = [0, -1, -1, -1, -1];

    Deque<int> queue = [0];
    while (!queue.is_empty) {
        var node = queue.pop_front();
        for (var next in edges[node as ulong]) {
            if (hops[next as ulong] >= 0) {
                continue;
            }
            hops[next as ulong] = hops[node as ulong] + 1;
            queue.push_back(next);
        }
    }
    assert(hops[4] == 2, "two hops from node 0 to node 4");

    # Both ends work: a window of the last three readings.
    var window = Deque<int>();
    for (var reading in [4, 8, 15, 16, 23]) {
        window.push_back(reading);
        if (window.count > 3) {
            window.pop_front();
        }
    }
    assert(window.front() == 15 and window.back() == 23, "the last three");
    assert(window[1] == 16, "indexed from the front");
    return 0;
}

An array converts to a Deque, so an array literal can initialize one. count, is_empty, capacity, reserve and clear work as they do on an Array. A for loop visits the elements from front to back; changing the deque while a loop iterates it panics ("Deque modified during iteration"). Popping, or reading front() or back(), of an empty deque panics, as does an index past the back.

PriorityQueue

A PriorityQueue is a binary heap: push adds an element in O(log n), pop removes the greatest in O(log n), and peek() reads the greatest without removing it. It is the frontier of Dijkstra's and A* searches, a scheduler's run queue, or the k largest values of a stream.

# A scheduler: the job with the earliest deadline runs first.
struct Job {
    var name: String;
    var deadline: int;

    construct(name: String, deadline: int) {
        this.name = name;
        this.deadline = deadline;
    }
}

main(): int {
    # The comparer is reversed, so the smallest deadline is the greatest.
    var jobs = PriorityQueue<Job>((a, b) => b.deadline.compare(a.deadline));
    jobs.push(Job("backup", 30));
    jobs.push(Job("email", 5));
    jobs.push(Job("report", 12));
    assert(jobs.peek().name == "email", "the earliest deadline");

    var order = "";
    while (!jobs.is_empty) {
        order = $"{order}{jobs.pop().name} ";
    }
    assert(order == "email report backup ", "by deadline");

    # Comparable elements need no comparer: the greatest comes out first.
    PriorityQueue<int> scores = [72, 95, 88, 61];
    assert(scores.pop() == 95, "the top score");
    var rest = scores.into_sorted_array();
    assert(rest == [61, 72, 88], "the rest, ascending");
    return 0;
}

Elements are ordered by compare<T>, so numbers, String, and any Comparable type need nothing more. To order by something else, pass a comparer to the constructor: a function that returns a negative number, zero or a positive number as its first argument sorts before, with or after its second. For the smallest first, reverse the comparer, (a, b) => b.compare(a). Elements that sort together come out in no particular order.

An array converts to a PriorityQueue, and PriorityQueue<T>(items, compare) builds one from an array with a comparer; both take O(n), and copy the array. into_sorted_array() empties the queue and returns its elements from smallest to greatest. pop and peek of an empty queue panic.

Neither type is [Shared]: like an Array, each stays on one thread.

Iteration

A for loop visits each element of a collection in turn. You can loop over an Array, over the code points of a String, over a range of numbers (0..count), and over any type of your own that follows the iterator protocol.

Looping over an array

for (var x in source) { ... } runs the body once per element, with x bound to the element:

struct Item {
    int value;
    construct(this.value = 0) {}
}

make_items(): Array<Item> {
    var items = Array<Item>();
    items.append(Item(20));
    items.append(Item(22));
    return items;
}

main(): int {
    var nums = Array<int>();
    nums.append(1);
    nums.append(2);
    nums.append(39);

    # The basic loop: x takes each element in order.
    var total = 0;
    for (var x in nums) {
        total = total + x;
    }
    assert(total == 42, "sum of the elements");

    # The loop variable may be typed, and the parentheses are optional.
    long wide = 0;
    for (long x in nums) {
        wide = wide + x;
    }
    for var x: int in nums {
        wide = wide - x;
    }
    assert(wide == 0, "typed loop variables");

    # break and continue work as in a while loop.
    var odd = 0;
    for (var x in nums) {
        if (x % 2 == 0) {
            continue;
        }
        if (x > 10) {
            break;
        }
        odd = odd + x;
    }
    assert(odd == 1, "only 1 is odd and below 10");

    # A struct element is shared: changing a field changes the element,
    # but rebinding the loop variable does not touch the array.
    var items = make_items();
    for (var item in items) {
        item.value = item.value * 10;
        item = Item(99);
    }
    assert(items[0].value == 200, "first element was updated");
    assert(items[1].value == 220, "second element was updated");

    # Iterating a temporary keeps it alive for the whole loop.
    var sum = 0;
    for (var item in make_items()) {
        sum = sum + item.value;
    }
    assert(sum == 42, "temporary array stays alive");

    # The loop is shorthand for driving the iterator yourself.
    var it = nums.iterate();
    var manual = 0;
    while (it.next()) {
        manual = manual + it.current();
    }
    assert(manual == 42, "the same elements, by hand");

    # Modifying the array after the loop is fine.
    nums.append(100);
    assert(nums.count == 4, "appended after the loop");
    return 0;
}

The example shows each part of the loop:

  • The loop variable can be declared with var or with a type: for (var x in nums), for (long x in nums), and for (var x: int in nums) all work.
  • The parentheses are optional, as with if and while: for var x in nums { ... }. The braces are required.
  • break and continue work as they do in a while loop.
  • The loop variable is a copy, like any var. Assigning a new value to it does not change the collection. For a struct element, though, the copy is another reference to the same object (see Memory and reference counting), so item.value = ... does change the element.
  • A temporary source stays alive. The loop holds a reference to what it iterates, so for (var item in make_items()) is safe.

Looping over a string

A String yields its code points one at a time. Each one is a String holding a single code point, the same value that indexing gives you (word[i]):

main(): int {
    var word = "héllo ✓";

    # A String yields one code point at a time, as a one-code-point String.
    var count = 0;
    var copy = "";
    for (var c in word) {
        assert(c.length == 1, "each piece is one code point");
        copy.append(c);
        count = count + 1;
    }
    assert(count == 7, "7 code points");
    assert(copy == word, "the pieces rebuild the string");

    # Each piece is the same value as indexing the string.
    var i = 0;
    for (var c in word) {
        assert(c == word[i], "same as word[i]");
        i = i + 1;
    }

    # An empty string runs the body zero times.
    for (var c in "") {
        assert(false, "never runs");
    }
    return 0;
}

Looping over a range

a..b is the numbers from a up to, but not including, b, and a..>b includes b. Looping over one is how you count:

main(): int {
    # `a..b` counts from a up to, but not including, b.
    var total = 0;
    for (var i in 0..5) {
        total += i;
    }
    assert(total == 10, "0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4");

    # `a..>b` includes b.
    var product = 1;
    for (var i in 1..>5) {
        product *= i;
    }
    assert(product == 120, "5 factorial");

    # The bounds give the type: `count` is a ulong, so i is too.
    var names = ["Ada", "Grace", "Edsger"];
    ulong letters = 0;
    for (var i in 0..names.count) {
        letters += names[i].size;
    }
    assert(letters == 14, "letters in every name");

    # A range that starts past its end is empty.
    for (var i in 3..1) {
        assert(false, "never runs");
    }

    # A range is a value: test membership, or use the iterator adapters.
    var digits = 0..10;
    assert(digits.contains(9) && !digits.contains(10), "half-open");
    var evens = 0;
    for (var even in (1..>10).filter((n) => n % 2 == 0)) {
        evens += even;
    }
    assert(evens == 30, "2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10");
    return 0;
}

  • The bounds give the type. A range's element type is inferred from its bounds like a generic call's type argument, so 0..names.count counts in ulong. The bounds must be integers; anything else is an error at the operator:

    main.pep:2:22: error: range bounds must be integers, not 'String'
    2 |     for (var c in "a".."z") {
      |                      ^~

  • Precedence. A range binds more loosely than arithmetic and shifts, and more tightly than comparisons, so 0..n + 1 is 0..(n + 1). Two range operators in a row (1..2..3) are an error; add parentheses. ... is not a range operator.

  • An empty range runs no iterations. A range whose start is past its end (3..1, 5..>4) is empty, and a..a is too. A closed range ending at its type's largest value (250..>top with a byte top of 255) stops there without overflowing.

  • A range is a value, a Range<T>. It has contains(x) and the is_empty property, and it is an Iterator<T>, so it has the adapters and consumers (map, filter, take, sum, ...). Looping over one allocates nothing; the optimizer turns it into a plain counting loop.

The iterator protocol

The for loop is not tied to Array and String. It works with any type that has the right methods, described by two traits in the runtime (runtime/iterator.pep, documented in the Iterators reference):

export trait Iterator<T> {
    next(): bool;    # advance; true if there is a current element
    current(): T;    # the element next() just moved to
}

export trait Iterable<T> {
    iterate(): Iterator<T>;
}
  • An iterator steps through elements. next() moves to the next element and returns true, or returns false when there are no more (and keeps returning false after that). current() returns the element next() moved to.
  • An iterable is a collection that hands out a fresh iterator from iterate(). Array<T> returns an ArrayIterator<T>, String returns a StringIterator, and HashMap<K, V> and HashSet<K> return a HashMapIterator<K, V> and a HashSetIterator<K>.

for (var x in source) { body } behaves exactly like this:

{
    var it = source.iterate();   # or `var it = source;` when source is itself an iterator
    while (it.next()) {
        var x = it.current();
        { body }
    }
}

The loop chooses by the methods the source's type has, like a C++ range-based for: it uses iterate() if the type has one, and otherwise uses the source itself as the iterator if it has both next() and current(). A type with neither is a compile error:

main.pep:4:19: error: type 'Foo' is not iterable: implement Iterable<T> (iterate()) or Iterator<T> (next() and current())
    4 |     for (var x in f) {
      |                   ^

HashMap<K, V> yields each entry as a tuple (K, V), so for (var (name, age) in ages) names both parts; HashSet<K> yields its members. Both visit entries in no particular order. Changing a value (ages[name] = … for a key already present) is fine while looping, but adding or removing an entry stops the program at the iterator's next step.

Adapters

Iterator<T> has default methods that wrap an iterator in another one. Each works lazily, one element at a time as the loop asks for it:

  • map(transform) yields transform(x) for each element x; its element type is whatever transform returns.
  • filter(keep) yields only the elements for which keep(x) is true.
  • enumerate() yields (index, x) tuples, counting from 0 in ulong; enumerate<int>() counts in int instead.
  • zip(other) yields (x, y) pairs, one element from each iterator in step, and stops when either runs out.
  • take(n) yields at most the first n elements; skip(n) yields the elements after the first n.
  • chain(other) yields this iterator's elements, then other's.
  • flat_map(transform) yields the elements of the iterator transform(x) returns for each element x, one after another: ["ab", "cd"].iterate() .flat_map((w) => w.iterate()) yields a, b, c, d.
  • take_while(keep) yields the leading elements that pass; skip_while(skip) yields the elements from the first one that fails.
  • step_by(n) yields the first element, then every nth one after it.
  • chunks(n) yields the elements in arrays of n (the last may be shorter); windows(n) yields every run of n consecutive elements. Each array is new, so keeping one is safe.
  • peekable() yields the same elements and adds peek(), which returns the next element as an optional without moving to it.

They return iterators, so they chain, and a for loop can use the result directly; destructure a tuple to name its parts.

The consumers run an iterator (as far as they need to) and return a value:

  • to_array() collects what is left into a new Array.
  • count() returns how many elements are left, as a ulong.
  • last() returns the last element as an optional.
  • for_each(action) calls action with each element.
  • fold(initial, combine) folds each element into a value: (1..>5).fold(1, (product, n) => product * n) is 120.
  • any(test) and all(test) return whether some or every element passes; they stop at the first element that settles the answer. all is true for no elements.
  • reduce(combine) is fold starting from the first element, as an optional that is Empty for none.
  • find(test) returns the first element that passes as an optional, Empty when none does; position(test) returns its position.
  • sum() adds the elements with + and returns 0 (the type's default value) for none; sum<long>() adds them as longs. min() and max() return the smallest and largest by compare, as an optional that is Empty for none; among equal elements they return the first. They need element types that have + or are Comparable, such as the numbers and String. min_by(compare) and max_by(compare) order by a function instead, as Array.sort does.
  • to_set() collects into a HashSet, to_map<K, V>() collects (key, value) tuples into a HashMap (a later key replaces an earlier one), and join(separator) joins String elements.

The adapters do not allocate per element: an optimized build of a chain such as (0..n).filter(f).map(g).take(k).sum() runs as fast as the loop written out by hand.

struct Person {
    String name;
    int age;
    construct(this.name = "", this.age = 0) {}
}

main(): int {
    var people = Array<Person>();
    people.append(Person("Ada", 36));
    people.append(Person("Bo", 12));
    people.append(Person("Cyd", 40));

    # filter keeps the adults, map turns each one into a name.
    var names = Array<String>();
    for (var name in people.iterate().filter((p) => p.age >= 18).map((p) => p.name)) {
        names.append(name);
    }
    assert(names.count == 2, "two adults");
    assert(names[0] == "Ada", "Ada first");
    assert(names[1] == "Cyd", "then Cyd");

    # Adapters work on any Iterator, including a String's.
    var kept = 0;
    for (var c in "hello".iterate().filter((c) => c != "l")) {
        kept += 1;
    }
    assert(kept == 3, "h, e, o");

    # enumerate pairs each element with its position, and zip pairs two
    # iterators in step; destructure the tuple to name both parts.
    var ranked = "";
    for (var (i, person) in people.iterate().enumerate()) {
        ranked += $"{i}:{person.name} ";
    }
    assert(ranked == "0:Ada 1:Bo 2:Cyd ", "numbered from 0");
    var seats = ["window", "aisle"];
    var seated = 0;
    for (var (person, seat) in people.iterate().zip(seats.iterate())) {
        seated += 1;   # Cyd gets no seat: zip stops at the shorter
    }
    assert(seated == 2, "two pairs");

    # flat_map yields the elements of the iterator it returns for each one.
    var letters = people.iterate().flat_map((p) => p.name.iterate()).count();
    assert(letters == 8, "Ada, Bo and Cyd");

    # to_array collects what an iterator yields.
    var ages = people.iterate().map((p) => p.age).to_array();
    assert(ages.count == 3 && ages[2] == 40, "every age");

    # Consumers run the iterator and return one value.
    assert(people.iterate().any((p) => p.age < 18), "Bo is a child");
    assert(people.iterate().map((p) => p.age).sum() == 88, "total age");
    assert(people.iterate().map((p) => p.age).max().value() == 40, "oldest");
    assert(people.iterate().find((p) => p.age > 36).value().name == "Cyd", "first over 36");
    assert(people.iterate().skip(1).take(1).count() == 1, "just Bo");
    return 0;
}

Every type that declares Iterator<T> gets them: ArrayIterator<T> (from Array.iterate()), StringIterator, ranges, and your own iterators once you write extend YourType with Iterator<T>;. The adapter holds its own copy of the iterator it wraps (the runtime's iterators are value structs, boxed when they become an Iterator<T>), so a chain built from a temporary stays alive while the loop runs, and it.map(f), it.to_array() and the other consumers leave it where it was. All of them but filter and to_array are generic methods (see Generics), so they are not callable through an Iterator<T> trait value; being generic also means each one is compiled only for the iterators that call it.

Reading files and directories

Input that can fail partway, such as a directory listing or a file read line by line, yields a Result per element: an IoResult<T> from the io module. Handle each error where it happens; there is nothing to check after the loop.

import [File, Directory, Path] from io;

main(): int {
    var dir = Directory.temp().join("pepper-iteration-streams-example");
    Directory.remove_all(dir);
    assert(Directory.create_all(dir).is_ok(), "created the folder");
    assert(File.write_text(dir.join("notes.txt"), "first\nsecond\r\nthird").is_ok(), "wrote notes");
    assert(File.write_text(dir.join("todo.txt"), "").is_ok(), "wrote todo");

    # A Directory yields its entries one at a time, each an IoResult<DirEntry>.
    var names = 0;
    for (var entry in Directory.open(dir).value()) {
        if (entry.is_err()) {
            print(entry.error().message);
            break;
        }
        assert(entry.value().is_file, "both entries are files");
        names += 1;
    }
    assert(names == 2, "two entries");

    # A File's lines() yields each line, without its line ending.
    var file = File.open(dir.join("notes.txt")).value();
    var lines = Array<String>();
    for (var line in file.lines()) {
        lines.append(line.value());
    }
    assert(lines.count == 3 && lines[1] == "second", "three lines, \\r\\n removed");

    # Adapters work on streams too: number the lines.
    var again = File.open(dir.join("notes.txt")).value();
    var last = "";
    for (var (i, line) in again.lines().enumerate()) {
        last = $"{i}: {line.value()}";
    }
    assert(last == "2: third", "the last line, numbered");

    assert(Directory.remove_all(dir).is_ok(), "cleaned up");
    return 0;
}
  • A Directory is iterable. for (var entry in dir) reads the listing one entry at a time (Directory.iterate() returns a DirectoryIterator), without building an array the way dir.entries() does. Each element is an IoResult<DirEntry>. A directory that cannot be read yields one error and then ends.
  • lines() yields each line of an open File, or of any other io.Reader such as a socket, from what it reads next, as an IoResult<String> without the \n or \r\n. The last line counts even without a line ending. A read error, or a line that is not valid UTF-8, is yielded as an error and ends the lines.
  • chunks(size) yields the rest of a Reader in arrays of at most size bytes, one read each, as IoResult<u8[]>s.
  • An error ends the sequence: after an Err element, next() returns false.
  • listener.incoming() accepts connections on a TcpListener, yielding each one as an IoResult<TcpStream>. It is the exception to the rule above: a failed accept is yielded and the loop goes on, since the next connection may succeed. It ends only once the listener is closed, so a server loop breaks or returns when it is done.
  • Leaving early cleans up. The listing is closed when the loop ends, including by break or return, because the iterator is released then.

Writing your own iterator

To make your own type work in a for loop, give it next() and current() (an iterator), or give it an iterate() method that returns such a type (an iterable):

# An iterator: next() advances, current() returns the element.
struct Countdown {
    int remaining;
    int now;

    construct(this.remaining = 0) {}

    bool next() {
        if (remaining == 0) {
            return false;
        }
        now = remaining;
        remaining = remaining - 1;
        return true;
    }

    int current() {
        return now;
    }
}

# Declaring the trait documents the intent; the loop goes by the methods.
extend Countdown with Iterator<int>;

# An iterable: iterate() hands out a fresh iterator for each loop.
struct Evens {
    int limit;

    construct(this.limit = 0) {}

    EvensIterator iterate() {
        var it = EvensIterator();
        it.limit = limit;
        it.now = -2;
        return it;
    }
}

struct EvensIterator {
    int limit;
    int now;

    bool next() {
        now = now + 2;
        return now < limit;
    }

    int current() {
        return now;
    }
}

extend EvensIterator with Iterator<int>;
extend Evens with Iterable<int>;

# A generic function can loop over any type that supports the protocol.
sum<C>(C values): int {
    var total = 0;
    for (var v in values) {
        total = total + v;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    var total = 0;
    for (var n in Countdown(3)) {
        total = total + n;
    }
    assert(total == 6, "3 + 2 + 1");

    # A loop over an iterator in a variable uses that object up.
    var c = Countdown(2);
    for (var n in c) {
        total = total + n;
    }
    assert(!c.next(), "the countdown is exhausted");

    # An iterable starts a new pass every time.
    var evens = Evens(10);
    assert(sum<Evens>(evens) == 20, "0 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 8");
    assert(sum<Evens>(evens) == 20, "a second pass sees the same elements");

    var nums = Array<int>();
    nums.append(30);
    nums.append(12);
    assert(sum<Array<int>>(nums) == 42, "arrays work too");
    return 0;
}

Some things to keep in mind:

  • Declaring the trait is optional. The loop looks only at which methods a type has. Writing extend Countdown with Iterator<int>; documents your intent, and the compiler then checks that Countdown has both next() and current() (see Traits and extensions). Declaring it also lets the type be used as an Iterator<int> value, and a for loop over such a value calls the methods through the trait. It also gives the type the adapters and consumers (map, filter, fold, to_array(), ...).
  • Looping over an iterator uses it up. When the source is itself an iterator stored in a variable, the loop drives that variable in place, so it is exhausted afterwards, and a loop left with break can be resumed by looping over it again. A const variable holding a value iterator cannot be looped over, since next() changes it. An iterable starts a new, independent pass every time you loop over it.
  • Generic code can loop over a type parameter; each specialization checks the protocol for its own type (see Generics).
  • Calling current() out of turn panics in the runtime's iterators: before the first next() you get ArrayIterator.current() before next(), and after next() returned false you get ArrayIterator.current() past the end. Your own iterators should follow the same rule.

Modifying a collection while you loop over it

Changing an Array or a String while a loop is iterating over it stops the program with a panic, because the iterator could otherwise skip or repeat elements, or read past the end:

var nums = Array<int>();
nums.append(1);
nums.append(2);
for (var x in nums) {
    nums.append(x);   # panics: Array modified during iteration
}

Every method that changes an Array counts, including storing an element with nums[i] = v. For a String, append and grow count, and the message is String modified during iteration. The check happens on the iterator's next step, so modifying the collection after the loop is finished is fine.

To change elements as you go, loop over an index with while and store through it, or collect the changes in a second array and apply them after the loop.

Loop scope

The loop variable and anything declared in the loop body exist only inside the loop. Each pass gets a new loop variable, and struct values declared in the body are released at the end of every pass, whether the pass ends normally or by continue, break, or return. Leaving the loop early also releases the hidden iterator, so a destructor on a custom iterator runs at that point.

Using the loop variable or a body local after the loop is an error, the same as for any name that is out of scope:

main.pep:6:12: error: use of undeclared identifier 'i'
    6 |     return i;
      |            ^

The loop variable, or a local in the loop body, may have the same name as a variable declared before the loop. It hides the outer variable inside the loop, and the outer variable keeps its value afterwards.

Structs

A struct groups related values into one named type, and gives that type behavior through methods. Pepper has no classes and no inheritance: a struct holds data, methods and extensions add behavior, and traits describe what a type can do.

Every struct value is a reference to an object, so assigning a struct or passing it to a function shares the object rather than copying it. The memory chapter explains exactly when objects are created and destroyed.

Declaring a struct

Declare a struct with struct, a name, and its fields in braces. Struct names are PascalCase by convention.

# A struct groups related values into one type.
struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
}

# Fields can also be declared C-style, with the type first.
struct Counter {
    int count;          # no initializer: starts at zero
    String label = "clicks";
}

main(): int {
    # Without a constructor, `Point()` makes a Point with every field
    # at its initial value.
    var p = Point();
    assert(p.x == 0 && p.y == 0, "fields start at their initializers");

    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    assert(p.x * p.x + p.y * p.y == 25, "fields can be read and written");

    var c = Counter();
    assert(c.count == 0, "a numeric field without an initializer is zero");
    assert(c.label == "clicks", "a String field can have an initializer");

    # A struct value is a reference: `q` names the same Point as `p`.
    var q = p;
    q.x = 10;
    assert(p.x == 10, "p and q are the same object");
    assert(p === q, "=== tests whether two references name the same object");
    assert(!(p === Point()), "a new Point is a different object");
    return 0;
}

Things to notice:

  • A field is declared like a variable: var x: int = 0; or, C-style, int x = 0;. The initializer is optional.
  • A field without an initializer starts at its type's default: zero for numbers, false for bool, and null for a struct type such as String or another struct. Reading a field through a null reference crashes the program, so give struct-typed fields a value before you use them.
  • A struct with no constructor can be created with its name and empty parentheses, Point(). There is no new keyword at the call site.
  • p.x reads a field and p.x = 3 writes it.
  • a === b is true when a and b refer to the same object, and a !== b when they do not. See Comparing structs for ==.

A struct can have a field whose type is a struct declared later in the file, a field of its own type, or fields that lead back to it through other structs (a Team holding a Player that holds the Team). A struct-typed field holds a reference, so a linked list or a tree is just a struct that names itself:

# A field can hold the struct's own type: each Link points at the next one.
struct Link {
    var value: int;
    var next: Link;

    construct(this.value = 0) {}
}

# Two structs can refer to each other, in either declaration order.
struct Team {
    var name: String;
    var lead: Player;

    construct(this.name = "") {}
}

struct Player {
    var name: String;
    # A weak back pointer: the team owns its lead, so the player's link
    # back to the team must not keep the team alive (see the memory chapter).
    var team: Weak<Team>;

    construct(this.name = "") {}
}

sum(first: Link): int {
    var total = 0;
    var link: Link = first;
    while (link !== __null) {
        total = total + link.value;
        link = link.next;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    var list = Link(1);
    list.next = Link(2);
    list.next.next = Link(3);
    assert(sum(list) == 6, "the list holds 1, 2 and 3");
    assert(list.next.next.next === __null, "the last link has no next");

    var team = Team("Owls");
    team.lead = Player("Ada");
    team.lead.team = Weak<Team>(team);
    with (var t = team.lead.team) {
        assert(t.name == "Owls", "the player reaches its team");
    }
    return 0;
}

Objects that refer to each other in a loop keep each other alive, so make back pointers such as a child's parent a Weak<T> (see Cycles leak).

Constructors

A constructor sets up a new object. Declare it with construct, followed by its parameters and a body. Callers create the object by calling the struct's name like a function.

struct Rect {
    var width: int;
    var height: int;
    var area: int;

    # `this.width = 1` declares a parameter that is stored straight into the
    # field `width`; `1` is its default when the caller leaves it out.
    construct(this.width = 1, this.height = 1) {
        area = width * height;
    }
}

struct Temperature {
    var celsius: float;

    # Ordinary parameters work too, written like a function's: `name: Type`.
    construct(fahrenheit: float = 32.0) {
        celsius = (fahrenheit - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var r = Rect(3, 4);
    assert(r.width == 3 && r.height == 4, "arguments fill the fields");
    assert(r.area == 12, "the constructor body runs after the fields are set");

    var tall = Rect(2);
    assert(tall.width == 2 && tall.height == 1, "omitted arguments use their defaults");

    var unit = Rect();
