    assert(unit.area == 1, "every parameter has a default, so Rect() works");

    var boiling = Temperature(212.0);
    assert(boiling.celsius == 100.0, "212 F is 100 C");
    assert(Temperature().celsius == 0.0, "the default is 32 F");
    return 0;
}
  • A parameter written this.width = 1 stores its argument directly into the field width, before the body runs. The = 1 is required: it is the value used when the caller omits that argument.
  • Ordinary parameters are written as in a function, name: Type, with an optional default: fahrenheit: float = 32.0. The C-style form, float fahrenheit = 32.0, is accepted too.
  • Inside the body, fields are in scope by name. Use this.name when a parameter has the same name as a field.
  • A struct may declare several constructors with different parameter lists; a call picks one by its arguments, as for any overloaded function. At most one of them may be [Implicit]. A struct has at most one destructor.

A this.field parameter must have a default. Leaving it out is an error:

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    construct(this.x) {}
}

main.pep:3:21: error: expected '='
    3 |     construct(this.x) {}
      |                     ^

A struct without a constructor accepts no arguments:

main.pep:7:13: error: too many arguments to 'Point': expected 0, have 2
    7 |     var p = Point(1, 2);
      |             ^~~~~

Note: new is the older, deprecated spelling of construct. It still compiles, with a warning that offers the fix (see Deprecations).

Implicit conversions

A constructor marked [Implicit] also converts. Wherever a value flows into a place whose type is the struct, and the value has the constructor's parameter type, the compiler calls the constructor for you:

struct Celsius {
    var degrees: double;

    # `[Implicit]` lets a `double` become a `Celsius` wherever one is expected.
    [Implicit]
    construct(double degrees) {
        this.degrees = degrees;
    }
}

struct Label {
    var text: String;

    # Without `[Implicit]`, callers write `Label("...")` themselves.
    construct(String text) {
        this.text = text;
    }
}

describe(t: Celsius): String {
    return (t.degrees > 30.0) ? "hot" : "mild";
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe(35.0) == "hot", "an argument converts");
    var today: Celsius = 21.5;            # a typed variable converts
    assert(describe(today) == "mild", "already a Celsius");

    var label = Label("kitchen");         # no conversion: call the constructor
    assert(label.text == "kitchen", "explicit constructor call");

    var n = 12.0;                         # no slot type: stays a double
    assert(n == 12.0, "untyped local");
    return 0;
}

The standard library uses this for io.Path, which converts from a String, so dir.join("logs") and io.File.open("notes.txt") work without writing io.Path(...), and for Error, so Result<int>.err("bad input") works.

  • Where it applies: a variable's initializer when the variable's type is written, an assignment, a function, method or constructor argument (operators and a[i] = value included), a call through a function value, and a return from a function with a declared return type.
  • Where it does not: the receiver of a method call ("docs".join("x") does not turn "docs" into a Path), a var whose type is inferred (var n = 12.0; stays a double), and __null, which stays a null reference.
  • One conversion per value. The value must already have the constructor's parameter type, or reach it by a widening that loses nothing: a smaller integer to a larger one, an integer literal that fits, float to double, or a struct to a trait it declares. Conversions never chain: if Tag converts from Name and Name from String, a String does not become a Tag.
  • Overloads prefer anything else. Among overloads, a member that takes the value as it is, or by any other conversion, beats one that needs an [Implicit] constructor.
  • Each conversion is a constructor call, so it allocates a new object. The VS Code extension shows the call as an inlay hint around the converted value, and hovering the value names the constructor. The converted value is a temporary like any constructor call's result: it is released after the call it was passed to (see Memory and reference counting).
  • Only a constructor that can be called with one argument may be [Implicit]: one parameter, or a first parameter followed by parameters that all have defaults. It may not convert from the struct itself or, in a generic struct, from a bare type parameter (construct(T value)):
main.pep:2:5: error: 'Implicit' constructor of 'Span' must be callable with one argument
    2 |     [Implicit]
      |     ^~~~~~~~~~

Conversions are opt-in: a constructor without [Implicit] never runs on its own. When a value would fit such a constructor, the type error says so:

main.pep:6:27: error: cannot pass a value of type 'String' as argument 1 of 'show', which has type 'Label'
    6 | main(): int { return show("x"); }
      |                           ^~~
main.pep:3:5: note: 'Label' has a constructor from 'String': call 'Label(...)', or mark the constructor [Implicit]
    3 |     construct(String text) { this.text = text; }
      |     ^~~~~~~~~

Destructors

A destructor runs when an object is destroyed, which happens when the last reference to it goes away. Declare it with destruct and a body, with no parentheses. Use it to release something the object holds that Pepper does not manage for you, such as a file handle from C.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const closed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Connection {
    var name: String;

    construct(this.name = "") {}

    # The destructor runs once, when the last reference to the object goes
    # away. Use it to release whatever the object holds.
    destruct {
        closed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

main(): int {
    {
        var c = Connection("db");
        assert(closed.load() == 0, "still in use");
    }
    # `c` went out of scope at the closing brace.
    assert(closed.load() == 1, "the destructor ran at the end of the block");
    return 0;
}

You never call a destructor yourself. After it runs, Pepper releases the object's fields, so a destructor can still read them. The memory chapter lists every point where an object can be destroyed.

Methods

A method is a function declared inside a struct. You call it on an object with a dot, v.length_squared(), and inside it this refers to that object.

struct Vector {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    # A method: name, parameters, then the return type after `:`.
    length_squared(): int {
        # Fields can be named directly inside a method...
        return x * x + y * y;
    }

    # ...or through `this`, the object the method was called on.
    dot(other: Vector): int {
        return this.x * other.x + this.y * other.y;
    }

    # Methods can change fields, and can call other methods.
    scale(factor: int) {
        x = x * factor;
        y = y * factor;
    }

    # The return type can also come first, C-style.
    bool is_zero() {
        return length_squared() == 0;
    }

    # A static method belongs to the type, not to one object: there is
    # no `this`. Call it on the type name.
    static unit_x(): Vector {
        return Vector(1, 0);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var v = Vector(3, 4);
    assert(v.length_squared() == 25, "method call");
    assert(v.dot(Vector(1, 1)) == 7, "method with an argument");

    v.scale(2);
    assert(v.x == 6 && v.y == 8, "a method can modify its object");

    assert(Vector().is_zero(), "methods can be called on a temporary");
    assert(Vector.unit_x().x == 1, "static method called on the type");
    return 0;
}
  • Methods are written like functions: name(parameters): ReturnType { ... }. Leave out the return type for a method that returns nothing. The C-style form, bool is_zero() { ... }, works too.
  • Inside a method, the object's fields and other methods can be named directly (x, length_squared()), or through this (this.x). A parameter or local with the same name as a field hides the field; use this. to reach the field.
  • A bare call names the struct's own method before a top-level function of the same name, unless no method by that name takes those arguments: then it calls the function. So a copy(): Buffer method can call the free function copy(label).
  • A method can change the fields of its object. Because struct values are references, the caller sees the change.
  • Calling a method does not copy the object or add a reference to it. The result of a method call is a new reference, like any function result.
  • Several methods can share a name when their parameters differ; each call picks the best fit (see Overloading).

Static methods

A method marked static belongs to the type rather than to one object. It has no this, and you call it on the type name: Vector.unit_x(). Static methods are the usual way to offer named constructors, such as the standard library's Result<int>.ok(42).

Inside the struct, any method, static or not, can call a static method by its bare name: unit_x() in a method of Vector means Vector.unit_x().

# Static methods belong to the type; inside it, they are called by name.
struct Vector {
    var x: double = 0.0;
    var y: double = 0.0;
    construct(this.x = 0.0, this.y = 0.0) {}

    static unit_x(): Vector {
        return Vector(1.0, 0.0);
    }

    # A static method calls another by its bare name.
    static scaled_unit_x(factor: double): Vector {
        var unit = unit_x();
        return Vector(unit.x * factor, unit.y * factor);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var v = Vector.scaled_unit_x(3.0);
    assert(v.x == 3.0 && v.y == 0.0, "called on the type name outside it");
    return 0;
}

Operators

A struct can define what the operators do for it. Declare a method whose name is the operator, written like any other method: ==(other: Money): bool. The C-style form with the return type first, bool ==(Money other), is accepted too.

struct Money {
    var cents: int = 0;

    construct(this.cents = 0) {}

    # `a == b` calls `a.==(b)`. Without this method, `==` on two structs
    # compares identity, like `===`.
    ==(other: Money): bool {
        return cents == other.cents;
    }

    # `!=` is derived from `==` when the struct does not define it.

    # `a < b` calls `a.<(b)`.
    <(other: Money): bool {
        return cents < other.cents;
    }

    # `a + b` calls `a.+(b)` and returns a new Money.
    +(other: Money): Money {
        return Money(cents + other.cents);
    }

    # `-a` calls `a.-()`: a unary operator takes no parameters.
    -(): Money {
        return Money(0 - cents);
    }

    # `a - b` calls `a.-(b)`. The unary and binary `-` overload each other,
    # told apart by their number of parameters.
    -(other: Money): Money {
        return Money(cents - other.cents);
    }

    # `a += b` needs its own method; it is not rewritten to `a = a + b`.
    +=(other: Money): Money {
        cents += other.cents;
        return this;
    }
}

struct Shelf {
    var slots: Array<String>;

    construct() {
        slots = Array<String>();
        slots.append("empty");
        slots.append("empty");
    }

    # An indexer with one parameter handles reads: `shelf[i]`.
    [](index: int): String {
        return slots[index];
    }

    # An indexer with two parameters handles writes: `shelf[i] = value`.
    [](index: int, value: String): String {
        slots[index] = value;
        return value;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var price = Money(250);
    assert(price == Money(250), "== compares cents");
    assert(price != Money(100), "!= compares cents");
    # `===` and `!==` always compare identity: equal cents, different objects.
    assert(price !== Money(250), "!== compares identity");
    var same = price;
    assert(same === price, "=== is true for the same object");

    var total = price + Money(50);
    assert(total.cents == 300, "+ makes a new value");
    assert(price.cents == 250, "+ left its operands alone");

    assert(price < total, "< compares cents");

    var refund = -price;
    assert(refund.cents == -250, "unary - calls -()");
    assert((total - price).cents == 50, "binary - calls -(other)");

    total += Money(25);
    assert(total.cents == 325, "+= updated total in place");

    var shelf = Shelf();
    shelf[1] = "books";
    assert(shelf[1] == "books", "indexer write, then read");
    assert(shelf[0] == "empty", "the other slot is unchanged");
    return 0;
}

When the left operand is a struct that declares the operator, a + b becomes the call a.+(b). The right operand is the method's single parameter, and it can be any type. These binary operators can be defined:

KindOperators
Arithmetic+ - * / % **
Bitwise& | ^
Bitwise shifts<< >>
Comparison and logical== != < <= > >= && ||
Compound assignment+= -= *= /= %= <<= >>= &= |= ^=

Keep these rules in mind:

  • An operator can be declared once per right-operand type (+(Money) and +(int)), and a + b picks by b's type, as for any overloaded method.
  • Each operator is its own method, with one exception: when a struct defines == but not !=, a != b means !(a == b). A struct that defines == and is used as a HashMap or HashSet key also needs a matching hash<T> (see Hashing and equality). += is not rewritten to a = a + b; define each one you want to use.
  • Comparison operators must return bool; any other return type is an error (comparison operator '==' must return 'bool', not 'String'). Logical operators should return bool too. Arithmetic, bitwise and compound assignment operators usually return the struct's own type; a compound assignment usually changes this and returns it.
  • The left operand decides: a + b uses the method on a's type. For a number on the left, such as 2 * v, see A number on the left.
  • Operators that start with < (<, <=, <<, <<=) can only be declared in the name: Type form, <(other: V): bool: in the C-style form the parser reads bool < as the start of generic arguments.

The result of an operator has the type its method returns, so with -(other: V): int, var r = a - b; is an int.

A number on the left

2.0 * v uses the operator of the left operand's type, double, which a struct cannot change. Declare it in an extension of the number type instead, where this is the number:

# A number on the left of an operator: `2 * v` with a struct `v`.
struct Vector {
    var x: double;
    var y: double;

    construct(this.x = 0.0, this.y = 0.0) {}

    # `v * 2.0` calls `v.*(2.0)`.
    *(scale: double): Vector {
        return Vector(x * scale, y * scale);
    }
}

# `2.0 * v` uses the operator of the left operand's type, so `double`
# declares it in an extension; `this` is the number.
extend double {
    *(v: Vector): Vector {
        return v * this;
    }
}

# `2` is an `int`, which needs its own.
extend int {
    *(v: Vector): Vector {
        return v * (this as double);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var v = Vector(1.0, 2.0);
    var a = v * 2.0;
    var b = 2.0 * v;
    var c = 2 * v;
    assert(a.x == 2.0 && b.x == 2.0 && c.y == 4.0, "both orders");
    # Numbers on both sides still use the built-in operator.
    assert(2 * 3 == 6, "built-in");
    return 0;
}

  • The number type is the left operand's own: 2 is an int and 2.0 a double, so each needs its own extension (extend int, extend double). Without one, 2 * v is invalid operands to binary expression ('int' and 'Vector').

  • The operator takes one operand, which may be any type except a number, bool, enum or pointer: numbers on both sides always use the built-in operator.

    main.pep:2:14: error: operator '+' of 'int' cannot take an operand of type 'int': the built-in operator applies
    2 |     +(other: int): int { return 0; }
      |              ^~~

  • Comparisons work the same way, and 2.0 != v means !(2.0 == v) when the extension declares only ==. Compound assignments (n *= v) do not apply, since the number cannot hold the result.

  • The extension is visible like any other: where its file is imported, if it is exported.

Unary operators

A unary operator is a method with no parameters; its operand is this.

OperatorDeclarationop x calls
Negation-(): Vx.-()
Bitwise complement~(): Vx.~()
Logical not!(): boolx.!()
Truth test!!(): boolx.!!() (see below)

The C-style form works here too: V -(), bool !!(). ! and !! must return bool (truth-test operator '!!' must return 'bool', not 'int'), and !, ~ and !! take no parameters. -a on a number is unchanged. A struct may declare both a unary -() and a binary -(other: V): they overload each other, told apart by their number of parameters.

Truth tests and conditions

A condition asks a value "true or false?". For bool the answer is the value, for a number it is "not zero", and for a raw pointer (__ptr<T>) or a function value it is "not null". A struct answers through its truth-test operator, !!(): bool, like C++'s operator bool:

# A struct that declares `!!(): bool` can be used as a condition.
struct Budget {
    var cents: int = 0;

    construct(this.cents = 0) {}

    # The truth test: `if (budget)` calls `budget.!!()`.
    !!(): bool {
        return cents > 0;
    }
}

struct Label {
    var text: String;

    construct(this.text = "") {}
}

spend(budget: Budget, amount: int): int {
    var spent = 0;
    # A condition, an operand of `&&`, and the operand of `!` all call `!!`.
    while (budget && amount > 0) {
        budget.cents -= 1;
        amount -= 1;
        spent += 1;
    }
    if (!budget) {
        print("budget used up");
    }
    return spent;
}

main(): int {
    var budget = Budget(3);
    assert(spend(budget, 2) == 2, "spent 2 of 3");
    assert(budget ? true : false, "a ternary condition calls !! too");
    assert(spend(budget, 5) == 1, "only 1 left");
    assert(!!budget == false, "!!x calls the truth test");

    # A struct without `!!` is not a condition: `if (label)` is an error.
    # Compare with `__null` to ask whether a reference is set.
    var label: Label;
    assert(label === __null, "no Label yet");
    label = Label("sale");
    assert(label !== __null, "now there is one");
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# budget used up

These are the boolean contexts. In each, a struct value x becomes x.!!():

  • the condition of if, else if and while;
  • the condition of condition ? a : b;
  • each operand of &&, ||, and and or (unless the struct declares && or || itself, which then takes the whole operation);
  • the operand of !: without its own ! method, !x is !(x.!!()).

!!x is the truth test itself: on a struct it calls x.!!(); on a bool or a number it is still two negations. Optional declares !!, so if (found) asks whether an optional holds a value.

A struct that does not declare !! cannot be used as a condition at all:

main.pep:6:9: error: 'Node' cannot be used as a condition: declare '!!(): bool' on it, or compare with '__null'
    6 |     if (node) {
      |         ^~~~

A struct value is a reference, but a condition never tests it for null. To ask whether a reference is set, compare it with __null (node !== __null), or better, use an Optional for a value that may be missing. A trait value is treated the same way: it is a condition only when its trait declares !!.

Comparing structs

Without an == method, a == b on two structs compares identity: it is true only when both refer to the same object, exactly like a === b. The same goes for !=. Define == when two distinct objects with the same contents should count as equal, as String and Array do; != then follows from it. To compare field by field, mark the struct [Equatable], which derives == and hash together. === and !== always compare identity, whatever methods the struct declares, so "a" + "b" == "ab" is true while "a" + "b" === "ab" is false.

A struct never equals a number: unless the struct declares an == (or !=) taking one, comparing a struct value such as an Optional with an integer is an error (cannot compare 'Optional<ulong>' with an integer), since it could only ever compare the object itself. Test an optional with is_empty() (or if (found)) and read its value with value().

Indexers

An indexer lets you write object[index]. Declare it as a method named []:

  • With one parameter, [](index: int): String, it handles reads: shelf[i].
  • With two parameters, [](index: int, value: String): String, it handles writes: shelf[i] = value. The second parameter is the value being stored.

The C-style form, String [](int index), is accepted too. Only parameters without a default count, so either kind can end with a defaulted parameter, such as the location: __ptr<char> = __caller_location() that Array uses to report an out-of-range index at the caller's line (see Assertions and panics).

A struct can have both. With both, compound assignment through an index (counts[i] += 1) reads with the first and writes with the second. Array and String are indexed this way.

Assignment through a chain of indexes, library["fiction"][0] = "Dune", reads with every index but the last and writes with the last, as if the value read were held in a variable first (var fiction = library["fiction"]; fiction[0] = "Dune";). Since a struct is held by reference, the write changes the object the outer struct holds. Assigning through an index whose type has only the reading indexer is an error (cannot assign through '[]': 'Shelf' declares a '[]' getter but no setter).

# A struct declaring `[]` can be indexed: one parameter reads, two write.
struct Shelf {
    var titles: Map<String, String>;
    var sections: Map<String, Shelf>;

    construct() {
        titles = Map<String, String>();
        sections = Map<String, Shelf>();
    }

    # `shelf["name"]` reads a section.
    [](name: String): Shelf {
        return sections[name];
    }

    # `shelf["name"] = section` writes one.
    [](name: String, section: Shelf): Shelf {
        sections[name] = section;
        return section;
    }

    # `shelf[slot]` and `shelf[slot] = title` overload `[]` by type.
    [](slot: ulong): String {
        return titles[$"{slot}"];
    }

    [](slot: ulong, title: String): String {
        titles[$"{slot}"] = title;
        return title;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var library = Shelf();
    library["fiction"] = Shelf();
    # A chained assignment writes into the shelf the first index reads,
    # like `var fiction = library["fiction"]; fiction[0] = ...;`.
    library["fiction"][0] = "Dune";
    library["fiction"]["classics"] = Shelf();
    library["fiction"]["classics"][0] = "Emma";
    assert(library["fiction"][0] == "Dune", "set through two indexers");
    assert(library["fiction"]["classics"][0] == "Emma", "and through three");
    return 0;
}

Properties

A property is a struct member that is read and written like a field (account.name, account.name = "Savings") but whose get and set accessors can run code. A property that needs somewhere to keep its value gets it from the compiler: its implied storage, reachable as field inside its accessors. You declare a separate private field only when you want one.

Declaring properties

A property is a field declaration followed by an accessor block instead of ;:

# A property is read and written like a field, but its `get` and `set`
# accessors can run code.
struct Account {
    # An auto property: implied storage, read and written by anyone.
    var owner: String { get; set; }

    # Read-only outside the struct: only Account's own code assigns it.
    var balance: long { get; }

    # A custom `set` over implied storage: `field` is the storage and
    # `value` is the new value.
    var name: String {
        get;
        set {
            assert(!value.is_empty, "an account name cannot be empty");
            field = value;
        }
    } = "unnamed";

    # Computed: no accessor is omitted and none uses `field`, so it takes
    # no space.
    var is_empty: bool {
        get {
            return balance == 0;
        }
    }

    # Explicit storage, when you want it.
    var _deposits: ulong;
    var deposits: ulong {
        get {
            return _deposits;
        }
    }

    # An initializer initializes the implied storage.
    var limit: long { get; set; } = 100;

    construct(this.owner = "") {}

    deposit(amount: long) {
        balance += amount;   # Account's own code may set a get-only property
        _deposits += 1;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var account = Account("Ann");
    assert(account.owner == "Ann", "a constructor parameter can set a property");
    assert(account.is_empty, "a computed property runs its get");

    account.owner = "Bob";
    account.name = "Savings";
    assert(account.name == "Savings", "the set stored the name");

    account.deposit(30);
    account.deposit(12);
    assert(account.balance == 42 && account.deposits == 2, "methods update the storage");
    assert(!account.is_empty, "the computed property follows the balance");

    # `account.balance = 0;` would not compile: 'balance' has no 'set'.

    account.limit += 50;   # a get, then a set
    assert(account.limit == 150, "compound assignment reads and writes");
    return 0;
}
  • get; and set; with no body are the defaults: get returns the storage, and set stores the new value in it. Either may have a body instead.
  • A property has implied storage when an accessor is omitted (get; or set;) or an accessor body uses field. Otherwise it is computed: it takes no space, and its get runs every time it is read.
  • An initializer after the accessors (var limit: long { get; set; } = 100;) initializes the storage, so it needs a property that has storage. It does not run set.
  • Inside an accessor, field is the storage, and inside set, value is the new value (a by-value parameter). Both are contextual: outside accessors they are ordinary names, so a local or a member called field or value elsewhere keeps working. Inside an accessor, a bare field always means the storage; reach a member of that name as this.field.
  • A property must have a get: { set; } alone is an error.
  • A property is declared with var and an explicit type; it cannot be const. There are no static properties.

Reading and writing

  • p.count calls get, and p.count = x calls set. A default accessor is not a call at all: an auto property ({ get; set; }) compiles to the same loads and stores as a field.
  • p.count += 1, p.count++ and the other compound assignments are a get and then a set. p is evaluated once.
  • A constructor parameter this.name assigns the property, through its set when it has one. A field initializer and the struct's own field initialization do not.
  • Inside the struct's methods, a property is reached by its bare name, like a field: balance += amount; is this.balance += amount;.
  • A property's accessors are ordinary method calls for reference counting: get returns a temporary that owns one reference, and value is a by-value parameter, acquired on entry and released on exit.

Read-only properties

{ get; } alone makes a property read-only outside the struct: assigning it from other code is an error at the property's name.

main.pep:6:7: error: cannot assign to 'balance': it has no 'set' accessor
    6 |     a.balance = 3;
      |       ^~~~~~~
main.pep:2:9: note: 'balance' declared here
    2 |     var balance: long { get; }
      |         ^~~~~~~

The struct's own constructors and methods may assign a get-only property with implied storage; that writes the storage directly. An extension's methods are not the struct's own code: they cannot assign it either.

Properties in traits and extensions

A trait can require a property, var area: double { get; } or { get; set; }, with no accessor bodies. A struct meets the requirement with a property of the same name and type (auto or computed), or with a plain field. Reading or writing the property through a trait value calls the struct's accessors.

An extension can add computed properties only, since it cannot add storage to the struct:

# A trait can require a property; a struct meets it with a property of the
# same name and type.
trait Shape {
    var area: double { get; }
    var label: String { get; set; }
}

struct Square {
    var side: double { get; set; } = 1.0;
    var area: double {
        get {
            return side * side;
        }
    }
    var label: String { get; set; } = "square";
}

extend Square with Shape;

# An extension can add computed properties, which need no storage.
extend Square {
    var perimeter: double {
        get {
            return side * 4.0;
        }
    }
}

describe(shape: Shape): String {
    shape.label = "seen";
    return $"{shape.label}: {shape.area}";
}

main(): int {
    var square = Square();
    square.side = 3.0;
    assert(square.area == 9.0, "the computed area follows the side");
    assert(square.perimeter == 12.0, "an extension's property reads like any other");
    assert(describe(square) == "seen: 9.0", "a trait value reaches the struct's accessors");
    assert(square.label == "seen", "the set through the trait reached the struct");
    return 0;
}

An extension property that would need storage is an error:

main.pep:5:9: error: an extension cannot add storage: property 'y' must be computed, with accessor bodies that do not use 'field'

An enum can declare computed properties too, under the same rule, and no set, since its values never change.

Properties of [Shared] structs

The fields of a [Shared] struct are const, so the storage of its properties is too:

  • A property with implied storage must be { get; }, and only the struct's constructors assign it. A set, with or without a body, is an error at set, with a note at [Shared].
  • A computed get over the struct's const fields is allowed, as any method is.

A [Shared] struct's properties are get only, by design: an assignment x.p = v would read as a write to a struct whose fields cannot change. To change what a thread-safe member holds (an Atomic<int>, or a value behind a Mutex), declare a method that says what it does, such as store_hits(value) or add_name(name).

How properties compile

The compiler lowers a property to plain members: a field for its storage (named after the property when its get is the default, __field_name otherwise), a getter method __get_name() and, with a set, a setter __set_name(value). Every read and write of the property becomes a storage access or an accessor call once the receiver's type is known. The accessor methods appear in debuggers and in profiles under those names.

Value structs

A struct is normally a reference to an object on the heap. A struct marked [Value] is a value instead, like a number or a tuple: it is stored inline in whatever holds it (a local, a field, an array element), and assigning it, passing it, or returning it copies it. Creating one allocates nothing.

# A value struct is stored inline and copied like a number.
[Value]
struct Span {
    var start: int;
    var end: int;

    construct(this.start = 0, this.end = 0) {}

    length(): int {
        return end - start;
    }

    # Assigns a field of `this`, so it changes the value it is called on.
    grow(by: int) {
        end = end + by;
    }
}

# A reference struct holding a value: the span is part of the line's object.
struct Line {
    var text: String;
    var span: Span;

    construct(this.text = "") {}
}

# The parameter is a copy: growing it does not change the caller's span.
grown(span: Span, by: int): Span {
    span.grow(by);
    return span;
}

main(): int {
    var a = Span(2, 5);
    var b = a;          # a copy
    b.grow(10);
    if (a.length() != 3 || b.length() != 13) {
        return 1;
    }

    var c = grown(a, 1);
    if (a.length() != 3 || c.length() != 4) {
        return 2;
    }

    # Through a reference, the change lands in the object's own span.
    var line = Line("hello");
    var same = line;
    line.span.grow(5);
    if (same.span.length() != 5) {
        return 3;
    }

    # An element read from an array is a copy: change it, then store it back.
    var spans = Array<Span>();
    spans.append(a);
    var first = spans[0];
    first.grow(1);
    spans[0] = first;
    if (spans[0].length() != 4) {
        return 4;
    }

    # Values compare field by field.
    if (a != Span(2, 5)) {
        return 5;
    }
    return 0;
}

Use a value struct for small types that describe a value rather than an identity: a span, a point, a color. An enum can be a value too (see Value enums); Optional and Result are. Keep a reference struct for anything that is shared and changed through several names, or that is large.

Declaring one

Put [Value] on its own line above the struct. Everything else is written as for any struct: fields, constructors, methods, operators, generic parameters, and extensions.

[Value]
struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
}

A variable or field of a value struct type that is not given a value holds the zero value: every field zero, false, or null.

Copies

  • var b = a; makes b an independent copy. Changing b leaves a as it was.
  • A parameter is a copy of the argument. A function can change its parameter without the caller seeing it; return the changed value instead.
  • A field of a value struct is part of whatever holds it. In a reference struct, line.span.grow(5) changes the span inside line's object, and every reference to that object sees it.
  • Reading an element of an array, or the result of any call, gives a copy. To change an element, read it into a variable, change it, and store it back (spans[0] = first;).

A field that is itself a reference (a String, an Array) is copied as a reference, so both copies share that object, as two variables holding the same String do. Its count is kept like any other reference's: copying the value acquires it, and the copy going out of scope releases it. Use copy for a deep copy.

Methods that change this

In a method, this is the value the method was called on, not a copy, so a method that assigns a field (end = end + by;), or calls another method that does, changes that value. The compiler works out which methods change this from their bodies. Calling one on something that would only change a copy is an error, because the change would be lost:

main.pep:9:12: error: cannot call mutating method 'grow' on a temporary 'Span'
    9 |     make().grow(1);
      |            ^~~~
main.pep:9:5: note: 'make' returns a copy; store it in a variable, change it, and assign it back
    9 |     make().grow(1);
      |     ^~~~

The same holds for assigning a field of a call's result (spans[0].end = 3;) and for changing a const variable's value. A closure made in a method holds a copy of this, so it cannot change this either.

Comparing and hashing

== and != compare two values field by field, and hash combines the fields' hashes, unless the struct declares its own == or hash (declare both together; see Hashing and equality). A value has no identity, so === and !== are errors on it, and it is never null: comparing one with __null is an error too.

What a value struct cannot do

Each of these is an error at the code to change:

  • ===, !==, or __null on a value.
  • __weak<T> or __refcount of a value: there is no object to count.
  • A destruct block: nothing destroys a value. Its reference fields are still released.
  • [Shared]: a value struct is thread-safe when its fields are, and needs no atomic counts.
  • A field whose type is the struct itself, directly or through other value structs: the value would be infinitely large. Hold it through a reference struct or an Array instead.
  • A parameter or result of an extern function: pass a pointer to C instead.

Value structs as trait values

A value struct can declare traits like any struct. Where it flows into a slot of a trait type, such as an argument of type Iterator<int>, it is boxed: copied into a new object that the trait value refers to. The box is a copy, so a mutating method called through the trait value changes the box and not the original, and two conversions of one value make two boxes. Copying the trait value shares the box, as for any trait value.

The runtime's iterators (ArrayIterator, StringIterator, the map and set iterators, ChannelIterator, and the map, filter, enumerate, zip, take, skip, chain and other adapters) are value structs, so a for loop over an Array, a String or any map or set allocates no iterator.

Equality, hashing and ordering

HashMap<K, V> and HashSet<K> find a key by hashing it with hash<K> and comparing it with ==. What those two mean for a type decides which keys count as the same. OrderedMap<K, V> finds keys the same way. For maps that keep their keys in order, see Maps and sets; what < and sorting mean for a type is Ordering with Comparable, below.

Key type==hash<K>
Numbers, bool, char, pointersthe valuethe value's bits
Stringthe contentthe content
A tupleelement by elementthe elements' hashes, combined
A value structfield by fieldthe fields' hashes, combined
An [Equatable] struct or enumfield by fieldthe fields' hashes, combined
Any other structidentity (===)the object's address

Struct keys use identity by default

A struct is a reference. Unless it says otherwise, two references are the same key only when they refer to the same object. Another object with equal fields is a different key:

struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
}

main(): int {
    var origin = Point(0, 0);
    var visits = HashMap<Point, int>();
    visits[origin] = 1;

    # A struct key is found by identity: the same object finds its entry...
    assert(visits.contains(origin), "the stored object");

    # ...but another object with equal fields is a different key.
    assert(!visits.contains(Point(0, 0)), "an equal but distinct object");
    return 0;
}

Identity is right for objects that stand for one thing: a connection, a node in a graph, a task. It is wrong for a struct that describes a value, such as a point or a record looked up by its fields.

Deriving both with [Equatable]

Mark the struct [Equatable], and the compiler writes both halves from its fields, so they cannot drift apart. It compares and hashes like a tuple of its fields: a field of a struct type uses that struct's == and hash, a String its content, and a null field equals only null. Mark a field [Equatable(exclude = true)], or [Equatable(include = false)], to leave it out of both; a field with neither takes part:

# `[Equatable]` derives `==` and the hash from the fields, so they always
# agree.
[Equatable]
struct Person {
    String name;
    int id;
    # Not part of the identity: two records for the same person may differ.
    [Equatable(exclude = true)]
    String nickname;

    construct(this.name = "", this.id = 0, this.nickname = "") {}
}

# An enum whose cases carry values compares the case and then its values.
[Equatable]
enum Token {
    Word(text: String),
    Number(value: int),
    End,
}

main(): int {
    HashSet<Person> people = [Person("Ada", 1, "A"), Person("Ada", 1, "Countess")];
    assert(people.count == 1, "equal people are one member");
    assert(people.contains(Person("Ada", 1)), "the nickname is ignored");
    assert(!people.contains(Person("Ada", 2)), "a different id");
    assert(Person("Ada", 1) == Person("Ada", 1, "B"), "== is derived");

    var counts = HashMap<Token, int>();
    counts[Token.Word("pepper")] = 2;
    counts[Token.End] = 1;
    assert(counts[Token.Word("pepper")] == 2, "found by case and value");
    assert(Token.Word("salt") != Token.Word("pepper"), "different values");
    assert(Token.Number(0) != Token.End, "different cases");
    return 0;
}
  • An enum whose cases carry values can be [Equatable] too: two values are equal when they hold the same case and its values are equal.
  • A generic struct derives both for each specialization, from the fields its type arguments give it.
  • include and exclude are bools, and saying both in a way that contradicts (include = true, exclude = true) is an error. On the struct itself, [Equatable] takes no arguments.
  • An [Equatable] struct cannot also declare == or override hash<T>; either is an error. To compare some other way, drop the attribute and declare both by hand (below).
  • An Array field compares by its elements but hashes by its address, so it adds nothing to the hash. Equal keys still hash equally; keys that differ only in such a field share a hash, which costs speed. The same goes for an Array in a tuple.
  • [Equatable] does not apply to a value struct or an enum whose cases carry nothing: they already compare and hash by content.

Keying a struct by its content

To decide yourself what counts as equal, give the struct both halves of the pair:

  • an == operator that says when two keys are the same, and
  • an override of hash<T> for the struct (see Overriding a generic function for one type), hash<Point>(value: Point): u64.
struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;

    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    # Two points are equal when their coordinates are...
    ==(other: Point): bool {
        return x == other.x and y == other.y;
    }
}

# ...so equal points must hash equally: hash the same fields `==` compares.
# A tuple hashes each element in turn, which combines them.
hash<Point>(value: Point): u64 {
    return hash<(int, int)>((value.x, value.y));
}

struct Person {
    String name;
    int id;
    # Not part of the identity: two records for the same person may differ.
    String nickname;

    construct(this.name = "", this.id = 0, this.nickname = "") {}

    ==(other: Person): bool {
        return id == other.id and name == other.name;
    }
}

# A String field hashes by its content, through hash<String>.
hash<Person>(value: Person): u64 {
    return hash<(String, int)>((value.name, value.id));
}

main(): int {
    var visits = HashMap<Point, int>();
    visits[Point(1, 2)] = 1;
    visits[Point(1, 2)] = visits[Point(1, 2)] + 1;   # the same key
    assert(visits.count == 1, "one entry");
    assert(visits[Point(1, 2)] == 2, "found by content");
    assert(Point(1, 2) != Point(2, 1), "!= is the negation of ==");

    HashSet<Person> people = [Person("Ada", 1, "A"), Person("Ada", 1, "Countess")];
    assert(people.count == 1, "equal people are one member");
    assert(people.contains(Person("Ada", 1)), "the nickname is ignored");
    assert(!people.contains(Person("Ada", 2)), "a different id");
    return 0;
}

The two must agree: keys that are == must have the same hash. The simplest way to keep that promise is to hash exactly the fields that == compares, by hashing a tuple of them: hash<(int, int)>((value.x, value.y)). A tuple's hash combines its elements' hashes, and each element uses its own type's hash, so a String field contributes its content. Unequal keys may share a hash. That costs speed, not correctness.

With == declared, != is its negation, as for any struct. The struct may also overload == for other types (==(rhs: int)); the map and set compare keys with the == that takes the struct itself.

Keep these rules in mind:

  • Declare both or neither. With == but no hash<T>, two equal keys usually hash differently, so a lookup would miss an entry that is there. With hash<T> but no ==, keys would still compare by identity, so an equal object would never find another's entry. Either is a compile error when the struct is used as a HashMap or HashSet key:

    main.pep:5:5: error: 'Point' declares '==' but no 'hash<Point>', so as a HashMap or HashSet key, equal values will not find each other
    5 |     ==(other: Point): bool {
      |     ^~
note: declare 'hash<Point>(value: Point): u64' hashing the fields '==' compares, or remove '==' and mark 'Point' '[Equatable]' to derive both

    The runtime's own structs are not checked. An Array key's == compares elements but its hash is its address, so find it with the same Array object, not an equal one.

  • Don't change a key's fields while it is in a map or set. The entry stays where its old hash put it, so lookups by its new or its old fields both miss it. Remove it, change it, then insert it again.

  • One override per program. hash<Point> replaces hash<T> for Point everywhere, including inside HashMap, so it may be declared in only one file, and that file must declare Point or be in its module (see overriding a generic function).

  • The hash is not keyed, so it does not resist keys chosen by an attacker to collide.

Value structs compare and hash by their fields

A value struct has no identity, so == and hash already compare and hash it field by field. Declare your own pair only to change what counts as equal, here to ignore case:

# A value struct compares and hashes by its fields with no code at all.
[Value]
struct Cell {
    int row;
    int column;

    construct(this.row = 0, this.column = 0) {}
}

# A value struct may still declare its own pair, here to ignore case.
[Value]
struct Tag {
    String text;

    construct(this.text = "") {}

    ==(other: Tag): bool {
        return text.lower() == other.text.lower();
    }
}

hash<Tag>(value: Tag): u64 {
    return hash<String>(value.text.lower());
}

main(): int {
    var board = HashMap<Cell, String>();
    board[Cell(0, 0)] = "rook";
    assert(board[Cell(0, 0)] == "rook", "fields decide");

    var tags = HashSet<Tag>();
    tags.insert(Tag("Pepper"));
    assert(tags.contains(Tag("PEPPER")), "case is ignored");
    return 0;
}

Ordering with Comparable

A type whose values sort in one order declares the Comparable trait. It asks for one method, compare(other), which returns a negative number, zero or a positive number as the value sorts before, with or after other, and gives the type the rest:

  • the operators <, <=, > and >=;
  • min(other), max(other) and clamp(low, high) (which panics when low sorts after high);
  • a place as a Map key or Set element, in that order;
  • the constraint T: Comparable in a generic function, whose body can then use all of the above on a T.
struct Version {
    var major: int;
    var minor: int;

    construct(this.major = 0, this.minor = 0) {}

    # The one method Comparable asks for.
    compare(other: Version): int {
        var order = major.compare(other.major);
        if (order != 0) {
            return order;
        }
        return minor.compare(other.minor);
    }
}

extend Version with Comparable;

# A generic function asks for an order with `T: Comparable`.
largest<T: Comparable>(items: Array<T>): T {
    var best = items[0];
    for (var item in items) {
        best = best.max(item);
    }
    return best;
}

main(): int {
    # `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` come from `compare`.
    assert(Version(1, 2) < Version(1, 10), "1.2 sorts before 1.10");
    assert(Version(2, 0).min(Version(1, 9)).major == 1, "min");
    assert(Version(3, 0).clamp(Version(1, 0), Version(2, 0)).major == 2, "clamp");

    # Numbers and strings are Comparable too.
    assert(largest([3, 9, 2]) == 9, "numbers");
    assert(largest(["pear", "apple"]) == "pear", "strings");
    assert((15).clamp(0, 10) == 10, "clamp a number");

    # A Comparable struct is a Map key, in its order.
    var releases = Map<Version, String>();
    releases[Version(2, 0)] = "second";
    releases[Version(1, 5)] = "first";
    assert(releases.first().value().1 == "first", "sorted by compare");

    # An array of a Comparable type sorts in its order; a comparer gives
    # any other.
    var versions = [Version(2, 1), Version(1, 5)];
    versions.sort();
    assert(versions[0].major == 1, "sorted");
    versions.sort((a, b) => b.compare(a));
    assert(versions[0].major == 2, "sorted in reverse");
    return 0;
}

A type that declares its own < (or min, or any of the others) keeps it; the trait's version fills in only what the type leaves out.

compare must give a total, consistent order: the same two values always compare the same way, a.compare(b) has the opposite sign of b.compare(a), and if a sorts before b and b before c, a sorts before c. Map, Set and sorting depend on it.

Sorting

An array of Comparable elements sorts in their own order with sort(), stably, as sort((a, b) => a.compare(b)) would. Floats sort in the total order, NaN last. Any other order still takes a comparer: items.sort((a, b) => b.compare(a)) sorts in reverse.

Numbers, char and String

Every number type and char is Comparable by value, and String by content, the order of String.compare. Their compare returns -1, 0 or 1 (String.compare any negative or positive number).

float and double compare in a total order: NaN sorts after every number and with every other NaN, and -0.0 sorts with 0.0. Their <, <=, > and >= keep IEEE behavior, false whenever a NaN takes part, while compare, clamp and Map keys follow the total order, so a NaN key cannot break a map.

Not yet

  • Tuples and Optional are not Comparable, and Comparable is not derived from a struct's fields: a struct writes its compare, as Version does above.

Traits and extensions

Pepper has no inheritance. Instead, you add behavior to a type with an extension, and describe a set of behavior that several types share with a trait. Extensions can be written anywhere, so you can add methods to a library type, such as String, from your own code.

A trait is also a type: a value of type Shape holds any struct, or enum whose cases carry values, that has the Shape trait, and calls its methods (see Traits as types).

Extensions

An extend block adds methods to a struct declared elsewhere, whether in the same file, another file, or the standard library:

struct Temperature {
    var celsius: float = 0.0;
    construct(this.celsius = 0.0) {}
}

# `extend` adds methods to a struct declared elsewhere.
extend Temperature {
    fahrenheit(): float {
        return celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0;
    }

    static freezing(): Temperature {
        return Temperature(0.0);
    }

    bool ==(Temperature other) {
        return celsius == other.celsius;
    }
}

# Library types can be extended too.
extend String {
    exclaim(): String {
        var s = String();
        s.append(this);
        s.append("!");
        return s;
    }
}

# One specialization of a generic library type can be extended, and its
# methods can loop over `this`.
extend Array<int> {
    total(): int {
        var sum = 0;
        for (var x in this) {
            sum += x;
        }
        return sum;
    }
}

struct Box<T> {
    var value: T;
}

# Extending the generic struct adds the method to every Box<...>.
extend Box<T> {
    get(): T {
        return value;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var t = Temperature(100.0);
    assert(t.fahrenheit() == 212.0, "extension method");
    assert(Temperature.freezing() == Temperature(0.0), "static method and operator from an extension");

    assert("hello".exclaim() == "hello!", "String extension");

    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(2);
    numbers.append(3);
    assert(numbers.total() == 5, "Array<int> extension loops over this");

    var b = Box<int>();
    b.value = 5;
    assert(b.get() == 5, "Box<int>");
    var s = Box<String>();
    s.value = "five";
    assert(s.get() == "five", "Box<String>");
    return 0;
}
  • An extension can hold anything a struct body can hold except fields, a constructor, and a destructor: methods, static methods, operators, and indexers.
  • Methods in an extension behave exactly like methods declared in the struct. They can use this and name the struct's fields directly, and they are called the same way.
  • A type can have any number of extensions.
  • An extension method may share its name with the struct's methods if its parameter types differ: it joins their overload set.
  • An extension in another file is usable only where that file (or its module) is imported, and only if it is exported; the standard library's extensions are usable everywhere. See Visibility.

Extending generic structs

extend Box<T>, using the struct's own type parameter name, adds the methods to every specialization: Box<int>, Box<String>, and so on. The example above does this.

When Box constrains its parameter (struct Box<T: Shape>), the extension keeps the constraint without restating it; extend Box<T: Shape> may restate it as documentation (see constraints). A constraint the struct does not have limits the extension to the specializations that meet it: extend Box<T: Named> { ... } adds its methods to Box<Square> but not to Box<String>, and extend Box<T: Shape> with Shape makes a Box of shapes a shape (see constrained extensions).

extend Box<int> targets one specialization: its methods exist only on Box<int>, and calling one on a Box<String> is an error (no member named 'doubled' in 'Box<String>').

A library type's specialization can be extended the same way. The example's extend Array<int> adds total(), which loops over this with for.

An extension cannot add fields; declare every field in the struct itself.

Traits

A trait names a set of methods. Declare one with trait and method signatures ending in ;. Then declare that a type has the trait with extend Type with Trait, and provide the methods in that extension:

# A trait names a set of methods that a type provides.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    name(): String;

    # A method with a body is a default: every type with the trait gets it.
    describe(): String {
        return "a " + name();
    }
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

# `extend ... with` declares that Square has the Shape trait, and adds the
# trait's methods to it.
extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }

    name(): String {
        return "square";
    }
}

# A trait can be generic, and can declare static methods; `this` as a type
# stands for the type that has the trait.
trait From<T> {
    static this from(T value);
}

extend Square with From<int> {
    static Square from(int side) {
        return Square(side);
    }
}

# A trait whose methods all have defaults needs no body: end the extension
# with `;`, the same as writing an empty `{}`.
trait Labeled {
    label(): String {
        return "shape";
    }
}

extend Square with Labeled;

main(): int {
    var sq = Square(3);
    assert(sq.area() == 9, "trait method called on the struct");
    assert(sq.name() == "square", "second trait method");
    assert(sq.describe() == "a square", "default method from the trait");
    assert(Square.from(4).area() == 16, "static method from a generic trait");
    assert(sq.label() == "shape", "default method from a bodiless extension");
    return 0;
}
  • A trait can have type parameters, like From<T>.
  • A trait can declare static methods. In a trait, this used as a type stands for the type that has the trait.
  • extend Square with Shape, Printable { ... } attaches several traits at once.
  • When the type already has every method the traits need, from its own methods or the traits' defaults, the extension can end with ; instead of a body: extend Square with Labeled; is the same as extend Square with Labeled {}. Only an extension with a with clause can leave out its body; pep-fmt writes an empty one as ;.
  • A trait can declare several methods of one name with different parameter types; the type implements each with the method whose parameter types match (see Overloading).
  • The methods in the extension are ordinary methods of the struct, so you call them on a Square as usual.
  • A generic parameter can require a trait, total_area<T: Shape>, so that only types declared to have it are accepted (see constraints).
  • The runtime declares traits too. ToString (to_string(): String) makes a type usable in an interpolated string.

The compiler checks that the type has every method the trait declares, either in the extension or in the struct itself. A missing method is an error at the extension, with a note at the trait's method:

main.pep:9:8: error: 'Square' does not implement 'area', required by trait 'Shape'
    9 | extend Square with Shape {
      |        ^~~~~~
main.pep:2:5: note: 'area' declared here
    2 |     area(): int;
      |     ^~~~

A method that implements a trait should name its parameters as the trait does, since a call through a value of the trait type names its arguments with the trait's names. A different name is a warning, whose fix renames the parameter and its uses:

main.pep:8:10: warning: parameter 'factor' of 'area' is named 'scale' in trait 'Shape'
    8 |     area(factor: int): int { return side * side * factor; }
      |          ^~~~~~
main.pep:2:5: note: 'area' declared here
    2 |     area(scale: int): int;
      |     ^~~~

Default method bodies

A trait method can have a body. A type that has the trait and does not define that method gets the trait's body as its own method; a type that defines the method keeps its own. Inside a default body, the trait's type parameters and this stand for the types named in the with clause:

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    sides(): int { return 4; }
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
}

Here Square(3).sides() returns 4.

A default method can have type parameters of its own (see Generic methods). The runtime's Iterator<T> uses this for its map<U> and filter adapters, which every type that declares Iterator<T> gets.

A default body sees only what its trait declares: a bare call to one of the trait's methods calls it on this, and any other bare name means what it means where the trait is declared (a top-level function or variable), even when a conforming type happens to have a method or field of that name. Call through this explicitly only for the trait's own methods.

A closure in a default body can use this and the trait's methods too. Each type that gets the default gets its own copy of the closure, which captures this as that type, as a closure in one of its own methods would (see this in methods):

# A closure in a trait's default method can use `this` and the trait's
# methods.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;

    # Every type with Shape gets this method, and its own copy of the
    # closure, which captures `this`.
    scaled_area(): (int) => int {
        return (factor: int) => area() * factor;
    }
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var square = Square(3);
    var scale = square.scaled_area();
    assert(scale(2) == 18, "closure in a default method");

    # The closure keeps the square alive and sees its current side.
    square.side = 4;
    assert(scale(2) == 32, "sees the current value");
    return 0;
}

Numbers, bool and enums

A number type (int, long, byte, char, float, double and the rest), bool, or an enum whose cases carry no values can declare a trait too, with an extension written the same way. Inside its methods, this is the value:

trait Describe {
    describe(): String;
    # A default method works for value types too.
    shout(): String { return describe() + "!"; }
}

trait Zero {
    static zero(): this;
}

# A number type conforms like a struct; `this` is the value.
extend int with Describe {
    describe(): String { return this < 0 ? "negative" : "non-negative"; }
}

extend int with Zero {
    static zero(): int { return 0; }
}

enum Light {
    Red,
    Green,
}

# An enum whose cases carry no values can conform too.
extend Light with Describe {
    describe(): String { return this == Light.Red ? "stop" : "go"; }
}

# Each call is resolved for the type argument: no trait value is made.
describe_all<T: Describe>(items: Array<T>): String {
    var text = "";
    for (var item in items) {
        text = text + item.describe() + " ";
    }
    return text;
}

zero_of<T: Zero>(): T { return T.zero(); }

main(): int {
    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(-1);
    numbers.append(2);
    assert(describe_all(numbers) == "negative non-negative ", "numbers");
    assert(Light.Green.shout() == "go!", "enum");
    assert((5).describe() == "non-negative", "a call on a value");
    assert(zero_of<int>() == 0, "a static member through T");
    return 0;
}

  • The type then meets the constraint T: Describe (see constraints), and its methods can be called on a value (x.describe()) or, for a static one, on the type (int.zero(), or T.zero() in a generic). Each call goes straight to the method: there is no object and no vtable.

  • It is never a trait value. A number or such an enum cannot be stored in a Describe variable, passed as one, or added to an Array<Describe>:

    main.pep:7:15: error: 'int' cannot be converted to trait 'Doubled': only structs and enums whose cases carry values can be trait values
    7 | main(): int { Doubled d = 3; return 0; }
      |               ^~~~~~~
main.pep:4:8: note: 'int' conforms to 'Doubled' here, which makes it meet the constraint, not a trait value
    4 | extend int with Doubled {
      |        ^~~

  • An extension of a number type may also add methods without a trait (extend int { ... }), and operators for a number on the left of another type (extend double { *(v: Vector): Vector { ... } } makes 2.0 * v work; see A number on the left). An enum declares its methods inside the enum, so an extension of one must name a trait.

  • The spellings of one type are one type: extend int is also extend i32.

Traits as types

A trait's name is also a type. A variable, parameter, field, return value, or collection element of type Shape holds any struct, or enum whose cases carry values, that declares Shape, and calling a method on it runs that type's own method:

# A trait used as a type holds any struct that declares the trait.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    name(): String;
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

struct Rect {
    var width: int = 1;
    var height: int = 1;
    construct(this.width = 1, this.height = 1) {}
}

extend Rect with Shape {
    area(): int { return width * height; }
    name(): String { return "rect"; }
}

# One function accepts every Shape; each call runs the value's own method.
measure(shape: Shape): int {
    return shape.area();
}

main(): int {
    # A Square converts to a Shape wherever a Shape is expected.
    var s: Shape = Square(3);
    assert(measure(s) == 9, "square through a trait parameter");
    assert(s.name() == "square", "method of the concrete type");

    # Collections can hold different types that share a trait.
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    shapes.append(Square(2));
    shapes.append(Rect(2, 5));
    var total = 0;
    for (var shape in shapes) {
        total = total + shape.area();
    }
    assert(total == 14, "sum of areas");

    # Two trait values are equal when they refer to the same object.
    var same: Shape = s;
    assert(same == s, "same object");
    return 0;
}

  • Conversion is implicit. A Square becomes a Shape wherever a Shape is expected: an initializer, an assignment, an argument, a return value.

  • Conformance is declared. Only a type that declares the trait with extend Type with Trait converts. Having the right methods is not enough:

    main.pep:11:20: error: 'Circle' does not conform to trait 'Shape'
   11 |     var s: Shape = Circle();
      |                    ^~~~~~
main.pep:6:8: note: declare it with 'extend Circle with Shape'
    6 | struct Circle {
      |        ^~~~~~

  • A trait value is a shared reference to the struct, like any other struct value (see Memory). When the last reference goes away, whether it was a Shape or a Square, the struct's own destructor runs.

  • Only instance methods are callable through the trait. Static methods, generic methods, and methods whose signature uses this as a type, need the concrete type; calling one through a trait value is an error.

  • Methods must match the trait's signature. An implementation with different parameter or return types is an error. The one exception is a trait method that returns a trait type: the implementation may return a struct that declares that trait, as iterate() does in Iteration.

  • == and != on trait values compare identity: they are equal when they refer to the same object.

  • copy copies the struct behind a trait value and returns it as the same trait type (see Copying trait values). It panics when that struct cannot be copied.

Converting a trait value back

A trait value remembers the struct it holds, so it converts back to that struct, or to another trait the struct declares. A type pattern names the type, like an enum case, and binds the value as that type:

# A trait value converts back to the struct it holds, or to another trait
# that struct declares, with `is`, `match` and `as?`.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

trait Named {
    name(): String;
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
}

extend Square with Named {
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

struct Rect {
    var width: int = 1;
    var height: int = 1;
    construct(this.width = 1, this.height = 1) {}
}

extend Rect with Shape {
    area(): int { return width * height; }
}

# A type pattern tests for a struct and binds the value as that struct.
describe(shape: Shape): String {
    return match (shape) {
        Square(square) => $"a square of side {square.side}",
        Rect(rect) => $"a {rect.width} by {rect.height} rectangle",
        else => "another shape",
    };
}

main(): int {
    var shape: Shape = Square(3);
    assert(describe(shape) == "a square of side 3", "match on the struct");
    assert(describe(Rect(2, 5)) == "a 2 by 5 rectangle", "another struct");

    # `is` tests without converting; as an `if` condition it can bind.
    assert(shape is Square, "a square");
    assert(!(shape is Rect), "not a rectangle");
    if (shape is Square(square)) {
        assert(square.side == 3, "bound as a Square");
    }

    # `as?` gives an optional: Empty when the value is something else.
    var square = shape as? Square;
    assert(square.value().side == 3, "converted to Square");
    var rect = shape as? Rect;
    assert(rect.is_empty(), "not a Rect");

    # Converting to another trait works when the struct declares both.
    var named = shape as? Named;
    assert(named.value().name() == "square", "a Square is Named");
    var other: Shape = Rect(1, 1);
    assert((other as? Named).is_empty(), "a Rect is not Named");
    return 0;
}

  • value is Square tests whether the value holds a Square. As the whole condition of an if or while, value is Square(square) also binds it, as for enums.

  • match (value) { Square(square) => ..., Rect(rect) => ..., else => ... } picks the arm of the value's struct. Any struct may declare a trait, so a match expression on a trait value needs an else arm.

  • value as? Square converts the value, giving Square?: Empty when the value holds something else, or is null. as without the ? is an error for a trait value, since the conversion can fail.

  • Another trait works the same way: value as? Named and value is Named succeed when the struct behind the value declares Named too.

  • A generic struct is named with its type arguments: Cell<int>(cell).

  • A value struct's trait value holds a copy of it (see boxing), and converting back copies it out again.

  • The bound value is another reference to the same object, like any copy (see Memory); a test holds no reference after it.

  • Naming a struct that does not declare the trait is an error, since the value can never hold one:

    main.pep:9:18: error: 'Point' does not implement 'Shape', so a 'Shape' value never holds one
    9 |     if (shape is Point) {
      |                  ^~~~~

Weak references and atomics

Weak<Shape> is a weak reference to a trait value: it holds the struct's weak reference and its vtable, and a with block upgrades it to a Shape while a strong reference is left:

# A weak reference can point at a trait value: it keeps the struct behind
# it without keeping it alive.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
}

main(): int {
    var shape: Shape = Square(3);
    var weak = Weak<Shape>(shape);

    # While a strong reference is left, `with` reaches the value as a Shape.
    with (var live = weak) {
        assert(live.area() == 9, "upgraded to a Shape");
    } else {
        assert(false, "still alive");
    }

    # Once the last strong reference goes, the Square is destroyed.
    shape = __null;
    assert(weak.expired(), "destroyed");
    with (var live = weak) {
        assert(false, "expired: the body is skipped");
    }
    return 0;
}

Atomic<Shape> is ruled out. Atomic<T> needs a thread-safe T, and a trait value may hold any struct, thread-safe or not; it is also two pointers wide, more than one atomic instruction swaps on every platform. The error is the one for any type that is not thread-safe:

main.pep:8:32: error: 'Shape' does not conform to 'Shared', required by 'T' in 'Atomic'
    8 |     var current = async.Atomic<Shape>();
      |                                ^~~~~

To share a trait value between threads, keep it in a Mutex<Shape> and swap it with replace, or use Atomic<Square> for one [Shared] struct type.

Generics

Generics let you write a struct or a function once and use it with many types. Add type parameters in angle brackets after the name, then use them like any other type name. The standard library's Array<T>, HashMap<K, V>, and Result<TValue, TError> are all ordinary generic types written this way (Result is a generic enum).

Pepper generics work like C++ templates: each distinct set of type arguments, such as Stack<int> or Stack<String>, produces its own copy of the code, compiled for those exact types. There is no runtime cost for using them.

Generic structs

# `T` is a type parameter: each use such as `Stack<int>` or
# `Stack<String>` makes a separate, fully typed version of the struct.
struct Stack<T> {
    var items: Array<T>;

    construct() {
        items = Array<T>();
    }

    push(item: T) {
        items.append(item);
    }

    pop(): T {
        return items.pop();
    }

    peek(): T {
        # `top` is inferred as `T`: an `int` in `Stack<int>`, a `String`
        # in `Stack<String>`.
        var top = items.last();
        return top;
    }

    is_empty(): bool {
        return items.is_empty;
    }
}

# Several parameters are separated by commas.
struct Entry<K, V> {
    var key: K;
    var value: V;
    construct(K key, V value) {
        this.key = key;
        this.value = value;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var numbers = Stack<int>();
    numbers.push(1);
    numbers.push(2);
    assert(numbers.peek() == 2, "peek looks at the top");
    assert(numbers.pop() == 2, "last in, first out");
    assert(numbers.pop() == 1, "then the first");
    assert(numbers.is_empty(), "empty again");

    var words = Stack<String>();
    words.push("hello");
    assert(words.pop() == "hello", "the same code works for Strings");

    var e = Entry<String, int>("answer", 42);
    assert(e.key == "answer" && e.value == 42, "two type parameters");
    return 0;
}
  • Name the type parameters after the struct's name: struct Stack<T>, struct Entry<K, V>. Inside the struct, fields, parameters, return types, and locals can all use them.
  • Name the type arguments whenever you use the struct: Stack<int>(), var s: Stack<String>;.
  • Stack<int> and Stack<String> are different types.
  • A type argument is a type. The one exception is a number, which only the lane count of a SIMD vector accepts (Vector<int, 4>); a struct of your own cannot compute with a number parameter.
  • Each type argument makes a separate copy of the struct, so a struct whose copy needs a copy with a larger argument never ends: struct Foo<T> with a field var inner: Foo<Array<T>> makes Foo<int> need Foo<Array<int>>, which needs Foo<Array<Array<int>>>, and so on. The compiler stops 64 levels deep with an error at the type that asks for the next level ('Foo' is specialized 65 levels deep, past the limit of 64), with a note where the chain started.

Generic functions

A free function takes type parameters the same way:

larger<T>(a: T, b: T): T {
    if (a > b) {
        return a;
    }
    return b;
}

struct Circle {
    var radius: int = 1;
    area(): int { return 3 * radius * radius; }
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 2;
    area(): int { return side * side; }
}

# The body can use anything the type argument provides: this works for
# any T that has an `area()` method returning a number.
total_area<T>(shapes: Array<T>): int {
    var sum = 0;
    for (var shape in shapes) {
        sum += shape.area();
    }
    return sum;
}

# `T()` calls the type argument's constructor.
fresh<T>(): Array<T> {
    var items = Array<T>();
    items.append(T());
    return items;
}

# A closure in generic code is compiled with each use too: for `T = int`
# it calls `larger<int>`.
larger_later<T>(a: T, b: T): () => T {
    return () => larger(a, b);
}

main(): int {
    # Type arguments come from the arguments, or can be written out.
    assert(larger(3, 9) == 9, "ints");
    assert(larger<float>(2.5, 1.5) == 2.5, "floats");

    var circles = Array<Circle>();
    circles.append(Circle());
    circles.append(Circle());
    assert(total_area(circles) == 6, "circles");

    var squares = Array<Square>();
    squares.append(Square());
    assert(total_area<Square>(squares) == 4, "squares");
    assert(total_area(fresh<Circle>()) == 3, "a constructed Circle");
    var pick = larger_later(4, 7);
    assert(pick() == 7, "a closure calling a generic function");
    return 0;
}

Pepper infers the type arguments from the arguments, so larger(3, 9) calls larger<int>. You can always write them out, larger<float>(2.5, 1.5), or write only the leading ones and let the arguments give the rest: pick<int>(1, "x") for pick<T, U>(a: T, b: U). You must write them when the arguments do not determine every type parameter, for example one that appears only in the return type:

main.pep:4:13: error: cannot infer the type arguments of 'make' from its arguments; write them: make<T>(...)
    4 |     var b = make();
      |             ^~~~
main.pep:1:1: note: declared here
    1 | make<T>(): Box<T> { return Box<T>(); }
      | ^~~~

A generic function used as a value, not called, takes its type arguments from the function type it is given: var f: (int, int) => int = larger; is larger<int> (see Function types).

A parameter whose type is a trait takes its type arguments from the trait the argument's type declares: given total<T>(items: Iterator<T>), the call total(Countdown(4)) infers T = int from extend Countdown with Iterator<int>.

Inference works through closures in both directions. In transform(words, (w) => w.size), where transform<T, U>(items: Array<T>, f: (T) => U), words gives T, which types the closure's parameter w, and the closure's result gives U.

A closure inside a generic function or method is compiled with each use of it, so the generic calls in its body take their type arguments from that use: in larger_later<T>(a: T, b: T) above, () => larger(a, b) calls larger<int> when T is int.

Because each use is compiled for its concrete types, the body may use any operator, field, or method that the type arguments provide. total_area<T> calls shape.area(), so it works with any T that has an area() method returning a number, and using it with a type that lacks one is a compile error inside total_area. To state the requirement up front, and have the compiler report it where the function is used, give T a constraint.

That includes constructing one: T() (or T(args)) calls the type argument's constructor, so fresh<Circle>() above makes a Circle. In a constrained generic, which offers only what its constraints declare, it is an error.

Generic methods

A method can have type parameters of its own, in a struct, a generic struct, an extension, or a trait's default method. They are inferred at each call like a function's, or written after the method name:

struct Box<T> {
    T value;
    construct(T v) { value = v; }

    # A method with a type parameter of its own: `U` is chosen per call.
    map<U>(f: (T) => U): Box<U> {
        return Box<U>(f(value));
    }
}

main(): int {
    var b = Box<int>(4);

    # `U` comes from what the closure returns...
    var tens = b.map((x) => x * 10);
    assert(tens.value == 40, "tens");

    var text = tens.map((x) => "forty");
    assert(text.value == "forty", "text");

    # ...or is written after the method name.
    var wide = b.map<long>((x: int): long => x + 1);
    assert(wide.value == 5, "wide");
    return 0;
}
  • Write the type arguments with no space before < or after >: b.map<long>(f). With a space, a.b < c is a comparison.
  • A generic method cannot be called through a trait value, since each of its uses is compiled separately. Call it on the concrete type.
  • Many iterator adapters (map, zip, chunks, peekable, ...) and consumers (fold, sum, min, to_set, ...) are generic default methods of Iterator<T>, some with a type parameter that defaults to T, so each is compiled only for the iterators that call it; see Iteration.

Default type arguments

A type parameter can have a default, written Name=Type. When a use leaves that argument out, the default fills it in:

struct Measurement<TValue, TUnit=String> {
    var value: TValue;
    var unit: TUnit;
}

main(): int {
    # `Measurement<float>` fills TUnit with its default, String.
    var length = Measurement<float>();
    length.value = 2.5;
    length.unit = "m";
    assert(length.unit == "m", "TUnit defaulted to String");

    # Any argument can still be given explicitly.
    var count = Measurement<int, int>();
    count.unit = 7;
    assert(count.unit == 7, "TUnit given as int");

    # The standard library's Result uses a default the same way:
    # Result<int> means Result<int, Error>.
    var ok = Result<int>.ok(42);
    assert(ok.value() == 42, "Result with the default error type");
    return 0;
}

Arguments are matched to parameters in order, so put the parameters that have defaults last. A generic method's default may name a type parameter of the struct or trait around it: Iterator<T> declares sum<TSum=T>(), so sum() adds in the element type and sum<long>() in long. The standard library declares enum Result<TValue, TError=Error>, so Result<int> means Result<int, Error>. See Error handling with Result.

Constraints

A type parameter can require a trait: write the trait after a colon, T: Shape. Every type argument for T must then conform to Shape. Several constraints are joined with &, and a constrained parameter can still have a default, written after them:

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

trait Named {
    name(): String;
}

struct Circle {
    var radius: int = 1;
    area(): int { return 3 * radius * radius; }
}

extend Circle with Shape;

struct Square {
    var side: int = 2;
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

extend Square with Shape;
extend Square with Named;

# Every T must conform to Shape.
total_area<T: Shape>(shapes: Array<T>): int {
    var sum = 0;
    for (var shape in shapes) {
        sum += shape.area();
    }
    return sum;
}

# Several constraints are joined with `&`.
label<T: Shape & Named>(item: T): String { return item.name(); }

# A constrained parameter can have a default, which must conform too.
struct Gallery<TTag, TShape: Shape = Square> {
    var items = Array<TShape>();
    add(item: TShape) { items.append(item); }
    total(): int { return total_area(items); }
}
