main(): int {
    var circles = Array<Circle>();
    circles.append(Circle());
    circles.append(Circle());
    assert(total_area(circles) == 6, "circles");
    assert(label(Square()) == "square", "label");

    # Gallery<String> is Gallery<String, Square>.
    var gallery = Gallery<String>();
    gallery.add(Square());
    assert(gallery.total() == 4, "default");

    # A trait type conforms to its own trait.
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    shapes.append(Circle());
    shapes.append(Square());
    assert(total_area(shapes) == 7, "trait values");
    return 0;
}

Constraints work on generic structs, enums whose cases carry values, functions, methods, traits and type aliases. A constraint may name the parameters before it in the same list: sum<T, I: Iterator<T>>(values: I).

A type argument conforms to a trait when:

  • it is a struct declared to have the trait with extend Circle with Shape. For a generic struct, extend Box<T> with Shape makes every Box<X> conform, and extend Box<int> with Shape only Box<int>. A generic trait must match exactly: extend Counter with Iterator<int> conforms to Iterator<int>, not to Iterator<long>. Having the right methods is not enough; the extension is what declares it.
  • it is the trait type itself (Array<Shape> passed as Array<T> with T: Shape), as long as every member of the trait can be called through a value of the trait type (see traits as types).
  • it is a type parameter constrained by that trait: inside wrap<T: Shape>, Gallery<String, T> is allowed.

A number type, char, bool or an enum whose cases carry no values conforms when it declares the trait the same way (extend int with Shape; see numbers, bool and enums), for constraints only: it never becomes a trait value. Pointers, tuples and function types conform to no trait.

The Shared constraint

T: Shared is built in: it requires a type that is safe to share between threads, by the same rule as a field of a [Shared] struct. The types that conform are listed in What threads can share; no extend can make another type conform. It gives T no methods, and it joins other constraints with & (T: Shared & Named):

import async;

[Shared]
struct Settings {
    const workers: int;
    construct(this.workers = 1) {}
}

# A cell that any thread may read: its value must be thread-safe.
[Shared]
struct Cell<T: Shared> {
    const value: T;
    construct(value: T) { this.value = value; }
}

share<T: Shared>(value: T): Cell<T> { return Cell<T>(value); }

main(): int {
    var count = share(3);
    var settings = share(Settings(4));
    assert(count.value == 3 and settings.value.workers == 4, "shared cells");

    # The runtime states the same rule: spawn<T: Shared>.
    async.run(() => {
        var task = async.spawn<Settings>(() => { return Settings(2); });
        assert(task.join().value().workers == 2, "spawned");
    });
    return 0;
}

The standard library states the rule this way where it applies: spawn<T: Shared>, run_blocking<T: Shared> and Lazy<T: Shared>, so async.spawn<String>(...) is reported at String, with a note saying why it is not thread-safe ('String' is not declared [Shared]). In a constraint, Shared always means this built-in, so a trait cannot be named Shared. A generic that passes its own T to one of these (say run_blocking<T>) needs T: Shared too.

A constraint can name another type parameter of the same declaration: count_all<T, I: Iterator<T>>(source: I). Inference reads it too: the argument gives I, and the Iterator<...> that I declares gives T. A trait's default method may name the trait's own parameters (put_all<I: Iterator<T>> in trait Sink<T>), which take the arguments of the conformance (extend Sum with Sink<int>).

# `I`'s constraint names `T`: the argument's type gives `I`, and the
# `Iterator<T>` it declares gives `T`.
count_all<T, I: Iterator<T>>(source: I): int {
    var count = 0;
    while (source.next()) {
        count += 1;
    }
    return count;
}

first<T, I: Iterator<T>>(source: I): T {
    source.next();
    return source.current();
}

main(): int {
    var words = Array<String>();
    words.append("pepper");
    words.append("salt");

    # Both inferred: I = ArrayIterator<String>, T = String.
    assert(count_all(words.iterate()) == 2, "count");
    assert(first(words.iterate()) == "pepper", "first");

    # Written type arguments may stop early; the rest are inferred.
    assert(count_all<String>(words.iterate()) == 2, "partial");
    return 0;
}

The compiler checks every use: a type argument you write, one it infers from a call, a default, and a concrete override. The error points at the type argument, or at the call argument the type came from:

main.pep:11:21: error: 'Circle' does not conform to trait 'Shape', required by 'T' in 'Gallery'
   11 |     var g = Gallery<Circle>();
      |                     ^~~~~~
main.pep:7:19: note: constraint declared here
    7 | struct Gallery<T: Shape> {
      |                   ^~~~~
main.pep:4:8: note: declare it with 'extend Circle with Shape'
    4 | struct Circle {
      |        ^~~~~~

A type parameter passed on to a constrained one must carry the constraint itself: wrap<T>(item: T): Gallery<String, T> is an error that suggests T: Shape. The language server offers both the extension and the constraint as quick fixes.

  • A constraint must name a trait: T: Point, with Point a struct, is an error.
  • An extension of a constrained struct keeps its constraints: extend Gallery<TTag, TShape> needs no TShape: Shape of its own. You may restate them as documentation, extend Gallery<TTag, TShape: Shape>. A constraint the struct does not have makes a constrained extension.
  • In an overload set, a generic member whose inferred type arguments do not meet its constraints is not viable, and the error lists why.
  • A constrained name is always a type parameter, never an override's type argument: describe<Point: Shape> declares a generic function whose parameter happens to be named Point.

Inside a constrained generic

The compiler also checks the generic itself, once, whether or not anything uses it: inside largest<T: Shape & Ordered>, a value of type T offers exactly what Shape and Ordered declare. It may:

  • call their instance methods and operators (item.area(), best < item),
  • call their static members through the parameter (T.unit()),
  • convert to one of their trait types (var shape: Shape = item;),
  • be stored, passed, returned, and compared with ==, !=, === and !==.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    scaled(by: int): this;
    static unit(): this;
}

trait Ordered {
    <(other: this): bool;
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    scaled(by: int): Square { return Square(side * by); }
    static unit(): Square { return Square(1); }
    <(other: Square): bool { return side < other.side; }
}

extend Square with Shape;
extend Square with Ordered;

# Inside the body, a T offers what Shape and Ordered declare.
largest<T: Shape & Ordered>(items: Array<T>): T {
    var best = items[0];
    for (var item in items) {
        if (best < item) {
            best = item;
        }
    }
    return best;
}

# Static members are called through the parameter.
unit_area<T: Shape>(): int { return T.unit().area(); }

# A T converts to the trait types of its constraints.
as_shape<T: Shape>(item: T): Shape {
    var shape: Shape = item.scaled(2);
    return shape;
}

main(): int {
    var squares = Array<Square>();
    squares.append(Square(2));
    squares.append(Square(3));
    assert(largest(squares).side == 3, "largest");
    assert(unit_area<Square>() == 1, "static member");
    assert(as_shape(Square(3)).area() == 36, "conversion");
    return 0;
}

Anything else is an error at the member or operator, even before any use: a field, a method no constraint declares, a constructor T(), a call of a constraint's method with the wrong number or types of arguments, or initializing, assigning or returning a T as another type. (Passing a T to a function that takes another type is still reported in each specialization.)

main.pep:5:45: error: no member named 'perimeter' in 'T'
    5 | total<T: Shape>(item: T): int { return item.perimeter(); }
      |                                             ^~~~~~~~~
main.pep:5:10: note: 'T' is constrained by 'Shape', which has no member 'perimeter'
    5 | total<T: Shape>(item: T): int { return item.perimeter(); }
      |          ^~~~~

A method that two constraints both declare is an error too ('name' is declared by both 'Named' and 'Titled'; call it through one of them).

Each use is still compiled for its type argument, so a call goes straight to that type's own method, with no trait value in between. A parameter without a constraint keeps working as before: its uses are checked in each specialization. In a list that mixes the two, such as f<T: Shape, U>, only the uses of T are checked in the generic.

Constrained extensions

An extension of a generic struct can add a constraint the struct does not have: extend Box<T: Named> { ... }. Its members exist only on the specializations whose type argument meets it, so Box<Square> has label() and Box<String> does not. With with, the constraint makes a conditional conformance: after extend Box<T: Shape> with Shape, a Box<Square> is a Shape (it can be passed where T: Shape is required and converted to a Shape value), and a Box<String> is not.

trait Shape {
    area(): int;
}

trait Named {
    name(): String;
}

struct Square {
    area(): int { return 4; }
    name(): String { return "square"; }
}

extend Square with Shape;
extend Square with Named;

struct Box<T> {
    var item: T;
    construct(item: T) { this.item = item; }
}

# Only a Box of something Named has `label()`.
extend Box<T: Named> {
    label(): String { return "box of " + item.name(); }
}

# A Box of shapes is itself a shape.
extend Box<T: Shape> with Shape {
    area(): int { return item.area() * 2; }
}

main(): int {
    var box = Box<Square>(Square());
    assert(box.label() == "box of square", "constrained extension");

    Shape shape = box;
    assert(shape.area() == 8, "conditional conformance");

    # Box<String> is still a Box, without `label()` or `area()`.
    var text = Box<String>("plain");
    assert(text.item == "plain", "any Box");
    return 0;
}
  • Every Box<X> keeps the struct's own members and constraints; an extension adds to them, it never removes any.
  • Inside the extension, T offers the struct's constraints and the extension's, as in any constrained generic.
  • A call of a member the specialization does not have names the constraint it misses:
main.pep:20:9: error: no member named 'label' in 'Box<Circle>'
   20 |     box.label();
      |         ^~~~~
main.pep:15:15: note: 'label' requires 'Circle' to conform to 'Named'
   15 | extend Box<T: Named> {
      |               ^~~~~

and a type argument that misses a conditional conformance says so too ('Box<String>' conforms to 'Shape' only when 'String' conforms to 'Shape').

  • Only the struct's own parameters can carry an extension's constraints: extend Box<int: Shape> is an error.
  • A conformance that holds for every Box needs its members on every Box: extend Box<T> with Named cannot rest on a name() that only extend Box<T: Named> provides. Make the conformance conditional instead (extend Box<T: Named> with Named).
  • Several extensions may declare the same trait with different constraints; a specialization conforms when it meets any of them.
  • Inside another generic, a call such as b.label() on a Box<T> is checked in each specialization, like any member of a generic struct.

Overriding a generic function for one type

You can give a generic function a separate definition for a specific type argument. Write the concrete type where the type parameter would go:

# The generic version handles every type...
describe<T>(value: T): String {
    return "something";
}

# ...and these definitions replace it for two specific types.
describe<int>(value: int): String {
    return "an int";
}

describe<String>(value: String): String {
    return "a String";
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe<float>(1.5) == "something", "the generic version");
    assert(describe<int>(7) == "an int", "the int override");
    assert(describe<String>("hi") == "a String", "the String override");

    # The standard library's hash<String> is such an override: it hashes
    # a String by its content instead of by identity.
    assert(hash<String>("pepper") == hash<String>("pepper"), "content hash");
    return 0;
}

A call whose type argument matches an override, such as describe<int>(7), uses the override; every other call uses the generic version. The standard library uses this to give hash<String> a content-based hash, while hash<T> hashes other structs by identity; a struct keyed by its content overrides hash<T> the same way (see Hashing and equality).

An override can name a built-in type (int, bool, String, and so on) or a struct, such as describe<Point>. It must be declared next to the generic function or next to one of its type arguments: in the file that declares either, or in another file of the same module. Here main.pep overrides shapes.pep's describe<T> for its own Point, and the generic code in shapes.pep uses the override too:

# A generic function, and code that calls it for any type.
export describe<T>(v: T): int {
    return 0;
}

export describe_twice<T>(v: T): int {
    return describe<T>(v) * 2;
}

import "shapes";

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

# Overrides shapes.pep's describe<T> for Point, from another file.
describe<Point>(p: Point): int {
    return p.x + p.y;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    assert(describe<Point>(p) == 7, "the override");
    assert(describe_twice<Point>(p) == 14, "generic code in shapes.pep uses it too");
    assert(describe<int>(5) == 0, "other types keep the generic version");

    # The standard library's generics, such as hash<T>, can be overridden
    # for a struct the same way.
    return 0;
}

A function whose type parameters all name types the file can see (its own, the ones it imports, under any name such as P after import [Point as P] from geo, and the standard library's) is an override when the file can also see a generic function of that name and number of type parameters (its own, an imported one, or the standard library's); otherwise a struct's name is just the name of a type parameter. The generic may be spelled by any name the file has for it (show<Point> after import [describe as show]). A type argument must name a struct, not a type alias or a trait. A generic and another function of the same name in one file are overloads, unless they have the same parameters, or the generic's type parameters all name structs the file can see without a generic of that name to override: either is an error, since it usually means an override whose type argument the file cannot see, or of a generic the file's own function of that name hides.

This placement rule (Rust calls it the orphan rule) means a file that can see both the generic and the type can also see every override that applies to them, so the compiler can check each file on its own. An override that neither of them is declared beside is an error:

main.pep:2:1: error: cannot override 'hash' for 'int' here: an override must be in the file or module that declares 'hash' or one of its type arguments
    2 | hash<int>(value: int): ulong {
      | ^~~~

The standard library's generics, such as hash<T> and to_string<T>, can be overridden for your own structs, but not for built-in types: the standard library declares both. Wrap the built-in type in a struct of your own instead.

To add methods to a generic struct from outside its declaration, use an extension.

Type aliases

A type alias gives an existing type another name. Use one to shorten a long type that you write often, such as HashMap<String, Array<int>>, or to say what a value means, such as Score instead of int.

Declaring an alias

Write type, the new name, =, and the type it stands for:

# An alias is another name for an existing type.
type Score = int;
type Names = Array<String>;
type Handler = (int) => int;

struct Player {
    var name: String;
    var best: Score = 0;        # aliases work in fields...
}

type Team = Player;

double_it(x: int): int {
    return x * 2;
}

# ...and in parameters and return types.
apply(h: Handler, x: Score): Score {
    return h(x);
}

main(): int {
    var s: Score = 21;
    var plain: int = s;         # Score and int are the same type
    assert(apply(double_it, plain) == 42, "function type alias");

    var names = Names();        # construct through the alias
    names.append("Ada");
    assert(names.count == 1, "Names is Array<String>");

    var p = Team();
    p.best = s;
    var q: Player = p;          # Team and Player are the same type
    assert(q.best == 21, "struct alias");
    return 0;
}

An alias is only a spelling, not a new type. The compiler replaces every use of the alias with its target before it checks anything else, so Score and int are interchangeable: you can assign one to the other, pass one where the other is expected, and error messages name the target type.

You can use an alias anywhere a type can appear: local and module-level variables, parameters, return types, struct fields, generic arguments, and casts. An alias of a struct also works where the struct's name would: to construct it (Team()) and to call its static methods.

Generic aliases

An alias can have type parameters of its own, including defaults, just like a generic struct:

# Generic aliases take their own type parameters.
type Predicate<T> = (T) => bool;
type Lookup<V> = HashMap<String, V>;
type Outcome<T, E=Error> = Result<T, E>;

is_even(x: int): bool {
    return x % 2 == 0;
}

count_matching(values: Array<int>, test: Predicate<int>): int {
    var n = 0;
    for (var v in values) {
        if (test(v)) {
            n += 1;
        }
    }
    return n;
}

parse_digit(text: String): Outcome<int> {
    if (text == "7") {
        return Outcome<int>.ok(7);
    }
    return Outcome<int>.err(Error("not a digit I know"));
}

main(): int {
    var values = Array<int>();
    values.append(1);
    values.append(2);
    values.append(4);
    assert(count_matching(values, is_even) == 2, "Predicate<int> is (int) => bool");

    var ages = Lookup<int>();   # HashMap<String, int>
    ages.insert("Ada", 36);
    assert(ages.contains("Ada"), "Lookup<int> is HashMap<String, int>");

    # Outcome<int> fills E with its default: Result<int, Error>.
    assert(parse_digit("7").value() == 7, "ok");
    assert(parse_digit("x").is_err(), "err");
    return 0;
}

The arguments at the use site fill the alias's parameters in order, and omitted ones take their defaults. Outcome<int> becomes Result<int, Error>, and Lookup<int> becomes HashMap<String, int>. Aliases are especially handy for function types, which are long to write out: Predicate<int> reads better than (int) => bool.

Aliases across files

Like other top-level declarations, an alias is private to the file (or module) that declares it. Mark it export to let files that import it use it; see Visibility and Modules and imports.

Recursive aliases

An alias must not refer to itself, directly or through other aliases. The compiler reports the cycle at the alias, with a note at each alias it passes through:

type Celsius = Degrees;
type Degrees = Celsius;

main.pep:1:6: error: type alias 'Celsius' refers to itself
    1 | type Celsius = Degrees;
      |      ^~~~~~~
main.pep:2:6: note: through type alias 'Degrees', declared here
    2 | type Degrees = Celsius;
      |      ^~~~~~~

Overloading

Several free functions in one file can share a name when their parameter lists differ. Each call picks the one whose parameters fit its arguments best:

# Overloaded free functions: one name, several parameter lists.

import io;

describe(n: long): String { return "a number"; }
describe(x: double): String { return "a fraction"; }
describe(s: String): String { return "some text"; }
describe(s: String, times: int): String { return "text, repeated"; }

# An exact match beats a widening, which beats a conversion; an
# `[Implicit]` constructor comes last.
size(p: io.Path): int { return 1; }
size(n: long): int { return 2; }

main(): int {
    var small: int = 7;
    assert(describe(small) == "a number", "int widens to long");
    assert(describe(2.5) == "a fraction", "exact match");
    assert(describe("hi") == "some text", "a literal promotes to String");
    assert(describe("hi", 3) == "text, repeated", "picked by argument count");

    assert(size(4) == 2, "an integer literal fits a long");
    assert(size("notes.txt") == 1, "only io.Path takes a String, by its [Implicit] constructor");
    return 0;
}

The functions of one name in one file are an overload set, and each is a member of it; the files of one module may share a set, and so do the sets a file imports, the runtime's, and its own functions of that name. Methods of one name in a struct are a set too, and so are its static methods, its operators, its constructors, and the methods its extensions add.

Declaring overloads

  • The parameter lists must differ in the number or the types of the parameters. Parameter names and default values do not count (though named arguments can pick between members that differ in types), and neither does the return type:

    main.pep:2:1: error: functions that differ only in their return type cannot be overloaded
    2 | f(x: int): long { return 2; }
      | ^
main.pep:1:1: note: previous declaration is here
    1 | f(x: int): int { return 1; }
      | ^

    Two functions with the same parameter types and the same return type are a redefinition of 'f'.

  • A file's own functions join imported ones. A file's functions of a name and the functions its imports bind to that name are one set (see Imported sets merge).

Files of one module share a set

When an import or a re-export takes one name from two files of the same module, and both are functions declared under that name, it takes their union: one set of every member. Here shapes/module.pep re-exports area from two files:

# Each file adds members to `area`; the module exports one set.
export * from "square";
export * from "rect";

export area(side: int): int {
    return side * side;
}

export area(width: int, height: int): int {
    return width * height;
}

import "shapes";

main(): int {
    assert(area(3) == 9, "square.pep's member");
    assert(area(2, 5) == 10, "rect.pep's member");
    return 0;
}

A file of the module sees the members its own file and the module's files it imports declare (see Visibility). That holds for unexported functions too: functions of one name that files of a module declare, exported or not, are one set wherever those files are imported. Members from different files must still differ in their parameters (redefinition of 'area'). Names that are not all functions, such as two structs Point, and a renaming re-export (export size as area beside an area) are still exported twice.

Imported sets merge

Sets of one name from different modules merge too, as they do in Swift: where two imports bind describe, and where the file declares describe itself, an unqualified describe(…) picks among every member. Here two modules each export one member and the file adds a third:

export describe(n: int): String {
    return "a number";
}

export describe(flag: bool): String {
    return "a flag";
}

import "numbers";
import "flags";

# The file's own `describe` joins the two modules' sets.
describe(text: String): String {
    return "some text";
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe(3) == "a number", "numbers' member");
    assert(describe(true) == "a flag", "flags' member");
    assert(describe("hi") == "some text", "this file's member");
    return 0;
}

Unlike files of one module, two modules may each export a member with the same parameters. That is no error until a call cannot tell them apart:

main.pep:3:22: error: call to 'parse' is ambiguous
    3 | main(): int { return parse(1); }
      |                      ^~~~~
a.pep:1:8: note: candidate function
    1 | export parse(x: int): int { return 1; }
      |        ^~~~~
b.pep:1:8: note: candidate function
    1 | export parse(x: int): int { return 2; }
      |        ^~~~~

A qualifier (a.parse(1)) picks one module's set. A file's own member hides an imported member with the same parameters, so a file can replace one member of an imported set. Only functions merge: a struct or variable of the name hides imported functions of it (or, named in an import list, is 'parse' is imported but also declared in this file).

The runtime's sets

The prelude's functions, such as the runtime's print and to_string, are a set too, which a file's own and imported functions of the name join. Here point.pep adds a print member and the file adds a to_string member, and the runtime's members still take every other call:

export struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;

    construct(x: int, y: int) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }
}

# Joins the runtime's `print(String)` wherever it is imported.
export print(p: Point) {
    print($"({p.x}, {p.y})");
}

import "point";

# The file's own `to_string` joins the runtime's.
to_string(p: Point): String {
    return $"Point({p.x}, {p.y})";
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point(1, 2);
    print(p);       # point's member
    print("text");  # the runtime's member
    assert(to_string(p) == "Point(1, 2)", "this file's member");
    assert(to_string(42) == "42", "the runtime's member");
    return 0;
}

A member may not take a runtime member's parameters, since a call could not tell the two apart. With the same return type (or one left to inference) it is a redefinition:

main.pep:1:1: error: redefinition of 'print'
    1 | print(text: String) {}
      | ^~~~~
runtime/string.pep:1864:8: note: previous definition is here
 1864 | export print(text: String) {
      |        ^~~~~

and with another return type it is the same error as for two members of one file:

main.pep:1:1: error: functions that differ only in their return type cannot be overloaded
    1 | to_string(value: int): int { return value; }
      | ^~~~~~~~~
runtime/string.pep:1635:8: note: previous declaration is here
 1635 | export to_string(value: int): String {
      |        ^~~~~~~~~

Give the function another name or other parameters instead. A struct or variable named like a runtime function hides all of its members.

Members may differ in visibility

Exported members are what other files see; a private member is a candidate only for calls in its own file, or in its module's files. Here shapes.pep exports area(int) and keeps the two-argument form as a helper:

# One set: `area(int)` is exported; `area(int, int)` is private to this file.
export area(side: int): int {
    return area(side, side);
}

area(width: int, height: int): int {
    return width * height;
}

import "shapes";

main(): int {
    # Only the exported member is a candidate here: `area(2, 3)` would be
    # an error, since `area(int, int)` is private to shapes.pep.
    assert(area(3) == 9, "the exported member");
    return 0;
}

A call that only the private member fits is an error in another file, and its notes list only the exported members:

main.pep:2:22: error: no matching function for call to 'area'
    2 | main(): int { return area(2, 3); }
      |                      ^~~~
shapes.pep:2:8: note: candidate function not viable: requires 1 argument, but 2 were provided
    2 | export area(side: int): int {
      |        ^~~~

Importing the name (import [area] from "shapes", or the whole file) brings every exported member, and import [area as size] renames the whole set. A re-export (export area;, export * from "shapes") passes on the exported members too; a set whose members are all private is re-exported whole.

extern functions do not overload

An extern function does not overload, by design: an extern is a C function, which has one symbol, and keeping one extern per name keeps the binding to C one-to-one. To put a family of C functions such as abs and llabs behind one name, give each extern a name of its own ([Link(name = ...)] binds it to the C symbol) and overload Pepper functions that call them. With optimization on (-O2), LLVM inlines the small wrappers:

# C's `abs` and `llabs` behind one Pepper name. An extern binds one C
# symbol, so each gets its own name, and Pepper functions overload them.
[Link(name = "abs")]
extern int c_abs(int x);
[Link(name = "llabs")]
extern i64 c_llabs(i64 x);

magnitude(x: int): int { return c_abs(x); }
magnitude(x: long): long { return c_llabs(x); }

main(): int {
    assert(magnitude(-3) == 3, "int");
    var big: long = -5000000000;
    assert(magnitude(big) == 5000000000, "long");
    return 0;
}

Overloading the extern itself is an error that says so (extern 'abs' cannot be overloaded; rename it and overload Pepper functions named 'abs' that call it).

How a call picks a member

A member is viable when the call has between its required and total number of parameters and each argument converts to its parameter. For each argument, the conversion has a rank, best first:

RankWhat converts
exactthe same type; a string literal to __ptr<char> or StringConstant
promotionan integer widening that loses nothing (int to long, u8 to int; the narrower target ranks better, so a short picks int over long), float to double, an integer literal to any integer type it fits, a struct to a trait it declares, __null to a reference, a string literal to String
conversionany other numeric conversion (bool included), and pointer conversions
implicit constructora value to a struct whose [Implicit] constructor takes it

One viable member is better than another when none of its arguments ranks worse and at least one ranks better, as in C++. Between two members whose arguments rank the same, a non-generic one is better than a generic one, and of two generic ones the more specialized is better: the one whose parameter types the other's could take but not the reverse. So describe<A, B>(pair: (A, B)) takes a tuple argument over describe<T>(value: T), which takes anything else. The call picks the member that is better than every other viable one. When there is none, the call is an error that lists the candidates:

main.pep:3:22: error: call to 'f' is ambiguous
    3 | main(): int { return f(1); }
      |                      ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function
    1 | f(x: long): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function
    2 | f(x: short): int { return 2; }
      | ^

An integer literal fits every integer type that holds its value equally well, so f(1) above is ambiguous; an int member would take it exactly. Two widenings to types of the same width (a ushort to long and ulong) are ambiguous too; convert the argument yourself (f(n as long)). When no member is viable, each note says why:

main.pep:5:12: error: no matching function for call to 'f'
    5 |     return f(s);
      |            ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function not viable: no known conversion from 'String' to 'int' for 1st argument
    1 | f(x: int): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function not viable: requires 2 arguments, but 1 was provided
    2 | f(x: int, y: int): int { return 2; }
      | ^

A call with named arguments considers only the members that have a parameter of each name it uses and get every required parameter, and binds the names before ranking the arguments as above. So two overloads whose later parameters have different names can be told apart by naming one (pick(1, b = 2) against pick(a: int, b: int = 0) and pick(a: String, c: int = 0)). The members it considers must put each named argument at the same position; when they do not, the call is an error: named arguments bind differently in the overloads of 'f'.

The member picked decides the call's type, so var x = half(9.0); is a double when half(x: double): double is picked. In the editor, hovering the call shows the member it picked and how many others the set has, and go-to-definition goes to that member.

Generic members

A set can mix generic and non-generic members. A generic member is viable when its type arguments can be inferred from the call, and ranks as an exact match for the arguments that inferred them. When a generic and a non-generic member tie, the non-generic one wins. Writing type arguments (describe<int>(7)) considers only the generic members:

# Generic and non-generic overloads, and overloads called from generic code.

# A non-generic overload wins a tie with a generic one.
describe<T>(value: T): String { return "something"; }
describe(value: int): String { return "an int"; }

# Generic overloads can differ in their number of parameters.
last<T>(a: T): T { return a; }
last<T>(a: T, b: T): T { return b; }

kind(n: int): String { return "number"; }
kind(s: String): String { return "text"; }

# Each specialization resolves `kind` for its own `T`.
label<T>(value: T): String { return kind(value); }

main(): int {
    assert(describe(7) == "an int", "non-generic wins the tie");
    assert(describe(1.5) == "something", "only the generic fits");
    assert(describe<int>(7) == "something", "type arguments pick generic overloads");

    assert(last(1) == 1, "one argument");
    assert(last(1, 2) == 2, "two arguments");

    assert(label(3) == "number", "label<int> calls kind(int)");
    assert(label("x") == "text", "label<String> calls kind(String)");
    return 0;
}

A call inside a generic function or a generic struct's method whose argument types depend on a type parameter is resolved again for each specialization, so label<String> above calls kind(s: String).

An override such as describe<Point>(p: Point) belongs to the generic member with the same number of type parameters and parameters; it is not a member itself.

Methods and operators

A struct's methods of one name are an overload set, and a call picks among them the same way, whether it is written m.add(x), this.add(x), or add(x) inside a method. Static methods overload among themselves (Money.of(250)), and operators are methods, so +(Money) and +(int) can coexist:

# Overloaded methods, static methods and operators.

struct Money {
    var cents: long;

    construct(long cents = 0) {
        this.cents = cents;
    }

    # Methods of one name in a struct overload like free functions.
    add(other: Money): Money { return Money(cents + other.cents); }
    add(dollars: int, cents: int): Money { return Money(this.cents + dollars * 100 + cents); }

    # Static methods overload among themselves.
    static of(cents: long): Money { return Money(cents); }
    static of(text: String): Money { return Money(text.size as long); }

    # Operators are methods, so they overload by operand type too.
    +(other: Money): Money { return add(other); }
    +(more: int): Money { return Money(cents + more); }
}

main(): int {
    var a = Money.of(250);
    var b = a.add(1, 5);                  # add(int, int)
    assert(b.cents == 355, "two ints");
    assert(a.add(b).cents == 605, "a Money");

    var c = a + b + 10;                   # +(Money), then +(int)
    assert(c.cents == 615, "operators");
    assert(Money.of("four").cents == 4, "static of(String)");

    # A method used as a value takes the member its type names.
    var plus: (Money) => Money = a.add;
    assert(plus(a).cents == 500, "method value");
    return 0;
}

  • Unary and binary operators of one symbol are one set: a unary -() and a binary -(other: Money) are told apart by their number of parameters (see Unary operators).

  • A static method and an instance method may not share a name, since a bare of(x) inside a method could mean either:

    main.pep:3:12: error: static method 'get' cannot share its name with an instance method of 'S'
    3 |     static get(x: String): int { return 2; }
      |            ^~~
main.pep:2:5: note: previous declaration is here
    2 |     get(x: int): int { return 1; }
      |     ^~~

  • In a generic struct, each specialization resolves its own calls: in Holder<int>, has(x: T) takes an int. Two members that become the same after substitution (has(x: T) and has(x: String) in Holder<String>) are only an error when a call cannot tell them apart.

  • A method as a value (m.add, Money.of) picks its member from the expected function type, like a free function below; without one the error is cannot infer the type of 'f' from overloaded method 'Money.add'.

Extensions and traits

An extension's methods join the struct's overload set of their name, and a trait may declare several methods of one name. Each of a trait's overloads is implemented by the conforming type's method with the same parameter types, and a call through a value of the trait type picks among the trait's members the same way:

struct Square {
    var side: int = 0;

    construct(this.side = 0) {}

    area(): int {
        return side * side;
    }
}

# An extension's methods join the struct's overload set of their name.
extend Square {
    area(scale: int): int {
        return area() * scale;
    }
}

# A trait may declare overloads too; each is its own member.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    area(scale: int): int;

    # A default joins the conforming type's set of its name.
    describe(): int {
        return area() * 100 + area(2);
    }
}

# Each trait member is implemented by the method with its parameter types.
extend Square with Shape;

total(shape: Shape): int {
    return shape.area() + shape.area(10);
}

main(): int {
    var square = Square(3);
    assert(square.area(2) == 18, "the extension's overload");
    assert(total(square) == 99, "each call through the trait takes its own member");
    assert(square.describe() == 918, "the default body calls both");
    return 0;
}
  • An extension member with a body method's parameters is redefinition of 'area', with a note at the method it repeats.
  • A call sees only the extensions visible in its file (see Visibility): a private extension's overload is never a candidate in another file, so importing a file can add candidates to a call. If an added candidate makes a call ambiguous, the error's notes point at each candidate, the extension's included.
  • A trait's default method is copied into a conforming type that lacks a method with its parameter types, even when the type has other methods of that name; the copy joins their set.
  • A missing overload is named with its parameter types: 'Square' does not implement 'area(int)', required by trait 'Shape'.

Constructors

A struct may declare several constructors. A call Span(...) picks among them exactly as a call picks among functions:

struct Span {
    var start: int = 0;
    var length: int = 0;

    # Constructors overload like functions: each takes its own parameters.
    construct(this.length = 0) {}

    construct(start: int, end: int) {
        this.start = start;
        length = end - start;
    }

    construct(text: String) {
        length = text.length as int;
    }
}

main(): int {
    assert(Span().length == 0, "no arguments");
    assert(Span(5).length == 5, "one int");

    var middle = Span(2, 7);
    assert(middle.start == 2 && middle.length == 5, "two ints");

    assert(Span("pepper").length == 6, "a String");

    # As a value, the expected function type picks the constructor.
    var make: (int, int) => Span = Span;
    assert(make(1, 4).length == 3, "the (int, int) constructor");
    return 0;
}
  • Two constructors with the same parameter types are constructor of 'Span' cannot be redeclared, with a note at the first.
  • No constructor fits is no matching constructor for initialization of 'Span', and a tie is call to constructor of 'Span' is ambiguous; the notes point at each candidate constructor.
  • A generic struct's constructors resolve in each specialization: Pair<int>(1, 2) picks among Pair<int>'s constructors.
  • At most one constructor may be [Implicit]: an implicit conversion needs one constructor to call.
  • [Deprecated] on one constructor warns only at the calls that resolve to it.
  • A constructor as a value (var make: (int, int) => Span = Span;) picks its member from the expected function type, like a function below.

Overloaded functions as values

The name of an overload set, written without a call, is a value only where the expected function type picks one member exactly: a typed variable, an argument, a return from a function with a declared return type, or an assignment. A closure whose parameters have no types, passed to an overloaded function, picks the member whose function parameter has its number of parameters:

# An overloaded function used as a value, and closures passed to overloads.

twice(n: int): int { return n * 2; }
twice(s: String): String { return s + s; }

apply(f: (int) => int, n: int): int { return f(n); }

# Overloads that differ in the type of a function parameter.
run(f: (int) => int): int { return f(10); }
run(f: (int, int) => int): int { return f(10, 20); }

main(): int {
    # The declared type picks the overload.
    var doubler: (int) => int = twice;
    assert(doubler(4) == 8, "twice(int)");

    # So does the parameter it is passed to.
    assert(apply(twice, 5) == 10, "twice(int) again");

    # A closure without parameter types picks the overload of its arity.
    assert(run((a) => a + 1) == 11, "one parameter");
    assert(run((a, b) => a + b) == 30, "two parameters");
    return 0;
}

Without an expected type, the compiler asks for one:

main.pep:4:13: error: cannot infer the type of 'g' from overloaded function 'f'
    4 |     var g = f;
      |             ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function
    1 | f(x: int): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function
    2 | f(x: long): int { return 2; }
      | ^
main.pep:4:13: note: declare the type, for example 'var g: (int) => int = f;'
    4 |     var g = f;
      |             ^

An expected type that matches no member is address of overloaded function 'f' does not match required type '(bool) => int'.

Function types and closures

Functions in Pepper are values. You can store a function in a variable, a field or an array, pass it to another function, and return it. This lets you choose behavior at run time: a sort order, a callback, a step in a pipeline. A function value is a named function, a method, a constructor, or a closure: an anonymous function written where it is used.

Function types

A function type is written (parameter types) => return type:

TypeMeaning
(int) => inttakes an int, returns an int
(String, int) => booltakes a String and an int, returns a bool
() => voidtakes nothing, returns nothing
(int) => (int) => inttakes an int, returns an (int) => int

=> is right-associative, so the last row is a function that returns a function. A function type carries no parameter names, so a call through a function value passes its arguments by position: named arguments are an error there. A function type can be used anywhere a type can: for variables, parameters, return types, struct fields, generic arguments such as Array<(int) => int>, and type aliases.

Written with shared in front, as in shared () => void, a function type is thread-safe: its values can be passed to other threads. See Sharing function values between threads.

Referring to a named function

The name of a free function, written without a call, is a value of that function's type. Calling a function value calls the function:

# Function types and references to named functions.
square(x: int): int { return x * x; }
negate(x: int): int { return -x; }

# A parameter can take a function: its type is '(parameter types) => return type'.
apply(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(x);
}

twice(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(f(x));
}

# Generic functions can take function values too.
apply_twice<T>(f: (T) => T, x: T): T {
    return f(f(x));
}

main(): int {
    # A function's name without a call is a value of its function type.
    var f = square;                 # f: (int) => int
    assert(f(3) == 9, "call through a local");

    var g: (int) => int = negate;   # the type can be written out
    assert(g(4) == -4, "explicit function type");

    # Function variables can be reassigned to another function of the same type.
    f = negate;
    assert(f(6) == -6, "reassigned");

    assert(apply(square, 5) == 25, "pass a function as an argument");
    assert(twice(square, 3) == 81, "(3 * 3) * (3 * 3)");
    assert(twice(negate, 7) == 7, "negating twice");
    assert(apply_twice<int>(square, 2) == 16, "generic");
    return 0;
}
  • var f = square; infers f's type, (int) => int, from the function. An overloaded name, or an overloaded method (p.move), needs a declared type instead, which picks the member.
  • An extern function is a value too, of the type its C prototype gives: var f = abs; is an (int) => int. A variadic one, such as snprintf, is not.
  • A function-typed variable can be reassigned to any function of the same type.
  • A parameter of function type, such as f: (int) => int, lets the caller pass in the behavior. Generic functions can take function parameters too.

Methods, constructors and generic functions

Methods, constructors and specializations of generic functions are values too:

# Methods, constructors and generic functions used as values.
struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;
    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}

    norm(): int {
        return x + y;
    }

    shifted(dx: int): Point {
        return Point(x + dx, y);
    }

    # Inside a method, a bare method name is `this.norm`.
    norm_of_this(): () => int {
        return norm;
    }
}

struct Box<T> {
    T value;
    construct(v: T) {
        value = v;
    }

    map<U>(f: (T) => U): Box<U> {
        return Box<U>(f(value));
    }

    # Inside a method, a generic method's bare name with its type
    # arguments is `this.map<String>`.
    mapper(): ((T) => String) => Box<String> {
        return map<String>;
    }
}

larger<T>(a: T, b: T): T {
    return a > b ? a : b;
}

combine(f: (int, int) => int, a: int, b: int): int {
    return f(a, b);
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point(3, 4);

    # A bound method: the method of one object, which it keeps alive.
    var norm = p.norm;
    assert(norm() == 7, "bound method");
    assert(p.norm_of_this()() == 7, "bare method name");

    # An unbound method takes the object as its first argument.
    var norm_of: (Point) => int = Point.norm;
    assert(norm_of(Point(1, 1)) == 2, "unbound method");

    # A struct's name is its constructor.
    var make: (int, int) => Point = Point;
    assert(make(5, 6).y == 6, "constructor");

    # A generic function with its type arguments names one specialization.
    assert(combine(larger<int>, 2, 9) == 9, "generic function");

    # Where a function type is expected, it picks the specialization.
    assert(combine(larger, 4, 1) == 4, "inferred specialization");

    # A generic method, with its type arguments written or picked by the
    # function type.
    var b = Box<int>(3);
    var to_long = b.map<long>;
    assert(to_long((x: int): long => x * 2).value == 6, "generic method");
    var to_text: ((int) => String) => Box<String> = b.map;
    assert(to_text((x: int) => "three").value == "three", "inferred generic method");
    assert(b.mapper()((x: int) => "3").value == "3", "bare generic method name");

    var steps = Array<(int) => Point>();
    steps.append(p.shifted);
    steps.append(Point(10, 0).shifted);
    assert(steps[1](5).x == 15, "methods in an array");
    return 0;
}
WrittenTypeCalls
p.norm() => intp.norm(), on the object p referred to when the value was made
Point.norm(Point) => intnorm on the object passed as the first argument
Point.origin (a static method)() => PointPoint.origin()
Point(int, int) => Pointthe constructor
Box<int>(int) => Box<int>the constructor of Box<int>
larger<int>(int, int) => intthe specialization larger<int>
b.map<long> (a generic method)((int) => long) => Box<long>b.map<long>(...), on the object b referred to

  • Bound methods. p.norm keeps a reference to the object, like a closure () => p.norm() that captured p, so the object lives as long as the value does. The expression before the . is evaluated once, when the value is made. A bound method is a function value, not the value the method returns: passing p.name where a String is expected is an error. Call it, p.name(). The methods of an enum whose cases carry nothing are not values at all (see enums).

  • Inside a method. A bare method name is a value too, as a bare call is a call: norm means this.norm, and a static method's bare name means Point.origin. This works in closures, extensions and trait default methods as well. A local or parameter of the same name hides the method. Storing norm (or this.norm) in a field of this would be a reference cycle, and is an error, as for closures.

  • Traits and extensions. A method declared in an extension works the same way, and so does a method of a trait-typed value (shape.area), which calls through the trait.

  • Generic functions. Where a function type is expected, the generic function's name alone is enough: the expected type picks the specialization, as a call's arguments do. var f: (int, int) => int = larger; and combine(larger, 2, 9) both mean larger<int>, and a type parameter that appears only in the return type is bound from the expected return type. With no function type to go by, as in var f = larger;, write the type arguments:

    main.pep:3:13: error: cannot infer the type arguments of 'larger' used as a value; write them (larger<T>) or give the value a function type

  • Generic methods. A method with type parameters of its own is a value once they are known: written (b.map<long>, Box<int>.map<long>, Box<int>.wrap<int>) or picked by the function type it flows into, as for generic functions: var m: ((int) => String) => Box<String> = b.map; is b.map<String>. Without either, var m = b.map; is an error that asks for them. Inside a method, the bare name with its type arguments (map<String>) is this.map<String>, a value even when the method takes no arguments; the parentheses (map<String>(f)) call it.

  • A type with a constructor that takes no arguments. Box<int> on its own names the constructor only when the constructor needs at least one argument; otherwise it is a call, Box<int>(). The same goes for a generic function whose parameters all have defaults.

Storing and returning functions

Function values go wherever other values go: struct fields, arrays, module-level variables and return values. A type alias gives a long function type a short name, and can have type parameters of its own.

# Function values in fields, arrays, globals, and return values.

import async;

square(x: int): int { return x * x; }
negate(x: int): int { return -x; }
increment(x: int): int { return x + 1; }

struct Transform {
    var op: (int) => int;
    construct(this.op = square) {}
    run(x: int): int { return op(x); }
}

# Choose a function at run time and return it.
pick(squared: bool): (int) => int {
    if squared {
        return square;
    }
    return negate;
}

# A module-level function variable. Every module-level variable is const
# and thread-safe: an Atomic lets it change, and a function type every thread
# can reach is declared shared.
const handler = async.Atomic<shared (int) => int>(increment);

# A type alias can name a function type, even a generic one.
type Combine<T> = (T, T) => T;
add(a: int, b: int): int { return a + b; }
fold(values: int[], combine: Combine<int>, start: int): int {
    var total = start;
    for (var v in values) {
        total = combine(total, v);
    }
    return total;
}

# A function that returns nothing has the return type void.
const events = async.Atomic<int>(0);
record(n: int) { events.fetch_add(n); }

main(): int {
    var t = Transform();
    assert(t.run(4) == 16, "the default op squares");
    t.op = negate;
    assert(t.op(4) == -4, "call through a field");

    var pipeline = Array<(int) => int>();
    pipeline.append(increment);
    pipeline.append(square);
    pipeline.append(negate);
    var value = 2;
    for (var step in pipeline) {
        value = step(value);
    }
    assert(value == -9, "-((2 + 1) * (2 + 1))");
    assert(pipeline[1](5) == 25, "call an array element");

    assert(pick(true)(5) == 25, "call a returned function directly");
    var chosen = pick(false);
    assert(chosen(5) == -5, "call a stored returned function");

    assert(handler.load()(1) == 2, "global function value");
    handler.store(square);
    assert(handler.load()(3) == 9, "replaced global");

    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(1);
    numbers.append(2);
    numbers.append(3);
    assert(fold(numbers, add, 10) == 16, "10 + 1 + 2 + 3");

    var callback: (int) => void = record;
    callback(2);
    callback(5);
    assert(events.load() == 7, "void function values");
    return 0;
}
  • Fields. A field of function type is called like a method: t.op(4). Inside the struct, op(x) and this.op(x) both call it.
  • Arrays. pipeline[1](5) indexes the array and calls the element.
  • Module-level variables. Every module-level variable is const and thread-safe (see Module-scope variables), so one whose function changes is an Atomic of a shared function type: handler.load()(1) calls the current function and handler.store(square) replaces it.
  • Return values. pick(true)(5) calls the function that pick returns.
  • void results. A function without a return value has a function type ending in => void, such as (int) => void.

Closures

A closure literal is a parameter list, =>, and a body. The body is an expression or a block:

# Closure literals: anonymous functions that capture values.
struct Counter {
    int count;
    construct(this.count = 0) {}
    add(n: int) { count += n; }
}

apply(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(x);
}

# A closure can outlive the function that made it: it keeps its own copy
# of 'n'.
make_adder(n: int): (int) => int {
    return (x) => x + n;
}

struct Scaler {
    int factor;
    construct(this.factor = 1) {}

    # Inside a method, a closure can use 'this' and the struct's members.
    scaler(): (int) => int {
        return (x) => x * factor;
    }
}

main(): int {
    # Parameter types written out: the closure's type is (int) => int.
    var double = (x: int) => x * 2;
    assert(double(21) == 42, "expression body");

    # With a function type to fill, the parameter types can be left out.
    var add: (int, int) => int = (a, b) => a + b;
    assert(add(40, 2) == 42, "types from the variable");
    assert(apply((x) => x * x, 5) == 25, "types from the parameter");

    # A block body, with the return type written after the parameters.
    var clamp = (x: int, low: int, high: int): int => {
        if x < low { return low; }
        if x > high { return high; }
        return x;
    };
    assert(clamp(7, 0, 5) == 5, "block body");

    # Captured values.
    var add_five = make_adder(5);
    assert(add_five(10) == 15, "captured parameter");
    var offset = 100;
    var shift = (x: int) => x + offset;
    assert(shift(1) == 101, "captured local");

    # A captured struct is shared, so the closure can change the object.
    var counter = Counter();
    var bump = () => counter.add(1);
    bump();
    bump();
    assert(counter.count == 2, "shared struct");

    var triple = Scaler(3).scaler();
    assert(triple(4) == 12, "captured this");

    # A closure can return a closure.
    var adder: (int) => (int) => int = (a) => (b) => a + b;
    assert(adder(2)(3) == 5, "curried");
    return 0;
}

  • Parameter types. (x: int) => x * 2 writes the parameter type. When the closure goes straight into a slot of function type (a typed variable, a parameter, an assignment, a return, a field), the types come from that slot, so (a, b) => a + b is enough. A parameter of a generic function counts too: passing (x) => x + 1 to apply<T>(f: (T) => T, x: T) with x an int types the closure's x as int (see Generics). With no slot to take them from, a parameter without a type is an error:

    main.pep:2:14: error: cannot infer the type of parameter 'x'; write it: (x: Type) => ...

  • Return type. It is inferred from the body, or from the slot. To write it, put it after the parameters: (x: int): long => x. When the slot returns a trait, a body that returns a struct declaring it is enough, also when the struct is what binds the trait's type arguments: passing (n) => [n, n].iterate() to count<U>(make: (int) => Iterator<U>) binds U, and the closure returns the Iterator<U>.

  • Body. An expression body is the value the closure returns. A block body uses return like a function. A closure whose type returns void can have an expression body such as () => counter.add(1); the value is discarded.

  • Calling. A closure is called like any function value, and can be called where it is written: ((x: int) => x + 1)(2).

Captured values

A closure can use the local variables and parameters around it. It keeps a copy of each one it uses, made when the closure is created, so it can outlive the function that created it (make_adder above).

A captured variable must never be assigned, before or after the closure is created, inside the closure or outside it. Then the copy and the variable can never differ:

var count = 0;
var f = () => count;
count = 5;   # error

main.pep:4:5: error: cannot assign to 'count' because a closure captures it
main.pep:3:19: note: captured here; a closure keeps a copy, so the variable must not change

The rule applies to ++, -- and compound assignments too. Only the variable is fixed: a captured struct is a reference to the same object, so the closure can call its methods and change its fields (counter above). To share a changing number, capture a struct that holds it, such as a Counter or an Atomic<int>.

this in methods

A closure written in a method can use this, the struct's fields and its methods. It captures this (one reference to the object), never a copy of the fields, so it sees the fields' current values. In a trait's default method, a closure can use this and the trait's methods the same way.

Storing such a closure in a field of the same object would make the object and the closure keep each other alive forever (a reference cycle), so that direct case is an error:

main.pep:4:15: error: storing a closure that captures 'this' in field 'measure' of 'this' creates a reference cycle that is never freed

Capture a weak reference to the object instead.

Type checking

A function value must match the type it flows into exactly: the same parameter types in the same order and the same return type. The aliases of a primitive type count as the same type, so (i32) => i32 and (int) => int match. A mismatch in an initializer, an assignment, an argument or a return is a compile error, as is calling a function value with the wrong number of arguments:

square(x: int): int { return x * x; }

main(): int {
    var f: (String) => int = square;   # error
    return f(1, 2);                    # error
}

main.pep:4:30: error: cannot initialize variable 'f' of type '(String) => int' with a value of type '(int) => int'
    4 |     var f: (String) => int = square;   # error
      |                              ^~~~~~
main.pep:5:12: error: too many arguments to function of type '(String) => int': expected 1, have 2
    5 |     return f(1, 2);                    # error
      |            ^

The compiler reports one error at a time, so the second appears once the first is fixed.

Calling a variable that does not hold a function is an error at the call, which names the variable's type:

main.pep:3:12: error: called object type 'String' is not a function
    3 |     return name(1);
      |            ^~~~

Sharing function values between threads

A plain function type such as () => void can hold any function value, including a closure that captures a String or an Array. Such values stay on the thread that made them: their reference counts are plain increments, like those of a struct that is not [Shared] (see What threads can share).

A function type written with shared in front, such as shared () => void or shared (long) => void, is thread-safe. Its reference counts are atomic, and its values hold only thread-safe state, so any thread may copy, call and drop them. It goes wherever a thread-safe type is required: the body of a thread (ThreadBody is shared () => void), a field of a [Shared] struct, a module-scope variable, or async.Atomic<shared (int) => int>.

# shared function types: function values that threads can share.
import async;

const total = async.Atomic<long>(0);

# A named function holds no state, so it is always thread-safe.
add_one() {
    total.fetch_add(1);
}

# A [Shared] struct's fields must be thread-safe: a function field is shared.
[Shared]
struct Task {
    const weight: long;
    const run: shared (long) => void;
    construct(this.weight = 1, this.run = (n: long) => {}) {}
}

# A plain function type takes any function of the same signature.
apply(f: (long) => long, x: long): long {
    return f(x);
}

main(): int {
    # A closure converts to a shared type when everything it captures is
    # thread-safe: here nothing but the module-scope Atomic.
    var add: shared (long) => void = (n: long) => { total.fetch_add(n); };
    var task = Task(10, add);

    # A thread body is a shared () => void. This closure captures a
    # [Shared] struct.
    var worker = async.Thread.spawn(() => { task.run(task.weight); });
    var other = async.Thread.spawn(add_one);
    worker.join();
    other.join();
    assert(total.load() == 11, "both threads ran");

    # A shared value can be used where a plain one is expected.
    var step: long = 5;
    var add_step: shared (long) => long = (x: long) => x + step;
    assert(apply(add_step, 1) == 6, "shared value passed as plain");

    # A plain closure may capture anything, but stays on this thread.
    var name = "worker";
    var greet = () => name + " done";
    assert(greet() == "worker done", "plain closure");
    return 0;
}

  • What converts to shared. A named function, which holds no state; a method, constructor or generic function value with nothing captured, such as Point.norm or Box<int>; and a closure literal (or a bound method such as p.norm) whose captured values are all thread-safe: numbers, Atomic<T> and other [Shared] structs, shared function values, and the rest of that list. The value must be written where the shared type is expected, so that it is made thread-safe from the start.

  • What does not. A closure that captures a value that is not thread-safe is reported at the capture, with a note at the captured variable:

    main.pep:5:46: error: closure passed as 'shared () => void' captures 'name' of type 'String', which is not thread-safe
    5 |     var t = async.Thread.spawn(() => { print(name); });
      |                                              ^~~~
main.pep:4:9: note: capture a thread-safe value instead, such as an 'async.Atomic<T>' or a '[Shared]' struct
    4 |     var name = "worker";
      |         ^~~~

    A closure in a method that uses this or a member captures this, so it is thread-safe only in a [Shared] struct. A value that already has a plain type (a variable, a parameter, a call result) never becomes shared, even when it holds nothing:

    main.pep:3:32: error: cannot initialize variable 'f' of type 'shared () => void' with a value of type '() => void'
    3 |     var f: shared () => void = g;
      |                                ^

  • From shared to plain. A shared value converts to the plain type of the same signature anywhere: shared (long) => long can be passed to a parameter of type (long) => long. The conversion allocates a small plain function value that holds the shared one and calls it, so the plain copy counts with plain increments while the shared value keeps its atomic ones.

  • Inference. A variable initialized with a closure, such as var f = () => 1;, has a plain type. Write the type to make it shared: var f: shared () => int = () => 1;.

  • shared is special only directly before a function type; elsewhere it is an ordinary name.

Null function values

A function-typed variable or field that has never been assigned is null. Calling it stops the program with the message called a null function value:

var handler: (int) => int;
handler(1);   # panics: called a null function value

Names and shadowing

A local variable, parameter or field with the same name as a free function hides the function inside its scope. Inside a function with a parameter named square, square means the parameter, not the function.

Memory

A function value is a reference, like a struct value, and follows the same reference-counting rules (see Memory and reference counting). Referring to a named function allocates nothing: every reference to square shares one static function object, and so does a generic function named without its type arguments (larger as an (int, int) => int). A method, constructor or generic function value allocates one small object, like a closure; a bound method's object holds a reference to its receiver.

Creating a closure allocates one object holding the captured values, like constructing a struct. Copying the closure adds a reference to that object, and when the last reference goes, the object releases what it captured.

A plain function value's counts are plain increments; a shared one's are atomic, like a [Shared] struct's (see Sharing function values between threads).

C function pointers

A C function pointer type, extern (P...) => R, holds a bare address that C can call, not a function value: it takes a named function or a closure that captures nothing, and never a closure that captures values. That is by design; see Passing a Pepper function to C for how a callback gets the state it needs.

Memory and reference counting

Pepper frees memory for you, without a garbage collector and without ownership annotations. Every struct object keeps a count of the references to it, and the object is destroyed the moment that count drops to zero. Because the rules are simple and the same everywhere, you can always tell when an object will be destroyed and its destructor will run.

If you know C++, the whole model fits in one sentence: every struct value behaves exactly like a std::shared_ptr<T> passed by value.

Values and references

Numbers, bool, and the other primitive types are plain values: assigning one copies it, as in C. So is a tuple, whose elements are copied the way each element would be on its own, and so is a struct or enum marked [Value], such as Optional<T> and Result<T> (see value enums).

Everything else, including your own structs, String, Array, HashMap, and function values, is a reference to an object on the heap. Assigning a reference, passing it to a function, or storing it in a field or an array shares the object. Nothing is copied.

struct Account {
    var balance: int = 0;
}

# The parameter is another reference to the caller's object, so changes to
# its fields are visible to the caller.
deposit(account: Account, amount: int) {
    account.balance += amount;
}

# Rebinding the parameter itself only changes this function's reference.
replace(account: Account) {
    account = Account();
    account.balance = 999;
}

main(): int {
    var mine = Account();
    var yours = mine;               # shares the object; nothing is copied
    yours.balance = 50;
    assert(mine.balance == 50, "assignment shares the object");

    deposit(mine, 25);
    assert(mine.balance == 75, "a function can change the shared object");

    replace(mine);
    assert(mine.balance == 75, "rebinding a parameter does not affect the caller");

    # To get an independent object, make a new one and copy the fields.
    var copy = Account();
    copy.balance = mine.balance;
    copy.balance = 0;
    assert(mine.balance == 75, "the copy is a separate object");
    return 0;
}
  • var yours = mine; makes a second reference to the same Account. Changes through either name are visible through both.
  • A parameter is one more reference to the caller's object. The function can change the object's fields, but assigning a new object to the parameter only changes the function's own reference.
  • To get an independent object, create a new one. Pepper does not copy structs for you; some library types offer a method for it, such as Array's clone().

A struct-typed variable or field that has not been given a value, such as var next: Account;, is null: it refers to no object. Reading a field or calling a method through a null reference crashes the program. Use === or !== to check whether two references name the same object, or whether one is null (next === __null). A struct is not a condition by itself, so if (next) is an error unless the struct declares the truth test !! (see Truth tests and conditions). For a value that may be absent, prefer Optional<T>, whose type says so.

When objects are destroyed

A reference is held by whatever stores it: a local variable, a parameter, a field, an element of a container, or a temporary value in the middle of an expression. Each of those releases its reference exactly once, when it goes away. When the last reference is released, the object is destroyed: its destructor runs, and then its fields release their own references, which may destroy further objects in turn.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Tracked {
    var name: String;
    construct(this.name = "") {}
    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

struct Holder {
    var item: Tracked;
}

make(name: String): Tracked {
    var t = Tracked(name);
    return t;                   # the caller receives the object
}

main(): int {
    # 1. A local is released when its scope ends.
    {
        var a = Tracked("a");
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 1, "a was destroyed at the end of its block");

    # 2. While another reference exists, the object stays alive.
    var b = Tracked("b");
    var also_b = b;
    b = Tracked("b2");          # b lets go of the first object...
    assert(destroyed.load() == 1, "...but also_b still holds it");
    also_b = b;                 # the last reference moves away
    assert(destroyed.load() == 2, "the first object is destroyed now");

    # 3. Fields and containers hold references too.
    var holder = Holder();
    {
        var c = Tracked("c");
        holder.item = c;
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 2, "holder.item keeps c alive after its scope");
    holder = Holder();          # the old Holder dies and releases c
    assert(destroyed.load() == 3, "releasing the holder released its field");

    var list = Array<Tracked>();
    list.append(Tracked("d"));
    assert(destroyed.load() == 3, "the array holds d");
    list.clear();
    assert(destroyed.load() == 4, "clearing the array released d");

    # 4. Returned objects belong to the caller; unused results are
    #    destroyed right away.
    var e = make("e");
    assert(destroyed.load() == 4, "e is alive in main");
    make("temporary");
    assert(destroyed.load() == 5, "a result nobody keeps is destroyed immediately");
    return 0;
}

Destroying an object first runs its destructor, then releases its fields in reverse declaration order; an object a field release destroys is destroyed completely, its own fields included, before the next field is released. So an object's destructor always runs before those of the objects it held.

A chain of any length can be released: a linked list of a million links, or a document nested a million levels deep, is destroyed without running out of stack. This changes the order above only for a recursive type: a struct whose fields can lead, through any number of steps, back to a value of its own type. A field that holds an object of the same cycle (a list's next, a tree's left and right, a node's children array and the nodes in it, a trait value, a closure and what it captures) is released only after the object holding it is completely destroyed, its other fields included, and the chain is destroyed in a loop: an object's destructor still runs before those of the objects it held, the last-declared of those fields still goes first, and an array's elements go in index order, but an object's other fields are released before the chain below it. A cycle that runs through anything else, such as a tuple or the elements of another container (a HashMap, an Optional), nests as usual until it is about 16 KiB of stack deep; past that, further objects wait on a list for the current thread and are destroyed, in the order they were released, when the outermost release has finished its own object. Either way, every object is destroyed before the release that started it returns, and a type no cycle runs through is destroyed exactly as described above.

import async;

const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Link {
    var next: Link;
    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

# A node of a tree, holding its children in an array.
struct Tree {
    var children: Array<Tree> = Array<Tree>();
    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

main(): int {
    # A million links, each holding the next one.
    var head = Link();
    var node = head;
    for (var i in 0..999999) {
        node.next = Link();
        node = node.next;
    }
    node = Link();
    # Releasing the head destroys the whole chain, without one stack frame
    # per link.
    head = Link();
    assert(destroyed.load() == 1000000, "every link was destroyed");

    # A tree a hundred thousand levels deep, through its children arrays.
    var root = Tree();
    var branch = root;
    for (var i in 0..99999) {
        var child = Tree();
        branch.children.append(child);
        branch = child;
    }
    branch = Tree();
    root = Tree();
    assert(destroyed.load() == 1100000, "every node was destroyed");
    return 0;
}

Concretely, a reference is released when:

  • A local variable goes out of scope, at the closing brace of the block that declared it, or when the function returns.
  • A variable or field is overwritten. b = Tracked("b2"); releases the object b held before, after taking the new one. Assigning a variable to itself (a = a) changes nothing.
  • A parameter's function returns. The function held its parameters for as long as it ran.
  • The object that holds a field is destroyed, or a container removes an element (clear(), overwriting list[i], and so on). remove_at() and pop() are the exception: they hand the container's reference to the caller, so var x = list.remove_at(0); leaves the count unchanged.
  • A temporary is no longer needed. A result that is not stored anywhere, like the one from make("temporary");, is released at the end of the statement. The same goes for a call result passed straight to another function, and for the object in make().name.

Returning a local hands its reference to the caller, so the object survives the function. Calling a method on an object does not add a reference to it: inside the method, this refers to the caller's object.

Cycles leak

Reference counting cannot free a cycle: objects that refer to each other, directly or through a chain, keep each other's counts above zero even after nothing else refers to them. Their destructors never run and their memory is never freed.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Person {
    var name: String;
    var friends: Array<Person>;

    construct(this.name = "") {
        friends = Array<Person>();
    }

    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

main(): int {
    # Two people who list each other as friends form a cycle: each keeps
    # the other alive, so neither is ever destroyed.
    {
        var ann = Person("Ann");
        var bob = Person("Bob");
        ann.friends.append(bob);
        bob.friends.append(ann);
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 0, "the cycle leaked both objects");

    # Break the cycle before letting go, and both are destroyed.
    {
        var cat = Person("Cat");
        var dan = Person("Dan");
        cat.friends.append(dan);
        dan.friends.append(cat);
        dan.friends.clear();    # Dan no longer holds Cat
    }
    assert(destroyed.load() == 2, "without the cycle, both were destroyed");
    return 0;
}

To avoid a cycle, make one direction of it a weak reference (next section), or break the cycle yourself before the last outside reference goes away: clear the container, or overwrite the field, that closes the loop.

A closure holds a reference to every struct it captures, including this, so a closure stored inside an object it captures closes a cycle too. The compiler reports the direct case, a method storing a closure that captures this in a field of this.

Weak references

A Weak<T> points at an object without keeping it alive. Use it for back pointers: a child's parent, a document's folder, an observer's subject. The owner holds strong references down the tree, and everything that points back up holds a Weak<T>, so there is no cycle.

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const destroyed = async.Atomic<int>(0);

struct Folder {
    var name: String;
    var files: Array<Document>;

    construct(this.name = "") {
        files = Array<Document>();
    }

    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

struct Document {
    var title: String;
    # A weak back pointer: the folder owns its documents, not the other way
    # round, so there is no cycle.
    var folder: Weak<Folder>;

    construct(String title, Folder folder) {
        this.title = title;
        this.folder = Weak<Folder>(folder);
    }

    destruct {
        destroyed.fetch_add(1);
    }

    String path() {
        with (var f = folder) {
            return f.name + "/" + title;
        } else {
            return "(deleted)/" + title;
        }
        return "";
    }
}

main(): int {
    var kept = Document("draft", Folder("none"));
    {
        var home = Folder("home");
        var notes = Document("notes", home);
        home.files.append(notes);
        assert(notes.path() == "home/notes", "the folder is alive");
        kept = notes;
    }
    # The folder went away with `home`; the weak pointer did not keep it.
    assert(kept.path() == "(deleted)/notes", "the folder is gone");
    assert(kept.folder.expired(), "and the weak reference knows it");
    return 0;
}
  • Weak<T>(object) makes the weak reference. It does not change the object's reference count.
  • A with block reaches the object: with (var f = folder) { ... } binds f to an ordinary strong reference for the length of the block. When the object has already been destroyed, the body is skipped and the else block runs. See Scoped blocks with with.
  • expired() reports whether the object has been destroyed.
  • T may be a trait: Weak<Shape> upgrades to a Shape (see Weak references and atomics).
  • The object is destroyed on time. When its last strong reference goes, its destructor runs and its fields are released, even if weak references remain. Only the object's small header stays allocated until the last weak reference is gone.

In C++ terms, a struct value is a std::shared_ptr<T> and Weak<T> wraps the built-in __weak<T>, a std::weak_ptr<T>: Weak<T>(object) is weak_ptr(object), and entering it with with is lock().
