Inside a constructor, this already holds the object's first reference, like the shared_ptr that make_shared fills in: a constructor may pass this to a function or store it, and a weak reference made from it upgrades, without the object being destroyed when those copies are dropped.

References and threads

Reference counts are plain, fast increments, so a struct's objects must stay on one thread. A struct declared [Shared] has atomic counts instead, and its references can be copied and dropped on any thread. The compiler requires such a struct's fields to be const and thread-safe. See What threads can share.

Function values follow the same split: a plain function type such as () => void has plain counts and stays on one thread, and a shared function type such as shared () => void has atomic counts.

Copying a value with copy

copy(value) makes a copy of a value that shares no object that is not thread-safe with the original, so the copy can go to another thread: pass copy(x) to a channel to send a value you keep using.

var names = Array<String>();
names.append("ada");
var copied = copy(names);
copied[0].append(" lovelace");   # names[0] is still "ada"
  • Every struct object the value reaches is copied once. An object referenced twice is copied once and stays shared inside the copy, and a cycle becomes the same cycle among the copies.
  • Thread-safe objects are not copied: a [Shared] struct or a shared function value in the original is the same object in the copy. For a thread-safe value, copy returns the value itself.
  • A weak reference to an object that was copied points at its copy. A weak reference to an object outside the copied value becomes null.
  • A struct is copied field by field, without running its constructor.

A struct with a destructor or a raw pointer (__ptr<T>) field is not trivially copyable: copying its fields would share what it owns, such as a buffer it frees. Such a struct says how to copy itself by implementing Copyable<T>, with a copy(): T method that builds the copy and copies each value it holds with copy(value). String, Array, HashMap and HashSet implement it. String.copy() also copies a single String; it replaces the deprecated clone(). Array.clone() is unchanged: it copies the Array but shares its elements.

# A struct with a destructor is not trivially copyable, so it implements
# `Copyable<T>` to say how `copy` copies it.
struct Buffer {
    __ptr<u8> data;
    ulong size;
    String label;

    construct(size: ulong) {
        data = _pep_malloc(size);
        this.size = size;
        label = "buffer";
    }

    destruct {
        _pep_free(data);
    }

    copy(): Buffer {
        var made = Buffer(size);
        var i: ulong = 0;
        while (i < size) {
            made.data[i] = data[i];
            i = i + 1;
        }
        # The free function `copy`: it continues the running copy.
        made.label = copy(label);
        return made;
    }
}

extend Buffer with Copyable<Buffer>;

struct Message {
    Buffer body;
    Buffer again;
}

main(): int {
    var message = Message();
    message.body = Buffer(4);
    message.body.data[0] = 9;
    message.again = message.body;

    var copied = copy(message);
    copied.body.data[0] = 1;
    copied.body.label.append(" (copy)");
    assert(message.body.data[0] == 9, "the original buffer is unchanged");
    assert(message.body.label == "buffer", "the original label is unchanged");
    # The buffer appears twice, so its copy is one object.
    assert(copied.again === copied.body, "one copy of the shared buffer");
    return 0;
}

Inside copy(), the call copy(label) is the free function, not the method: a bare call in a method names the struct's own method only when one by that name takes those arguments. While a copy runs, copy(value) continues it rather than starting another, so an object the outer copy already made is reused and sharing is kept. That is why a Copyable value is copied with copy(x): calling x.copy() directly still works, but each copy(value) inside it is then a copy of its own. A value whose contents can lead back to it calls register_copy(this, made) before copying them, so the cycle finds the copy being built.

The copy(copies: Copies): T form of Copyable<T>, which took the copy's context as an argument and copied with copies.copy(value), still works in this release, with a warning at Copies.

Copying a value that reaches a struct that is not trivially copyable and does not implement Copyable<T> is an error at the copy call. It names the struct, shows each field on the way to it, says why it cannot be copied, and shows a Copyable<T> to fill in (the editor offers to insert it):

main.pep:14:13: error: cannot copy 'Log' because it contains 'Handle', which is not trivially copyable
   14 |     var c = copy(log);
      |             ^~~~
main.pep:9:5: note: 'Log' reaches it through field 'out'
    9 |     Handle out;
      |     ^~~~~~
main.pep:1:8: note: 'Handle' has a destructor, so copying its fields would release what it owns twice
    1 | struct Handle {
      |        ^~~~~~
note: implement 'Copyable<Handle>' to say how to copy it:
    extend Handle with Copyable<Handle> {
        copy(): Handle {
            # Build the copy; copy each struct field with copy(field).
            panic("copying 'Handle' is not implemented");
            return this;
        }
    }

Some types cannot be copied at all: an io.File owns an operating-system handle, so the error says to send its path instead. A plain function value cannot be copied, because it may capture anything; declare it shared.

Copying trait values

copy of a trait value copies the struct behind it, as copy of that struct would, and returns the copy as the same trait type. Sharing works across the boundary: a struct reached twice, through a trait value or directly, is copied once.

# `copy` of a trait value copies the struct behind it, whichever it is.
trait Shape {
    area(): int;
    grow();
}

struct Square {
    var side: int = 1;
    construct(this.side = 1) {}
}

extend Square with Shape {
    area(): int { return side * side; }
    grow() { side = side + 1; }
}

struct Rect {
    var width: int = 1;
    var height: int = 1;
    construct(this.width = 1, this.height = 1) {}
}

extend Rect with Shape {
    area(): int { return width * height; }
    grow() { width = width + 1; }
}

main(): int {
    var shapes = Array<Shape>();
    var square = Square(2);
    shapes.append(square);
    shapes.append(Rect(2, 3));
    shapes.append(square);

    var copied = copy(shapes);
    for (var shape in copied) {
        shape.grow();
    }
    assert(shapes[0].area() == 4, "the original Square is unchanged");
    assert(shapes[1].area() == 6, "the original Rect is unchanged");

    # The Square appears twice, so its copy is one object, grown twice.
    assert(copied[0] == copied[2], "one copy of the shared Square");
    assert(copied[0].area() == 16, "the copied Square grew twice");
    assert(copied[1].area() == 9, "the copied Rect grew once");
    return 0;
}

Which struct a trait value holds is known only when the program runs, so the compiler cannot check that it can be copied. Copying a trait value that holds a struct that cannot be copied (one with a destructor and no Copyable<T>, an io.File, a MutexGuard) panics:

cannot copy the 'Owner' behind a trait value, which is not trivially copyable

Handing a reference over with move

move(x) gives up x's reference: the call returns the same object, and x is left null. Nothing is copied and no count changes. It is how a value built in a local variable goes to a channel, a Mutex or another [Move] parameter, which takes a new value, without the cost of copy(x):

var lines = Array<String>();
lines.append("first");
var log = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(move(lines));   # lines is now null

move is an ordinary function from the prelude (runtime/copy.pep), but the compiler checks every call:

  • Only a local variable can be moved (move(h.s) is an error), and only when it holds the one reference to a new value: nothing else refers to it or to anything it reaches. A parameter can be moved only when it is [Move], since the caller handed its value over.

    main.pep:8:24: error: 'a' cannot be moved: 'b' also references its value
    8 |     names.replace(move(a));
      |                        ^
note: only a variable that holds the one reference to a new value can hand it over; pass 'copy(...)' instead

Only a variable still in scope counts: one declared in a block that has ended no longer references anything. A closure references what it captures, so a captured value can be moved once no closure that holds it is left: its block has ended, it was only passed to a call that does not keep it, or the function that made it has returned. A closure still in a variable, stored in a field, or returned and kept still holds the value:

import async;

struct Counter {
    var n: int;

    construct(n: int) {
        this.n = n;
    }
}

repeat(times: int, f: () => void) {
    for (var _ in 0..times) {
        f();
    }
}

main(): int {
    var counters = async.Channel<Counter>();

    var a = Counter(0);
    {
        var bump = () => {
            a.n += 1;
        };
        bump();
    }
    # `bump` is gone with its block, so `a` holds the only reference.
    counters.send(move(a));

    var b = Counter(10);
    # `repeat` calls the closure but does not keep it.
    repeat(3, () => {
        b.n += 1;
    });
    counters.send(move(b));

    # var c = Counter(0);
    # var show = () => print($"{c.n}");
    # counters.send(move(c));   # error: 'show' also references its value

    print($"{counters.receive().value().n}");  # 1
    print($"{counters.receive().value().n}");  # 13
    return 0;
}

What ? or a pattern binding takes out of a call's result can be moved too: the Result or Optional the call returned is a temporary, which lets go of its value once the value is read. One kept in a variable still holds it:

import async;

struct Connection {
    var id: int;

    construct(id: int) {
        this.id = id;
    }
}

connect(id: int): Result<Connection, String> {
    return Result<Connection, String>.ok(Connection(id));
}

open_both(pool: async.Channel<Connection>): Result<void, String> {
    # The `Result` is a temporary: once `?` has read it, `first` holds
    # the only reference to the connection.
    var first = connect(1)?;
    pool.send(move(first));
    if (connect(2) is Ok(second)) {
        pool.send(move(second));
    }

    # var kept = connect(3);
    # var third = kept?;
    # pool.send(move(third));   # error: 'kept' also references its value
    return Result<void, String>.ok();
}

main(): int {
    var pool = async.Channel<Connection>();
    open_both(pool);
    print($"{pool.receive().value().id}");  # 1
    print($"{pool.receive().value().id}");  # 2
    return 0;
}

In a loop, the check counts every reference the loop's body makes, wherever in the body it is made: a statement after the move runs again before the next pass's move. So a loop can move a variable it gives a new value each pass, but not one it also stores in a variable from outside the loop, even after the move:

import async;

struct Counter {
    var n: int;

    construct(n: int) {
        this.n = n;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var counters = async.Channel<Counter>();

    var a = Counter(1);
    for (var i in 0..3) {
        counters.send(move(a));
        # A new value before the next pass, so `a` holds the only reference.
        a = Counter(i + 2);
    }

    # var last = Counter(0);
    # var b = Counter(1);
    # for (var i in 0..3) {
    #     counters.send(move(b));   # error: 'last' also references its value
    #     b = Counter(i + 2);
    #     last = b;                 # still there on the next pass
    # }

    var total = 0;
    for (var _ in 0..3) {
        total += counters.receive().value().n;
    }
    print($"{total}");  # 6
    return 0;
}

  • A moved variable cannot be read again until it is assigned a new value, including on the next pass through a loop:

    main.pep:8:12: error: 'a' is used after its value was moved
    8 |     return a.count;
      |            ^
main.pep:7:19: note: 'a' was moved here; assign it a new value before using it again
    7 |     names.replace(move(a));
      |                   ^~~~

The runtime also moves values out of raw memory (move(buffer[head])), which is a promise the compiler cannot check: only runtime files may do it. The parameter of move is marked [MoveSource], which is also only allowed in the runtime, so a hand-off always shows at the call as move(x); a function of your own that takes over its argument uses [Move].

Where objects live

Every object, String buffer and Array buffer comes from the runtime's allocator. A block of up to 128 bytes (most objects and short strings) comes from a small block allocator: blocks are grouped by size into classes (multiples of 16 bytes up to 128, then four classes per power of two). Each class's blocks are cut from 64 KiB spans, and a thread hands out a class's blocks from one span at a time, so objects made one after another sit close together in memory. Allocating, and freeing on the thread that allocated, take no lock; a block freed on another thread goes back to its span with one atomic step. Larger blocks come from the C library's calloc and go back with free. A small block's size is rounded up to its class, so a 40-byte object takes 48 bytes.

An empty Array allocates nothing. Array<T>() makes no object until the Array is written (append, insert, reserve, ...) or shared (assigned to a second variable, stored in a field or element, passed or returned): reading it (count, is_empty, contains, a for loop over it) allocates nothing. The first write or share allocates the object, so every name for the Array still sees the same appends:

struct Node {
    String name;
    # Most nodes never get children, and an empty Array costs nothing.
    Array<Node> children = Array<Node>();
    construct(name: String) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var a = Array<int>();           # no allocation
    assert(a.count == 0 && a.is_empty, "reading allocates nothing");
    for (var x in a) {
        assert(false, "an empty Array has no elements");
    }
    var b = a;                      # allocates the Array: a and b share it
    b.append(1);                    # allocates its buffer
    assert(a.count == 1, "both names see the append");

    var leaf = Node("leaf");
    var root = Node("root");
    root.children.append(leaf);
    assert(leaf.children.is_empty && root.children.count == 1, "only root's children were allocated");
    return 0;
}

Structs that hold an Array which usually stays empty (a tree node's children, a list of comments) cost nothing extra for it.

The environment variable PEPPER_SMALL_BLOCK_LIMIT, read when the program starts, sets the largest size the small block allocator serves, in bytes, up to 4096 (a larger value counts as 4096). 0 turns it off, and then every block comes from the C library:

PEPPER_SMALL_BLOCK_LIMIT=0 ./main      # every block from calloc
PEPPER_SMALL_BLOCK_LIMIT=512 ./main    # blocks up to 512 bytes from the classes

With it off, a program can use another C allocator, such as mimalloc, by loading it in front of the C library (LD_PRELOAD=libmimalloc.so on Linux).

Small blocks live in address space the program reserves at start (4 GiB, committed 64 KiB at a time as it is used, and never returned to the operating system); a program that fills it falls back to calloc. On WebAssembly, which cannot reserve address space, every block comes from calloc.

Summary

CodeWhat happens to references
var b = a;b takes a new reference to a's object.
b = c;b takes a reference to c's object and holds it, then releases its old one. A destructor that runs then and reads b finds c's object.
f(a)The parameter takes a reference for the duration of the call.
return a;The caller receives a reference to a's object.
a.method()No change: this refers to a's object.
f(move(a))No change: a's reference goes to the call, and a is left null.
make(); (result unused)The result is released at the end of the statement.
var w = Weak<T>(a);No change to a's count; w does not keep the object alive.
var c = copy(a);c refers to new objects; a's count does not change.
end of a blockEvery local declared in the block releases its reference.

Scoped blocks with with

A with block enters a scope object, binds what it hands out, and cleans up when the object is destroyed. It plays the role of Python's with and C#'s using, but the cleanup is ordinary destruction: it runs through the same reference counting as every other object (see Memory and reference counting).

import async;

# A module-scope counter: const, and changed through an Atomic.
const open_sessions = async.Atomic<int>(0);

# A scope object: enter() hands out what the block works with, and the
# destructor calls exit() when the last reference goes away.
struct Session {
    var user: String;

    construct(this.user = "") {
        open_sessions.fetch_add(1);
    }

    destruct {
        this.exit();
    }

    Session enter() {
        return this;
    }

    exit() {
        open_sessions.fetch_sub(1);
    }
}

extend Session with Scoped<Session>;

# enter() may return a null reference: then the body is skipped and the
# `else` block runs.
struct Lookup {
    var found: Session;

    construct(Session session) {
        found = session;
    }

    Session enter() {
        return found;
    }

    exit() {}
}

extend Lookup with Scoped<Session>;

first_user(): String {
    with (var session = Session("ada")) {
        # `return` leaves the block too: the session still closes.
        return session.user;
    }
    return "";
}

main(): int {
    with (var session = Session("grace")) {
        assert(open_sessions.load() == 1, "open inside the block");
        assert(session.user == "grace", "bound to what enter() returned");
    }
    assert(open_sessions.load() == 0, "closed at the end of the block");

    assert(first_user() == "ada", "the value was returned");
    assert(open_sessions.load() == 0, "closed on return as well");

    var hits = 0;
    with (var s = Lookup(Session("linus"))) {
        hits += 1;
    } else {
        hits -= 100;
    }
    with (var s = Lookup(__null)) {
        hits -= 100;
    } else {
        hits += 1;
    }
    assert(hits == 2, "the body ran for a session, the else block for null");
    return 0;
}

The header

with (var name = scope) { ... } else { ... }
with (Type name = scope) { ... }
with (scope) { ... }
  • name is bound to scope.enter(), not to scope itself. A Session can hand out itself; a Weak<T> hands out a strong reference to the object it points at, or null once that object is gone.
  • Without a binding, the block still holds the result of enter() until it ends. An enter() that returns nothing (declared without a return type) has nothing to bind, and binding it is an error.
  • The parentheses are optional, as with if, while and for. The braces are required.
  • name cannot be reassigned inside the block.

Skipping the body

When enter() returns a struct reference that is null, the body is skipped and the optional else block runs instead. else is only allowed when enter() returns a struct type, since nothing else can be null.

The Scoped<T> protocol

A type works in a with block when it has the methods of the Scoped<T> trait (runtime/scoped.pep, documented in the Scoped reference):

export trait Scoped<T> {
    enter(): T;  # what the header binds; null skips the body
    exit();      # the cleanup; call it from the destructor
}

A with block goes by the methods a type has, not by the trait: a type without enter() is a compile error in a with header. Declaring the trait (extend Session with Scoped<Session>;) documents the intent, and the compiler then checks that the type has both enter() and exit().

When exit() runs

The block keeps two locals: the scope object and the bound value. Both are released on every path out of the block (the end of the body, return, break and continue), the bound value first. Implementations call exit() from their destructor:

destruct {
    this.exit();
}

so exit() runs when the scope object's last reference is released:

  • A scope object created in the header (with (var s = Session("grace"))) is released by the block, so exit() runs at the end of the block.
  • A scope object that something else also holds (a field, another local) lives on after the block, and exit() waits for its last owner. This is the same rule as any other object.
  • A copy of the bound value that outlives the block (stored in a field, returned) keeps that value alive, but not the scope object.

A panic stops the program without running destructors, so exit() does not run then.

Threads and shared data

The async module starts and manages operating-system threads. Pepper keeps threads safe by controlling what they can share: only thread-safe values can be reached from more than one thread, and the compiler checks the types that claim to be.

On WebAssembly (--target wasm32-wasip1) a program has one thread: Thread.spawn panics. Mutexes, channels and atomics still work, as long as nothing waits for another thread (see WebAssembly).

Starting and joining threads

import async;

const finished = async.Atomic<int>(0);

# A thread body is a function that takes nothing and returns nothing.
count_to_a_million() {
    var me = async.Thread.current();
    assert(me.name() == "counter", "a spawned thread sees its own Thread");
    var total: long = 0;
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 1000000) {
        total = total + 1;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    finished.fetch_add(1);
}

main(): int {
    var main_thread = async.Thread.current();
    assert(main_thread.name() == "main", "the main thread is named main");

    var first = async.Thread.spawn(count_to_a_million, "counter");
    var second = async.Thread.spawn(count_to_a_million, "counter");
    assert(first.id() != second.id(), "every thread has its own id");

    first.join();
    second.join();
    assert(first.is_finished(), "join waits for the body to return");
    assert(finished.load() == 2, "both bodies ran");

    # A thread with 8 MiB of stack on every system.
    async.Thread.spawn(count_to_a_million, "counter", 8388608).join();
    assert(finished.load() == 3, "the third body ran");

    # How many threads can run at once, and on how many cores.
    assert(async.logical_cpus() >= async.physical_cpus(), "hyperthreads count once in physical_cpus");
    return 0;
}
  • Thread.spawn(body, name) starts a new thread that runs body, a function of type ThreadBody (an alias for shared () => void), and returns its Thread. The name is optional.
  • Thread.spawn(body, name, stack_size) gives the thread stack_size bytes of stack. Without it a thread gets the system's default: usually 8 MiB on Linux (ulimit -s), 1 MiB on Windows and 512 KiB on macOS. A thread that recurses deeply, such as one walking a deeply nested tree, passes a size so it has the same room everywhere. The stack is reserved address space: memory is used only as the thread reaches it.
  • join() waits for the body to return. After join(), the joining thread sees everything the other thread did. A thread can be joined once.
  • Thread.current() returns the calling thread's Thread. For a spawned thread it is the same object that spawn returned. The main thread's is named main.
  • id() returns the thread's ThreadId, a number that no other thread in the program has. Ids come from the runtime, starting at 1, and are not the operating system's thread ids. A ThreadId can be compared and used as a HashMap key.
  • is_finished() reports whether the body has returned. is_joinable() reports whether join() may be called.
  • Thread.sleep(milliseconds) pauses the calling thread (in a task, only the task: see Tasks).
  • Dropping every reference to a Thread without joining it detaches the thread. It keeps running, and its resources are freed when it finishes.
  • A panic or failed assert on any thread ends the whole program.

The body can be a named function or a closure. A closure passes data to the thread through its captures:

var total = async.Atomic<long>(0);
var step: long = 5;
var worker = async.Thread.spawn(() => { total.fetch_add(step); });
worker.join();

The body is a shared function value, so the closure may capture only thread-safe values (numbers, Atomic<T>, [Shared] structs, shared function values). The compiler checks each capture and reports one that is not thread-safe where the closure uses it:

main.pep:5:46: error: closure passed as 'shared () => void' captures 'name' of type 'String', which is not thread-safe
    5 |     var t = async.Thread.spawn(() => { print(name); });
      |                                              ^~~~
main.pep:4:9: note: capture a thread-safe value instead, such as an 'async.Atomic<T>' or a '[Shared]' struct
    4 |     var name = "worker";
      |         ^~~~

Every module-scope variable is const and thread-safe, so any thread may use one (see below).

The Thread reference documents every method.

Processor counts

  • async.logical_cpus() returns how many threads the machine can run at the same moment. A core with hyperthreading (SMT) counts two or more times. This is a good default size for a pool of CPU-bound worker threads. In a Linux container with a CPU quota (docker run --cpus), it is the quota rounded up, when that is fewer (see Containers).
  • async.physical_cpus() counts each physical core once. On Linux it reads the kernel's CPU topology, on macOS hw.physicalcpu, and on Windows GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx. Inside a virtual machine it counts the cores the hypervisor presents, because the guest cannot see the host's hardware.

Thread-local variables

A module-scope var marked [ThreadLocal] has a separate copy on every thread, like C++ thread_local or a Rust #[thread_local] static:

import async;

import [Thread] from async;

# A separate `depth` on every thread, each starting at 0.
[ThreadLocal]
var depth: int = 0;

const deepest = async.Atomic<int>(0);

descend(levels: int) {
    depth += 1;
    if (depth > deepest.load()) {
        deepest.store(depth);
    }
    if (levels > 1) {
        descend(levels - 1);
    }
    depth -= 1;
}

work() {
    descend(5);
}

main(): int {
    depth = 100;   # changes only the main thread's copy
    var a = Thread.spawn(work);
    var b = Thread.spawn(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(deepest.load() == 5, "each thread counted from its own 0");
    assert(depth == 100, "the main thread's copy is its own");
    return 0;
}
  • Every thread's copy starts from the initializer, which must be a constant: a number, bool or char literal (negated, or cast), an enum case, or nothing, for the type's default (zero, or null for a struct). To start from anything else, leave the initializer out and set the value on the thread's first use.
  • Reading or assigning one touches only the calling thread's copy, so it is a plain var: it need not be const like other module-scope variables, and needs no atomics or locks. A read is a single load from the thread's storage (a %fs-relative load on x86-64 Linux), not a call.
  • Its type must be thread-safe (see What threads can share): a number, a raw pointer, a [Shared] struct, a shared function type, or a tuple or [Value] struct of them. A value of any other type, such as a String, goes in a ThreadLocal<T>.
  • When a thread started with Thread.spawn exits (the async runtime's workers and blocking threads included), each of its thread-locals is set to its default and the struct it held is released, last declared first. The main thread's are never released, like every other module-scope variable, and a thread started by C code does not release its own.
  • A task sees the thread-locals of the worker thread it runs on, as with a ThreadLocal<T>.

[ThreadLocal] applies only to a module-scope variable. A variable whose type is not thread-safe, or whose initializer is not a constant, is reported at the type or the initializer:

main.pep:3:14: error: thread-local variable 'scratch' has type 'Plain', which is not thread-safe
    3 | var scratch: Plain;
      |              ^~~~~
note: a per-thread value of any type is an 'async.ThreadLocal<T>' (after 'import async')
main.pep:1:8: note: 'Plain' is not declared [Shared]
    1 | struct Plain { var x: int; }
      |        ^~~~~

main.pep:3:18: error: thread-local variable 'depth' must start from a constant
    3 | var depth: int = start();
      |                  ^~~~~
note: every thread starts from this value; leave it out and assign the value on the thread's first use instead

Per-thread values with ThreadLocal

ThreadLocal<T> is a variable with a separate value on every thread, of any type:

import async;

import [Thread, ThreadLocal] from async;

# One variable, a separate value on every thread.
const calls = ThreadLocal<int>();
const totals = async.Atomic<long>(0);

record_call() {
    calls.set(calls.get() + 1);
}

work() {
    record_call();
    record_call();
    record_call();
    totals.fetch_add(calls.get());   # 3 on every thread
}

main(): int {
    record_call();
    var a = Thread.spawn(work);
    var b = Thread.spawn(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(totals.load() == 6, "each thread counted its own calls");
    assert(calls.get() == 1, "the main thread's value is its own");
    return 0;
}
  • get() returns the calling thread's value, or the default of T (zero, or null for a struct) until that thread calls set.
  • set(value) replaces only the calling thread's value.
  • is_set() and clear() test for and remove the calling thread's value.
  • When a thread started with Thread.spawn exits, its value is released, even if the ThreadLocal itself was destroyed first. As with [ThreadLocal] variables, the main thread's value is released only by clear(), and a thread started by C code leaks the values it did not clear.
  • Each thread keeps its values in a table of its own, held in [ThreadLocal] variables, so get() costs a few loads and no call, and a program can have any number of ThreadLocals.

A ThreadLocal is usually a module-scope variable. Its T does not need to be thread-safe, because each value stays on the thread that stored it. For a T that is not thread-safe, such as a String, the value is reached like a Mutex's (see What a lock body may do):

  • with (var value = local.enter()) { ... } binds this thread's value; the else block runs when the thread has none;
  • get() is a compile error;
  • set(value) takes a new value: a constructor call, a string literal, copy(x), or move(x).

Otherwise a function called while a Mutex is locked could keep part of the locked value in a thread-local, and a later get() would hand it out after the lock was released. The ThreadLocal reference has the details.

Tasks that take turns on one worker thread share its ThreadLocal values; a TaskLocal<T> gives each task its own.

What threads can share

Every struct value is a counted reference (see Memory and reference counting). Updating a count from two threads at once can free an object too early or never, so by default a struct's counts are plain, fast increments, and its objects must stay on one thread.

A struct declared [Shared] has atomic reference counts, so references to one object can be copied and dropped on any thread:

import async;

# A struct that threads can share: declared [Shared], every field const and
# thread-safe.
[Shared]
struct Settings {
    const port: int;
    const retries: int;
    construct(this.port = 0, this.retries = 0) {}
}

# async.Atomic<T> of a [Shared] struct: threads read the current settings, and one
# of them can replace them.
const current = async.Atomic<Settings>(Settings(8080, 3));
const seen = async.Atomic<long>(0);

read_settings() {
    var settings = current.load();
    seen.fetch_add(settings.port);
}

main(): int {
    var readers = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 4) {
        readers.append(async.Thread.spawn(read_settings));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    for (var reader in readers) {
        reader.join();
    }
    assert(seen.load() == 4 * 8080, "every reader saw the settings");

    current.store(Settings(9090, 5));
    assert(current.load().port == 9090, "replaced");
    return 0;
}

The compiler checks every [Shared] struct:

  • Every field must be const. It is set once, by the constructor, and never assigned again, so threads cannot race on it. To change shared state, give the struct a thread-safe member such as an Atomic<T>.

  • Every field must have a thread-safe type. These are all the thread-safe types, the same ones the constraint T: Shared accepts:

    • every number type (int, long, byte, char, short, float, double and the rest), bool, and void;
    • enums whose cases carry no values, which are stored as integers;
    • [Shared] structs, and enums whose cases carry values that are declared [Shared];
    • weak references to thread-safe types;
    • raw pointers (__ptr<T>, and void*) to thread-safe types;
    • shared function types, such as shared () => void (see Function types), and C function pointer types (extern (int) => int);
    • tuples whose elements are all thread-safe;
    • inside a generic, a type parameter constrained T: Shared.

    Nothing else is. A struct is never thread-safe on its own, even when all its fields are numbers: a struct value is a reference to a reference-counted object, and only a [Shared] struct counts those references atomically. So String, Array and other structs that are not [Shared] are not thread-safe, and neither is a plain function type such as () => void:

    main.pep:3:14: error: field 'F' of shared struct 'H' has type '() => void', which is not thread-safe
    3 |     const F: () => void;
      |              ^~~~~~~~~~
note: declare the function type 'shared () => void' to share it between threads

A generic [Shared] struct whose parameter has no constraint is checked for each set of type arguments, and the error points at the code that asked for the specialization:

[Shared]
struct Cell<T> {
    const value: T;
}

make<T>(): Cell<T> { return Cell<T>(); }

main(): int {
    var c = make<String>();
    return 0;
}

main.pep:9:13: error: 'make<String>' requires thread-safe type arguments; 'String' is not thread-safe
    9 |     var c = make<String>();
      |             ^~~~~~~~~~~~
main.pep:6:29: note: 'Cell<String>' is required here, in 'make<String>'
    6 | make<T>(): Cell<T> { return Cell<T>(); }
      |                             ^~~~~~~
main.pep:3:18: note: required by field 'value' declared here
    3 |     const value: T;
      |                  ^
runtime/string.pep:54:15: note: 'String' is not declared [Shared]

A generic can state the rule up front with the built-in constraint T: Shared: [Shared] struct Cell<T: Shared> accepts exactly the type arguments above, and a wrong one is reported where it is written ('String' does not conform to 'Shared', required by 'T' in 'Cell'). The standard library's Atomic<T>, spawn, run_blocking and Lazy<T> do this, so Atomic<String> is reported at String.

A field that is not const, or that has a type that is not thread-safe, is reported at the field:

main.pep:3:9: error: field 'Count' of shared struct 'Counter' must be 'const'
    3 |     int Count;
      |         ^~~~~
note: threads change a shared struct's state through a thread-safe member such as 'async.Atomic<T>' (after 'import async')

Thread, ThreadLocal<T> and Atomic<T> are [Shared] themselves, and so are the synchronization types below: Channel<T>, Mutex<T>, Condition<T>, RwLock<T>, Semaphore, Barrier, Latch, Once and Lazy<T>.

Module-scope variables

Every module-scope variable is implicitly shared, exported or not: any function can use it, and any function can run on any thread. So it follows the same two rules as a field of a [Shared] struct:

  • It must be const. To change the value, give it a thread-safe type such as Atomic<T>, or a ThreadLocal<T> for a value per thread. The one exception is a [ThreadLocal] variable, which every thread has its own copy of.
  • It must have a thread-safe type from the list above. A String, an Array, a struct that is not [Shared], a trait value, or a plain function value cannot be a module-scope variable; keep it in a local, or in a ThreadLocal<T>.
const MAX_WORKERS = 8;                  # a number
const jobs_done = async.Atomic<long>(0);  # changed with fetch_add
const settings = Settings(8080, 3);     # a [Shared] struct
const scratch = ThreadLocal<String>();  # a String per thread
const double: shared (int) => int = (x: int) => x * 2;  # a shared function
[ThreadLocal]
var depth: int = 0;                     # a copy per thread

A variable that breaks a rule is reported at its name or type:

main.pep:1:5: error: module-scope variable 'hits' must be 'const'
    1 | var hits = 0;
      |     ^~~~
note: every thread can reach a module-scope variable; change its state through a thread-safe type such as 'async.Atomic<T>' (after 'import async'), or declare it '[ThreadLocal]' to give each thread its own copy

main.pep:2:15: error: module-scope variable 'origin' has type 'Plain', which is not thread-safe
    2 | const origin: Plain = Plain();
      |               ^~~~~
main.pep:1:8: note: 'Plain' is not declared [Shared]
    1 | struct Plain { var x: int; }
      |        ^~~~~

Module-scope variables are initialized before main runs, in the order they are declared, and each file's after those of the files it imports and of the runtime. So an initializer may use the variables of the files it imports.

Channels

A Channel<T> carries values from threads that send to threads that receive, with any number of each, like a Go channel. (In a task, a wait parks only the task, and so do the waits of Mutex and Condition below.)

import async;

# The main thread sends numbers to a pool of workers, and the workers send
# their squares back on a second channel.
const jobs = async.Channel<long>(16);    # bounded: send waits while 16 are queued
const results = async.Channel<long>();   # unbounded: send never waits

square_numbers() {
    # The loop ends once `jobs` is closed and empty.
    for (var n in jobs) {
        results.send(n * n);
    }
}

# A `shared` function value is thread-safe, so a channel can carry work.
const tasks = async.Channel<async.ThreadBody>();
const ran = async.Atomic<long>(0);

run_tasks() {
    for (var task in tasks) {
        task();
    }
}

main(): int {
    var workers = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 4) {
        workers.append(async.Thread.spawn(square_numbers));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    var n: long = 1;
    while (n <= 100) {
        jobs.send(n);
        n = n + 1;
    }
    jobs.close();   # no more work: each worker's loop ends
    for (var worker in workers) {
        worker.join();
    }
    results.close();

    var total: long = 0;
    for (var square in results) {
        total = total + square;
    }
    assert(total == 338350, "the sum of the first 100 squares");

    # receive() returns a Result: an error once the channel is closed and
    # empty. A closed channel refuses new values.
    assert(results.receive().is_err(), "nothing left");
    assert(!results.send(1), "closed");

    var runner = async.Thread.spawn(run_tasks);
    tasks.send(() => { ran.fetch_add(1); });
    tasks.send(() => { ran.fetch_add(10); });
    tasks.close();
    runner.join();
    assert(ran.load() == 11, "the runner ran both tasks");
    return 0;
}
  • Channel<T>(capacity) makes a channel that holds at most capacity values; send waits while it is full. Channel<T>() (capacity 0) is unbounded, and send never waits.
  • send(value) queues a value and returns true, or returns false if the channel is closed. try_send(value) does not wait: it also returns false when a bounded channel is full.
  • receive() waits for the next value and returns a Result<T>: the value, or an error once the channel is closed and empty. try_receive() returns an error right away when nothing is waiting, and receive_for(milliseconds) when the time runs out.
  • close() ends the stream and wakes every waiting sender and receiver. Values already queued are still received. Only close() closes a channel: dropping it, or ending the threads that use it, does not.
  • for (var v in channel) receives until the channel is closed and empty. Several threads can loop over one channel; each value goes to one of them.
  • Values from one sender arrive in the order they were sent.
  • The count property and is_closed() report the channel's state, which other threads may change right after.

send and try_send take a new value, which nothing on the sending thread references, and hand it to the receiver without copying it: a constructor call, a literal, a call that returns a fresh value (through a shared function value too, when its arguments are new: it reaches nothing else that is not thread-safe), move(x) (a variable that holds the only reference) or copy(x) (when the sender keeps using x). A String, an Array or a struct of them can be sent, and changing the original after sending a copy does not change what was sent:

import async;

# A plain struct: no destructor and no raw pointer, so `copy` copies it field
# by field. Its Strings and Array are not thread-safe, but a Channel takes
# only new values, and a copy is one.
struct Order {
    String customer;
    Array<String> items;
    Order next;

    construct(this.customer = "") {
        items = Array<String>();
    }
}

const orders = async.Channel<Order>();
const letters = async.Atomic<long>(0);

count_letters() {
    for (var order in orders) {
        for (var item in order.items) {
            letters.fetch_add(item.length as long);
        }
    }
}

main(): int {
    # copy() makes a new object for everything that is not thread-safe.
    var tea = Order("ada");
    tea.items.append("tea");
    var copied = copy(tea);
    copied.items[0].append(" and cake");
    assert(tea.items[0] == "tea", "the original is unchanged");

    # Objects referenced twice stay shared in the copy, and cycles are kept.
    var a = Order("a");
    var b = Order("b");
    a.next = b;
    b.next = a;
    var pair = copy(a);
    assert(pair.next.next === pair, "the copy has the same cycle");
    a.next = __null;
    pair.next = __null;

    # send() takes a new value: send a copy to keep changing the order.
    var worker = async.Thread.spawn(count_letters);
    var order = Order("grace");
    order.items.append("coffee");
    orders.send(copy(order));
    order.items.append("biscuits");
    # Or hand the value itself over with `move`; `last` is null afterwards.
    var last = Order("hopper");
    last.items.append("tea");
    orders.send(move(last));
    orders.close();
    worker.join();
    assert(letters.load() == 9, "the worker saw only what was sent");
    return 0;
}

Sending a variable that something else may still reference is an error, and the editor offers both fixes:

main.pep:7:16: error: 'line' is not a new value, but parameter 'value' takes a value that nothing else references
    7 |     lines.send(line);
      |                ^~~~
      |                move(line)
runtime/async/channel.pep:173:17: note: 'value' is declared [Move] here
  173 |     send([Move] value: T): bool {
      |                 ^~~~~
note: hand it over with 'move(line)', or pass a new value, such as 'copy(line)'

A thread-safe value (a number, a [Shared] struct, a shared function value such as a ThreadBody) passes freely, which makes a channel of ThreadBody values a work queue. Since nothing is copied, a channel can carry any type, trait values and values that cannot be copied (an io.File) included.

The Channel reference documents every method.

Waiting on several channels with Select

A Select<E> waits on several channels at once and takes the first value any of them receives (or, with a send arm, sends to the first with room), like Go's select. Each channel is added with a function that turns its values into an E, usually a case of an enum of your own that carries the value, so the channels may carry different types and a match handles the result:

import async;

# Every value the select can return: one case per channel.
enum Event {
    Line(text: String),
    Reading(value: long),
    Stop,
}

const lines = async.Channel<String>();
const readings = async.Channel<long>();
const stop = async.Channel<bool>();

read_lines() {
    lines.send("first");
    lines.send("second");
    lines.close();
}

read_sensor() {
    var i: long = 1;
    while (i <= 3) {
        readings.send(i * 10);
        i = i + 1;
    }
    readings.close();
}

main(): int {
    var select = async.Select<Event>();
    select.receive(lines, (text: String): Event => Event.Line(text));
    select.receive(readings, (value: long): Event => Event.Reading(value));
    select.receive(stop, (unused: bool): Event => Event.Stop);

    var threads = [async.Thread.spawn(read_lines), async.Thread.spawn(read_sensor)];
    var text = 0;
    var total: long = 0;
    var running = true;
    while (running) {
        match (select.wait()) {
            Ok(event) => {
                match (event) {
                    Line(line) => {
                        text = text + 1;
                    }
                    Reading(value) => {
                        total = total + value;
                    }
                    Stop => {
                        running = false;
                    }
                }
            }
            Err(error) => {
                # Every channel is closed and empty (`stop` included, below).
                running = false;
            }
        }
        if (text == 2 && total == 60) {
            stop.close();
        }
    }
    for (var thread in threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    assert(text == 2 && total == 60, "every value arrived once");
    return 0;
}
  • receive(channel, wrap) adds a channel. wrap runs on the waiting thread, with the value received.
  • wait() waits until a channel has a value and returns it as an E, in a Result<E>. wait_for(milliseconds) gives up after that long, and try_wait() does not wait at all.
  • The value is taken under that channel's own lock, so no other receiver can take it between "ready" and "take".
  • When several channels have values, each wait starts just after the channel that fired last, so one busy channel cannot starve the others.
  • A channel that is closed and empty is skipped. Once every channel is, wait() returns an error (every channel is closed). A timeout's error is the time ran out.
  • A Select belongs to the thread (or task) that made it; it is not [Shared]. In a task, waiting parks the task, and a cancel or the task's timeout ends the wait.

A Select can also wait to send, like a case ch <- v in Go's select. send(channel, value, sent) adds a send arm: wait() fires it once channel has room (a bounded channel that is full waits), and returns what sent returns. Here a loop keeps receiving jobs while each result waits for room in a bounded channel:

import async;

# What one wait did: a job arrived, or a result went out.
enum Step {
    Job(value: long),
    Sent,
}

const jobs = async.Channel<long>();
# Holds one result at a time, so sending can wait.
const results = async.Channel<long>(1);

feed() {
    var i: long = 1;
    while (i <= 5) {
        jobs.send(i);
        i = i + 1;
    }
    jobs.close();
}

main(): int {
    var select = async.Select<Step>();
    select.receive(jobs, (value: long): Step => Step.Job(value));
    var feeder = async.Thread.spawn(feed);
    var received = 0;
    var waiting = 0;
    var total: long = 0;
    while (received < 5 || waiting > 0) {
        match (select.wait()) {
            Ok(step) => {
                match (step) {
                    Job(value) => {
                        received = received + 1;
                        # Goes into `results` once it has room; until then
                        # the select keeps receiving jobs.
                        select.send(results, value * value, (): Step => Step.Sent);
                        waiting = waiting + 1;
                    }
                    Sent => {
                        waiting = waiting - 1;
                        # Take the result back out, so the next send has room.
                        total = total + results.receive().value();
                    }
                }
            }
            Err(error) => {
                panic(error.message);
            }
        }
    }
    feeder.join();
    assert(total == 55, "every square was sent once");
    return 0;
}
  • value must be a new value, as for Channel.send (move(x), copy(x), a constructor call, ...). The select holds it and moves it into the channel only when that arm fires, under the channel's lock, so it is never sent when another arm fires first.
  • A send arm fires once: after its value is sent it leaves the select, so the next wait() does not send it again. Add another with send for the next value.
  • A send arm whose channel is closed is skipped like a closed receive channel, and its value is dropped with the select.

The Select reference documents every method.

Mutexes and conditions

A Mutex<T> owns a value that one thread at a time can use. The way to reach the value is a with block:

import async;

# Each balance is an Atomic, but moving money changes both, and no thread
# may see it in neither account. A Mutex makes the pair of updates one step.
[Shared]
struct Accounts {
    const checking: async.Atomic<long>;
    const savings: async.Atomic<long>;
    construct(long checking = 0, long savings = 0) {
        this.checking = async.Atomic<long>(checking);
        this.savings = async.Atomic<long>(savings);
    }
}

const accounts = async.Mutex<Accounts>(Accounts(1000, 0));
const bad_totals = async.Atomic<long>(0);

move_to_savings() {
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 1000) {
        with (var a = accounts.lock()) {
            a.checking.fetch_sub(1);
            a.savings.fetch_add(1);
        }   # unlocked here, on every path out of the block
        i = i + 1;
    }
}

audit() {
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 1000) {
        with (var a = accounts.lock()) {
            if (a.checking.load() + a.savings.load() != 1000) {
                bad_totals.fetch_add(1);
            }
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var mover = async.Thread.spawn(move_to_savings);
    var auditor = async.Thread.spawn(audit);
    mover.join();
    auditor.join();
    assert(bad_totals.load() == 0, "the auditor never saw money missing");

    # try_lock does not wait: the body runs if the lock was free, and the
    # else block runs if another thread held it.
    with (var a = accounts.try_lock()) {
        assert(a.savings.load() == 1000, "everything was moved");
    } else {
        assert(false, "no other thread holds the lock now");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • with (var v = mutex.lock()) { ... } waits until no other thread holds the lock, binds the value, and unlocks when the block ends by any path: the end of the body, return, break or continue. Everything a thread did while it held the lock is visible to the next thread that takes it.
  • try_lock() does not wait. With with (var v = mutex.try_lock()) { ... } else { ... }, the body runs if the lock was free and the else block runs if it was not.
  • A Mutex is not re-entrant: calling lock() again on the thread that holds it panics instead of deadlocking. is_held() reports whether the calling thread holds it.
  • A panic while a Mutex is held ends the program, so a Mutex is never left "poisoned".
  • Taking a free lock is one atomic instruction, and a thread that finds it held spins briefly before it sleeps. Locks sleep on the operating system's wait-on-address call (futex on Linux, __ulock_wait on macOS, WaitOnAddress on Windows), as Rust's do.

T is a struct type: a struct of your own, an Array<String>, or a [Shared] struct whose Atomic fields must change as a unit. Mutex<int> is an error (use async.Atomic<int>). A Mutex of values that are not thread-safe is kept apart from the rest of the program by the compiler; see What a lock body may do.

  • Mutex<T>(value) and replace(value) take a new value: a constructor call, a string literal, a call that returns a fresh value, copy(x), or move(x), never a variable something else still references. The caller hands its reference over, so nothing is copied.
  • replace(value) swaps the whole value under the lock and returns the old one, which the caller then owns outright.

A value built in a local variable goes in with move, which hands over the variable's reference instead of copying the value:

import async;

main(): int {
    # Build the list here, then hand it to the Mutex: `move` gives up
    # `lines`' reference, so nothing is copied and `lines` is empty after.
    var lines = Array<String>();
    lines.append("first");
    var log = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(move(lines));

    var line = "second";
    with (var list = log.lock()) {
        # `line` holds the only reference to its String, so it can move in.
        list.append(move(line));
    }

    # Swap in a new list; the old one comes back without a copy either.
    var next = Array<String>();
    next.append("third");
    var old = log.replace(move(next));
    print($"{old.count}");     # 2
    print(old[1]);               # second
    return 0;
}

A Condition<T> lets a thread that holds a Mutex sleep until another thread changes the value. Get one with mutex.condition():

import async;

# A baker makes pies and eaters take them. The eaters sleep on a Condition
# until there is a pie, or until the bakery closes.
[Shared]
struct Bakery {
    const pies: async.Atomic<long>;
    const closed: async.Atomic<int>;
    construct() {
        pies = async.Atomic<long>(0);
        closed = async.Atomic<int>(0);
    }
}

const bakery = async.Mutex<Bakery>(Bakery());
const changed = bakery.condition();
const eaten = async.Atomic<long>(0);

eat() {
    while (true) {
        with (var b = bakery.lock()) {
            # Wait in a loop: a wakeup can be spurious, and another eater
            # may take the pie first.
            while (b.pies.load() == 0 && b.closed.load() == 0) {
                changed.wait();   # unlocks, sleeps, locks again
            }
            if (b.pies.load() == 0) {
                return;   # closed and nothing left; the block unlocks
            }
            b.pies.fetch_sub(1);
        }
        eaten.fetch_add(1);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var eaters = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 3) {
        eaters.append(async.Thread.spawn(eat));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    i = 0;
    while (i < 50) {
        with (var b = bakery.lock()) {
            b.pies.fetch_add(1);
            changed.notify_one();
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
    with (var b = bakery.lock()) {
        b.closed.store(1);
        changed.notify_all();
    }
    for (var eater in eaters) {
        eater.join();
    }
    assert(eaten.load() == 50, "every pie was eaten once");
    return 0;
}
  • wait() must run while the caller holds the Mutex, normally inside its with block. It unlocks, sleeps until notified, and locks again before returning. It panics if the caller does not hold the Mutex.
  • A thread can wake without a notification (a spurious wakeup), and another thread may get to the value first, so always wait in a loop that re-checks what it waits for.
  • wait_for(milliseconds) gives up after that long and returns false.
  • notify_one() wakes one waiting thread, and notify_all() wakes them all.

wait_while(predicate) writes that loop for you: it waits while predicate returns true for the locked value, asking again after every wakeup, and returns with the Mutex still locked. wait_while_for(milliseconds, predicate) gives up after that long and returns false:

import async;

# A worker takes jobs from a queue, sleeping while it is empty.
const jobs = async.Mutex<Array<long>>(Array<long>());
const changed = jobs.condition();
const done = async.Atomic<long>(0);

work() {
    var taken = 0;
    while (taken < 5) {
        with (var queue = jobs.lock()) {
            # Waits while the predicate holds; spurious wakeups are handled.
            # The predicate is given the locked value: it cannot capture it.
            changed.wait_while((waiting: Array<long>): bool => waiting.count == 0);
            done.fetch_add(queue.remove_at(0));
            taken = taken + 1;
        }
    }
}

main(): int {
    var worker = async.Thread.spawn(work);
    var i: long = 1;
    while (i <= 5) {
        with (var queue = jobs.lock()) {
            queue.append(i);
            changed.notify_all();
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
    worker.join();
    assert(done.load() == 15, "every job was taken once");

    with (var queue = jobs.lock()) {
        # Gives up after 10 milliseconds: nothing is queued.
        var ready = changed.wait_while_for(10, (waiting: Array<long>): bool => waiting.count == 0);
        assert(!ready, "the time ran out");
    }
    return 0;
}

The predicate is given the locked value as its parameter, since a closure cannot capture part of a locked value. It must be a closure written at the call, and the compiler checks its body as it checks a lock body (see What a lock body may do): it cannot keep any part of the value, or bring in a value from outside.

main.pep:10:26: error: 'queue[0]' is part of the value locked by 'queue' and cannot outlive the lock
   10 |             saved.append(queue[0]);
      |                          ^~~~~~~~
main.pep:9:27: note: locked here
    9 |         ready.wait_while((queue: Array<String>): bool => {
      |                           ^~~~~
note: 'String' is not thread-safe, so no part of the locked value may be kept outside the block; take 'copy(queue[0])'

The Mutex reference documents Mutex, MutexGuard and Condition.

What a lock body may do

A value that is not thread-safe counts its references plainly, so no thread may hold a reference into a Mutex's value while the Mutex is unlocked. The compiler checks each with block over a lock so that none can:

import async;

# A Mutex of values that are not thread-safe: a list of Strings that
# several threads add to.
const names = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(Array<String>());
const tags = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(Array<String>());

add_names(prefix: String) {
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 3) {
        with (var list = names.lock()) {
            list.append("worker");            # a new String: fine
            list.append(prefix + "!");        # `+` returns a new String: fine
            list.append(copy(prefix));        # a copy of an outside value: fine
            var n = list.count;             # a number leaves freely
            if (list.contains(prefix)) {      # comparing keeps nothing
                n = n + 1;
            }
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
}

# Part of the locked value leaves the block only as a copy.
first_name(): String {
    with (var list = names.lock()) {
        if (list.count > 0) {
            return list[0].copy();
        }
    }
    return "";
}

main(): int {
    var a = async.Thread.spawn(() => { add_names("a"); });
    var b = async.Thread.spawn(() => { add_names("b"); });
    a.join();
    b.join();

    var first = first_name();
    first.append(" (mine)");   # changing the copy leaves the list alone
    with (var list = names.lock()) {
        assert(list.count == 18, "every name was added");
        assert(list[0] == "worker", "the locked String is unchanged");
    }

    # replace swaps in a new value and hands back the old one, which the
    # caller then owns outright.
    var old = names.replace(Array<String>());
    assert(old.count == 18, "the old list");

    # A variable of an outer block outlives an inner lock, so it keeps only a
    # copy of the inner value (`seen = tag_list` is an error).
    with (var list = names.lock()) {
        var seen = Array<String>();
        with (var tag_list = tags.lock()) {
            tag_list.append("new");
            seen = copy(tag_list);
        }
        list.append(seen[0]);   # the outer block's own value may take it
        assert(list.count == 1, "the copied tag");
    }

    # A thread's own value that is not thread-safe is reached through `with`.
    var scratch = async.ThreadLocal<String>();
    scratch.set("draft");
    with (var text = scratch.enter()) {
        text.append(" 2");
    }
    with (var text = scratch.enter()) {
        assert(text == "draft 2", "this thread's value");
    }
    return 0;
}

Inside the block, every value that is not thread-safe is either part of the locked value (the binding, its fields and elements, and what calls on them return), from outside (a parameter, this, or a variable declared before the block), or new. A new value may join either side; the other two must never meet:

  • Moving in. A call, constructor or assignment that would link an outside value with the locked one is an error. Pass a new value instead: copy(line), a literal, or the result of a call that returns a fresh value. A variable that holds the only reference to its value can hand it over with move(line).

    main.pep:8:21: error: 'line' cannot move into the value locked by 'names'
    8 |         list.append(line);
      |                     ^~~~
main.pep:7:28: note: locked here
    7 |     with (var list = names.lock()) {
      |                            ^~~~
note: 'String' is not thread-safe, so the locked value cannot share it with the rest of the program; pass 'copy(line)'

  • Moving out. Storing part of the locked value outside the block, or returning it from the block, is an error; take a copy (copy(list[0]), or list[0].copy(), which returns a fresh value).

    main.pep:8:17: error: 'list[0]' is part of the value locked by 'names' and cannot outlive the lock
    8 |         first = list[0];
      |                 ^~~~~~~

  • Closures. A closure written in the block cannot capture part of the locked value, since a function value could carry it out.

  • Two locks. Values locked by two nested blocks stay apart as well. A variable declared in the outer block, before the inner one, is from outside to the inner block: it outlives the inner lock, so it may hold the outer block's value but no part of the inner one's, whether it would hold it directly, in a field, through a closure, or from one pass of a loop to the next.

  • Numbers pass freely, as do every thread-safe value and every new one.

Which calls link which values comes from what the called function does: the compiler works out, for every function, whether it keeps an argument (as append keeps its element) and whether its result shares anything with its arguments. A result that shares nothing, such as that of +, substr, copy() or a constructor, is fresh, and may cross in either direction. The language server shows "Returns a fresh value" when hovering over such a function. A call through a function value links its result with its arguments and with what the function value captured, so it is fresh only when the function value and its arguments are new. A value an extern function hands back, and a value read through raw memory that a [Shared] struct holds, are never fresh: something else may reference them. The runtime takes the few values it hands out that nothing else references out of raw memory with move(p[i]), a promise the compiler cannot check and allows only in the runtime: a channel's receive() (the value send handed over) and a Mutex's replace().

A function that returns a tuple has one such fact per element: after var (fresh, same) = split(line);, fresh may move into a locked value while same, which split returned from its argument, may not.

The guard a lock() returns can only be the scope of a with header: storing it in a variable or field is an error, so no lock outlives its block.

Two attributes carry these rules, and code outside the runtime may use them too:

  • [Isolated] on a struct makes it a guard: it can only be the scope of a with header, and the block is checked as above. MutexGuard<T> and ThreadLocalGuard<T> are [Isolated].
  • [Move] on a parameter (construct([Move] T value)) requires a new value for it at every call: a constructor call, a literal, a fresh result, copy(x), move(x), or any thread-safe value. The caller hands its reference over, so the function receives it without a count step.

Checking confinement at run time

Raw memory (__ptr<T>) and extern code are promises the compiler cannot check, so a program that uses them can still keep a reference into a locked value. Set the environment variable PEP_CHECK_SYNC when running a program to check at every unlock that nothing outside the locked value refers into it:

$ PEP_CHECK_SYNC=1 ./main
PEP_CHECK_SYNC: an object in the value locked by a 'Mutex<Box>' is still referenced from outside it

The check copies the locked value to count the references inside it, so it costs time and memory in proportion to the value's size at each unlock; it is off unless the variable is set. It checks a Mutex<T> whose T is not thread-safe and can be copied.

Reader/writer locks

An RwLock<T> lets many threads read a value at once, or one thread write it:

import async;

# A price list that many threads read and one thread now and then updates.
# A writer changes both prices together, so a reader never sees one updated
# and the other not.
[Shared]
struct Prices {
    const coffee: async.Atomic<long>;
    const tea: async.Atomic<long>;
    construct() {
        coffee = async.Atomic<long>(300);
        tea = async.Atomic<long>(250);
    }
}

const prices = async.RwLock<Prices>(Prices());
const mismatches = async.Atomic<long>(0);

check_prices() {
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 1000) {
        with (var p = prices.read()) {   # many readers at once
            if (p.coffee.load() - p.tea.load() != 50) {
                mismatches.fetch_add(1);
            }
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
}

raise_prices() {
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 100) {
        with (var p = prices.write()) {   # no reader sees the middle
            p.coffee.fetch_add(10);
            p.tea.fetch_add(10);
        }
        i = i + 1;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var threads = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 3) {
        threads.append(async.Thread.spawn(check_prices));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    threads.append(async.Thread.spawn(raise_prices));
    for (var thread in threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    assert(mismatches.load() == 0, "no reader saw a half-done update");
    with (var p = prices.read()) {
        assert(p.coffee.load() == 1300, "every raise landed");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • with (var v = lock.read()) { ... } waits until no writer holds or waits for the lock; any number of threads may read at the same time.
  • with (var v = lock.write()) { ... } waits until no other thread holds the lock at all.
  • try_read() and try_write() do not wait: the else block runs when the lock is not free.
  • replace(value) swaps the whole value under the write lock and returns the old one.
  • Writers come first: while a writer waits, new readers wait behind it, so readers cannot keep it out forever. A thread that reads must therefore not ask to read again before its block ends, and asking to write while holding the lock panics instead of deadlocking.

T must be thread-safe, as for Atomic<T>: typically a [Shared] struct whose Atomic fields a writer changes together. Readers that hold the value at once each copy a reference to it, so a value that is not thread-safe, such as an Array<String>, would have its reference counts changed by several threads at a time; it is a compile error at the type argument. Put such a value in a Mutex<T>. When readers only need the latest value and writers replace it whole, an Atomic<T> holding a [Shared] struct does the same job without a lock.

Semaphores, barriers and latches

Three types coordinate threads by counting. Each is [Shared], so keep it in a module-scope variable or pass it to threads:

  • A Semaphore(permits) lets at most permits threads hold a permit at once. acquire() waits for a free permit and takes it, try_acquire() takes one only if one is free, and release() gives one back. with (semaphore.permit()) { ... } holds a permit for the block and gives it back on every path out.
  • A Barrier(count) makes groups of count threads meet: wait() sleeps until count threads have called it, then all go on together. It returns true on exactly one of them, the leader, and resets for the next round.
  • A Latch(count) opens once count_down() has been called count times. wait() sleeps until it is open, and is_ready() asks without waiting. It is one-shot: counting down an open latch panics.
import async;

const WORKERS = 4;

# At most two workers use the printer at once.
const printer = async.Semaphore(2);
const printing = async.Atomic<long>(0);
const most_printing = async.Atomic<long>(0);

# Every worker finishes a step before any starts the next.
const step_done = async.Barrier(WORKERS);
const steps_led = async.Atomic<long>(0);

# The main thread waits until every worker has set up.
const ready = async.Latch(WORKERS);

work() {
    ready.count_down();
    var step = 0;
    while (step < 3) {
        with (printer.permit()) {
            var now = printing.fetch_add(1) + 1;
            if (now > most_printing.load()) {
                most_printing.store(now);
            }
            printing.fetch_sub(1);
        }   # the permit is given back here
        if (step_done.wait()) {
            steps_led.fetch_add(1);   # one leader per step
        }
        step = step + 1;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var workers = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < WORKERS) {
        workers.append(async.Thread.spawn(work));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    ready.wait();
    assert(ready.is_ready(), "every worker counted down");
    for (var worker in workers) {
        worker.join();
    }
    assert(most_printing.load() <= 2, "the semaphore let two in at most");
    assert(steps_led.load() == 3, "each step had exactly one leader");
    return 0;
}

Each is a Mutex over its counts with a Condition to sleep on, so in a task their waits park the task, not its worker.

Once and Lazy

Once runs a function exactly once, however many threads ask, and Lazy<T> builds a value the first time a thread asks for it:

import async;

[Shared]
struct Settings {
    const workers: long;
    construct(this.workers = 1) {}
}

const builds = async.Atomic<long>(0);

load_settings(): Settings {
    builds.fetch_add(1);
    return Settings(async.logical_cpus() as long);
}

# Built by the first thread that calls get(), not before main runs.
const settings = async.Lazy<Settings>(load_settings);

# Runs initialize() once, however many threads call it.
const setup = async.Once();
const setups = async.Atomic<long>(0);

initialize() {
    setups.fetch_add(1);
}

work() {
    setup.call(initialize);
    assert(settings.get().workers >= 1, "every thread sees the settings");
}

main(): int {
    assert(!settings.is_built(), "nothing is built before first use");
    var workers = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 4) {
        workers.append(async.Thread.spawn(work));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    for (var worker in workers) {
        worker.join();
    }
    assert(builds.load() == 1, "the settings were built once");
    assert(setups.load() == 1, "initialize ran once");
    assert(setup.is_done(), "done");
    return 0;
}
  • once.call(body) runs body if no call has run one yet. Threads that call it while the body runs wait for it, and every caller sees what the body did. is_done() reports whether it has run.
  • Lazy<T>(initializer) takes a shared () => T function. The first get() runs it; later calls, from any thread, return the same value. is_built() reports whether it has run.
  • A Lazy<T> is the usual way to give a module-scope variable a value that is expensive to build, or that cannot be built before main runs. Its T must be thread-safe, since every thread gets the same value.

The Once reference has the details.

Limitations

  • Lazy<T> holds only thread-safe values.
  • A value received from a channel moves into a locked value directly (list.append(jobs.receive().value())), but not through a variable declared outside the block: such a variable is an outside value, whatever it holds, so it needs copy, or move when it holds the only reference (list.append(move(job))).
  • A Mutex is not re-entrant, and neither is an RwLock.
  • The value a Select's wait() returns is not a new value for a lock body, since it comes from wrap, a function value the Select keeps, and may share what wrap captured; copy it to move it into a locked value.
  • Deadlocks are not detected, except locking a Mutex twice on one thread, or asking to write an RwLock the thread holds, which panic.

Atomics

An atomic value can be read and updated by several threads at once without a data race: every operation on it happens as one indivisible step. Pepper provides this through async.Atomic<T>, the equivalent of C++ std::atomic<T>.

Threads themselves, and the rules for what they can share, are in Threads and shared data.

Atomic<T>

Atomic<T> belongs to the async module, with the other types threads share: import async and write async.Atomic<T>, or bring the name in with import [Atomic] from async. The Atomic reference documents every method.

import async;

main(): int {
    var a = async.Atomic<int>(41);
    assert(a.load() == 41, "the initial value");

    a.store(1);
    assert(a.load() == 1, "store replaces the value");

    # The fetch_ operations return the value from before the change.
    assert(a.fetch_add(5) == 1, "fetch_add returns the old value");
    assert(a.load() == 6, "1 + 5");
    assert(a.fetch_sub(2) == 6, "fetch_sub returns the old value");
    assert(a.load() == 4, "6 - 2");

    var flags = async.Atomic<uint>(12);          # 0b1100
    flags.fetch_and(10);                   # 0b1000
    assert(flags.load() == 8, "fetch_and");
    flags.fetch_or(1);                     # 0b1001
    assert(flags.load() == 9, "fetch_or");
    flags.fetch_xor(9);                    # 0b0000
    assert(flags.load() == 0, "fetch_xor");

    # compare_exchange stores only if the current value is the expected one.
    assert(a.compare_exchange(4, 10), "4 matched, so 10 is stored");
    assert(!a.compare_exchange(4, 20), "10 does not match 4");
    assert(a.load() == 10, "the failed exchange changed nothing");

    # exchange always stores, and returns what was there.
    assert(a.exchange(3) == 10, "exchange returns the old value");
    assert(a.load() == 3, "and stores the new one");

    assert(a.is_lock_free(), "an int fits a native atomic instruction");
    return 0;
}
MethodWhat it does
Atomic<T>(value)Creates an atomic holding value (zero, or null for a struct type, if you leave it out).
load()Reads the value.
store(v)Replaces the value with v.
compare_exchange(expected, desired)Stores desired only if the value is currently expected; returns whether it did.
exchange(v)Stores v and returns the value it replaced.
fetch_add(v), fetch_sub(v)Adds or subtracts v; returns the value from before. Overflow wraps around.
fetch_and(v), fetch_or(v), fetch_xor(v)Combines the value bitwise with v; returns the value from before.
is_lock_free()Reports whether the operations use native atomic instructions.

Each operation compiles to a native atomic instruction. load has acquire ordering, store has release ordering, and compare_exchange and the fetch_ operations are acquire-release. exchange is a compare_exchange retry loop.

Some details differ from C++:

  • compare_exchange does not update expected when it fails. Call load() to get the current value before you retry.
  • The comparison is bitwise. For a floating-point T, 0.0 and -0.0 are different values. For a struct T, it compares references (whether both are the same object), not the objects' contents.
  • The fetch_ operations are for integer types. Calling one on a floating-point or struct T compiles, but stops the program when it runs.
  • is_lock_free() is true for any number type of 8 bytes or less, and for any struct type.
  • T must be thread-safe. Atomic is a [Shared] struct, so it is declared Atomic<T: Shared>: T is a number, bool, an enum, a [Shared] struct, or another type in What threads can share. Atomic<String> is a compile error at String (see the Shared constraint). A tuple is thread-safe, but its value cannot be stored atomically, so Atomic of a tuple is an error too, and so is Atomic of a trait type (see Weak references and atomics).

Common patterns

import async;

# An Atomic can only hold a thread-safe struct: one declared [Shared], whose
# fields are const and thread-safe.
[Shared]
struct Config {
    const version: int;
    construct(this.version = 0) {}
}

# A module-scope Atomic that every function can share.
const next_id = async.Atomic<long>(0);

new_id(): long {
    return next_id.fetch_add(1) + 1;
}

# The compare-and-swap retry loop: build any read-modify-write update.
double_it(async.Atomic<int> value) {
    var current = value.load();
    while (!value.compare_exchange(current, current * 2)) {
        current = value.load();
    }
}

main(): int {
    assert(new_id() == 1, "first id");
    assert(new_id() == 2, "second id");

    var n = async.Atomic<int>(21);
    double_it(n);
    assert(n.load() == 42, "doubled");

    # Copies of an Atomic share one slot, because Atomic is a struct.
    var same = n;
    same.store(7);
    assert(n.load() == 7, "both names see the store");

    # An Atomic can hold a struct reference.
    var first = Config(1);
    var current = async.Atomic<Config>(first);
    assert(current.load().version == 1, "load returns the reference");

    # compare_exchange compares references: the same object, not equal contents.
    var lookalike = Config(1);
    var second = Config(2);
    assert(!current.compare_exchange(lookalike, second), "a different object");
    assert(current.compare_exchange(first, second), "the same object");
    assert(current.load().version == 2, "swapped");

    var old = current.exchange(first);
    assert(old.version == 2, "exchange hands back the old reference");
    return 0;
}
  • A shared counter. fetch_add(1) hands out unique, increasing numbers, even when many threads call it at once.
  • A compare-and-swap loop. To apply any update that the fetch_ operations do not cover, load the current value, compute the new one, and compare_exchange; if another thread changed the value in between, the exchange fails and you try again with a fresh load().
  • Sharing an Atomic. Atomic is a [Shared] struct, so copying one copies a reference: every copy shares the same slot, on any thread. To share a value, pass the Atomic around or keep it in a module-scope variable.
  • Atomic struct references. An Atomic<T> whose T is a [Shared] struct type holds a counted reference, and follows the same rules as any other reference (see Memory and reference counting): store and a successful compare_exchange take a reference to the new value and release the one they replace, and load and exchange give you your own reference. The swap in the slot is itself atomic, so concurrent stores never leak or release a value twice. When the Atomic itself is destroyed, it releases the reference it holds.

Atomics and threads

Atomic<T> is how threads share a value that changes. Keep it in a module-scope variable, or in a const field of a [Shared] struct, and every thread sees the same slot. Threads and shared data shows it together with Thread.spawn.
