Tasks

A task is a function that runs alongside others. Each task has its own small stack, and the tasks on a thread take turns: one runs until it waits (for a timer, for another task, or by yielding), and then another runs. A runtime has a few such threads, its workers, so tasks also run in parallel. This is the model of Go's goroutines and of libuv or tokio event loops, without async/await: a function that waits looks like any other function, and any function can wait, however deep in the call stack. A socket call that has to wait parks only its task, so one worker can serve thousands of connections.

WASI cannot switch stacks, so on WebAssembly (--target wasm32-wasip1) starting tasks (async.run, async.run_with) panics (see WebAssembly).

Tasks live in the async module:

import async;

main(): int {
    var log = Array<String>();
    async.run(() => {
        # A task starts when the running task next waits.
        var worker = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => {
            log.append("worker starts");
            async.yield_now();
            log.append("worker ends");
            return 42;
        });
        log.append("first task");
        var answer = worker.join().value();   # waits; the worker runs
        assert(answer == 42, "join returns the body's value");
        log.append("joined");
    });
    assert(log[0] == "first task" && log[1] == "worker starts", "tasks take turns");
    assert(log[2] == "worker ends" && log[3] == "joined", "join waited");
    return 0;
}
  • async.run(body) runs body as the first task and returns once it has returned and every task it started has finished. run_with(options, body) does the same with settings; RuntimeOptions().stack_size(bytes) sets how much stack each task reserves (256 KiB by default).
  • Task<T>.spawn_local(body) starts a task on the running task's worker and returns its Task<T>. The new task runs the next time the running task waits. T is the body's result type; use Task<void> for a body that returns nothing.
  • task.join() waits for the task and returns a Result<T, TaskError>: the body's value, or an error if the task was cancelled.
  • async.yield_now() lets every other ready task run first.
  • task.is_finished() says whether the body has returned.

A task from spawn_local stays on the thread of the task that started it, so it may use any value that task uses, as the closures above share log. Nothing needs to be thread-safe.

Several workers

run turns the calling thread into the first worker and starts one more thread per logical CPU after it (RuntimeOptions().workers(count) sets how many workers in all). async.spawn<T>(body) starts a task that whichever worker is free first runs, in parallel with the others:

import async;

sum(from: long, to: long): long {
    var total: long = 0;
    var i = from;
    while (i < to) {
        total = total + i;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(4), () => {
        # Two halves of the work, on two workers at the same time.
        var low = async.spawn<long>(() => { return sum(0, 500000); });
        var high = async.spawn<long>(() => { return sum(500000, 1000000); });
        var total = low.join().value() + high.join().value();
        assert(total == 499999500000, "both halves were added");
    });
    return 0;
}

Because such a task may run on another thread, its body must be a shared function: it may capture only thread-safe values, as a thread's body. Its result crosses threads too, so spawn constrains it T: Shared: a thread-safe type such as a number, a [Shared] struct, or a shared function type. async.spawn<String> is a compile error at String. join, cancel and is_finished work as for spawn_local, from the task that started it.

A task, once started, stays on its worker until it finishes, so the tasks it starts with spawn_local share values with it safely. An idle worker takes the next task that no worker has started yet. A task that computes without waiting still holds up the other tasks on its own worker (not the other workers), so a long computation should call yield_now() now and then.

async.spawn_on_each_worker(body) starts one task per worker, each on its own worker, and returns them in worker order. It is how a server runs an accept loop on every worker (see Sockets).

Blocking calls

Some work would hold a worker up: a call that blocks in the operating system (reading a file, a C library that waits) or a long computation. async.run_blocking<T>(body) runs body on a separate thread and parks the calling task until it returns, so the worker keeps running its other tasks meanwhile:

import async;

const ticks = async.Atomic<int>(0);

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(1), () => {
        # Keeps running on the one worker while the blocking call waits.
        var ticker = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            while (ticks.load() < 3) {
                async.sleep(5);
                ticks.fetch_add(1);
            }
        });
        var answer = async.run_blocking<int>(() => {
            async.Thread.sleep(50);   # blocks a pool thread, not the worker
            return 42;
        });
        assert(answer == 42, "the blocking call's result");
        assert(ticks.load() > 0, "the worker ran the ticker meanwhile");
        ticker.join();
    });
    return 0;
}

The runtime keeps a pool of threads for these calls. It starts one when a call finds none idle, up to RuntimeOptions().blocking_threads(count) (64 by default); past that, calls wait for a free one. As for spawn, body must be a shared function and T must be thread-safe. body always runs to the end: cancelling the task, or a timeout around the call, takes effect once the call has returned. Outside a task, run_blocking just calls body.

Waiting

async.sleep puts a task to sleep and runs the others meanwhile, so many tasks can wait at the same time on one thread. It takes an os.Duration (see The operating system), or a number of milliseconds; a duration that is not a whole number of milliseconds rounds up:

import async;
import os;

main(): int {
    var order = Array<int>();
    async.run(() => {
        var tasks = Array<async.Task<void>>();
        var i = 0;
        while (i < 3) {
            var n = i;
            # The later a task starts, the shorter it sleeps.
            tasks.append(async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                async.sleep(os.Duration.from_milliseconds(((3 - n) * 20) as ulong));
                order.append(n);
            }));
            i = i + 1;
        }
        for (var task in tasks) {
            task.join();
        }
    });
    # All three slept at the same time, on one thread.
    assert(order[0] == 2 && order[1] == 1 && order[2] == 0, "shortest sleep first");
    return 0;
}

Outside a task, sleep blocks the thread, and yield_now does nothing.

Tasks are never interrupted. A task that computes for a long time without waiting keeps every other task waiting, so a long loop should call yield_now() now and then.

Thread.sleep in a task is async.sleep.

Mutexes, channels and conditions

The synchronization types work in tasks too. When a task has to wait for a Mutex, for a value from a Channel or for room in a bounded one, in Condition.wait, for an RwLock, or in Semaphore.acquire, Barrier.wait or Latch.wait, it parks and its worker runs other tasks, just as it does for a socket. The task that holds the lock or will send the value can be on the same worker, on another worker, or a plain thread:

import async;

struct Log {
    var lines: Array<String>;
    construct() {
        this.lines = Array<String>();
    }
}

const log = async.Mutex<Log>(Log());
const jobs = async.Channel<int>(2);

main(): int {
    # One worker: every task below shares one thread.
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(1), () => {
        # The consumer parks in the channel until a value arrives.
        var consumer = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => {
            var total = 0;
            for (var job in jobs) {
                total = total + job;
            }
            return total;
        });
        # A task may hold the lock while it waits; the other task parks
        # until it is free.
        var writer = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            with (var l = log.lock()) {
                l.lines.append("first");
                async.sleep(10);
                l.lines.append("second");
            }
        });
        async.yield_now();
        with (var l = log.lock()) {
            l.lines.append("third");
        }
        writer.join();

        # The producer parks while the bounded channel is full.
        var i = 1;
        while (i <= 5) {
            jobs.send(i);
            i = i + 1;
        }
        jobs.close();
        assert(consumer.join().value() == 15, "every job arrived");
    });
    with (var l = log.lock()) {
        assert(l.lines[2] == "third", "the lock waited for the writer");
    }
    return 0;
}
  • Each task counts as its own holder of a Mutex, so two tasks on one worker exclude each other, and a task may hold a lock across its own waits (a sleep, a socket call, another lock).
  • A cancel, or a timeout around the call, ends a channel wait: send returns false and receive returns an error (and a for loop over the channel ends). A task waiting for a Mutex still gets the lock, and Condition.wait still waits for a notification, since the caller's loop would only wait again; wait_for returns when its own time runs out.
  • A Select parks its task on every channel at once, and a cancel or timeout ends its wait with an error. Condition.wait_while parks like wait.
  • Outside a task they block the thread, as before.

Task-local values

A TaskLocal<T> is a variable with a separate value in every task, as a ThreadLocal<T> has one per thread. Tasks that take turns on one worker share its thread, so only a TaskLocal can tell them apart:

import async;

# The id of the request the running task is handling.
const request_id = async.TaskLocal<long>();

# Deep in the call chain, without the id passed down as a parameter.
current_request(): long {
    return request_id.get();
}

main(): int {
    # One worker: the three tasks take turns on one thread, so a
    # ThreadLocal could not tell them apart.
    async.run_with(
        async.RuntimeOptions().workers(1),
        () => {
            var tasks = Array<async.Task<bool>>();
            for (var id in [1, 2, 3]) {
                tasks.append(
                    async.Task<bool>.spawn_local(
                        () => {
                            request_id.set(id);
                            async.yield_now();  # the other tasks set their ids meanwhile
                            return current_request() == id;
                        }
                    )
                );
            }
            for (var task in tasks) {
                assert(task.join().value(), "each task sees its own id");
            }
            # This task never set one.
            assert(!request_id.is_set(), "a task starts with no value");
        }
    );
    return 0;
}
  • set(value) stores the calling task's value and get() returns it (the default of T, zero or null, until the task sets one). is_set() and clear() work as on a ThreadLocal.
  • A task starts with no value, even one started by a task that has one, and its values are released when it finishes.
  • Code outside any task (before async.run, or on a plain Thread) has one value per thread, like a ThreadLocal.
  • For a T that is not thread-safe, such as a String, reach the value with with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }, as for a ThreadLocal; get() is then a compile error.

Sockets

A socket call in a task that would have to wait (for a connection, for data, or for room to send) parks the task and lets the others run until the socket is ready. The socket API is the same one a plain program uses; only the waiting differs:

import async;
import io;

# Echoes everything a client sends until it closes the connection.
serve(stream: io.TcpStream) {
    var buffer = Array<u8>();
    while (true) {
        var r = stream.read(buffer, 4096);   # parks this task until data arrives
        if (r.is_err() || r.value() == 0) {
            return;
        }
        stream.write_all(buffer);
        buffer.clear();
    }
}

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var address = listener.local_address().value();
        var clients = 10;

        # The server: one task per connection, all on this thread.
        async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            while (true) {
                var accepted = listener.accept();
                if (accepted.is_err()) {
                    return;   # cancelled when the first task returns
                }
                var (stream, peer) = accepted.value();
                async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => { serve(stream); });
            }
        });

        # The clients, as tasks on the same thread.
        var replies = Array<async.Task<ulong>>();
        var i = 0;
        while (i < clients) {
            var k = i;
            replies.append(async.Task<ulong>.spawn_local(() => {
                var stream = io.TcpStream.connect(address).value();
                var message = $"hello from {k}";
                stream.write_all(message);
                var buffer = Array<u8>();
                stream.read_exact(buffer, message.size);
                return buffer.count;
            }));
            i = i + 1;
        }
        for (var reply in replies) {
            assert(reply.join().value() > 0, "the server echoed the message");
        }
    });
    return 0;
}

Outside a task, the same calls block the thread as before. A socket belongs to the worker whose task made it: tasks started with spawn_local can share it, and each spawned task makes its own.

Waiting on several sockets

To wait on whichever of several sockets is ready first, give each socket a task that reads it and sends what it read to a channel, and wait on the channels with a Select. Closing a channel when its socket closes lets the select stop waiting on it. Tasks are cheap, so this costs little, and the reading code stays the ordinary blocking-style loop:

import async;
import io;

# What the select returns: bytes that arrived on one of the connections.
enum Event {
    Data(from: int, count: ulong),
}

# Reads `stream` until the peer closes it, sending the size of each read to
# `into`, then closes `into` so the select stops waiting on it.
forward(stream: io.TcpStream, into: async.Channel<ulong>) {
    var buffer = Array<u8>();
    while (true) {
        var r = stream.read(buffer, 4096);   # parks this task, not the others
        if (r.is_err() || r.value() == 0) {
            into.close();
            return;
        }
        into.send(r.value());
        buffer.clear();
    }
}

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var address = listener.local_address().value();
        var first = io.TcpStream.connect(address).value();
        var (from_first, first_peer) = listener.accept().value();
        var second = io.TcpStream.connect(address).value();
        var (from_second, second_peer) = listener.accept().value();

        # One task per socket turns what it reads into channel messages.
        var first_bytes = async.Channel<ulong>();
        var second_bytes = async.Channel<ulong>();
        async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => { forward(from_first, first_bytes); });
        async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => { forward(from_second, second_bytes); });

        first.write_all("hello");
        first.shutdown_write();
        second.write_all("hi there");
        second.shutdown_write();

        # The select then waits on both sockets at once, through their channels.
        var select = async.Select<Event>();
        select.receive(first_bytes, (count: ulong): Event => Event.Data(0, count));
        select.receive(second_bytes, (count: ulong): Event => Event.Data(1, count));
        ulong first_total = 0;
        ulong second_total = 0;
        var running = true;
        while (running) {
            match (select.wait()) {
                Ok(event) => {
                    match (event) {
                        Data(from, count) => {
                            if (from == 0) {
                                first_total = first_total + count;
                            } else {
                                second_total = second_total + count;
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
                Err(error) => {
                    running = false;   # both connections closed
                }
            }
        }
        assert(first_total == 5 && second_total == 8, "every byte arrived once");
    });
    return 0;
}

Files

File.read, write and write_all in a task park the task until the system call is done, and the worker runs other tasks meanwhile. With the IoUring backend the kernel does the read or write itself; with the others a thread from run_blocking's pool makes the blocking call. Opening, seeking, metadata and the other File calls still block the thread, as they are quick on local disks. A cancel or a timeout does not cut a read or write short: it takes effect once the call returns.

The array a read fills or a write sends from is in use until the call returns, so growing it from another task meanwhile panics ("Array: the buffer is in use by an I/O operation"). A String passed to write_all is copied first.

Accepting on every worker

An io.SharedTcpListener is a listening socket that any thread can accept on. Give each worker an accept loop with spawn_on_each_worker; each connection goes to one of the waiting workers, and the stream it returns belongs to that worker:

import async;

import io;

const served = async.Atomic<int>(0);

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(4), () => {
        var listener = io.SharedTcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var port = listener.local_address().value().port();

        # One accept loop per worker; each connection goes to one of them.
        async.spawn_on_each_worker(() => {
            while (true) {
                var accepted = listener.accept();
                if (accepted.is_err()) {
                    return;   # cancelled when the first task returns
                }
                var (stream, peer) = accepted.value();
                served.fetch_add(1);
                async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                    stream.write_all("hello").value();
                });
            }
        });

        var i = 0;
        while (i < 8) {
            var client = io.TcpStream.connect_host("127.0.0.1", port).value();
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (client.read(reply, 64).value() > 0) {
            }
            assert(reply.count == 5, "greeted");
            i = i + 1;
        }
    });
    assert(served.load() == 8, "every connection was accepted once");
    return 0;
}

The listener has no close(), since other workers may be waiting on it. It closes when the last reference goes: here, once run has cancelled the loops.

Moving a stream to another worker

stream.into_transfer() moves a connection out of a TcpStream into an io.SocketTransfer, a thread-safe token that a shared function can capture or a Channel can carry, and io.TcpStream.adopt(transfer) takes it out again on the receiving worker. The old stream is closed afterwards, only the first adopt gets the connection, and a token no one adopts closes the connection when it goes:

import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run_with(async.RuntimeOptions().workers(2), () => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var port = listener.local_address().value().port();
        var client = async.Task<ulong>.spawn_local(() => {
            var stream = io.TcpStream.connect_host("127.0.0.1", port).value();
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (stream.read(reply, 64).value() > 0) {
            }
            return reply.count;
        });

        var (stream, peer) = listener.accept().value();
        # A stream is not thread-safe; its transfer token is.
        var transfer = stream.into_transfer();
        var handler = async.spawn<void>(() => {
            var mine = io.TcpStream.adopt(transfer).value();
            mine.write_all("from any worker").value();
        });
        handler.join();
        assert(client.join().value() == 15, "the moved stream answered");
    });
    return 0;
}

When no task is ready to run, a worker blocks until a socket is ready, the next timer is due, or another worker wakes it; while tasks are running, it also checks the sockets every few dozen tasks, so a busy task cannot starve the network.

Backends

How the runtime waits for sockets is its I/O backend, an async.Backend:

BackendWhereHow
EpollLinuxepoll, edge-triggered
IoUringLinux 5.11 and laterio_uring: the kernel does stream sockets' receives and sends and files' reads and writes itself, submitted in batches, with deferred completion work; never picked automatically, since container seccomp profiles and hardened kernels often refuse it
KqueuemacOSkqueue, edge-triggered
IocpWindowsan I/O completion port, fed by AFD poll requests (as tokio and libuv do)
Polleverywherepoll() (WSAPoll on Windows), which looks at every waiting socket on each wait: fine for a few connections, slow for thousands

Backend.Automatic, the default, picks epoll, kqueue or IOCP, whichever the system has. RuntimeOptions().backend(kind) asks for one (and run_with panics if the system does not have it), and the PEPPER_IO_BACKEND environment variable (epoll, io_uring, kqueue, iocp or poll) overrides the automatic choice without changing the program, for testing and benchmarks. async.current_backend() says which one is running.

io_uring pays off as the amount of multiplexed I/O grows: many operations in flight, submitted and completed in batches through the ring rather than one system call each. With the IoUring backend, a stream socket's read and write in a task go to the kernel as a receive or send request, which it runs once the socket is ready; the worker submits every request queued since its last look, and collects every completion, in one system call. In our echo benchmark that makes about an eighth of epoll's system calls, runs as fast as epoll from 64 to 1,024 connections (half again as fast as io_uring used only for readiness), and stays about 10% behind at 4,096.

A cancel or a timeout asks the kernel to stop a request and waits for it to finish, since the kernel is writing into or reading from the array until then. A receive that got data before the cancel took effect returns that data instead of failing, so no bytes are lost. As with files, growing the array from another task meanwhile panics. Accepting, connecting, UDP sockets, and a second task reading (or writing) a socket that one already reads (or writes) still wait for readiness.

Timeouts

async.timeout(milliseconds) limits how long the waits inside a with block may take:

import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();

        # Nobody connects, so the accept gives up after 50 milliseconds.
        with (var deadline = async.timeout(50)) {
            var accepted = listener.accept();
            assert(accepted.is_err() && accepted.error().is_timed_out(), "accept timed out");
            assert(deadline.is_expired(), "the limit has passed");
        }

        # A join gives up too; the task itself carries on until cancelled.
        var slow = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => {
            async.sleep(1000000);
            return 42;
        });
        with (async.timeout(20)) {
            var result = slow.join();
            assert(result.error().is_timed_out(), "join timed out");
        }
        slow.cancel();
    });
    return 0;
}

Once the limit passes, a socket call that has to wait fails with an IoError for which is_timed_out() holds, join fails with a TaskError for which is_timed_out() holds (the task it waited for carries on), and sleep returns early. Code that does not wait is never interrupted. The limit ends with the block. Timeouts nest, and an inner one cannot extend an outer one. deadline.is_expired() says whether the limit has passed. timeout panics outside a task.

Cancelling

task.cancel() asks a task to stop. Nothing stops it by force: from then on async.is_cancelled() is true inside it, sleep returns at once, and join on it fails with a TaskError whose is_cancelled() is true. A task waiting in join returns the same error when it is cancelled itself, and a socket call waiting in a cancelled task fails with an IoError whose is_cancelled() is true. When the first task of a run returns, every task still running is cancelled, on every worker, and run waits for each to finish:

import async;

main(): int {
    var polls = Array<int>();
    async.run(() => {
        var poller = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            while (!async.is_cancelled()) {
                polls.append(1);
                async.sleep(5);
            }
        });
        async.sleep(30);
        poller.cancel();
        var result = poller.join();
        assert(result.is_err() && result.error().is_cancelled(), "a cancelled task's join fails");

        # A task still running when the first task returns is cancelled too,
        # and run waits for it to finish.
        async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            async.sleep(1000000);   # returns at once when cancelled
        });
    });
    assert(polls.count > 0, "the poller ran until cancelled");
    return 0;
}

If every task is waiting for another task and none can continue, run panics instead of waiting forever.

How it works

Each task runs on a fiber: a stack of its own and a saved set of registers. Switching tasks saves the running task's registers on its stack and restores the other's, a few instructions of assembly on Linux and macOS (the __switch_context intrinsic) and the Fibers API on Windows. A task's stack is reserved address space with a guard page below it; only the pages the task touches use memory, and a task that overflows its stack ends the program with panic: stack overflow, as a thread does (see Assertions and panics). Stacks are reused for later tasks.

Each worker has its own ready queue, timers and backend. Workers talk through a queue of messages each (a spawned task finished, was cancelled, or was woken by a Mutex, Condition or Channel) and a doorbell that ends a worker's wait in its backend from another thread: an eventfd with epoll and io_uring, a user event with kqueue, a posted completion with IOCP, and a pipe (on Windows, a loopback UDP socket that a second socket sends to) with poll(). run_blocking's pool threads are plain threads that report back through the same messages.

Current status

  • File calls other than read, write and write_all (opening, seeking, sync, directories) block the thread in a task.
  • The tasks of a thread share its ThreadLocal values, on every system; a TaskLocal<T> gives each task its own.

The reference page documents every function.

Modules and imports

As a program grows, you split it into files, and group related files into modules. An import makes another file's or module's exported declarations available in the importing file. What a file exports is covered in Visibility.

Importing a file

The simplest import names another file, as a string, relative to the importing file. The .pep extension is optional:

# Every import comes before the file's declarations.
import "util";                       # util.pep's exports, unqualified
import "util" as u;                  # the same exports, as u.name
import [thrice as triple] from "util";
import "helpers/text";               # a file in a subfolder

main(): int {
    assert(twice(BASE) == 20, "unqualified names from util.pep");
    assert(u.thrice(2) == 6, "qualified by the alias");
    assert(triple(3) == 9, "renamed by the import list");
    assert(shout("hi") == "hi!", "from helpers/text.pep");

    # An imported function is a value like any other.
    var f = u.twice;
    assert(f(4) == 8, "function reference through a qualifier");
    return 0;
}

util.pep sits next to main.pep, and text.pep is in a helpers folder:

export const BASE = 10;

export twice(n: int): int {
    return n * 2;
}

export thrice(n: int): int {
    return n * 3;
}

export shout(s: String): String {
    return s + "!";
}

An import comes in one of these forms:

FormWhat it makes available
import "util";Every export of util.pep, unqualified: twice(BASE).
import "util" as u;Every export, qualified by the name you choose: u.twice(1).
import [thrice as triple, twice] from "util";Only the listed exports, unqualified, each under its own name or the one after as.
import geometry;A module's exports, qualified by the module's name: geometry.Point.
import geometry as g;A module's exports, qualified by g.
import [area, Point as Pt] from geometry;The listed exports of a module, unqualified.

An import ends with a semicolon.

An import binds names only in the file that contains it. The exports of a file that this file did not import are not visible to it, even when another file of the program imports them. Here geometry/module.pep imports shapes.pep, but main.pep imports only the module:

import geometry;
main(): int { return area(1, 2); }

main.pep:2:22: error: 'area' is exported by deps/geometry/shapes.pep, which this file does not import; add an import for it
    2 | main(): int { return area(1, 2); }
      |                      ^~~~
deps/geometry/shapes.pep:3:8: note: declared here
    3 | export area(w: int, h: int): int {
      |        ^~~~

Imports come first

Every import, and every export ... from, comes before all of a file's declarations and export name re-exports:

main(): int { return 0; }
import geometry;

main.pep:2:1: error: imports must come before all declarations
    2 | import geometry;
      | ^~~~~~

Modules

A module is a folder that contains a module.pep file. The module is named after its folder, and its exports are exactly what its module.pep exports. The other files in the folder are the module's own files: module.pep imports them and chooses what to pass on to the module's users. A file of a module sees the declarations of the module's files it imports, exported or not, except those marked private (see Files of a module see each other through imports). Loading any file of a module loads its module.pep, and with it every file the module imports.

This example has a geometry module next to main.pep:

modules-folders/
    main.pep
    geometry/
        module.pep      # the module's interface
        shapes.pep      # a file of the module
        solids/
            module.pep  # a module nested inside geometry

# A file of the geometry module. Its exports are visible to the files of
# the module that import it, not to the module's importers.
export area(w: int, h: int): int {
    return w * h;
}

export struct Box<T> {
    var value: T;
}

# A module nested in the geometry folder.
export volume(w: int, h: int, d: int): int {
    return w * h * d;
}

# The geometry module: what this file exports is the module's interface.
import "shapes";
import "solids" as solids;

export struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

export make(x: int, y: int): Point {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = x;
    p.y = y;
    return p;
}

reset_count(): int {
    return 0;
}

export area as rect_area;           # shapes.pep's area, renamed
export Box;                         # shapes.pep's Box, under its own name
export reset_count as reset;        # a private function, exported as reset
export solids.volume as box_volume; # from the nested module

import "geometry" as g;
import [rect_area, Point as Pt] from "geometry";

# Qualified names work in types, too.
corner(): g.Point {
    return g.make(1, 1);
}

main(): int {
    var p: g.Point = g.make(3, 4);
    assert(p.x == 3, "qualified function and type");

    Pt q = corner();
    assert(q.y == 1, "the struct under its import-list name");

    assert(g.rect_area(2, 3) == 6, "re-exported under a new name");
    assert(rect_area(2, 5) == 10, "imported unqualified");
    assert(g.reset() == 0, "a private function, re-exported");
    assert(g.box_volume(2, 3, 4) == 24, "re-exported from a nested module");

    var b = g.Box<int>();
    b.value = 7;
    var boxes: g.Box<int>[] = g.Box<int>[]();
    boxes.append(b);
    assert(boxes[0].value == 7, "a generic struct through a qualifier");
    return 0;
}

main.pep imports the folder with a string, import "geometry", because the module lives next to it. A string import names either a file (geometry.pep) or a module folder (geometry/) relative to the importing file. A module imports a module nested in its own folder the same way: geometry/module.pep imports "solids".

Re-exports

export name as new_name; exports name to importers under new_name, and export name; exports it under its own name. The name may be declared in the file (even privately) or imported from another file or module, qualified or not. This is how a module.pep publishes what its other files define.

The semicolon is required. Without it, export Box followed by a declaration would read as an exported C-style declaration whose type is Box.

The exports of the module's other files are not the module's exports. In the example, users of geometry can call g.rect_area, but not g.area:

main.pep:2:22: error: 'area' is not exported by 'geometry' (deps/geometry/module.pep)
    2 | main(): int { return geometry.area(1, 2); }
      |                      ^~~~~~~~~~~~~

Re-exporting a whole file or module

A module.pep that only passes on its files' exports would repeat every name. export ... from passes them on in one line, in the same shapes as the import ... from forms:

FormWhat importers get
export * from "rect";Every export of rect.pep, each under its own name.
export * from geometry;Every export of the module geometry.
export [perimeter as outline, Side] from "measure";Only the listed exports, each under its own name or the one after as.
# The shapes module: its interface is its files' exports, passed on whole or
# by name.
export * from "rect";                               # every export of rect.pep
export [perimeter as outline, Side] from "measure"; # two, one renamed

import "shapes";

main(): int {
    var r = make_rect(3, 4);
    assert(area(r) == 12, "from export * of rect.pep");
    assert(outline(r) == 14, "from the export list, renamed");

    var s = Side();
    s.length = 5;
    assert(s.length == 5, "a struct from the export list");
    return 0;
}

  • It re-exports; it doesn't import. export * from "rect"; makes no name visible in the file that contains it. Inside a module that does not matter, since the module's files see each other's declarations anyway; a file outside it imports the names as usual (import "rect";).

  • Only exports travel. Private declarations stay behind, and extensions stay visible only as they always are.

  • Collisions are errors. If two re-exports, or a re-export and one of the file's own exports, publish one name for different declarations, the compiler reports it at the export ... from that adds the second one. List the names you want instead, or rename one with as. The exception is functions declared under one name: they join one overload set. Anything else collides:

    shapes/module.pep:2:1: error: 'area' is exported twice by module 'shapes'
    2 | export * from "measure";
      | ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
shapes/module.pep:1:1: note: also exported here
    1 | export * from "rect";
      | ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

  • Like imports, export ... from lines come before every declaration and take attributes such as [Target(...)]. A deprecated declaration stays deprecated through every re-export.

A module's files stay inside it

A string import from a file of a module must name a file of the same module, or a module folder. Reaching into another module's files, or out of your own module, is an error:

main.pep:1:8: error: "geometry/shapes.pep" belongs to another module; import that module's folder instead
    1 | import "geometry/shapes";
      |        ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

geometry/bad.pep:1:8: error: "../main.pep" is outside this file's module; a module imports only its own files
    1 | import "../main";
      |        ^~~~~~~~~

A file outside any module, such as your program's main.pep, may import files in its own folder or below, except files inside a module folder there.

Files of one module may import each other, even in a cycle.

Dependencies and search paths

A module that is not part of your program's own folders, such as a library you depend on, is imported by name rather than by string:

import geometry;

main(): int {
    var p: geometry.Point = geometry.make(3, 4);
    return p.x - 3;
}

An identifier import looks for a folder geometry/module.pep on the search paths: first each directory you pass with -I, in order, then the runtime directory. If geometry lives in a deps folder, compile with:

pepper build main.pep -I deps -o main

An identifier import never looks next to the importing file. A module that is not found is reported with the places the compiler looked:

main.pep:1:8: error: cannot find module 'nowhere': no nowhere/module.pep in deps, /home/you/pepper/runtime
    1 | import nowhere;
      |        ^~~~~~~

The standard library's io module is found this way, in the runtime directory: import io; then io.File, or import [File, Path] from io;.

A module nested in another module's folder is imported with a dotted name: import geometry.solids; finds geometry/solids/module.pep and binds its last name, so its declarations are solids.volume (or, with import geometry.solids as s;, s.volume).

Projects and packages

A project's pep.toml lists the packages it depends on, and each key is the name source code imports:

[dependencies]
geometry = { github = "someone/geometry", version = "1.2" }

import geometry; then finds the package's root module.pep in the project's .pep/deps, with no -I, and import geometry.solids; the module in its solids folder. pepper build with no file builds the project.

  • Each package imports by its own keys. A dependency's files import the packages its own pep.toml lists, under its names for them. When two packages need different major versions of one package, each import reaches the major its key asks for, and the two majors' types are different types.
  • A dev-dependency ([dev-dependencies]) is imported only in a test build (--test) and by the files in examples/, and a build-dependency ([build-dependencies]) only by the package's build script; an import of either anywhere else is an error at the name.
  • A dependency only some platforms have ([target.'OS(Windows)'.dependencies]) is imported under the same condition, [Target(OS(Windows))] import winapi;, so builds for other targets skip the import (see Platform-specific imports).
  • A build script's generated module is imported as generated by the package's own files (see Generated modules).

See Projects: pep.toml.

The runtime prelude and --import

The runtime itself is not a module: its files are loaded into every program, and their exports, such as String, Array, and Result, are visible everywhere without an import.

--import NAME adds a module, or a file NAME.pep, found on the search paths to that prelude, so every file sees its exports without importing it. A name that resolves to neither is an error:

error: --import no_such_module: cannot find module 'no_such_module' (no no_such_module/module.pep) or file no_such_module.pep in /home/you/pepper/runtime

A prelude module may redefine an export of the runtime, such as panic: it is loaded ahead of the runtime and its definition wins. It must declare the name itself (export panic(...)); re-exporting another function under a runtime export's name is an error, since the runtime's own files would keep calling their version. When the runtime's function is overloaded, the prelude module replaces only the overloads it declares, matched by parameter types, defaulted ones included: an export assert(condition: bool, message: String, location: __ptr<char> = __caller_location()) replaces the String form, and a string literal message still calls the runtime's __ptr<char> form.

Only functions may be redefined this way. A struct, trait, type alias or variable that a prelude module exports under a name the runtime (or another prelude module) already exports is an error in the module loaded first, with a note at the other:

alt/module.pep:1:15: error: redefinition of 'MapIterator'
    1 | export struct MapIterator<K, V> { var key: K; var value: V; }
      |               ^~~~~~~~~~~
runtime/iterator.pep:182:15: note: also exported here

How imported names behave

  • Qualified names work wherever a name does: in expressions (g.rect_area(1, 2), or a module variable such as u.BASE), in types (var p: g.Point, g.Box<int>[], a return type g.Point), and in generic constructions (g.Box<int>()). A generic construction is recognized only for a qualifier imported earlier in the file; elsewhere a.b < c, d > (e) is two comparisons.
  • Local names shadow imports. A local variable, parameter, generic parameter, or struct member hides a qualifier or an imported name of the same name.
  • A file may not import a name it also declares at top level: 'make' is imported but also declared in this file. Functions are the exception: a file's own functions of a name join the imported ones in one overload set.
  • An import list wins. A name listed in import [...] takes priority over the same name from a whole-file import. When two whole-file imports provide the same name differently, using that name is an error because it is ambiguous, unless both are functions declared under that name, which join one overload set.
  • A local may share an imported declaration's name. If g.rect_area is shapes.pep's area, calling g.rect_area(1, 2) inside a function with a parameter named area calls shapes.pep's function. The one exception is a re-exported runtime name: if a module exports the runtime's print as say, a local named print where you call say is an error that asks you to rename one of them.

Each module (and each file outside a module) has its own namespace, for its exported declarations as well as its private ones, so modules may reuse names freely: two modules may both export parse, and a.parse and b.parse stay apart. See Each module has its own namespace. Here metric and imperial each export a Length, a parse and a unit:

# Both modules export `Length`, `parse` and `unit`; each keeps its own.
import "metric" as metric;
import "imperial" as imp;
import [unit as imperial_unit] from "imperial";

main(): int {
    var a: metric.Length = metric.parse("abc");
    var b: imp.Length = imp.parse("abc");
    assert(a.metres == 3.0, "metric.parse");
    assert(b.feet == 9.0, "imperial.parse");
    assert(metric.unit() == "m", "qualified by the alias");
    assert(imperial_unit() == "ft", "renamed by the import list");
    return 0;
}

Platform-specific imports

An import or a re-export may carry attributes like any declaration. With a [Target(...)] attribute it applies only on matching platforms and is ignored elsewhere (see Platform selection):

[Target(OS(Linux))]
import linux;

[Target(OS(Linux))]
export linux_open as open;

[Target(OS(Windows))]
export * from "windows";

Visibility

Visibility decides which declarations other files may use. A top-level declaration has one of three levels:

WrittenVisible to
private f()its own file only
f()the files of its module
export f()any file that imports it

With no modifier, a declaration is internal to its module: the files of one module see each other's declarations, and nothing else does. A file outside any module is a module of its own, so its declarations are private to the file. This lets a module, or a file, keep its helpers to itself and offer a small, clear surface to the code that imports it.

private is optional. It is recommended for a helper that only its own file uses, so it does not leak into the rest of the module, and it is needed only where two files of one module would otherwise declare the same name (see Keeping a declaration to its file).

Exporting declarations

Put export in front of a declaration to make it usable from other files that import this one (see Modules and imports for how to import). You can export every kind of top-level declaration:

  • functions, including extern declarations of C functions
  • structs
  • enums
  • type aliases
  • traits
  • extensions
  • module-scope variables, which are always const and thread-safe (see Module-scope variables)

Here is a library file with a mix of exported and private declarations, and a program that uses it:

import async;

# Everything here is private to lib.pep unless it says `export`.

export struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

export type Points = Point[];

export trait Describe {
    describe(): String;
}

# A module-scope variable is `const` and thread-safe: change it through
# an Atomic.
export const points_made = async.Atomic<int>(0);

export origin(): Point {
    return make(0, 0);
}

export at(x: int, y: int): Point {
    return make(x, y);
}

# Private: only lib.pep can call make().
make(x: int, y: int): Point {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = x;
    p.y = y;
    points_made.fetch_add(1);
    return p;
}

# An exported extension: its methods are usable wherever Point is.
export extend Point with Describe {
    describe(): String {
        return "point";
    }
}

# A private extension: only lib.pep can call p.norm().
extend Point {
    norm(): int {
        return x * x + y * y;
    }
}

export norm_of(p: Point): int {
    return p.norm();
}

# `export` goes after attributes, directly before the declaration.
[Target(OS(Windows))]
export platform_name(): String { return "Windows"; }

[Target(!OS(Windows))]
export platform_name(): String { return "not Windows"; }

import "lib";

main(): int {
    var p = at(3, 4);             # exported function
    var o: Point = origin();      # exported struct, used as a type
    Points list = Points();       # exported type alias
    list.append(p);
    list.append(o);

    assert(p.x == 3, "fields are as visible as their struct");
    assert(p.describe() == "point", "method from an exported extension");
    assert(norm_of(p) == 25, "an exported function may use private helpers");
    assert(points_made.load() == 2, "exported module variable");
    assert(platform_name().length > 0, "exported, with an attribute");
    return 0;
}

main.pep can call at, origin, and norm_of, use Point and Points as types, and read the counter in points_made, an exported const Atomic<int>. It cannot use make or call p.norm(). Trying to is an error that tells you how to fix it:

import "lib";

main(): int {
    var q = make(1, 2);
    return 0;
}

main.pep:4:13: error: 'make' is private to lib.pep; declare it with 'export' to use it from another file
    4 |     var q = make(1, 2);
      |             ^~~~
lib.pep:29:1: note: declared here
   29 | make(x: int, y: int): Point {
      | ^~~~

The same applies to private structs, enums, type aliases, traits, and variables: naming one from another file reports 'name' is private to file.pep.

Files of a module see each other through imports

Inside a module, export is not needed for one file to use another's declarations, but an import is: a file sees the top-level declarations of another file of its module, exported or not, once it imports that file (import "rules";), as a C file sees another's declarations through its header. export means visible outside the module, through its module.pep.

Here the inventory module keeps its rules in rules.pep, which exports nothing, and stock.pep imports it to use them:

# Module-internal: no `export`, yet every file of `inventory` can use these.
const RESTOCK_LEVEL = 5;

struct Shelf {
    var count: int;
}

needs_restock(shelf: Shelf): bool {
    return shelf.count < RESTOCK_LEVEL;
}

# Uses `Shelf`, `needs_restock` and `RESTOCK_LEVEL` from rules.pep, which
# this file imports: a file of a module sees another through an import.
import "rules";

export struct Stock {
    var _shelf: Shelf;

    construct(count: int) {
        _shelf = Shelf();
        _shelf.count = count;
    }

    low(): bool {
        return needs_restock(_shelf);
    }

    missing(): int {
        if low() {
            return RESTOCK_LEVEL - _shelf.count;
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

# The module's interface: only what this file exports reaches importers.
export * from "stock";

# `rules.pep` exports nothing, so importing it only makes it part of the
# module.
import "rules";

import "inventory";

main(): int {
    var s = Stock(2);
    assert(s.low(), "two is below the restock level");
    assert(s.missing() == 3, "three more reach it");
    # `needs_restock(...)` here would be an error: it is internal to the
    # module 'inventory'.
    return 0;
}

A file's own declarations come first, then what its imports bring in (the files of its module it imports included), then the runtime's. A file of the module that names a declaration of another one it does not import gets an error that names the file to import. Without its import "rules";, stock.pep would report:

inventory/stock.pep:5:17: error: 'Shelf' is declared in inventory/rules.pep, another file of this module, which this file does not import; add an import for it
    5 |     var _shelf: Shelf;
      |                 ^~~~~

So a file's dependencies are exactly its imports, and the compiler checks and caches each file against what it imports alone. A module's files are the files of the program in its folder (and in subfolders that are not modules themselves): a file joins the program when the module imports it, so module.pep imports a file with nothing to export, like rules.pep, just to include it. A [Target(...)] on that import (see Platform-specific imports) includes the file only on some platforms.

Outside the module, its internal declarations stay hidden. Using one is an error that names the module:

main.pep:3:13: error: 'Shelf' is internal to module 'inventory'; export it from the module to use it here
    3 |     var s = Shelf();
      |             ^~~~~
inventory/rules.pep:4:8: note: declared here
    4 | struct Shelf {
      |        ^~~~~

The files of a module still share one set of names, so two of them may not both declare a struct, enum, type alias, trait, or variable of one name: the second is a redefinition of 'name', with a note at the first, unless one of them is private. Functions are different: functions of one name in several files of a module are one overload set, as they are within a file. Extensions are shared the same way: a file sees the methods the files of its module it imports add, exported or not, unless the extension is private.

Keeping a declaration to its file

Put private in front of a top-level declaration to keep it to its own file: the other files of its module do not see it. You can mark every kind of declaration that export applies to. Two files of one module may then each declare a private helper of the same name, and each file's code reaches its own. Here summary.pep and detail.pep each have a private WIDTH and label, and share the module-internal pad:

# `private` keeps these to this file: detail.pep may declare its own
# `WIDTH` and `label` without a clash.
private const WIDTH: ulong = 10;

private label(count: int): String {
    return $"{count} item(s)";
}

# Module-internal: no modifier, so detail.pep can use it too.
pad(text: String, width: ulong): String {
    if (text.size >= width) {
        return text;
    }
    return text + " ".repeat(width - text.size);
}

export summary_line(count: int): String {
    return pad(label(count), WIDTH);
}

# The same names as summary.pep's private ones, and private here too.
import "summary";

private const WIDTH: ulong = 12;

private label(name: String): String {
    return $"- {name}";
}

export detail_line(name: String): String {
    return pad(label(name), WIDTH) + "|";
}

# The module's interface: one function from each file.
export * from "summary";
export * from "detail";

import "report";

main(): int {
    assert(summary_line(3) == "3 item(s) ", "summary.pep's own label and width");
    assert(detail_line("pen") == "- pen       |", "detail.pep's own label and width");
    # `label(3)` here would be an error: it is private to summary.pep.
    return 0;
}

A private declaration stays out of the rest of the module entirely:

  • Another file of the module that names it, without a declaration of its own by that name, gets an error saying to remove private. Were detail.pep to have no label of its own, calling label(3) there would report:

    report/detail.pep:6:16: error: 'label' is private to report/summary.pep; remove 'private' to use it from the other files of its module
    6 |     return pad(label(3), WIDTH) + "|";
      |                ^~~~~
report/summary.pep:5:9: note: declared here
    5 | private label(count: int): String {
      |         ^~~~~

  • A private function joins no overload set of the module: functions of one name in the other files form their set without it, and its own file sees only its own.

  • A private extension's methods are usable only in its file.

Code outside the module never sees a private declaration, as it never sees a module-internal one ('label' is internal to module 'report').

In a file outside any module, private changes nothing: its declarations are already private to it. A declaration cannot be both export and private:

main.pep:1:8: error: a declaration cannot be both 'export' and 'private'
    1 | export private f(): int { return 0; }
      |        ^~~~~~~

Members of structs and extensions

Fields and methods declared inside a struct's body are reached through the struct, so they share the struct's visibility: if you can use the struct, you can use all of its members.

To let other code read a value but not write it, make it a property with only a get: var balance: long { get; } can be assigned only by the struct's own constructors and methods.

Methods added by an extension share the extension's visibility instead. In the example, norm() is added by a private extension, so only lib.pep (or, in a module, the module's files) can call it, even though Point itself is exported:

main.pep:4:14: error: 'norm' is declared in a private extension in lib.pep; declare the extension with 'export' to use it from another file
    4 |     return p.norm();
      |              ^~~~
lib.pep:46:5: note: declared here
   46 |     norm(): int {
      |     ^~~~

An exported extension's methods are usable where its file is imported, not everywhere: a file sees the extensions it declares itself, the exported extensions of the files it imports, the exported extensions of every file of a module it imports (import geo reaches geo/ext.pep's), and those of the runtime, which every file sees. Here measure.pep adds manhattan() to Point, and main.pep imports it to call it:

import "point";

# An exported extension: files that import measure.pep can call these.
export extend Point {
    manhattan(): int {
        return abs(x) + abs(y);
    }
}

# Private to this file.
abs(v: int): int {
    if (v < 0) { return -v; }
    return v;
}

import "point";
import "measure";                      # brings Point's manhattan() into scope

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 3;
    p.y = -4;
    assert(p.manhattan() == 7, "an extension from an imported file");
    return 0;
}

Without import "measure";, the call is an error. If no file of the program imports measure.pep, the method does not exist at all (no member named 'manhattan' in 'Point'); if another file does, the error says which import is missing:

main.pep:8:14: error: 'manhattan' is declared in an extension in measure.pep, which this file does not import; add an import for it
    8 |     assert(p.manhattan() == 7, "an extension from an imported file");
      |              ^~~~~~~~~
measure.pep:5:5: note: declared here
    5 |     manhattan(): int {
      |     ^~~~~~~~~

Two kinds of call are checked where they take effect rather than here:

  • A method of a trait you can see (s.area() where area is a method of a trait Shape you declare, import, or get from the standard library): the call may go through a value of that trait, which works whatever file declares the conformance. A file can return a Shape whose struct and conformance stay private, and callers still call area on it.
  • A call on a receiver whose type is not known in this file: this.m() in a trait's default method, or x.m() (or x.f().m()) where x is a parameter typed by a type parameter, the function's or its struct's (measure<X>(x: X)). Such a call resolves where the generic is used, with that file's imports.

When the extension is in a file of another module, the error names the module to import instead (import its module 'geo'), since a file of another module is reached only through its module.

Inside a struct's methods (and a trait's default methods), a bare call to a name that an extension you cannot see adds as a method is an error too, rather than a call to the top-level function of that name: the compiler would otherwise bind it to the method. Rename one of them, or import the extension's file if the method is what you meant. That import may point back at a file that imports this one (a struct's file importing the file that extends it); such cycles are allowed.

Extending a struct does not make a private struct visible to other files.

Visibility is checked before types are known, so members are matched by name: a call x.m() is accepted if any struct body visible to the file (its own, or exported) or any extension visible to it, as above, declares a member named m.

Where export and private go

export and private go directly before the declaration's keyword or name, after any attributes:

[Target(OS(Windows))]
export platform_name(): String { return "Windows"; }

[Inline]
private twice(x: int): int { return x * 2; }

Writing it before the attributes is a parse error:

main.pep:2:8: error: unexpected '['
    2 | export [Target(OS(Windows))] f(): int { return 1; }
      |        ^

export controls visibility between Pepper files only. Making a function callable from C with C linkage is a separate matter, handled by the [Export] attribute described in Calling Pepper from C.

The runtime's exports

The runtime's public surface (String, Array, HashMap, HashSet, Result, Error, hash, assert, panic, and the rest of the standard library reference) is exported the same way, and is visible in every file without an import. The runtime's own helpers are private, so calling one, such as _pep_check_sync_enabled, reports '_pep_check_sync_enabled' is private to followed by the path of the runtime's internals.pep.

Each module has its own namespace

A private declaration belongs to its file (or its module) alone, so two files outside any module, or two modules, may each declare a private name without clashing. Within a module, private does the same for two of its files (see Keeping a declaration to its file). Here main.pep and lib.pep each have their own Counter and make, and each file's code reaches its own:

# lib.pep's private helpers: no other file can see them, and no other
# file's names can clash with them.
struct Counter { var n: int; }

make(): Counter {
    var c = Counter();
    c.n = 10;
    return c;
}

export lib_total(): int {
    return make().n;
}

import "lib";

# main.pep has its own private Counter and make(), unrelated to lib.pep's.
struct Counter { var n: int; var step: int; }

make(): Counter {
    var c = Counter();
    c.n = 1;
    c.step = 2;
    return c;
}

main(): int {
    var c = make();                    # main.pep's make()
    assert(c.n + c.step == 3, "main's own Counter");
    assert(lib_total() == 10, "lib's make() is its own");
    return 0;
}

This holds across modules too: two modules may each have a util.pep with a private helper. Files are told apart by their path inside their module (io/file.pep), not by their file name alone. Within one module, the files share their names instead, except private ones (see Files of a module see each other through imports).

Exported names work the same way between modules: each module's exports are its own, so two modules may export the same name, and importers tell them apart by qualifier (a.parse and b.parse) or by an import list (import [parse as parse_b] from b). Using a name that two whole-file imports both provide is an error at the use (see Modules and imports). A private name may repeat an exported one from another file; in the file that declares it, the file's own declaration is the one that name refers to.

Two kinds of file keep their exported names program-wide, because every file reaches them without an import or by its bare name: the runtime (and any --import module), and the program's main file. So an export may not repeat a runtime name: exported 'String' is also declared in followed by the runtime's file.

A few kinds of declaration are not private in this sense:

  • extern declarations name a C function, which is the same function in every file. Several files may declare the same extern.
  • Concrete overrides of a generic function, such as hash<int> alongside hash<T>, take the generic function's name: they replace its version for those types wherever it is called. So each override may be declared in only one file (override 'hash<int>' is also declared in b.pep), and overriding one the runtime already provides, such as hash<String>, is also an error. An override must be for a generic function you can see: overriding another file's private generic function reports that it is private. An override may be for a struct, such as hash<Point>, and must be declared in the file or module that declares the generic or one of its type arguments (see Generics).
  • Declarations that a [Target(...)] attribute drops for the platform being compiled (see Platform selection) are never compiled. This is why the first lib.pep above can declare platform_name twice.

Naming conventions

Pepper code, including the standard library, follows one set of naming rules. The compiler does not enforce them, but every example in this book, the runtime, and the tools in this repository follow them, and code you contribute should too.

WhatStyleExamples
Structs, traits, type aliasesPascalCaseString, HashMap, IoResult
Generic parametersone capital letter, or PascalCaseT, K, V, TValue, TError
Data members (fields)snake_caseunit_name, is_file
Methods and free functionssnake_caseappend, remove_at, read_to_string
Parameters and local variablessnake_casecapacity, best_so_far
Constants (a const holding a fixed value)SCREAMING_CASEMAX_REQUESTS, LINE_WIDTH
Other module-scope variablessnake_caserequest_count
Private data members and methods_ then snake_case_readings, _is_empty
# Types are PascalCase; acronyms are written as words (`HttpClient`, not `HTTPClient`).
struct TemperatureLog {
    # Public data members are snake_case.
    var unit_name: String = "celsius";
    # Private data members start with `_`.
    var _readings: Array<int> = Array<int>();
    var _total: int = 0;

    # Methods and their parameters are snake_case.
    add_reading(degrees: int) {
        _readings.append(degrees);
        _total = _total + degrees;
    }

    average(): int {
        return _is_empty() ? 0 : _total / (_readings.count as int);
    }

    # A private method starts with `_` too.
    _is_empty(): bool {
        return _readings.count == 0;
    }
}

# Generic parameters are a single capital letter or PascalCase.
struct Pair<TFirst, TSecond> {
    var first: TFirst;
    var second: TSecond;

    construct(TFirst first, TSecond second) {
        this.first = first;
        this.second = second;
    }
}

# Free functions and local variables are snake_case.
largest_of<T>(values: Array<T>): T {
    var best_so_far = values[0];
    for (var value in values) {
        if (value > best_so_far) {
            best_so_far = value;
        }
    }
    return best_so_far;
}

main(): int {
    var log = TemperatureLog();
    log.add_reading(20);
    log.add_reading(24);
    assert(log.average() == 22, "average of the readings");
    assert(log.unit_name == "celsius", "public member");

    var pair = Pair<String, int>("answer", 42);
    assert(pair.second == 42, "generic struct");

    var numbers = Array<int>();
    numbers.append(3);
    numbers.append(9);
    numbers.append(4);
    assert(largest_of<int>(numbers) == 9, "generic function");
    return 0;
}

Types

A type name is PascalCase: each word starts with a capital letter, and there are no underscores. Write an acronym as a word, so IoError and HttpClient, not IOError or HTTPClient.

An enum's cases are PascalCase too (Color.Red, Status.NotFound).

A generic parameter is either a single capital letter (T, U, K, V) or a PascalCase name, which by convention starts with T (TValue, TError). Use a single letter when the parameter's role is obvious, and a name when a declaration has several parameters that a reader has to tell apart.

Members, functions, and variables

Everything else a program names is snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores. That covers a struct's data members, its methods, free functions, parameters, local variables, and module-scope variables.

The exception is a constant: a const, at module scope or in a function, whose value is fixed, such as a number, string, or character. Its name is SCREAMING_CASE, uppercase words joined by underscores (MAX_REQUESTS, LINE_WIDTH). A module-scope const that holds an object, such as const request_count = async.Atomic<int>(0);, is a variable and stays snake_case.

Spell words out. A name is read far more often than it is typed, so prefer iterate, index, and directory to iter, idx, and dir. Keep an abbreviation only when it is the usual name for the thing, such as io or c_str.

An extern declaration keeps the name the C library gives the function, whatever its style (GetCurrentProcessId), because that name is what the linker looks up. The same goes for the fields of a struct that mirrors a C struct.

Built-in type names

Unlike the conventions above, this rule is enforced. No top-level declaration may take the name of a built-in type: void, bool, char, byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float, double, and their sized spellings (i8, u8, i16, u16, i32, u32, i64, u64, f32, f64). Names resolve by spelling across the whole program, so such a declaration would take the type's place in every file, the runtime's included. The compiler reports it at the name:

main.pep:1:7: error: 'double' is the name of a built-in type; choose another name
    1 | const double = (x: int): int => x * 2;
      |       ^~~~~~

Locals, parameters and members may still use these names, since they are visible only where they are declared.

Private members

Pepper's private keyword applies only to top-level declarations (see Visibility); any code that can reach an object can name all of its members. A leading _ marks a data member or method as private to its struct instead: code outside the struct, and its extensions, should not use it. The rest of the name is snake_case, as for a public member (_readings, _is_empty).

The standard library relies on this convention: its generated reference leaves _ members out, and doc comments are required only on members without the prefix.

A top-level declaration does not need the prefix to be private: it is internal to its module (or, outside any module, private to its file) unless it is exported, and private keeps it to its file (see Visibility). The runtime also uses the prefix on top-level helpers it exports but that are not part of its public API, such as _pep_malloc, which the compiler calls by name, or a helper one runtime module shares with another: the reference leaves them out too.

Documentation comments

Comments explain code to the people who read it. Pepper has one comment syntax, #, and a convention on top of it for documentation: lines starting with ## directly above a declaration document that declaration. Your editor shows them when you hover over a use of the name, and the standard library reference in this book is generated from them.

Comments

A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. It can take a whole line or follow code:

# Count the lines that are not blank.
var count = 0;   # blank lines are skipped below

Pepper has no block comment syntax: to comment out several lines, start each with #. (// is not a comment in Pepper.)

Doc comments

A doc comment is a run of consecutive lines that start with ##, directly above the declaration it documents:

## Returns the larger of `a` and `b`.
##
## @param a the first value
## @param b the second value
## @returns `a` when it is at least `b`, otherwise `b`
larger(a: int, b: int): int {
    return a >= b ? a : b;
}
  • The text of each line is what follows ## . A line that is just ## is a blank line in the documentation, which separates paragraphs.
  • The comment must sit directly above the declaration, with no blank line in between. Attributes and export or static may come between the comment and the declaration, so put the comment above the attributes.
  • Only lines that start with exactly two # count. A single # is an ordinary comment, and a line starting with three or more, such as a decorative #######, is not documentation.
  • A doc comment works on functions, structs, enums and their cases, traits, extensions, type aliases, module-scope variables, and the fields, properties, constructors and methods inside a struct, enum, trait or extension.

What to write

Start with a description: what the declaration does, in the third person ("Returns ...", "Appends ..."), followed by what a caller needs to know, such as edge cases, who owns what, how long it takes, and differences between platforms. The description is Markdown, so put code in backticks.

After the description come tags, each starting a line with @. A tag's text runs until the next tag.

TagUse it for
@typeParam T descriptioneach generic parameter of a generic struct, trait, type alias or function
@param name descriptioneach parameter of a function, method or constructor
@returns descriptionwhat the function returns, whenever it returns a value
@panics descriptioneach way a caller can make the function panic (a failed assert, a call to panic)
@examplesample code, indented on the lines that follow; line breaks are kept
@see namea related declaration
@note texta remark that does not fit elsewhere

Write tag descriptions like clang writes errors: lowercase start, no trailing period. A field or a type alias usually needs only one line: ## The number of bytes in the buffer.

Keep notes that matter only to the people maintaining the code in ordinary # comments inside the body. The doc comment is the contract with callers.

Here is a small documented library:

# A small library, documented the way the standard library is.
# This line and the one above are ordinary comments: they start with a
# single '#'. Doc comments start with '##'.

## A last-in, first-out collection.
##
## Elements come out in the reverse of the order they went in.
##
## @typeParam T the type of the elements
## @example
##     var s = Stack<int>();
##     s.push(1);
##     s.push(2);
##     var top = s.pop();   # top == 2
struct Stack<T> {
    ## The elements, bottom first.
    var items: Array<T> = Array<T>();

    ## Adds `value` on top of the stack.
    ##
    ## @param value the element to add
    push(value: T) {
        items.append(value);
    }

    ## Removes and returns the element on top of the stack.
    ##
    ## @returns the element that was pushed last
    ## @panics if the stack is empty
    ## @see Stack.push
    pop(): T {
        assert(items.count > 0, "pop() on an empty Stack");
        return items.remove_at(items.count - 1);
    }

    ## Returns the number of elements.
    ##
    ## @returns how many elements the stack holds
    count(): ulong {
        return items.count;
    }
}

## Returns the larger of `a` and `b`.
##
## @param a the first value
## @param b the second value
## @returns `a` when it is at least `b`, otherwise `b`
## @note ties return `a`
larger(a: int, b: int): int {
    # An implementation note for maintainers, not part of the docs.
    return a >= b ? a : b;
}

main(): int {
    var s = Stack<int>();
    s.push(1);
    s.push(2);
    assert(s.pop() == 2, "the last element comes out first");
    assert(s.count() == 1, "one element is left");
    assert(larger(3, 7) == 7, "larger returns the larger value");
    return 0;
}

Where doc comments appear

  • In your editor. The Pepper language server shows a declaration's doc comment when you hover over its name, anywhere it is used. The description comes first, followed by sections for the type parameters, parameters, return value, panics, related declarations, notes and examples.
  • In the standard library reference. The reference pages are generated from the doc comments in the runtime, one page per runtime file. A ## block at the very top of a file, followed by a blank line, introduces that file's page. Building this documentation explains how to regenerate them.
  • In a package's reference. pepper doc package builds the same pages for a package, from its own sources, and pepper doc package --check reports its undocumented declarations the way the runtime's check does (see pep-doc package).

The standard library is fully documented

Every public declaration in the runtime must have a doc comment: every exported declaration whose name does not start with _, and every field, constructor and method of such a struct, trait or extension whose name does not start with _. Names starting with _ are internals shared between runtime files and are exempt.

A test enforces this, and reports a clang-style error for each gap: a missing doc comment, a comment with no description, a missing @param, @typeParam or @returns, a tag with no description, a @returns on a function that returns nothing, or a @param naming a parameter that does not exist. If you contribute to the runtime, run the test suite before you send a change. The compiler does not check the doc comments in your own programs, but following the same format gets you the same editor support, and pepper doc package --check checks a package's.

Unit tests

A unit test is a function marked [Test]: it takes no parameters, returns nothing, and passes when it returns. It checks what the code under test does with expect_equal and the other expect_* functions, which are in the prelude, so a test file needs no import:

# Counts the words in `text`: the runs of characters between spaces.
word_count(text: String): ulong {
    ulong count = 0;
    for (var word in text.split(" ")) {
        if (!word.is_empty) {
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

[Test]
counts_the_words() {
    expect_equal(word_count("salt and pepper"), 3);
    expect_equal(word_count("  spaced   out "), 2);
}

[Test]
an_empty_string_has_no_words() {
    expect_equal(word_count(""), 0);
    expect_true(word_count(" ") == 0);
}

[Test]
[ShouldPanic("out of bounds")]
reading_past_the_last_word_panics() {
    var words = "salt pepper".split(" ");
    var third = words[2];
}

# A normal build leaves the tests out and runs this.
main(): int {
    print(word_count("salt and pepper"));
    return 0;
}

pepper test (the pep-test tool) builds the tests and runs them:

$ pepper test words_test.pep
running 3 tests
test counts_the_words ... ok (4 ms)
test an_empty_string_has_no_words ... ok (3 ms)
test reading_past_the_last_word_panics ... ok (5 ms)
3 passed, 0 failed

Given a folder, or nothing (the current folder), it runs every test in the .pep files under it. Its exit status is 0 only when every test passes.

Checks

Each check panics when it fails, as assert does, and reports what it compared at the line of the call, so a failing test says where and why:

words_test.pep:14:5: panic: expect_equal failed
  actual:   2
  expected: 3
CheckFails when
expect_equal(actual, expected)actual == expected is false; prints both
expect_not_equal(actual, unexpected)the two are equal; prints the value
expect_true(condition)condition is false
expect_false(condition)condition is true

expect_equal and expect_not_equal take two values of one type that has == and a text form (see to_string in String interpolation). assert and panic fail a test too: any panic does.

Tests that should panic

[ShouldPanic] turns a test around: it passes only when it panics. With a message, [ShouldPanic("out of bounds")], the panic's message must also contain that text, so a test does not pass on some other panic. A [ShouldPanic] test that returns fails.

How tests run

Each test runs in a child process of its own, so a panic, a crash or a test that never ends fails only that test, and the others carry on. Tests run in parallel, one per logical CPU (--jobs 1 runs them one at a time, in order), and a test still running after 60 seconds fails (--timeout changes the limit). Tests share no state: each process starts fresh.

A test also fails when it leaks: the test program counts the live allocations before and after the test, and a test that returns with more (or fewer) than it started with fails, saying how many it left behind:

error: test 'counts_the_words' left 1 allocation behind

What a program makes once and keeps until it ends, such as a global made on first use, is not a leak. A test that is first to use it wraps that use in keep_for_the_program, which runs it and leaves what it allocates out of the count:

keep_for_the_program(() => {
    tls.TlsConnector.create();   # loads the TLS library, which stays loaded
});

There is no setup or teardown: a fixture is a plain function that a test calls, and what it makes is released when the test's scope ends, as everywhere else. A struct whose destructor cleans up makes a fixture that tears itself down. TempFolder, which every test file can use, is one: a fresh folder under the system's temporary folder, removed with what is in it when the test returns:

import io;

[Test]
writes_a_file() {
    var folder = TempFolder("writes_a_file");
    var path = folder.path.join("notes.txt");
    io.File.write_text(path, "hello");
    expect_equal(io.File.read_to_string(path).value(), "hello");
}

Where tests live

A test can sit beside the code it tests, where it can call the file's private functions, as above. Or tests can live in their own files, such as a module's tests/ folder, where they import the module and see its public API; pepper test -I <dir> adds the folder that holds the module to the import path:

geometry/
  module.pep
  shapes.pep
  tests/
    area_test.pep      # import geometry; [Test] functions

pepper test -I . geometry/tests

pep-test looks at each .pep file under the folders it is given and builds those with a line that starts with [Test]. The test files of one folder build into one test program, whose tests are their [Test] functions. Folders whose names start with . are skipped.
