Each file keeps the scope it has in any program. A folder inside a module (a test/ folder below its module.pep, say) holds files of that module, which see each other's names: two of them that declare the same helper, or the same test name, collide (redefinition of 'helper'). Mark such a declaration private in each file, or rename it. Test files outside a module see only each other's exports, so their names never collide.

Test builds

A normal build leaves [Test] functions out, so they cost nothing, and a file of tests can keep a main of its own. pep-build --test, which pep-test uses, builds the test program instead:

  • it keeps the [Test] functions and defines the build option TEST, so code only the tests use (a fixture that would be unused otherwise) can be marked [BuildOption("TEST")];
  • it replaces the entry file's main with one that answers --list (each test, one per line) and --run NAME (run one test), which is how pep-test drives it. Given several files of one folder, it builds the tests of them all into one program, and --run FILE::NAME tells apart two tests of one name.

A [Test] function that platform selection leaves out ([Target(OS(Linux))] in a build for Windows) is not part of the test program: --list does not show it.

A [Test] function that takes parameters, returns a value or is generic is an error, as are [Test] on a method and [ShouldPanic] without [Test]:

main.pep:2:8: error: test 'checks' must take no parameters
    2 | checks(x: int) {}
      |        ^

The language server checks a file that declares a [Test] function as a test build does: with the build option TEST and testing loaded, so errors, hover and go-to-definition work inside test bodies with no setting (see pep-lsp).

Tests that compare a program's printed output with an expected file are not supported yet.

Deprecation

When an API is on its way out, mark it [Deprecated("message")]. Code that uses it still compiles, but every use gets a warning that shows your message, the same way clang reports [[deprecated]]. That gives the code that depends on the API time to move before you remove it.

struct Temperature {
    int celsius;

    # A method on its way out: it still works, but every call warns.
    [Deprecated("use 'fahrenheit' instead", "fahrenheit")]
    to_f(): int { return fahrenheit(); }

    fahrenheit(): int { return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32; }
}

# The second argument names the replacement: the warning carries a fix that
# renames the call.
[Deprecated("use 'boiling' instead", "boiling")]
boiling_point(): Temperature { return boiling(); }

boiling(): Temperature {
    var t = Temperature();
    t.celsius = 100;
    return t;
}

main(): int {
    # Both calls warn, and both still work.
    var old = boiling_point();
    assert(old.to_f() == 212, "the old API still works");

    var t = boiling();
    assert(t.fahrenheit() == 212, "100 C is 212 F");
    return 0;
}

Compiling this prints a warning at each use of a deprecated name, with a note at its declaration. The second of the two is:

main.pep:25:16: warning: 'to_f' is deprecated: use 'fahrenheit' instead [deprecated]
   25 |     assert(old.to_f() == 212, "the old API still works");
      |                ^~~~
      |                fahrenheit
main.pep:6:5: note: 'to_f' declared here
    6 |     to_f(): int { return fahrenheit(); }
      |     ^~~~

Warnings never stop the build. The program above compiles and runs.

The replacement

The attribute takes an optional second argument: the name that replaces the deprecated one.

[Deprecated("use 'copy' instead", "copy")]
clone(): Counter { ... }

With a replacement, the warning comes with a fix that renames the use. The compiler shows the new name under the old one, as in the warning above, and the language server offers the rename as a quick fix. The fix only renames, so give a replacement only when the new declaration can be used the same way. Otherwise leave it out and explain the change in the message.

An empty message is allowed. The warning then says only 'name' is deprecated.

What it applies to

Put [Deprecated(...)] before any declaration other code refers to by name:

  • a function or an extern
  • a struct, an enum, a trait, or a type alias
  • a module-scope variable
  • a field, a method, or a constructor of a struct, or a method of an enum
  • a method in a trait or in an extension (put it on each method, not on the extend block)

A doc comment goes above the attribute, as it does for any attribute.

To rename a parameter while calls still name the old one, put [Rename("old", "new")] on the function instead (see Other names for a parameter).

Which uses warn

Every use of the declaration warns, at the name you wrote:

  • a call, a reference to a function or variable, or a construction S() (a deprecated constructor is reported at the struct's name)
  • a type name, anywhere a type is written
  • a member access x.name, a method call x.name(), a static call S.name(), and a bare field or method name inside the struct's own methods
  • an entry in an import list, import [name] from m, and a qualified use m.name, where the warning points at name
  • a call the compiler writes for you, at the token that stands for it: a for loop's next() and current() at for, a with block's enter() at with, and an operator overload at its operator (a + b at +; a deprecated == also warns at a != that uses it). These warnings offer no rename fix.

These do not warn:

  • the declaration itself
  • a use inside a declaration that is deprecated too, including the methods of a deprecated struct and closures written inside a deprecated function, so old code can keep calling old code without noise
  • a re-export, export name as other or export [name] from source, which passes the name on without using it

Mistakes in the attribute

A malformed attribute is an error at the attribute:

main.pep:1:1: error: 'Deprecated' expects a message string: [Deprecated("message")]
    1 | [Deprecated]
      | ^~~~~~~~~~~~

The other errors are 'Deprecated' expects the replacement as a string, the replacement 'a b' is not a name, too many arguments to 'Deprecated': expected at most 2, have 3, duplicate 'Deprecated' attribute, and 'Deprecated' cannot be applied to an extension or a destructor.

Compiler errors

When the compiler cannot build your program, it tells you what is wrong and exactly where, in the same format as clang. This chapter shows how to read an error and lists some common ones.

Reading an error

Here is a program with a mistake in it:

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    var total = p.x + p.z;
    return total;
}

Compiling it prints:

main.pep:8:25: error: no member named 'z' in 'Point'
    8 |     var total = p.x + p.z;
      |                         ^

An error has three parts:

  1. The header: the file, line and column, then error: and the message. Editors and terminals recognize file:line:column and can jump to it.
  2. The source line the error is on, with its line number.
  3. A caret (^) under the exact token you need to change, with ~ under the rest of the token when it is longer than one character. Here, the member name z, not the whole statement.

Messages follow clang's style: they start in lowercase, put names and types in single quotes ('z', 'Point'), and say what to do when there is an obvious fix. The fixed program is:

# The program from "Reading an error", after the fix.

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    var total = p.x + p.y;
    assert(total == 7, "x + y");
    return 0;
}

Notes

Some errors are explained by a second place in your code. The compiler shows that place as a note: after the error, in the same format. When one file calls a function that another file did not export, the note points at the declaration:

main.pep:4:12: error: 'helper' is private to lib.pep; declare it with 'export' to use it from another file
    4 |     return helper();
      |            ^~~~~~
lib.pep:1:1: note: declared here
    1 | helper(): int { return 1; }
      | ^~~~~~

When a brace is never closed, the error is at the end of the file, and the note shows the brace that opened the block:

main.pep:5:1: error: expected '}'
    5 | 
      | ^
main.pep:1:13: note: to match this '{'
    1 | main(): int {
      |             ^

One error at a time

The compiler stops at the first error it finds and exits with status 1, so fix that error and compile again. It never produces an executable from a program with an error.

On a terminal, errors are colored like clang's. Set the NO_COLOR environment variable to turn colors off. Output that goes to a file or a pipe is never colored.

Warnings do not stop the build, and the compiler prints them whether or not it also finds an error. Besides the linker's own warnings, which the compiler passes through (see Linking), the warnings are: deprecations; a method whose parameter names differ from its trait's (see Traits); an else arm of a match that every case already handles (see Enums); a comparison with a build option that is not defined (see Build options); and an [Export] that has no effect, or a --lib build that exports nothing (see Calling Pepper from C). A package's build script can print warnings of its own (see Build scripts).

Deprecations

A use of a declaration marked [Deprecated("message")] warns at the name, with the message and a note at the declaration. When the attribute names a replacement, the warning shows the rename under the code, and the language server offers it as a quick fix. See Deprecation.

main.pep:9:15: warning: 'clone' is deprecated: use 'copy' instead [deprecated]
    9 |     var b = a.clone();
      |               ^~~~~
      |               copy
main.pep:4:5: note: 'clone' declared here
    4 |     clone(): Counter { return this.copy(); }
      |     ^~~~~

Syntax of the language itself that is on its way out keeps compiling for a while too, with a warning that names its replacement and shows the fix under the code it replaces:

main.pep:3:5: warning: `new` is deprecated; constructors are spelled `construct`, matching `destruct` [deprecated]
    3 |     new(this.x = 1) {}
      |     ^~~
      |     construct
DeprecatedReplacement
new(...) constructorconstruct(...)
A struct, enum, type alias, trait or variable that two files of one module both declare, privately (now an error: files of a module share their names)one declaration, or two names
A declaration of another file of the module, used without importing that file (now an error)import "file"; in the file that uses it
io.Path.join_str(String)io.Path.join(Path), which accepts a String
String.clone()String.copy()
ThreadLocal<T>.get() for a T that is not thread-safe (now an error)with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }
io.Path.is_dir()io.Path.is_directory()
io.File.set_len(ulong)io.File.set_length(ulong)
io.File.write_string(String)io.File.write_all(String)
io.TcpStream.write_string(String), io.UnixStream.write_string(String), tls.TlsStream.write_string(String)write_all(String)
io.File.seek(Offset, int)io.File.seek(io.SeekFrom)
io.File.std_file(int, String)io.File.std_file(io.StdStream, String)
HashMap.cap(), HashSet.cap()the capacity property
arguments(), exit(code) in the preludeprocess.arguments(), process.exit(code) (import process)
Channel.send(x), try_send(x) with a variable something else references (now an error: send no longer copies)send(move(x)), or send(copy(x)) to keep using x
[Sending] parameter attribute (now an error)[Move]
io.Print traitio.Writer (which also needs write(data))
ArraySlice<T>, ArraySliceIterator<T>ArrayView<T>, ArrayViewIterator<T>
Atomic<T> without an import (now an error: it moved to the async module)async.Atomic<T> after import async, or import [Atomic] from async
math.parse_int(text, base)long.parse(text, base), with no import
Optional<T>() (now an error: Optional is an enum)Optional<T>.Empty
Optional cases None and Some(v) (now an error: renamed)Empty and Value(v)
Optional<T>.some(v), Optional<T>.none()the cases Optional<T>.Value(v), Optional<T>.Empty
Optional.is_some(), Optional.is_none()is_value(), is_empty()
[LinkName("symbol")] on an extern (now an error)[Link(name = "symbol")]
A parameter's former name, kept by [Rename("old", "new")]the new name (see named arguments)
Copyable<T> implemented as copy(copies: Copies): T, with copies.copy(x) and copies.register(original, made)copy(): T, with copy(x) and register_copy(original, made) (see copying)
hint.likely(condition), hint.unlikely(condition)[Likely] or [Unlikely] above the if or match arm (see branch hints)

Errors in the editor

The Pepper language server, used by the VS Code extension, reports the same errors at the same places while you type. It underlines the token the caret would point at, and shows each note as related information that you can click to jump to.

Common errors

These are some errors you are likely to meet, with the exact text the compiler prints.

A name that was never declared, often a typo:

main.pep:3:16: error: use of undeclared identifier 'nope'
    3 |     return a + nope;
      |                ^~~~

main.pep:2:12: error: call to undeclared function 'frob'
    2 |     return frob(1);
      |            ^~~~

A call of a local or parameter that is not a function, such as one holding what a generic function with no required arguments returned:

main.pep:6:12: error: called object type 'String' is not a function
    6 |     return f() == "n" ? 0 : 1;
      |            ^

A type name that does not exist, often a misspelled type or a missing import:

main.pep:2:12: error: unknown type name 'Frob'
    2 |     var x: Frob = 1;
      |            ^~~~

A field or method the struct does not have:

main.pep:6:7: error: no member named 'move' in 'Point'
    6 |     p.move(1);
      |       ^~~~

The wrong number of arguments. When the function has default parameters, the message gives the range:

main.pep:4:12: error: too few arguments to 'add': expected 2, have 1
    4 |     return add(1);
      |            ^~~

main.pep:3:12: error: too many arguments to 'f': expected at most 2, have 3
    3 |     return f(1, 2, 3) + f();
      |            ^

A call no overload fits, or that two fit equally well. Each note is a candidate, and says why it does not fit (see Overloading):

main.pep:3:22: error: call to 'f' is ambiguous
    3 | main(): int { return f(1); }
      |                      ^
main.pep:1:1: note: candidate function
    1 | f(x: long): int { return 1; }
      | ^
main.pep:2:1: note: candidate function
    2 | f(x: short): int { return 2; }
      | ^

A struct used as a condition without a truth-test operator. A struct is never tested for null implicitly: declare !!(): bool on it, or compare with __null (see Truth tests and conditions):

main.pep:6:9: error: 'Node' cannot be used as a condition: declare '!!(): bool' on it, or compare with '__null'
    6 |     if (node) {
      |         ^~~~
main.pep:1:8: note: 'Node' declared here
    1 | struct Node {
      |        ^~~~

A syntax error. The parser says what it expected at the first place the code stopped making sense:

main.pep:2:14: error: expected ')'
    2 |     if (true {
      |              ^

main.pep:2:13: error: expected expression
    2 |     var x = ;
      |             ^

A value of the wrong type. Numbers convert among themselves, as in C, but a number is never a struct and one struct type is never another, except that a struct converts to a trait it declares, and a value converts to a struct whose constructor from its type is [Implicit]. A raw pointer is never a struct either: a __ptr<char> is not a String (copy it with String(p)), and a String is not a __ptr<char> (pass its c_str()). Two specializations of one generic struct are different types: Array<int> is not Array<String> and Array<Derived> is not Array<Base>. Type arguments compare exactly, at every depth, after aliases resolve and omitted arguments take their defaults (Result<int> is Result<int, Error>). The check applies wherever a value flows into a typed place: a variable's initializer, an assignment, an argument, a return, and each arm of c ? a : b, whose false arm must convert to the true arm's type:

main.pep:2:13: error: cannot initialize variable 'x' of type 'int' with a value of type 'String'
    2 |     int x = "hello";
      |             ^~~~~~~

main.pep:3:12: error: cannot pass a value of type 'int' as argument 1 of 'g', which has type 'String'
    3 |     return g(5);
      |            ^

main.pep:3:19: error: cannot pass a value of type '__ptr<char>' as argument 2 of 'assert', which has type 'String'; use 'String(...)' to copy a C string
    3 |     assert(false, p);
      |                   ^

main.pep:2:12: error: cannot return a value of type 'String' from 'f', which returns 'int'
    2 |     return "a";
      |            ^~~

main.pep:2:20: error: cannot initialize variable 'a' of type 'Array<int>' with a value of type 'Array<String>'
    2 |     Array<int> a = Array<String>();
      |                    ^~~~~~~~~~~~~

main.pep:3:35: error: incompatible operand types ('Array<int>' and 'Array<String>')
    3 |     var a = flag ? Array<int>() : Array<String>();
      |                                   ^~~~~~~~~~~~~

A struct used as a trait it does not declare (see Traits as types):

main.pep:11:20: error: 'Circle' does not conform to trait 'Shape'
   11 |     var s: Shape = Circle();
      |                    ^~~~~~
main.pep:6:8: note: declare it with 'extend Circle with Shape'
    6 | struct Circle {
      |        ^~~~~~

A value that is not thread-safe given to another thread (see Threads): here a thread body, a shared function value, that captures a String:

main.pep:5:46: error: closure passed as 'shared () => void' captures 'name' of type 'String', which is not thread-safe
    5 |     var t = async.Thread.spawn(() => { print(name); });
      |                                              ^~~~
main.pep:4:9: note: capture a thread-safe value instead, such as an 'async.Atomic<T>' or a '[Shared]' struct
    4 |     var name = "worker";
      |         ^~~~

The same name declared twice in one scope:

main.pep:3:9: error: redefinition of 'n'
    3 |     var n = 2;
      |         ^
main.pep:2:9: note: previous definition is here
    2 |     var n = 1;
      |         ^

A function's parameters share the outermost scope of its body, as in C++, so a local of the same name as a parameter is a redefinition too:

main.pep:2:9: error: redefinition of 'x'
    2 |     var x = 5;
      |         ^
main.pep:1:3: note: previous definition is here
    1 | f(x: bool): int {
      |   ^

The same holds for top-level types: two structs, traits, enums or type aliases of one name in a file, or exported by two prelude modules, report redefinition of 'Point'.

Two functions that differ only in their return type, in one file or beside a runtime function of the name, which a call could not tell apart:

main.pep:1:1: error: functions that differ only in their return type cannot be overloaded
    1 | to_string(value: int): int { return value; }
      | ^~~~~~~~~
runtime/string.pep:1621:8: note: previous declaration is here
 1621 | export to_string(value: int): String {
      |        ^~~~~~~~~

Looping over something that cannot be iterated (see Iteration):

main.pep:3:19: error: type 'int' is not iterable: implement Iterable<T> (iterate()) or Iterator<T> (next() and current())
    3 |     for (var i in 5) {
      |                   ^

An import that names nothing (see Modules and imports):

main.pep:1:8: error: cannot find "nope.pep" or the module folder "nope" next to this file
    1 | import "nope";
      |        ^~~~~~

Code nested too deeply. Parentheses, blocks, else ifs, prefix operators, type arguments and patterns nest the program one level deeper, and so does each operator of a chain (a + b + c is two levels) and each member, call or index of a chain (f(x) is two levels: the call and its argument), and an interpolated string's {hole} is two levels too. A file may nest at most 256 levels, which bounds the stack the compiler and the language server need. The error points at the token that crosses the limit, here the 255th + of a long sum:

main.pep:2:1030: error: code is nested too deeply: the limit is 256 levels; split it into smaller expressions or functions
    2 |     return 0 + 1 + 1 + ... + 1;
      |                             ^

Split the expression into steps (var part = ...;), or move the inner part into a function.

A generic that asks for a larger copy of itself (see Generics). Each type argument makes a separate copy of a generic, so a Foo<T> holding a Foo<Array<T>> never runs out of copies to make. The compiler stops 64 levels deep, at the type that asks for the next level, with a note where the chain started:

main.pep:2:16: error: 'Foo' is specialized 65 levels deep, past the limit of 64; a generic whose instance asks for a larger instance of itself never ends
    2 |     var inner: Foo<Array<T>>;
      |                ^~~~~~~~~~~~~
main.pep:6:13: note: asked for by 'main' here
    6 |     var f = Foo<int>();
      |             ^~~~~~~~

A cast that reinterprets memory. as converts values, like static_cast (see Casting with as); a pointer to an integer, or to a pointer of another type, needs unsafe_cast:

main.pep:3:15: error: cannot cast '__ptr<int>' to 'ulong' with 'as'; use 'unsafe_cast<ulong>(...)' to reinterpret
    3 |     var a = p as ulong;
      |               ^~

Errors while the program runs

Some problems can only be found while the program runs, such as an array index out of range, an integer overflow, a division by zero, or a failed assert. These are not compiler errors: the program prints a message and stops immediately (it aborts, so it exits with a failure status instead of returning from main). See assert and panic.

Attributes

An attribute is a name in square brackets that tells the compiler something about the declaration below it. Each attribute goes on its own line, above its target, as pep-fmt writes it:

[Target(OS(Linux))]
[Deprecated("use 'open' instead", "open")]
export open_file(path: String): int { ... }

A parameter's attributes stay on its line, in front of it (send([Move] value: T)).

The built-in attributes are each covered in the chapter for what they do:

AttributeGoes onChapter
[Value]a struct or enumValue structs, value enums
[Equatable]a struct or enumDeriving == and hash
[Implicit]a constructorImplicit conversions
[Alias], [Rename]a parameterOther names for a parameter
[Shared]a structWhat threads can share
[ThreadLocal]a module-scope varThread-local variables
[Isolated]a structWhat a lock body may do
[Move], [MoveSource]a parameterHanding a reference over with move
[NotCopyable], [Locked]a struct; a parameterthe reference
[Unsafe]a functionRemoving the checks
[Likely], [Unlikely]an if or a match armBranch hints
[Cold]a functionCold functions
[Target]most declarations, and blocksPlatform selection
[BuildOption]a declaration or a blockBuild options
[Link]an extern functionLinking
[Export]a functionCalling Pepper from C
[Test], [ShouldPanic]a functionUnit tests
[Deprecated]most declarationsDeprecation
[Attribute]a structAttributes of your own

A struct marked [Attribute] is an attribute of your own, which a static block reads at compile time (see Reflection and attributes). The built-in ones are declared the same way, in the runtime, so the reference lists each with its fields.

Reflection and attributes

A program can look at its own types while it compiles: list a struct's fields, read the attributes written on them, and generate code for each one. This is how one function can turn any struct into JSON, declare a command-line option per field, or compare two values field by field.

The work happens in the compiler, in a static block, so it costs nothing at run time and needs no type information in the program. This is the model of Zig's comptime and C++'s static reflection, not of Java or C# runtime reflection.

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
    var label: String;
}

# One function describes any struct: the `static` block runs in the
# compiler, once per type `describe` is called with.
describe<T>(value: T): String {
    var out = StringBuilder();
    static (out, value) {
        out.append(reflect.name<T>());
        out.append("(");
        for (var field in reflect.properties<T>()) {
            # `field.name` is a compile-time string; `field.get(value)` reads
            # the field. Both statements use `out`, a captured runtime
            # value, so they are emitted once per field.
            out.append($"{field.name} = {field.get(value)}");
            if (!field.is_last) {
                out.append(", ");
            }
        }
    }
    out.append(")");
    return out.to_string();
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 3;
    p.y = 4;
    p.label = "corner";
    assert(describe(p) == "Point(x = 3, y = 4, label = corner)", "one line per field, in declaration order");
    return 0;
}

static blocks

A static block is written inside a function. It names, in parentheses, the runtime values it may emit code against: its capture list.

static (out, value) {
    ...
}

static { ... } with no list is pure compile-time work, such as a check with reflect.assert.

Each statement in the block either runs in the compiler or is emitted into the function:

  • A statement that uses a captured name, or a runtime local the block declares, is emitted. Its compile-time parts are filled in first: out.append(field.name) emits out.append("x").
  • Everything else runs in the compiler: var declarations whose value uses no captured name, if on a compile-time condition (only the branch taken is kept), for over a compile-time list, which is unrolled, one copy of its body per element, and while on a compile-time condition, which emits its body once per iteration.
  • An if whose condition uses a captured name is emitted as a runtime if; its branches can still hold compile-time steps.

A var with a captured name in its value is a runtime local, and using it counts as using a capture. Using a runtime value that is not captured is an error at that name:

main.pep:9:24: error: 'total' is a runtime value; add it to the static block's capture list

Each pass of an unrolled for or while, and the branch an if keeps, is its own block, like the body of a real loop.

A closure in an emitted statement is an ordinary closure: it captures runtime locals as any closure does. Its body cannot use a compile-time value such as field.name, since the closure outlives the block's expansion; copy the value into a runtime local first, and the closure captures that local:

static (options, calls) {
    for (var field in reflect.fields<Options>()) {
        var text = $"{field.get(options)}";
        calls.append(() => text);
    }
}

Compile-time loops

break and continue in a compile-time for or while run in the compiler: continue drops the rest of the pass, and break ends the unrolling. They cannot sit in a runtime if, whose condition the compiler does not know:

main.pep:10:17: error: 'break' in a runtime 'if' cannot leave a compile-time loop; the condition is not known while compiling

A while that runs 100,000 times is taken to be endless and stops the compile at its while.

struct Row {
    var id: int;
    var _cache: int;
    var name: String;
    var score: int;
    var notes: String;
}

# The sum of the public `int` fields of `Row` before 'notes': `continue`
# and `break` steer the unrolled `for`.
sum_leading_ints(row: Row): int {
    var total = 0;
    static (total, row) {
        for (var field in reflect.fields<Row>()) {
            if (field.name.starts_with("_")) {
                continue;
            }
            if (field.name == "notes") {
                break;
            }
            if (reflect.is_same<field.Type, int>()) {
                total += field.get(row);
            }
        }
    }
    return total;
}

# A compile-time `while` emits its body once per iteration: here, the
# first four powers of three, as four additions.
powers_of_three(): int {
    var sum = 0;
    static (sum) {
        var power = 1;
        while (power < 30) {
            sum += power;
            power = power * 3;
        }
    }
    return sum;
}

main(): int {
    var row = Row();
    row.id = 2;
    row.score = 40;
    assert(sum_leading_ints(row) == 42, "id and score; _cache is skipped");
    assert(powers_of_three() == 1 + 3 + 9 + 27, "one addition per iteration");
    return 0;
}

In generic code

In a generic function, a static block runs once for each specialization, when its type arguments are known: describe<Point> and describe<Line> each get their own expansion. Code the block emits can call other generic functions, such as describe(field.get(value)) for a field that is itself a struct, and those are specialized in turn. A mistake in a block is reported when some specialization uses it, with the pass it happened in and, when a generic asked for that specialization, a note at each use that led to it ('dump<Point>' is used by 'main' here):

main.pep:14:13: error: 'print' cannot be called at compile time
main.pep:12:27: note: in pass 1 of 2 (member 'x')
note: a 'static' block can call the 'reflect' functions and the methods of what they return; calling other functions at compile time is not supported yet
main.pep:10:1: note: in the static block of 'dump<Point>'

At module scope

A static block outside any function runs once, while compiling. It has nothing to capture and emits no code; instead, each const declared at the top of the block becomes a module-scope constant holding what the block computed. Its other vars, and anything declared in its loops and branches, stay in the compiler. export static exports its constants, and attributes written above the block ([Target(...)]) apply to them too.

export struct Pixel {
    var red: u8;
    var green: u8;
    var blue: u8;
    var alpha: u8;
}

export enum Channel {
    Red,
    Green,
    Blue,
    Alpha
}

# A module-scope `static` block runs once, while compiling. Each `const` at
# its top becomes a module-scope constant holding what the block computed;
# `export static` exports them.
export static {
    var bytes = 0;
    for (var field in reflect.properties<Pixel>()) {
        reflect.assert(reflect.is_same<field.Type, u8>(), $"'{field.name}' must be one byte");
        bytes += 1;
    }
    const PIXEL_BYTES = bytes;
    const LAST_CHANNEL = reflect.cases<Channel>()[reflect.cases<Channel>().count - 1].get();
}

import "sizes";

main(): int {
    assert(PIXEL_BYTES == 4, "one byte per field of Pixel");
    assert(LAST_CHANNEL == Channel.Alpha, "the last case of Channel");
    return 0;
}

A constant takes a number, bool, character or enum case; a module-scope variable cannot be a String, since it must be thread-safe. At module scope, a case's get() is the case itself, and a statement that would emit code is an error:

main.pep:7:9: error: a module-scope 'static' block cannot emit code; declare a 'const' with what it computes

What the compiler can evaluate

Compile-time values are integers, floating-point numbers, bool, strings, enum cases, and what the reflect functions return: members, cases, functions, lists and attributes. Expressions can use literals, the arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, + on strings, interpolated strings ($"{field.name}: "), ?:, assignment to a compile-time var (n += 1), and indexing a list. A string has length, is_empty, starts_with, ends_with and contains; a list has count and is_empty.

Emitted code can use a compile-time number, bool, string or enum case; the compiler writes it as a literal.

Seeing what a block does

A static block runs inside the compiler, so a print in it would be emitted into the program instead of showing anything while compiling. These show what the block computes:

  • reflect.print(value) writes value as a note each time the compiler runs it, on every compile, including one that succeeds. In an unrolled loop each note says which pass printed it:

    main.pep:9:17: note: static print: "describing Point"
    9 |         reflect.print($"describing {reflect.name<T>()}");
      |                 ^~~~~
main.pep:11:21: note: static print: "x"
   11 |             reflect.print(field.name);
      |                     ^~~~~
main.pep:10:27: note: in pass 1 of 2 (member 'x')
   10 |         for (var field in reflect.properties<T>()) {
      |                           ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

  • reflect.assert(condition, message) and reflect.error(message) stop the compile at that point with message, which can be an interpolated string holding the values that matter (reflect.assert(n < 8, $"{reflect.name<T>()} has {n} fields")). Like every error in a block, it carries the pass and, in generic code, the specialization it happened in (see In generic code).

  • The emitted code runs like code written by hand. Each statement a block emits keeps the source line of the statement it came from, so a runtime print it emits shows values as the program runs, and a debugger breakpoint on that line (with -g) stops there, in every pass. Stepping goes through an unrolled loop pass by pass, stopping on the for line and then on the body, and the debugger shows the compile-time variables, such as the loop's field (see Stepping through a static block).

  • --emit-static writes the program's source with each block replaced by what it emits (see the next section).

  • --emit-llvm writes the program's LLVM IR into the build directory (.pep/build/<name>.ll), where the function a block expanded in shows exactly what it emitted, one copy per specialization (describe<Point>). --emit-ast prints the program as parsed, before any block runs, so it does not show the expansion.

Seeing what a static block emits

pepper build main.pep --emit-static writes a copy of the program with each static block replaced by the statements it emits, the way a C compiler's -E shows the preprocessed source. Nothing is compiled; the copy goes into main.static/ (or the folder -o names) and builds into the same program. For the describe example at the top of this page, the copy keeps describe<T> as written and adds what it is for Point:

# 'describe' specialized for T = Point, with its static blocks expanded
describe<Point>(value: Point): String {
    var out = StringBuilder();
    # static (out, value) expanded from reflection-basics.pep:11:5 for T = Point
    {
        out.append("Point");
        out.append("(");
        {
            out.append($"x = {value.x}");
            {
                out.append(", ");
            }
        }
        {
            out.append($"y = {value.y}");
            {
                out.append(", ");
            }
        }
        {
            out.append($"label = {value.label}");
        }
    }
    # end static
    out.append(")");
    return out.to_string();
}
  • Each pass of an unrolled for or while is a block of its own, one after another; a compile-time if leaves only the branch it took; the compile-time vars and steps are gone.
  • Compile-time values are written as literals: field.name becomes "x" (inside an interpolated string, its text), field.Type the type, field.get(value) value.x, case.matches(v) v is Shape.Circle, and function.call() a call by name. A case's value, item.get(v), becomes a match that reads it.
  • Everything else in the file is copied byte for byte, comments included. --emit-static=keep also keeps each block as # comments above its expansion.
  • A block in a generic function expands differently for each type, so the copy adds a concrete override per specialization the program uses, as above. A block in a method of a generic struct, or in a generic method, stays as written, with each specialization's expansion above it as comments.
  • An error in the emitted code shows when the copy is built, at the line of the copy that has it.
  • To debug the program in the expanded source, build it with -g --debug-static=expanded: the copy is written beside the program as main.static.pep, and the debugger steps through it (see Stepping through a static block). In a method of a generic struct or a generic method, where the copy shows the expansion only as comments, the debugger shows the block as written.

pep-build lists the details.

The reflect functions

reflect is built in: a static block uses it without an import. The reference has an entry for each function and for the members, cases and functions they return.

FunctionReturns
reflect.name<T>()the type's name, as written ("Box<int>")
reflect.properties<T>()the public fields and properties of a struct, in declaration order
reflect.fields<T>()every field of a struct, private ones and a property's storage included; only in the file that declares T
reflect.cases<E>()an enum's cases, in order
reflect.functions_with<A>()every function in the program that carries attribute A
reflect.is_struct<T>(), is_enum<T>(), is_trait<T>()what kind of type T is
reflect.is_reference<T>()whether T is a reference type, whose slots can be null: a struct or an enum whose cases carry values, unless it is [Value]
reflect.is_same<A, B>()whether A and B are the same type (int and i32 are)
reflect.has_attribute<T, A>(), reflect.attribute<T, A>()attribute A on struct or enum T
reflect.has_build_option("NAME")whether the build defines build option NAME (-D NAME)
reflect.build_option("NAME"), reflect.build_option("NAME", default)the build option's value as a String; without a default, an error when the build does not define it
reflect.print(value)writes value as a note while compiling (see Seeing what a block does)
reflect.error(message)fails the compile with message
reflect.assert(condition, message)fails the compile with message when condition is false

fields exists for code a struct's author writes, such as a field-by-field ==; anywhere else it is an error, which points at properties:

main.pep:4:24: error: 'fields' of 'Account' is only available in the file that declares 'Account'; use 'properties'

A member (from properties or fields) has:

  • name, index, is_last, is_const, is_property
  • type_name: its type as a string; field.Type is the type itself, usable wherever a type is written: var copy: field.Type = ..., reflect.is_same<field.Type, String>(), parse<field.Type>(text). This works for a compile-time var holding a member too (var first = case.values[0]; gives first.Type).
  • has_attribute<A>() and attribute<A>()
  • get(value) and set(value, x), which emit value.name and value.name = x

A case (from cases) has:

  • name, value (its integer value, or the tag of a case that can carry values), index, is_last, has_attribute<A>(), attribute<A>()
  • values: the values the case carries, as members, in order; empty for a case that carries none. A value's get(v) reads it from v, which must hold this case; set is an error, since a case's values are fixed.
  • matches(v), which emits a test of whether v holds this case
  • get(values...), which emits the case made with those values: case.get() for a case that carries none, case.get(r) for Circle(radius: int)

A function (from functions_with) has name, has_attribute<A>(), attribute<A>(), and call(arguments...), which emits a direct call.

enum Level {
    Low,
    High = 10,
}

struct Settings {
    var name: String;
    var retries: int;
    var verbose: bool;
    var level: Level;
}

# A compile-time `if` keeps only the branch it takes, so each field is
# written by the code that fits its type.
render<T>(value: T): String {
    var out = StringBuilder();
    static (out, value) {
        for (var field in reflect.properties<T>()) {
            out.append($"{field.name}=");
            if (reflect.is_same<field.Type, String>()) {
                out.append($"\"{field.get(value)}\"");
            } else if (reflect.is_enum<field.Type>()) {
                out.append(level_name(field.get(value)));
            } else {
                out.append($"{field.get(value)}");
            }
            out.append(";");
        }
    }
    return out.to_string();
}

# `reflect.cases<E>()` lists an enum's cases; `case.get()` is the case
# itself in emitted code.
level_name(level: Level): String {
    var name = "";
    static (level, name) {
        for (var case in reflect.cases<Level>()) {
            if (level == case.get()) {
                name = case.name;
            }
        }
    }
    return name;
}

# `field.set(value, x)` assigns a field.
reset_counts<T>(value: T) {
    static (value) {
        for (var field in reflect.properties<T>()) {
            if (reflect.is_same<field.Type, int>()) {
                field.set(value, 0);
            }
        }
    }
}

main(): int {
    var settings = Settings();
    settings.name = "fast";
    settings.retries = 3;
    settings.level = Level.High;
    assert(
        render(settings) == "name=\"fast\";retries=3;verbose=false;level=High;",
        "each field is written by the code for its type"
    );
    reset_counts(settings);
    assert(settings.retries == 0, "set assigns the int fields");
    return 0;
}

struct Account {
    var owner: String;
    var _balance: int;

    construct(this.owner = "", this._balance = 0) {}

    # `reflect.fields<T>()` lists private fields too, so it is available
    # only in the file that declares `T`: code its author writes, like this
    # field-by-field `==`.
    ==(other: Account): bool {
        var same = true;
        static (same, other) {
            for (var field in reflect.fields<Account>()) {
                same = same && field.get(this) == field.get(other);
            }
        }
        return same;
    }
}

main(): int {
    assert(Account("ann", 5) == Account("ann", 5), "equal fields compare equal");
    assert(!(Account("ann", 5) == Account("ann", 6)), "a private field takes part");
    return 0;
}

enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Rect(width: int, height: int),
    Point,
}

# `case.matches(value)` tests which case a value holds, and each of the
# case's `values` reads its value with `get`.
describe<E>(value: E): String {
    var out = "";
    static (out, value) {
        for (var case in reflect.cases<E>()) {
            if (case.matches(value)) {
                out = case.name;
                for (var item in case.values) {
                    out = out + $" {item.name}={item.get(value)}";
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}

# `case.get(values...)` makes a case; here, each value is `size`.
square<E>(name: String, size: int): E {
    var out: E;
    static (out, name, size) {
        for (var case in reflect.cases<E>()) {
            if (name == case.name) {
                if (case.values.count == 0) {
                    out = case.get();
                } else if (case.values.count == 1) {
                    out = case.get(size);
                } else if (case.values.count == 2) {
                    out = case.get(size, size);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}

main(): int {
    assert(describe(Shape.Rect(3, 4)) == "Rect width=3 height=4", "a case's values");
    assert(describe(Shape.Point) == "Point", "a case without values");
    assert(describe(square<Shape>("Rect", 5)) == "Rect width=5 height=5", "a made case");
    assert(describe(square<Shape>("Circle", 2)) == "Circle radius=2", "one value");
    return 0;
}

Attributes

An attribute is a struct marked [Attribute]. Writing it above a declaration records a compile-time value of that struct, which has_attribute<A>() tests for and attribute<A>() returns.

# An attribute is a struct marked `[Attribute]`. Its fields hold what a
# use of it says; a field with an initializer may be left out.
[Attribute]
struct Name {
    const value: String;
}

[Attribute]
struct Ignore {}

struct User {
    [Name("user_id")]
    var id: int;
    var email: String;
    [Ignore]
    var session: int;
}

# The keys a struct's fields are written under: each field's `[Name]` if
# it has one, else the field's own name, skipping `[Ignore]`d fields.
keys<T>(): String[] {
    var keys: String[] = [];
    static (keys) {
        for (var field in reflect.properties<T>()) {
            if (!field.has_attribute<Ignore>()) {
                var key = field.name;
                if (field.has_attribute<Name>()) {
                    key = field.attribute<Name>().value;
                }
                keys.append(key);
            }
        }
    }
    return keys;
}

main(): int {
    var found = keys<User>();
    assert(found.count == 2, "the [Ignore]d field is skipped");
    assert(found[0] == "user_id", "[Name] renames the key");
    assert(found[1] == "email", "a field without [Name] keeps its name");
    return 0;
}
  • Fields of an attribute struct are numbers, bool, char, String, or enums whose cases carry no values.
  • Arguments are constants: literals, a negated number, an enum case (Level.High), or strings joined with +. They can be named: [Check(weight = 3)].
  • Without a constructor, the arguments set the fields in order, and a field with an initializer may be left out. The initializer is a constant of the same kinds, strings joined with + included. A constructor may take this.field parameters, or parameters its body assigns to fields (this.long_name = long_name;), which is all its body may do.
  • An attribute from another module can be named through it, with or without arguments: [serialize.Ignore], [serialize.Name("key")].
  • An attribute that names neither a built-in attribute nor an [Attribute] struct is an error, at its name: unknown attribute 'Optoin'.
  • Built-in attributes (Target, Shared, Deprecated, ...) are [Attribute] structs too, declared in the runtime (attributes), so a block reads them like its own: function.attribute<Deprecated>().message. Target holds its condition as written ("!OS(Windows)"). The compiler still checks and acts on each one itself.
struct Settings {
    var width: int;
    [Deprecated("use 'width' instead", "width")]
    var size: int;
}

# Lists the deprecated fields of `T` with what replaces each, read from the
# built-in `Deprecated` attribute like any `[Attribute]` struct.
deprecated_fields<T>(): String {
    var out = "";
    static (out) {
        for (var field in reflect.properties<T>()) {
            if (field.has_attribute<Deprecated>()) {
                out = out + $"{field.name} -> {field.attribute<Deprecated>().replacement};";
            }
        }
    }
    return out;
}

main(): int {
    assert(deprecated_fields<Settings>() == "size -> width;", "one deprecated field");
    return 0;
}

Attributes can go on structs, enums and their cases, fields, functions, methods, constructors, parameters and module-scope variables.

[Attribute]
struct Check {
    const weight: int = 1;
}

[Check]
check_addition(): bool {
    return 1 + 1 == 2;
}

[Check(weight = 3)]
check_strings(): bool {
    return "ab" + "c" == "abc";
}

# `reflect.functions_with<A>()` lists every function in the program that
# carries `A`; `check.call()` calls it directly.
run_checks(): int {
    var score = 0;
    static (score) {
        for (var check in reflect.functions_with<Check>()) {
            if (check.call()) {
                score += check.attribute<Check>().weight;
            }
        }
    }
    return score;
}

main(): int {
    assert(run_checks() == 4, "each [Check] function runs once, weighted");
    return 0;
}

Not supported yet

  • Calling functions other than the reflect functions at compile time.
  • Reflecting methods and constructors (reflect.methods<T>()).
  • Limiting where an attribute may be used ([AttributeTargets(...)]).
  • Tracing the blocks the compiler runs.
  • Type information at run time.

Build options

Some code should be optional at build time: linking a library such as libcrypto or zlib when it is there, tracing that only a debug build wants, a backend chosen when the program is built. Build options set that on the command line with -D, as in C compilers, and the code tests them with BuildOption.

pep-build main.pep -D USE_LIBCRYPTO -D LOG_LEVEL=2 -D BACKEND=zlib -o app
  • -D NAME defines an option. It counts as NAME=1, as in C.
  • -D NAME=VALUE defines it with a value, which may be any text.
  • Repeat -D for more options. When two name the same option, the later one wins.

pep-build --test defines TEST, which keeps the [Test] functions and can mark code only tests use (see Unit tests). A package's [features] that a build turns on define options too, named <package>_<feature> (http_tls; see Features), and so do the pep:build-option=NAME lines a package's build script prints, named <package>_<NAME> (see Build scripts).

A name is a letter or _, then letters, digits and _. Any other name is an error:

error: invalid build option name '2FAST' in '-D 2FAST'; a name is a letter or '_' followed by letters, digits and '_'

# Build options: compile with `pep-build main.pep -D FAST_MATH -D LOG_LEVEL=2`
# to pick the other versions.

# `[BuildOption("NAME")]` keeps a declaration when `-D NAME` is given, and
# `!BuildOption(NAME)` inside a `Target` keeps its fallback otherwise.
[BuildOption("FAST_MATH")]
scale(x: int): int {
    return x << 1;
}

[Target(!BuildOption(FAST_MATH))]
scale(x: int): int {
    return x * 2;
}

# A `static` block reads an option's value while compiling, with a default
# for a build that does not set it.
log_level(): int {
    var level = 1;
    static (level) {
        if (reflect.build_option("LOG_LEVEL", "1") == "2") {
            level = 2;
        }
    }
    return level;
}

main(): int {
    if (scale(21) != 42) {
        return 1;
    }
    var level = log_level();
    if (level < 1 || level > 2) {
        return 2;
    }
    return 0;
}

Selecting code

[BuildOption("NAME")] keeps a declaration or a block only when the build defines NAME. It is shorthand for [Target(BuildOption(NAME))], and it goes everywhere [Target(...)] goes: functions, externs, structs, methods, module-scope variables, imports, re-exports and { } blocks in a function (see Platform selection).

Inside Target, BuildOption(NAME) combines with OS(...), Arch(...), !, &&, || and parentheses. Used alone, it is true when NAME is defined, whatever its value, and false when it is not, with no warning:

[BuildOption("USE_LIBCRYPTO")]
[Link("crypto")]
extern int SHA256_Init(__ptr<void> context);

[Target(!BuildOption(USE_LIBCRYPTO))]
_sha256_compress(...) { ... }   # the portable fallback

[Target(BuildOption(TRACE) && OS(Linux))]
import "linux_trace";

Several attributes on one item combine with "and", as [Target] does.

Options the runtime reads

OptionEffect
USE_LIBCRYPTOdigest's SHA-256 and SHA-1 use libcrypto (CNG on Windows); see Cryptographic hashes
USE_ZLIBcompress uses zlib; see Compression
TESTdefined by pep-build --test; see Unit tests

Comparing values

BuildOption(NAME) may be compared with a literal using ==, !=, <, <=, > and >=, on either side. The literal's type says how the value is read:

LiteralThe value is read asExample
integera signed 64-bit integer, decimal or 0x hexBuildOption(LOG_LEVEL) >= 2
floata doubleBuildOption(SCALE) > 1.5
true / falsetrue/false, 1/0, on/off or yes/no, in any case (== and != only)BuildOption(TRACE) == true
stringtext, compared byte for byteBuildOption(BACKEND) == "zlib"
[Target(BuildOption(LOG_LEVEL) >= 2 && OS(Linux))]
_trace(message: String) { ... }

[Target(BuildOption(BACKEND) == "zlib")]
import "zlib_backend";

A value the literal's type cannot read is an error at the comparison:

main.pep:1:28: error: build option 'LEVEL' is 'high', which is not an integer
    1 | [Target(BuildOption(LEVEL) >= 2)]
      |                            ^~~~

Comparing two build options, or a build option with anything but a literal, is an error too.

A comparison with an option the build does not define is false, whatever the operator, and the compiler warns at it, since a missing option there is usually a mistake:

main.pep:3:13: warning: build option 'LOG_LEVEL' is not defined; the comparison is false
    3 |     [Target(BuildOption(LOG_LEVEL) >= 2)] {
      |             ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
note: define it with '-D LOG_LEVEL=<value>'

Reading values in static blocks

A static block reads build options while compiling:

  • reflect.has_build_option("NAME") is whether the build defines NAME.
  • reflect.build_option("NAME") is its value, as a String. It is an error when the build does not define NAME.
  • reflect.build_option("NAME", "default") is its value, or default when the build does not define it.

The build cache and the editor

The options and their values are part of the build cache's key, so building with other options never reuses objects built with different ones.

The language server analyzes with the options in the VS Code setting pepper.buildOptions, a list written as -D takes them (["USE_ZLIB", "LOG_LEVEL=2"]). It has none by default, so code that needs an option shows dimmed, and comparisons with options warn until the setting names them.

Not yet

  • A pep.toml table declaring the options a package takes, with their types and defaults.
  • Arithmetic on options, and comparing two options.

Platform selection

Some code only makes sense on one platform: a Windows API call, a Linux-specific constant, a type whose size differs between operating systems. The [Target(...)] attribute keeps a declaration or a block only when you compile for a matching platform, so one source file can hold every platform's version side by side.

The target is the platform you compile on, unless you name another with --target (see Cross-compiling below).

Writing a condition

Target takes one boolean condition built from these predicates:

  • OS(...) is true on the named operating system: Windows, Mac (or MacOS), Linux, Wasi (WebAssembly, see below), IOS or Android (see iOS and Android). As in C, where TARGET_OS_MAC holds on every Apple OS and __linux__ on Android, OS(Mac) is also true on iOS and OS(Linux) on Android: they share the kernel and most of the C library, so code for macOS or Linux usually works there unchanged. Write OS(Mac) && !OS(IOS) for macOS alone, and OS(Linux) && !OS(Android) for desktop and server Linux alone.
  • Arch(...) is true on the named processor architecture: x64, aarch64, or wasm32.
  • BuildOption(NAME) is true when the build defines NAME with -D, and can be compared with a literal (BuildOption(LOG_LEVEL) >= 2); see Build options.

Values are matched case-insensitively, so OS(windows) works too. Combine predicates with && (or and), || (or or), !, and parentheses:

[Target(OS(Windows))]                     # Windows
[Target(!OS(Windows))]                    # Linux and macOS
[Target(OS(Linux) && Arch(x64))]          # Linux on x64 only
[Target(OS(Windows) || OS(Mac))]          # Windows and macOS
[Target(!(OS(Windows) || OS(Mac)))]       # Linux

An item may carry several attributes. They are combined with "and": the item is kept only when every Target on it matches. Other attributes on the same item, such as [Link(...)], do not affect the selection.

What it applies to

Put [Target(...)] before any top-level declaration: a function, an extern, a struct, an enum, a trait, an extension, a type alias, a module-scope variable, an import, or a re-export. It also works on the methods inside a struct, trait or extension, and on an enum's cases. When two declarations share a name, give them conditions that never match on the same platform, so exactly one survives:

# One name, a different declaration per platform.

# Type aliases: a Windows HANDLE is a pointer, a POSIX descriptor an int.
[Target(OS(Windows))] type Handle = __ptr<void>;
[Target(!OS(Windows))] type Handle = int;

# Module-scope variables (const and thread-safe, like every global).
[Target(OS(Windows))] const max_path = 260;
[Target(!OS(Windows))] const max_path = 4096;

# Functions.
[Target(OS(Windows))]
platform_name(): String { return "Windows"; }

[Target(OS(Mac))]
platform_name(): String { return "macOS"; }

[Target(OS(Linux))]
platform_name(): String { return "Linux"; }

# Structs, and methods inside them.
[Target(Arch(x64))]
struct Cpu {
    var name: String = "x64";
}

[Target(Arch(aarch64))]
struct Cpu {
    var name: String = "aarch64";
}

struct Word {
    [Target(Arch(x64) || Arch(aarch64))]
    bits(): int { return 64; }
}

main(): int {
    var name = platform_name();
    print(name);
    print(Cpu().name);
    assert(Word().bits() == 64, "every supported target is 64-bit");

    [Target(OS(Windows))] {
        assert(sizeof<Handle>() == 8, "a HANDLE is a pointer");
        assert(name == "Windows", "the Windows function was kept");
    }
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        assert(sizeof<Handle>() == 4, "a descriptor is an int");
        assert(max_path == 4096, "the POSIX variable was kept");
    }
    return 0;
}

The attribute goes before export, not after it: [Target(OS(Windows))] export f(). Writing export [Target(OS(Windows))] f() is a parse error.

A project's pep.toml takes the same conditions for the packages only some platforms need ([target.'OS(Windows)'.dependencies]): a build sees them only for a target the condition selects, so guard their imports with it too. See Projects: pep.toml.

Blocks inside a function

Inside a function body, attach [Target(...)] to a block { ... }. The block is kept or removed like a declaration. Blocks may nest, and may appear inside if and loop bodies.

This is the usual way to wrap C functions that differ per platform: declare each platform's extern with its own condition, and call each one from a block with the same condition.

# A portable wrapper over a C function that has a different name on
# each platform. kernel32 is linked by default on Windows, and getpid is
# in the C library everywhere else.

[Target(OS(Windows))] extern uint GetCurrentProcessId();
[Target(!OS(Windows))] extern int getpid();

process_id(): long {
    [Target(OS(Windows))] {
        return GetCurrentProcessId() as long;
    }
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        return getpid() as long;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var id = process_id();
    print($"process {id}");
    assert(id > 0, "a running process has a positive id");
    return 0;
}

What happens to code that does not match

Code whose condition does not match is removed before type checking. That is what makes the examples above work: a call to GetCurrentProcessId, which exists only on Windows, is fine in a block that is removed everywhere else. Removed code is not checked for errors beyond parsing, so a typo in it goes unnoticed until you build on the platform that keeps it. The VS Code extension shows it dimmed, from its attribute to its end, with a hint saying it is not compiled for the platform you are building on. A file that is mostly code for another OS (a Linux-only file opened on Windows) is still checked as that OS's build would check it, so hover and go-to-definition work in it. In such a file, an error only your own platform's build would report (portable code calling a function only the other OS has) appears when you build, not in the editor.

It still has to parse, and every Target condition is validated on every platform, even one inside removed code. A misspelled value is always an error, never a silent "no match":

[Target(OS(Darwin))]
f(): int { return 1; }

main.pep:1:1: error: unknown OS value `Darwin` (expected Windows, Mac, MacOS, Linux, Wasi, IOS, Android) in [Target(OS(Darwin))]
    1 | [Target(OS(Darwin))]
      | ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Other mistakes the compiler reports:

  • Target takes exactly one condition: [Target(OS(Windows), Arch(x64))] is an error; write [Target(OS(Windows) && Arch(x64))].
  • Only OS(...), Arch(...) and BuildOption(...) may appear inside it. A bare name ([Target(Windows)]), another call ([Target(Foo(x))]), not in place of !, or a nested Target is an error.
  • OS(...) and Arch(...) are only valid inside Target(...), and the brackets hold one attribute: [OS(Windows)] and [Target(OS(Windows)) && Export] are parse errors.
  • Struct fields cannot carry [Target(...)]. Select the whole struct instead, as Cpu does in the first example.

Cross-compiling

--target <triple> compiles for another platform: [Target(...)] selects that platform's code, and the compiler emits that platform's machine code and object format. The supported targets are each OS on each architecture:

TripleOSArch
x86_64-unknown-linux-gnuLinuxx64
aarch64-unknown-linux-gnuLinuxaarch64
x86_64-apple-darwinmacOSx64
aarch64-apple-darwinmacOSaarch64
x86_64-pc-windows-msvcWindowsx64
aarch64-pc-windows-msvcWindowsaarch64
wasm32-wasip1Wasiwasm32
aarch64-apple-iosiOSaarch64
aarch64-apple-ios-simulatoriOS (simulator)aarch64
x86_64-apple-ios-simulatoriOS (simulator)x64
aarch64-linux-androidAndroidaarch64
x86_64-linux-androidAndroidx64

clang's other spellings work too: arm64 for aarch64, amd64 for x86_64, any vendor, and an OS version (arm64-apple-macosx14.0, aarch64-apple-ios17.0, aarch64-linux-android33). Any other triple is an error that lists these. wasm32-wasi, wasm32-unknown-wasi and wasm32-unknown-wasip1 all mean wasm32-wasip1. The iOS and Android targets, their versions and their SDKs are described in iOS and Android.

pepper build --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu main.pep -o main

Linking an executable for another platform needs that platform's system libraries and LLVM's linker, lld: the compiler looks for it beside clang, in its LLVM install and on the PATH, also under the versioned name Ubuntu's lld-20 package uses (ld.lld-20). Name the directory that holds the libraries (the sysroot) with --sysroot <dir>, or set PEPPER_SYSROOT_<TRIPLE>, the triple in capitals with _ for each - (PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_APPLE_DARWIN):

  • Linux: a directory with the target's glibc and GCC runtime (/usr/aarch64-linux-gnu from Debian's or Ubuntu's libc6-dev-arm64-cross and libgcc-13-dev-arm64-cross, which clang also finds without --sysroot). From another OS, copy a Linux machine's at the same paths: the C startup files and libc, libm, libgcc_s and the dynamic loader from /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu, and crtbegin*.o, crtend*.o and libgcc* from /usr/lib/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/<version>.

  • macOS: a macOS SDK (MacOSX.sdk, xcrun --show-sdk-path on a Mac). Linking reads only its SDKSettings.json and the library stubs in usr/lib.

  • Windows: a directory laid out like a Visual Studio install, with the MSVC libraries and the Windows SDK, as xwin writes it:

    xwin --accept-license --arch x86_64 splat --use-winsysroot-style --preserve-ms-arch-notation --output ~/winsysroot

CI links each of these from the other two (from Linux x64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64, for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-pc-windows-msvc) and runs the programs on their own OS; its scripts, scripts/ci-export-sysroot.sh and scripts/ci-provision-cross.sh, show the setup end to end.

When the link fails, the error ends with a note naming what is missing:

note: linking for 'x86_64-pc-windows-msvc' needs that platform's system libraries and LLVM's linker (lld): pass '--sysroot <dir>' or set PEPPER_SYSROOT_X86_64_PC_WINDOWS_MSVC

The -m options are read for the target: -mcpu is an AArch64 option and -march=x86-64-v3 an x86 one, and native, which names the CPU of the machine you compile on, is an error for a target of another architecture.

The compiler only builds for the target; copy the executable to a machine of that platform to run it.

WebAssembly

--target wasm32-wasip1 compiles to a WebAssembly module for WASI preview 1, which runtimes such as wasmtime run from the command line:

pep-build --target wasm32-wasip1 --sysroot /opt/wasi-sdk main.pep -o main.wasm
wasmtime run --dir . main.wasm

Linking needs a wasi-sdk (its sysroot holds wasi-libc and clang's builtins) and LLVM's wasm-ld, which the compiler finds as it finds lld (also as wasm-ld-20). Name the SDK directory, or its share/wasi-sysroot, with --sysroot, or set PEPPER_SYSROOT_WASM32_WASIP1 or WASI_SDK_PATH. wasi-sdk 25 is the version tested. The program needs a runtime's --dir to reach a directory and -S inherit-env (wasmtime) to see the environment. Directory.temp() is TMPDIR, else /tmp, so grant one (--dir /tmp) to use it.

WASI preview 1 is a small system, and wasm32 is a 32-bit target, so some things work differently:

  • OS(Wasi) code selects the WASI versions of the runtime's platform layer. Code written for !OS(Windows) also compiles for WASI, so check that it only calls what wasi-libc has.
  • There are no threads and no stack switching: Thread.spawn panics, and so does starting tasks (async.run, async.run_with). Mutexes, channels and atomics still work, as long as nothing waits for another thread.
  • Sockets, TLS, HTTP connections and starting processes return an IoError saying they are not supported on WASI.
  • Files work through the directories the runtime grants. Metadata has no permission bits (read_only is false) and no creation time, and set_permissions and set_read_only return an error; set_executable and the mode of OpenOptions and Directory.create do nothing. Timestamps and symlinks work.
  • os reports OperatingSystem.Wasi, "wasm32", an empty host name and version, and no total memory.
  • Pointers and C's long and size_t are 32 bits; see 32-bit targets.

Calling C

Pepper programs can call functions written in C: the C standard library, your operating system's API, or any other library with a C interface. You declare the C function's prototype with extern, make sure the library that defines it is linked, and then call it like any Pepper function.

Declaring a C function

An extern declaration is a C prototype, written the way C writes it: the return type, the name, and the parameter types, each followed by a parameter name. It has no body.

extern ulong strlen(char* s);
extern int strcmp(char* a, char* b);
extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

After that, strlen("hello") calls the C library's strlen. The compiler does not check your prototype against any C header, so it must match the real C function exactly. A wrong parameter or return type compiles, and then passes or reads the wrong bits when the program runs.

Match C types with Pepper types of the same size:

CPepper
char, signed char, unsigned charchar or i8, u8 or byte
short, unsigned shortshort or i16, ushort or u16
int, unsigned intint or i32, uint or u32
long long, unsigned long long, int64_t, size_t (64-bit)long or i64, ulong or u64
float, doublefloat, double
T*T* in the prototype

Pepper's long is always 64 bits. C's long is 64 bits on Linux and macOS but 32 bits on Windows, so a C function that takes long needs a different prototype per platform (see [Link(name = ...)] below for an example).

32-bit targets

On a 32-bit target (wasm32-wasip1, see WebAssembly), pointers, C's long and size_t are 32 bits. There, an extern's long and ulong stand for C's pointer-sized long/ssize_t and unsigned long/size_t: the call passes the low 32 bits and widens the result back to 64 (sign-extending a long, zero-extending a ulong), so extern ulong strlen(char* s); works unchanged. A Pepper function passed to C as a callback is converted the same way in the other direction. i64 and u64 stay 64 bits on every target; use them for C's long long, int64_t and off_t. WebAssembly checks every call's signature, so a prototype with the wrong width traps instead of returning garbage.

Some things to know about extern declarations:

  • The prototype uses C syntax only. The name(parameter: type): type form that Pepper functions use is a parse error on an extern, and __ptr<T> as a parameter type is an error too: write char*, not __ptr<char>.
  • An extern is private to its file (or module), like every declaration. Write export extern ... to let files that import this one call it (see Visibility).
  • Several files may declare the same extern, since every declaration names the same C function. The runtime already declares malloc, free and a few others privately, and your program can declare them again.
  • An extern is linked by name. If no linked library defines it, the program compiles and then fails to link, with the linker reporting an undefined symbol. See Linking for how to add libraries.
  • An extern is a function value too, of the function type its prototype gives (abs is an (int) => int), so it can be stored and passed like a Pepper function. Where a C function pointer type is expected, it is the C function's own address (see Passing a Pepper function to C). A variadic extern (one ending in ..., below) is not a value: wrap a call to it in a closure.
# An extern function is a function value, like a Pepper function.
extern int abs(int x);
extern ulong strlen(char* s);

apply(f: (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(x);
}

main(): int {
    # Its type comes from the prototype: `abs` is an `(int) => int`.
    var absolute = abs;
    assert(absolute(-3) == 3, "through a local");
    assert(apply(abs, -4) == 4, "as an argument");

    # A `char*` parameter is a `__ptr<char>` in the function type.
    var length: (__ptr<char>) => ulong = strlen;
    var word = "four";
    assert(length(word.c_str()) == 4, "strlen");

    # Where a C function pointer is expected, it is the C function itself.
    var pointer: extern (int) => int = abs;
    assert(pointer(-5) == 5, "C function pointer");
    return 0;
}

Passing strings

Pepper's String is a reference-counted object, not a C string, so a String value cannot be passed where C expects char*.

  • A string literal passed to an extern is passed as a NUL-terminated C string, with no allocation: strlen("hello") is 5. The same is true wherever a literal flows into a __ptr<char>, __ptr<u8>, or __ptr<void> in Pepper code (a variable, field, argument, or return value), so String("hello") copies the literal's five bytes.
  • A StringConstant passes its constant NUL-terminated bytes with no copy, by itself where a __ptr<char> is expected or through c_str(). The pointer is valid for the whole run of the program and is never __null.
  • A String value is passed with c_str(), which returns the String's buffer, NUL-terminated, as a __ptr<char>. A String is not guaranteed to be NUL-terminated otherwise, so always go through c_str() when C needs the terminator. The pointer belongs to the String: it is valid until the String is destroyed or grows (for example with append or +=). An empty String() has no buffer, so its c_str() is __null; check before you pass it to a C function that does not accept NULL.
  • To turn a C string back into a String, pass the pointer to the constructor: String(p) copies a NUL-terminated C string, and String(p, size) copies size bytes. If you already know the number of code points, pass it as a third argument: String(p, size, String.length_of(p, size)). The constructor copies the bytes, so you still own (and may free) the C buffer. A C string is never passed or stored where a String is expected without this copy: that is an error.
# Passing strings to C, and turning C strings back into Strings.

extern ulong strlen(char* s);
extern int strcmp(char* a, char* b);
extern char* strchr(char* s, int c);

main(): int {
    # A string literal passed to an extern is a NUL-terminated C string.
    assert(strlen("hello") == 5, "a literal is passed as a C string");
    assert(strcmp("abc", "abc") == 0, "equal C strings compare as 0");

    # So is one stored in a __ptr<char>, or passed to the String
    # constructor, which copies it.
    __ptr<char> greeting = "hello";
    assert(strlen(greeting) == 5, "a literal in a __ptr<char> is a C string");
    assert(String("hello").size == 5, "String(literal) copies its bytes");

    # A String value goes through c_str().
    var name = "Pepper";
    name += " and C";
    assert(strlen(name.c_str()) == name.size, "c_str() is the String's bytes");

    # A char* result is a __ptr<char>. Copy it into a String with the
    # constructor: the byte size and the number of code points.
    var rest = strchr(name.c_str(), 32);   # 32 is ' '
    assert(rest != __null, "strchr found a space");
    var size = strlen(rest);
    var copy = String(rest, size, String.length_of(rest, size));
    assert(copy == " and C", "the copy holds the tail of the C string");
    return 0;
}

Passing a String value directly to an extern's char* parameter is an error:

main.pep:4:19: error: cannot pass 'String' to parameter 1 of extern 'strlen' of type '__ptr<char>'; pass its 'c_str()'
    4 |     return strlen(name) as int;
      |                   ^~~~

The reverse is an error too: a char* (or any raw pointer, void* included) is never a String, so passing one where a String is expected, assigning it to a String variable, or returning it as one is rejected. Copy it into a String with String(p) first:

main.pep:3:19: error: cannot pass a value of type '__ptr<char>' as argument 2 of 'assert', which has type 'String'; use 'String(...)' to copy a C string

Passing arrays

An Array<T> is a reference-counted object too, so C gets its elements through a pointer:

  • data() returns a __ptr<T> to the first element. C may read and write the elements through it. The pointer belongs to the Array: it is valid until the Array is destroyed or its buffer grows (for example with append). An empty Array's data() is __null.
  • append_from(p, count) appends count elements copied from p, as String(p, size) does for bytes, so you still own (and may free) the C buffer.
# Passing an Array's elements to C, and filling an Array from a C buffer.

extern void* memset(void* s, int c, ulong n);
extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

main(): int {
    # data() points at the elements, so C can read or write them in place.
    var bytes = Array<u8>();
    bytes.append(1);
    bytes.append(2);
    bytes.append(3);
    memset(bytes.data() as __ptr<void>, 7, bytes.count);
    assert(bytes[2] == 7, "C wrote through data()");

    # An empty Array has no elements to point at: data() is __null.
    var none = Array<u8>();
    assert(unsafe_cast<__ptr<u8>>(none.data()) == __null, "empty is __null");

    # append_from copies count elements out of a C buffer, which you still own.
    __ptr<u8> buffer = unsafe_cast<__ptr<u8>>(malloc(4));
    memset(buffer as __ptr<void>, 9, 4);
    var copy = Array<u8>();
    copy.append_from(buffer, 4);
    free(buffer as __ptr<void>);
    assert(copy.count == 4 && copy[3] == 9, "append_from copied the buffer");
    return 0;
}

Variadic functions

A C function with a variable argument list, such as printf or snprintf, ends its prototype with ... after at least one named parameter:

extern int snprintf(char* buffer, ulong size, char* format, ...);

The call uses the C calling convention for variadic functions, which differs from a plain call on some targets (such as macOS on Apple silicon). Each argument past the named ones gets C's default argument promotions: integers narrower than int widen to int, and float widens to double. Match your format string to the promoted type: %d for a u8, %f for a float, and %lld (not %ld) for a long, because C's long is 32 bits on Windows.

... must come last and must follow a named parameter: extern int f(...); is a parse error.

# Calling a C function that takes a variable argument list.

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

# On Windows, snprintf lives in legacy_stdio_definitions.
[Target(OS(Windows))] [Link("legacy_stdio_definitions")]
extern int snprintf(char* buffer, ulong size, char* format, ...);
[Target(!OS(Windows))]
extern int snprintf(char* buffer, ulong size, char* format, ...);

main(): int {
    var buffer = malloc(64) as __ptr<char>;
    u8 small = 200;     # widened to int
    float half = 0.5;   # widened to double
    long big = 5000000000;
    var written = snprintf(buffer, 64, "%d %.1f %lld %s", small, half, big, "ok");
    var text = String(buffer, written as ulong, String.length_of(buffer, written as ulong));
    free(buffer);
    assert(text == "200 0.5 5000000000 ok", "snprintf formatted every argument");
    return 0;
}

On Windows, the C runtime defines snprintf and its relatives inline in its headers, so the linkable symbols live in a separate library, legacy_stdio_definitions. The example links it with [Link] on Windows only.

Pointers

C code deals in raw pointers, and Pepper has a raw pointer type for talking to it: __ptr<T>, such as __ptr<void>, __ptr<char> or __ptr<__ptr<int>>. A void* returned by an extern is a __ptr<void> in Pepper, and a __ptr<T> can be passed to an extern that takes a C pointer.

A pointer supports these operations:

OperationMeaning
p[i]reads or writes the element i places from p; its type is T, so var v = p[i] declares a T
p + nthe address n elements after p (n bytes for __ptr<void>)
p == __null, p != __nullcompares with the null pointer
p == q, p != qcompares two addresses (a pointer also compares with an integer address)
p as __ptr<void>, v as __ptr<T>the same address, to and from __ptr<void>
unsafe_cast<__ptr<U>>(p)the same address, seen as pointing at U
unsafe_cast<ulong>(p), unsafe_cast<__ptr<T>>(n)the address as an integer, and back

as converts a pointer only to and from __ptr<void>, like static_cast in C++. Any other pointer conversion reinterprets memory, so it is spelled unsafe_cast (see Reinterpreting with unsafe_cast).

__null is the null pointer. sizeof<T>() gives the size of a type in bytes, which you need to allocate memory for C. The compiler built-ins reference lists these and the other __ intrinsics.

T* spelling is for extern prototypes only, since they mirror C. Everywhere else (parameters, return types, struct fields, locals, globals, type aliases, generic arguments and casts) you write __ptr<T>, and T* is a compile error:

clear(p: void*, n: ulong) { }

main.pep:1:10: error: C pointer syntax `void*` is only allowed in extern declarations; use `__ptr<void>`
    1 | clear(p: void*, n: ulong) { }
      |          ^~~~

# Raw pointers: __ptr<T> in Pepper code, T* in extern prototypes.

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);
extern void* memset(void* p, int value, ulong size);

struct Buffer {
    var data: __ptr<u8> = __null;
    var size: ulong = 0;
}

make_buffer(size: ulong): Buffer {
    var b = Buffer();
    b.data = malloc(size) as __ptr<u8>;
    b.size = size;
    memset(b.data, 0, size);
    return b;
}

sum(values: __ptr<int>, count: int): int {
    var total = 0;
    var i = 0;
    while (i < count) {
        total = total + values[i];
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

# `var` takes the element type from the pointer: `big` is a ulong, so a value
# above 2^32 reads back whole.
first(values: __ptr<ulong>): ulong {
    var big = values[0];
    return big;
}

main(): int {
    # Indexing reads and writes elements of T.
    var numbers = malloc(4 * sizeof<int>()) as __ptr<int>;
    numbers[0] = 10;
    numbers[1] = 20;
    numbers[2] = 30;
    numbers[3] = 40;
    assert(sum(numbers, 4) == 100, "indexing reads what was written");

    var wide = malloc(sizeof<ulong>()) as __ptr<ulong>;
    wide[0] = 5000000000;
    assert(first(wide) == 5000000000, "var v = p[i] has the pointee's type");
    free(wide);

    # p + n moves by n elements, not n bytes.
    var third = numbers + 2;
    assert(third[0] == 30, "numbers + 2 points at the third element");
    assert(unsafe_cast<ulong>(third) - unsafe_cast<ulong>(numbers) == 8, "two ints are eight bytes");

    # __ptr<void> strides by bytes; cast to see the memory another way.
    var raw = numbers as __ptr<void>;
    var bytes = raw as __ptr<u8>;
    assert(bytes[4] == 20, "the second int starts at byte 4 (little-endian)");
    free(raw);

    # Pointers can live in struct fields, and compare with __null.
