    var b = make_buffer(16);
    assert(b.data != __null, "malloc returned memory");
    assert(b.data[15] == 0, "memset cleared it");
    free(b.data);
    b.data = __null;

    # A pointer to pointers: indexing yields the inner pointer, and indexing
    # again reads or writes through it.
    var rows = malloc(2 * sizeof<__ptr<int>>()) as __ptr<__ptr<int>>;
    var row = malloc(sizeof<int>()) as __ptr<int>;
    rows[1] = row;
    rows[1][0] = 7;
    assert(rows[1][0] == 7, "rows[1][0] reads through the row pointer");
    assert(row[0] == 7, "rows[1] is the row pointer");
    free(row);
    free(rows);
    return 0;
}

Pointers are not reference-counted and nothing checks them: indexing past the end of an allocation, using memory after free, or forgetting to free it behaves exactly as it would in C. Keep raw pointers inside small functions or structs that own the memory, and give the rest of your program ordinary Pepper types.

Owning a C resource: Handle<T>

A C library hands out objects that it frees with a function of its own (fclose, free, LLVMDisposeModule). Pepper's reference counting does not know about them, so the runtime's Handle<T> ties one to Pepper's lifetimes, like C#'s SafeHandle: it holds the raw value and a release function, and calls the function once, when the last reference to the handle goes away.

# A C resource owned by a Handle: `free` runs when the last reference to
# the handle goes away.

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);
extern void* memset(void* p, int value, ulong size);

# A buffer from C, freed with the struct that holds it.
struct Buffer {
    var _memory: Handle<__ptr<void>>;
    var size: ulong { get; }

    construct(size: ulong) {
        _memory = Handle<__ptr<void>>(malloc(size), (p) => free(p));
        this.size = size;
    }

    fill(value: u8) {
        memset(_memory.value, value as int, size);
    }

    at(index: ulong): u8 {
        return (_memory.value as __ptr<u8>)[index];
    }
}

main(): int {
    var buffer = Buffer(16);
    buffer.fill(7);
    if (buffer.at(15) != 7) {
        return 1;
    }

    # release() frees early; the handle then no longer owns the memory.
    var scratch = Handle<__ptr<void>>(malloc(8), (p) => free(p));
    scratch.release();
    return scratch.is_owned() ? 2 : 0;
}
  • Handle<T>(value, release) takes ownership of value. T is usually __ptr<void> or an integer descriptor.
  • value reads the raw value, to pass to C.
  • A handle is a reference, so copies share the resource; it is released when the last copy goes away. Keep it in a field of the struct that wraps the resource, as Buffer does.
  • release() frees the resource early, and detach() gives it back without freeing it. Either way the release function never runs again, and is_owned() becomes false.
  • release is a function value, so a closure may capture what the release needs. A captured reference stays alive until the release runs, which is how a C object that must not outlive its parent (an LLVM module and its context) keeps the parent alive.

Passing a Pepper function to C

A Pepper function value is a reference-counted object, not a C function pointer. For C, Pepper has a separate type, extern (P...) => R: the address of a function that C calls with the C calling convention. Declare a callback parameter of a C function with it, and pass a named function, or a closure that captures nothing:

# `extern (P...) => R` is a C function pointer type: qsort calls `compare`
# with pointers to two elements.
extern void qsort(void* base, ulong count, ulong size, extern (void*, void*) => int compare);

ascending(a: __ptr<void>, b: __ptr<void>): int {
    __ptr<int> x = a;
    __ptr<int> y = b;
    return x[0] - y[0];
}

main(): int {
    __ptr<int> numbers = _pep_malloc(4 * sizeof<int>());
    numbers[0] = 30;
    numbers[1] = 10;
    numbers[2] = 40;
    numbers[3] = 20;

    # A named function converts to the C function pointer type.
    qsort(numbers, 4, sizeof<int>(), ascending);
    assert(numbers[0] == 10 && numbers[3] == 40, "ascending");

    # So does a closure that captures nothing; its parameter types come
    # from the C function pointer type.
    qsort(numbers, 4, sizeof<int>(), (a, b) => {
        __ptr<int> x = a;
        __ptr<int> y = b;
        return y[0] - x[0];
    });
    assert(numbers[0] == 40 && numbers[3] == 10, "descending");

    # A C function pointer is a value like a number: store it, call it.
    var compare: extern (__ptr<void>, __ptr<void>) => int = ascending;
    assert(compare(numbers, numbers + 1) > 0, "40 sorts after 30");

    _pep_free(numbers);
    return 0;
}

  • What converts. A named free function, an extern function, a static method (Order.descending), or a closure literal that captures nothing, whose parameter and return types match the C function pointer type exactly. A closure literal takes its parameter types from the type, as it does from any function type.

  • Nothing captured. C calls the function with its arguments alone, so a closure that captures a value, or a bound method (p.get), cannot convert:

    main.pep:4:43: error: closure passed as C function pointer type 'extern (__ptr<void>, __ptr<void>) => int' captures 'bias'; a C function pointer cannot hold captured values
    4 |     qsort(_pep_malloc(4), 0, 4, (a, b) => bias);
      |                                           ^~~~
main.pep:3:9: note: pass what the callback needs through the C function's context argument instead
    3 |     var bias = 1;
      |         ^~~~

    This is a design decision, not a missing feature: a C function pointer is a bare address, and giving each capturing closure an address of its own would mean writing executable code at run time, which some platforms forbid. A callback that needs state gets it another way (see Callbacks that need state).

    A function value held in a variable does not convert either, since it may be a closure.

  • C types only. C knows nothing of reference counts, so the parameter and return types must be numbers, bool, pointers, or other C function pointer types. A struct is an error: C function pointer type 'extern (String) => int' cannot use 'String'; C passes only numbers, 'bool' and pointers. Write pointers as void* in an extern declaration and as __ptr<void> elsewhere, as for any pointer.

  • A value like a number. A C function pointer has no reference count. Store it in a variable, field or module-scope const, return it, pass it to other threads, or call it: compare(a, b) calls through it with the C calling convention. Calling a null one (from C) panics. It converts to void* but not to a Pepper function type; wrap it in a closure that calls it, (x) => f(x), to use it as one.

__function_pointer(name) also gives a function's address, as an untyped __ptr<void>. It takes a free function, or a static method of the struct whose method uses it. Inside a generic struct the static method is the one for the current type arguments, which is how Thread.spawn gives the operating system its thread entry point. Prefer a C function pointer type where the signature is known, since the compiler then checks it.

Callbacks that need state

Since a C function pointer holds no captured values, a callback that needs state gets it another way:

  • The C function's context argument. Most C APIs that take a callback also take a void* context argument that they hand back to it; pass a pointer to the data the callback needs through that.
  • A thread-local or module-scope value. Set a [ThreadLocal] variable, an async.ThreadLocal<T> or an Atomic<T> before calling C, and read it in the callback, which is a named function:
# A C function pointer holds no captured values, so a callback that needs
# state reads it from somewhere C does not have to carry: here, a
# thread-local the caller sets before handing the callback to C.
extern void qsort(void* base, ulong count, ulong size, extern (void*, void*) => int compare);

# The value to sort around, for the calling thread.
[ThreadLocal]
var pivot: int = 0;

distance(x: int): int {
    var d = x - pivot;
    return d < 0 ? -d : d;
}

closest_first(a: __ptr<void>, b: __ptr<void>): int {
    __ptr<int> x = a;
    __ptr<int> y = b;
    return distance(x[0]) - distance(y[0]);
}

main(): int {
    __ptr<int> numbers = _pep_malloc(4 * sizeof<int>());
    numbers[0] = 10;
    numbers[1] = 40;
    numbers[2] = 22;
    numbers[3] = 31;

    pivot = 30;
    qsort(numbers, 4, sizeof<int>(), closest_first);
    assert(numbers[0] == 31 && numbers[3] == 10, "closest to 30 first");

    _pep_free(numbers);
    return 0;
}

Binding to a different symbol name

[Link(name = "symbol")] binds an extern to a C symbol whose name differs from the declared one. Pepper code calls the extern by its declared name, and the object file refers to symbol, even when a Pepper function is named symbol too: each call reaches its own function. Use it to give a C function a clearer name, to avoid clashing with a Pepper name, or, together with [Target], to bind one Pepper name to a different symbol on each platform. lib names the library that defines the symbol in the same attribute, as [Link("library")] does on its own:

# [Link(name = "symbol")] binds a Pepper name to a C symbol with a different name.

# llabs takes a 64-bit long long on every platform: `i64` in an extern is
# 64 bits everywhere, where `long` follows the size of a pointer.
[Link(name = "llabs")]
extern i64 absolute(i64 value);

# A Pepper function may be named after the C symbol: each call reaches its own.
llabs(value: i64): i64 {
    return value;
}

# C's long is 64 bits on Linux and macOS but 32 bits on Windows and
# WebAssembly, so the 64-bit labs is only right on the first two.
[Target(OS(Windows) || OS(Wasi))]
[Link(name = "llabs")]
extern i64 abs64(i64 value);
[Target(OS(Linux) || OS(Mac))]
[Link(name = "labs")]
extern long abs64(long value);

# `lib` names the library that defines the symbol, as [Link("m")] does.
[Target(OS(Linux))]
[Link(lib = "m", name = "cbrt")]
extern double cube_root(double value);

main(): int {
    assert(absolute(-7) == 7, "absolute calls llabs");
    assert(llabs(-7) == -7, "llabs calls the Pepper function");
    assert(abs64(-5000000000) == 5000000000, "abs64 calls a 64-bit abs");
    [Target(OS(Linux))]
    {
        var root = cube_root(27.0);
        assert(root > 2.999 && root < 3.001, "cube_root calls cbrt from libm");
    }
    return 0;
}

Real uses of the per-platform form include macOS on Intel, where the 64-bit-inode version of stat is named stat$INODE64:

[Target(OS(Mac) && Arch(x64))]
[Link(name = "stat$INODE64")]
extern int stat(char* path, void* buf);
[Target(OS(Mac) && Arch(aarch64))]
extern int stat(char* path, void* buf);

[Link] takes the library as its one positional argument or as lib, and the symbol as name; each is a non-empty string, and an extern names at most one symbol. Anything else is an error, such as:

main.pep:1:7: error: 'Link' has no argument named 'symbol'; use 'lib', 'path' or 'name'
    1 | [Link(symbol = "labs")] extern long pep_abs(long v);
      |       ^~~~~~

The earlier [LinkName("symbol")] was removed; it is an error that suggests the [Link(name = "symbol")] that replaces it.

LLVM intrinsics

An extern whose [Link(name = ...)] symbol starts with llvm. is not a C function but an LLVM intrinsic: a call to it compiles to the operation itself, usually one instruction, and nothing is linked. The runtime's bit and math methods (Bit operations) are written this way; declare one yourself for an intrinsic they do not cover, such as a CPU-specific one:

# An extern bound to an LLVM intrinsic: a call is the instruction itself.
[Link(name = "llvm.umin")]
extern ulong smaller(ulong a, ulong b);

# `llvm.ctlz` takes a second argument that must be a constant.
[Link(name = "llvm.ctlz")]
extern ushort leading_zeros(ushort value, bool is_zero_poison);

main(): int {
    assert(smaller(7, 3) == 3, "llvm.umin.i64");
    assert(leading_zeros(1, false) == 15, "llvm.ctlz.i16");
    return 0;
}

  • The extern's prototype is the intrinsic's signature, in the types Pepper maps to LLVM's: byte and char are i8, ushort and short i16, uint and int i32, ulong and long i64, bool i1, float and double themselves, any pointer ptr, and a void return is void. Intrinsics that take or return vectors or structs cannot be declared yet.

  • Name an overloaded intrinsic by its base name (llvm.ctpop): the overload is picked from the prototype (llvm.ctpop.i32 for a uint). The mangled name works too.

  • A prototype that matches no overload is an error at the extern, with LLVM's reason:

    main.pep:2:13: error: 'popcount' does not match the signature of LLVM intrinsic 'llvm.ctpop': intrinsic has incorrect argument type
    2 | extern long popcount(int value);
      |             ^~~~~~~~

  • Some arguments must be constants, such as llvm.ctlz's is_zero_poison; passing a variable is an error at the argument:

    main.pep:5:19: error: argument 2 to 'leading_zeros' must be a constant
    5 |     return leading_zeros(1, zero_poison);
      |                             ^~~~~~~~~~~

An unknown name (llvm.nonsense) is an error too. A target-specific intrinsic (llvm.x86.*, llvm.aarch64.*) only exists on its architecture, so pair it with [Target(Arch(...))].

Linking the library

A C function is only callable if the library that defines it is linked into your program. The C library is always linked. For anything else, attach [Link("name")] to the extern or pass -l name to the compiler. A package that bundles the C source compiles it with a [native] table in its pep.toml, or a build script. The Linking chapter covers all of these.

[Target(OS(Windows))]
[Link("gdi32")]
extern ulong GetStockObject(int kind);

Calling Pepper from C

C code can call Pepper functions: mark each one [Export], and build the program as a library with --lib static or --lib shared. The compiler writes a C header beside the library that declares every exported function.

# A library C code calls: build it with `pepper build counter.pep --lib
# static` (or `--lib shared`), which also writes `counter.h`.
#
# `main` is not needed in a library; this one calls the exported functions
# from Pepper, so the example runs as a program too.

[Export]
add(a: int, b: int): int {
    return a + b;
}

# A struct crosses to C as an opaque handle, `Counter*`.
struct Counter {
    var count: int;

    construct(this.count = 0) {}
}

# The C name can differ from the Pepper name.
[Export(name = "counter_new")]
make_counter(start: int): Counter {
    return Counter(start);
}

[Export]
counter_increment(counter: Counter): int {
    counter.count += 1;
    return counter.count;
}

# A C function pointer, called back.
[Export]
apply(f: extern (int) => int, x: int): int {
    return f(x);
}

# A String arrives as UTF-8 bytes and their size, and leaves as a
# NUL-terminated copy that C frees with `pepper_string_free`.
[Export]
greet(name: String): String {
    return "hello, " + name;
}

main(): int {
    var counter = make_counter(41);
    assert(counter_increment(counter) == 42, "the counter counts");
    assert(add(2, 3) == 5, "add adds");
    assert(greet("C") == "hello, C", "greet greets");
    return 0;
}

pepper build counter.pep --lib static     # libcounter.a and counter.h
pepper build counter.pep --lib shared     # libcounter.so and counter.h

The header declares the functions with C types:

typedef struct Counter Counter;

void counter_retain(Counter* handle);
void counter_release(Counter* handle);

void pepper_string_free(char* text);

int32_t add(int32_t a, int32_t b);
int32_t apply(int32_t (*f)(int32_t), int32_t x);
int32_t counter_increment(Counter* counter);
Counter* counter_new(int32_t start);
char* greet(const char* name, size_t name_size);

and a C program calls them like any C function:

#include <stdio.h>
#include "counter.h"

static int32_t twice(int32_t x) { return 2 * x; }

int main(void) {
    Counter* counter = counter_new(41);
    printf("%d\n", counter_increment(counter));   /* 42 */
    counter_release(counter);
    printf("%d\n", apply(twice, add(2, 3)));      /* 10 */
    char* greeting = greet("C", 1);
    printf("%s\n", greeting);                       /* hello, C */
    pepper_string_free(greeting);
    return 0;
}

cc main.c -I. -L. -lcounter -lm -o main    # Linux; macOS needs no -lm

Exporting a function

  • [Export] goes on a free function that is not generic. Its C name is its Pepper name; [Export(name = "c_name")] gives it another, which must be a C identifier. Two exports with one C name are an error.
  • [Export] anywhere else (a struct, a method, an extern, a variable, a generic function) is a warning, and does nothing.
  • An exported function is still a Pepper function: Pepper code calls it by its Pepper name.
  • Do not confuse [Export] with the export keyword, which makes a declaration visible to other Pepper files (see Visibility). A function can be either, both or neither.

What crosses to C

Each parameter and the result must be a type C can hold:

PepperC (in the header)
boolbool
char, i8, u8, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong (and their i16... spellings)char, int8_t, uint8_t, int16_t, uint16_t, int32_t, uint32_t, int64_t, uint64_t
float, doublefloat, double
__ptr<T>T* for a number type, else void*
extern (P...) => Ra C function pointer, R (*name)(P...)
Stringa parameter: const char* name, size_t name_size; a result: char* (see Strings)
a structan opaque handle, Name*

Anything else is an error at the parameter or result that C cannot hold:

main.pep:2:15: error: cannot export 'total': C cannot hold 'Array<int>'
    2 | total(values: Array<int>): int {
      |               ^~~~~~~~~~
note: only a non-generic struct passes to C, as a handle

A generic struct (Array<int>), a value struct, an enum, a trait, a tuple, Optional and a Pepper function type cannot cross. Pass an array as a pointer to its elements and a count, or wrap it in a struct of your own and pass a handle.

Strings

A String crosses as UTF-8 bytes, copied each way, so neither side keeps a pointer into the other's memory:

  • A String parameter is two C parameters: a pointer to the bytes and their size, const char* name, size_t name_size. The bytes need no NUL terminator, and may contain NULs. The function gets its own copy for the call; C keeps its buffer. A size of 0 (with any pointer, NULL included) is the empty string.
  • A String result is a NUL-terminated copy of its bytes, as char*, which the C code owns and frees with pepper_string_free, never with free. An empty String is "", never NULL. A string with NULs inside ends at its first one for C; return a pointer and a size instead when that matters.
  • The header declares pepper_string_free when some export returns a String.

Handles

A struct reaches C as a pointer to an incomplete C type (Counter*), which C code passes back but never looks inside. Handles follow Pepper's reference counting:

  • A handle a function returns is one reference, which the C code owns. It releases it with <name>_release (counter_release) when it is done; the last release frees the object, running its destructor.
  • A handle C passes in stays C's: the function borrows it for the call.
  • <name>_retain adds a reference, for C code that keeps a handle in two places; each retain needs a release.
  • The names are the struct's name in snake case: ByteBuffer gets byte_buffer_retain and byte_buffer_release. The header declares them for every struct an export passes.

A handle must not be null, and is freed at most once: C gets no checks on either.

Why a string is freed but a handle is released

The two look alike from C, a pointer Pepper hands over, but they are different things, and the names say which:

  • A handle is a live Pepper object. Pepper may hold references to it too: a field, a global, another thread. C holds one or more of those references, so it uses the same counting Pepper does: <name>_retain adds one, <name>_release drops one, and the object is destroyed only when the last reference anywhere goes away. Releasing is not freeing.
  • A returned string is not a Pepper object. It is a plain copy of the bytes, made at the boundary like strdup makes one, with no count and no other owner. Pepper keeps no reference to it, so there is nothing to retain or share; the C code owns it outright and gives it back once with pepper_string_free.
  • Why not free: the copy comes from Pepper's allocator, which tracks live allocations, serves short strings from its own small block pools (see Where objects live) and, on Windows, may use a different C runtime's heap than the caller's. pepper_string_free returns it to the allocator that made it.

A String parameter needs neither: Pepper copies the bytes for the call, and C's buffer stays C's.

Building the library

--lib static writes an archive of the program's objects: libname.a (name.lib on Windows). --lib shared links a shared library: libname.so, libname.dylib on macOS, or name.dll on Windows, with its import library name.lib. -o chooses another name. Either way the header is written beside the library, named for it without the lib prefix (counter.h).

The compiler writes the archive itself, in the format of the platform it builds for (with --target, another one's: GNU's for Linux and Android, the BSD format Apple's linkers read for macOS and iOS, the COFF archive for Windows), with the index of the symbols its objects define, so no archiver needs to be installed and a static library for another platform needs no system root. A shared library links like an executable, with clang. With --lto=full the library is optimized as one module first, as an executable is (see --lto in pep-build).

  • A library needs no main. One that has a main keeps it, and C code that links the library cannot have its own.
  • Only the exported functions and their handle functions are visible outside a shared library; everything else in it is hidden.
  • A program that links the static library must also link the C libraries Pepper's runtime uses. The header lists them in a comment at the top, such as /* Link the static library with: -lm */ on Linux. A shared library links them itself.
  • On Windows, --lib static and --lib shared both write name.lib (the archive, or the DLL's import library), so build them into different folders.
  • A C program links at most one Pepper static library: each holds its own copy of the runtime, and two would define it twice. Shared libraries keep their runtimes to themselves, so a program may load several.
  • A library's thread-locals (its own and the runtime's) use the initial-exec TLS model, as a program's do, where reading one costs a load, except on Android (see below). On Linux this makes a .so built from either kind need static TLS (readelf -d shows FLAGS STATIC_TLS): a program that links it always loads it, but a dlopen of it works only while glibc's spare static TLS (512 bytes by default, which the glibc.rtld.optional_static_tls tunable raises) has room for its thread-locals. macOS and Windows have no such limit.
  • On Android every app loads its native code with dlopen, and bionic refuses initial-exec there, so an Android library's thread-locals use the general-dynamic model, which costs a call (__tls_get_addr on x86_64, a TLS descriptor's on arm64) per access.

Swift, Kotlin and Java code can call the exports with its own values instead: --bindings swift and --bindings java write bindings beside the header (see iOS and Android).

Initialization, panics and threads

  • Module-scope variables are initialized when the library is loaded, before C calls any exported function (a static library's initializer runs with the program's other static constructors).
  • A panic in Pepper code called from C prints its message and aborts the process, as it does in a Pepper program: it never unwinds into C.
  • Exported functions may be called from any thread, including threads C created. The thread-safety rules of threads still hold: a handle to a struct that is not [Shared] must stay on one thread at a time, and C does not check that.

Linking

The Pepper compiler turns your program into a native executable in two steps: it compiles your files and the runtime into object files (one per source file; see Output files), and then links them with the system libraries it needs. When you call C functions, linking is where their definitions come from, so this chapter explains what is linked by default and how to add more.

What the compiler links

The compiler uses clang as its link driver, rather than calling the platform's linker directly, because clang already knows each platform's startup files, C library and SDK locations. It uses the clang from the LLVM installation the compiler was built with when there is one, and otherwise the first clang on your PATH.

Every program is linked with:

  • Linux: the C library, which clang adds, and the math library (m), which the Pepper compiler adds (a floating-point ** calls its pow), and, when the compiler runs on a glibc older than 2.34, pthread and dl, where that glibc keeps threads and dlsym (a newer one has them in the C library).
  • macOS: libSystem, which contains the C library, plus the SDK and platform-version flags. clang adds all of these, using the Xcode Command Line Tools.
  • Windows: the Microsoft C runtime (the UCRT, vcruntime and the CRT startup library), which clang adds, plus kernel32, user32 and shell32, which the Pepper compiler adds. A program that uses async also links synchronization, which the runtime names with [Link] for its locks (WaitOnAddress). clang finds the Visual Studio and Windows SDK libraries itself, so you do not need a Developer Command Prompt.

Any library file named lib<name>.a in the runtime directory is linked too.

Anything else must be linked explicitly. On Linux, that includes pthread on older systems. Android keeps pthread and rt in its C library and has no library of either name, so the compiler drops -l pthread and -l rt when linking for Android: one [Link("pthread")] serves both.

Linking a library from the source: [Link]

Attach [Link("name")] (or [Link(lib = "name")]) to an extern declaration to link the library that defines it. The compiler passes -lname to the linker, just like -l on the command line. Name the library the way the linker does: m for libm, gdi32 for gdi32.lib.

# [Link("name")] on an extern links the library that defines it.

# gdi32 is not one of the libraries Windows programs link by default.
[Target(OS(Windows))] [Link("gdi32")] extern ulong GetStockObject(int kind);

# pthread_self is in libpthread on older Linux systems, in libc on newer
# ones, and in libSystem on macOS; linking pthread works on all of them.
[Target(!OS(Windows))] [Link("pthread")] extern ulong pthread_self();

# The math library is separate from the C library on Linux.
[Target(OS(Linux))] [Link("m")] extern double pow(double base, double exponent);
[Target(!OS(Linux))] extern double pow(double base, double exponent);

main(): int {
    [Target(OS(Windows))] {
        # 5 is NULL_BRUSH, a stock object that always exists.
        assert(GetStockObject(5) != 0, "gdi32 was linked");
    }
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        assert(pthread_self() != 0, "pthread was linked");
    }
    assert(pow(2.0, 10.0) == 1024.0, "the math library was linked");
    return 0;
}
  • The library is linked only if the extern survives platform selection. Combining [Link] with [Target], as above, links a library only on the platforms that need it.
  • Each library is linked once, however many externs name it.
  • The library is linked even when nothing calls the extern.
  • The same attribute can also bind the extern to a differently named C symbol: [Link(lib = "m", name = "cbrt")] (see Binding to a different symbol name).

Putting [Link] in the source keeps the knowledge of which library a function comes from next to its declaration, so nobody building your program has to remember a command-line flag.

Linking C code a package builds: [native] and build scripts

A package can ship a C library's source instead of asking its users to install the library. When the C needs only compiling and linking, a [native] table in its pep.toml says which files to compile and what to link, with no script:

[native]
sources = ["c/*.c"]
include = ["c/include"]
link    = ["m"]

The build compiles each source with clang for the build's target and links the objects into the program. Since it runs no package code, --no-build-scripts allows it, as long as its flags are ones that cannot make clang load code (see [native]).

For anything more, such as generating a header or running configure, a build script compiles the C code with clang for the build's target, and prints the objects and libraries to link (pep:object=..., pep:link=...).

Linking a library from the command line: -l

The -l option links a library for one build:

pepper build main.pep -l m -o main

Repeat it for more libraries (-l m -l pthread).

A library the linker does not find on its own (one outside the system's library directories, such as a Homebrew install on macOS) needs its folder on the search path. -L dir adds one, like -L for clang:

pepper build main.pep -L /opt/homebrew/opt/llvm@20/lib -o main

Repeat it for more folders. The folders are searched for -l libraries and [Link] libraries alike, in the order given, before the default ones. On Windows, clang passes each one to the linker as /LIBPATH:.

Library search directories in the source and the environment

A library that ships with your program, such as a vendored build in a vendor/ folder, can name its folder in the [Link] attribute with path:

[Link(lib = "probe", path = "vendor/lib")]
extern int probe_version();

A relative path is relative to the folder of the file that declares the extern, not to where you run the compiler, so the program builds the same from anywhere. Like the library, the folder is searched only when the extern survives platform selection, so a [Target] can give each platform its own folder.

The PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable adds folders for every build, separated like PATH (:, or ; on Windows):

PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/homebrew/lib pepper build main.pep -o main

The linker searches -L folders first, then [Link] paths, then PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH, then the runtime's folder and the system's.

When linking fails

If a function you declared with extern is not defined by any linked library, compilation succeeds and the link fails. The compiler prints what the linker said, which names the missing symbol:

error: Link failed: clang exited with exit status: 1
/usr/bin/ld: .pep/build/main.units/main.o: in function `main':
main:(.text+0x25ba): undefined reference to `no_such_function'
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation)

The object the linker names is the one for the file that made the call, in .pep/build/<name>.units/. Symbols of your own functions appear as the compiler spells them for the linker: main and a method such as Point.length keep their names, and any other name is written _P followed by the name with _ doubled and other characters as _ and two hex digits, so a function parse appears as _Pparse and Array<int>.count as _PArray_3cint_3e.count. That way a Pepper function never collides with a C library function of the same name, such as exit. extern functions keep their C names.

To fix it, check the spelling of the extern against the C function (or use [Link(name = "symbol")] when the names differ), then add the library that defines it with [Link] or -l.

If the compiler cannot run clang at all, the error says Link failed: cannot run clang. Install clang (on Linux, from your package manager) or the Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS.

Warnings from the linker are passed through unchanged, even when the link succeeds.

Output files

With no -o, the executable is named after the first source file, without an extension, in the directory where you run the compiler. Windows will not run a file without .exe, so pass -o main.exe there. The object files and other intermediate files go in .pep/build/ under the current directory, or in the directory you pass to --build: one object per file of the program in <name>.units/, and <name>.o, which runs the program's global initializers. Unchanged objects come from the build cache in .pep/cache/ (--no-cache skips it).

With --lib static or --lib shared, the output is a library and a C header instead (see Building the library).

iOS and Android

Pepper compiles natively for iOS and Android through the same LLVM backend it uses everywhere else: --target picks the platform, and the result is ordinary machine code for an iPhone, an iPad, the iOS simulator, or an Android phone. An app calls the Pepper code through C, as any C library is called: mark the functions [Export], build a library with --lib static (see Calling Pepper from C), or on iOS an .xcframework or a Swift package (--lib xcframework, --lib swift-package) and on Android an .aar (--lib aar), and call it from Swift directly, or from Kotlin and Java through JNI.

Targets

TripleRuns on
aarch64-apple-iosiPhone and iPad
aarch64-apple-ios-simulatorthe iOS simulator on an Apple silicon Mac
x86_64-apple-ios-simulatorthe iOS simulator on an Intel Mac
aarch64-linux-androidAndroid phones and tablets (arm64-v8a)
x86_64-linux-androidthe Android emulator on x64 (x86_64)

  • Versions. A triple can name the oldest OS version the code runs on: aarch64-apple-ios17.0, aarch64-apple-ios17.0-simulator, aarch64-linux-android33. Without one, iOS code runs on iOS 15 and later and Android code on API level 30 (Android 11) and later. Pepper's runtime needs API level 30, so an older one is an error:

    error: unsupported target 'aarch64-linux-android24': Pepper's runtime needs Android API level 30 or later (write 'android30')

  • Spellings. arm64 works for aarch64, as do Rust's -sim for -simulator and any vendor (aarch64-unknown-linux-android). x86_64-apple-ios means the simulator, since no iPhone is x64.

  • CPU. Code for an iPhone runs on every arm64 iPhone (clang's apple-a7); add -mcpu=apple-a14 to use what newer ones have. Android x64 code uses SSE4.2 and POPCNT, which the Android x86_64 ABI requires.

Building

A library for an app needs no SDK, only the compiler:

pepper build --target aarch64-apple-ios --lib static greeter.pep -o ios/libgreeter.a
pepper build --target aarch64-linux-android --lib static greeter.pep -o android/libgreeter.a

The compiler writes each archive itself, in the format the platform's linkers read (BSD's for iOS, GNU's for Android), so nothing from Xcode or the NDK is needed to make it. Each writes greeter.h beside the library. Build the library once for each target the app ships: the device and the simulator on iOS, and each Android ABI.

Linking, for a shared library or an executable to run in the simulator or an emulator, needs the platform's SDK:

  • iOS links with LLVM's ld64.lld against an iOS SDK. On a Mac with Xcode the compiler asks xcrun for it (iphoneos, or iphonesimulator for the simulator). Elsewhere name it with --sysroot, or set PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_APPLE_IOS (and PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_APPLE_IOS_SIMULATOR, and so on): the variable is named for the triple without its version. Homebrew's llvm@20 does not ship ld64.lld: brew install lld@20 (or scripts/setup-llvm.sh) installs it, and the link needs that bin folder and llvm@20's on the PATH (see Setting up LLVM).
  • Android links with the NDK's own clang, which brings the NDK's linker, compiler-rt and unwinder. Name the NDK with --sysroot <ndk> or PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_LINUX_ANDROID, or set ANDROID_NDK_HOME or ANDROID_NDK_ROOT; otherwise the newest NDK in the Android SDK ($ANDROID_HOME/ndk/<version>, as Android Studio installs it) is used. NDK r27 is the version tested.

When the SDK is missing, the link error says where to point the compiler:

note: linking for 'aarch64-linux-android30' needs the Android NDK (https://developer.android.com/ndk/downloads): pass '--sysroot <ndk>' or set PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_LINUX_ANDROID, ANDROID_NDK_HOME or ANDROID_HOME

Selecting code for a platform

[Target(OS(IOS))] and [Target(OS(Android))] select code for one of them. Most code needs neither: iOS is Darwin, like macOS, and Android runs the Linux kernel, so OS(Mac) is true on iOS and OS(Linux) on Android, as TARGET_OS_MAC and __linux__ are in C (see Platform selection). The runtime's macOS and Linux code serves them, with a few declarations narrowed where they differ. At run time, os.system_os() returns OperatingSystem.IOS or OperatingSystem.Android.

Bindings

Swift, Kotlin and Java call the library's [Export]ed functions (see Calling Pepper from C) through bindings the compiler generates beside the C header, so the app passes its own values and writes no glue: --bindings swift or --bindings java with --lib, and --lib swift-package and --lib aar (below) write them themselves. Names are camel case (count_words is countWords), and each export crosses as:

PepperSwiftJava and Kotlin
boolBoolboolean
i8, u8, charInt8, UInt8, CCharbyte
short, ushortInt16, UInt16short
int, uintInt32, UInt32int
long, ulongInt64, UInt64long
float, doubleFloat, Doublefloat, double
an enumits stored integerits stored integer
StringStringString
a structa class owning one referencea class owning one reference, AutoCloseable
__ptr<T>UnsafeMutablePointer<T>? (UnsafeMutableRawPointer? for void)long
extern (A) => R@convention(c) functionnone: an error

Java has no unsigned types: u8 through ulong keep their bits in the signed type of their size. A String crosses as UTF-8 both ways (a Java string's own bytes, not JNI's modified UTF-8), and a string Pepper returns ends at its first NUL. JNI cannot pass a C function pointer, so an export that takes or returns one is an error at its type when Java bindings are built, as are an export whose camel-case name is a Java keyword or another's, and a struct named as the library's own class.

A struct handle is an object that owns one reference to the Pepper value: Swift's class releases it in deinit, and Java's in close(), which try-with-resources and Kotlin's use call (a handle never closed leaks its value; there is no finalizer, which would release it on another thread). Its reference count is a plain one unless the struct is [Shared], so a handle stays on one thread, as the Pepper value would.

Calling Pepper from Swift

--bindings swift writes, beside the header, greeter.swift: a Swift function for each export, over the C module Cgreeter that the module.modulemap it also writes declares. Compile it with the app's Swift code, find the module map with -I, and link the library:

pepper build --target aarch64-apple-ios-simulator --lib static --bindings swift greeter.pep -o libgreeter.a
xcrun --sdk iphonesimulator swiftc -target arm64-apple-ios15.0-simulator -parse-as-library \
  -I . App.swift greeter.swift -L . -lgreeter -o App.app/App

print(greet("iOS"))         // String in, String out: the C copy is freed
let tally = tallyNew()      // a Pepper struct, released when `tally` goes
print(tallyAdd(tally, 3))

Without the bindings, Swift calls the C functions directly through the header as a bridging header (-import-objc-header greeter.h): a String crosses as a pointer and a size, and a returned string is freed with pepper_string_free.

Packaging for Xcode and SwiftPM

--lib xcframework builds the library for every iOS target at once, as one .xcframework Xcode adds as a single dependency: a device slice and a simulator slice holding both simulator architectures, each with the header and a module map, so Swift imports its C functions by name with no bridging header. --lib swift-package puts it in a Swift package with the Swift bindings. Neither needs Xcode or an SDK: the compiler builds each static library and writes the rest itself.

pepper build --lib xcframework greeter.pep -o Greeter.xcframework
pepper build --lib swift-package greeter.pep -o Greeter

The name comes from the output (Greeter): the module (import Greeter), the library (libGreeter.a) and its header (Greeter.h). In the Swift package the module Greeter is the Swift bindings, over the C module CGreeter, which code that calls the C functions directly imports instead:

Greeter/
  Package.swift
  Sources/Greeter/Greeter.swift   the bindings
  CGreeter.xcframework/
    Info.plist
    ios-arm64/                    libGreeter.a, Headers/Greeter.h, Headers/module.modulemap
    ios-arm64_x86_64-simulator/   the same, its libGreeter.a holding arm64 and x86_64

In Xcode, drag Greeter.xcframework into the target's Frameworks, Libraries, and Embedded Content (Do Not Embed: it is static), or add the package with Add Package Dependencies… › Add Local…. A package depends on it by path:

dependencies: [.package(path: "../Greeter")],
targets: [
    .target(name: "App", dependencies: [.product(name: "Greeter", package: "Greeter")]),
]

import Greeter

print(greet("iOS"))

The slices are built for iOS 15 and later. A library that links others ([Link], -l) names them in its header, as --lib static does; the app links them itself.

Calling Pepper from Kotlin or Java

--bindings java (with --lib shared) writes, beside the header, greeter.jar: the class pepper.greeter.Greeter, a static native method for each export, which loads libgreeter.so when first used, and a class for each struct. Their JNI functions, which convert Java's values, are compiled into the library from greeter_jni.c, also written there. The jar's class files are written by the compiler, so it needs no JDK.

pepper build --target aarch64-linux-android --lib shared --bindings java greeter.pep \
  -o jniLibs/arm64-v8a/libgreeter.so

import pepper.greeter.Greeter

println(Greeter.greet("Android"))
Greeter.tallyNew().use { tally -> println(Greeter.tallyAdd(tally, 3)) }

With Gradle, put each ABI's .so in src/main/jniLibs/<abi>/ (arm64-v8a, x86_64) and the jar in the module's dependencies, or add the .aar below, which holds both.

Packaging for Gradle

--lib aar builds the library as a shared library for every Android ABI at once, with the Java bindings, as one Android library (.aar) a Gradle build adds as a single dependency. It needs no Gradle and no JDK: the compiler builds each .so with the NDK (found as for any Android link, above) and writes the archive itself.

pepper build --lib aar greeter.pep -o greeter.aar

The name comes from the output (greeter, which takes letters, digits and _): the library libgreeter.so, its header greeter.h, and the Java package, pepper.greeter, also the manifest's. It holds:

greeter.aar
  AndroidManifest.xml       minSdkVersion 30
  classes.jar               the Java bindings: pepper.greeter.Greeter, and a class per struct
  R.txt, res/               empty: the library has no resources
  include/greeter.h
  jni/arm64-v8a/libgreeter.so
  jni/x86_64/libgreeter.so
  LICENSE-OpenSSL.txt       only when the library imports tls (see Shipping)

Add it to the app module, and Gradle puts each ABI's .so in the APK and the classes on the app's class path:

dependencies {
    implementation(files("libs/greeter.aar"))
}

Each .so holds the Pepper code and the JNI functions, so the app calls Greeter.greet("x") with no C of its own.

Threads

Exported functions may be called from any thread (see Initialization, panics and threads), so the app decides where Pepper code runs. Keep long work off the main thread (iOS's main queue, Android's UI thread): call it from a background queue, a coroutine on Dispatchers.Default, or a Pepper thread or task the library starts itself. Pepper code never calls back into UIKit or Android's views on its own; hand results back to the main thread on the app's side.

What works differently

The runtime runs the documentation's examples on both platforms, with these differences:

  • Starting processes. An iOS app cannot start other programs, and the process module's Command.spawn returns an IoError there. On Android it works, but an app has few programs to start.
  • TLS on iOS. The tls module uses the system's Security.framework (Secure Transport), so TlsConnector and http.Client's https:// URLs work with nothing bundled: the server's certificate is checked against the system's roots and any added with add_root_certificate, and ALPN works. Secure Transport speaks TLS 1.2 at most, so a server that accepts only TLS 1.3 fails the handshake. A TLS server (TlsAcceptor.create) and a client certificate (TlsConnector.set_identity) return an IoError there for now. iOS checks a server's certificate more strictly than OpenSSL: it must name the host in its subject alternative names, carry the serverAuth extended key usage and, when issued after June 2019, be valid for at most 825 days, even from a private certificate authority.
  • TLS on Android. Android ships no OpenSSL a program may load, so the toolchain carries a static OpenSSL 3 for each ABI (runtime/tls/android/<triple>/libssl.a and libcrypto.a), and a program that imports tls (or http) links it: TlsConnector, TlsAcceptor and http.Client's https:// URLs work as on Linux, TLS 1.3 included. A connector trusts the system's certificate store (the Conscrypt module's, /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts, on Android 14 and later; /system/etc/security/cacerts before), less the certificates the user turned off in Settings, plus those the user installed (/data/misc/user/0/cacerts-added) where the process may read them, and any added with add_root_certificate. Unlike an app's Java networking, this ignores the app's network security configuration. OpenSSL adds about 4 MB to a stripped binary. An app linking a Pepper static library adds the libraries its header names (-lssl -lcrypto) from that folder: -L <toolchain>/runtime/tls/android/aarch64-linux-android.
  • Files. An app reads and writes inside its own container: pass the path the platform gives (FileManager's documents directory, Context.getFilesDir()) to the Pepper code. os.home_directory() and the temporary directory point into the container on iOS. Android has no /tmp: without TMPDIR, io.Directory.temp() is /data/local/tmp, which an app cannot write, so an app passes its cache directory. A Unix socket's path is at most 104 bytes there, and the container's own path takes most of them, so give a socket there a short name. On Android, an app creates Unix socket files in its own data folder (Context.getFilesDir()); SELinux refuses them elsewhere, and from an adb shell program everywhere, with a permission error.
  • Backtraces. Android's backtraces come from the NDK's unwinder (bionic's backtrace needs API level 33), and both platforms name functions from the binary's own symbols, so strip a release build only after keeping a copy for symbolication.
  • Standard output goes to the Xcode console and the simulator's --stdout file on iOS. On Android it goes nowhere in an app: log with the platform's logger instead (__android_log_write through an extern).

Shipping

  • Pepper compiles ahead of time, so iOS's ban on JIT compilation does not apply. Bitcode is no longer required by the App Store.
  • A static library is linked into the app's own binary, so its code is covered by the app's signature; strip the release build's symbols as usual (Xcode's Strip Linked Product, the Android Gradle plugin's strip of jniLibs). A Pepper library adds the runtime parts the program uses: the prototype app's library below is about 1 MB unstripped.
  • Each Android ABI needs its own .so; Google Play requires arm64-v8a.
  • An Android library's thread-locals (its own and the runtime's) use the general-dynamic TLS model, since the app loads its .so with dlopen and bionic refuses initial-exec there; each access costs a call. A library for desktop Linux keeps initial-exec, which is faster but needs static TLS, so a dlopen of its .so may fail (see Building the library).
  • OpenSSL's license. An Android program or app that imports tls (or http) contains OpenSSL, which is under the Apache License 2.0, so it must give its users a copy of that license: ship runtime/tls/android/LICENSE.txt from the toolchain with it (a --lib shared build for Android writes it beside the .so as LICENSE-OpenSSL.txt, and --lib aar puts that in the .aar), as an app does in its open-source licenses screen (Google Play Services' oss-licenses plugin, or a page of the app's own), and say that the app includes OpenSSL. The iOS build bundles nothing.

Debugging

-g writes DWARF, which LLDB reads in both Xcode and Android Studio. Build the library with -g and the app in its debug configuration, and set breakpoints in the .pep files by path.

Testing

pepper test --target builds a package's [Test] functions for the simulator or Android and runs them there, reporting as on the desktop (see Testing on iOS and Android):

pepper test --target aarch64-apple-ios-simulator   # in the booted simulator
pepper test --target x86_64-linux-android          # on the running emulator

An Android test runs as an adb shell program, which SELinux allows less than an app: it cannot make a Unix socket file or a hard link in the folders it can write, such as /data/local/tmp. Mark a test that needs them [Target(!OS(Android))], or leave the part that does out, as the runtime's own tests do.

The prototype apps

docs/examples/mobile/ holds a small app for each platform that calls the same Pepper library, greeter.pep:

  • ios/: a SwiftUI app (PepperDemo.swift), and build.sh, which builds it with swiftc and the library's --bindings swift for the simulator and for devices, installs it in a booted simulator, launches it and checks its output; and package/, a Swift package whose tests import Greeter from the package --lib swift-package writes and call its bindings, which package.sh builds and runs in the simulator with xcodebuild test.
  • android/: an activity in Java that calls the bindings of the library's --lib aar (pepper.greeter.Greeter), and build.sh, which builds the .aar, checks its layout, and builds the APK with the Android SDK's own tools (javac, d8, aapt2, apksigner; Gradle is not needed), installs it in the emulator, starts it and checks its log.

scripts/mobile-test.sh runs both on a Mac with Xcode and the Android SDK: it runs the runtime's [Test]s in the simulator and in the emulator with pep-test --target, builds every documentation example for the iOS simulator and for Android, runs each in the simulator (xcrun simctl spawn) and in the emulator (adb shell), then builds and runs the two apps and the Swift package's tests. On iOS it also runs scripts/mobile/tls_check.pep in the simulator against openssl s_server on the Mac, with a certificate authority made for the run: it trusts that authority, connects to localhost and 127.0.0.1, checks that ALPN chose http/1.1, sends GET /, checks that a connector without the authority is refused, and fetches the server through http.Client. It needs no internet access. Set PEPPER_MOBILE_TLS_URL to an https:// URL to also fetch that public host through the system's roots. On Android the same check runs in the emulator against the same kind of server, which adb reverse makes the emulator's localhost, with the same opt-in public fetch. The Android run also works on Linux, for the host's ABI (x86_64 there), as CI runs it: scripts/ci-provision-android.sh sets up an emulator on a GitHub-hosted Linux runner, since Apple silicon runners cannot run one. CI's mobile workflow (.github/workflows/mobile.yml) runs the script on both, with the commit's own compiler (see Testing the runtime and the compiler).

bash scripts/mobile-test.sh target/bin/pep-build /tmp/mobile all

From a checkout, programs for Android that import tls need the static OpenSSL in the runtime first, which the toolchain already carries:

bash scripts/openssl-android.sh fetch runtime

scripts/openssl-android.sh build <ndk> <output-dir> builds that archive (OpenSSL 3.5, for each ABI, with the NDK's clang), and the openssl-android workflow publishes it on the openssl-<version> release whenever the version the script pins has not been published.

Not supported yet

  • TLS on iOS: servers, client certificates and TLS 1.3 (which need a SecIdentity and Network.framework).
  • Bindings: [T] and Data (an export takes no array), Result as throws (an export returns no Result), callbacks (a C function pointer is Swift-only), and a struct's exports as methods of its class.
  • Packaging: pep.toml keys for --lib xcframework and --lib aar, an .aar for an API level other than 30, Mac Catalyst and macOS slices in the .xcframework, and --lib jnilibs (each ABI's .so laid out for Gradle's jniLibs).
  • Other targets: 32-bit Android (armeabi-v7a, x86), Mac Catalyst, tvOS, watchOS and visionOS.

Optimizer hints

Hints tell the optimizer what it cannot see in the code. A hint never changes what a program computes, only how fast it runs, so a wrong hint costs speed and nothing else.

  • Which way a branch goes: write [Likely] or [Unlikely] above the if or match arm (see branch hints).
  • A function rarely called: [Cold] above it (see cold functions).
  • Memory a loop will soon touch: the hint module's prefetches.
FunctionTells the optimizer
hint.prefetch_read(address)address will be read soon: start loading its cache line now.
hint.prefetch_write(address)address will be written soon.

A prefetch never faults, even for an address that is not mapped, and does nothing where the CPU has no prefetch instruction.

# Prefetching: start loading memory a loop will soon read.
import hint;

main(): int {
    var text = "a long text that a loop will read";
    hint.prefetch_read(text.c_str());
    var spaces = 0;
    for (var index in 0..text.length) {
        if (text.byte_at(index) == ' ') {
            spaces += 1;
        }
    }
    assert(spaces == 7, "a hint changes nothing the program computes");
    return 0;
}

The prefetches are LLVM's llvm.prefetch intrinsic (see LLVM intrinsics). They matter only with optimization (-O2 and up, where the runtime's functions inline into the caller); at -O0 they cost a call and do nothing.

Cold functions

[Cold] above a function, method or constructor marks it rarely called: the optimizer never inlines it and treats a call to it as the unlikely side of a branch. Split the rare work out of a hot function into a [Cold] one, so the hot function stays small enough to inline into its callers:

# A hot method with its rare work split out into a [Cold] one.
struct Counter {
    var count: int;
    var wraps: int;

    construct() {
        count = 0;
        wraps = 0;
    }

    # Called on every event: small enough to inline.
    add() {
        if (count == 1000) {
            _wrap();
        }
        count += 1;
    }

    # Called once per thousand events: kept out of line.
    [Cold]
    _wrap() {
        count = 0;
        wraps += 1;
    }
}

main(): int {
    var counter = Counter();
    for (var index in 0..2500) {
        counter.add();
    }
    assert(counter.wraps == 2 && counter.count == 500, "[Cold] changes nothing the program computes");
    return 0;
}

[Cold] is LLVM's cold and noinline function attributes. The runtime's allocator marks its slow paths this way.

Deprecated hints

hint.likely(condition) and hint.unlikely(condition) are deprecated: each use warns and suggests the attribute.

SIMD vectors

A SIMD vector holds several numbers of one type, its lanes, and computes on all of them with one instruction. The simd module has two types:

  • Vector<T, N>: N lanes of the number type T.
  • Mask<N>: N booleans, what a lane-wise comparison gives.
import simd;

# The index of the first byte of `text` that is not ASCII, or its size:
# sixteen bytes per step, then one at a time for the rest.
first_non_ascii(text: String): ulong {
    var bytes = unsafe_cast<__ptr<byte>>(text.c_str());
    ulong i = 0;
    while (i + 16 <= text.size) {
        var high = simd.Vector<byte, 16>.load(bytes + i).greater_equal(0x80 as byte).to_bits();
        if (high != 0) {
            return i + high.trailing_zeros();
        }
        i = i + 16;
    }
    while (i < text.size && bytes[i] < 0x80) {
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return i;
}

main(): int {
    # A vector holds `N` lanes and computes on all of them at once.
    var a = simd.Vector<int, 4>(10);
    a[1] = 20;
    var b = a * 2 + 1;
    assert(b[0] == 21 && b[1] == 41 && b.sum() == 104, "lane-wise arithmetic");

    # A comparison gives a mask, one bool per lane.
    var big = b.greater(30);
    assert(big.to_bits() == 2 && big.any() && !big.all(), "a mask");
    var capped = big.select(simd.Vector<int, 4>(30), b);
    assert(capped.maximum() == 30, "select");

    # Floats, and conversions between lane types.
    var halves = a.convert<float>() * 0.5;
    assert(halves[1] == 10.0 && halves.square_root()[0] < 2.3, "floats");

    assert(first_non_ascii("plain ascii, then caf\u{e9}") == 21, "a scan");
    assert(first_non_ascii("short") == 5, "no match");
    return 0;
}

Bring them in with import simd; and write simd.Vector<byte, 16>, or import [Vector, Mask] from simd; and write Vector<byte, 16>.

Lane types and counts

  • T is an integer or floating-point type: byte, char, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float or double. These conform to the module's Lane trait; any other type is an error at the type argument:

    main.pep:3:25: error: 'String' does not conform to trait 'Lane', required by 'T' in 'Vector'

  • N is written as a number, a power of two from 1 to 64:

    main.pep:3:30: error: lane count of 'Vector<int, 3>' must be a power of two from 1 to 64, not '3'

    A number is a type argument only here, for a lane count; it is not a general constant parameter, so code cannot compute with N (use the count property for the lane count as a value).

  • Sixteen bytes (Vector<byte, 16>, Vector<short, 8>, Vector<int, 4>, Vector<float, 4>, Vector<double, 2>) fits a vector register on every target Pepper supports and is the width to reach for first. A wider vector works everywhere: where the target's registers are narrower, each operation takes several instructions.

A vector is a value struct: it is stored inline, copied like a number, and safe to share between threads (a [Shared] struct's field, a module constant).

Operations
MakeVector<T, N>() (every lane 0), Vector<T, N>(x) (every lane x)
Lanesv[i], v[i] = x (panics when i >= N), v.count
Arithmetic+ - *, unary -, with a vector or a scalar: v * 2
Division/ %: integer lanes panic on a zero divisor lane, and on the lowest value divided by -1; float lanes follow IEEE
Bitwise (integers)& | ^ ~, << >> by an int count (panics outside 0.. the lane width; >> is arithmetic for signed T), rotate_left, rotate_right
Floatssquare_root, floor, ceiling
Bothmin, max, abs
Horizontalsum, minimum, maximum
Comparisonsequal, not_equal, less, less_equal, greater, greater_equal, with a vector or a scalar, giving a Mask<N>
Whole vector== (every lane equal), != (some lane differs)
Rearrangingshuffle(indices), reverse, interleave_low, interleave_high
Typesconvert<U>() (lane by lane, like as), reinterpret<U, M>() (the same bits)
MemoryVector<T, N>.load(array, index), v.store(array, index) (panic unless index + N <= array.count); load, store, load_aligned, store_aligned on a __ptr<T>

A mask has any(), all(), & | ^ ~, m[i], select(a, b) (each lane from a where the mask is true, else from b) and to_bits(), which packs lane i into bit i of a ulong. With trailing_zeros() (see integer bit methods) that finds the first true lane, which is how a scan for a byte, or for a byte that is not ASCII, finds its match sixteen bytes at a time.

Some differences from scalar arithmetic are deliberate:

  • Integer lanes wrap around on overflow in +, -, *, unary - and abs, as vector instructions do; scalar arithmetic panics instead.

  • Comparisons that give a lane per lane are methods, because a comparison operator must return bool (see operators). == and != compare whole vectors.

  • shuffle takes each index modulo N, so every index picks a lane. With constant indices an optimized build makes it one shuffle instruction.

  • convert from float to integer saturates: a lane outside the target type's range becomes its nearest value, and NaN becomes 0.

  • The bitwise operators, shifts and rotates exist only for integer lanes, and square_root, floor and ceiling only for float lanes:

    main.pep:4:15: error: no member named 'square_root' in 'Vector<int, 4>'

Targets and optimization

The operations compile to LLVM vector instructions, which the target turns into its own: SSE2 on x86-64 (wider with -march=x86-64-v3 for AVX2, see pep-build), NEON on arm64, and WebAssembly's simd128 with -msimd128. A target without vector instructions, such as wasm32-wasip1 without -msimd128, computes the same results one lane at a time. Nothing picks instructions at run time: the -m options decide.

Each operation is a small method that the compiler always inlines, so an optimized build (-O2) of a loop over vectors has no calls in it, only the vector instructions. At -O0 it still runs, more slowly, like the rest of an unoptimized program.

Backtraces and the debugger

The debug module walks the call stack and talks to a debugger. Bring it in with import debug.

FunctionDoes
debug.capture()Records the call stack as a Backtrace: the return address of each call, innermost first.
trace.frames()Resolves the addresses to StackFrames: function, file, line, column, address and inlined.
debug.print_backtrace()Writes the current stack to standard error, as a panic does.
debug.output(text)Writes to the platform's debugger channel.
debug.is_debugger_attached()Whether a debugger is attached.
debug.breakpoint()Stops in the debugger, as a breakpoint on that line would.
# Capturing the call stack and resolving it to functions and lines.
import debug;

struct Parser {
    var depth: int;

    construct() {
        depth = 0;
    }

    # Records where it was called from, as an error report might.
    where(): debug.Backtrace {
        return debug.capture();
    }
}

main(): int {
    var parser = Parser();
    var trace = parser.where();
    var frames = trace.frames();
    for (var frame in frames) {
        print(frame.to_string());
    }
    # The outermost frame is main. (With -O and no -g, `where` is inlined
    # into main and has no frame of its own; WebAssembly cannot walk its
    # stack, so there a backtrace is empty.)
    if (frames.count > 0) {
        assert(frames[frames.count - 1].function == "main", "the outermost call");
    }
    debug.output("done");
    return 0;
}

Built with -g, this prints:

Parser.where at debug-backtrace.pep:13:16
main at debug-backtrace.pep:19:24
done

Built with -g -O2, the optimizer inlines where into main, and the backtrace still shows it, marked as inlined:

Parser.where at debug-backtrace.pep:13:16 (inlined)
main at debug-backtrace.pep:19:24
done

Capturing is cheap; resolving is not

capture() only records addresses, so a program can capture a stack whenever it might want to report one later, such as when it creates an error value. The work happens in frames() and to_string(), which read the program's symbol table and line table each time they are called.

A function name needs the program's symbol table, which every build keeps unless the executable is stripped. A file, line and column need the debug info a -g build carries:

PlatformFunction namesSource lines
LinuxThe executable's ELF symbol tableIts DWARF line table
macOSThe executable's symbol tableThe .dSYM bundle a -g build writes beside the executable (with dsymutil, from Xcode's command line tools)
WindowsDbgHelp, from the .pdb every build writes beside the executableDbgHelp, from the .pdb of a -g build (no columns)
WASInonenone

A WebAssembly program cannot walk its own stack, so on WASI a backtrace is empty.

Inlined calls

A function the optimizer inlined into its caller has no frame of its own on the stack. In a -g build, frames() puts it back: it expands each address into the chain of inlined calls it is inside, as addr2line -i and debuggers do, with one StackFrame per call, innermost first. Each of these frames has inlined set and is at the line of its own call, and the frame after them, which is not inlined, is the real one. All of them share its address. Linux and macOS read the inlined calls from the DWARF debug info, and Windows asks DbgHelp. On Windows an inlined call to a generic function is named without its type arguments (helper, not helper<int>), since the .pdb records inlined calls that way.

Without -g there is no record of what was inlined, so an optimized build's backtrace shows only the real frames, each named after the function the code was inlined into.

Which frames are left out

frames() leaves out, at the top of the stack, the frames of capture itself and of the runtime's panic code, and the runtime's operator methods a panic came through: a panic in a[i] starts at the line with a[i], not in Array<int>.__index_get. It also leaves out the C runtime's frames below main. frames(full = true) keeps them all.

Backtraces on panic

A panic prints the stack after its message in a build without -O:

main.pep:3:9: panic: index out of range
backtrace:
  0: inner at main.pep:3:9
  1: main at main.pep:8:12

An optimized build prints the message alone. The PEPPER_BACKTRACE environment variable overrides the build: PEPPER_BACKTRACE=1 prints a backtrace in any build, PEPPER_BACKTRACE=full also prints the frames frames() leaves out, and PEPPER_BACKTRACE=0 never prints one. Without -g, each frame shows its function but no file or line.

Only the first panic in a process prints a backtrace. If a second thread panics at the same time, it prints just its message.

The debugger channel

debug.output(text) writes a line where a debugger shows it:

  • Windows: OutputDebugStringW. Visual Studio's Output window and WinDbg show it, and so does DebugView when no debugger is attached. It goes nowhere else.
  • Linux, macOS and WASI: standard error. These systems have no separate channel, and debuggers show the program's own output.

debug.is_debugger_attached() reads TracerPid in /proc/self/status on Linux, P_TRACED on macOS, and IsDebuggerPresent on Windows. It is always false on WASI.

debug.breakpoint() executes the processor's debug trap. A debugger stops there and can continue the program. With no debugger attached, the trap ends the program, so guard it:

if (debug.is_debugger_attached()) {
    debug.breakpoint();
}

break is a keyword, so the function is called breakpoint.

See Debugging for running a program under gdb, lldb or Visual Studio.

Files and directories

The io module reads and writes files, lists and creates directories, and inspects and changes what the file system records about them: permission bits, timestamps and symbolic links. Every call that touches the file system returns an IoResult, whose error says what went wrong portably (is_not_found(), is_permission_denied(), is_already_exists(), ...; see Error handling with Result).

  • Path is a file-system path. Joining, parent(), file_name(), extension() and normalize() work on its text alone; exists(), metadata(), canonicalize() and the set_* methods below ask the file system.
  • File is an open file. File.open reads, File.create writes a new or emptied file, and OpenOptions describes anything else (append, create only if missing, ...). read_to_string, write_text, read_bytes, write_bytes, copy, rename and remove work on a whole file by path.
  • Directory creates and removes directories (create, create_all, remove, remove_all) and lists one, all at once with entries() or one entry at a time with for.
  • Metadata is a snapshot of a path's kind, size, permission bits and timestamps, from Path.metadata() (which follows symlinks), Path.symlink_metadata() (which does not) or File.metadata().
  • glob finds the paths that match a pattern such as src/**/*.pep, and Watcher reports changes in a directory tree (see Finding files by pattern and Watching for changes).
# Write, read, list and remove files with io.
import io;

main(): int {
    var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-files-basics-example");
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    io.Directory.create_all(folder.join("notes")).value();

    # Whole files at once.
    var path = folder.join("notes").join("today.txt");
    io.File.write_text(path, "buy milk\n").value();
    assert(io.File.read_to_string(path).value() == "buy milk\n", "read back");

    # An open File, with OpenOptions for anything but read or replace.
    var log = io.OpenOptions().append(true).create(true).open(folder.join("log.txt")).value();
    log.write_all("started\n").value();
    log.close().value();

    # Metadata, and a directory's entries.
    var m = path.metadata().value();
    assert(m.is_file && m.size == 9, "a 9-byte file");
    var names = Array<String>();
    for (var entry in io.Directory.open(folder).value()) {
        names.append(entry.value().name);
    }
    assert(names.count == 2, "log.txt and notes");

    io.Directory.remove_all(folder).value();
    return 0;
}

On Windows, a path of 248 characters or more works like any other: io makes it absolute and gives it the \\?\ prefix, which lifts Windows' 260-character limit whatever the system's long-path setting. A shorter path is passed as it is.

Permissions

A file's permission bits say who may read, write and run it. They are the platform's own bits, as Metadata.permissions reports them:

  • On Linux and macOS, the POSIX mode_t bits: read, write and execute for the owner, the group and everyone else, plus setuid, setgid and sticky. Pepper has no octal literals, so rwxr-xr-x (octal 755) is written 493, and a comment gives the octal. On a directory, read lets one list it, write lets one add and remove entries, and execute lets one reach anything inside it.
  • On Windows, the FILE_ATTRIBUTE_* word. Only FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY is a permission; whether a file runs depends on its extension.
  • WASI has no permission bits.

Three ways to change them:

  • set_permissions(mode) on a Path or an open File sets the raw bits (chmod and fchmod). On Windows it applies only the read-only bit of mode, and on WASI it returns an error.
  • set_read_only(bool) is the portable read-only switch. On POSIX, read-only clears every write bit and writable sets only the owner's, so this never opens a file to others. On Windows it sets or clears FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY.
  • set_executable(bool) adds an execute bit wherever there is a read bit, as chmod +x does, or clears them all. It does nothing on Windows and WASI.

A file or directory can also be created with its bits, so that it never exists with the default ones even for a moment: OpenOptions.mode(m) for a new file, and Directory.create(path, mode = m) or create_all(path, mode = m) for a directory. The process umask still applies, as it does to open and mkdir. These are ignored on Windows and WASI.

Timestamps

Metadata.modified and Metadata.accessed are nanoseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC. set_modified(time) and set_accessed(time) on a Path or an open File set one and leave the other (utimensat and futimens; SetFileTime on Windows, which keeps 100 ns). Writing to a file sets its modification time, and adding or removing an entry sets a directory's, so set a time after the contents are final.

# Permission bits and timestamps: make a script executable, protect a file,
# and copy a modification time.
import io;

main(): int {
    var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-files-permissions-example");
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    # 448 is octal 700: only the owner may list or enter it (POSIX only).
    io.Directory.create(folder, mode = 448).value();

    # Created with mode 493 (octal 755, rwxr-xr-x) less the umask, so the
    # script is never readable by others without being executable.
    var script = folder.join("run.sh");
    var file = io.OpenOptions().write(true).create_new(true).mode(493).open(script).value();
    file.write_all("#!/bin/sh\necho hello\n").value();
    file.close().value();

    # The portable way: add an execute bit where there is a read bit.
    var notes = folder.join("notes.sh");
    io.File.write_text(notes, "#!/bin/sh\n").value();
    notes.set_executable(true).value();
    [Target(OS(Linux) || OS(Mac))] {
        assert((notes.metadata().value().permissions & 64) != 0, "the owner may run it");
    }

    # Read-only: no write bits on POSIX, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY on Windows.
    [Target(!OS(Wasi))] {
        notes.set_read_only(true).value();
        assert(notes.metadata().value().read_only, "read-only");
        notes.set_read_only(false).value();
    }

    # Give the script the same modification time as the notes.
    var modified = notes.metadata().value().modified;
    script.set_modified(modified).value();
    assert(script.metadata().value().modified == modified, "same time");

    io.Directory.remove_all(folder).value();
    return 0;
}

On Windows, an open File must have been opened for writing to change its read-only bit or its times.

Symbolic links

File.symlink(target, link) and Directory.symlink(target, link) create a symbolic link at link pointing to target. POSIX makes one kind of link either way; Windows makes a file link and a directory link differently, and a file link to a directory does not open, so use the one that matches the target. The target is stored as given and need not exist; a relative target is resolved from the directory holding the link.

Path.read_link() returns the target a link stores, without following it. Path.symlink_metadata() describes the link itself, and metadata() what it points to. Directory.remove_all removes links and never follows them.

# Symbolic links: make one to a file and one to a directory, and read them.
import io;

main(): int {
    var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-files-symlinks-example");
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    io.Directory.create_all(folder.join("releases").join("1.2")).value();
    io.File.write_text(folder.join("app-1.2.conf"), "port = 80\n").value();

    # Windows needs Developer Mode or an administrator to make symlinks.
    [Target(!OS(Windows))] {
        # A relative target is resolved from the folder holding the link.
        var config = folder.join("app.conf");
        io.File.symlink(io.Path("app-1.2.conf"), config).value();
        assert(io.File.read_to_string(config).value() == "port = 80\n", "read through the link");
        assert(config.read_link().value() == io.Path("app-1.2.conf"), "the stored target");
        assert(config.symlink_metadata().value().is_symlink, "the link itself");

        var current = folder.join("current");
        io.Directory.symlink(io.Path("releases").join("1.2"), current).value();
        assert(current.is_directory(), "a directory through the link");
    }

    # remove_all removes links, never what they point to.
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder).value();
    return 0;
}

Making a symlink on Windows needs Developer Mode or an administrator; without either it fails with is_permission_denied().

Moving a file to another thread

A File is not thread-safe, so a thread cannot capture one. To hand an open file to another thread, such as the pipe from a child process's output to a thread that reads it while this one writes to the child, file.into_transfer() moves its handle into an io.FileTransfer, a thread-safe token that a shared function can capture or a Channel can carry, and io.File.adopt(transfer) takes it out again on the other thread. The File it came from is closed afterwards, only the first adopt gets the handle, and a token no one adopts closes the file when it goes. A stream moves the same way, as a SocketTransfer (see Moving a stream to another worker).

# Hand an open File to another thread with into_transfer and adopt.
import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-files-transfer-example.txt");
    io.File.write_text(path, "read on another thread").value();
    var file = io.File.open(path).value();
    # A File is not thread-safe; its transfer token is.
    var transfer = file.into_transfer();
    var size = async.Atomic<ulong>(0);
    var reader = async.Thread.spawn(() => {
        var mine = io.File.adopt(transfer).value();
        size.store(mine.read_all().value().count);
    });
    reader.join();
    assert(size.load() == 22, "the other thread read the file");
    assert(!file.is_open(), "the File it came from is closed");
    io.File.remove(path);
    return 0;
}

Finding files by pattern

io.glob(pattern) returns the existing paths that match a shell-style pattern, sorted, and io.glob_matches(pattern, path) tests a path's text against one without touching the file system:

  • * matches any run of characters within one path component, and ? one character; neither matches /.
  • ** as a whole component matches any number of directories, none included: src/**/*.pep matches src/main.pep and src/net/http.pep.
  • [abc], [a-z] and [!abc] (or [^abc]) match one character listed, in the range, or not listed.
  • {pep,md} matches either alternative; alternatives may hold any pattern, braces included.

Patterns separate components with / on every system; on Windows a \ in the path being matched counts as / too. There is no escape character, so that Windows paths stay as they are: [*] matches a literal *. An unclosed [ or { matches itself, so every pattern is valid. Matching is case-sensitive, and * matches a leading . like any other character.

glob starts at the longest leading part of the pattern without wildcards, so src/**/*.pep lists only under src, and a relative pattern gives relative paths. ** does not descend into symlinked directories, so a link cycle cannot loop. Directories it cannot read are skipped, and a pattern whose start does not exist matches nothing.

# Find files by pattern with io.glob, and test a path with io.glob_matches.
import io;

main(): int {
    var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-files-glob-example");
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    io.Directory.create_all(folder.join("src").join("net")).value();
    io.File.write_text(folder.join("README.md"), "").value();
    io.File.write_text(folder.join("src").join("main.pep"), "").value();
    io.File.write_text(folder.join("src").join("net").join("http.pep"), "").value();

    # `**` crosses directories; `*` stays within one name. Patterns use `/`
    # on every system, and the paths come back sorted.
    var base = folder.to_string().replace("\\", "/");
    var sources = io.glob(base + "/src/**/*.pep");
    assert(sources.count == 2, "main.pep and net/http.pep");
    assert(io.glob(base + "/*.{md,txt}").count == 1, "README.md");

    # Matching text alone touches no files.
    assert(io.glob_matches("src/**/*.pep", "src/net/http.pep"), "matches");
    assert(!io.glob_matches("*.pep", "src/main.pep"), "`*` stops at `/`");
    assert(io.glob_matches("file[0-9].txt", "file7.txt"), "a class");

    io.Directory.remove_all(folder).value();
    return 0;
}

Watching for changes

io.Watcher.open(directory) watches a directory and everything below it. Each wait() returns the changes recorded since the last one, or waits for the next: a list of FileChanges, each a ChangeKind (Created, Removed, Modified) and the path it happened to. A rename reports the old path removed and the new one created. When the system drops changes because they came too fast, wait reports one Overflow change for the directory: list it again to catch up. close() stops watching, and a wait running in another task then fails.

In a task (see Tasks) wait parks only the task, so others run while it waits, and the task's cancel or async.timeout ends it. Outside a task it blocks the thread.

# Watch a directory tree for changes with io.Watcher, inside a task.
import async;
