import io;

main(): int {
    var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-files-watch-example");
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    io.Directory.create_all(folder).value();
    var watcher = io.Watcher.open(folder).value();
    async.run(
        () => {
            var path = folder.join("hello.txt");
            io.File.write_text(path, "hi").value();
            # In a task the wait parks only the task, and a timeout ends it.
            with (async.timeout(5000)) {
                var changes = watcher.wait().value();
                for (var change in changes) {
                    if (change.kind == io.ChangeKind.Created && change.path.to_string() == path.to_string()) {
                        print($"created {change.path.file_name().value()}");
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    );
    watcher.close();
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder).value();
    return 0;
}

Each system watches its own way, and that shows in a few places:

  • Linux uses inotify, with a watch on every directory of the tree. A new directory gets one as its creation is read, and what it already holds by then is reported created. The number of watches is limited (/proc/sys/fs/inotify/max_user_watches), and open fails past it.
  • macOS uses kqueue, which holds an open descriptor for every directory and file of the tree, so a large tree may need a higher ulimit -n. A directory that changed is listed again to tell what came and went.
  • Windows uses ReadDirectoryChangesW, which watches the whole tree with one handle. One write often reports Modified twice; repeats next to each other in one batch are dropped.
  • WASI cannot watch: open fails.

Archives

archive.TarReader.extract uses all of the above: it restores each file's mode and modification time and makes the archive's symlinks, as long as they stay inside the directory it extracts into. See Compression and archives.

Processes

The process module starts other programs and holds what belongs to the running one: its arguments, its exit, its id, its executable, and its working directory. Bring it in with import process.

On WebAssembly (--target wasm32-wasip1) a program cannot start another: run, spawn, exec and executable_path return an IoError saying it is not supported on WASI. Its arguments, exit and environment work (see WebAssembly).

Running a program

Command describes a program to start. Its setters return the same Command, so they chain. run() starts the program, waits for it to end, and returns an Output: the status it ended with, and the text it wrote to stdout and stderr.

import io;
import process;

# Runs a copy of this program as a child, so the example needs no other
# program on any system: the child's first argument says what to do.
main(args: String[]): int {
    if (args.count > 1) {
        io.File.stdout().write_all("hello from " + args[1]);
        io.File.stderr().write_all("a warning");
        return 3;
    }

    var self = process.executable_path().value().to_string();
    var output = process.Command(self).argument("the child").run().value();
    assert(output.stdout == "hello from the child", "standard output is collected");
    assert(output.stderr == "a warning", "and so is standard error");
    assert(!output.status.success(), "the child failed");
    assert(output.status.code().value() == 3, "with exit code 3");

    # A program that is not found fails to start.
    var missing = process.Command("no-such-program").run();
    assert(missing.is_err() && missing.error().is_not_found(), "not found");
    return 0;
}
  • The program is found the way a shell finds it. A bare name is searched for on the PATH (on Windows, also next to the running program and in the system directories, with .exe added when the name has no extension). Anything with a path separator is a path.
  • Each argument reaches the program as one argument, whatever it holds. No shell splits it or expands * or $NAME. On Windows, where a program receives a single command line, each argument is quoted so that the C runtime splits it back out as it was.
  • run() collects standard output and error, both at once, so a child that fills one pipe while the parent reads the other does not stall. Standard input is the null device unless it was set. The output is decoded as UTF-8, with each invalid byte sequence replaced by U+FFFD; read a child's binary output from a pipe with spawn() instead.
  • A program that cannot be started is an error (is_not_found() when it does not exist). A program that runs and fails is a successful result whose status says so.

exec() runs the program in place of the running one, as a shell's exec does: the program's exit status becomes this process's own, and exec() returns only when the program cannot be started, with the error. On POSIX the program takes over the process; Windows cannot replace a process, so there the program is started, waited for, and its exit status passed on. Output that print buffered is flushed first, and the standard streams must stay inherited (otherwise the error has is_invalid_input()).

Exit status

ExitStatus.success() is true for exit code 0. code() returns the exit code, and signal() the POSIX signal that ended the process (such as 9 for SIGKILL). Each is an optional: a process killed by a signal has no exit code, and a process that exited has no signal. Windows has no signals, so there every process has a code; a POSIX parent sees only the low 8 bits of it.

Talking to a child

spawn() starts the program and returns a Child at once. Each of the three standard streams is Stream.Inherit (shared with the parent, the default), Stream.Pipe (connected to the parent), or Stream.Null. A piped stream is an io.File from child.stdin(), child.stdout() or child.stderr(), so the file read and write methods apply.

import io;
import process;

main(args: String[]): int {
    if (args.count > 1) {
        # The child: read standard input to the end, and write it back in
        # capitals.
        var text = io.File.stdin().read_string().value();
        io.File.stdout().write_all(text.upper());
        return 0;
    }

    var self = process.executable_path().value().to_string();
    var child = process.Command(self)
        .argument("upper")
        .stdin(process.Stream.Pipe)
        .stdout(process.Stream.Pipe)
        .spawn()
        .value();
    child.stdin().write_all("pear and apple");
    child.stdin().close();  # the child reads to the end, so end it
    var shouted = child.stdout().read_string().value();
    var status = child.wait().value();
    assert(shouted == "PEAR AND APPLE", "the child's output");
    assert(status.success(), "the child succeeded");
    return 0;
}
  • Close a piped standard input when you are done writing, or a child that reads to the end never finishes. wait() closes it too, before waiting.
  • Read piped output before waiting. A child that fills a pipe stops until the parent reads it, so waiting first can wait forever.
  • wait() returns the exit status, and again on later calls. try_wait() returns none while the child runs. kill() ends the child at once (SIGKILL, or TerminateProcess on Windows); wait for it afterwards.
  • Wait for every child. On POSIX a child that ended stays in the process table until it is waited for. Releasing a Child neither waits for it nor kills it.

In a task, run(), wait() and reads from a pipe park the task rather than block its worker, so other tasks keep running.

Environment and working directory

A child inherits the parent's environment. environment(name, value) sets a variable for the child, remove_environment(name) leaves one out, and clear_environment() starts from an empty environment. On Windows, names ignore case. working_directory(path) starts the child in another directory. The running process reads and changes its own environment with os.environment(name) and os.set_environment(name, value) (see The operating system).

import io;
import os;
import process;

main(args: String[]): int {
    if (args.count > 1) {
        io.File.stdout().write_all(os.environment("GREETING").value_or("unset"));
        return 0;
    }

    var self = process.executable_path().value().to_string();
    var greeted = process.Command(self).argument("child").environment("GREETING", "hello").run().value();
    assert(greeted.stdout == "hello", "the child sees the variable");

    var cleared = process.Command(self).argument("child").clear_environment().run().value();
    assert(cleared.stdout == "unset", "an empty environment");

    # The child starts in another directory; the parent's stays as it was.
    var before = process.working_directory().value();
    var elsewhere = process.Command(self).argument("child").working_directory(io.Directory.temp()).run();
    assert(elsewhere.is_ok(), "started in the temporary directory");
    assert(process.working_directory().value() == before, "unchanged");
    return 0;
}

The running process

  • process.arguments() returns the program's command-line arguments, the same array main(args: String[]) receives (see Functions). On Windows they are read as UTF-16, so every character arrives as UTF-8; on POSIX an argument is whatever bytes the parent passed.
  • process.exit(code) ends the program at once with status code, as C's exit does: the handlers registered with C's atexit run, and printed output is flushed. In a copy process.fork() started, the handlers, which are the parent's, are skipped, from whichever of its threads exit is called.
  • process.id() is the process's id.
  • process.executable_path() is the absolute path of the running program's executable, so a tool can find files installed next to it.
  • process.working_directory() and process.change_working_directory(path) read and change the directory relative paths are resolved against, as io.Directory.current() and io.Directory.set_current(path) do.

arguments() and exit() without import process still work, but are deprecated and warn.

Signals

process.signals([...]) returns an async.Channel<Signal> that receives each signal it names instead of the signal's default action, which ends the program. A server or tool waits on it to shut down cleanly: stop accepting work, flush, remove temporary files.

SignalPOSIXWindows
InterruptSIGINT (Ctrl-C)CTRL_C_EVENT, CTRL_BREAK_EVENT
TerminateSIGTERMCTRL_CLOSE_EVENT, CTRL_LOGOFF_EVENT, CTRL_SHUTDOWN_EVENT
HangupSIGHUPnever sent
import process;
import [Signal] from process;

main(): int {
    var stop = process.signals([Signal.Interrupt, Signal.Terminate]);
    # Serve until Ctrl-C or a request to terminate arrives: here, for at most
    # a tenth of a second.
    var signal = stop.receive_for(100);
    if (signal.is_ok()) {
        print("shutting down cleanly");
    }
    # Closing the channel gives the signals back their default action.
    stop.close();
    return 0;
}

No program code runs inside the operating system's signal handler: on POSIX the handler only writes the signal's number to a pipe, and a runtime thread sends it on the channel. So the channel is the whole interface, and works as any channel does: receive() waits, a task can select on it alongside its other channels, and try_receive() polls between steps of a long job.

  • Every open channel that names a signal receives it.
  • Closing a channel stops it receiving; once no open channel names a signal, its default action returns.
  • On Windows the system ends the program a few seconds after Terminate (the console closing, a log-off or a shutdown) whatever it does, so keep that cleanup short.
  • WebAssembly has no signals: the channel never receives.
  • Writing to a socket whose peer has gone returns an IoError rather than raising SIGPIPE; the runtime asks for that on every socket.

Finding a program

process.find_executable(name) looks a program up on the PATH as a shell does, returning the path of the first match that may be run, or none, so a tool can say what to install before trying to run it. process.is_executable(path) tells whether a file may be run.

var perf = process.find_executable("perf");
if (perf.is_empty()) {
    print("perf is not installed");
}

See the process module reference.

The operating system

The os module reports what the operating system provides beyond the running process: environment variables, clocks, and facts about the machine and the user. Bring it in with import os. The full API is in the reference.

Environment variables

os.environment(name) returns a variable's value as a String?: none when it is not set, and an empty String when it is set to nothing. os.environment_variables() returns them all as a HashMap<String, String> from name to value.

import os;

main(): int {
    # An optional: none when the variable is not set.
    var runtime = os.environment("PEPPER_RUNTIME").value_or("runtime");
    assert(!runtime.is_empty, "a fallback when unset");
    assert(os.environment("PEPPER_SURELY_NOT_SET").is_empty(), "unset");

    var count = 0;
    for (var (name, value) in os.environment_variables()) {
        if (name.starts_with("PEPPER_")) {
            print($"{name}={value}");
        }
        count = count + 1;
    }
    assert(count > 0, "a process has an environment");
    return 0;
}
  • On Windows, names ignore case (Path finds PATH), and values are read as UTF-16, so text outside the ANSI code page survives.
  • On POSIX a value is whatever bytes the parent passed; one that is not valid UTF-8 is returned as it is.

Changing the environment

os.set_environment(name, value) sets a variable for the running process, and os.remove_environment(name) removes one. Later reads see the change, and so do the children the process starts afterwards.

import os;

main(): int {
    var name = "PEPPER_EXAMPLE_GREETING";
    os.set_environment(name, "hello");
    assert(os.environment(name).value() == "hello", "set");

    os.set_environment(name, "");
    assert(os.environment(name).value() == "", "set to nothing");

    os.remove_environment(name);
    assert(os.environment(name).is_empty(), "removed");
    return 0;
}
  • Every read and change the runtime makes goes through one lock, so Pepper code never races with itself over the environment, from any thread.
  • C code that calls getenv itself is outside that lock. On POSIX, setenv races with such a call on another thread (Rust 2024 marks its set_var unsafe for this reason), so set variables before starting threads that run C code reading them.
  • A name that is empty or contains = or a NUL byte, or a value that contains a NUL byte, panics.
  • On Windows names ignore case, and the C runtime's own getenv copy does not see the change. On WASI the change stays inside the program.
  • To give only a child a different environment, use process.Command's environment, remove_environment and clear_environment (see Processes).

Time

Three value types cover time. Each is a value struct: copied, compared with ==, < and the other comparisons, and never allocated.

  • Duration is a span of time in nanoseconds, never negative. Make one with from_seconds, from_milliseconds, from_microseconds or from_nanoseconds, read it back with seconds(), milliseconds() and the others (rounded down), and add, subtract, multiply or divide it. Printing one shows it in the largest unit it reaches: 2.5s, 15ms, 40ns.
  • Instant reads a monotonic clock, for measuring how long something takes. It only moves forward, whatever the system's date is set to. later - earlier is the Duration between two instants, and start.elapsed() the time since one.
  • SystemTime reads the wall clock: nanoseconds since the Unix epoch (1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC). unix_seconds() is what file systems and most protocols record. Since the wall clock can be set back, duration_since(earlier) is an optional: none when earlier is later. The time module turns it into a date and time, in UTC or a time zone, and back.
import os;

main(): int {
    # Measure with the monotonic clock: subtracting two instants gives a
    # Duration.
    var start = os.Instant.now();
    long total = 0;
    for (var i in 0..100000) {
        total = total + i;
    }
    var elapsed = os.Instant.now() - start;
    print($"summed in {elapsed}");   # such as "1.234ms"

    var timeout = os.Duration.from_seconds(2) + os.Duration.from_milliseconds(500);
    assert(timeout.milliseconds() == 2500, "whole milliseconds");
    assert(timeout.to_string() == "2.5s", "the largest unit it reaches");
    assert(elapsed < timeout, "durations compare");

    # The wall clock counts from the Unix epoch.
    var now = os.SystemTime.now();
    assert(now.unix_seconds() > 1700000000, "after November 2023");
    var tomorrow = now + os.Duration.from_seconds(86400);
    assert(tomorrow.duration_since(now).value() == os.Duration.from_seconds(86400), "a day later");
    assert(now.duration_since(tomorrow).is_empty(), "no negative durations");
    return 0;
}

Subtracting a longer Duration, or a later Instant, panics: neither can be negative.

The machine and the user

import os;

main(): int {
    print($"{os.system_name()} {os.system_version()} on {os.architecture()}");
    print($"host {os.hostname()}: {os.logical_cpus()} logical processors, {os.physical_cpus()} cores");
    print($"{os.total_memory() / 1048576} MiB of memory in {os.page_size()}-byte pages");

    var user = os.user_name().value_or("unknown");
    var home = os.home_directory();
    print($"user {user}, home {home.is_value() ? home.value().to_string() : "unknown"}");
    print($"temporary files go in {os.temp_directory()}");

    var executable = os.system_os() == os.OperatingSystem.Windows ? "tool.exe" : "tool";
    assert(executable.starts_with("tool"), "picked a name");
    return 0;
}
FunctionReturns
system_os()the OperatingSystem the program was built for: Linux, Mac, Windows or Wasi
system_name()the same as text: "linux", "macos" or "windows"
system_version()the kernel release on Linux, the product version on macOS (14.5), major.minor.build on Windows
architecture()"x64", "aarch64" or "wasm32", as [Target(Arch(...))] names them
hostname()the machine's host name
logical_cpus(), physical_cpus()processor counts, the same as async's, capped by a Linux container's CPU quota
total_memory(), page_size()physical memory, or a Linux container's lower memory limit, and the virtual memory page size, in bytes
peak_memory()the most physical memory the process has held at once (its peak resident set), in bytes; 0 on WASI
user_name()the user the program runs as, or none
home_directory()HOME (on Windows USERPROFILE), or the user database's entry, or none
temp_directory()the directory for temporary files, the same as io.Directory.temp()
is_elevated()whether the program runs as root, or elevated ("Run as administrator") on Windows; never on WASI

Containers

On Linux, total_memory() and logical_cpus() report what a container lets the program use, as the JVM and Go do, so a pool or a cache sized from them fits inside it. Both read the process's cgroup and each cgroup above it, under /sys/fs/cgroup, with cgroup v2 or v1:

  • total_memory() returns the smallest of the physical memory and every memory limit found (memory.max, or v1's memory.limit_in_bytes), as docker run --memory sets it.
  • logical_cpus() returns the smaller of the online processors and the smallest CPU quota (cpu.max, or v1's cpu.cfs_quota_us over cpu.cfs_period_us), rounded up to whole processors: docker run --cpus=1.5 counts as 2. physical_cpus() is never more than that.

Where no limit is set, or the files cannot be read, they report the machine.

Current limitations

  • async.timeout still takes milliseconds, not a Duration.

Command-line options

The cli module parses a program's command line. Declare each option and positional argument on a cli.Parser, call parse, then read the values through the handles the declarations returned, or declare them all at once as the fields of a struct. The help, --version and the error messages all come from the declarations. Bring it in with import cli; the full API is in the reference.

# Command-line parsing: declare options and arguments, then parse.
import cli;

main(args: String[]): int {
    var parser = cli.Parser("greet", "Greets someone", version = "1.0");
    var greeting = parser.option("greeting", "g", "what to say", default_value = "hello");
    var loud = parser.flag("loud", "l", "shout it");
    var times = parser.option<int>("times", "n", "how many times to say it", value_name = "COUNT", default_value = "1");
    var names = parser.positionals("names", "who to greet");

    # `parse` prints --help and --version and exits; on a mistake it writes
    # the error and the usage to standard error and returns false.
    if (!parser.parse(args)) {
        return 2;
    }

    var people = names.is_set ? names.values() : ["world"];
    for (var person in people) {
        var line = $"{greeting.value()}, {person}";
        for (var _ in 0..times.value()) {
            print(loud.is_set ? line.upper() : line);
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

greet --help prints:

Greets someone

usage: greet [OPTIONS] [names]...

Arguments:
  <names>...  who to greet

Options:
  -g, --greeting <GREETING>  what to say [default: hello]
  -l, --loud                 shout it
  -n, --times <COUNT>        how many times to say it [default: 1]
  -h, --help                 show this help
  -V, --version              show the version

The raw arguments stay where they were: main(args: String[]) receives them, and process.arguments() returns them. parse takes them as main receives them, program name first.

Declaring

DeclarationHandleReads
flag(name, short_name, help, global)Flagis_set and occurrences (properties)
option<T>(name, short_name, help, value_name, default_value, required, global, implicit_value)Argument<T>value(), value_or(fallback), is_set
multiple<T>(name, short_name, help, value_name, required, global)ArgumentList<T>values(), is_set
positional<T>(name, help, required, default_value)Argument<T>value(), value_or(fallback), is_set
positionals<T>(name, help, required)ArgumentList<T>values(), is_set

T is the type of the value (see Typed values); leave it out for a String: option("output") is option<String>("output").

  • An option's name is its long name without --; short_name is one character without -, or empty for none. One of the two may be empty: option("", "o") is an option spelled only -o, as a C compiler's -I, -D and -o are. Pass the rest by name: option("output", "o", "the executable to write", default_value = "a.out").
  • value() returns the value given, else the default; it panics when the argument was left out and has no default, so use value_or or check is_set for an optional one. is_set (a property, like occurrences and is_selected) is false for a value that came from the default.
  • Positional arguments fill in declaration order. A required one cannot follow an optional one, and positionals takes every value that is left, so it comes last.
  • -h/--help is always there, and -V/--version when the parser has a version. Declaring -h or -V yourself takes the short name; the long forms keep working.
  • A mistake in the declarations, such as a name declared twice or a short name longer than one character, panics: it is a bug in the program, not in its input.

On the command line

  • A value follows its option as --output a.out, --output=a.out, -o a.out, -oa.out or -o=a.out. It is taken as it is, even when it starts with -.
  • Short flags combine: -vq is -v -q, and -vo a.out gives -v and then -o a.out. -vvv counts three occurrences.
  • Options and positional arguments mix in any order. -- ends the options, so rm -- -file removes a file named -file, and - alone is a positional argument (by custom, standard input).
  • An option that takes one value keeps the last one given.
  • An option declared with an implicit_value takes a value only when it is attached (--emit-ast=json, -O3); given alone, it has the implicit value, and the argument after it is not its value. The help shows it as --emit-ast[=<FORMAT>] or -O[<LEVEL>].

Typed values

A declaration with a type argument reads its values as that type, and a value that is not one fails the parse:

greet: error: invalid value 'x' for '--times': expected an integer
TA value isAn error expects
Stringany text
int, longan integer, as int.parse reads itan integer
uint, ulongan integer that is not negativea non-negative integer
byte, short, ushortan integer in the type's rangean integer from 0 to 255
float, doublea number, as double.parse reads ita number
io.Pathany text, as a path
an enum whose cases carry no valuesa case's name in kebab case: DebugInfo is debug-info'fast' or 'debug-info'
  • An enum's help lists its cases: [possible values: fast, debug-info].
  • default_value is written as on the command line, so the help shows it as it is: option<int>("jobs", default_value = "4"). A default that is not a value of the type panics.
  • Any other type is a compile error at the call.

Errors

parse writes a clang-style error, the usage and a hint to standard error and returns false, so the program can exit with 2:

greet: error: unknown option '--lound'; did you mean '--loud'?
usage: greet [OPTIONS] [names]...
Run 'greet --help' for more information.

The messages:

  • unknown option '--x' (with did you mean '--y'? for a near miss) and unknown option '-x'
  • missing value for '-o'
  • option '--loud' takes no value (for --loud=yes)
  • invalid value 'x' for '--times': expected an integer
  • missing required option '--target', missing required argument '<source>'
  • unexpected argument 'x' when there is no positional argument left for it
  • unknown command 'x' and missing command: expected 'add' or 'update'

A mistake parse cannot see, such as two options that cannot be used together, is reported the same way with usage_error, which returns 2:

if (test.is_set and library.is_set) {
    return parser.usage_error("'--test' cannot be used with '--lib'");
}

try_parse does the same parse and writes nothing. It returns a Result<String?>: an error holding the message, some text when --help or --version asked for it (print it and exit with 0), or none when the arguments were parsed. Tests use it, and so can a program that reports errors its own way.

Declaring options as a struct

add_options declares an option or positional argument for each public field of a struct, and every successful parse stores the values in that struct's fields. The attributes [cli.Option] and [cli.Positional] on the fields carry what the builder calls take as arguments:

# Command-line parsing: declare the options as a struct's fields.
import cli;

struct Options {
    [cli.Option("g", "what to say")]
    var greeting: String = "hello";
    [cli.Option("l", "shout it")]
    var loud: bool;
    [cli.Option("n", "how many times to say it", value_name = "COUNT")]
    var times: int = 1;
    [cli.Positional("who to greet")]
    var names: String[];
}

main(args: String[]): int {
    var options = Options();
    var parser = cli.Parser("greet", "Greets someone", version = "1.0");
    parser.add_options(options);
    if (!parser.parse(args)) {
        return 2;
    }

    var people = options.names.is_empty ? ["world"] : options.names;
    for (var person in people) {
        var line = $"{options.greeting}, {person}";
        for (var _ in 0..options.times) {
            print(options.loud ? line.upper() : line);
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Its help and errors are the same as the builder example's above: the declarations are the same ones.

Field typeDeclaresAfter a parse
boolflagwhether it was given
Toption<T>the value given, else the field's starting value
T?option<T>the value given, or Empty
T[]multiple<T>the values given, in order
  • T is any type of Typed values: String, a number type, io.Path or an enum. A field's starting value is the default the help shows, except an empty String or a null io.Path, which means none.
  • An option is named after its field, with each _ written -: import_path is --import-path. Any other field type is a compile error at the call: 'add_options' cannot declare field 'table' of type 'Map<String, int>'; use bool, String, a number type, io.Path or an enum, or one of those as T? or T[].
  • [cli.Option(short_name, help, name, value_name, required, global)] sets the rest, every argument optional: [cli.Option("o", "the executable to write")], [cli.Option(required = true)].
  • [cli.Positional(help, name, required)] makes the field the next positional argument. A T one is required when it has no default or required is set; a T? one may be left out; a T[] one takes every value left (positionals), and required asks for at least one.
  • Each parse sets every field again, so a flag left out is false even if the field started true.
  • A parse that fails, or that asks for --help or --version, leaves the fields as they were.
  • The two styles mix: call flag and option on the same parser, and add_options on a command's parser for that command's options. A command's struct is filled only when that command is given.

Subcommands

command(name, about) declares a subcommand, as in git add or pep-package update, and returns its own Parser to declare its options and arguments on. The first argument that is not an option names the command; after parse, is_selected tells which command was given.

# Subcommands, and handling the outcome yourself with try_parse.
import cli;

main(): int {
    var parser = cli.Parser("pkg", "Manages packages");
    var verbose = parser.flag("verbose", "v", "say more");
    var add = parser.command("add", "Adds a dependency");
    var name = add.positional("name", "the package to add");
    var dev = add.flag("dev", "d", "only for development");
    var update = parser.command("update", "Updates dependencies");
    var packages = update.positionals("packages", "what to update; everything when none");

    # The arguments as `main(args: String[])` would receive them.
    var parsed = parser.try_parse(["pkg", "-v", "add", "--dev", "yaml"]);
    assert(parsed.is_ok() && parsed.value().is_empty(), "parsed, no help asked for");
    assert(add.is_selected && !update.is_selected, "the add command");
    assert(verbose.is_set && dev.is_set && name.value() == "yaml", "its values");

    # A mistake is an error with a clang-style message.
    parsed = parser.try_parse(["pkg", "updat"]);
    assert(parsed.error().message == "unknown command 'updat'; did you mean 'update'?", "a suggestion");

    # --help gives the text to print, for the command it follows.
    parsed = parser.try_parse(["pkg", "update", "--help"]);
    print(parsed.value().value());
    return 0;
}
  • A parser with commands needs one, and cannot have positional arguments of its own.
  • Options before the command's name belong to the parent, and everything after it to the command, so pkg -v add x works and pkg add -v x does not, unless -v is global.
  • A global option (flag("verbose", "v", global = true), and the same argument on option and multiple) may also be given after the name of any command below its parser, at any depth, and each command's help lists it. A command cannot declare an option with a global option's name, and a required global option may be given anywhere on the line.
  • --help after a command shows that command's help, and errors show its usage.
  • Commands nest: a command's parser can declare commands too.

Shell completions

completions(shell) returns a script that completes the program's command line in Bash, Zsh, fish or PowerShell (cli.Shell), from the declarations: options (with the global ones in each command), commands, an enum's cases, and file names for a value that is a String or an io.Path. A program prints it on request, often from a command of its own, as pkg completions fish does here:

# Shell completion scripts, printed by a command of the program's own.
import cli;

main(): int {
    var parser = cli.Parser("pkg", "Manages packages");
    parser.flag("verbose", "v", "say more", global = true);
    var add = parser.command("add", "Adds a dependency");
    add.positional("name", "the package");
    var completions = parser.command("completions", "Prints a shell completion script");
    var shell = completions.positional<cli.Shell>("shell", "bash, zsh, fish or powershell");

    # The arguments as `main(args: String[])` would receive them.
    var parsed = parser.try_parse(["pkg", "completions", "fish"]);
    assert(parsed.is_ok() && completions.is_selected, "the completions command");
    print(parser.completions(shell.value()));
    return 0;
}

The user installs what it prints where the shell looks for it:

ShellInstall the script as
bash~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/pkg, or source it from ~/.bashrc
zsh_pkg in a directory on $fpath
fish~/.config/fish/completions/pkg.fish
powershelldot-sourced from $PROFILE

Not yet

  • Windows-style /option forms: every platform uses - and --.

Logging

The log module writes lines with a level, a message, key/value fields and the place of the call, from any thread or task. Bring it in with import log.

# Leveled, structured logging: levels, fields, a target, and a JSON file.
import io;
import log;

main(): int {
    log.info("started");
    log.warning("disk almost full", [log.field("free_mb", 120)], target = "storage");
    log.debug("hidden: the default level is info");

    log.set_level(log.Level.Debug, "storage");
    if (log.enabled(log.Level.Debug, "storage")) {
        log.debug("scanning", [log.field("path", "/var/data")], target = "storage");
    }

    # From here on, lines go to a file as JSON Lines.
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("logging-basics.log");
    var file = io.File.create(copy(path)).value();
    log.set_output(move(file), log.Format.Json);
    log.error("cannot connect", [log.field("attempt", 3)], target = "db");
    log.set_output(io.File.stderr());

    var text = io.File.read_to_string(path).value();
    assert(text.starts_with("{\"time\":"), "one JSON object per line");
    assert(text.contains("\"level\":\"error\",\"target\":\"db\",\"message\":\"cannot connect\""), "the line's keys");
    assert(text.contains("\"attempt\":3}"), "the field, as JSON");
    io.File.remove(path);
    return 0;
}

On standard error this prints:

2026-10-17T23:48:53.555Z INFO  started (logging-basics.pep:6:5)
2026-10-17T23:48:53.555Z WARN  [storage] disk almost full free_mb=120 (logging-basics.pep:7:5)
2026-10-17T23:48:53.555Z DEBUG [storage] scanning path="/var/data" (logging-basics.pep:12:9)
FunctionDoes
log.error(message), warning, info, debug, traceWrites a line at that Level.
log.field(key, value)Makes a Field for a line's fields; the value is written as JSON.
log.set_level(level, target)Sets the least important level shown, for one target or (with no target) for all.
log.enabled(level, target)Whether a line at level for target would be written.
log.set_output(writer, format)Sends lines to a Writer in Format.Text or Format.Json.

Lines

Each logging function takes the message, then two optional arguments, usually named:

  • fields: an array of log.field(key, value). A text line shows each as key=value, with the value's JSON text (200, "/var/data", true).
  • target: the part of the program the line is about, such as "http". A text line shows it in brackets, and levels can be set for it alone.

Each line names the place of the call, as assert does. The time is UTC, to the millisecond. On a terminal the level is in color, unless the NO_COLOR environment variable is set (on Windows, only in a console already in virtual terminal mode, such as Windows Terminal).

Levels

The levels, most important first, are Error, Warning, Info, Debug and Trace. A target shows its level and every level above it; Off shows nothing. By default every target shows Info.

The PEPPER_LOG environment variable sets the levels when the program first logs: comma-separated items, each a level for every target or target=level for one. The names are off, error, warning (or warn), info, debug and trace, in any case. An item with an unknown level is reported on standard error and skipped.

$ PEPPER_LOG=warning,http=debug ./server

log.set_level changes them from code. A target named in PEPPER_LOG or set_level uses its own level; every other target uses the global one.

Cost

A line no target shows costs two atomic loads: no lock and no formatting. The arguments are still evaluated, so a message or field that is costly to build goes inside an if (log.enabled(...)), as in the example.

Output and threads

Lines go to standard error as text until log.set_output names a Writer, such as a file or a socket, and a format:

  • Format.Text: the readable lines above.
  • Format.Json: one JSON object per line (JSON Lines) with time, level, target (when there is one), message and location, then each field.

The log keeps the writer, so it must be a new value or one handed over with move(x). A File keeps its path, so make it from copy(path), as the example does.

Each line is built first and then written whole, with one write_all, under a Mutex, so lines from many threads and tasks never interleave. A task waiting for that lock parks instead of blocking its worker thread. A failed write is ignored.

Not yet

  • Levels cannot be removed at compile time.
  • The runtime's own modules (such as http) and the pep-* tools do not log through log yet.

Dates, times and time zones

The time module turns instants into calendar dates and times of day, and back: dates and times with no zone, fixed offsets from UTC, time zones with daylight saving time, and the text forms of RFC 3339, ISO 8601, HTTP and C's strftime. Bring it in with import time. The full API is in the reference.

An instant itself is an os.SystemTime: nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. time says what date and time that is somewhere, and which instant a date and time names.

The calendar is the proleptic Gregorian calendar, which extends today's rules to years before it was adopted, and leap seconds are ignored, as Unix time, Go and Java ignore them: every day has 86400 seconds.

Dates and times of day

Four value types carry no time zone. Each is copied, compared with ==, < and the other comparisons, and never allocated.

  • Date is a year, a month (1 to 12) and a day. It knows its weekday(), day_of_year() and whether its year is_leap_year(), and moves with add_days, add_months and add_years. A month or year later keeps the day when it can and otherwise takes the month's last day, so a month after January 31 is February 28 or 29.
  • Time is an hour, minute, second and nanosecond within a day.
  • DateTime is a Date and a Time together: what TOML calls a local date-time. Adding or subtracting an os.Duration moves it.
  • Weekday is an enum, Monday to Sunday, whose values are ISO 8601's numbers, 1 to 7.
import os;
import time;

main(): int {
    # A Date is a day on the calendar, with no time of day or zone.
    var leap_day = time.Date(2024, 2, 29);
    assert(leap_day.weekday() == time.Weekday.Thursday, "2024-02-29 was a Thursday");
    assert(leap_day.day_of_year() == 60, "the 60th day of the year");
    assert(leap_day.add_years(1) == time.Date(2025, 2, 28), "no February 29 in 2025");
    assert(time.Date(2024, 1, 31).add_months(1) == leap_day, "the last day of February");
    assert(time.Date(2024, 12, 25).days_since(leap_day) == 300, "days between dates");

    # Parts from outside the program are checked, not trusted.
    assert(time.Date.checked(2023, 2, 29).is_empty(), "2023 is not a leap year");
    assert(time.Date.parse("2024-02-29").value() == leap_day, "ISO 8601 text");

    # A DateTime adds a time of day; durations move it.
    var start = time.DateTime(2024, 3, 1, 23, 30);
    var end = start + os.Duration.from_seconds(90 * 60);
    print(end);  # 2024-03-02T01:00:00
    assert(end.date == time.Date(2024, 3, 2) && end.time == time.Time(1, 0), "past midnight");
    assert(start < end, "date times compare");
    return 0;
}

The constructors (Date(2024, 2, 29)) panic on parts that name no date or time, which suits values written in the program. For parts that come from outside it, checked returns an optional instead, and parse a Result. Years run from -999999 to 999999, and year 0 is 1 BC.

Offsets and timestamps

Offset is a fixed offset from UTC, east positive: Offset.from_hours(5, 30) is +05:30. OffsetDateTime is a DateTime at an Offset, which names one instant: RFC 3339's timestamp and TOML's offset date-time.

import time;

main(): int {
    # An OffsetDateTime is an RFC 3339 timestamp: a date and time at an
    # offset from UTC, which together name one instant.
    var meeting = time.OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-03-01T09:00:00+01:00").value();
    print(meeting.to_utc());  # 2024-03-01T08:00:00Z
    assert(meeting.offset == time.Offset.from_hours(1), "the offset it was written at");

    # The same instant at two offsets is not ==, but compares as equal.
    var utc = meeting.to_utc();
    assert(utc != meeting && !(utc < meeting) && !(utc > meeting), "one instant");
    assert(utc.to_system_time() == meeting.to_system_time(), "one SystemTime");

    # strftime codes lay a date out any way.
    assert(meeting.format("%A %e %B %Y, %H:%M %:z") == "Friday  1 March 2024, 09:00 +01:00", "strftime");
    assert(meeting.format("%G-W%V-%u") == "2024-W09-5", "the ISO week date");

    # HTTP's Date and Last-Modified headers, both ways.
    var header = meeting.to_http_date();
    assert(header == "Fri, 01 Mar 2024 08:00:00 GMT", "an IMF-fixdate, in GMT");
    assert(time.OffsetDateTime.parse_http_date(header).value() == utc, "and back");
    return 0;
}
  • OffsetDateTime.from_system_time(t, offset) is the instant t at offset (UTC by default), and to_system_time() goes back. to_offset and to_utc show the same instant at another offset.
  • == compares the date, time and offset, so the same instant written at two offsets is not ==. <, <=, > and >= compare instants.
  • DateTime.from_system_time(t) and to_system_time() read a DateTime as UTC.

Text

Each type's to_string() writes ISO 8601, and its static parse reads it:

TypeText
Date2024-02-29; outside the years 0 to 9999, signed: -0001-12-31, +10000-01-01
Time08:30:00, with the fraction of a second when there is one: 08:30:00.25
DateTime2024-03-01T09:00:00
Offset+01:00; parse also takes Z, +0100 and +01
OffsetDateTime2024-03-01T09:00:00+01:00, Z for UTC

parse also reads what TOML allows: a space or t for the T, z for the Z, and a time without its seconds (09:00). Digits of a fraction past the nanosecond are dropped.

format(pattern) lays a value out with strftime's % codes, such as %Y-%m-%d, %A, %B and %H:%M; the module reference lists them all. Names are English whatever the locale. %z, %:z and %s need an offset, so only an OffsetDateTime takes them; an unknown code panics.

HTTP dates (RFC 9110) go both ways: to_http_date() writes the IMF-fixdate of Date and Last-Modified headers, Fri, 01 Mar 2024 08:00:00 GMT, and OffsetDateTime.parse_http_date reads it and the two obsolete forms servers must still accept, RFC 850's and C's asctime.

Time zones

A TimeZone gives the offset from UTC at each instant in one place:

  • TimeZone.utc(), and TimeZone.fixed(offset) for an offset that never changes.
  • TimeZone.local(), the system's zone: the TZ environment variable or /etc/localtime on Linux and macOS, as the C library's localtime reads them, and the zone in Windows' settings. WebAssembly has no local zone, so it is UTC there.
  • TimeZone.named("Europe/Paris"), a zone of the IANA time zone database, with its daylight saving time and history, or an error when the system does not know the name.

zone.offset_at(t) is the offset at the instant t, and zone.at(t) its date and time there. zone.at_local(date_time) goes the other way, from a date and time on the zone's clocks to the instant. Where the clocks go back, a time happens twice, and at_local picks the earlier; where they go forward, a time never happens, and it moves on by the length of the gap. time.now() is the current date and time in the local zone, and time.now_utc() in UTC.

import os;
import time;

main(): int {
    # The local zone and UTC are always there.
    var now = os.SystemTime.now();
    print($"here: {time.TimeZone.local().at(now)}");
    print($"UTC:  {time.now_utc()}");

    # Named zones come from the system's time zone database.
    var found = time.TimeZone.named("Europe/Paris");
    if (found is Ok(paris)) {
        var bastille = time.OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-07-14T10:00:00Z").value();
        assert(paris.at(bastille.to_system_time()).to_string() == "2024-07-14T12:00:00+02:00", "summer time");

        # A local time in the zone gets the offset in effect then.
        var christmas = paris.at_local(time.DateTime(2024, 12, 25, 18, 0));
        assert(christmas.offset == time.Offset.from_hours(1), "winter time");

        # 02:30 never happens on the night the clocks go forward: it moves
        # on by the hour that was skipped.
        var skipped = paris.at_local(time.DateTime(2024, 3, 31, 2, 30));
        assert(skipped.to_string() == "2024-03-31T03:30:00+02:00", "the gap");
    }
    assert(time.TimeZone.named("Nowhere/Atlantis").is_err(), "an unknown zone");
    return 0;
}

Nothing is bundled: named zones come from the system.

  • On Linux and macOS, the TZif files under /usr/share/zoneinfo, or the folder the TZDIR environment variable names. A minimal Linux container may have none until its tzdata package is installed. The rule at the end of each file covers instants after its last listed change.
  • On Windows, ICU (icu.dll, part of Windows 10 version 1903 and later), which knows the same names, or the TZif files in the folder TZDIR names when it is set.
  • On WebAssembly, TZif files under /usr/share/zoneinfo (or TZDIR) when the host lends the program that folder.

Current limitations

  • format writes text but nothing reads a strftime pattern back; parse ISO 8601, RFC 3339 and HTTP dates with the parse functions.
  • Names in format are English only, and there are no locale formats (%c, %x, %X) or zone abbreviations (%Z).
  • On Android, named zones are not found: its database is one packed file, not a folder of TZif files.

Encodings: text, base64 and UUIDs

Networked programs keep writing bytes as text and back: credentials in an HTTP header, a token in a URL, a value in a query string, an identifier in a database. Files, protocols and C libraries also hand over text in encodings other than UTF-8. These live in a few places:

WhatWhereFunctions
Text encodings (UTF-16, ASCII, ...)import texttext.Utf16.encode, text.Utf16.decode, ...
Base64import base64base64.encode, base64.decode
Hexadecimalimport digestdigest.to_hex, digest.from_hex
Percent-escapesUri, in the preludeUri.encode, Uri.decode
Form dataUri, in the preludeUri.encode_form, Uri.decode_form
UUIDsimport uuidUuid.v4, Uuid.v7, Uuid.parse, to_string
# Encodings: base64, hexadecimal, percent-escapes and form data, and UUIDs.
import base64;
import digest;
import uuid;

main(): int {
    # base64: an HTTP basic authentication header, and a URL-safe,
    # unpadded token as JSON Web Tokens write them.
    var credentials = base64.encode("ada:secret".bytes());
    assert(credentials == "YWRhOnNlY3JldA==", "standard, padded");
    var token = base64.encode([251, 255, 0], true, false);
    assert(token == "-_8A", "URL-safe, unpadded");
    assert(base64.decode(token, true).value()[0] == 251, "decoded");
    assert(base64.decode("not base64!").is_err(), "rejected");

    # Hexadecimal, both ways.
    assert(digest.from_hex(digest.to_hex([1, 171])).value()[1] == 171, "round trip");

    # Percent-escapes for one path segment or query value, and form data.
    assert(Uri.encode("a b&c") == "a%20b%26c", "escaped");
    var query = Uri.encode_form([("q", "pepper lang"), ("page", "2")]);
    assert(query == "q=pepper+lang&page=2", "form-encoded");
    var pairs = Uri.decode_form(query).value();
    assert(pairs[0].1 == "pepper lang", "decoded");

    # UUIDs: random (v4) and time-ordered (v7).
    var id = uuid.Uuid.v4();
    assert(uuid.Uuid.parse(id.to_string()).value() == id, "round trip");
    assert(uuid.Uuid.v7().version() == 7, "time-ordered");
    return 0;
}

Text encodings

A String always holds UTF-8. The text module converts text to and from the bytes of an encoding (u8[]), for files, network protocols and C libraries that use another one:

# Text in other encodings: encode a String to bytes, decode bytes back.
import text;

main(): int {
    var greeting = "héllo 🙂";

    # UTF-8 is what a String holds; decode checks the bytes.
    var utf8 = text.Utf8.encode(greeting);
    assert(utf8.count == 11, "é takes two bytes, 🙂 four");
    assert(text.Utf8.decode(utf8).value() == greeting, "round trip");

    # UTF-16: two bytes per unit, little-endian unless asked otherwise.
    var utf16 = text.Utf16.encode(greeting);
    assert(utf16.count == 16, "🙂 takes a surrogate pair");
    assert(text.Utf16.decode(utf16).value() == greeting, "round trip");

    # ASCII has no é: strict gives none, lossy writes '?'.
    assert(text.Ascii.encode(greeting).is_empty(), "not ASCII");
    assert(text.Ascii.encode_lossy("é").count == 1, "one '?'");

    # Code page 437, as old zip archives name entries: é is 0x82, and every
    # byte decodes, so decode gives a String.
    var dos = text.CodePage437.encode("café").value();
    assert(dos.count == 4 && dos[3] == 0x82, "one byte each");
    assert(text.CodePage437.decode(dos) == "café", "round trip");
    assert(text.CodePage437.encode(greeting).is_empty(), "no 🙂 in code page 437");

    # Strict decoding rejects invalid bytes; lossy decoding replaces them.
    var bad = Array<u8>();
    bad.append(104);
    bad.append(255);
    assert(text.Utf8.decode(bad).is_empty(), "0xFF is never UTF-8");
    assert(text.Utf8.decode_lossy(bad) == "h\u{FFFD}", "replaced");
    return 0;
}
TypeEncoding
text.Utf8UTF-8. encode copies the String's bytes; decode checks them. is_valid checks bytes without decoding, and find_invalid gives the offset of a String's first invalid byte. code_point_at reads one code point and append_code_point writes one.
text.Utf16UTF-16, two bytes per code unit, little-endian by default (encode(s, true) and decode(bytes, true) for big-endian). A code point past U+FFFF takes a surrogate pair.
text.AsciiASCII: code points below 128, one byte each. is_ascii checks a String.
text.CodePage437Code page 437, the IBM PC character set that old zip archives use for entry names: ASCII below 128, and one accented letter, Greek letter or box-drawing symbol for each byte above. Every byte decodes, so decode gives a String, not an Optional.
  • decode is strict: it gives Empty when the bytes are not valid in the encoding (a stray UTF-8 continuation byte, an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate, an odd UTF-16 byte count, an ASCII byte of 128 or more).
  • decode_lossy always succeeds: whatever is invalid becomes U+FFFD, the replacement character.
  • Ascii.encode gives Empty for text with a code point past 127, and CodePage437.encode for a character the code page lacks; encode_lossy writes ? for each instead.
  • No byte-order mark is written, and one that is read stays in the text.
  • io.File.read_string decodes with text.Utf8.decode, and an HTTP body's text() with decode_lossy.

The reference lists every function.

Base64

base64.encode(bytes) writes RFC 4648 base64 with the standard alphabet (A-Z a-z 0-9 + /) and = padding. Two optional arguments change that: url_safe = true uses - and _ in place of + and /, so the text can go in a URL or a file name, and padded = false leaves off the padding, as JSON Web Tokens do.

base64.decode(text) returns a Result<u8[]>. It accepts text with or without padding (pass url_safe = true for the other alphabet), and is strict otherwise: whitespace, a character outside the alphabet, a length no encoding gives, or unused bits that are not zero is an error. Remove line breaks from PEM or MIME text before decoding it. The functions work on whole arrays; there is no streaming encoder yet.

Hexadecimal

digest.to_hex(bytes) writes two lowercase digits per byte, and digest.from_hex(text) reads them back, in either case; an odd length or a character that is not a digit is an error.

Percent-escapes and form data

Uri.encode(text) escapes every byte outside RFC 3986's unreserved set (A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~), so the result is safe as one path segment or one query value: /, ?, &, = and % are escaped too. Uri.decode reverses it.

Uri.encode_form(pairs) writes names and values as application/x-www-form-urlencoded, the format of HTML forms and most query strings (q=pepper+lang&page=2), and Uri.decode_form(text) reads it back into an Array<(String, String)>, in order, keeping repeated names. In this format a space is +.

UUIDs

uuid.Uuid is a 128-bit identifier (RFC 9562), a value struct of two ulong halves, high and low, so == and hash work and it can key a map.

  • Uuid.v4() makes a random one: 122 bits from the operating system's secure source.
  • Uuid.v7() puts the wall clock's Unix time in milliseconds first, then 74 random bits, so ids made later sort later, both as values and as text. That keeps database indexes compact. Ids made in the same millisecond are in no particular order.
  • Uuid.parse(text) reads the usual form, 0190163d-8694-739b-aea5-966c26f8ad91, in either case, and to_string() (or interpolation) writes it in lowercase.
  • version() returns the version digit and bytes() the 16 bytes, for a database or a binary format.

The full API is in the reference: base64, uuid, hexadecimal and Uri.

Regular expressions

The regex module finds patterns in text: test whether text matches, find each match and its capture groups, and replace or split by a pattern.

# Regular expressions: match, capture, iterate, replace and split.
import regex;

main(): int {
    # Compile once, reuse. Backslashes are doubled inside a string literal.
    var date = regex.Regex("(?<year>\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})");
    assert(date.is_match("due 2026-10-01"), "a date somewhere");

    # The first match, with its groups. Positions are byte offsets.
    var found = date.find("due 2026-10-01").value();
    assert(found.text() == "2026-10-01" && found.start() == 4, "where");
    assert(found.group(2).value() == "10", "a numbered group");
    assert(found.group("year").value() == "2026", "a named group");

    # Every match, left to right.
    var total = 0;
    for (var number in regex.Regex("\\d+").find_all("1 22 333")) {
        total += int.parse(number.text()).value();
    }
    assert(total == 356, "1 + 22 + 333");

    # Replace with group references, and split.
    var swapped = regex.Regex("(\\w+)@(\\w+)").replace_all("ann@home bob@work", "$2:$1");
    assert(swapped == "home:ann work:bob", "groups swapped");
    var parts = regex.Regex("\\s*,\\s*").split("a , b,c");
    assert(parts.count == 3 && parts[1] == "b", "three pieces");

    # Flags go inside the pattern: (?i) ignores case.
    assert(regex.Regex("(?i)^hello").is_match("HeLLo there"), "any case");

    # An invalid pattern from outside the program: parse reports it.
    var bad = regex.Regex.parse("(unclosed");
    assert(bad.is_err(), "missing ')'");
    return 0;
}

Compiling a pattern

  • regex.Regex(pattern) compiles a pattern and panics when it is invalid. Use it for patterns written in the program.
  • regex.Regex.parse(pattern) returns a Result<Regex> instead, whose error names the problem and its byte offset: invalid regex '(a': missing ')' at offset 0. Use it for patterns that come from input.
  • Compile once and reuse the Regex; compiling costs more than a search.
  • Regex.escape(text) escapes every character with a meaning in a pattern, so the result matches text literally.

A pattern is a String, so each backslash is doubled in a string literal: "\\d+" is the pattern \d+.

Searching

MethodResult
is_match(text)whether there is a match anywhere; the fastest test
find(text)the leftmost Match, or Empty
find_at(text, start)the leftmost match starting at or after byte start
find_all(text)an iterator over every match, left to right, without overlaps
replace(text, replacement)text with the first match replaced
replace_all(text, replacement)text with every match replaced
split(text)the pieces of text between matches

A Match has text(), start() and end() (byte offsets, as String.find returns, for use with substr_bytes), and group(index) or group(name), which give the group's text or Empty when the group did not take part (as (a) in (a)|b matching b). Group 0 is the whole match; groups are numbered by their opening (. group_range(index) gives a group's offsets.

Matching is leftmost-first, as in Perl: the match that starts earliest wins, and among those, a greedy repetition prefers more and alternation prefers its earlier branch (a|ab finds a in ab).

find_all skips an empty match that comes right after the previous match, so a* finds a twice in aba, not also an empty match between them.

In a replacement, $1 or ${1} stands for group 1, ${name} for a named group, $0 for the whole match and $$ for a $. A group that did not take part gives empty text. Use braces when a digit or letter follows: ${1}0, not $10.

Syntax

The syntax is RE2's, the one Go's regexp and Rust's regex crate use.

SyntaxMatches
.any code point except a newline (any at all with (?s))
[abc], [a-z], [^a-z]a code point in, or not in, the set
[[:alpha:]], [[:^digit:]]a POSIX class: alnum, alpha, ascii, blank, cntrl, digit, graph, lower, print, punct, space, upper, word, xdigit
\d, \w, \san ASCII digit, word character ([0-9A-Za-z_]), or space ([\t\n\f\r ])
\D, \W, \Sanything else
\n, \t, \r, \f, \v, \aa control character
\x41, \x{1F642}the code point with that hexadecimal value
\., \*, \\, ...the punctuation character itself
x*, x+, x?zero or more, one or more, zero or one
x{n}, x{n,}, x{n,m}exactly n, at least n, from n to m (at most 1000)
x*?, x+?, x??, x{n,m}?the same, preferring fewer (lazy)
xy, x|yx then y; x or y
(x)a capture group
(?<name>x), (?P<name>x)a named capture group
(?:x)a group that does not capture
^, $the start and end of the text (of a line with (?m))
\A, \zthe start and end of the text, always
\b, \Ban ASCII word boundary, and anything else

Flags go in the pattern: (?i) makes the rest of the enclosing group case-insensitive, (?i:x) only x, and (?-i) turns a flag off.

FlagMeaning
icase-insensitive (ASCII letters)
mmulti-line: ^ and $ also match at line breaks
s. also matches a newline
Uswap greedy and lazy: x* is lazy and x*? greedy

Text

  • A pattern works on code points: . and [^a] match one whole code point, such as é or 🙂, never part of one.
  • \d, \w, \s, \b, the POSIX classes and case-insensitive matching are ASCII-only: \w does not match é.
  • Positions are byte offsets, like String.find and substr_bytes, not the code point positions of substr.

Linear time

Matching never backtracks. The engine (a Pike VM, as in RE2) steps every possible match through the text together, so a search takes time proportional to the size of the text times the size of the pattern, whatever both are. A pattern such as (a*)*b, which takes exponential time in a backtracking engine, is safe on untrusted input.

The price is two features that need backtracking. A pattern that uses one fails to compile:

  • Backreferences (\1): backreferences are not supported
  • Lookaround ((?=x), (?!x), (?<=x), (?<!x)): lookaround is not supported

Groups nest at most 250 deep, and a pattern whose compiled program would exceed 100,000 instructions (from large counted repetitions such as (a{1000}){1000}) is rejected.

Threads

A Regex never changes once it is compiled, and it is [Shared]: one Regex can serve every thread at once, so a pattern the program uses often can be compiled once at module scope:

import regex;

const identifier = regex.Regex("^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$");

is_identifier(text: String): bool {
    return identifier.is_match(text);
}

Each search keeps its working state to itself, and a Match (which holds the searched String) stays on the thread that found it.

The reference lists every method.

JSON

The json module reads JSON text into a JsonValue, lets you look values up and change them, and writes them back as compact or indented text. It also converts structs to JSON and back.

# JSON: parse text, look values up, change them, and write them back.
import json;

main(): int {
    var text = "{\"name\": \"pepper\", \"server\": {\"port\": 8080}, \"tags\": [\"fast\"]}";
    var parsed = json.parse(text, path = "config.json");
    if (parsed.is_err()) {
        print(parsed.error().to_string());   # config.json:1:17: error: ...
        return 1;
    }
    var root = parsed.value();

    # Lookups chain, and a missing key gives Null instead of panicking.
    assert(root["name"].as_string().value() == "pepper", "a string");
    assert(root["server"]["port"].as_int().value_or(80) == 8080, "a number");
    assert(root["server"]["host"].as_string().value_or("localhost") == "localhost", "a default");

    # Match on the case to handle every kind.
    var described = match (root["tags"]) {
        Array(items) => $"{items.count} tag",
        Null => "no tags",
        else => "not a list",
    };
    assert(described == "1 tag", "an array");

    # Change the value in place, then write it back. Keys keep their order.
    root["tags"].append(json.JsonValue.String("safe"));
    root["debug"] = json.JsonValue.Bool(false);
    assert(root.to_string() == "{\"name\":\"pepper\",\"server\":{\"port\":8080},\"tags\":[\"fast\",\"safe\"],\"debug\":false}", "compact");

    # Build a value from scratch.
    var reply = json.JsonValue.object();
    reply["id"] = json.JsonValue.Integer(42);
    reply["ok"] = json.JsonValue.Bool(true);
    assert(reply.to_pretty_string() == "{\n  \"id\": 42,\n  \"ok\": true\n}", "indented");

    # An error names the line and column.
    var bad = json.parse("{\n  \"a\": 1\n  \"b\": 2\n}", path = "bad.json");
    assert(bad.error().to_string() == "bad.json:3:3: error: expected ',' or '}'", "where");

    # JSONC: comments and trailing commas, on request.
    var settings = json.parse("{\n  // the theme\n  \"theme\": \"dark\",\n}", comments = true);
    assert(settings.value()["theme"].as_string().value() == "dark", "JSONC");
    return 0;
}

Values

json.JsonValue is an enum whose cases carry values, so match handles each kind:

CaseHoldsJSON
Nullnothingnull
Bool(value: bool)the booleantrue, false
Integer(value: long)an integer within ±(2^53 − 1)42, -7
Number(value: double)any other number2.5, 1e3, 9007199254740993
String(value: String)the string"hi"
Array(items: Array<JsonValue>)the elements[1, 2]
Object(members: OrderedMap<String, JsonValue>)the members, in insertion order{"a": 1}
  • Numbers keep their form. A number written without a fraction or an exponent is an Integer when it is within ±(2^53 − 1), the range every JSON implementation agrees on (RFC 7493). Any other number, including a larger integer, is a Number.
  • Make values with the cases (JsonValue.Integer(42), JsonValue.String("a"), JsonValue.Null), and containers with JsonValue.object() and JsonValue.array(items).
  • Containers are shared. An Array or Object holds its array or map by reference, so changing it through value[key] = ..., append, or the map from as_object() changes every holder of the value.

Looking values up

ExpressionResult
value["key"]the member, or Null when missing or not an object
value[index]the element, or Null when out of range or not an array
value.as_string(), as_bool(), as_double()the value, or Empty for another kind
value.as_int()an Integer, or a Number with no fraction that fits in a long; otherwise Empty
value.as_array(), as_object()the array or map itself, or Empty
value.is_null()whether it is Null
value.contains("key")whether an object has the member, even a null one

A lookup that finds nothing gives Null rather than panicking, so lookups chain and a default goes at the end: root["server"]["port"].as_int().value_or(8080).

Changing values

  • value["key"] = member sets an object's member. A new key goes at the end; an existing key keeps its place. It panics on a value that is not an object.
  • value[index] = element replaces an array's element, and value.append(element) adds one at the end. Both panic on a value that is not an array.
  • value.remove("key") removes an object's member and says whether it was there.

Parsing

json.parse(text) returns a Result<JsonValue, JsonError>. It is strict RFC 8259:

  • The text holds one value, with only spaces, tabs and line breaks around it. A byte-order mark at the start is skipped.
  • The text must be valid UTF-8; an invalid byte is an error at that byte.
  • A string cannot hold a raw control character (write \n), and a \u escape of an unpaired surrogate ("\uD800") is an error.
  • No comments, trailing commas, single quotes, NaN, leading zeros (01) or + signs.
  • When an object repeats a key, the last value wins, in the place of the first.

parse takes optional arguments, usually passed by name:

ArgumentDefaultMeaning
commentsfalseAccept JSONC, as VS Code's settings files are: // and /* */ comments, and a comma after the last element or member.
path""The name of the text, which the error's to_string() puts first.
max_depth1000How deeply arrays and objects may nest.

The parser keeps its own stack rather than recursing, so deep nesting in the text cannot overflow the call stack. max_depth still bounds it, because releasing a value releases its nested values recursively. Raise it with care: Windows gives a program's main thread a 1 MB stack, which a few thousand levels of nested objects can use up when the value is released.

Errors

A JsonError has the message, the line and column (from 1, counting bytes) and the byte offset. to_string() renders it like a compiler error:

config.json:3:3: error: expected ',' or '}'

Without a path, it starts at the line: 3:3: error: expected ',' or '}'.

Writing

  • value.to_string() writes compact text, with no spaces or line breaks: {"id":42,"tags":["a","b"]}. String interpolation uses it too.
  • value.to_pretty_string() puts each element and member on its own line, indented two spaces per level (to_pretty_string(indent = 4) for four), with a space after each :. An empty array or object stays [] or {}.
  • Strings are written as UTF-8, escaping ", \ and the control characters. to_string(ascii_only = true) and to_pretty_string(ascii_only = true) also escape everything outside ASCII as \u, with a surrogate pair past U+FFFF.
  • A Number is written as Pepper writes a double (0.5, 1000.0, 1e+16), so it reads back as a Number. NaN and the infinities, which JSON cannot spell, are written as null.
  • Objects keep their keys in insertion order, so parsing a document and writing it back keeps its order.

Documents with comments

parse skips a JSONC file's comments. To change a file people edit, such as a settings file, and write it back with its comments, read it with json.parse_document(text), which returns a Result<JsonDocument, JsonError>:

# JSON: change a JSONC settings file and write it back with its comments.
import json;

main(): int {
    var text = "{\n  // Spaces per level.\n  \"tab_size\": 4,\n  \"font\": \"Mono\", // the editor's\n  \"wrap\": true\n}";
    var parsed = json.parse_document(text, path = "settings.json");
    if (parsed.is_err()) {
        print(parsed.error().to_string());
        return 1;
    }
    var document = parsed.value();
    assert(document.to_string() == text, "unchanged text comes back as it was");

    # Change the value; each comment stays with its value.
    document.root["tab_size"] = json.JsonValue.Integer(2);
    document.set_comments("$.wrap", ["// Wrap long lines."]);
    assert(document.comments("$.tab_size")[0] == "// Spaces per level.", "by path");
    print(document.to_string());
    # {
    #   // Spaces per level.
    #   "tab_size": 2,
    #   "font": "Mono", // the editor's
    #   // Wrap long lines.
    #   "wrap": true
    # }
    return 0;
}

# Output:
# {
#   // Spaces per level.
#   "tab_size": 2,
#   "font": "Mono", // the editor's
#   // Wrap long lines.
#   "wrap": true
# }
  • document.root is the JsonValue; change it as any other.
  • Each comment belongs to a value, by its path from the root $ ($.editor.tab_size, $.files[0]): the comments on the lines before it, and those on the line it ends, after its comma. Comments before a closing bracket stay at the end of their array or object, and those around the whole value stay before or after it.
  • document.to_string() writes the text indented, as to_pretty_string does (to_string(indent = 4) for four spaces), with every comment back in its place. A file in that layout reads and writes back unchanged.
  • A comment whose value is removed is dropped. One whose path later names another value, such as an element shifted into its index, goes with that value.
  • document.comments(path) returns the comments before a value, and document.set_comments(path, ["// ..."]) replaces them.
  • parse_document takes path and max_depth as parse does, and always accepts JSONC.

Structs

json.encode(value) writes a struct as JSON text, and json.decode<T>(text) reads one back. There is no code to write per type: both walk the struct's properties with reflection while compiling, so the conversion costs what hand-written code would.

# JSON: convert structs to JSON text and back, through reflection.
import json;

enum Mode {
    Fast,
    Safe,
}

struct Tls {
    var cert: String;
}

struct ServerConfig {
    var host: String;
    [Required]
    var port: int;
    # The key is "max-connections", not the property's name.
    [Name("max-connections")]
    var max_connections: int;
    # Never written or read.
    [Ignore]
    var started_at: long;
    # `null` or missing when none.
    var tls: Tls?;
    var mode: Mode;
    var tags: Array<String>;
}

main(): int {
    var config = ServerConfig();
    config.host = "localhost";
    config.port = 8080;
    config.max_connections = 64;
    config.mode = Mode.Safe;
    config.tags = ["web"];
    var text = json.encode(config);
    assert(
        text == "{\"host\":\"localhost\",\"port\":8080,\"max-connections\":64,\"tls\":null,\"mode\":\"Safe\",\"tags\":[\"web\"]}",
        "properties in declaration order"
    );

    var decoded = json.decode<ServerConfig>("{\"port\": 443, \"tls\": {\"cert\": \"site.pem\"}}");
    if (decoded.is_err()) {
        print(decoded.error().to_string());
        return 1;
    }
    var back = decoded.value();
    assert(back.port == 443, "a number");
    assert(back.tls.value().cert == "site.pem", "a nested struct");
    assert(back.mode == Mode.Fast, "a missing key keeps its default");

    # An error names where in the document it is, by path, line and column.
    var bad = json.decode<ServerConfig>("{\"port\": 443, \"mode\": \"Slow\"}", path = "server.json");
    assert(bad.error().to_string() == "server.json:1:23: error: $.mode: 'Slow' is not a case of 'Mode'", "a path");
    var missing = json.decode<ServerConfig>("{}");
    assert(missing.error().to_string() == "1:1: error: $: missing required key 'port'", "[Required]");
    return 0;
}

A struct's public properties become an object's members, in declaration order. Each property's type converts as follows, and the same rules apply at the top level (json.decode<Array<int>>("[1, 2]")):

PepperJSON
an integer type (int, u8, long, ...)a number; reading one checks that it has no fraction and fits the type
float, doublea number
booltrue, false
Stringa string
an enuma case that carries no values as its name ("Safe"); one that carries values as an object with the case's name as its one key, holding the values by name ({"Circle": {"radius": 2}}); attributes choose other forms
T?the value, or null when Empty; a missing key reads as Empty
Array<T>an array
HashMap<String, V>, OrderedMap<String, V>, Map<String, V>an object
a structan object, recursively
json.JsonValueitself, for parts of a document with no fixed shape

A struct reference that holds nothing (a String, array, struct or reference enum field never assigned) is written as null, and null reads back as one, so a value round-trips. Reading a case's value whose key is missing is an error: $.shapes[0].Circle: missing value 'radius'. null for a number, bool or enum is an error.

Attributes

The serialize module's attributes, which json uses (they need no import of their own), change how a property is converted:

AttributeEffect
[Name("key")]writes and reads the property under key
[Ignore]leaves the property out of both
[Required]makes a missing key an error when reading

On an enum and its cases, they choose how a case is written:

AttributeEffect
[Name("key")] on a casewrites and reads the case under key instead of its own name
[Tag("kind")] on an enumwrites each case as an object naming it under kind, with its values beside the tag: {"kind": "Circle", "radius": 2}, {"kind": "Point"}
[Tag("kind", content = "data")] on an enumputs the values in an object under data instead: {"kind": "Circle", "data": {"radius": 2}}
[Untagged] on an enumwrites no tag: a case's values as an object ({"radius": 2}), and a case that carries none as its name ("Point")
# JSON: choose how an enum's cases are written with attributes.
import json;

# A tag beside the values: {"kind": "circle", "radius": 2}.
[Tag("kind")]
enum Shape {
    [Name("circle")]
    Circle(radius: int),
    Point,
}

# The values under their own key: {"type": "Click", "data": {"x": 1, "y": 2}}.
[Tag("type", content = "data")]
enum Event {
    Click(x: int, y: int),
    Close,
}

# No tag; reading takes the first case that fits.
[Untagged]
enum Size {
    Fixed(px: int),
    Auto,
}

main(): int {
    assert(json.encode(Shape.Circle(2)) == "{\"kind\":\"circle\",\"radius\":2}", "internally tagged");
    assert(json.encode(Shape.Point) == "{\"kind\":\"Point\"}", "a case with no values");
    assert(json.encode(Event.Click(1, 2)) == "{\"type\":\"Click\",\"data\":{\"x\":1,\"y\":2}}", "adjacently tagged");
    assert(json.encode(Size.Fixed(8)) == "{\"px\":8}", "untagged");
    assert(json.encode(Size.Auto) == "\"Auto\"", "untagged, no values");

    var shape = json.decode<Shape>("{\"kind\": \"circle\", \"radius\": 5}");
    if (shape.value() is Circle(radius)) {
        assert(radius == 5, "read back");
    } else {
        return 1;
    }
    var size = json.decode<Size>("\"Auto\"");
    assert(size.value() is Auto, "the first case that fits");
    var bad = json.decode<Shape>("{\"radius\": 5}");
    assert(bad.error().to_string() == "1:1: error: $: missing tag 'kind'", "a missing tag");
    return 0;
}

Reading an [Untagged] enum tries each case in order and takes the first that reads without an error (with UnknownKeys.Reject, an extra key is an error too), so a case whose values include another's goes first. When none reads, the error says so: $: found an object, which matches no case of 'Size'. A [Tag] enum's errors name its tag: $: missing tag 'kind', $.kind: 'Hex' is not a case of 'Shape'. A tag with the name of one of a case's values is a compile error, since both would be written under one key.

Reading

decode makes a struct with its constructor that takes no arguments, then reads in each property it finds a key for. A missing key leaves its property at its default, unless the property is [Required]. It takes optional arguments, usually passed by name:

ArgumentDefaultMeaning
unknown_keysUnknownKeys.IgnoreWhat to do with a key that names no property: skip it, or with UnknownKeys.Reject, fail naming it.
commentsfalseAccept JSONC, as parse does.
path""The name of the text, which the error's to_string() puts first.

An error has a line and column as in Errors. One in converting a value also has its value_path, where in the document the value is as a path from the root $, and its message starts with that path. The line and column are the value's, or the enclosing object's for a missing key:

server.json:3:13: error: $.server.port: expected a number, found a string
server.json:7:21: error: $.tags[2]: expected a string, found null
server.json:4:24: error: $["max-connections"]: 70000 does not fit in 'u16'
server.json:1:1: error: $: missing required key 'port'

json.to_json(value) and json.from_json<T>(value) do the same conversions to and from a JsonValue rather than text (with no text, a from_json error has no line: error: $.port: ...), and json.encode(value, indent = 2) writes indented text.

Types it cannot convert

A property whose type has no JSON form, such as a pointer, a function, or a Result (a result is not a value to send over the wire), is a compile error naming the property. Notes follow the conversion back to the call that asked for it:

runtime/json/convert.pep:358:25: error: 'encode' cannot convert property 'outcome' of type 'Result<int>' to JSON
...
main.pep:10:16: note: 'encode<Job>' is used by 'main' here
   10 |     var text = json.encode(job);
      |                ^~~~~~~~~~~

Current limits

  • parse skips comments; only a JsonDocument keeps them, and decode never does. A document is always written indented.
  • A struct's own conversion cannot be customized yet: a type converts as its properties do.
  • Map keys must be Strings.

The reference lists every function.

TOML

The toml module reads TOML 1.0 into a TomlValue, lets you look values up and change them, writes tables back as documents, edits a document in place without disturbing its comments, and converts structs to TOML and back. The package manager reads and edits pep.toml and pep.lock with it.

# TOML: parse a document, look values up, edit it in place keeping its
# comments, and read it into a struct.
import toml;

struct Package {
    [Required]
    var name: String;
    var version: String;
}

struct Manifest {
    [Required]
    var package: Package;
}

main(): int {
    var text = "[package]\nname = \"demo\"  # the name\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\n";
    var parsed = toml.parse(text, path = "pep.toml");
    if (parsed.is_err()) {
        print(parsed.error().to_string());   # pep.toml:2:6: error: ...
        return 1;
    }
    var root = parsed.value();
    assert(root["package"]["name"].as_string().value() == "demo", "a string");
    assert(root.lookup("package.version").value().as_string().value() == "0.1.0", "a dotted lookup");
    assert(root.try_get("dependencies").is_empty(), "a missing key");

    # Change a value, then write the tables back as a document.
    var package = root["package"];
    package["edition"] = toml.TomlValue.Integer(2026);
    assert(root.to_document() == "[package]\nname = \"demo\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nedition = 2026\n", "a document");

    # Edit the text in place: comments and layout stay as written.
    var document = toml.parse_document(text, path = "pep.toml").value();
    document.set(["dependencies", "yaml"], toml.TomlValue.String("0.3")).value();
    assert(
        document.to_string() == "[package]\nname = \"demo\"  # the name\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\n\n[dependencies]\nyaml = \"0.3\"\n",
        "an edit"
    );

    # Read it into a struct, with the serialize attributes json uses.
    Manifest manifest = toml.decode<Manifest>(text).value();
    assert(manifest.package.version == "0.1.0", "a struct");

    # An error names the line and column.
    var bad = toml.parse("name \"demo\"\n", path = "bad.toml");
    assert(bad.error().to_string() == "bad.toml:1:6: error: expected '=' after the key", "where");
    return 0;
}

Values

toml.TomlValue is an enum whose cases carry values:

CaseHoldsTOML
String(value: String)the string"hi", 'C:\path', """..."""
Integer(value: long)a 64-bit integer42, 0xff, 1_000
Float(value: double)a float, inf and nan included0.5, 1e10, inf
