Boolean(value: bool)the booleantrue, false
DateTime(value: TomlDateTime)a date, a time, or both1979-05-27T07:32:00Z, 1979-05-27, 07:32:00
Array(items: Array<TomlValue>)the elements[1, "two"]
Table(members: OrderedMap<String, TomlValue>)the keys, in the order written[server], { x = 1 }
  • Look values up with value["key"] and value[index], which panic on a miss, or try_get("key") and lookup("package.name"), which give an empty Optional. The as_ methods (as_string, as_int, as_float, as_bool, as_date_time, as_array, as_table) give an empty Optional for another kind; as_float also reads an integer.
  • Write a value on one line with to_string() (as after a key's =), or a table as a whole document with to_document().
  • There is no null. What json writes as null is left out, and a missing key reads as the property's default.

Errors

toml.parse(text, path = "pep.toml") checks every rule of TOML 1.0 and gives a TomlError that renders like a compiler error: pep.toml:4:12: error: expected '=' after the key. Arrays and inline tables may nest max_depth deep (1000 by default); parsing and writing use explicit stacks, so deep nesting never overflows the stack. The module passes all 709 TOML 1.0 cases of toml-test, which its tests run.

Editing a document in place

toml.parse_document(text) gives a TomlDocument, whose set(keys, value) and remove(keys) change only the lines they must, keeping every comment and blank line, the way cargo add edits Cargo.toml. A changed value is rewritten on one line; a new key goes after the last key of its table, indented like it; a new table goes at the end as a [header] section, or as { ... } with inline = true. Edits cannot reach inside an array of tables ([[bin]]); set or remove the whole array.

Structs

toml.encode(value) and toml.decode<T>(text) (and to_toml and from_toml, which work on a TomlValue) convert structs through reflection, with the serialize attributes JSON uses: [Name("key")], [Ignore] and [Required]. unknown_keys = toml.UnknownKeys.Reject makes an unknown key an error. See the reference for every function.

YAML

YAML 1.2 is read and written by the yaml package, which has the same shape as the json and toml modules: a YamlValue to look values up in and change, clang-style errors at the line and column, documents that keep their comments when edited, and struct conversion with the serialize attributes. It is a package rather than part of the runtime because few programs need YAML; add it with pepper package add pep-lang/pepper-yaml --name yaml.

import yaml;

main(): int {
    var parsed = yaml.parse("server:\n  port: 8080\n  debug: no\n", path = "config.yaml");
    if (parsed.is_err()) {
        print(parsed.error().to_string());
        return 1;
    }
    var root = parsed.value();
    print(root["server"]["port"].as_int().value());       # 8080
    print(root["server"]["debug"].as_string().value());   # no
    root["server"]["port"] = yaml.YamlValue.Integer(9090);
    print(root.to_string());
    return 0;
}
  • The core schema: yes, no, on and off are strings, not booleans, so NO (Norway) stays NO.
  • Safe for untrusted text: only the core schema's tags (!!str, !!int, ...) are read, and any other tag is an error; aliases may not stand for more than max_alias_nodes nodes, which stops the "billion laughs" attack.
  • Merge keys: yaml.parse(text, merge_keys = true) applies YAML 1.1's << (<<: *defaults), which CI and compose files use to reuse a mapping; the mapping's own keys win, and merged nodes count toward max_alias_nodes. By default << is an ordinary key, as YAML 1.2 says.
  • Several documents in one stream (---) are read by yaml.parse_all and written by yaml.write_all.
  • yaml.parse_document keeps comments, key order, flow or block style and scalar styles through edits, as json.parse_document keeps a JSONC file's comments.
  • yaml.encode and yaml.decode<T> convert structs exactly as json.encode and json.decode do.

The package's README lists what it reads and its limits: a mapping's keys are strings, and there is no streaming reader yet.

Compression and archives

The compress module compresses and decompresses DEFLATE data, plain or in its zlib and gzip framings, and the archive module reads and writes tar archives. Together they handle .gz and .tar.gz files. Both are written in Pepper, so a program that uses them links no extra library, unless it is built to use zlib (see Using zlib).

# Compress and decompress bytes in one call, or as streams.
import compress;
import io;

main(): int {
    var text = "the cat sat on the mat; ".repeat(100).bytes();

    # gzip, zlib and raw DEFLATE each have compress and decompress.
    var packed = compress.Gzip.compress(text);
    assert(packed.count < text.count / 10, "repetitive text shrinks");
    assert(compress.Gzip.decompress(packed).value() == text, "round trip");

    # Level 0 stores, 9 squeezes hardest; 6 is the default.
    var fast = compress.Zlib.compress(text, level = 1);
    assert(compress.Zlib.decompress(fast).value() == text, "any level reads back");

    # Corrupt data is an error, never a crash.
    packed[packed.count - 5] = packed[packed.count - 5] ^ 1;
    var bad = compress.Gzip.decompress(packed);
    assert(bad.is_err() && bad.error().is_invalid_input(), "the CRC-32 check fails");

    # Streams: a CompressWriter wraps any io.Writer, a DecompressReader any
    # io.Reader, such as a File. Here both are in memory.
    var sink = io.ByteWriter();
    var writer = compress.CompressWriter(sink, compress.Format.Gzip);
    writer.print_line("first line");
    writer.print_line("second line");
    writer.finish();

    var reader = compress.DecompressReader(io.ByteReader(sink.bytes), compress.Format.Gzip);
    var lines = 0;
    for (var line in reader.lines()) {
        lines += 1;
    }
    assert(lines == 2, "two lines");

    # The checksums are there on their own too.
    assert(compress.Crc32.of("123456789".bytes()) == 0xCBF43926, "CRC-32");
    return 0;
}

Formats

FormatStructWhere it is used
Format.Gzipcompress.Gzip.gz files, HTTP Content-Encoding: gzip
Format.Zlibcompress.ZlibPNG images, HTTP deflate
Format.Rawcompress.Deflatezip entries, other containers with their own framing
  • compress(data, level = 6) returns the compressed bytes. The level runs from 0 (stored, no compression) to 9 (smallest, slowest). Each level searches for matches with zlib's settings for it, so the output is about the size zlib makes at the same level, at a similar speed: on 12 MB of source text, compressing at level 6 takes about 1.2 times as long as the gzip command, and decompressing is a little faster than gzip -d.
  • decompress(data) returns an io.IoResult<u8[]>. Damaged or truncated data is an error whose is_invalid_input() holds, and gzip and zlib data is checked against its CRC-32 or Adler-32 checksum.
  • Gzip input may hold several members one after another (cat a.gz b.gz); they decompress to their contents joined. Bytes after the last member are an error. A gzip header's file name and comment are skipped, and a written header has neither.
  • A zlib stream made with a preset dictionary needs it to decompress; see Preset dictionaries.
  • decompress puts everything in memory. Use a DecompressReader for input from outside the program, so a small file that expands hugely cannot exhaust memory.

compress.Crc32 and compress.Adler32 compute the two checksums over data given in pieces (update, then value), or in one call with of.

Streams

compress.DecompressReader(source, format) is an io.Reader that decompresses source, any io.Reader, as it is read, so lines(), chunks(size) and read_all() work on it. It holds at most about 225 KiB of input and output, however large the data.

compress.CompressWriter(sink, format, level = 6) is an io.Writer that compresses what is written and writes the result to sink. Call finish() at the end: it writes the last block and the checksum. Dropping the writer does not finish it, and finish() does not close the sink.

io.ByteReader(bytes) and io.ByteWriter() stand in for a stream when the data is in memory.

Preset dictionaries

A short message compresses poorly, since the stream has no earlier bytes to refer back to. A preset dictionary gives it some: bytes that both sides agree on beforehand, such as the keys and common values of a JSON protocol, which the compressed data can then copy from as if they came just before it.

# Compress small messages against a preset dictionary of what they share.
import compress;

main(): int {
    # Short messages with the same keys compress poorly on their own: the
    # stream has no earlier bytes to refer back to.
    var dictionary = "{\"user\": \"\", \"action\": \"login\", \"status\": \"ok\"}".bytes();
    var message = "{\"user\": \"ada\", \"action\": \"login\", \"status\": \"ok\"}".bytes();

    var plain = compress.Zlib.compress(message);
    var primed = compress.Zlib.compress(message, dictionary);
    assert(primed.count < plain.count, "the dictionary supplies the repeated text");

    # Decompressing needs the same dictionary; the stream names it by its
    # Adler-32, so a missing or different one is an error.
    assert(compress.Zlib.decompress(primed, dictionary).value() == message, "round trip");
    assert(compress.Zlib.decompress(primed).is_err(), "no dictionary given");
    print($"{plain.count} bytes alone, {primed.count} with the dictionary");
    return 0;
}
  • Zlib.compress(data, dictionary, level = 6) and Zlib.decompress(data, dictionary) take one. The zlib header names the dictionary by its Adler-32, so decompress without one, or with a different one, is an is_invalid_input() error. A stream made without a dictionary decompresses as usual when one is given.
  • CompressWriter(sink, format, dictionary, level = 6) and DecompressReader(source, format, dictionary) take one for Format.Zlib or Format.Raw. Raw DEFLATE data carries no sign of it, so both sides must know to use it. Gzip has no dictionary, and asking for one panics.
  • Only the last 32 KiB of a dictionary can be referred to, since that is how far back DEFLATE reaches; put the most common text at its end.

Using zlib

Building with -D USE_ZLIB (see Build options) makes compress use zlib, the reference DEFLATE library, for compressing, decompressing, CRC-32 and Adler-32, in place of its Pepper code:

pep-build main.pep -D USE_ZLIB -o app
  • The API is the same, and so are the errors for damaged data, worded as the Pepper code words them where zlib tells the causes apart. Compressed output can differ byte for byte (zlib's gzip header names the operating system), but each side decompresses the other's.
  • Linux links -lz, from the development package (zlib1g-dev, zlib-devel). macOS has zlib already. Windows has none: install it (vcpkg install zlib) and name the folder holding zlib.lib with -L or PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH.
  • zlib compresses faster than the Pepper code at the same level, and makes output of about the same size.

Tar archives

# Write a .tar.gz, list it, and extract it.
import archive;
import compress;
import io;

main(): int {
    var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-compression-tar-example");
    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-compression-tar-example.tar.gz");

    # A TarWriter over a gzip CompressWriter over a File.
    var file = io.File.create(path).value();
    var gzip = compress.CompressWriter(file, compress.Format.Gzip);
    var tar = archive.TarWriter(gzip);
    tar.append_directory("app-1.0");
    tar.append_file("app-1.0/main.pep", "main(): int { return 0; }\n".bytes());
    tar.append_file("app-1.0/run.sh", "#!/bin/sh\n".bytes(), mode = 493);
    tar.finish();
    gzip.finish();
    file.close();

    # List the entries.
    var reader = archive.TarReader(compress.DecompressReader(io.File.open(path).value(), compress.Format.Gzip));
    var names = Array<String>();
    while (true) {
        var entry = reader.next_entry().value();
        if (entry.is_empty()) {
            break;
        }
        names.append(entry.value().path);
    }
    assert(names.count == 3 && names[0] == "app-1.0/", "a directory ends with '/'");

    # Extract without the top directory.
    reader = archive.TarReader(compress.DecompressReader(io.File.open(path).value(), compress.Format.Gzip));
    reader.extract(folder, strip_components = 1).value();
    assert(io.File.read_to_string(folder.join("main.pep")).value().starts_with("main"), "extracted");

    io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
    io.File.remove(path);
    return 0;
}

archive.TarReader(source) reads an archive from any io.Reader; wrap the file in a DecompressReader to read a .tar.gz.

  • next_entry() moves to the next entry and returns its TarEntry: path, kind (File, Directory, Symlink, HardLink or Other), size, mode, modified (seconds since 1970) and link_target. It returns Empty at the end of the archive.
  • The reader is an io.Reader of the current entry's contents: read, read_all(), lines(). Contents not read are skipped.
  • It reads ustar archives with the pax and GNU extensions for long paths, which covers GNU tar, bsdtar, and the .tar.gz snapshots that git archive, GitHub, GitLab and Codeberg make.

extract(target, strip_components = 0) writes the rest of the archive into the directory target:

  • It refuses, with an is_invalid_input() error, an entry whose path is absolute or holds a .. component, a \ or a :, so an archive cannot write outside target. archive.safe_components(path) is that check, for readers of other formats: it gives the path's components, or Empty for an unsafe path.
  • strip_components drops leading path components, as tar's --strip-components does. A GitHub snapshot puts everything under name-version/, which strip_components = 1 removes.
  • Files and directories are created, replacing a file already there. A hard link becomes a copy of the file it names. Devices and FIFOs are skipped.
  • Each file and directory gets the entry's modification time and, on Linux and macOS, its permission bits less the umask, as tar does, so a script keeps its executable bit. Setuid, setgid and sticky bits are never applied. A directory gets its mode and time after its contents are written, so a read-only directory can still be filled; one that already existed keeps its own. Windows and WASI apply no permission bits.
  • Symlinks are made after everything else, so no file is written through one. A link whose target is absolute or climbs out of target with .., or that would be made inside another symlink, is skipped. Windows, where making a symlink needs Developer Mode or an administrator, skips every symlink.

archive.TarWriter(sink) writes an archive: append_file(path, data), append_directory(path), append_symlink(path, target), append(entry, data) for any header, and append_stream(entry, source) to copy entry.size bytes from a stream. finish() writes the end marker. Paths longer than a ustar header holds get a pax header, so none is cut short.

Zip archives

.zip archives are read and written by the zip package, which builds on compress and archive. It is a package rather than part of the runtime because the package manager needs only .tar.gz; add it with pepper package add pep-lang/pepper-zip --name zip.

import zip;

main(): int {
    var writer = zip.Writer.create("bundle.zip").value();
    writer.add("version.txt", "1.0.0".bytes()).value();
    writer.finish().value();

    var archive = zip.Archive.open("bundle.zip").value();
    for (var entry in archive.entries()) {
        print($"{entry.name}: {entry.size} bytes");
    }
    archive.extract_all("out").value();
    return 0;
}
  • It reads and writes stored and DEFLATE entries, ZIP64 (archives and entries past 4 GiB, more than 65,535 entries), and UTF-8 names; names in older archives are decoded as code page 437 (text.CodePage437).
  • Entries compressed another way (bzip2, LZMA, zstd) or encrypted are listed, and reading one is an error naming the entry and the method.
  • extract_all checks every name with archive.safe_components before writing anything, and each entry's CRC-32 as it is written.

Cryptographic hashes

The digest module computes SHA-256, SHA-1 and BLAKE3 digests: fixed-size fingerprints of data, used to check that a download arrived intact, to name content by its hash, or to key a cache. It also computes message authentication codes with HMAC or BLAKE3's keyed mode, and derives keys. Bring it in with import digest; the full API is in the reference.

# Cryptographic hashes: one-shot, incremental, and as hexadecimal text.
import digest;

main(): int {
    # One call hashes a whole input, bytes or a String's UTF-8 bytes.
    var id = digest.to_hex(digest.sha256("hello"));
    assert(id == "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824", "SHA-256");

    # A hasher takes the input in pieces, such as the blocks of a file as
    # they are read; the digest does not depend on how it was split.
    var hasher = digest.Blake3();
    hasher.update("hel");
    hasher.update("lo");
    var whole = digest.blake3("hello");
    assert(hasher.finish() == whole, "same digest");
    assert(whole.count == 32, "32 bytes");

    # git names a file's content by the SHA-1 of a header and the bytes.
    u8[] nul = [0];
    var git = digest.Sha1();
    git.update("blob 6");
    git.update(nul);
    git.update("hello\n");
    assert(git.finish_hex() == "ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a", "git blob id");
    return 0;
}

One-shot and incremental

Each hash has a one-shot function and a hasher type:

HashFunctionHasherDigest size
SHA-256digest.sha256(input)digest.Sha25632 bytes
SHA-1digest.sha1(input)digest.Sha120 bytes
BLAKE3digest.blake3(input)digest.Blake332 bytes
  • The input is a u8[], or a String, which hashes its UTF-8 bytes (without a terminating NUL).
  • A hasher takes the input in pieces: call update any number of times, then finish for the digest. Splitting the input differently gives the same digest. finish also resets the hasher, so it can hash another input; reset discards the input so far.
  • A digest is a u8[]. digest.to_hex(bytes) writes it as lowercase hexadecimal, the way checksums are usually shown, and each hasher's finish_hex() does both steps; digest.from_hex(text) reads hexadecimal back into bytes.
  • An array literal passed straight to update is ambiguous between its u8[] and String overloads; give it a type first (u8[] nul = [0]; hasher.update(nul);).

Which hash

  • SHA-256 is the common choice for published checksums and anything that must interoperate.
  • BLAKE3 is faster and as strong; the compiler's build cache keys its objects with it.
  • SHA-1 is broken for collision resistance: someone can make two inputs with the same digest. Use it only where a format requires it, such as git object ids.

None of these is the hash for a hash table: HashMap and HashSet use hash<T>, which is much faster but neither cryptographic nor stable between versions.

Message authentication

A message authentication code (MAC) is a digest that only someone with a secret key can compute, so a receiver that shares the key can check that a message is authentic and unchanged. Webhook signatures, JWTs (HS256) and S3-style request signing all use HMAC.

# Message authentication: HMAC, BLAKE3's keyed mode and key derivation.
import digest;

main(): int {
    # A webhook signs its body with HMAC-SHA-256 under a shared secret;
    # the receiver computes the MAC again and compares in constant time.
    var body = "{\"event\":\"push\"}";
    var received = digest.hmac_sha256("webhook secret", body);
    var signature = "493db758cb288b3801a0084bcdd27bd565ca0fb9b0a149404d2b4442c9d79bcd";
    assert(digest.to_hex(received) == signature, "HMAC-SHA-256");
    var expected = digest.Hmac<digest.Sha256>("webhook secret");
    expected.update(body);
    assert(digest.equal_constant_time(expected.finish(), received), "authentic");

    # Derive a 32-byte key for one purpose from a shared secret, then use
    # it for BLAKE3's keyed mode.
    var derive = digest.Blake3.derive_key("example.com 2026-10-16 webhook MACs v1");
    derive.update("a shared secret");
    var mac = digest.Blake3.keyed(derive.finish());
    mac.update(body);
    assert(mac.finish().count == 32, "a 32-byte MAC");

    # BLAKE3 gives output of any length; the first 32 bytes are the digest.
    var hasher = digest.Blake3();
    hasher.update(body);
    var long_output = hasher.finish(64);
    assert(long_output.count == 64, "64 bytes");
    assert(digest.to_hex(long_output).starts_with(digest.to_hex(digest.blake3(body))), "a prefix");
    return 0;
}
  • HMAC (RFC 2104) works over SHA-256 or SHA-1: digest.hmac_sha256(key, message) and digest.hmac_sha1(key, message) are one-shot, both arguments u8[] or both String, and digest.Hmac<digest.Sha256>(key) is the incremental hasher, with the same update, finish, finish_hex and reset as the hashes. finish and reset keep the key. A key longer than 64 bytes is hashed first.
  • Check a MAC with digest.equal_constant_time(a, b), not ==: == stops at the first byte that differs, and timing it lets an attacker find a valid MAC a byte at a time.
  • BLAKE3's keyed mode, digest.Blake3.keyed(key), is a MAC with a 32-byte key; it panics on a key of any other length.
  • Key derivation: digest.Blake3.derive_key(context) returns a hasher whose digest is a key, derived from the input (a shared secret, say) for the purpose context names. Make context a hard-coded string unique to the application and purpose; different contexts give unrelated keys.
  • Extended output: every Blake3 hasher's finish(length) returns length bytes, in any of the three modes. The first 32 are the digest finish() returns.
  • PBKDF2 (RFC 8018): digest.pbkdf2_sha256(password, salt, rounds, length) derives length bytes from a password (u8[] or String) and a u8[] salt, with rounds iterations of HMAC-SHA-256 per 32-byte block. It is SCRAM's Hi(), as PostgreSQL, MongoDB and SASL logins use. To store new passwords, use Argon2id (pepper-crypto's crypto.hash_password) instead, which costs an attacker's GPUs memory as well as time. It panics when rounds is 0 or length is over RFC 8018's limit.

Using the system's crypto library

By default the hashes are written in Pepper, so a program that uses them links no extra library. Building with -D USE_LIBCRYPTO (see Build options) makes SHA-256 and SHA-1 call the platform's crypto library instead, which uses the CPU's SHA instructions where it has them: several times faster (about 1.7 GB/s instead of 250 MB/s for SHA-256 on an x86-64 with SHA-NI).

pep-build main.pep -D USE_LIBCRYPTO -o app
PlatformLibraryWhat it needs
LinuxOpenSSL's libcrypto (EVP_Digest*), linked as -lcryptothe development package (libssl-dev, openssl-devel)
macOSOpenSSL's libcrypto, linked as -lcryptoHomebrew's openssl@3, and its lib folder named with -L or PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH (-L $(brew --prefix openssl@3)/lib)
WindowsCNG (BCryptHash*), linked as bcrypt.libnothing: CNG is part of Windows 10 and later

The API and the digests are the same either way. Blake3 stays portable Pepper, since libcrypto has no BLAKE3.

Limitations

  • Without USE_LIBCRYPTO, SHA-256 and SHA-1 run at a few hundred megabytes per second. BLAKE3 is always the portable code, below the official BLAKE3, which uses SIMD and threads.
  • The hashes have no secret-dependent branches or table lookups, but they have not been audited for timing side channels, which matter only when hashing secrets. Copies of an HMAC key stay in memory until the hasher is freed; nothing wipes them.
  • HMAC works over SHA-256 and SHA-1; there is no SHA-512 to put under it.

Random numbers

The random module gives random numbers two ways: secure bytes from the operating system, for keys, tokens and identifiers, and Generator, a fast pseudo-random generator for everything else: games, simulations, sampling, shuffling and jitter. Bring it in with import random; the full API is in the reference.

# Random numbers: this thread's generator, a seeded one, and secure bytes.
import random;

main(): int {
    # This thread's generator, seeded from the operating system.
    var die = random.next_int(1..>6);
    assert(die >= 1 && die <= 6, "a die roll");
    var names = ["ada", "grace", "edsger"];
    random.shuffle(names);
    var pick = random.choose(names);
    assert(names.contains(pick), "one of the names");

    # A seeded generator gives the same numbers on every run and platform.
    var a = random.Generator(2024);
    var b = random.Generator(2024);
    assert(a.next_double() == b.next_double(), "same seed, same numbers");

    # Keys and tokens come from the operating system, not a generator.
    var key = random.bytes(32);
    assert(key.count == 32, "256 bits");
    return 0;
}

Secure bytes

FunctionGives
random.bytes(count)a new u8[] of count random bytes
random.fill(bytes)overwrites every element of an existing u8[]
random.secure_ulong()a random ulong

They come from getentropy on Linux, Android, macOS, iOS and WASI, and from BCryptGenRandom on Windows, so no one can predict them. Each call asks the kernel, which is slower than a generator. They panic only if the operating system cannot give random bytes, which a working system never does.

Generators

random.Generator is xoshiro256**: 256 bits of state, statistically strong output, and a few instructions a number. It is not secure: anyone who sees enough of its output can predict the rest.

  • Generator() seeds itself from the operating system, so each run gives different numbers.
  • Generator(seed) gives the same numbers for the same seed on every platform, for reproducible tests and simulations.
MethodGives
next_ulong()64 random bits
next_int(range)an int in range: 0..10 is 0 to 9, 1..>6 is 1 to 6
next_double()a double from 0 up to but not including 1
next_bool()true or false
choose(items)one element of an array
shuffle(items)puts an array in a random order, in place

Every number in a range is equally likely: next_int draws again rather than let the low numbers come up a little more often. An empty range, or choose on an empty array, panics.

A generator is a value struct: copying one copies its state, so the copy gives the same numbers as the original, and a function that takes a generator as a parameter draws from its own copy. A generator belongs to one thread.

This thread's generator

random.next_ulong, next_int, next_double, next_bool, choose and shuffle draw from a generator each thread has of its own, seeded from the operating system the first time the thread uses it. Code that needs a random number calls them without passing a generator around, and threads never share or lock one.

Networking

The io module has TCP, UDP and Unix domain sockets, IP and socket addresses, and host name lookup; the tls module encrypts TCP connections, and the http module speaks HTTP over them. In a plain program every call blocks the calling thread until it completes, like File. To serve several connections at once, give each one its own thread, or its own task: in a task, a call that has to wait parks only that task.

On WebAssembly (--target wasm32-wasip1) there are no sockets, host name lookups or TLS: each of those calls returns an IoError saying it is not supported on WASI (see WebAssembly).

Addresses

An IpAddress is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. A SocketAddress is an IP address and a port:

import io;

main(): int {
    var home = io.IpAddress.v4(127, 0, 0, 1);
    assert(home.is_loopback(), "127.0.0.1 is loopback");

    # Text is read strictly and printed in one canonical form.
    var six = io.IpAddress.parse("2001:DB8:0:0:0:0:0:1").value();
    assert(six.to_string() == "2001:db8::1", "IPv6 prints compressed and lowercase");
    assert(io.IpAddress.parse("256.1.1.1").error().is_invalid_input(), "256 is out of range");

    var service = io.SocketAddress.parse("[::1]:8080").value();
    assert(service.is_v6() && service.port() == 8080, "IPv6 with a port");
    assert(service.to_string() == "[::1]:8080", "brackets around IPv6");

    # A link-local IPv6 address names its interface after `%`: a number, or
    # a name such as `eth0` that is looked up on this machine.
    var link = io.SocketAddress.parse("[fe80::1%4000000000]:8080").value();
    assert(link.address().scope_id() == 4000000000, "the scope id");

    # A host name goes to the system resolver; an IP address is used as is.
    var local = io.resolve("localhost", 80).value();
    assert(local.count >= 1 && local[0].address().is_loopback(), "localhost is loopback");
    return 0;
}
  • IpAddress.v4(a, b, c, d) and IpAddress.v6(a, ..., h) build an address from its bytes or its eight 16-bit groups. loopback_v4(), loopback_v6(), unspecified_v4() (0.0.0.0) and unspecified_v6() (::) are the well-known ones. IpAddress() is 0.0.0.0.
  • IpAddress.parse reads dotted decimal IPv4 and the RFC 4291 text form of IPv6, and to_string() prints the RFC 5952 form: lowercase, zeros compressed, ::ffff:1.2.3.4 for an IPv4-mapped address. Parsing and printing are the same on every platform.
  • An IPv6 address may carry a scope id, the network interface a link-local address belongs to: fe80::1%eth0 or fe80::1%2 (RFC 4007). scope_id() reads it (0 for none) and with_scope_id(id) sets it. A name is looked up on this machine, and to_string() prints the interface's name when it has one, else the number. Sockets pass it to the system as sin6_scope_id. In a URI the % is escaped, http://[fe80::1%25eth0]/ (RFC 6874); the HTTP client decodes it.
  • SocketAddress(address, port) or SocketAddress.parse("1.2.3.4:80") make a socket address. IPv6 takes brackets: [::1]:80.
  • resolve(host, port) looks a host name up with the system resolver (the hosts file and DNS) and returns every address it has, with port attached. An IP address is returned as is. A name with no address fails with is_not_found().

TCP

A TcpListener waits for connections. Each TcpStream is one connection:

import io;

# A server and a client on this machine, taking turns on one thread: the
# system completes a connection before the server accepts it.
main(): int {
    # Port 0 asks the system for any free port.
    var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
    var address = listener.local_address().value();

    var client = io.TcpStream.connect(address).value();
    var (server, peer) = listener.accept().value();
    assert(peer == client.local_address().value(), "accept reports who connected");

    # The client sends a request and closes its sending side.
    assert(client.write_all("ping").is_ok(), "send the request");
    client.shutdown_write();

    # The server reads until the client is done: read returns 0 at the end.
    var request = Array<u8>();
    while (server.read(request, 4096).value() > 0) {
    }
    assert(request.count == 4, "the whole request arrived");

    # It answers, and the client reads exactly the bytes it expects.
    server.write_all("pong");
    var reply = Array<u8>();
    assert(client.read_exact(reply, 4).is_ok(), "read the reply");
    assert(reply[0] == 'p' && reply[1] == 'o', "the reply is pong");
    return 0;
}
  • TcpListener.bind(address) listens on a local address. Port 0 lets the system pick a free port, and local_address() says which one it picked. accept() waits for the next connection and returns the stream and the peer's address as a tuple. for (var connection in listener.incoming()) accepts one connection per step, yielding an IoResult<TcpStream> (see Iteration).
  • TcpStream.connect(address) connects to an address. TcpStream.connect_host(host, port) resolves a name and tries each of its addresses in turn.
  • read(buffer, max) waits until some data arrives, then appends up to max bytes of it to buffer, the same way File.read does. It returns 0 once the peer has closed its side. read_exact(buffer, count) loops until count bytes have arrived.
  • write(data) sends what the system will take in one call. write_all(data) loops until everything is sent; data is a u8[] or a String.
  • shutdown_write() tells the peer that nothing more is coming, while this side can still read.
  • set_no_delay(true) sends small writes immediately instead of combining them.
  • local_address() and peer_address() return the two ends of the connection.

Reading and writing any stream

A File, a TcpStream, a UnixStream and a tls.TlsStream have the io.Reader and io.Writer traits, so a function that takes an io.Reader (or <R: io.Reader>) reads from any of them:

import io;

# Any stream that is an io.Reader: a File, a socket, or a TLS stream.
count_lines(source: io.Reader): int {
    var count = 0;
    for (var line in source.lines()) {
        if (line.is_err()) {
            break;
        }
        count += 1;
    }
    return count;
}

# `print` and `print_line` write a value's text to any io.Writer, the way the
# global `print` writes to standard output.
main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("networking-print.txt");
    var file = io.File.create(path).value();
    file.print("total: ");
    file.print_line(42);
    file.print_line((1, "two"));
    file.close();
    assert(io.File.read_to_string(path).value() == "total: 42\n(1, two)\n", "the file holds both lines");
    assert(count_lines(io.File.open(path).value()) == 2, "a File is a Reader");
    io.File.remove(path);

    # The same calls work on a TcpStream (and a UnixStream).
    var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
    var client = io.TcpStream.connect(listener.local_address().value()).value();
    var (server, peer) = listener.accept().value();
    client.print_line($"hello from {client.local_address().value()}");
    client.print_line("bye");
    client.shutdown_write();
    assert(count_lines(server) == 2, "a TcpStream is a Reader");
    return 0;
}
  • io.Reader needs read(buffer, max) and gives lines(), the stream's lines as IoResult<String>s, and chunks(size), its bytes in arrays of at most size, both read as a for loop asks for them (see Iteration).
  • io.Writer needs write(data) and write_all(data: u8[]) and gives print(value) and print_line(value). They write the text that to_string makes of any value, as the global print does on standard output; print_line adds a \n. Both return an IoResult<void>, like write_all.
  • io.ByteReader(bytes) reads an array of bytes as a stream, and io.ByteWriter() collects what is written in its bytes array, for code that takes a stream when the data is in memory.
  • compress.DecompressReader and compress.CompressWriter wrap another stream (see Compression and archives).
  • Another type gets them by providing those methods and declaring extend MyStream with io.Reader; or extend MyStream with io.Writer;.
  • io.Print, which gave only print and print_line, is deprecated: use io.Writer.

UDP

A UdpSocket sends and receives datagrams. Each one arrives whole or not at all, and in no guaranteed order:

import io;

main(): int {
    var loopback = io.SocketAddress(io.IpAddress.loopback_v4(), 0);
    var sender = io.UdpSocket.bind(loopback).value();
    var receiver = io.UdpSocket.bind(loopback).value();

    var datagram = Array<u8>();
    datagram.append(1);
    datagram.append(2);
    datagram.append(3);
    sender.send_to(datagram, receiver.local_address().value());

    # One receive takes one whole datagram and says who sent it.
    var buffer = Array<u8>();
    var (count, from) = receiver.receive_from(buffer, 1500).value();
    assert(count == 3 && buffer[2] == 3, "the datagram arrived whole");
    assert(from == sender.local_address().value(), "from the sender");
    return 0;
}
  • UdpSocket.bind(address) opens a socket on a local address.
  • send_to(data, address) sends one datagram. receive_from(buffer, max) waits for one datagram, appends it to buffer, and returns the byte count and the sender. The part of a datagram beyond max bytes is lost.
  • After connect(address), send and receive use that peer, and datagrams from anyone else are dropped.
  • set_broadcast(true) allows sending to a broadcast address.

Unix domain sockets

A Unix domain socket connects processes on the same machine through a path in the file system instead of an IP address and port. UnixListener and UnixStream work like TcpListener and TcpStream:

import io;

# A server and a client over a Unix domain socket, taking turns on one
# thread, as in the TCP example.
main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-networking-unix.sock");
    # Binding fails if the socket file is still there from an earlier run.
    io.File.remove(path);
    var listener = io.UnixListener.bind(path).value();

    var client = io.UnixStream.connect(path).value();
    var server = listener.accept().value();

    assert(client.write_all("ping").is_ok(), "send the request");
    var request = Array<u8>();
    assert(server.read_exact(request, 4).is_ok(), "read the request");
    server.write_all("pong");
    var reply = Array<u8>();
    assert(client.read_exact(reply, 4).is_ok(), "read the reply");
    assert(reply[0] == 'p' && reply[1] == 'o', "the reply is pong");

    # Closing the listener leaves the socket file; remove it when done.
    listener.close();
    assert(io.File.remove(path).is_ok(), "remove the socket file");
    return 0;
}
  • UnixListener.bind(path) creates a socket file at path and listens on it. Binding fails with is_address_in_use() if a file is already there, and closing the listener does not remove the file, so a server removes it with File.remove before binding and when it is done.
  • UnixStream.connect(path) connects to it. It fails with is_not_found() when there is no socket file, and with is_connection_refused() when the file is there but nothing listens on it.
  • accept() returns just the stream: the client's end has no path.
  • Reading, writing, shutdown_write(), into_transfer() and adopt are the same as on a TcpStream, and SharedUnixListener is the counterpart of SharedTcpListener.
  • A path holds at most 107 bytes (103 on macOS); a longer or empty one fails with is_invalid_input().

Unix datagram sockets

UnixDatagram is the Unix domain counterpart of UdpSocket, on Linux and macOS only (Windows has no Unix datagram sockets, so it is declared with [Target(OS(Linux) || OS(Mac))]):

# Unix datagram sockets: a server bound to a path answers each datagram.
import io;

main(): int {
    # Linux and macOS only: Windows has no Unix datagram sockets.
    [Target(OS(Linux) || OS(Mac))]
    {
        var folder = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-udgram-example");
        io.Directory.remove_all(folder);
        io.Directory.create_all(folder).value();
        var server_path = folder.join("server.sock");
        var client_path = folder.join("client.sock");

        var server = io.UnixDatagram.bind(server_path).value();
        var client = io.UnixDatagram.bind(client_path).value();
        client.send_to("ping".bytes(), server_path).value();

        # Each receive takes one whole datagram and names its sender.
        var request = Array<u8>();
        var (n, sender) = server.receive_from(request, 1024).value();
        assert(n == 4 && sender == client_path, "one datagram from the client");
        server.send_to("pong".bytes(), sender).value();

        var reply = Array<u8>();
        client.receive(reply, 1024).value();
        assert(reply.count == 4, "the reply");

        # A pair is two sockets already connected to each other.
        var (a, b) = io.UnixDatagram.pair().value();
        a.send("hi".bytes()).value();
        var got = Array<u8>();
        assert(b.receive(got, 16).value() == 2, "through the pair");

        # Closing leaves the socket files; remove them.
        io.Directory.remove_all(folder).value();
    }
    return 0;
}
  • UnixDatagram.bind(path) creates a socket file to receive on, with the same path rules and errors as UnixListener.bind; unbound() makes one that can only send, and pair() two that are connected to each other.
  • send_to(data, path) sends one datagram; it fails with is_not_found() when there is no socket file and is_connection_refused() when nothing is bound to it any more. A datagram is never dropped silently. While the receiver's queue is full, a send waits on Linux; on macOS it fails at once with "No buffer space available" (ENOBUFS) and sends nothing, so try again later.
  • receive_from(buffer, max) returns the byte count and the sender's path, which is empty for an unbound sender. As with UDP, a datagram longer than max is cut.
  • connect(path), send and receive work as on a UdpSocket.

TLS

The tls module encrypts a TCP connection with TLS 1.2 or 1.3. A TlsConnector makes client connections and checks the server's certificate. A TlsAcceptor serves them with a certificate and key. Both produce a TlsStream, which reads and writes like a TcpStream:

import async;
import io;
import tls;
import "test_certificate";

# A TLS server and client on this machine, in two tasks.
main(): int {
    var connector = tls.TlsConnector.create();
    if (connector.is_err()) {
        # On Linux or macOS without OpenSSL 3.
        print(connector.error().message);
        return 0;
    }
    # A real server reads its certificate and key from files it was given.
    var certificate = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-example-cert.pem");
    var key = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-example-key.pem");
    io.File.write_text(certificate, test_certificate());
    io.File.write_text(key, test_private_key());
    var created = tls.TlsAcceptor.create(certificate, key);
    if (created.is_err()) {
        # On iOS, which has no TLS servers yet.
        print(created.error().message);
        io.File.remove(certificate);
        io.File.remove(key);
        return 0;
    }

    async.run(
        () => {
            var acceptor = created.value();
            # Mutual TLS: only clients with a certificate the test
            # certificate issued (here, the test certificate itself) get in.
            assert(acceptor.require_client_certificate(certificate).is_ok(), "ask clients for certificates");
            var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = listener.local_address().value().port();
            var server = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                var (tcp, peer) = listener.accept().value();
                var stream = acceptor.accept(tcp).value();
                var request = Array<u8>();
                stream.read_exact(request, 4);
                stream.write_all("pong");
                stream.shutdown();
            });

            # The client trusts the test certificate as well as the system's.
            var client = connector.value();
            assert(client.add_root_certificate(certificate).is_ok(), "trust the test certificate");
            assert(client.set_identity(certificate, key).is_ok(), "present a client certificate");
            var stream = client.connect_host("localhost", port).value();
            stream.write_all("ping");
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (stream.read(reply, 4096).value() > 0) {}
            assert(reply.count == 4 && reply[0] == 'p' && reply[1] == 'o', "the reply is pong");
            server.join();
        }
    );
    io.File.remove(certificate);
    io.File.remove(key);
    return 0;
}
  • TlsConnector.create() trusts the system's root certificates, and add_root_certificate(path) adds more from a PEM file, such as a private certificate authority. Make one connector and share it: it is [Shared].
  • connector.connect(tcp, host) runs the handshake over a connected TcpStream. It checks that the certificate is valid and was issued for host, which is also sent to the server (SNI). connect_host(host, port) connects the TCP stream first. An IP address in host is checked against the certificate's addresses.
  • TlsAcceptor.create(certificate_chain, private_key) reads PEM files, and acceptor.accept(tcp) runs the handshake over a connection a TcpListener accepted.
  • Mutual TLS: acceptor.require_client_certificate(roots) asks every client for a certificate and accepts only one issued by a certificate in the PEM file roots; connector.set_identity(certificate_chain, private_key) gives the client a certificate to present. A client with no certificate, or an untrusted one, fails the server's accept. With TLS 1.3 the client's connect can succeed first, and its next read then fails or returns 0.
  • ALPN: connector.set_protocols(["h2", "http/1.1"]) offers protocols to servers, most preferred first, and acceptor.set_protocols(...) lists the ones a server accepts, also most preferred first. The handshake picks the first of the server's that the client offers, and stream.protocol() names it on both sides. A client that offers no protocols connects with none chosen; one whose protocols the server accepts none of fails the handshake (the no_application_protocol alert of RFC 7301).
  • read, read_exact, write and write_all work on the decrypted bytes. shutdown() sends the TLS close_notify, and read returns 0 once the peer has sent one or closed the connection.
  • A failed handshake returns an error whose message says why, such as certificate verify failed: self-signed certificate.

On Linux and macOS the module uses OpenSSL 3, loaded when the first connector or acceptor is made: install it with the system's package manager, or brew install openssl@3 on macOS. If it is missing, create() returns an error. On Windows it uses the system's SChannel, which needs nothing installed; a private key (a server's or a client's) must be PKCS #8 (BEGIN PRIVATE KEY), and TLS 1.3 needs Windows 11 or Server 2022. On iOS it uses the system's Security.framework, which needs nothing bundled, for clients only and with TLS 1.2. On Android it uses an OpenSSL 3 that the toolchain carries and links into the program, with the system's trusted certificates (see iOS and Android).

Timeouts

A socket call waits as long as it takes unless a timeout limits it:

import io;

# A read that gives up when the peer stays silent, and a connect with a
# limit of its own.
main(): int {
    var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
    var address = listener.local_address().value();

    # connect_timeout gives up after 2 seconds instead of the system's limit.
    var client = io.TcpStream.connect_timeout(address, 2000).value();
    var (server, peer) = listener.accept().value();

    # The server says nothing, so the read gives up after 100 milliseconds.
    client.set_read_timeout(100).value();
    var reply = Array<u8>();
    var silent = client.read(reply, 4096);
    assert(silent.is_err() && silent.error().is_timed_out(), "the read timed out");

    # The stream is still open: once the server answers, the read succeeds.
    server.write_all("pong");
    assert(client.read_exact(reply, 4).is_ok(), "read the late reply");
    return 0;
}
  • set_read_timeout(milliseconds) limits how long a read (or a UDP datagram receive) waits for data, and set_write_timeout(milliseconds) how long a write waits for room to send. A call that waits longer fails with is_timed_out(), and the socket stays open for another try. Each wait counts on its own, so read_exact or write_all can take longer in all. 0, the default, means no limit; read_timeout() and write_timeout() return the current values. TcpStream, UdpSocket, UnixStream and UnixDatagram have them.
  • TcpStream.connect_timeout(address, milliseconds) gives up on a connection that is not established in time, instead of after the system's own limit, which is often minutes.
  • They work the same outside a task, where the thread blocks, and inside one, where only the task parks. In a task, async.timeout also limits every wait in its block, and whichever ends first wins.
  • A TlsStream waits through its TcpStream, so the TCP stream's timeouts limit its reads, writes and handshake too. Set them before connect or accept.

Errors

Every operation returns an IoResult. Besides the file-system predicates, IoError has these for networking:

PredicateWhen
is_connection_refused()nothing listens at the address
is_connection_reset()the peer reset or closed the connection (writing to a closed connection included)
is_address_in_use()another socket already has the address and port
is_address_not_available()the IP address is not one of this machine's
is_timed_out()the peer never answered, or a read, write or connect timeout expired
is_not_found()resolve found no address for the name, or UnixStream.connect found no socket file

Writing to a closed connection never raises SIGPIPE, so it cannot kill the process. The write returns an error instead.

Closing

A socket closes when the last reference to it goes, like a File, and close() closes it earlier and reports any error. A socket cannot be copied, so it cannot go through a channel to another thread. Use it on the thread that made it, or move it: into_transfer() turns a TcpStream (or a UnixStream) into a thread-safe SocketTransfer that TcpStream.adopt (or UnixStream.adopt) takes on another thread, and a SharedTcpListener is a listener any thread can accept on (see Tasks).

On POSIX a listener sets SO_REUSEADDR, so a server can restart right away. On Windows it does not, because there that option would let another program take over the port.

The reference pages for addresses, sockets and Unix domain sockets and TLS document every method.

HTTP

The http module has an HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 client and server, over plain TCP or TLS. Both run in tasks: a request that waits parks only its task. Over TLS the two sides pick HTTP/2 through ALPN when both have it (see HTTP/2); the Request and Response types, and the code that uses them, are the same for either version.

HTTP needs tasks and sockets, so it is not available on WebAssembly (--target wasm32-wasip1, see WebAssembly).

import async;
import http;
import io;

# Answers every request: `/hello` greets, anything else is not found.
handle(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    if (request.path() == "/hello") {
        var response = http.Response(200).set_text("hello, " + request.query());
        response.headers["Content-Type"] = "text/plain";
        return response;
    }
    return http.Response(404).set_text("nothing at " + request.path());
}

main(): int {
    async.run(
        () => {
            # Port 0 asks the system for any free port.
            var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = server.local_address().value().port();
            # serve() runs until async.run ends, so it gets a task of its own.
            async.spawn<void>(() => {
                server.serve(handle);
            });

            var base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + to_string(port);
            var client = http.Client();
            var response = client.get(base + "/hello?pepper").value();
            assert(response.status == 200, "found");
            assert(response.text() == "hello, pepper", "the handler's text");
            assert(response.headers["content-type"] == "text/plain", "names ignore case");

            var missing = client.get(base + "/elsewhere").value();
            assert(missing.status == 404 && missing.reason == "Not Found", "not found");

            var posted = client.post(base + "/hello", "text/plain", "a body").value();
            assert(posted.is_success(), "any method reaches the handler");
        }
    );
    return 0;
}

Messages

  • A Request has a method, a url, headers and a body. For a client the url is absolute (https://example.com/items?page=2); a server handler gets the request target (/items?page=2). uri() parses either as a Uri, and path() and query() return its parts.
  • A Response has a status, a reason, headers and a body. is_success() tests for a 2xx status.
  • Headers maps each field name to its values. Names ignore case (they are stored lowercased). headers["Accept"] reads the first value ("" when there is none) and headers["Accept"] = "text/html" replaces the field; get(name) returns an optional, add keeps earlier values, values(name) returns them all, and names() lists the fields in no defined order.
  • set_text and set_body fill a request or response and return it, so they chain. body() returns the bytes, for any body including binary ones; text() decodes them as UTF-8, replacing invalid bytes with U+FFFD.
  • set_reader(source) gives a request or response a body streamed from any io.Reader (a file, a compress.CompressReader) instead of one held in memory; see Streaming bodies.

URLs

Uri (in the prelude, so no import is needed) parses any URI reference following RFC 3986: an absolute URI with any scheme (https:, mailto:, file:) or a relative reference such as a request target. It splits the text into scheme, user_info, host, port, path, query and fragment; the parts that can be missing are optionals. Components keep their percent-escapes, and Uri.decode turns one into text; Uri.encode escapes text for a path segment or query value, and Uri.encode_form and Uri.decode_form write and read form data (see Encodings and UUIDs). base.resolve(reference) resolves a relative reference against a base URI, as a browser resolves a link (RFC 3986 section 5.2).

main(): int {
    # Any scheme parses; the scheme is lowercased and nothing else changes.
    var uri = Uri.parse("HTTPS://user@example.com:8443/caf%C3%A9?page=2#top").value();
    assert(uri.scheme == "https" && uri.host.value() == "example.com", "scheme and host");
    assert(uri.port.value() == 8443 && uri.user_info.value() == "user", "port and user information");
    assert(uri.path == "/caf%C3%A9" && uri.query.value() == "page=2", "path and query keep their escapes");
    assert(Uri.decode(uri.path).value() == "/café", "decoded path");
    assert(uri.path_and_query() == "/caf%C3%A9?page=2", "what an HTTP request line names");

    # Missing parts are Empty: a mailto URI has no authority.
    var mail = Uri.parse("mailto:someone@example.com").value();
    assert(mail.host.is_empty() && mail.path == "someone@example.com", "no authority");

    # A relative reference has no scheme, like a request target on a server.
    var target = Uri.parse("/items?page=2").value();
    assert(!target.is_absolute() && target.path == "/items", "relative");

    # resolve() turns a relative reference, such as a redirect's Location,
    # into the URI it names.
    var page = Uri.parse("https://example.com/docs/guide/intro").value();
    assert(page.resolve(Uri.parse("../api?v=2").value()).to_string() == "https://example.com/docs/api?v=2", "resolved");

    assert(Uri.parse("http://example.com/a b").is_err(), "a space must be percent-encoded");
    return 0;
}

Client

  • Client() trusts the system's root certificates for https:// URLs. Client(connector) uses a tls.TlsConnector of your own, for instance one that trusts a private certificate authority.
  • get(url), post(url, content_type, body) and send(request) open a connection, send the request and read the whole response, up to MAX_RESPONSE_BODY (64 MiB). open(request) returns at the header fields and leaves the body to read as a stream (see Streaming bodies). The client adds Host, Content-Length (or Transfer-Encoding: chunked) and Connection: close.
  • Any status is a successful result: check status. An error means there was no response: the URL is not http:// or https:// (is_invalid_input()), the connection or TLS handshake failed, or the response was not valid HTTP.
  • A request that could split the message is refused with is_invalid_input(): a header field value holding CR, LF or NUL, or a field name or method that is not an RFC 9110 token.
  • Redirects (301, 302, 303, 307, 308) are followed, up to max_redirects (10) per request, and response.url is where the response came from. A 303, and a 301 or 302 after a POST, becomes a GET without the body; a 307 or 308 repeats the method and body, except that a body from set_reader cannot be sent twice, so that redirect is returned. Leaving the origin drops Authorization, Proxy-Authorization and Cookie. Client(0) returns every redirect as it is.
  • Every request from a Client uses a new connection; a Session keeps them open (see Reusing connections).
  • For https:// the client offers HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 through ALPN, on its own connector or the one it was given, and speaks whichever the server picks.

Server

  • Server.bind(address) listens for HTTP; Server.bind_tls(address, acceptor) serves HTTPS with a tls.TlsAcceptor's certificate.
  • serve(handler) accepts connections on every worker of async.run and serves each in a task of its own, calling handler for each request with the body read in full. It returns when async.run ends. The handler is a shared (Request) => Response, since every worker calls it.
  • Connections stay open between requests unless the client asks to close or speaks HTTP/1.0. Chunked request bodies and Expect: 100-continue are understood.
  • The server adds Content-Length to each response (or, for a body from set_reader of unknown length, Transfer-Encoding: chunked), and the standard reason phrase when reason is empty (reason_phrase(status) returns it).
  • A request it cannot parse gets 400 Bad Request, header fields over 64 KiB get 431, and a body over MAX_REQUEST_BODY (16 MiB) gets 413.
  • A handler's response with a header field (or reason phrase) that could split the message gets 500 Internal Server Error instead, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.
  • Server.bind_tls offers HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 through ALPN, and a plain-TCP client that opens with the HTTP/2 preface (prior knowledge, or h2c) is served HTTP/2 too. See HTTP/2.

Streaming bodies

A body need not fit in memory. Both directions stream through io.Reader, the trait of files, sockets and the compress readers:

  • Responses to a client: client.open(request) returns the Response as soon as its header fields arrive. response.reader() is then a BodyReader that reads the body from the connection as it arrives, with no size limit, undoing chunked framing, and ends where the body ends. Read it with read, chunks or lines, or wrap it in a compress.DecompressReader. The connection closes at the end of the body, at close(), or when the last reference to the reader goes.
  • Requests from a client: request.set_reader(source) sends the body chunked; set_reader(source, length) sends it with Content-Length.
  • Responses from a server: a handler returns Response(200).set_reader(source), sent chunked to an HTTP/1.1 client (or with Content-Length when a length is given). An HTTP/1.0 client gets the body unframed, and the connection closes after it.
import async;
import http;
import io;

# `/download` streams a body of unknown length, which goes out chunked;
# `/upload` reports how many bytes it received.
handle(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    if (request.path() == "/download") {
        var data = "pepper\n".repeat(100000).bytes();
        return http.Response(200).set_reader(io.ByteReader(data));
    }
    return http.Response(200).set_text(to_string(request.body().count));
}

main(): int {
    async.run(
        () => {
            var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = server.local_address().value().port();
            async.spawn<void>(() => {
                server.serve(handle);
            });
            var base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + to_string(port);
            var client = http.Client();

            # open() returns at the header fields; the body is read as it
            # arrives and written to a file a chunk at a time.
            var response = client.open(http.Request("GET", base + "/download")).value();
            assert(response.headers["transfer-encoding"] == "chunked", "no length up front");
            var path = io.Directory.temp().join("pepper-download.txt");
            var file = io.File.create(path).value();
            for (var chunk in response.reader().chunks(65536)) {
                file.write_all(chunk.value());
            }
            file.close();

            # Send the file back as a request body read from the file.
            var upload = http.Request("PUT", base + "/upload").set_reader(io.File.open(path).value());
            assert(client.send(upload).value().text() == "700000", "every byte arrived");
            io.File.remove(path);
        }
    );
    return 0;
}

Switching protocols

A protocol that starts as an HTTP/1.1 request, such as WebSocket, can be served from a handler: it answers with Response().upgrade(protocol, takeover).

  • The server sends 101 Switching Protocols with Upgrade: protocol, Connection: Upgrade and the response's other headers, and no Content-Length or body. It then calls takeover in the connection's task with an http.Connection, and serves no more HTTP on it.
  • A Connection is an io.Reader and an io.Writer over the raw stream, TCP or, under Server.bind_tls, TLS. Its first reads return the bytes the client sent right after the request head, which the server had already read. It closes when takeover returns, or at close().
  • request.can_upgrade() says whether the connection can switch: true for HTTP/1.1, false for HTTP/1.0 and for a request on an HTTP/2 stream. For those, an upgrade response becomes 501 Not Implemented.
import async;
import http;
import io;
import text;

# `/shout` switches the connection to a made-up protocol that sends back
# every byte in upper case, until the client stops sending.
handle(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    if (!request.can_upgrade() || request.headers["upgrade"] != "shout") {
        return http.Response(400).set_text("send Upgrade: shout");
    }
    return http.Response().upgrade("shout", (connection) => {
        for (var chunk in connection.chunks(4096)) {
            connection.write_all(text.Utf8.decode_lossy(chunk.value()).upper().bytes());
        }
    });
}

main(): int {
    async.run(
        () => {
            var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = server.local_address().value().port();
            async.spawn<void>(() => {
                server.serve(handle);
            });
            var stream = io.TcpStream.connect(io.SocketAddress(io.IpAddress.loopback_v4(), port)).value();
            # The request head and the first bytes of the new protocol, together.
            stream.write_all(
                "GET /shout HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\nUpgrade: shout\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n\r\nhello".bytes()
            );
            stream.shutdown_write();
            var reply = Array<u8>();
            while (stream.read(reply, 4096).value() > 0) {}
            var reply_text = text.Utf8.decode_lossy(reply);
            assert(reply_text.starts_with("HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n"), "switched");
            assert(reply_text.ends_with("\r\n\r\nHELLO"), "spoke the new protocol");
        }
    );
    return 0;
}

Reusing connections

client.session() returns a Session, which sends requests with the client's settings and keeps each connection open after its response (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive). The next request to the same scheme, host and port uses it again, saving the TCP and TLS handshakes:

import async;
import http;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run(
        () => {
            var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
            var port = server.local_address().value().port();
            async.spawn<void>(() => {
                server.serve((request) => {
                    return http.Response(200).set_text("page " + request.query());
                });
            });
            var base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + to_string(port);

            var session = http.Client().session();
            for (var page in 1..>3) {
                var response = session.get(base + "/items?" + to_string(page)).value();
                assert(response.text() == "page " + to_string(page), "each page");
            }
            # One connection carried all three requests, and waits for more.
            assert(session.idle_count == 1, "kept open");
            session.close();
        }
    );
    return 0;
}
  • A connection goes back to the session when its response body has been read to its end (send reads it; for open, read the BodyReader to its end), unless the server said Connection: close.
  • max_idle_per_host (4) connections wait for each scheme, host and port; one idle longer than idle_timeout (90 seconds) is closed instead of used. idle_count says how many wait, and close() closes them.
  • A request that finds its reused connection closed by the server goes again on a new one, unless its body came from set_reader.
  • An HTTP/2 connection is not idle and taken in turn: every request to its origin shares it at once, each on a stream of its own. idle_count counts it while no request is using it.
  • A Session is not [Shared]: use one per thread or task. A Client is shared, and connections, which belong to one thread, cannot be. Tasks started with spawn_local may share a session, and over HTTP/2 their requests go out on one connection at the same time.

HTTP/2

HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) carries many requests on one connection at once, as streams, with header fields compressed (HPACK, RFC 7541) and each body flow-controlled so that one large transfer does not hold up the rest.

  • Choosing it: over TLS, the client offers h2 and http/1.1 through ALPN and Server.bind_tls accepts both, preferring h2, so two Pepper programs speak HTTP/2 with no setting to change. A server or client that offers only HTTP/1.1 gets HTTP/1.1. On plain TCP the client speaks HTTP/1.1; the server also takes HTTP/2 from a client that starts with its preface (prior knowledge).
  • Client: a Session keeps one HTTP/2 connection per origin, and requests from several tasks share it at once. A request outside a session opens a connection that closes after its body. A connection the server ends with GOAWAY is replaced by a new one for the next request.
  • Server: each stream is a request, answered by the same handler in a task of its own, so the requests of one connection run at the same time. The handler sees the Host field from :authority. A server lets a client open 100 streams at once.
  • Messages: field names go lowercase on the wire, as HTTP/2 requires, and fields that only mean something to HTTP/1.1 (Connection, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade, Keep-Alive) are left out. HTTP/2 has no reason phrase, so a response's reason is the standard one for its status. Bodies stream through io.Reader exactly as for HTTP/1.1; closing a response's reader early resets only its stream.

Current status

  • A server handler gets the request body read into memory in full, up to MAX_REQUEST_BODY (16 MiB).
  • HTTP/2 server push, stream priorities and the Upgrade: h2c handshake are not supported; a client speaks HTTP/2 only over TLS.
  • A server handler can take over only an HTTP/1.1 connection; WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) is not supported.

The reference pages for messages, the client, the server and Uri document every method.

Installing Pepper

Each release publishes the Pepper toolchain prebuilt for Linux, macOS and Windows, with an install script that downloads the right one. You need no LLVM development install to use it; building from source is for working on Pepper itself (see Getting started).

# Linux and macOS
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pep-lang/pepper/main/scripts/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pep-lang/pepper/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex

Each release also carries both scripts as assets, beside its archives.

The script only bootstraps. It picks this machine's archives (linux-x64, macos-arm64, macos-x64 or windows-x64) from the newest release that has them: the toolchain, pepper-<version>-<target>.tar.gz (.zip on Windows), and the installer, pepper-install-<version>-<target>.tar.gz, which holds only pep-install. It downloads both, checks the installer against its .sha256, unpacks pep-install into a temporary folder and runs pep-install setup --archive <toolchain>, which:

  1. checks the toolchain archive against its .sha256;
  2. unpacks it into ~/.pepper/toolchains/<version> (%LOCALAPPDATA%\pepper on Windows), makes it the default toolchain, and puts the entry point pepper and pep-install in ~/.pepper/bin; toolchains installed before stay (see Toolchains: pep-install);
  3. adds that folder's bin to the PATH: in ~/.profile, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile and ~/.zshrc and fish's conf.d, or in the Windows user's PATH;
  4. checks that programs can be linked (below), offering to install what is missing;
  5. builds and runs a small program with the new install, and fails if it cannot.

With --version (-Version) the script asks GitHub's API for that release by its tag. Without, it lists the repository's v<x.y.z> tags and asks for the release of each, newest version first, until one has this machine's archives. GitHub's list of releases often answers with no releases, so the script asks for that list only when it cannot get the tags. An answer that fails or comes back empty is asked again twice, 2 and then 5 seconds apart (five times, up to 30 seconds apart, for the list of releases). When the last one fails too, or the release does not exist (404), the script stops with the HTTP status and the API's message, such as GET .../releases/tags/v9.9.9 answered HTTP 404: Not Found.

The script downloads the toolchain itself, rather than leaving it to pep-install, because pep-install downloads with OpenSSL 3, which a fresh Mac and RHEL 8 do not have.

Open a new terminal afterwards so the PATH change takes effect, then pepper build hello.pep -o hello works as in Getting started.

What it installs

~/.pepper/
  bin/
    pepper              the entry point (The pepper command), which runs a toolchain's tools
    pep-install         installs and removes toolchains (pepper install)
  toolchains/
    0.4.0/
      bin/
        pep-build       the compiler, with LLVM inside it (on Windows, LLVM-C.dll beside it)
        pep-fmt  pep-test  pep-package  pep-profile  pep-run  pep-new  pep-init
        pep-lsp  pep-doc  pepper  pep-install
      runtime/          the runtime, which pep-build finds from its own folder
      LICENSE.md
  default-toolchain     the default toolchain's version

pepper runs the tools of the toolchain a folder uses: the default, unless pepper +<version>, PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN or the project's pep.toml names another (see Toolchains). pepper install add, use and update install more and change the default; update also updates pepper and pep-install themselves.

Running the script again installs the newest release beside the others and makes it the default. Only releases that carry the installer archive can be installed this way; pepper install add installs older ones into a home that is set up. A release from before toolchains (0.3.0 and earlier) cannot be set up at all, and neither is an install from before toolchains, with bin and runtime straight in ~/.pepper, moved: uninstall it first.

On Linux the binaries need glibc 2.28 or newer (RHEL 8, Debian 10, Ubuntu 18.10 and later); systems that use musl, such as Alpine, are not supported. There are no prebuilt binaries for Linux or Windows on arm64 yet. The macOS binaries are not signed: an archive downloaded with a browser makes Gatekeeper warn before it runs; one the script downloads does not.

What linking needs

pep-build compiles with the LLVM inside it, but links each program with clang, which also needs the platform's linker and C library:

PlatformNeedsThe script offers
Linuxclang and the C library's development filesapt-get install clang build-essential, dnf/yum install clang gcc glibc-devel, pacman -S clang gcc or zypper install clang gcc glibc-devel, whichever manager is present
macOSXcode's command line toolsxcode-select --install
WindowsLLVM (clang) and the MSVC libraries and Windows SDKLLVM with winget install LLVM.LLVM, else scoop install llvm; the Visual Studio Build Tools' C++ workload with winget

It asks before installing anything, unless given --yes (-Yes). With no terminal to ask on it installs nothing and says what to install.

Programs that use the tls module also need OpenSSL 3 (libssl.so.3 on Linux, Homebrew's openssl@3 on macOS; Windows uses SChannel). The script says so when it finds none, and on macOS offers brew install openssl@3.

pep-build looks for clang in this order, and uses the first it finds:

  1. in the LLVM named by PEPPER_LLVM_PREFIX, else by LLVM_SYS_<major>1_PREFIX (LLVM_SYS_201_PREFIX for LLVM 20);
  2. beside pep-build itself;
  3. on the PATH, as clang, then as clang-<major> for the LLVM it is built with (what Ubuntu's clang-20 package installs);
  4. where LLVM's packages put it when they leave it off the PATH: C:\Program Files\LLVM\bin and Scoop's llvm on Windows; Homebrew's llvm and llvm@<major> on macOS; /usr/lib/llvm-<major>/bin, then the newest /usr/lib/llvm-*/bin, on Linux.

When there is none, linking fails with an error that names what to install.

Options

install.sh [--version <x.y.z> | --archive <file>] [--prefix <dir>]
           [--yes] [--no-modify-path] [--no-prerequisites]
install.sh --uninstall [--prefix <dir>]
install.shinstall.ps1What it does
--version <x.y.z>-Version <x.y.z>Installs that release instead of the newest, or a prerelease such as 0.4.0-dev, the build of main (see below), which installing again refreshes
--archive <file>-Archive <file>Installs an archive already downloaded, checked against <file>.sha256 beside it, with the installer archive pepper-install-<version>-<target> (and its .sha256) beside it too. One not named for a release, such as a dev build, installs as the version its pep-build --version reports
--prefix <dir>-Prefix <dir>Installs into <dir> instead of ~/.pepper (%LOCALAPPDATA%\pepper)
-y, --yes-YesInstalls missing prerequisites without asking
--no-modify-path-NoModifyPathLeaves the PATH alone
--no-prerequisites-NoPrerequisitesNeither checks for nor installs what linking needs
--uninstall-UninstallRemoves the install, every toolchain in it, and the PATH entries the script added, with the home's own pep-install uninstall, else with the newest release's installer
-h, --helpGet-Help .\install.ps1Shows the usage

Piped into a shell, the script still takes options: curl ... | sh -s -- --version 0.4.0. irm ... | iex takes none, so install.ps1 reads two environment variables in their place:

VariableInstead of
PEPPER_HOME--prefix / -Prefix (both scripts)
PEPPER_VERSION-Version (install.ps1)

While the repository is private, its releases need a GitHub token to download: set GITHUB_TOKEN (or GH_TOKEN) to one that can read it, for example GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token). The raw script URLs above need it too, so download the script with gh first:

gh api repos/pep-lang/pepper/contents/scripts/install.sh -H "Accept: application/vnd.github.raw" > install.sh
GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token) sh install.sh

Uninstalling

sh install.sh --uninstall           # or: curl ... | sh -s -- --uninstall

.\install.ps1 -Uninstall

This removes the install folder (only when it holds bin/pep-build) and the PATH lines the script added. Prerequisites it installed, such as clang, stay.

How releases are built

The Release workflow (.github/workflows/release.yml) publishes:

  • the build of main, on each merge into main that changes the compiler, the runtime or the tools: main holds the version being developed as a prerelease (0.4.0-dev in VERSION and each tool's version()), and the workflow publishes it on the prerelease v0.4.0-dev, moving its tag to the merge and replacing its archives. CI runs it on the merge before its tests, which then install that build. CI and the workers install the newest published toolchain, that prerelease or a release with a higher version, whatever VERSION holds, instead of building the compiler. The newest release, the default, never picks a prerelease.
  • a release, on a vX.Y.Z tag, made by hand. Its stage 0, the compiler that builds it, is the build of main that .github/stage0 pins (see Stage 0), as for every build of main, so the release may take any version, not only the one main was developing:

    1. A pull request runs scripts/set-version.sh 0.9.0, which sets the version everywhere a tool reads it.

    2. Tag that merge v0.9.0 and push the tag. The workflow checks that the commit holds that version, builds it and publishes the release; the Docs workflow publishes the docs from the same tag. The VS Code extension is released from its own repository, pep-lang/vscode-pepper.

    3. Once it is published, the workflow pushes the branch release/start-0.10.0-dev, which starts the next minor version on main, unless main has already moved on or that branch has an open pull request (a branch left from an earlier release, as a patch release finds, is replaced); a major version is started by hand. GitHub Actions may not open pull requests in this repository, so the run's summary (and a warning) links to open its pull request; open it, and it merges once its CI passes, as any pull request does. Until it merges, merges to main publish no prerelease, since main holds the released version.

      gh pr create --base main --head release/start-0.10.0-dev --fill

For each platform, scripts/release-build.sh builds the tools, lays them out as above, archives them as pepper-<version>-<target>.tar.gz (.zip on Windows) with a .sha256, packs pep-install alone as the installer archive, pepper-install-<version>-<target>.tar.gz (.zip) with its own .sha256, and scripts/release-smoke-test.sh proves the archives work: unpacked outside the repository with no LLVM variables set, pepper build must build and run a program, and the binaries must load nothing beyond the system's C and C++ runtimes (on Linux, nothing newer than glibc 2.28: the Linux leg builds in a manylinux_2_28 container), and the installer's pep-install must run. The workflow then installs each archive with the install script. Last, it uploads the archives, their checksums, a SHA256SUMS and both scripts to the release. A pull request that changes these scripts runs every leg too, without publishing.

The pepper command

pepper is the entry point to every Pepper tool, the way go and git are: pepper <command> [arguments] runs a separate program named pep-<command> with the remaining arguments.

pepper build main.pep -o main     # runs pep-build main.pep -o main
pepper build                      # builds the project pep.toml describes
pepper run hello.pep a b          # builds hello.pep and runs it with a b
pepper fmt -w src                 # runs pep-fmt -w src
pepper -C my_app build            # runs pep-build in my_app
pepper +0.2 build                 # runs the installed 0.2.x toolchain's pep-build
pepper help                       # lists the commands it can find
pepper help build                 # runs pep-build --help
pepper --version                  # pepper's version; -v adds each command's

pepper is itself written in Pepper (tools/pepper/main.pep). The compiler is the program pep-build, so pepper build takes exactly the options the compiler does (see The compiler: pep-build).

Usage and options

pepper [+<version>] [-C <dir>]... <command> [arguments]
pepper help [<command>]
pepper --version [-v]
FormWhat it does
pepper <command> [arguments]Runs pep-<command> with the arguments (see How it finds a command)
+<version>Runs the command with that installed toolchain, such as +0.3.0 or +0.3 (see Toolchains)
-C <dir>Changes to <dir> before running the command (see Running in another folder)
