pepper help, -h, --helpPrints the usage, these options, and the commands it can find
pepper help <command>Runs pep-<command> --help
--versionPrints pepper and its version, and in a Pepper home the toolchain the folder uses and why
--version -v, --version --verboseAlso prints the version each command reports (its --version's first line, or (no version))

Options go before the command: everything after the command belongs to it, so pepper fmt --help is pep-fmt --help. pepper with no arguments, or with only -C and +<version> options, prints the usage to standard error and exits with status 2; so does a -C with no folder after it; an option other than -v or --verbose after --version is an error that exits with 2. An unknown command exits with 1. Otherwise the exit status is the command's.

The commands in this repository

CommandProgramWhat it does
pepper buildpep-buildCompiles a program, or with no file the project (The compiler: pep-build, Projects: pep.toml)
pepper newpep-newStarts a program or package in a new folder (Starting a project: pep-new and pep-init)
pepper initpep-initStarts a program or package in the current folder (Starting a project: pep-new and pep-init)
pepper runpep-runBuilds a program and runs it, like python script.py (Running a program: pep-run)
pepper installpep-installInstalls toolchains side by side and picks the default (Toolchains: pep-install)
pepper packagepep-packageAdds, removes, updates and fetches a project's dependencies (The package manager: pep-package)
pepper fmtpep-fmtFormats source (Formatting with pep-fmt)
pepper profilepep-profileProfiles a program and draws a flame graph (Profiling with pep-profile)
pepper testpep-testBuilds and runs the [Test] functions (Testing with pep-test)
pepper lsppep-lspRuns the language server, which editors start (The language server: pep-lsp)
pepper docpep-docGenerates the library reference and builds this book, or a package's reference (The documentation builder: pep-doc)

Every one of them, pep-build included, is a Pepper program under tools/, built with pep-build.

Building it

Build pepper with a pep-build (an installed one, or one you built from tools/compiler; see Building from source) and put it next to it:

target/bin/pep-build tools/pepper/main.pep -o target/bin/pepper

On Windows, name the output target\bin\pepper.exe.

How it finds a command

Outside a Pepper home, pepper <command> looks for pep-<command> (pep-<command>.exe on Windows) in the directory that holds the running pepper first, then in each directory on the PATH, and runs the first it finds. So the tools installed next to pepper win over others with the same name, and any program named pep-<name> on the PATH adds the command <name>: a tool of your own becomes pepper <name> once it is installed. On Linux and macOS only files with an execute permission count.

The command takes pepper's place, with its standard input, output and error: on Linux and macOS pepper execs it, so signals such as Ctrl-C reach the command directly and its exit status is pepper's. Windows cannot replace a process, so there pepper waits for the command, leaves Ctrl-C to it, and exits with its exit status. A command name is lowercase letters, digits, - and _; anything else, such as a path, is not a command.

An unknown command is an error that suggests the closest command and lists the ones pepper found:

$ pepper buidl main.pep
pepper: error: 'buidl' is not a pepper command; did you mean 'build'?

Commands:
  build
  fmt

Running in another folder

-C <dir> runs the command as if pepper had been started in <dir>, like git -C: pepper -C my_app build builds the project in my_app from anywhere. Repeated, each -C is relative to the one before, so pepper -C a -C b build runs in a/b; an empty -C "" changes nothing. A folder that cannot be entered is an error that exits with status 1:

$ pepper -C nowhere build
pepper: error: cannot change to 'nowhere': No such file or directory

-C and +<version> are the only options that go before a command. They work with help and the old form too.

Toolchains

Installed by pep-install, pepper lives in the Pepper home's bin folder (~/.pepper/bin, %LOCALAPPDATA%\pepper\bin on Windows), beside the installed toolchains, and runs the tools of one of them, or of a toolchain in a folder PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN_PATH lists (see More toolchain folders). The first of these that names a toolchain picks it:

  1. +<version> before the command: pepper +0.3.0 build;
  2. the PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN environment variable;
  3. toolchain = "0.3" in [package] of the nearest pep.toml at or above the folder the command runs in (after -C), so a project pins the compiler it builds with (see Projects: pep.toml);
  4. the default, which pepper install use sets.

A version is exact (0.3.0), or a prefix that picks the newest installed toolchain that starts so (0.3, 0), or latest for the newest installed. pepper then looks for pep-<command> in that toolchain's bin folder first, then beside pepper, then on the PATH, and runs it with PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN set to the exact version, so a pepper that command runs uses the same toolchain. pepper install always runs the home's own pep-install, which needs no toolchain.

When the toolchain picked is not installed, or none is installed, pepper says so and how to install it, and exits with status 1:

$ pepper build
pepper: error: toolchain 0.4 (pinned by /work/app/pep.toml) is not installed; install it with 'pepper install add 0.4'

pepper install which shows which toolchain a folder uses and why. Outside a Pepper home, as when it is built from this repository, pepper runs the tools beside it, and +<version> is an error.

The old form

Before pepper build, pepper was the compiler. A first argument that is a .pep file or an option still runs the compiler with the whole command line, after a warning:

$ pepper main.pep -o main
pepper: warning: 'pepper main.pep ...' is deprecated; use 'pepper build main.pep ...'

The old form will be removed in a later release.

Toolchains: pep-install

pep-install installs Pepper toolchains side by side and picks the default one, the way rustup and nvm do. pepper install runs it with the same arguments:

pepper install list               # the installed toolchains, marking the default and the one in use here
pepper install list --available   # the releases with an archive for this machine
pepper install add 0.3            # installs the newest 0.3.x; the default stays as it is
pepper install use 0.3.0          # makes it the default
pepper install update             # installs the newest release and makes it the default
pepper install add --force 0.3.0  # installs 0.3.0 again, replacing it
pepper install remove 0.2.1
pepper install which              # the toolchain this folder uses, why, and its pep-build
pepper install setup              # sets this machine up: installs, sets the default and the PATH, checks
pepper install uninstall          # removes the home and its PATH changes

pep-install <command> [arguments]

A toolchain is one release of the compiler, its runtime and the tools (pep-build, pep-fmt, pep-test, ...). The pepper command that pep-install sits beside runs the tools of the toolchain a folder uses: the one pepper +<version> names, else PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN's, else the one the project's pep.toml pins with toolchain = "0.3", else the default (see Toolchains).

To install a command-line tool built from a package, rather than a toolchain, use pepper package install.

Options and commands

Command or optionWhat it does
listLists the installed toolchains, newest first, marking the default and the one the current folder uses, with why
list --available, -aLists the releases that have an archive for this machine instead, marking those installed
add <version>Installs the newest release <version> names, unless it is installed; it becomes the default only when there was none
add --force <version>, -fInstalls it even when it is installed, replacing the home's copy
use <version>Makes the newest installed toolchain <version> names the default
updateInstalls the newest release, unless it is installed, and makes it the default; older toolchains stay installed. Then updates the home's pepper and pep-install from it
update --force, -fInstalls the newest release even when it is installed, replacing the home's copy
remove <version>Removes the installed toolchain <version> names; it must name just one, and not the default
whichPrints the toolchain the current folder uses and why, then the path of its pep-build; fails when that toolchain is not installed
setup [<version>]Sets this machine up for Pepper: installs the newest release <version> names (default latest), makes it the default, puts its pepper and pep-install in the home's bin, adds that to the PATH, offers to install what linking needs, and builds and runs a program to check (see Setting a machine up)
setup --archive <file>Installs the downloaded release archive <file> instead, checked against <file>.sha256 beside it
setup --yes, -yInstalls missing prerequisites without asking
setup --no-modify-pathLeaves the PATH and the shell startup files alone
setup --no-prerequisitesNeither checks for nor installs clang and the other prerequisites
uninstallRemoves the Pepper home and the PATH changes setup made for it
--path <dir>Also finds toolchains in <dir>, before those PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN_PATH lists; repeatable, before or after the command (see More toolchain folders)
-h, --helpPrints the commands; after a command, that command's options
-V, --versionPrints the version

A <version> is exact (0.3.0), or a prefix (0.3, 0) for the newest release, or installed toolchain, that starts so, or latest for the newest. A prerelease such as 0.4.0-dev, the build of main that each merge replaces, is picked only by naming it exactly; prefixes, latest and update leave prereleases out. Only releases are installed; there is no nightly channel.

The exit status is 0 on success, 1 when a command fails, and 2 for a mistake on the command line.

Where toolchains go

The Pepper home holds them:

~/.pepper/bin/pepper                 the entry point
~/.pepper/bin/pep-install
~/.pepper/toolchains/0.3.0/bin/      a toolchain's pep-build, pep-fmt, ...
~/.pepper/toolchains/0.3.0/runtime/  and its runtime
~/.pepper/default-toolchain          the default toolchain's version

The install scripts set up the home by running setup (see Setting a machine up): it installs the newest release this way and puts its pepper and pep-install in bin.

update replaces the home's pepper and pep-install with the new toolchain's when they differ. Each is written beside the old one and renamed into place, the old one first moved aside to <name>.old; on Windows, where a running program cannot be removed, that .old file is removed by the next update.

add --force and update --force install a toolchain that is already installed again, the way a fresh one is: downloaded, checked and unpacked beside its folder. The old folder is then moved aside, the new one put in its place and the old one removed, so no stale files remain, and a failed download or unpack leaves the old toolchain as it was. On Windows a toolchain one of whose programs is running (a pep-lsp the editor started, say) cannot be moved, and the install fails, leaving it in place.

The home is the folder above the running pep-install when that is a home (it has a toolchains folder), or the one whose toolchain it is (<home>/toolchains/<version>/bin), else PEPPER_HOME, else %LOCALAPPDATA%\pepper on Windows and ~/.pepper elsewhere.

Setting a machine up

setup is what the install scripts run, from the installer archive each release carries (pepper-install-<version>-<target>.tar.gz, .zip on Windows, holding only pep-install). It does what add and use do, then:

  • puts the toolchain's pepper and pep-install in the home's bin, as update does;
  • unless that folder is on the PATH already or --no-modify-path is given, adds it: on Windows to the user's PATH, elsewhere with a line in ~/.profile, and in ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile and ~/.zshrc when they exist (~/.zshrc also when the shell is zsh), and in fish's conf.d/pepper.fish when fish is installed. Each line follows a # Added by the Pepper installer comment;
  • unless --no-prerequisites is given, checks for what linking a program needs and offers to install what is missing, asking on the terminal first unless --yes is given: Xcode's command line tools on macOS, the Visual Studio Build Tools' C++ workload on Windows (with winget), and clang when the check program's build finds none (apt, dnf, yum, pacman or zypper on Linux, through sudo when not root; winget or Scoop on Windows). It notes when OpenSSL 3, which the tls module loads, is missing, and on macOS offers brew install openssl@3;
  • builds and runs a small program with the home's pepper, from an empty folder, and fails when it cannot.

A toolchain from before side-by-side toolchains, which has no pepper to put in bin, cannot be set up. An archive named for no release (a dev build, pepper-dev-<target>) is installed under the version its pep-build reports.

uninstall removes the home, refusing a folder that holds neither toolchains nor bin/pep-build, and the PATH lines setup added for that home's bin.

More toolchain folders

Toolchains are also found in the folders PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN_PATH lists, separated as PATH separates them (; on Windows, : elsewhere), and for pep-install in each --path folder, which come first. Each is laid out as the home's toolchains folder is, a folder per toolchain named by its version:

/opt/pepper/0.3.0/bin/pep-build
/opt/pepper/0.3.0/runtime/

PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN_PATH=/opt/pepper pepper +0.3.0 build main.pep
pepper install --path /opt/pepper use 0.3.0

The home's own toolchains folder is searched first, so a toolchain there wins over one of the same version elsewhere. list marks a toolchain found elsewhere with its folder; use, which and pepper +<version> take it as they take one in the home, and add and update count it as installed (--force installs into the home all the same). remove removes only toolchains in the home: a toolchain in another folder is left to whoever put it there. A project's pep.toml cannot add folders, since where toolchains are differs from one machine to the next.

Editors

The VS Code extension runs the language server of the toolchain the workspace uses, as pepper install which reports it, and offers to install Pepper, the toolchain the workspace needs, or a newer default when they are missing or old; see pep-lsp.

Downloads

add and update find this machine's archive (linux-x64, macos-arm64, macos-x64 or windows-x64) among the GitHub releases, as the install scripts do, download it and check it against its .sha256. The archive is unpacked beside the toolchain's folder first, so a download that fails or does not match its checksum leaves nothing behind.

VariableWhat it does
PEPPER_HOMEWhere toolchains go, when pep-install does not run from a home
PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN_PATHMore folders to find toolchains in (see More toolchain folders)
PEPPER_INSTALL_RELEASES_URLLists the releases from this URL instead of GitHub's API, for a mirror; it serves the same JSON
GITHUB_TOKEN, GH_TOKENA token sent to GitHub's API while the repository is private, and to nothing else

The compiler: pep-build

pep-build compiles a Pepper program into an executable, or into a library for C code to link. pepper build runs it with the same arguments, so everything on this page applies to both spellings:

pepper build main.pep -o main          # the same as: pep-build main.pep -o main

pep-build [OPTIONS] [<entry.pep>]

This page lists every option. pep-build --help prints the same list in short, and pepper help build runs it.

All options at a glance

OptionWhat it doesDefault
<entry.pep>The program's entry filethe project's, from pep.toml
-I <dir>Add a folder to search for imported modulesthe runtime's folder only
--import <name>Load a module into every file of the programnone
--entry <name>The function the program starts in, instead of main; it takes no parameters or one String[], and every main is left out (not with --test or --lib)main
--no-runtimeCompile without the standard librarythe runtime is used
-o <file>Name the executable or library (with --emit-static, the folder)<entry stem> in the current folder; a project's name in its folder
--lib static, --lib sharedBuild a library for C instead of an executablean executable
--lib xcframework, --lib swift-packageBuild an iOS .xcframework, or a Swift package around one, for an appan executable
--lib aarBuild an Android library (.aar) holding a shared library for each ABI, for an appan executable
--bindings swift, --bindings javaWith --lib static or --lib shared (java: --lib shared), also write Swift or Java bindings of the [Export]ed functions beside the headernone
--testBuild the [Test] functions of the entry file (or of several files of one folder) into a test programoff
--lockedFail, rather than fetch, when pep.lock is out of date with pep.tomloff, or PEPPER_LOCKED
--offlineFetch no dependency over the network; fail on one neither .pep/deps nor the download cache holdsoff, or PEPPER_OFFLINE
--frozenBoth --locked and --offlineoff
--no-build-scriptsFail, rather than run it, when a dependency has a build script; a [native] table still compiles, unless a dependency's has flags that could load code (which it allows)off, or PEPPER_NO_BUILD_SCRIPTS
--build <dir>Folder for intermediate files.pep/build (in a project's folder when building it)
--emit-llvmWrite LLVM IR instead of an executableoff
--emit-static, --emit-static=keepWrite the source with each static block expanded, instead of compilingoff
--emit-ast[=text|json]Print the syntax tree instead of compilingoff
--emit-linkedPrint every file's syntax tree after linking, as JSON, instead of compilingoff
--emit-checkedPrint what the checks after linking report, instead of compilingoff
--emit-modelPrint the program's sema model before any sema pass, as JSON, instead of compilingoff
--emit-model-step <N>With --emit-model, print the model after the first N sema steps0
--emit-stepsPrint the names of the sema steps, one per line, instead of compilingoff
-O, -O0 to -O3Optimization level-O0, or PEPPER_OPT_LEVEL
--lto=full, --lto=offLink-time optimizationoff
-march=, -mcpu=, -mtune=, -m<feature>, -mno-<feature> (-m <option>)The CPU to generate code forclang's default for the target
-g, --emit-debugEmit debug infooff
--debug-static=source, --debug-static=expandedWith -g, step through static blocks as written or expandedsource
--frame-pointersKeep every function's frame pointer, for profilersoff
--target <triple>Compile for another platformthe machine compiling
--sysroot <dir>The target's system librariesPEPPER_SYSROOT_<TRIPLE>
-l <lib>Link a C librarythe platform's defaults
-L <dir>Add a folder the linker searchesPEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH
--MSVCUse the MSVC linker (not ported)off
-D <name>[=<value>]Define a build optionnone
-F <names>, --features <names>Turn on features of the project's packageits default feature
--no-default-featuresLeave the project's package's default feature offoff
--allBuild every member of the project's workspacethe project alone, or every member in a root with no [package]
-p <name>, --package <name>Build this workspace member; repeatable
--no-runtime-checks=<list>Remove kinds of runtime checkevery check on
--no-cacheDo not use the build cachethe cache is used
--cache <dir>Folder for the build cachePEPPER_CACHE_DIR, else .pep/cache (in a project's folder when building it)
--verify-cacheCheck cache hits against fresh codeoff, or PEPPER_CACHE_VERIFY
--no-verify-cacheDo not check cache hits
-T <channel>, --TallPrint timings and cache decisionsoff
-v, --verboseAccepted; prints nothing more yetoff
--compile-part <dir>, --part <N>=<object>, --compilation-unit-worker <dir>, --members <names>, --member <dir>, --print-members, --build-script <dir>Internal: what a build runs in the children it starts, and what pep-test asks
-h, --helpPrint the options
-V, --versionPrint the version

An option that takes a value accepts it as the next argument or attached: -I lib, -Ilib, --target aarch64-apple-darwin and --target=aarch64-apple-darwin are all the same. -O, --emit-ast and --emit-static take a value only attached (-O3, --emit-ast=json), so the argument after them is never read as their value. Short options that take no value combine (-gv is -g -v). Options may come before or after the entry file, and every argument after -- is a file. An unknown option is an error, and the compiler exits with status 2 after a short usage message.

Inputs and imports

The entry file

pepper build main.pep

The file that holds main. The compiler finds the files it imports on its own (see Modules and imports), so a program of many files is compiled by naming its entry file alone. Only the first file named is compiled; any others are ignored.

With no file, the compiler builds the project whose pep.toml is in the current folder or the nearest folder above it: its [build] table names the entry file and the output, and the build goes in the project's .pep (see Projects: pep.toml). With no file and no pep.toml, it stops with error: no source files provided, and no pep.toml in <folder> or a folder above it.

cd my_app/src
pepper build              # builds my_app/pep.toml's program into my_app/

An entry file inside a project (under a folder with a pep.toml) imports the project's dependencies, and its [build] table's include folders and link libraries apply to it as well.

Before compiling a program in a project, the compiler fetches whatever pep.lock lists and the project's .pep/deps lacks or holds at another commit, and the Git dependencies that pep.toml, or the pep.toml of a path dependency it reaches, names and pep.lock does not list yet, by running pep-package fetch (beside pep-build, else on the PATH). Without pep-package, it checks the missing commits out with git itself, and asks for pepper package fetch to move a checkout at another commit. A dependency checked out on a branch is left as it is. See The package manager: pep-package.

--locked, --offline, --frozen

These make the fetch reproducible, for CI (see Reproducible builds):

  • --locked (or PEPPER_LOCKED=1) fails when pep.lock is out of date with pep.toml, instead of updating it. A Git dependency pep.toml names that pep.lock does not list is an error before anything is fetched; otherwise the build runs pep-package fetch --locked, even when nothing is missing, so a changed range is caught too.
  • --offline (or PEPPER_OFFLINE=1) fetches nothing over the network: pep-package runs with --offline, taking a locked package .pep/deps lacks from the download cache, and failing on one the cache lacks too. Without pep-package, a locked package .pep/deps lacks is an error that names it.
  • --frozen is both.
$ pepper build --offline
fetching the dependencies of app/pep.toml failed (pep-package -C app fetch --offline exited with 1):
pep-package: error: cannot fetch github:someone/geometry: --offline, and neither app/.pep/deps/github.com/someone/geometry nor the package cache holds the commit 0582024b9cd7; run 'pepper package fetch' without --offline (or PEPPER_OFFLINE) first

Build scripts and --no-build-scripts

Once the dependencies are fetched, and before it loads the program, the compiler runs the build script of each package the build turns on (the project's first): it builds the script for the machine it runs on, with itself and --build-script, into .pep/build/<package>-<hash>/, where the script's package sees only its [build-dependencies] and their own scripts run; then it runs the script in the package's folder, links what it says to, defines the build options it names, and resolves the package's import generated to the modules it wrote. A script whose inputs, the Pepper files it imports among them, have not changed since its last run is not run again. The script builds in the program's build cache, even under --no-cache, whose record of the script's build names the files it imports. The --emit-* modes run them too, since the program they load may import what a script generates.

After a package's script, if it has one, the compiler compiles the C its [native] table and the [target.'<condition>'.native] tables that hold for the target name, with its own clang for the target, the system root and the -O level, into .pep/build/<package>-<hash>/native/<target>/, and links the objects. An object whose source, included headers (from clang's -MD list) and flags have not changed is not compiled again.

--no-build-scripts (or PEPPER_NO_BUILD_SCRIPTS=1) fails instead of running a dependency's script, which runs that package's code on this machine; the project's own script still runs, and so does every [native] table, which runs no package code. A dependency's table is refused when one of its flags is not on the short list that cannot load code or name a file ([native] lists it), since a flag such as -fplugin= makes clang load a plugin from the package. The error is at the flag in the dependency's pep.toml:

app/.pep/deps/github.com/someone/native/pep.toml:8:10: error: '--no-build-scripts' (or PEPPER_NO_BUILD_SCRIPTS) refuses the clang flag '-fplugin=x' of the dependency 'native', which could load code or name a file; it allows only -O0 to -O3, -Os, -Oz, -std=, -march=, -mcpu=, -mtune= and plain -W, -f and -m options; read the flag, and build without that option to use it

A dependency's build script is refused outright:

error: the dependency 'native' has a build script, app/.pep/deps/github.com/someone/native/build.pep, which '--no-build-scripts' (or PEPPER_NO_BUILD_SCRIPTS) refuses to run; read it, and build without that option to run it

-I <dir>

Adds a folder to search for modules imported by name (import geometry; looks for geometry/module.pep). The -I folders are searched in the order given, then a project's [build] include folders, then the runtime's folder. A project's dependencies are found through its pep.toml instead. See Dependencies and search paths.

pepper build tools/pep-fmt/main.pep -o pep-fmt

--import <name>

Loads a module (<name>/module.pep) or a file (<name>.pep), found on the search paths, into every file of the program, the way the standard library's prelude is loaded. Its definitions come ahead of the runtime's, so one that redefines a runtime export wins. Repeat it for more modules. A name that cannot be found is an error that lists the folders searched. See The runtime prelude and --import.

--no-runtime

Compiles without the standard library: the runtime is neither looked for nor loaded, so only the program's own files and what -I reaches are compiled. For testing the compiler; ordinary programs need the runtime (print, String and Array all live there).

Without this option the compiler finds the runtime as Getting started describes, and PEPPER_RUNTIME names its folder outright.

Output

-o <file>

The path of the executable, or with --lib of the library. Without it, the output goes to the current folder, named after the entry file with no extension (main for main.pep); with --lib, the library's usual file name for that stem (libmain.a). Building a project with no file, it is the [build] table's output, else the package's name in the project's folder (libname.a with --lib), with .exe added when building for Windows and the name has no extension. Windows runs only files ending in .exe, so otherwise name the output there: -o main.exe. The folders the path names are made when they do not exist.

With --emit-static, it is the folder the expanded source goes into.

--lib static, --lib shared

Builds a library for C code to link instead of an executable, with a C header beside it that declares the program's [Export]ed functions. No main is needed.

  • --lib static writes an archive: libname.a (name.lib on Windows), holding the objects of the whole program, the runtime's included, with the index of their symbols that linkers search. The compiler writes it itself in the target's format (GNU's for Linux and Android, the BSD format Apple's linkers read for macOS and iOS, the COFF archive for Windows), so no archiver needs to be installed, and building one for another platform needs no system root: nothing is linked. A program linking it also links the libraries the program does, which the header names in a comment (/* Link the static library with: -lm */).
  • --lib shared links a shared library: libname.so, libname.dylib on macOS, name.dll (and its import library name.lib) on Windows. Its soname is its file name; on macOS and iOS its install name is @rpath/<file name>, so a program that links it finds it on its run path. Linking one for another platform needs its system root, as an executable does (--sysroot). For Android, when the program imports tls, the .so holds the toolchain's static OpenSSL, and its license goes beside it as LICENSE-OpenSSL.txt.

The header goes beside the library, named for it without the lib prefix (libname.a has name.h). A library that exports nothing is built with a warning. See Calling Pepper from C.

--bindings swift, --bindings java

With --lib static or --lib shared, also writes bindings beside the header name.h, so Swift, Kotlin or Java code calls the [Export]ed functions with its own values (a String in and out, an object for each struct handle), named in camel case:

  • --bindings swift writes name.swift, a Swift function for each export and a class for each struct handle, and the module.modulemap of the C module they import, Cname (the header). Compile name.swift with the app's Swift code and -I its folder.
  • --bindings java (only with --lib shared) writes name.jar, the class pepper.name.Name (in Pascal case) of a static native method for each export, which loads libname.so, and a class for each struct handle (AutoCloseable); and name_jni.c, the JNI functions of those methods, which the link compiles into the library. The class files are written by the compiler, so this needs no JDK, but the link needs a clang that finds jni.h, as the Android NDK's does. An export that passes a C function pointer, or whose name Java cannot use, is an error.

--lib swift-package and --lib aar write them themselves; with those, or without --lib, --bindings is a usage error. See iOS and Android.

--lib xcframework, --lib swift-package

Builds the static library of an iOS app's Pepper code for every iOS target at once, packaged as Xcode and SwiftPM take it. Each is named for its output, which must be a Swift module name (letters, digits and _):

  • --lib xcframework writes Name.xcframework (-o Name.xcframework; the output must end in .xcframework, since it is replaced whole): ios-arm64/ for devices and ios-arm64_x86_64-simulator/ for the simulator on Apple silicon and Intel Macs, each with libName.a, the header Name.h and a module.modulemap, so Swift can import Name, and the Info.plist listing them. The compiler builds the three static libraries by running itself with --lib static --target <triple>, side by side, each in a folder of the build folder's xcframework/, and writes the simulator's two archives into one universal file itself, as lipo would, so this needs no Xcode and works on any system.
  • --lib swift-package writes the folder Name (-o Name) holding CName.xcframework (as above, its module named CName), the Swift bindings of --bindings swift as Sources/Name/Name.swift, and a Package.swift whose library product Name is that Swift target over the binary target, for iOS 15 and later. An app adds it as a local package (.package(path: "Name")), or from the repository it is committed to.

They cannot be combined with --target or the --emit options. See iOS and Android.

--lib aar

Builds the shared library of an Android app's Pepper code for every Android ABI at once (arm64-v8a and x86_64), packaged as an Android library a Gradle build adds: name.aar (-o name.aar), named for its output, which takes letters, digits and _. It holds jni/<abi>/libname.so for each ABI, the header as include/name.h, an AndroidManifest.xml for the package pepper.name and API level 30, the Java bindings of --bindings java as classes.jar (each .so holds their JNI functions), the empty R.txt and res/ an .aar must have, and, when the program imports tls, OpenSSL's license as LICENSE-OpenSSL.txt. The compiler builds each library by running itself with --lib shared --bindings java --target <triple>, side by side, each in a folder of the build folder's aar/, and writes the zip itself, so this needs the Android NDK (found as for any Android link: --sysroot, ANDROID_NDK_HOME or ANDROID_HOME) but no Gradle or JDK. It cannot be combined with --target or the --emit options. See iOS and Android.

--test

Builds the entry file's tests into a test program, which pep-test runs. A build without it leaves every [Test] function out. With it:

  • the [Test] functions are kept, and the build option TEST is defined (as by -D TEST), for code only tests use ([BuildOption("TEST")]);
  • the runtime's testing module is loaded into every file (as by --import testing);
  • the entry file's main is replaced by one that answers --list (one line per test: name, file:line, returns or panics, and the text a [ShouldPanic] panic must contain, separated by tabs) and --run NAME [--timeout SECONDS] (run that test; a test still running after the timeout ends the program with exit status 124).

Only the entry file's [Test] functions become tests. Given several files of one folder (pep-build --test a_test.pep b_test.pep), it builds the tests of them all into one program: a generated entry file in that folder (_pep_test_main.pep, never written to disk) imports each file and registers its tests, and each file keeps the scope it has in any program. --list then gives each test's own file, and --run also takes FILE::NAME, as --list spells the file, to tell apart tests of one name in two files. It cannot be combined with --lib. See Unit tests.

--build <dir>

The folder for intermediate files: the program's objects and, with --emit-llvm, its IR. The default is .pep/build in the current folder, or in the project's folder when building a project with no file.

--emit-llvm

Writes the whole program's LLVM IR to <build>/<name>.ll (.pep/build/main.ll for main.pep), optimized at the -O level, and stops there: nothing is linked and no executable is written.

pepper build main.pep -O --emit-llvm      # .pep/build/main.ll

--emit-static, --emit-static=keep

Writes a copy of the program's source with each static block replaced by the code it emits, like a C compiler's -E, and stops there: nothing is compiled to code. Use it to see what a reflection loop, a serializer or a library's block does to the program (see Seeing what a static block emits).

pepper build main.pep --emit-static              # main.static/main.pep
pepper build main.pep --emit-static -o expanded  # expanded/main.pep
pepper build expanded/main.pep -o main           # the same program
  • Every file of the program in the entry file's folder (and the folders under it) is written into the output folder at the same relative path, so the folder builds as a whole program; files with no block are copied unchanged. The runtime and libraries found elsewhere are not copied. The originals are never overwritten.
  • The folder is -o's, else <entry stem>.static in the current folder.
  • Each expansion is a { ... } block between # static (out, value) expanded from main.pep:12:5 and # end static. --emit-static=keep also keeps the block as written, as # comments above it; --emit-static=expand is the default, the same as --emit-static.
  • A block in a generic function expands once per specialization. The generic function stays as written, and after it comes a concrete override for each type the program uses it with (describe<Point>(value: Point)), its blocks expanded, so the copy still builds into the same program. A block in a method of a generic struct, or in a generic method, stays, with each specialization's expansion above it as # comments.
  • When pep-fmt is next to the compiler or on PATH, it formats the copies, wrapping long lines.
  • Errors a block reports stop it, as they stop a build. Errors in the code a block emits are found when the copy is built, at the copy's line.

--emit-ast

Parses the entry file only and prints its syntax tree to standard output, instead of compiling. Imports are not followed and nothing is checked.

--emit-ast and --emit-ast=text print the tree as source-like text. --emit-ast=json prints it as one line of JSON: each node an object with its fields in declaration order, each enum case an object with the case's name as its one key, and each span {"start": ..., "end": ...} in bytes. The compiler's parser written in Pepper (tools/compiler) prints the same JSON, and its test compares the two over every source file in the repository.

--emit-linked

Loads the program as a build does (the entry file, every file its imports reach, and the runtime), links it, and prints it to standard output as one line of JSON instead of compiling. Nothing after linking is checked, so a program with type errors prints too; a file that cannot be read or parsed stops it, as it stops a build.

The JSON is an object with three keys:

  • files: every file in load order (the entry file first), each with its name as the program reached it, its namespace, its module_root folder (or null), whether it is part of the prelude (the runtime and --import files) or a prelude_part (another file of a forced module), the index of the file each of its imports names (or null when one did not resolve), which of them are folder_imports (a local import of a module folder), and its module, the syntax tree as --emit-ast=json prints it after linking renamed what the file imports and gave its private declarations their program-wide names (helper@io/file).
  • errors: the linking errors, by file and position, each with its file index, span, message, whether it is an unresolved import, and its note ([span, message], or null).
  • overload_unions: each overload set that spans files, by name, with its functions grouped by module.

-I, --import, --no-runtime, -D and --test apply as for a build. The compiler's linker written in Pepper (tools/compiler) prints the same JSON, and its test compares the two.

--emit-checked

Loads and links the program as --emit-linked does, runs the checks that come before type checking, and prints what they report instead of compiling: the errors, rendered as a build reports them, then the warnings. The errors are the linking errors; when there are none, a [__BuiltIn] declaration outside the runtime; when there is none of those either, every use of a declaration another file keeps private or this file does not import. The warnings are deprecated syntax, comparisons with a build option -D does not define, and uses of declarations marked [Deprecated]. A program with neither prints an empty line.

-I, --import, --no-runtime, -D and --test apply as for a build. The compiler written in Pepper (tools/compiler) prints the same text, and its test compares the two.

--emit-model

Loads, links and checks the program as --emit-checked does, builds the sema model of each file and joins them, and prints the model as one line of JSON instead of compiling: what the sema builder made of the syntax trees (for, with, match, ?, destructuring, ranges, collection literals and properties lowered), before any sema pass runs. Object keys are sorted, and so are the sets (private_functions and the extension_scopes). When the checks or the builder reject the program, it prints the rendered error and fails.

-I, --import, --no-runtime, -D and --test apply as for a build. The compiler written in Pepper (tools/compiler) prints the same JSON, and its test compares the two.

--emit-model-step <N>

With --emit-model, runs the first N steps of the sema passes before printing the model. A step is one pass run, in the order the compiler runs them (platform filters first, then [Equatable], closure lifting and the rest); --emit-steps lists them. When a step rejects the program, it prints the rendered error and fails. The compiler written in Pepper runs the same steps, and its test compares the model after each.

--emit-steps

Loads, links, checks and builds the program as --emit-model does, runs every sema pass, and prints the name of each step run, one per line, instead of compiling: the numbering --emit-model-step uses.

Optimization and code generation

-O, -O<level>

The optimization level: -O0 (no optimization, the default), -O1, -O2 or -O3. -O alone is -O2, and it does not take the next argument as its level, so pepper build -O main.pep works. Each level runs the pipeline clang runs at that level. Without the option, the level is PEPPER_OPT_LEVEL (0 to 3) when that is set and not empty.

At -O0 a panic prints a backtrace after its message; at any other level it prints the message alone, unless the program runs with PEPPER_BACKTRACE=1 (see Backtraces on panic).

--lto=full, --lto=off

Link-time optimization. With --lto=full, once every file is compiled the whole program is optimized again as one module, so a call into another file (the runtime included) can be inlined. --lto=off optimizes each file alone, which links sooner. The default is off: full optimizes the whole program again on every build, an edit's too, so it suits a release build. --lto=full at -O0 is an error that asks for -O.

With it, each file is optimized by LLVM's pre-link pipeline and kept as bitcode (in the build cache, as an object is), then the compiler links them into one module, makes every symbol internal but main and the C exports of [Export] functions, runs LLVM's link-time pipeline over the whole program, and writes its objects, one per logical CPU in parallel, which link as usual. No linker plugin is involved, so it works on every target. It applies to a library too (--lib).

-march=<cpu>, -mcpu=<cpu>, -mtune=<cpu>, -m<feature>, -mno-<feature>

The -m options choose the CPU the code is generated for, with clang's names and meanings (-m <option>, with a space, is the same as -m<option>):

  • On x86-64, -march=<cpu> names the CPU: x86-64-v3, znver4, or native for the machine compiling.
  • On AArch64, -mcpu=<cpu> names the CPU (apple-m2, native) and -march=<arch> the architecture (armv8.2-a+crypto).
  • -mtune=<cpu> changes only how instructions are scheduled.
  • -m<feature> adds a CPU feature (-mavx2), and -mno-<feature> removes one (-mno-avx2).

Without them the program runs on any machine of its kind: clang's default CPU for the target (x86-64; apple-m1 on Apple arm64). An option the target's architecture does not take is an error worded as clang words it: -mcpu= on x86-64 (unsupported option '-mcpu=' for target ...; use '-march' or '-mtune'), -march= on WebAssembly, an AArch64 -march= that is not armv<version>-a (invalid arch name), native for another platform's target, or an empty value. A CPU or feature name LLVM does not know is passed on, and LLVM warns about it. The last of each option wins; the features come after those the CPU implies. The chosen CPU, its features and its tuning are part of the build cache's key.

-g, --emit-debug

Emits debug info for gdb, lldb, Visual Studio and WinDbg: DWARF 4 in the executable on Linux and macOS, and CodeView on Windows, where the linker writes <output>.pdb beside the executable. On macOS it also runs dsymutil to write <output>.dSYM beside the executable, when the program is built for the Mac it runs on. It works with -O. See Debugging.

A Windows build without -g also writes <output>.pdb, holding only the program's function names, which is where backtraces read them.

Every link leaves out the functions and data nothing uses, except a Windows build with -g: its linker keeps them all, so the program is larger.

--debug-static=source, --debug-static=expanded

With -g, chooses which source the debugger shows for the code a static block emits (see Stepping through a static block):

  • source, the default: the block as written. Stepping stops on a compile-time loop's header once per pass, then on its body.
  • expanded: a copy of each file with its blocks expanded, as --emit-static writes it (unformatted), saved beside the output as <name>.static.pep (main.static.pep for main.pep; a file in a folder under the entry's keeps that folder). The debugger steps through the expanded statements, sum = sum + p.y;, and a breakpoint on one of its lines stops in that pass. The rest of the program stays in its own files. A build with it does not use the build cache.
pepper build -g --debug-static=expanded main.pep -o main   # main, main.static.pep

--frame-pointers

Keeps the frame pointer in every function, even when optimizing, as clang's -fno-omit-frame-pointer does. A sampling profiler then walks the stack of each sample by following frame pointers, which is fast and finds every frame of Pepper code; without them, optimized code reuses the register and a profiler loses the callers of whatever was running. It costs a register and a few instructions per call. pep-profile builds with it, -O and -g. It is part of the build cache's key.

Targets and cross-compiling

--target <triple>

Compiles for another platform, named by an LLVM target triple: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin, x86_64-apple-darwin, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, wasm32-wasip1, aarch64-apple-ios, aarch64-apple-ios-simulator, x86_64-apple-ios-simulator, aarch64-linux-android or x86_64-linux-android, with a version allowed where clang allows one (arm64-apple-macosx14.0, aarch64-apple-ios17.0, aarch64-linux-android33). An unsupported triple is an error that lists the supported ones. [Target(...)] selects code for the target. The default is the machine the compiler runs on. See Cross-compiling and iOS and Android.

--sysroot <dir>

The folder that holds the target's system headers and libraries, passed to the link driver, for linking with --target. Without it, the folder named by PEPPER_SYSROOT_<TRIPLE> when that is set: the triple in capitals, with _ for each character that is not a letter or digit (PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_APPLE_DARWIN for aarch64-apple-darwin). An iOS or Android triple's variable leaves out the OS version (PEPPER_SYSROOT_AARCH64_APPLE_IOS_SIMULATOR for aarch64-apple-ios17.0-simulator). For iOS it is an iOS SDK, which on a Mac defaults to the one xcrun names; for Android it is the NDK (see ANDROID_NDK_HOME below).

Linking

-l <lib>

Links a C library, as -l does for clang: -l m links libm. Repeat it for more libraries. A project's [build] table adds its link libraries. A program's [Link] attributes name libraries from the source instead. See Linking.

-L <dir>

Adds a folder the linker searches for libraries. Folders given with -L come first, then those of [Link(path = ...)], then those in PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATH (separated like PATH: :, or ; on Windows). See Library search directories.

pepper build main.pep -L libs -l foo        # links libs/libfoo

--MSVC

Reserved for linking with Microsoft's linker. It is not ported, so it is an error on every platform; Windows executables link with clang and lld.

The link driver is clang. When PEPPER_LLVM_PREFIX, else LLVM_SYS_<major>1_PREFIX (for the LLVM the compiler was built with, such as LLVM_SYS_201_PREFIX for LLVM 20), names an LLVM install, its bin/clang and lld are used; else a clang beside pep-build, then one on the PATH (clang, then clang-<major>), then one where LLVM's packages install it off the PATH. With none, the link fails with an error naming what to install. Installing Pepper lists the folders searched.

Build options

-D <name>, -D <name>=<value>

Defines a build option. A bare name is name=1, as in C. [BuildOption] and [Target(BuildOption(...))] select code by it, and static blocks read it with reflect.build_option. Repeat it for more options; of two that name the same option, the later wins. A name must be an identifier (-D 2FAST is an error). Build options are part of the build cache's key. See Build options.

pepper build main.pep -D USE_ZLIB -D LOG_LEVEL=2

-F <names>, --features <names>, --no-default-features

--features turns on features of the project's package, from the [features] of its pep.toml: a comma-separated list (--features tls,gzip), or the option repeated. Its default feature is on unless --no-default-features is given. Each feature on defines the build option <package>_<feature> (http_tls), and turns on what it lists, across the whole dependency graph; see Features. A feature the package does not have is an error that lists those it has:

unknown feature 'tsl' in '--features': package 'http' has 'default', 'tls', 'gzip'

--all, -p <name>, --package <name>

In a workspace, --all builds every member and -p (repeated for more) the members it names by package name, from the root or any member. Each member builds into its own output, as pepper build in its folder would, one after another, and the first that fails stops the rest; a member with no [build] entry and no main.pep, a library, is skipped. Their features are unified: the build of each turns on what every selected member turns on in a package they share, and --features turns a feature on in each member that has it. In a workspace's root with no [package] of its own, pepper build builds every member. -o names one output, so it takes one member.

pepper build --all          # every member
pepper build -p app -O      # the member named app, optimized

Runtime checks

--no-runtime-checks=<list>

Integer overflow, division by zero, an oversized shift, an index out of range and a call through a null reference panic at run time, at every optimization level. This option removes the kinds of check it names, as a comma-separated list, from an optimized build:

KindWhat is no longer checkedWhat happens instead
overflowInteger overflowArithmetic wraps
divideDivision by zero and MIN / -1Undefined behavior
shiftA shift count of at least the widthThe count is masked
boundsArray and string indexingUndefined behavior
nullCalls and matches through a null referenceUndefined behavior
allAll of the above

Removing bounds or null gives up memory safety. At -O0 the option has no effect and prints warning: '--no-runtime-checks' has no effect at -O0. To remove checks from one function at every level, mark it [Unsafe("overflow,bounds")] instead. See Integer overflow.

pepper build -O main.pep --no-runtime-checks=overflow,shift

The build cache

The compiler checks a program one compilation unit at a time: a file, or the files that import each other in a cycle, with the runtime as one. The build cache keeps each compilation unit's checked result and object, and each file's own object: a file whose sources, and whose imports' declarations, did not change is not compiled or checked again. PEPC_COMPILATION_UNIT_JOBS sets how many compilation units are checked at once (one per processor by default; PEPC_LAYER_JOBS, its old name, still works). The optimization level, link-time optimization, debug info, CPU, removed runtime checks and build options are part of each object's key. Deleting the cache folder is always safe.

--no-cache

Compiles every file without reading or writing the build cache.

--cache <dir>

Keeps the build cache in <dir>. Without it, the folder named by PEPPER_CACHE_DIR when that is set and not empty, else .pep/cache in the current folder, or in the project's folder when building a project with no file.

No path in the cache adds more than 72 characters to <dir>'s, so a project folder can sit deep without the cache passing Windows' 260-character path limit. The folder holds one subfolder per layout version (v3); a build ignores the others, so an old version's folder can be deleted.

--verify-cache, --no-verify-cache

--verify-cache checks the cache, for testing the compiler: every file the cache would reuse is compiled anyway, and the build fails if its code differs from the cached object's, or if skipping the reused files' bodies changes another file's code. Setting PEPPER_CACHE_VERIFY to anything but empty or 0 does the same. --no-verify-cache turns it off even when PEPPER_CACHE_VERIFY is set. The two options cannot be combined. It builds the program a second time, with an empty cache of its own in the build folder, and compares each object that build makes with the one the cache holds under the same key, so a check costs about a build from scratch. A failure names the cached objects that differ.

Tracing and diagnostics

-T <channel>, --Tall

-T turns on a trace channel, which prints to standard error. Repeat it for more channels; --Tall turns on every one.

  • -T time prints how long each stage of the compile took, and the compiler's peak memory once it ended (time: link bodies 1395 ms, peak 400 MB). A build in compilation units keeps its workers' timings in compilation-units.<pid>/<k>.stages in the build folder, each ending with that worker's peak memory.
  • -T passes prints how long each pass of the checker took, summed over its runs, slowest first (pass: 3116.171 ms 16x resolve_implicit_types), the passes run checking the runtime and each module included.
  • -T cache prints how the build cache supplied each object: hit (its sources, and its imports' declarations, are unchanged), hit (same code) (compiled again, to the same code), or miss; and whether linking was skipped.

Any other channel name is accepted and ignored.

-v, --verbose

Accepted for compatibility with other compilers; it prints nothing more yet.

Errors and warnings are printed like clang's, colored when standard error is a terminal; set NO_COLOR to turn color off. See Compiler errors.

Internal options

A build starts copies of the compiler to work side by side, and gives them these options; they are listed so a failed child's command line can be rerun by hand (the build prints it).

  • --compile-part <dir> --part <N>=<object>... compiles parts of the program a build split into <dir>: each --part names a part by its number and the object to write it to. Nothing else is read.
  • --compilation-unit-worker <dir>, after the build's own arguments, checks the compilation units the build passes through <dir> and compiles their objects.
  • --members <names> names, comma-separated, the workspace members a build of several (--all, -p) builds together, so each child unifies its features with theirs. With a file, --all and -p do the same.
  • --member <dir>, with no file, builds the project in <dir> rather than the one around the current folder; a build of several members starts each child with it, in its own folder, so relative paths such as -o keep their meaning.
  • --print-members prints the package name and folder of each member --all or -p selects, a tab between them, a line each, and builds nothing; pep-test --all and -p run it.

Help and version

  • -h, --help prints every option with a line of description.
  • -V, --version prints pep-build and its version.

Environment variables

VariableWhat it doesOption that overrides it
PEPPER_RUNTIMEThe folder holding the standard library; nothing else is searched--no-runtime skips the runtime
PEPPER_OPT_LEVELThe optimization level (0 to 3) without -O; also the level the test suite's JIT uses-O<level>
PEPPER_LIBRARY_PATHMore folders the linker searches, after -L and [Link(path = ...)]-L comes first
PEPPER_SYSROOT_<TRIPLE>The system libraries for linking with --target <triple>--sysroot
ANDROID_NDK_HOME, ANDROID_NDK_ROOTThe Android NDK for linking with an Android --target, when neither --sysroot nor PEPPER_SYSROOT_<TRIPLE> names one--sysroot
ANDROID_HOME, ANDROID_SDK_ROOTThe Android SDK, whose newest ndk/<version> links an Android --target when nothing above names an NDK--sysroot
WASI_SDK_PATHThe wasi-sdk for linking with --target wasm32-wasip1, when neither --sysroot nor PEPPER_SYSROOT_WASM32_WASIP1 names one--sysroot
PEPPER_CACHE_DIRThe build cache folder--cache, --no-cache
PEPPER_CACHE_VERIFYAnything but empty or 0 checks the build cache--no-verify-cache
PEPPER_LOCKEDAnything but empty or 0: the same as --locked
PEPPER_OFFLINEAnything but empty or 0: the same as --offline
PEPPER_LLVM_PREFIXThe LLVM install whose clang and lld link the program
LLVM_SYS_<major>1_PREFIXThe same, when PEPPER_LLVM_PREFIX is not set (LLVM_SYS_201_PREFIX for LLVM 20)
PEPPER_PACKAGE_GITHUB_URL, PEPPER_PACKAGE_GITLAB_URL, PEPPER_PACKAGE_CODEBERG_URLWhere a build fetching a project's locked dependencies clones that host's repositories from, when pep-package is not installed (see pep-package)
NO_COLORSet and not empty: errors are not colored

Exit status

pep-build exits with 0 when the program compiled, 1 when it did not (the errors are on standard error), and 2 for a command line it cannot parse. A crash of the compiler itself exits with 101 after printing what went wrong; please report it.

Projects: pep.toml

A pep.toml file marks the root of a project. It names the project, says how pepper build builds it, and lists the packages it depends on, so a project builds with pepper build and nothing else:

cd my_app
pepper build          # builds the program pep.toml describes
./my_app

pepper new my_app starts a project with a pep.toml, a main.pep and a test, and pepper new my_lib --lib a package (see Starting a project: pep-new and pep-init). A pep.toml can say more:

[package]
name = "my_app"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Draws shapes"
authors = ["Ada <ada@example.com>"]
license = "MIT"
repository = "https://github.com/me/my_app"

[build]
entry = "src/main.pep"

[dependencies]
geometry  = { github = "someone/geometry", version = "1.2" }
json      = { gitlab = "group/pepper-json", version = "0.4.x" }
fast_json = { github = "other/json", version = "2" }   # renamed: 'json' was taken
http      = { codeberg = "someone/http", branch = "main" }
shapes    = { path = "../shapes" }

[dev-dependencies]
fixtures  = { github = "someone/fixtures", version = "1" }   # only tests and examples import it

[build-dependencies]
codegen   = { github = "someone/codegen", version = "1" }    # only the build script imports it

[target.'OS(Windows)'.dependencies]
winapi    = { github = "someone/winapi", version = "1" }     # only builds for Windows see it

[features]
default   = ["tls"]
tls       = ["dep:openssl"]          # a build with it defines 'my_app_tls' and uses openssl

A package is a project other projects depend on: a repository (or folder) with a pep.toml at its root. Its root module.pep is the module its dependency name imports, and any folder inside it holding a module.pep is a module of the package too.

[package]

KeyWhat it is
nameThe project's name: letters, digits and _, not starting with a digit. Required. pepper build names the executable after it.
versionIts version, major.minor.patch
descriptionOne line saying what it is
authorsAn array of names
licenseIts license, such as MIT
repositoryWhere its source lives
toolchainThe toolchain it builds with: 0.3.0, 0.3 for the newest installed 0.3.x, or latest. A pepper installed by pep-install runs that toolchain's tools in the project (see Toolchains); the compiler itself only checks that it is a version
minimum_toolchainThe oldest toolchain release that builds it: 0.11.0, or a prerelease such as 0.11.0-dev, which comes before 0.11.0. Resolving versions, pepper package skips a version of a package whose minimum_toolchain is newer than its own toolchain (see Resolving versions). Unlike toolchain, which picks the toolchain the project itself builds with, it says what the package's users need

[build]

pepper build with no file builds the project: it finds the nearest pep.toml in the current folder or a folder above it, and builds the [build] table's entry file into its output. Every path is relative to the folder holding pep.toml, and the build's intermediate files and cache go in that folder's .pep, wherever pepper build runs.

KeyWhat it isDefault
entryThe file that holds mainmain.pep
outputThe executable; building for Windows adds .exe to a name with no extensionthe package's name
includeAn array of extra folders to search for modules, as -I addsnone
linkAn array of C libraries to link, as -l addsnone
scriptThe package's build script, which builds its C code, or generates Pepper code, before its Pepper code is builtbuild.pep, when there is one

Options on the command line still apply: pepper build -O builds the project optimized, and -o names another output. A file argument builds that file instead (pepper build tools/gen.pep); the project's dependencies, include folders and link libraries still apply to it, since it is in the project.

Build scripts

A package that binds a C library can carry the library's C source and build it itself, so its users install nothing. Its build script, a Pepper program in build.pep at the package's root (or the file [build]'s script names), compiles the C code, and prints what the build must link. It can also write Pepper modules the package imports (Generated modules) and define build options its code reads. Every build of a program that uses the package (a dependency, or the project itself) compiles the script for the machine it runs on and runs it before it loads the program, even when it builds for another platform with --target. The script imports the runtime and its package's [build-dependencies], and stands apart from the code it builds: building it does not load its package's root module, which may import what the script generates, though it may import a file beside it. Cargo users know it as build.rs.

native/
├── pep.toml
├── module.pep        # extern int native_add(int a, int b); and the API around it
├── build.pep
└── c/add.c

# build.pep: compiles c/add.c for the build's target and links it.
import [Path] from io;
import os;
import process;

main(): int {
    var object = Path(os.environment("PEP_OUT_DIR").value()).join(Path("add.o"));
    var compiled = process
        .Command(os.environment("PEP_CLANG").value())
        .arguments(["--target=" + os.environment("PEP_TARGET").value(), "-c", "c/add.c", "-o", object.to_string()])
        .run();
    if (compiled.is_err() or !compiled.value().status.success()) {
        return 1;
    }
    print($"pep:object={object}");
    print("pep:rerun-if-changed=c");
    return 0;
}

The script runs in the package's folder, with these environment variables:

VariableWhat it holds
PEP_TARGETThe triple the program is built for (x86_64-pc-windows-msvc), as --target names it
PEP_TARGET_OS, PEP_TARGET_ARCHIts OS (linux, macos, windows, wasi, ios, android) and architecture (x86_64, aarch64)
PEP_HOSTThe triple of the machine the build runs on
PEP_OPT_LEVELThe optimization level, 0 to 3
PEP_FEATURESThe package's features the build turns on, separated by commas
PEP_PACKAGE_NAME, PEP_PACKAGE_DIRThe package's name and folder
PEP_OUT_DIRA folder of the package's own for what the script makes, and the package's generated modules: .pep/build/<package>-<hash>/out, <hash> naming where the package is (below --build's folder when given)
PEP_CLANGThe clang the build links with (see What the compiler links), empty when there is none; it compiles C for any target LLVM supports
PEP_SYSROOTThe target's system root (--sysroot), empty when there is none

What the script prints on standard output, a line each, tells the build what to do; other lines are its own and ignored:

LineWhat it does
pep:object=<file>Links an object file or a static library (.a, .lib)
pep:link=<name>Links a library by name, as -l does
pep:link-path=<dir>Adds a folder the linker searches, as -L does
pep:build-option=<NAME>[=<value>]Defines the build option <package>_<NAME>, as -D does (a bare NAME is NAME=1); the package's code reads it as a feature's
pep:warning=<text>Shows warning: <package>: <text>
pep:rerun-if-changed=<path>Runs the script again when the file, or any file in the folder, changes
pep:rerun-if-env-changed=<name>Runs the script again when the environment variable changes

A relative path is relative to the package's folder. A line starting pep: that is none of these is an error, as is a script that exits with a status other than 0, which shows what it printed. What the script printed on standard error is passed on.

When it runs again. The build keeps the script's output in .pep/build/<package>-<hash>/stamp, and uses it again until something the script depends on changes: its own file, every Pepper file it imports (files of its own beside it, and its build-dependencies' sources; not the runtime), its package's pep.toml, the project's pep.lock (which holds its build-dependencies' revisions), the variables above, and what its rerun-if-changed and rerun-if-env-changed lines name; or until its PEP_OUT_DIR, or an object it named, is gone. The files it imports are the ones the build cache recorded its last build used, so after the cache is emptied the script runs again. A script that reads other files at run time, such as its C sources, names them with rerun-if-changed; a change to a file it neither imports nor names leaves its last output in use. Builds that run side by side (pepper test) run one package's script one at a time.

Generated modules

A script can write Pepper code, such as bindings made from a C header or tables computed at build time, into PEP_OUT_DIR: its module.pep there is the module the package's code imports as generated, and a folder there holding a module.pep is generated.<folder>. Only the package's own files see it, and its imports resolve against the package's dependencies.

# build.pep: generates the module that names what it was built for.
import [File, Path] from io;
import os;

main(): int {
    var out = Path(os.environment("PEP_OUT_DIR").value());
    var target = os.environment("PEP_TARGET").value();
    File.write_text(out.join(Path("module.pep")), "export built_for(): String {\n    return \"" + target + "\";\n}\n");
    print("pep:build-option=FAST=1");
    return 0;
}

# module.pep of the package `native`
import generated;

export describe(): String {
    return "native for " + generated.built_for();
}

[BuildOption("native_FAST")]
export fast(): bool {
    return true;
}

A generated module is part of the program like any file: its build cache key covers its text, so a script that writes something new rebuilds what imports it. A package with no build script has no generated module, and a dependency the package names generated is imported in its place. An import of a module the script did not write is an error at the import:

module.pep:1:8: error: the build script of 'native', native/build.pep, wrote no module 'generated': no native/.pep/build/native-1a2b3c4d/out/module.pep

The language server finds a package's generated modules after a build has made them in the project's .pep/build, and does not see the build options a script defines.

What a build script can do. A build script is a program like any other: it runs with your permissions, can read and write any file you can, start programs and use the network. Building a project that depends on a package with a build script runs that package's code on your machine, before any of its code is in a program you chose to run. So:

  • pepper package add, update and fetch name each package that arrives (new, or at another commit) with a build script, and the file to read: note: native 1.0.0 (github:someone/native) has a build script, which every build of the project compiles and runs on this machine: read ....
  • pepper build --no-build-scripts (or PEPPER_NO_BUILD_SCRIPTS=1, which pepper test and pepper run builds see too) fails instead of running a dependency's script, naming it. The project's own script still runs: it is your code. A [native] table, which runs no package code, compiles under it too, unless a dependency's has flags that could load code (see [native]).

The package build, added to [build-dependencies] (pepper package add --build pep-lang/pepper-build --name build), does the common work: build.cc compiles C with the target's clang, flags and system root, build.pkg_config finds a library with pkg-config (pointing it at the system root when cross-compiling), and build.emit and build.env print the pep: lines and read the variables above.

A package whose C needs only compiling and linking says so in a [native] table instead, with no script.

[native]

C sources the build compiles for its target and links, with no build script: the common case of a package that bundles a C library.

[native]
sources    = ["c/*.c"]           # files, or globs of them
include    = ["c/include"]       # -I
defines    = ["SQLITE_OMIT_LOAD_EXTENSION", "LEVEL=2"]   # -D
flags      = ["-Wno-unused"]     # more clang flags
link       = ["m"]               # libraries to link, as -l adds
pkg-config = ["zlib"]            # libraries pkg-config describes

[target.'OS(Windows)'.native]
sources = ["c/win/*.c"]
link    = ["ws2_32"]
KeyWhat it is
sourcesThe C files to compile, or globs of them (*, **, ?, [...], {a,b}, as io.glob takes); a pattern that names no file is an error at the pattern
includeFolders to search for headers
definesMacros, NAME or NAME=value
flagsMore flags for clang, for every source
linkLibraries to link by name, such as m or ws2_32
pkg-configLibraries to find with pkg-config: its --cflags compile the sources, and its --libs are linked. It is the pkg-config that PKG_CONFIG names, else the one on the PATH; building for another system, it is pointed at the system root's .pc folders (PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR and PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR) unless PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR is set, and without --sysroot that is an error. A library it does not find is an error naming it

Every path is relative to the package's folder. A [target.'<condition>'.native] table, with the same keys, adds to [native] in a build whose target the condition (what [Target(...)] takes) selects: the C is part of the program, so --target decides, not the machine the build runs on. A package may have only target tables.

Each source is compiled with the clang the build links with, as a build script's PEP_CLANG, for the build's target (--target=<triple>), its system root (--sysroot), its optimization level (-O), and, for Linux and Android, -fPIC, then these flags, in the package's folder. The objects are linked into the program. A dependency's [native] table is compiled for every program that uses the package, and since it runs no package code, --no-build-scripts allows it. A flag can make clang load code from the package (-fplugin=, -Xclang -load) or read or write a file, so under --no-build-scripts a dependency's flags must each be one of these, or the build fails with an error at the flag:

  • -O0 to -O3, -Os, -Oz;
  • -std=<name>, and -march=, -mcpu= and -mtune= with a value of letters, digits, ., _, + and -;
  • -W<name> (-Wall, -Wno-pointer-sign, -Werror=format), of letters, digits, _, +, - and =, so never -Wl,, -Wa, or -Wp,;
  • -f<name> (-fwrapv, -fno-strict-aliasing), of letters, digits, _, + and -, so never one with a = value, except -fplugin, -fpass-plugin, -fprofile…, -fmodule…, -fimplicit-module…, -fsave-…, -ftime-trace…, -fcrash-…, -fintegrated-as, -fproc-stat-report… and -fexperimental-openacc-macro-override, and their -fno- forms;
  • -m<name> (-mavx2, -mno-sse4.2), of letters, digits, ., _, + and -, except -mllvm, -mmlir and -mlink….

Everything else is refused, -I, -D, -include, -Xclang, @file and -- options among them (include and defines give the first two).

With a build script. A package may have both: its script runs first, and its PEP_OUT_DIR is searched for headers, so the C can include one the script generates.

When it compiles again. Each object is kept in .pep/build/<package>-<hash>/native/<target>/ (<target> its triple), named after its source's path (c/add.c makes c_add.c.o), beside a key that covers clang, the flags, the source's text, and the text of every header it includes, which clang lists as it compiles (-MD). A build compiles a source again only when its key changes or its object is gone; editing a header recompiles exactly the sources that include it.

[dependencies]

Each key is the name source code imports, and its value says where the package comes from and which revision to use:

[dependencies]
geometry = { github = "someone/geometry", version = "1.2" }

import geometry;
import geometry.solids;     # the module in the package's solids/ folder

main(): int {
    print("{0} {1}", geometry.area(3, 4), solids.volume(2));
    return 0;
}
KeyWhat it is
github, gitlab, codebergThe repository, owner/name (on GitLab, group/subgroup/name too)
pathA folder on disk, relative to this pep.toml, instead of a repository
packageWith a repository: the member of the repository's workspace it is, by its [package] name (see A member as a Git dependency)
versionA semver range of the repository's version tags: 1.2, 0.4.x, >=1.0, <2
branchA branch
tagA tag
commitA commit
optionaltrue: a build uses it only when a feature turns it on
featuresAn array of the dependency's features to turn on
default-featuresfalse leaves the dependency's default feature off
workspacetrue: its source and revision are its workspace's

A dependency has exactly one source, and at most one of version, branch, tag and commit; with none, it follows the repository's default branch. A path dependency takes only a version, which a build ignores and publish asks for.

Imports

import geometry imports the package's root module, its module.pep. import geometry.solids imports the module in its solids folder, and binds the last name, so its declarations are solids.volume; as names it otherwise (import geometry.solids as s). A dotted import whose first name is not a dependency looks for the nested folder on the search paths: import a.b finds a/b/module.pep.

Because the name lives only in pep.toml, a package that moves to another host or organization, or a switch to a fork, changes one line of pep.toml and no source file. Two packages whose repositories share a name get different keys:

json      = { gitlab = "group/pepper-json" }
fast_json = { github = "other/json" }

Where dependencies live

A dependency from a Git host lives in the project's .pep/deps/<host>/<owner>/<name>, such as .pep/deps/github.com/someone/geometry. One copy serves the whole project: each package's own pep.toml names the packages it needs under its own keys, and an import in one of its files resolves against those keys, to the same copies. When packages need different majors of one package, each major is a copy of its own, <name>@v<major>, and an import resolves to the copy of the major its key's range asks for (see Two majors of one package).

pepper package fetches them there and records the commit of each, the dependencies' dependencies included, in pep.lock beside pep.toml; commit pep.lock with pep.toml. pepper build fetches what pep.lock lists and .pep/deps lacks or holds at another commit, so a fresh clone builds with pepper build alone, with git or, where git is missing, by downloading each locked commit's archive over HTTPS and checking it against the checksum pep.lock records. See The package manager: pep-package, which also says how versions are chosen when several packages need one.

pepper package add someone/geometry       # adds it to pep.toml and fetches it
pepper build

In CI, pepper build --locked and pepper test --locked fail when pep.lock is out of date with pep.toml instead of updating it, and --offline builds with only what .pep/deps and the shared download cache hold (--frozen is both; PEPPER_LOCKED=1 and PEPPER_OFFLINE=1 do the same). See Reproducible builds. They apply to dev-dependencies as to the rest.

A project that sets [fetch] vendor (pepper package vendor does) keeps its dependencies in that folder of the repository instead, and builds with no network and no download cache; see [fetch].

[dev-dependencies]

A package the project's tests and examples use but its code does not, such as a test helper, goes in [dev-dependencies], written as in [dependencies]:

[dev-dependencies]
fixtures = { github = "someone/fixtures", version = "1" }
  • Who sees them: a test build (pepper test, which builds with pep-build --test) and a build of a file in the project's examples folder, or a folder below it. Any other build of the project, such as pepper build, does not: an import of one there is an error that says to move it to [dependencies].
  • Not part of the package: a project that depends on this package neither fetches nor resolves its dev-dependencies, so one that conflicts with the dependent's own dependencies does no harm.
  • Locked with the rest: pep.lock records them beside the other packages, each that only dev-dependencies lead to marked dev = true, and pepper build fetches them with the rest.
  • Needs toolchain 0.11.0: an older toolchain rejects a pep.toml with [dev-dependencies] as an unknown table, a dependency's included. So a package that has one sets minimum_toolchain = "0.11.0" (or later) in [package], and pepper package on an older toolchain skips its versions instead of failing to build them. pepper package publish checks it (see pep-package).

pepper package add --dev adds one, and pepper package remove removes one from either table (see pep-package). A name may be in only one of the two tables.

main.pep:1:8: error: 'fixtures' is a dev-dependency, which only tests and the files in examples/ import; move it to '[dependencies]' to import it here
    1 | import fixtures;
      |        ^~~~~~~~

[build-dependencies]

A package the build script imports, such as a code generator or a helper for compiling C, goes in [build-dependencies], written as in [dependencies]:

[build-dependencies]
codegen = { github = "someone/codegen", version = "1" }
  • Who sees them: only the package's build script, which is built for the machine the build runs on, so they are too; they are never linked into the program. The script sees no other dependency of its package (an import of one says to add it here), and the package's code does not see its build-dependencies. A name may be in [dependencies] too, for both to import.
  • Part of the package: unlike dev-dependencies, every package's build-dependencies are resolved, a dependency's included, since its script runs in your build. One the package's other packages need too is one copy, at one version, as for any dependency.
  • Locked and vendored with the rest: pep.lock records them beside the other packages, each that only build-dependencies lead to marked build = true (and pepper package tree marks it [build]), pepper build fetches them, pepper package vendor copies them, audit checks them, and [overrides] and two majors apply to them as to the rest. A build-dependency's own build script runs in the build of the script that imports it.
  • Not optional: optional = true there is an error; a script reads its package's features from PEP_FEATURES.
  • Only on some hosts: [target.'<condition>'.build-dependencies] holds those a script needs only on some machines; see below.
  • Added with pepper package add --build (see pep-package).
  • Needs toolchain 0.11.0, as [dev-dependencies] does.
main.pep:1:8: error: 'codegen' is a build-dependency, which only the package's build script imports; add it to '[dependencies]' to import it here
    1 | import codegen;
      |        ^~~~~~~

[target.'<condition>'.dependencies]

A package only some platforms need, such as a binding to a Windows API, goes in a [target] table whose key is the condition, written as in [dependencies]:

[target.'OS(Windows)'.dependencies]
winapi = { github = "someone/winapi", version = "1" }

[target.'OS(Linux) && Arch(x64)'.dependencies]
epoll = { github = "someone/epoll", version = "0.3" }
