Formatting with pep-fmt

pep-fmt rewrites Pepper source in one standard style, so that every Pepper file reads the same and nobody has to argue about layout. It changes only whitespace, line breaks, the order of imports, and the form of function declarations; the program means exactly what it meant before.

pep-fmt is written in Pepper. It reads files with the Pepper compiler's own parser (tools/compiler/parse), so it accepts exactly the syntax the compiler does.

Running it

Build it with the compiler, with the tools folder on the import path:

pepper build tools/pep-fmt/main.pep -o pep-fmt

Give it files or directories, like gofmt:

pep-fmt main.pep            # print the formatted file to standard output
pep-fmt -w main.pep src/    # rewrite each file that is not formatted
pep-fmt --check src/        # list each file that is not formatted
pep-fmt < main.pep          # no files: standard input to standard output

Options

pep-fmt [OPTIONS] [paths]...
OptionWhat it does
<paths>Files to format, and directories to search for .pep files; none means standard input
-w, --writeRewrite each file that is not formatted, instead of printing it
--checkPrint the path of each file that is not formatted, and exit with 1 if there is one
-h, --helpPrint the options
-V, --versionPrint pep-fmt and its version

-w and --check need at least one path. pepper fmt runs pep-fmt with the same arguments.

A directory stands for every .pep file under it, in name order, skipping directories whose names start with . (such as .git and the .pep build cache). -w (or --write) rewrites only the files whose formatting changes. --check changes nothing, prints the path of each file that -w would rewrite, and exits with status 1 if there is one, which suits a CI step. The two can be combined.

If a file does not parse, pep-fmt leaves it untouched, prints the first syntax error to standard error, and exits with status 1 after the other files. Standard input is named <stdin>:

main.pep:2:14: error: expected ')'

Errors the compiler finds after parsing, such as a number too large for its type, do not stop pep-fmt. A few mistakes that parse, but whose text the syntax tree does not keep (a second destructor, a second get or set in a property, a second else arm, a property's value written before its accessors), are reported as cannot lay out this file and leave the file untouched.

A file that cannot be read or written also exits with status 1, and an unknown option, or -w or --check without a path, exits with status 2 after printing the usage (pep-fmt -h prints the full help). pep-fmt parses its options with the cli module.

The style

Layout. Indentation is 4 spaces. A brace goes on the same line as the declaration or statement that owns it, and else goes between the braces:

if count > 0 {
    print($"{count}");
} else {
    print("none");
}

A block stays on one line only when it holds a single break, continue or return and was written on one line: if done { return; }.

Line width. Lines are at most 120 columns. A list that does not fit (arguments, parameters, an import list) moves to its own indented line, and if it still does not fit, puts one item on each line:

report_values(
    first_argument, second_argument, third_argument, fourth_argument, fifth_argument, a_much_longer_argument
);
report_values(
    first_argument,
    second_argument,
    an_argument_so_long_that_the_whole_list_no_longer_fits_on_one_line_even_after_moving_it_down_one
);

A long expression breaks before each operator, and a chain of three or more method calls that does not fit breaks before each .:

if (first_condition_that_is_long(value) and second_condition_that_is_long(value)
    or third_condition_that_is_long(value)) {
    run();
}
total = first_value_that_is_long_enough
    + second_value_that_is_long_enough
    + third_value_that_is_long_and_longer_still;
var count = words
    .iterate()
    .filter((w) => w.length > 4)
    .map((w) => w.length * 2)
    .count_them_all();

Comments and string literals are never reflowed, so a line can stay longer than 120 columns when it has nowhere to break.

Attributes go one per line, each on its own line above the declaration:

[Target(OS(Linux))]
[Deprecated("use 'open' instead", "open")]
export open_file(path: String): int { return 0; }

A parameter's attributes are the exception: they stay on the parameter's line, in front of it, as in construct([Sending] T value).

Declarations. Pepper functions and methods are written with the parameter types after the names and the return type last, add(a: int, b: int): int. The C-style form, int add(int a, int b), is kept for extern functions, which mirror C prototypes; pep-fmt rewrites it everywhere else, including operator methods (bool ==(Point other) becomes ==(other: Point): bool, and bool !!() becomes !!(): bool), indexers (T [](ulong index) becomes [](index: ulong): T) and constructor parameters. A void return type is left out when the function has a body (void run() and run(): void both become run()); a declaration without a body, such as a trait method, keeps it.

Blank lines. At most one blank line in a row. Top-level structs, traits, extensions and functions with a body are separated by one blank line.

Comments stay where they are, attached to the code next to them. Trailing comments on consecutive lines are aligned, two spaces after the longest line:

var total = 0;      # the running sum
var count = 0;      # how many values
var average = 0.0;  # total / count

Imports that are next to each other (no blank line or comment between them) are sorted: modules first (import io;), then files of this module (import "util";), each by name.

Kept as written: parentheses around conditions (if x and if (x) are both fine), fields declared either way (int x; or var x: int;), and the file's line endings (\n or \r\n).

Turning it off for a section

Code between a # format: off comment and a # format: on comment is left exactly as written, for layouts the style would undo, such as a table of numbers:

# format: off
const IDENTITY = matrix(1, 0, 0,
                        0, 1, 0,
                        0, 0, 1);
# format: on

Each comment goes on its own line, between declarations or statements, and the pair must be in the same block (or both at the top level). Without a # format: on, the region runs to the end of the block or file.

Profiling with pep-profile

pep-profile runs a program under a sampling profiler and writes a flame graph of where it spends its time: an SVG that any browser opens, with one box per function, as wide as the share of samples the function was on the stack for, above the function that called it. Hover over a box to see its numbers; click it to zoom in, and click "Reset zoom" to zoom back out.

pepper profile main.pep                     # build it, run it, write main.svg
pepper profile ./server -- --port 8080      # an executable, with its arguments
pepper profile --pid 4242 --duration 10     # a running process, for 10 seconds
pepper profile -i main.json -o main.svg     # draw a recording made earlier

pep-profile records with a profiler that is already installed rather than sampling the program itself:

ProfilerPlatformsInstall
samplyLinux, macOS, Windowscargo install --locked samply
perfLinuxyour distribution's linux-tools (or perf) package
samplemacOScomes with macOS

It uses samply when it is installed, and otherwise perf on Linux or sample on macOS; on Windows, samply is the one supported. When none is installed it says what to install. --profiler picks one.

On Windows, samply records the system's ETW events, which needs administrator rights: run pep-profile from an Administrator terminal ("Run as administrator"). Without them it stops at once and says so, rather than waiting on a UAC prompt. Drawing a recording with --input needs no rights.

pep-profile is written in Pepper (tools/pep-profile). Build it with the compiler, with tools/ on the import path, and put it next to pepper so that pepper profile finds it:

target/bin/pep-build tools/pep-profile/main.pep -o target/bin/pep-profile

Usage and options

pep-profile [options] <program.pep | executable> [-- arguments...]
pep-profile [options] --pid <PID>
pep-profile [options] --input <FILE>
OptionWhat it doesDefault
<program>The .pep file or executable to profile, then its arguments
-o <file>, --output <file>The flame graph to writethe program's name with .svg
-F <hz>, --frequency <hz>Samples per second999
-d <seconds>, --duration <seconds>Stop recording after this longwhen the program ends; 10 s with --pid
-p <pid>, --pid <pid>Record a running process instead of starting one
-i <file>, --input <file>Draw a recording made earlier instead of recording
--profiler <name>Record with samply, perf or sample, or the profiler at a paththe first installed
--symbolizer <path>The llvm-symbolizer that names frames, or nonefound on the PATH
-l, --linesEnd each frame's name with its file and lineoff
--idleKeep the samples of threads that were waiting, not running (samply)off
--title <text>The flame graph's titleFlame graph: <name>
--renderer <name>What draws the flame graph: builtin, inferno or flamegraph.plbuiltin
--folded <file>Also write the folded stacks
--raw <file>Also keep the profiler's own recording
-I <dir>, --import-path <dir>A folder pep-build searches for imports, when building a .pep file
--openOpen the flame graph when it is writtenoff
-h, --helpPrint the options
-V, --versionPrint the version

Give exactly one of a program, --pid and --input. The program's own arguments go after it; put -- before them when any starts with -, so that pep-profile does not read them as its own options. pep-profile exits with 0 once the flame graph is written, whatever the program's own exit status, with 1 when it cannot record or draw one, and with 2 for a usage error.

Profiling a program

Given a .pep file, pep-profile first builds it with pep-build, found next to pep-profile or on the PATH, as

pep-build main.pep -O -g --frame-pointers -o <scratch>/main

-O profiles the code that ships; -g gives the frames their names and lines; and --frame-pointers keeps the frame pointer in every function, so that the profiler walks each sampled stack quickly and completely (see pep-build). Pass -I for each folder the program imports from. An executable is run as it is: build it with the same options to get the same detail.

The program runs with the terminal's standard input and output. Recording stops when it exits, or after --duration seconds. With perf, --duration stops the program with timeout; with samply and sample the program keeps running once recording stops, and sample then ends it.

--pid records a process that is already running, for --duration seconds (10 by default). samply and perf need permission to do that: on Linux, kernel.perf_event_paranoid must allow it (samply asks for 1 or lower) or the profiler must run as root; on macOS, sample can attach to your own processes.

samply also records each thread while it waits, as samples that used no CPU. On Windows, a thread pool that Windows starts in every process sits waiting the whole run, and alone would fill half the graph. So pep-profile leaves out every sample of a samply recording in which its thread used no CPU, and the graph shows where the program ran. --idle keeps them, to see where threads block. It changes nothing with perf or sample.

Names in the flame graph

Every frame is named the way the source names it:

  • A function or method by its name: work, Point.length, Box<int>.get. A generic specialization keeps its type arguments.
  • A closure by where it is written: closure at main.pep:14.
  • A function the optimizer inlined still has a frame of its own, inside the function it was inlined into.
  • With --lines, a frame also gives the file and line it is at: work (main.pep:17). A function then gets one frame per line that was running, which shows where in a long function the time goes.

These names come from the program's debug info, read by llvm-symbolizer, which LLVM installs: pep-profile looks for llvm-symbolizer and its versioned names (llvm-symbolizer-20) on the PATH, then in $PEPPER_LLVM_PREFIX/bin, $LLVM_SYS_<major>1_PREFIX/bin and the usual LLVM install folders. --symbolizer names one, and --symbolizer none skips it. Without one, frames take the profiler's symbol names, which pep-profile demangles: Pepper's linker name _PArray_3cint_3e.count shows as Array<int>.count, and a closure as closure #0 in main. Inlined functions then have no frames of their own, and --lines adds nothing.

Recordings

--raw <file> keeps the profiler's recording: samply's profile (with its symbols beside it, in <file> with .syms.json in place of .json), perf's perf.data, or sample's report. A samply profile opens in the Firefox Profiler (samply load <file>), which shows the samples over time; perf.data opens in perf report.

--input <file> draws a flame graph from such a recording instead of making a new one, telling the format from what the file holds:

  • a samply profile (JSON);
  • a perf.data file (read with perf script), or the text perf script -F ip,sym,symoff,dso writes;
  • the report sample writes;
  • folded stacks, as --folded writes them.

Frames are named from the libraries the recording names, when they are still on this machine.

--folded <file> writes the folded stacks the flame graph is drawn from, in the "collapsed" format other flame graph tools read: one line per distinct stack, its frames from the outermost in, joined by ;, then a space and its sample count.

_start;__libc_start_main_impl;main;work;Box<int>.get 533

Renderers

The flame graph is drawn by a renderer built into pep-profile, so it needs nothing else installed. --renderer inferno draws it with inferno's inferno-flamegraph (cargo install inferno), and --renderer flamegraph.pl with Brendan Gregg's flamegraph.pl, each found on the PATH, for their extra features such as search.

Testing with pep-test

pep-test builds the [Test] functions of Pepper files and runs them, each in a child process of its own, reporting which pass. Writing tests is covered in Unit tests.

pepper test                          # every test under the current folder
pepper test src/words_test.pep       # the tests of one file
pepper test -f words src             # only tests whose name contains "words"
pepper test --list src               # list them without running them
pepper test --shard 2/4 src          # the second of four parts of them
pepper test -I . geometry/tests      # tests that import the module geometry

running 3 tests
test counts_the_words ... ok (4 ms)
test an_empty_string_has_no_words ... ok (3 ms)
test reading_past_the_last_word_panics ... ok (5 ms)
3 passed, 0 failed

pep-test is written in Pepper (tools/pep-test). Build it with the compiler and put it next to pepper and pep-build, so that pepper test finds it and it finds the compiler:

target/bin/pep-build tools/pep-test/main.pep -o target/bin/pep-test

Usage and options

pep-test [options] [path]...
OptionWhat it doesDefault
<path>A .pep file to test, or a folder to search for files holding [Test] functions; repeatablethe current folder
-f <text>, --filter <text>Run only the tests whose name contains the text; repeated, any of themevery test
-l, --listList the tests instead of running them
-j <count>, --jobs <count>How many tests run at onceone per logical CPU
--target <triple>Builds the test programs for this target and runs the tests there: in the iOS simulator for an iOS simulator triple, on an Android emulator or device for an Android one (see Testing on iOS and Android)this machine
--shard <i>/<n>Run only the ith of n parts of the tests (1 to n), so the n runs 1/n to n/n run each test onceevery test
-t <seconds>, --timeout <seconds>Fail a test still running after this long; 0 for no limit60
-I <dir>, --import-path <dir>A folder pep-build searches for imports; repeatable
-L <dir>, --library-path <dir>A folder the linker searches for libraries, for pep-build; repeatable
-D <option>, --define <option>A build option for pep-build, NAME or NAME=VALUE; repeatable
--build-environment <name>=<value>Sets an environment variable for each pep-build that builds a test program, and not for the tests, which run with pep-test's environment; repeatable. For example, --build-environment PEPC_NO_COMPILATION_UNITS=1 builds each test program as one, while tests that build programs of their own still use compilation units
--lockedPassed to pep-build: fail, rather than fetch, when the project's pep.lock is out of date (also PEPPER_LOCKED=1)
--offlinePassed to pep-build: fetch nothing over the network, building with what .pep/deps and the download cache hold (also PEPPER_OFFLINE=1)
--frozenBoth --locked and --offline
-F <names>, --features <names>Passed to pep-build: features of the project's package to turn on, comma-separated; repeatable (see Features)the default feature
--no-default-featuresPassed to pep-build: leave the project's package's default feature off
--allTest every member of the project's workspace, with their features unified; no <path> with it
-p <name>, --package <name>Test this workspace member, by package name; repeatable, the members' features then unified
-h, --helpPrints the usage and these options
-V, --versionPrints pep-test and its version

--locked, --offline and --frozen govern the fetch each pep-build does for a project (see pep-build); pep-build reads PEPPER_LOCKED and PEPPER_OFFLINE itself.

The exit status is 0 when every test program builds and every test passes, 1 when a test fails or a program does not build, and 2 for a usage error.

What it does

  1. Finds the files. A file named on the command line is tested as it is. In a folder, and the folders below it (except those whose names start with .), it takes each .pep file with a line that starts with [Test].
  2. Builds one test program per folder, of that folder's test files, with pep-build --test (found next to pep-test, else on the PATH), in parallel. Each file keeps the scope it has in any program, so test files in a module's folder see each other's names, and a helper two of them declare must be private (see Unit tests). A test build sees the project's [dev-dependencies] (see Projects: pep.toml). A program that does not build is reported with the compiler's errors, and the other folders' tests still run.
  3. Lists each program's tests with --list and keeps those that match --filter. With --shard I/N it keeps every Nth of those, starting with the Ith: tests next to each other in the list, such as one file's slow ones, land in different shards, and every test is in exactly one, as long as the N runs see the same files. With --list it prints them and stops: the test's name, or file::name when the tests come from more than one file.
  4. Runs each test as program --run FILE::NAME --timeout SECONDS, each in its own process, up to --jobs at once, and prints test NAME ... ok (TIME) or ... FAILED (TIME) as each ends (in order with --jobs 1). TIME is how long the test's process ran: whole milliseconds (12 ms), or seconds with two decimals from one second up (1.25 s). A test that passes after more than 60% of its timeout is followed by warning: test NAME took TIME, over 60% of its N s timeout: it will time out once its machine is busier. A test passes when its process exits with 0; a [ShouldPanic] test passes when its process panics with a message that contains the attribute's text.
  5. Reports the failures, each with what the test printed (the panic's message and location) and why it failed, then a summary: 2 passed, 1 failed, with the number of tests --filter left out, of tests left to other shards, and of test programs that did not build when there are any. Each shard builds every test program: only the tests' runs are split.

The test programs are built in a temporary folder that is removed at the end. A test runs in the current folder, with PEPPER_BACKTRACE=0 unless PEPPER_BACKTRACE is set, so a panic prints its message without a backtrace. Each test gets a temporary folder of its own (TMPDIR, and TMP and TEMP for Windows, name it), removed when the test ends, so what a test that panics or times out leaves there, such as a TempFolder whose destructor never ran, is removed too.

Testing on iOS and Android

With --target, each test program builds for that target (pep-build --target, which needs the platform's SDK; see iOS and Android), and every request to it, --list and each --run, goes to where that target runs. The report is the same as on this machine.

pepper test --target aarch64-apple-ios-simulator src   # on a Mac, in the booted simulator
pepper test --target x86_64-linux-android src          # on the running emulator
  • iOS simulator (aarch64-apple-ios-simulator, or x86_64-apple-ios-simulator on an Intel Mac): each program runs in a booted simulator with xcrun simctl spawn, from this Mac's file system, so its temporary folder is the one pep-test makes here. simctl starts it in another folder, so pep-test names the current one in PEPPER_TEST_DIRECTORY and the program goes back there first: data files beside a test are found as on the Mac. simctl passes no USER, and the simulator's user database lacks the Mac's user, so os.user_name() finds none. The simulator is the one whose UDID PEPPER_IOS_SIMULATOR holds, else the booted one (booted). Boot it first (xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 16"). A device triple (aarch64-apple-ios) is a usage error: nothing here can start a program on an iPhone.
  • Android (aarch64-linux-android, x86_64-linux-android): adb, from the PATH or $ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools, pushes each program to a folder of its own under /data/local/tmp on the device that ANDROID_SERIAL names, or the only one connected, and runs it there with adb shell, from that folder. The folder of each program's test files is pushed too, to the same path below it, so a test that reads a data file beside it by a path from the current folder (such as tls/test/key.pem, from runtime/) finds it. Each test gets a temporary folder there, removed when it ends, and the whole folder is removed at the end. Start the emulator first, and build for its ABI (x86_64 on an x64 host, aarch64 on Apple silicon).

A target that is neither runs its programs here, as any program (such as x86_64-apple-darwin on an Apple silicon Mac).

The test program

pep-build --test builds a folder's test program (see pep-build), which pep-test runs with one of two requests:

  • --list prints a line per test, its fields separated by tabs: the name, file:line, returns or panics (a [ShouldPanic] test), and the text the panic must contain.
  • --run NAME [--timeout SECONDS] runs one test (NAME, or FILE::NAME with the file as --list gives it) and exits with 0 when it returns having released everything it allocated; a test that leaves an allocation behind (or releases one too many) exits with 1 and says so on standard error. A panic aborts the program, and so does a stack overflow, after panic: stack overflow; a test that runs past the timeout ends it with exit status 124. However the program ends (the test returns, panics, crashes or times out), every process the test started ends with it (a job object on Windows, a process group elsewhere): one left running would hold the pipes to its output open, and pep-test would wait on it. With PEPPER_TEST_DIRECTORY set and not empty, the program first makes that folder its current one (and exits with 2 when it cannot enter it).

On Windows, a test program turns off Windows Error Reporting for its crashes and abort(), so a test that panics or crashes ends at once, without a dialog.

The language server: pep-lsp

pep-lsp is Pepper's language server. An editor starts it and talks to it over standard input and output with the Language Server Protocol: it reports compiler errors and warnings as you type, and provides hover, completion, go to definition, document outlines and inlay hints. It checks code with the compiler's own front end, and finds the standard library the way the compiler does (see Where the compiler finds the standard library).

Warnings in the files a document imports show on those files too, such as a use of a deprecated function in a library the document calls. A file open in the editor shows its own analysis instead.

The VS Code extension (pep-lang/vscode-pepper) runs it. When pepper install manages your Pepper home, the extension runs the pep-lsp of the toolchain the first workspace folder uses, as pepper install which reports it there, so the editor checks code with the same compiler and standard library as pepper build. If that fails (say the project pins a toolchain that is not installed), a warning says why and the bundled server runs. Run Pepper: Restart Language Server after switching toolchains.

The extension also offers to install what is missing, running it as a task whose terminal shows the progress and any error, then offers to reload the window to pick the toolchain up:

  • with no Pepper home, Install Pepper runs the install script;
  • when the toolchain the workspace uses is not installed, Install runs the pepper install add <version> (or pepper install update) that pepper install which suggests;
  • when the default toolchain is older than the extension, Update runs pepper install update. A toolchain a project pins, or PEPPER_TOOLCHAIN names, is left as it is.

Don't Ask Again stops an offer for good. For another editor, run the toolchain's pep-lsp (or pepper lsp) for .pep files.

The server is written in Pepper, in tools/pep-lsp, on the lsp package, a framework for writing a language server for any language in Pepper. To build it from a checkout of the repository, with this checkout's standard library:

PEPPER_RUNTIME=$PWD/runtime pep-build -O tools/pep-lsp/main.pep -o target/pep-lsp/pep-lsp

When the server crashes

pep-lsp runs the server in a child process (pep-lsp --serve) and passes messages between the editor and it. If the server crashes (a bug in the compiler or the server ends it with a panic), pep-lsp answers the requests it left unanswered with an empty result, logs the server ended ...; restarting it to the editor's output, and starts a new one, which gets the open documents again. If the new one crashes too before you change anything, the document you changed last is left out until you change it again, so one text that crashes the server cannot keep it down; after five crashes in a row pep-lsp gives up and exits.

Checking as you type

The server checks a file as the root of its own program, the way pepper build checks one: one compilation unit at a time, starting with the standard library and working up through each file's imports. A compilation unit is one file, or the files that import each other in a cycle. It saves what it learned about each compilation unit in the build cache, in the .pep/cache folder of the file's project (the folder holding its pep.toml, else the file's own folder), or in $PEPPER_CACHE_DIR when that is set. When you edit a file, only the file you are editing is checked again. Every other compilation unit loads from the cache, unless its files changed on disk or a declaration it depends on changed. The cache outlives the server, so a restarted editor answers quickly once the files have been checked once. Delete the folder to start over.

The first time, when the cache has nothing yet (it lacks even the standard library's compilation unit), the server checks the whole program at once, which is quicker than one compilation unit after another, and meanwhile a copy of itself (pep-lsp --fill-cache) fills the cache: it checks the compilation units the file depends on in parallel, in more copies (pep-lsp --compilation-unit-worker), one per processor at most, as pepper build does. Until it is done, an edit is checked again on the record of the whole program the first check left: only the bodies and declarations the edit changed or added are checked, and their errors and warnings show at once. An edit that does more (one that changes a declaration's signature, say) waits for the copy, then loads the compilation units it checked. When the cache has some compilation units but not others, the server checks the missing ones that way itself.

Command-line options

pep-lsp [--stdio]
OptionWhat it does
--stdioTalk over standard input and output: the default, accepted for editors that pass it
--serveInternal: run the server in this process, without the supervisor that restarts it. The supervisor starts it so
--compilation-unit-worker <dir>Internal: check compilation units for the server that started it, which passes them through <dir>. The server starts these itself. --layer-worker is its deprecated spelling
--fill-cache <dir>Internal: check the compilation units the build cache lacks, in --compilation-unit-worker copies, for the server that started it, which passes the program through <dir>. The server starts it itself when the cache is empty
-h, --helpPrint the options and exit
-V, --versionPrint pep-lsp and its version, and exit

Any other argument is an error, and the server exits with status 2 without starting.

Initialization options

The server's settings arrive in the initializationOptions of the LSP initialize request, read once when it starts:

{
  "inlayHints": { "implicitConversions": true, "parameterNames": true },
  "buildOptions": ["USE_ZLIB", "LOG_LEVEL=2"]
}
OptionTypeDefaultWhat it does
inlayHints.implicitConversionsbooleantrueShow the constructor call an [Implicit] conversion inserts, such as Path( ... ) around a String passed where a Path is expected
inlayHints.parameterNamesbooleantrueShow the parameter name before a literal argument passed by position (resize(width: 800, height: 600))
buildOptionsarray of strings[]The build options to analyze with, as the compiler's -D takes them: NAME or NAME=VALUE. One that does not parse is left out. A document that declares a [Test] function is also analyzed with TEST, and testing loaded, as pep-test builds it

VS Code settings

The extension passes its settings to the server as the initialization options above, and restarts the server when one changes:

SettingDefaultWhat it does
pepper.lspPathemptyThe pep-lsp to run; empty uses the project's toolchain's. The server restarts whenever that file is rebuilt
pepper.inlayHints.implicitConversionstrueinlayHints.implicitConversions
pepper.inlayHints.parameterNamestrueinlayHints.parameterNames
pepper.buildOptions[]buildOptions

Inlay hints also need VS Code's own editor.inlayHints.enabled. The command Pepper: Restart Language Server (pepper.restartServer) restarts the server on demand.

The documentation builder: pep-doc

pep-doc builds this book. It generates the standard library reference from the runtime's documentation comments, checks the book, and renders it with mdBook, which must be on the PATH (a binary from its releases).

It also builds a package's reference (pep-doc package).

It is a Pepper program (tools/pep-doc), and it works on the Pepper checkout that holds the folder it is run in, except pep-doc package, which works on the package that holds it. scripts/pepper-tests.sh builds it beside pep-build, with the other Pepper tools, and pepper doc runs it. To build it alone, from the repository root:

pepper build -O tools/pep-doc/main.pep -o target/bin/pep-doc
target/bin/pep-doc reference

pep-doc [<command>] [options]

Commands

pep-doc reference

Regenerates docs/src/reference/ and the reference's entries in docs/src/SUMMARY.md from the doc comments under runtime/, and prints each file it changed. Run it after changing a runtime doc comment, and commit the result.

pep-doc check

Changes nothing, and fails (exit status 1) when:

  • the committed reference does not match the runtime, naming the stale pages;
  • a chapter has Markdown that renders broken without an mdBook error, such as an include indented inside a list item;
  • a public declaration in runtime/ (or tools/syntax) has no doc comment, or one without a description or a tag the documentation standard requires, as a clang-style error at the declaration;
  • a tool's option, command, option value, trace channel, environment variable or setting is missing from the tool's page in this book, naming the tool and the page;
  • a Pepper tool's version() (in tools/<tool>/main.pep, or pep-lsp's in tools/pep-lsp/arguments.pep) is not the version in the repository's VERSION file, which scripts/set-version.sh sets them all to.

The tools' options come from their --help: pep-build's and the Pepper tools' (pepper, pep-fmt, pep-profile, pep-package, pep-install, pep-run, pep-test, pep-new, and pep-init, whose page is pep-new's), which scripts/pepper-tests.sh builds in target/pepper-tests/bin beside a link to its pep-build, so run it first.

  • --tools <DIR>: the folder holding the built tools (default: target/pepper-tests/bin under $PEPPER_TARGET_DIR or target/).

CI runs it, after the tests.

pep-doc build

Regenerates the reference, renders the book into <site>/<version>/, and refreshes the site's versions.json and index.html. Other versions in the site are left as they are, so every published version stays available. This is the command when none is given.

  • --version <VERSION>: the version to build, X.Y.Z or dev (the default). Anything else is an error.
  • --site <DIR>: the site folder (default: target/docs-site).
pep-doc build --version 0.3.0 --site site     # renders into site/0.3.0/

pep-doc serve

Regenerates the reference and serves the book locally with mdbook serve, opening it in the browser and rebuilding as chapters change.

pep-doc package

Builds the reference of the package that holds the current folder: the nearest pep.toml up from it, which must have a [package]. Unlike the other commands, it needs no Pepper checkout, so pepper doc package works in any package:

cd geometry
pepper doc package           # writes .pep/doc/, renders it into .pep/doc/html/
  • Pages: one per .pep file with a public declaration or a ## introduction, made as the standard library reference's are, from the doc comments. A module.pep page is titled by the module (geometry, geometry.solids), any other by the file's path. Tests (test/ and tests/ folders, _test.pep files), examples/, hidden folders such as .pep/, and folders with their own pep.toml (a workspace's members, vendored packages) are left out; run it in each member of a workspace.
  • Features: a declaration that a feature gates says so under its signature ("Available with the feature tls"), linking to the front page's list of features. It is gated when its attributes require the feature's build option (<package>_<feature>): [BuildOption("http_tls")], or BuildOption(http_tls) in a [Target(...)], alone or joined by &&. One under ! or || is not marked.
  • Front page: the package's name, version and description, a line per page, its [features] with what each turns on, and its dependencies, each linked to its docs: for a GitHub repository, the GitHub Pages site the package template publishes (https://<owner>.github.io/<name>/), for another host its repository, and for a path dependency nothing.
  • Output: an mdBook in .pep/doc/ (book.toml, and src/ with the pages, README.md and SUMMARY.md, rewritten on each run), rendered with mdBook into .pep/doc/html/. When mdBook cannot run, the error says where the Markdown is.

Options:

  • --check: changes nothing, and fails (exit status 1) when a public declaration has no doc comment, or one without a description or a tag the documentation standard requires, as pep-doc check does for the runtime: a clang-style error at each.
  • --site <DIR>: renders into <DIR>/<version>/ instead, the version being pep.toml's (dev without one), and refreshes <DIR>'s versions.json and index.html, which opens the newest release, as build does for this book. Earlier versions stay.

Hosting a package's docs

The package template (pepper new --lib, and pep-lang/pepper-package-template) publishes each release's reference with GitHub Pages, with no server: on a vX.Y.Z tag its CI's docs job runs pepper doc package --site on the repository's gh-pages branch, which keeps a folder per version, and pushes it. Turn on GitHub Pages for the gh-pages branch once, in the repository's Settings, Pages. A toolchain whose pep-doc has no package skips the job.

pep-doc help

Prints the commands and options, as -h and --help do.

Options

OptionWhat it does
--version <VERSION>With build: the version to build
--site <DIR>With build: the site folder; with package: the site to render into
--checkWith package: check the doc comments, changing nothing
-h, --helpPrint the commands and options
-V, --versionAs the only argument: print pep-doc and its version

An unknown command is an error. Each command exits with 0 on success and 1 on failure, with the reason on standard error.

See Building this documentation for how the book is organized and published.

Debugging

Build with -g to debug a Pepper program in gdb, lldb, Visual Studio or WinDbg. The compiler then describes the program to the debugger, which can:

  • stop at a file:line breakpoint;
  • step through the source one statement at a time;
  • show a backtrace with the source line of every Pepper frame;
  • print parameters, locals, module-scope variables and struct fields.
pepper build -g main.pep -o main        # Linux: DWARF in the executable
pepper build -g main.pep -o main        # macOS: DWARF, and main.dSYM beside it
pepper build -g main.pep -o main.exe    # Windows: CodeView, and main.pdb beside it

On macOS the linker leaves the DWARF in the object files, so -g also runs dsymutil (from Xcode's command line tools) to gather it into main.dSYM. lldb finds the bundle beside the program; so do the program's own backtraces, which read their source lines from it. Without dsymutil the program still builds, and its backtraces name functions but not lines.

-g and -O work together. Optimized code still steps and shows a backtrace, and a call the optimizer inlined still appears as its own frame. A variable the optimizer removed shows as optimized out.

A session

This program builds an array of points and adds up the first one:

# Build with `-g` to debug this program: break on line 18 and print `first`.
struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
}

total(p: Point): int {
    return p.x + p.y;
}

main(): int {
    var points = Array<Point>();
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 1;
    p.y = 2;
    points.append(p);
    var first = points[0];
    return total(first) - 3;
}

Stop on line 18, after first is assigned, and look around. In gdb:

$ pepper build -g debugging.pep -o debugging
$ gdb ./debugging
(gdb) break debugging.pep:18
(gdb) run
Breakpoint 1, main () at debugging.pep:18
18	    return total(first) - 3;
(gdb) info locals
points = 0x5555555592f0
p = 0x5555555592c0
first = 0x5555555592c0
(gdb) print *first
$1 = {__refcount = 3, __weakcount = 1, x = 1, y = 2}
(gdb) step
total (p=0x5555555592c0) at debugging.pep:8
8	    return p.x + p.y;
(gdb) backtrace
#0  total (p=0x5555555592c0) at debugging.pep:8
#1  main () at debugging.pep:18

lldb takes the same steps with b debugging.pep:18, r, frame variable and bt. In Visual Studio, open the executable as a project (File > Open > Project/Solution), set a breakpoint in the source file and start debugging. The .pdb beside the executable is found automatically.

What the debugger sees

  • Functions under the names you wrote: total, Point.length, Array<int>.append. Methods the compiler writes for a struct, such as __acquire and __release, are marked artificial and placed on the struct's line. A closure is named for where it is written: closure at main.pep:14.

  • Structs. A variable of a struct type holds a reference, so the debugger shows an address. Dereference it (print *first) to see the fields. The fields include the __refcount and __weakcount head, which helps when chasing an ownership bug.

  • Numbers under their Pepper names (int, ulong, u8).

  • Enums. A plain enum shows its case by name. An enum with payloads shows as a struct holding its tag, __tag, whose value names the case (Rect), and the payload fields of every case, each named Case__field (Rect__width), which a debugger expression can name: print shape.Rect__width. With Pepper's formatters loaded (see below) it shows only its case and that case's values instead. A value enum ([Value], such as Optional and Result) is that struct itself, held inline, with no reference counts.

  • Tuples as a struct with members 0, 1, and so on.

  • Trait values as the object they refer to and its vtable.

  • Generics. Each instantiation is its own type, such as Array<long>.

  • Module-scope variables under their names.

  • String, Array and Optional read naturally once the debugger loads Pepper's formatters (see below): a String as its text, an Array as its count and elements, an Optional as its case, Empty or Value, and its value. A String and an Array also show their reference counts as [ref count] (strong references) and [weak count].

  • Other enums with payloads read the same way with the formatters: as their case and that case's values, such as Rect with width and height.

Stepping through a static block

A static block unrolls its compile-time loops into one pass per element, and the debugger steps through those passes as it would a loop that runs: it stops on the for (or while) line at the start of each pass, then on each line of the body. A compile-time if stops once on its line, then in the branch it kept. The compile-time variables (the loop's field, a var of the block) are locals of each pass, so the debugger shows which pass it is in:

# Build with `-g` and step through `total`: each pass of the `static`
# block's loop stops on the `for` line, then on its body, with `field`
# holding the pass's member.
struct Point {
    var x: int = 1;
    var y: int = 2;
    var z: int = 3;
}

total(p: Point): int {
    var sum = 0;
    static (sum, p) {
        for (var field in reflect.properties<Point>()) {
            sum = sum + field.get(p);
        }
    }
    return sum;
}

main(): int {
    return total(Point()) - 6;
}

$ pepper build -g debugging-static.pep -o debugging-static
$ gdb ./debugging-static
(gdb) break total
(gdb) run
(gdb) next
11	    var sum = 0;
(gdb) next
13	        for (var field in reflect.properties<Point>()) {
(gdb) next
14	            sum = sum + field.get(p);
(gdb) print field
$1 = {name = 0x55555559073f "x", type_name = 0x555555590a57 "int", index = 0, is_last = false, is_const = false, is_property = false}
(gdb) next
13	        for (var field in reflect.properties<Point>()) {
(gdb) next
14	            sum = sum + field.get(p);
(gdb) print field.name
$2 = 0x5555555909ba "y"

To step through the code each pass emits instead, with the compile-time values filled in, build with --debug-static=expanded. Beside the program it writes debugging-static.static.pep, the source with the block expanded as --emit-static writes it, and the debugger shows that file for the block's code:

$ pepper build -g --debug-static=expanded debugging-static.pep -o debugging-static
$ gdb ./debugging-static
(gdb) break debugging-static.static.pep:18
(gdb) run
Breakpoint 1, total (p=0x55555559c6b0) at debugging-static.static.pep:18
18	            sum = sum + p.y;
(gdb) print field.name
$1 = 0x5555555909ba "y"

The rest of the function, and the program, stays in its own files.

A breakpoint on a line of the body stops in every pass. A member or case shows as a structure of what reflect reads from it (name, index, is_last, and so on); a list does not show. The stop on the header is a nop the compiler adds only to unoptimized -g builds; optimized code steps through the body's lines without it.

Formatters for the runtime's types

The runtime ships formatters for each debugger in runtime/debuggers/. The sessions below stop in a program holding var name = "pepper";, an Array<int> values of 3 and 4, and var found = Optional<int>.Value(7);.

  • gdb. On Linux a -g program carries gdb_printers.py in its .debug_gdb_scripts section. gdb loads it from directories on its auto-load safe path, so add the program's directory to it, on the command line or in ~/.gdbinit:

    gdb -iex "add-auto-load-safe-path ." ./debugging

    (gdb) print name
$1 = "pepper" = {[ref count] = 1, [weak count] = 1}
(gdb) print values
$2 = Array<int> of count 2 = {[ref count] = 1, [weak count] = 1, [0] = 3, [1] = 4}
(gdb) print found
$3 = Value = {value = 7}

  • lldb. Import lldb_formatters.py, once per session or in ~/.lldbinit:

    (lldb) command script import runtime/debuggers/lldb_formatters.py
(lldb) frame variable name *values found
(String *) name = 0x00005555555592c0 "pepper"
(Array<int>) *values = count=2 {
  [ref count] = 1
  [weak count] = 1
  [0] = 3
  [1] = 4
}
(Optional<int>) found = Value {
  value = 7
}

  • Visual Studio and WinDbg. A -g program's .pdb carries pepper.natvis, and an entry for each of the program's enums with payloads, so nothing needs loading.

Building with -g

Debug info changes the code each file compiles to, so -g builds keep their own objects in the build cache, apart from builds without it. With -g, editing a file recompiles the files that import it, even when the edit only moves a declaration: their code records the line numbers of the generics they instantiate from it.

Backtraces without a debugger

A program can print its own stack: a panic does in a build without -O, and the debug module's capture() and print_backtrace() do on request. debug.output, debug.is_debugger_attached and debug.breakpoint talk to an attached debugger. See Backtraces and the debugger.

Standard library reference

The standard library is the Pepper runtime: the files under runtime/ that every program is compiled with. The pages listed first (from Built-in functions to URI) are the prelude, available without an import. Each module after them (io, async, json, ...) is brought in with an import, such as import io or import [File, Path] from io; its other pages are listed under it.

These pages are generated from the doc comments in the runtime's source (see Documentation comments), so they always match the version of Pepper they were built with. Use the version picker at the top of the page to read the reference for another release.

The prelude

The prelude is the part of the standard library every program gets without an import: the files at the top of runtime/. Each module after it (io, async, json, ...) is brought in with an import.

  • Built-in functions: assert and panic, which every program can call without an import.
  • Built-in attributes: The built-in attributes, declared as [Attribute] structs so a static block can read them like its own: field.has_attribute<Deprecated>() tests for one and function.attribute<Deprecated>().message reads its value (see the reflection chapter).
  • The reflect module (compile time): reflect exists only inside a static block, which runs while compiling.
  • Compiler built-ins: The types and functions the compiler provides itself: raw pointers, weak references, atomics, checked arithmetic and the other __ intrinsics the runtime is built on.
  • Arguments and exit (deprecated): The running program's arguments and exit, kept for the deprecated prelude arguments() and exit(); the process module has them now.
  • String: A mutable, reference-counted string of UTF-8 text.
  • Numbers: Reading numbers from text, and arithmetic that says what to do on overflow.
  • Comparable: Ordering: Comparable, the trait of types whose values sort in one order, which every number type, char and String declare.
  • Ranges: Ranges of numbers: a..b and a..>b.
  • Array: A growable, contiguous, zero-indexed sequence of T values.
  • HashMap and HashSet: Hashing: hash<T>(value), the 64-bit hash HashMap and HashSet use for their keys, and the hash maps and sets themselves.
  • Map and Set: Sorted collections: Map<K, V> and Set<K>, kept in key order on a red-black tree, and compare<T>, the ordering they sort keys by.
  • OrderedMap: OrderedMap<K, V>: a hash map that keeps its keys in the order they were first inserted.
  • BitSet: BitSet: a set of small non-negative integers, stored one bit each.
  • Deque: Deque: a double-ended queue over a growable ring buffer.
  • PriorityQueue: PriorityQueue: a binary heap that hands out its greatest element first.
  • Iterators: Something a for loop can step through, one element at a time.
  • Scoped: The scope protocol behind with (var x = scope) { ... } else { ... }.
  • Weak: Weak references: Weak<T> points at an object without keeping it alive.
  • Handle: Handle<T>: owns a resource that Pepper's reference counting does not know about, such as a C library's object, and releases it when the last reference to the handle goes away, like C#'s SafeHandle.
  • Result: Result<T, E>: the value of an operation that can fail, either Ok holding its value or Err holding its error, like Rust's Result.
  • Optional: A value of type T that may be absent: either Value, holding a T, or Empty, holding nothing, like Rust's Option<T> and Swift's Optional.
  • Copying: Deep copies: copy(value) makes a copy that shares no object that is not thread-safe with the original, so it can be handed to another thread; Copyable<T> lets a type say how it is copied.
  • URI: URI references (RFC 3986): parse any URI, such as https://example.com/a?b#c, mailto:someone@example.com or /items?page=2, into its parts.
  • Test checks: Checks for tests: expect_equal, expect_not_equal, expect_true and expect_false, which every program can call without an import.

Built-in functions

assert and panic, which every program can call without an import.

Source: runtime/internals.pep

assert

assert(condition: bool, message: String)

Panics with message when condition is false; otherwise does nothing.

The check always runs; there is no release mode that removes it. A string literal message picks the __ptr<char> overload instead, which builds no String. Any other message is evaluated before the call.

Parameters

  • condition — the condition that must hold
  • message — the text to print on failure; a null String prints a generic message

Panics

  • if condition is false: prints the location and message, and aborts (see panic)

Example

assert(count > 0, "count must be positive");

assert

assert(condition: bool, message: __ptr<char>)

Checks that condition holds; if not, panics with message, a NUL-terminated C string. A string literal message picks this overload, so an assertion that holds builds no String.

Parameters

  • condition — the condition that must hold
  • message — the text to print on failure, or __null for a generic message

Panics

  • if condition is false: prints the location and message, and aborts (see panic)

Example

assert(count > 0, "count must be positive");

panic

panic(message: String)

Prints message and aborts the program. It never returns.

Flushes every C output stream, so output printed so far is not lost, then writes location: panic: message and a newline to standard error ("Assertion failed with no additional information" when message is null), followed in a build without -O by a backtrace of the calls that led there (PEPPER_BACKTRACE overrides the build; see the debug module's print_backtrace), and calls C abort(). No destructors or releases run, and the process ends abnormally (SIGABRT on POSIX).

The location is the call's file:line:col, which the compiler passes in a hidden parameter, the way a C++ std::source_location default argument works. A function that panics on its caller's behalf, as the runtime's indexers do, declares that parameter itself and passes it on, so the panic names its caller's line:

check_positive(value: int, location: __ptr<char> = __caller_location()) {
    if (value <= 0) {
        panic("expected a positive value", location);
    }
}

Parameters

  • message — the text to print

Panics

  • always

Example

panic("unreachable");

panic

panic(message: __ptr<char>)

Reports message, a NUL-terminated C string (a generic message when it is __null), as a panic and aborts, as panic(String) does. A string literal message picks this overload, so it allocates nothing.

Parameters

  • message — the text to print, or __null

Panics

  • always

Example

panic("unreachable");

PanicHook

type PanicHook = shared (String, String) => void

The function a panic runs before it prints its message: see set_panic_hook. It receives the panic's message and its location (file:line:col, or an empty string when the panic has none).

set_panic_hook

set_panic_hook(hook: PanicHook)

Installs hook as the process's panic hook, replacing the one installed before (take that one with take_panic_hook first to chain them).

Every panic, on any thread, calls the hook on the panicking thread before it prints its message and backtrace, then prints and aborts as always: the hook cannot stop the panic. A full-screen terminal program uses it to leave the alternate screen, so the message lands where the user can read it. That covers panic, a failed assert, an index out of range, an overflowing operator and every other check the compiler or the runtime adds. A stack overflow skips the hook: the thread has no stack left to run it on.

A panic inside the hook does not run the hook again: it prints the first panic's message, then its own, and aborts. Two threads that panic at once each run the hook, at the same time. Keep the hook short, and keep it from taking a lock the panicking code may hold: it would wait forever instead of letting the program end.

Parameters

  • hook — runs with the panic's message and location

Example

var previous = take_panic_hook();
set_panic_hook((message, location) => {
    leave_alternate_screen();
    previous(message, location);
});

take_panic_hook

take_panic_hook(): PanicHook

Removes the process's panic hook and returns it, so that a panic again only prints its message.

Returns

  • the hook set_panic_hook installed last, or one that does nothing when there is none

Example

var hook = take_panic_hook();   # panics no longer run it
set_panic_hook(hook);           # and now they do again

Built-in attributes

The built-in attributes, declared as [Attribute] structs so a static block can read them like its own: field.has_attribute<Deprecated>() tests for one and function.attribute<Deprecated>().message reads its value (see the reflection chapter). The compiler acts on each attribute itself; these declarations only describe the values it records.

Source: runtime/attributes.pep

Attribute

[Attribute] struct Attribute

Marks a struct as an attribute, which can then be written above a declaration and read back in a static block.

Deprecated

[Attribute] struct Deprecated

Marks a public declaration as deprecated: each use outside a deprecated declaration warns with message.

Fields

message

const message: String

What the warning says, such as "use 'open' instead".

replacement

const replacement: String = ""

The name that replaces the declaration, offered as a fix; empty when there is none.

Alias

[Attribute] struct Alias

Gives a parameter a second permanent name that a call may use: [Alias("size", "count")] lets a call name count as size.

Fields

alias

const alias: String

The second name.

const parameter: String

The parameter it names.

Rename

[Attribute] struct Rename

Keeps a parameter's former name working behind a deprecation warning: [Rename("n", "count")].

Fields

The former name.

new_name

const new_name: String

The parameter's name now.

Link

[Attribute] struct Link

Names the C library an extern links against, its C symbol, or both: [Link("m")], [Link(name = "sym")], [Link("ssl", path = "vendor")].

Fields

lib

const lib: String = ""

The library; empty when only the symbol is given.

path

const path: String = ""

A folder the linker searches for libraries, relative to the file that declares the extern unless absolute; empty for none.

name

The C symbol, when it differs from the declared name; empty otherwise.

Target

[Attribute] struct Target

Keeps a declaration only on the platforms its condition matches: [Target(OS(Linux))], [Target(!OS(Windows))].

Fields

condition

const condition: String

The condition as written, such as !OS(Windows).

BuildOption

[Attribute] struct BuildOption

Keeps a declaration only when the build defines a build option with -D: [BuildOption("USE_ZLIB")] is [Target(BuildOption(USE_ZLIB))].

Fields

name

const name: String

The build option's name, such as USE_ZLIB.

Likely

[Attribute] struct Likely

Marks the if or match arm below it as the branch usually taken, so the optimizer lays it out as the straight-line path.

Unlikely

[Attribute] struct Unlikely

Marks the if or match arm below it as a branch rarely taken, such as error handling, so the optimizer moves it out of the fast path.

NotCopyable

[Attribute] struct NotCopyable

Forbids copying a struct with copy(value), giving the reason in the error.

Fields

reason

const reason: String

Why the struct cannot be copied.

Value

[Attribute] struct Value

Makes a struct a value: stored inline and copied on assignment, with no reference count.

Equatable

[Attribute] struct Equatable

Makes a struct, or an enum whose cases carry values, compare and hash by its fields, like a tuple of them, instead of by identity: the compiler derives its == and its hash, so equal values find each other as HashMap and HashSet keys.

On a field of such a struct, it says whether the field takes part: [Equatable(exclude = true)] or [Equatable(include = false)] leaves it out of both == and the hash. A field with neither takes part. On the struct itself it takes no arguments.

Fields

include

bool include = true

Whether the field takes part in == and the hash; false leaves it out.

exclude

bool exclude = false

Whether the field is left out of == and the hash.

Shared

[Attribute] struct Shared

Makes a struct safe to share between threads: its counts step atomically and its fields must be const and thread-safe.

ThreadLocal

[Attribute] struct ThreadLocal

Gives a module-scope var a separate value on every thread, like C++ thread_local: each thread starts from the initializer, which must be a constant, and reads and writes only its own copy, with no locks or atomics.

The variable's type must be thread-safe (a number, a raw pointer, a [Shared] struct, a shared function type); for any other type, use async.ThreadLocal<T>. A struct value is released when a thread started with async.Thread.spawn exits; the main thread's, like every other module-scope variable, is never released.

Example

[ThreadLocal]
var calls: int = 0;

count_call() {
    calls += 1;
}

Isolated

[Attribute] struct Isolated

Makes a struct a guard that can only be the scope of a with block and never escapes it.

Implicit

[Attribute] struct Implicit

Lets a one-parameter constructor convert implicitly wherever a value of its parameter's type flows into the struct's type.

Move

[Attribute] struct Move

Marks a parameter that takes its argument's reference: the caller's variable may not be used again.

MoveSource

[Attribute] struct MoveSource

Marks the parameter of a function that moves a value out of its source, as move does.

Locked

[Attribute] struct Locked

Marks a function-typed parameter that is called while a lock is held, so it may use the locked value.

Unsafe

[Attribute] struct Unsafe

Removes runtime checks from one function's body, as --no-runtime-checks removes them from a whole build: [Unsafe("overflow")], [Unsafe("overflow,bounds")] or [Unsafe("all")]. It applies at every optimization level. Calls the function makes keep their own checks, except the index check that an Array or String method makes for its caller, which bounds removes too. Removing bounds or null gives up memory safety in that function.

Fields

checks

const checks: String

The checks to remove, comma-separated: overflow, divide, shift, bounds, null, or all.

Cold

[Attribute] struct Cold

Marks a function rarely called, such as an allocator's slow path or error handling, so the optimizer never inlines it and its callers' fast paths stay small enough to inline themselves.

Test

[Attribute] struct Test

Marks a function as a unit test: pep-test (pepper test) builds it into a test program and runs it in a child process of its own. The function takes no parameters and returns nothing; it passes when it returns and fails when it panics (see expect_equal). A build without --test leaves [Test] functions out.

ShouldPanic

[Attribute] struct ShouldPanic

Marks a [Test] function as one that passes only when it panics: [ShouldPanic] takes any panic, and [ShouldPanic("index out of range")] only a panic whose message contains that text.

Fields

message

const message: String = ""

Text the panic's message must contain; empty for any panic.

Export

[Attribute] struct Export

Makes a free function callable from C, in a library built with --lib static or --lib shared: [Export], or [Export(name = "c_name")] for a C symbol other than its name.

Fields

name

const name: String = ""

The C symbol, when it differs from the function's name; empty otherwise.

__BuiltIn

[Attribute] struct __BuiltIn

Declares a compiler built-in in the runtime, for the reference and the editor: the compiler ignores the declaration, whose functions end in ;. [__BuiltIn("reflect.name")] names the built-in when it is not the declaration's own name. Only the runtime may use it.

Fields

name

const name: String = ""

The built-in's name, when it differs from the declaration's; empty otherwise.

The reflect module (compile time)

reflect exists only inside a static block, which runs while compiling. It needs no import. Everything here is evaluated by the compiler: the values are compile-time numbers, bools, strings, lists, and the members, cases, functions and attributes below. The Reflection and attributes chapter explains how a block mixes them with the code it emits.

The compiler provides reflect itself; this file only declares it, with [__BuiltIn], for this reference and the editor.

Compiler built-ins

The types and functions the compiler provides itself: raw pointers, weak references, atomics, checked arithmetic and the other __ intrinsics the runtime is built on. Every program can use them without an import, but most code should not: the runtime wraps each in a safe API (Atomic<T>, Weak<T>, math.checked_add, ...).

The compiler provides these itself; this file only declares them, with [__BuiltIn], for this reference and the editor.

Source: runtime/builtins.pep

__ptr

struct __ptr<T>

A raw pointer to a T in memory the program manages itself, as C's T*. It is how the runtime and C interop reach memory directly; nothing checks that it is valid.

p[i] reads or writes the ith element, p + n and p - n move by n elements (bytes for __ptr<void>), and == and != compare addresses. A pointer is true when it is not null (__null). as converts to and from __ptr<void>; unsafe_cast converts to any other pointer or to an integer. A string literal converts to __ptr<char>.

Returns

String

Source: runtime/string.pep

String

struct String

A mutable, reference-counted string of UTF-8 text. A string literal ("text") is a String wherever a String is expected; its own type is StringConstant.

Two measures describe a String, and each API says which one it uses:

  • Code points (Unicode characters): length, is_empty, the indexer s[i], substr, and iteration.
  • Bytes of UTF-8: size, find, starts_with, and ends_with. The byte size is the authoritative length, so the data may contain NUL bytes. It is never derived from a terminator.

A String's bytes are not guaranteed to be followed by a NUL. Only c_str() guarantees one, so call it to hand the text to C; anything else that reads the bytes must stop at size.

A String is a reference type: var b = a; shares one object, so append, +=, and grow are visible through every reference. Use copy() or + for an independent copy. Equality (==) compares content.

A StringIterator panics when the String has been changed by append, +=, or grow since the iterator was created, so modifying a String while a for loop iterates it panics.

To build text from values, use an interpolated string ($"{name}: {count:>4}") or String.format("{0}: {1:>4}", name, count), a compiler intrinsic whose braces name its arguments by position (see the String interpolation chapter).

Example

var s = "héllo";
assert(s.length == 5, "5 code points");
assert(s.size == 6, "6 bytes: 'é' is 2");
s.append(" world");
assert(s.find("world") == 7, "find returns a byte offset");
assert(s[1] == "é", "the indexer counts code points");
for (var c in s) {
    print(c);   # one code point per line
}

Properties

length

var length: ulong { get; }

The number of Unicode code points. O(1).

See also

  • size

size

var size: ulong { get; }

The number of bytes of UTF-8. O(1).

See also

  • length

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the String has no code points. O(1).

Constructor

String()

construct(data: __ptr<char> = __null, size: ulong = 0, length: ulong = 0)

Creates a String by copying size bytes of data into a new NUL-terminated buffer. With no arguments, it creates an empty String with no buffer; its c_str() is still a valid empty C string.

When data is not __null and size is 0, data is treated as a NUL-terminated C string:

  • with length nonzero, size becomes the byte length of its first length code points (0 if the C string is not valid UTF-8);
  • with length 0, size becomes the C string's whole byte length.

When length is 0, it is counted from the bytes. A nonzero length is trusted, not checked against the data. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to copy; __null for an empty String (then pass no sizes, because they are stored as given)
  • size — the number of bytes to copy from data; 0 treats data as a NUL-terminated C string
  • length — the number of code points in those bytes

Example

var empty = String();
var s = "abc";
var copy = String(s.c_str(), s.size, s.length);

Static methods

length_of

static length_of(data: __ptr<char>, size: ulong): ulong

Returns the number of Unicode code points in the first size bytes at data. Runs in O(size).

Returns 0 when data is __null, when size is 0, or when the bytes are not valid UTF-8: any malformed or truncated sequence makes the whole count 0.

Parameters

  • data — the UTF-8 bytes to measure
  • size — the number of bytes to measure

Returns

  • the number of code points, or 0 for invalid UTF-8

Methods

bytes

bytes(): u8[]

Returns a new array holding the String's UTF-8 bytes, without a terminating NUL. Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new array of size bytes

Example

var data = "hi".bytes();
assert(data.count == 2 && data[0] == 104, "the bytes of 'h' and 'i'");

grow

grow(new_size: ulong)

Extends the byte buffer to new_size bytes and fills the new bytes with zeros. Does nothing when new_size is not greater than size.

A low-level primitive for append. It updates size but not length, so the zero bytes it adds are not counted as code points until the caller overwrites them and fixes the length. When it grows the buffer, it invalidates running iterators and may reallocate the buffer, which invalidates pointers from c_str(). Runs in O(new_size).

Parameters

  • new_size — the new byte length

append

append(rhs: String)

Appends the content of rhs to this String in place, updating size and length.

Always invalidates running iterators, even when rhs is empty, so appending during iteration panics. It may reallocate the buffer. Every reference to this String sees the change. Runs in O(size + rhs.size).

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to append; it is not modified

Example

var s = "TEST";
s.append("ING");   # s == "TESTING"

operator []

[](idx: int): String

Returns the code point at code-point index idx as a new one-code-point String.

A negative idx counts from the end (s[-1] is the last code point). length is added until the index is non-negative, so any negative index wraps, and s[-7] of a 3-code-point String is s[2]. Runs in O(idx) because it walks the UTF-8 bytes. Use for (var c in s) to visit every code point in O(size).

Parameters

  • idx — the code-point index; negative counts from the end

Returns

  • a new String that holds the one code point

Panics

  • if idx is not less than length after the negative index is normalized, which includes any index into an empty String

Example

var s = "TEST";
assert(s[0] == "T", "first");
assert(s[-1] == "T", "last");

operator ==

==(rhs: String): bool

Returns whether this String and rhs have the same content, compared byte by byte. Strings with different length are unequal without comparing bytes. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to compare with

Returns

  • true when both hold the same bytes

operator ==

==(rhs: StringConstant): bool

Returns whether this String holds the same bytes as the StringConstant rhs, a literal included. Runs in O(size) and copies nothing.

Parameters

  • rhs — the text to compare with

Returns

  • true when both hold the same bytes

operator +=

+=(rhs: String): String

Appends rhs in place, like append, and returns this same String, not a copy. s += t modifies the object that every reference to s shares, and invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • rhs — the String to append

Returns

  • this String, after appending

Example

var s = "a";
s += "b";   # s == "ab"

iterate

iterate(): StringIterator

Returns an iterator over the String's code points, which makes String Iterable<String>: for (var c in s) visits each code point as a one-code-point String, the same value s[i] gives.

The iterator holds a reference to this String. The whole loop runs in O(size). Modifying the String during iteration makes the iterator panic.

Returns

  • a new iterator, positioned before the first code point

Example

var n = 0;
for (var c in "héllo") {
    n = n + 1;   # 5 iterations
}

c_str

c_str(): __ptr<char>

Returns the String's buffer as a NUL-terminated C string.

This is the one API that guarantees a NUL after the content: a String is not otherwise guaranteed to be NUL-terminated, so code that needs the terminator calls c_str() rather than relying on the buffer.

The pointer is owned by the String. It is valid until the String is destroyed or append, +=, or grow reallocates it. It is never __null: a String built with no data (String()) returns a constant empty C string, so it can go to C as it is. C functions stop at the first NUL byte in the content.

Returns

  • the String's NUL-terminated byte buffer

copy

copy(): String

Returns a new String with the same content and its own buffer, so later changes to either String do not affect the other. Runs in O(size).

This is also how copy(value) copies a String (the Copyable<String> implementation).

Returns

  • an independent copy of this String

Example

var a = "abc";
var b = a.copy();
b.append("d");   # a is still "abc"

clone

[Deprecated("use 'copy' instead", "copy")] clone(): String

Deprecated: use copy instead. Returns a new String with the same content and its own buffer.

Returns

  • an independent copy of this String

find

find(needle: String, from: ulong = 0): long

Returns the byte offset of the first occurrence of needle, or -1 when it does not occur.

The offset counts bytes, not code points. To use it with s[i] or substr, convert it with String.length_of(s.c_str(), offset). An empty needle is found at 0 unless this String is empty, in which case the result is -1. The result is also -1 when needle is not valid UTF-8, or when this String holds invalid UTF-8 before the first match. Bytes past the match are not checked, so searching on from each match (as split and replace do) reads the String once in all. The search is the C library's memmem, which compares many bytes per step (Windows, which has none, jumps between matches of the first byte with memchr).

With from, the search starts at that byte offset, which must be a code point boundary (an offset find returned, plus a match's size, is one); an offset past the end, or inside a code point, finds nothing. The result still counts from the start of the String.

Parameters

  • needle — the text to search for
  • from — the byte offset to start searching at; 0 by default

Returns

  • the byte offset of the first match at or after from, or -1 when there is none

Example

var s = "TESTING";
assert(s.find("STI") == 2, "byte offset");
assert(s.find("xyz") == -1, "absent");
assert("a,b,c".find(",", 2) == 3, "the second comma");

rfind

rfind(needle: String): long

Returns the byte offset of the last place needle occurs in this String, or -1 when it does not occur. An empty needle is found at size. Runs in O(size * needle.size).

Parameters

  • needle — the text to search for

Returns

  • the byte offset of the last match, or -1 when there is none

Example

assert("a/b/c".rfind("/") == 3, "the last slash");
assert("abc".rfind("x") == -1, "absent");

split

split(separator: String): String[]

Splits the String at every occurrence of separator and returns the pieces between them, in order. Adjacent separators give an empty piece, and so does a separator at either end: "a,,b".split(",") is ["a", "", "b"] and ",a".split(",") is ["", "a"]. A String without separator, the empty String included, gives one piece: the whole String. Runs in O(size * separator.size).

Parameters

  • separator — the text to split at

Returns

  • a new Array with one new String per piece

Panics

  • if separator is empty

Example

var parts = "a,b,,c".split(",");
assert(parts.count == 4, "four pieces");
assert(parts[2] == "", "an empty piece");

split_once

split_once(separator: String): (String, String)?

Splits the String at the first occurrence of separator: the text before it and the text after it, or none when it does not occur. Runs in O(size * separator.size).

Parameters

  • separator — the text to split at

Returns

  • the pieces before and after the first separator, or none

Panics

  • if separator is empty

Example

var header = "Host: example.com".split_once(": ");
assert(header.is_value(), "has a colon");
var (name, value) = header.value();
assert(name == "Host" && value == "example.com", "split");

join

join(parts: String[]): String

Returns the pieces of parts joined into one String, with this String between each two of them: ", ".join(names). No parts give an empty String, and one part gives a copy of it. Runs in O(total size).

Parameters

  • parts — the pieces to join

Returns

  • a new String

Example

var parts = Array<String>();
parts.append("a");
parts.append("b");
assert(", ".join(parts) == "a, b", "joined");

replace

replace(from: String, to: String): String

Returns a copy of this String with every occurrence of from replaced by to, scanning left to right without overlaps: "aaa".replace("aa", "b") is "ba". Runs in O(size * from.size) plus the result's size.

Parameters

  • from — the text to replace
  • to — the text to put in its place

Returns

  • a new String

Panics

  • if from is empty

Example

assert("a\r\nb".replace("\r\n", "\n") == "a\nb", "line endings");

contains

contains(needle: String): bool

Returns whether needle occurs in this String (find(needle) >= 0). Because of that, an empty String contains nothing, not even "". Runs in O(size * needle.size).

Parameters

Returns

Returns whether this String begins with the bytes of prefix. An empty prefix always matches. Runs in O(prefix.size).

Returns

Returns whether this String ends with the bytes of suffix. An empty suffix always matches. Runs in O(suffix.size).

substr(start: ulong, count: ulong): String

Returns a new String of up to count code points starting at code-point index start. Both arguments count code points, not bytes.

count is clamped to the code points that remain. When start is at or past length, the result is an empty String. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • start — the code-point index of the first code point to copy
  • count — the maximum number of code points to copy

Returns

  • a new String that holds the selected code points

Example

var s = "TEST";
assert(s.substr(1, 2) == "ES", "middle");
assert(s.substr(0, 99) == "TEST", "count is clamped");
assert(s.substr(4, 5) == "", "start past the end");

operator !=

Returns whether this String and rhs differ in content, the negation of ==. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

Returns

operator !=

Returns whether this String differs from the StringConstant rhs.

Parameters

Returns

operator +

Returns a new String that holds this String followed by rhs. Neither operand is modified. Runs in O(size + rhs.size).

Parameters

Returns

Example

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns this String, so a String is ToString and can be interpolated ($"name: {name}"). The result is the same object, not a copy. O(1).

Returns

  • this String

byte_at

byte_at(index: ulong): byte

Returns the byte at byte offset index of the UTF-8 data. O(1).

The offset counts bytes, not code points, so a byte inside a multi-byte code point is returned as it is. Compare the result with a character literal (s.byte_at(0) == '#').

Parameters

  • index — the byte offset, less than size

Returns

  • the byte at index

Panics

  • if index is not less than size ("String byte_at index out of bounds")

Example

var s = "a=b";
assert(s.byte_at(1) == '=', "second byte");

substr_bytes

substr_bytes(start: ulong, size: ulong): String

Returns a new String of the size bytes starting at byte offset start. Both arguments count bytes, not code points, so offsets from find can be used directly. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • start — the byte offset of the first byte to copy
  • size — the number of bytes to copy

Returns

  • a new String that holds those bytes

Panics

  • if start + size is greater than size ("String substr_bytes range out of bounds")
  • if start or start + size falls inside a multi-byte code point ("String substr_bytes splits a code point")

Example

var s = "key=value";
var eq = s.find("=") as ulong;
assert(s.substr_bytes(0, eq) == "key", "before '='");
assert(s.substr_bytes(eq + 1, s.size - eq - 1) == "value", "after '='");

compare(other: String): int

Compares this String with other byte by byte, for sorting. For valid UTF-8 this is code-point order; a String that is a prefix of the other orders first. Runs in O(min(size, other.size)).

Parameters

Returns

  • a negative number when this String orders before other, 0 when both hold the same bytes, and a positive number when it orders after

Example

assert("apple".compare("banana") < 0, "a before b");
assert("ab".compare("abc") < 0, "a prefix orders first");
assert("x".compare("x") == 0, "equal");
