trim_end

trim_end(): String

Returns a new String without the whitespace at the end: spaces, tabs, carriage returns, line feeds, vertical tabs and form feeds (ASCII only). Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new String with the trailing whitespace removed

Example

assert("code;  \r\n".trim_end() == "code;", "trailing whitespace");
assert("  indented".trim_end() == "  indented", "leading kept");

trim_start

trim_start(): String

Returns a new String without the whitespace at the start: spaces, tabs, carriage returns, line feeds, vertical tabs and form feeds (ASCII only). Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new String with the leading whitespace removed

Example

assert("  \tcode".trim_start() == "code", "leading whitespace");

trim

trim(): String

Returns a new String without the whitespace at either end, as trim_start and trim_end do. Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new String with the leading and trailing whitespace removed

Example

assert(" \t value \r\n".trim() == "value", "both ends");

lower

lower(): String

Returns a new String with the ASCII letters A to Z changed to a to z. Every other character, including non-ASCII letters, is kept as it is, so the result is valid UTF-8 of the same size. Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new String in lowercase

Example

assert("Content-Type".lower() == "content-type", "ASCII lowered");
assert("Ärger".lower() == "Ärger", "non-ASCII kept");

upper

upper(): String

Returns a new String with the ASCII letters a to z changed to A to Z. Every other character, including non-ASCII letters, is kept as it is, so the result is valid UTF-8 of the same size. Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new String in uppercase

Example

assert("get".upper() == "GET", "ASCII raised");

lines

lines(): String[]

Splits the String into lines and returns them without their line endings. A line ends at "\n" or "\r\n". A final line with no ending is included, but the end of the String after a final line ending does not start another line, so "a\nb\n" and "a\nb" both give ["a", "b"], and "" gives no lines. Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new Array with one new String per line

Example

var lines = "first\r\nsecond\n\nfourth".lines();
assert(lines.count == 4, "four lines");
assert(lines[1] == "second", "\\r\\n removed");
assert(lines[2] == "", "an empty line");

repeat

repeat(count: ulong): String

Returns a new String that holds this String count times in a row. count 0, or an empty String, gives an empty String. Runs in O(size * count).

Parameters

  • count — how many copies to join

Returns

  • a new String of size * count bytes

Example

assert("ab".repeat(3) == "ababab", "three copies");
var indent = " ".repeat(8);   # eight spaces

StringConstant

[Value] struct StringConstant

The text of a string literal: a pointer to its bytes, which never change and are never freed, with their byte size and code-point length. A string literal's type is StringConstant, and so is a const with no written type initialized from one (const NAME = "pepper";); where a String is expected, the literal is a String (see the Strings chapter of the book).

A StringConstant is a [Value] type: copying one copies the pointer and steps no reference count, and any thread may read it. Its bytes always end in a NUL byte, so c_str() goes to C as it is. It has String's read API, measured the same way (length in code points, size and offsets in bytes); the methods that make new text return a String. A StringConstant converts to a String wherever a String is expected, as if String had an [Implicit] constructor from it: the conversion, like String(text), copies the bytes. Where C expects a char*, it passes its own bytes, as c_str() does.

Example

StringConstant name = "pepper";
assert(name.length == 6, "6 code points");
assert(name.starts_with("pep"), "the read API of String");
String copy = name;   # a new String with its own bytes
copy.append("!");

Properties

length

var length: ulong { get; }

The number of Unicode code points. O(1).

See also

  • size

size

var size: ulong { get; }

The number of bytes of UTF-8, not counting the NUL terminator. O(1).

See also

  • length

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the text has no code points. O(1).

Constructor

StringConstant()

construct(data: __ptr<char> = __null, size: ulong = 0, length: ulong = 0)

Creates a StringConstant over the size bytes at data. The compiler calls it for each string literal. The bytes must be followed by a NUL byte and must never change or be freed while the program runs; no other bytes meet that, so code outside the runtime has no reason to call it with arguments. With no arguments, it is the empty text.

Parameters

  • data — the constant NUL-terminated bytes
  • size — the number of bytes before the NUL terminator
  • length — the number of code points in those bytes

Returns the text as a NUL-terminated C string, with no copy. It is never __null, and it stays valid for the whole run of the program.

Returns a new String with a copy of the text. Converting a StringConstant to a String, or calling String(text), calls it. Runs in O(size).

to_string

to_string(value: double): String

Returns the shortest decimal text that reads back as exactly value, as Swift prints a Double.

A whole number keeps a .0 ("3.0"), so the text always reads as a floating-point number. Values from 1e-4 up to 1e16 print in decimal; others use an exponent ("1e+16", "1.5e-05"). The special values are "nan", "inf" and "-inf". For a fixed number of fraction digits, interpolate with a precision instead: $"{value:.2}".

The digits come from the Ryu algorithm, which takes a fixed, small number of steps per value.

Parameters

  • value — the number to convert

Returns

  • a new String such as "0.1" or "-2.5"

Example

assert(to_string(0.1) == "0.1", "shortest");
assert(to_string(3.0) == "3.0", "keeps the point");
assert(to_string(1.0e20) == "1e+20", "exponent");

to_string(value: float): String

Returns the shortest decimal text that reads back as exactly value as a float, laid out as to_string(double) lays it out.

Parameters

  • value — the number to convert

Returns

  • a new String such as "0.1"

Example

float third = 1.0 / 3.0;
assert(to_string(third) == "0.33333334", "a float's digits");

to_string

to_string<A, B>(value: (A, B)): String

Returns the text of a pair, "(1, x)": each element's to_string text, separated by ", ", in parentheses. A String element is its text without quotes. Tuples of up to eight elements convert this way.

Type parameters

  • A — the type of the first element
  • B — the type of the second element

Parameters

  • value — the tuple to convert

Returns

  • a new String such as "(1, two)"

Example

assert(to_string((1, "two")) == "(1, two)", "a pair");
var nested = (1, (2.5, true));
assert($"{nested}" == "(1, (2.5, true))", "nested");

print

print(text: String)

Writes text and a line break to standard output.

Any other value prints through print(value), which writes its to_string text. To combine values, interpolate them (print($"total: {n}")), or pass a format string and arguments, which prints what String.format makes of them (print("{0} of {1}", a, b)). A string with no arguments after it is printed as written, braces included.

Each line is flushed as it is printed, as Rust's println! does, so the output appears as the program runs even when standard output is a pipe or a file (where C would buffer it until the program exits).

Parameters

  • text — the text to print

Example

print("hello");
var n = 3;
print($"n = {n}");
print("{0} + {1} = {2}", 1, 2, 1 + 2);   # 1 + 2 = 3

print

print<T>(value: T)

Writes the text of value and a line break to standard output: what $"{value}" would make of it, through to_string. That covers numbers, bool (true or false), tuples, and any type with a to_string() method or a to_string<T> override; another type is a compile error at the argument.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value

Parameters

  • value — the value to print

Example

print(42);          # 42
print(0.5);         # 0.5
print((1, "two"));  # (1, two)

to_string

to_string<T>(value: T): String

Returns the text of value by calling its to_string() method: the overload for any type that is ToString.

Declare a concrete override for a type that has no to_string() method of its own, or whose interpolated text should differ from it; like hash<Point>, an override is used by the whole program, including interpolated strings.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value; it must have a to_string() method unless an override to_string<T> exists

Parameters

  • value — the value to convert

Returns

  • the String that value.to_string() returns

Example

struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
}

to_string<Point>(value: Point): String {
    var x = value.x;
    var y = value.y;
    return $"({x}, {y})";
}

ToString

trait ToString

Something with a text form: a to_string() method returning a String.

An interpolated string ($"total: {a + b}") converts each value it holds with to_string(value), so a struct that implements ToString can be interpolated, as can the integers, bool, and String, which have to_string overloads. String, StringBuilder and io.Path implement it.

Example

struct Point {
    var x: int = 0;
    var y: int = 0;
    construct(this.x = 0, this.y = 0) {}
}

extend Point with ToString {
    to_string(): String {
        return $"({x}, {y})";
    }
}

var p = Point(1, 2);
assert($"p = {p}" == "p = (1, 2)", "interpolated");

Methods

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the text of this value.

Returns

  • a String

StringBuilder

struct StringBuilder

Builds a String from many pieces without copying the text built so far on every append.

String.append grows its buffer to the exact new size, so a long run of appends can copy the text repeatedly. A StringBuilder doubles its buffer when it is full, so appending is amortized O(piece size). Call to_string() for the result; the builder can keep appending afterward.

Example

var out = StringBuilder();
out.append("line ").append(to_string(3)).append("\n");
var text = out.to_string();   # "line 3\n"

Properties

size

var size: ulong { get; }

The number of bytes of UTF-8 appended so far. O(1).

length

var length: ulong { get; }

The number of code points appended so far. O(1).

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether nothing has been appended since the builder was created or last cleared. O(1).

Constructor

StringBuilder()

construct(capacity: ulong = 0)

Creates an empty StringBuilder, optionally with room for capacity bytes before it has to grow.

Parameters

  • capacity — the number of bytes to allocate up front

Methods

append

append(text: String): StringBuilder

Appends the text of text and returns this builder, so calls can be chained. Runs in amortized O(text.size).

Parameters

  • text — the String to append; it is not modified

Returns

  • this StringBuilder

Example

var b = StringBuilder();
b.append("a").append("b");   # b.to_string() == "ab"

clear

clear()

Removes all the text and keeps the buffer for reuse. O(1).

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns a new String holding the text appended so far. The builder is unchanged. Runs in O(size).

Returns

  • a new String

StringIterator

[Value] struct StringIterator

An Iterator<String> over a String's code points, returned by String.iterate() and used by for (var c in s).

Call next() to advance, then current() for the code point it moved to. Both methods panic if the String has been modified since the iterator was created. Create it with String.iterate(): a default-constructed StringIterator() has no String to walk.

Example

var it = "ab".iterate();
while (it.next()) {
    print(it.current());   # "a", then "b"
}

Methods

next

next(): bool

Advances to the next code point. Runs in O(1) per code point.

Returns false once it passes the end, and on every call after that. A malformed UTF-8 sequence is yielded, together with the rest of the bytes, as one final "code point".

Returns

  • true when positioned on a code point, false at the end

Panics

  • if the String was modified since the iterator was created

current

current(): String

Returns the code point that the last successful next() moved to, as a new one-code-point String.

Returns

  • a new String that holds the current code point

Panics

  • if the String was modified since the iterator was created
  • if next() has not been called yet
  • if next() has returned false (the iterator is past the end)

Numbers

Reading numbers from text, and arithmetic that says what to do on overflow.

Every number type has a static parse: int.parse("42") gives an int?, empty when the text is not a number of that type. The integer types take a base from 2 to 36; float and double read decimal notation. Each spelling of a type is the same type, so i32.parse is int.parse.

Integer +, - and * panic on overflow. Each integer type also has wrapping_add (the result modulo 2^bits), checked_add (none on overflow), saturating_add (clamped to the type's range) and overflowing_add (the wrapped result and whether it overflowed), with sub and mul forms of each.

Each integer type also has bit operations that compile to one instruction on most CPUs (leading_zeros, trailing_zeros, count_ones, count_zeros, swap_bytes, reverse_bits, rotate_left, rotate_right), and min, max and, when signed, abs. float and double have square_root, floor, ceiling, truncate, round, abs, copy_sign, multiply_add, min and max, the trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential and logarithmic functions of C's <math.h> with their names spelled out (sine, arc_tangent2, logarithm10, ...), cube_root, hypotenuse, remainder, and is_nan, is_infinite, is_finite and sign_bit. The math module has their constants (math.PI).

Example

var port = int.parse("8080");
assert(port.is_value() && port.value() == 8080, "parsed");
assert(byte.parse("256").is_empty(), "too big for a byte");
int big = 2147483647;
assert(big.wrapping_add(1) == -2147483648, "wraps around");
assert(big.checked_add(1).is_empty(), "does not fit");
assert((40 as uint).trailing_zeros() == 3, "40 is 0b101000");

Source: runtime/number.pep

Static methods

parse

static parse(text: String, base: int = 10): char?

Parses text as a char (i8) written in base: an optional + or -, then one or more digits, and nothing else. Digits past 9 are the letters, either case. No spaces, prefixes (0x) or separators are accepted.

Parameters

  • text — the text to parse
  • base — the base the digits are written in, from 2 to 36; 10 by default

Returns

  • the value, or none when text is not an integer in base or the value is outside -128 to 127

Panics

  • if base is less than 2 or greater than 36

Example

assert(i8.parse("-128").value() == -128, "the lowest");

Methods

is_digit

is_digit(): bool

Whether this is an ASCII decimal digit, 0 to 9, like C's isdigit.

Like every classification method on char, it looks at ASCII only, as C does in the "C" locale: a negative char (a byte of UTF-8 text above 127) is never a digit, letter, space or punctuation. Unlike C's functions, it is defined for every value, negative ones included.

Returns

  • true for 0 to 9

leading_zeros

leading_zeros(): int

Returns the number of zero bits above the highest set bit: 8 for zero, 0 when the highest bit is set. One instruction on most CPUs (llvm.ctlz).

Returns

  • the count of leading zero bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert(((1 as char)).leading_zeros() == 7, "one bit, at the bottom");

trailing_zeros

trailing_zeros(): int

Returns the number of zero bits below the lowest set bit: 8 for zero. One instruction on most CPUs (llvm.cttz), so it finds the first set bit of a mask without a loop.

Returns

  • the count of trailing zero bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert((8 as char).trailing_zeros() == 3, "8 is 0b1000");

count_ones

count_ones(): int

Returns the number of bits that are set (the population count, llvm.ctpop).

Returns

  • the count of one bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert((11 as char).count_ones() == 3, "three bits set");

count_zeros

count_zeros(): int

Returns the number of bits that are clear.

Returns

  • the count of zero bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert((11 as char).count_zeros() == 5, "three bits set");

swap_bytes

swap_bytes(): char

Returns this value with its bytes in reverse order: a one-byte value is itself. Each integer type has this method; see int.swap_bytes.

Returns

  • this value

reverse_bits

reverse_bits(): char

Returns this value with its bits in reverse order: the lowest bit becomes the highest (llvm.bitreverse).

Returns

  • the value with its 8 bits reversed

Example

assert(((1 as char)).reverse_bits().leading_zeros() == 0, "bottom to top");

rotate_left

rotate_left(count: int): char

Returns this value's bits rotated left by count: the bits shifted out at the top come back in at the bottom (llvm.fshl). count is taken modulo 8, so a negative count rotates right.

Parameters

  • count — how many places to rotate

Returns

  • the rotated value

Example

assert((9 as char).rotate_left(7) == (9 as char).rotate_right(1), "the same rotation");

rotate_right

rotate_right(count: int): char

Returns this value's bits rotated right by count: the bits shifted out at the bottom come back in at the top (llvm.fshr). count is taken modulo 8, so a negative count rotates left.

Parameters

  • count — how many places to rotate

Returns

  • the rotated value

Example

assert(((1 as char)).rotate_right(1) == ((1 as char)).rotate_left(7), "the bottom bit to the top");

Returns the smaller of this value and other.

Parameters

Returns

max

max(other: char): char

Returns the larger of this value and other.

Parameters

Returns

abs(): char

Returns the absolute value: this without its sign. The lowest value, -128, has no positive counterpart in a char, so it panics, as its negation does.

Returns

Panics

Example

Returns this * other, clamped to the highest byte on overflow.

Parameters

  • other — the value to multiply by

Returns

overflowing_mul

overflowing_mul(other: byte): (byte, bool)

Returns this * other modulo 2^8, and whether the operation overflowed.

leading_zeros

leading_zeros(): int

Returns the number of zero bits above the highest set bit: 8 for zero, 0 when the highest bit is set. One instruction on most CPUs (llvm.ctlz).

Returns

  • the count of leading zero bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert(((1 as byte)).leading_zeros() == 7, "one bit, at the bottom");

trailing_zeros

trailing_zeros(): int

Returns the number of zero bits below the lowest set bit: 8 for zero. One instruction on most CPUs (llvm.cttz), so it finds the first set bit of a mask without a loop.

Returns

  • the count of trailing zero bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert((8 as byte).trailing_zeros() == 3, "8 is 0b1000");

count_ones

count_ones(): int

Returns the number of bits that are set (the population count, llvm.ctpop).

Returns

  • the count of one bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert((11 as byte).count_ones() == 3, "three bits set");

count_zeros

count_zeros(): int

Returns the number of bits that are clear.

Returns

  • the count of zero bits, from 0 to 8

Example

assert((11 as byte).count_zeros() == 5, "three bits set");

swap_bytes

swap_bytes(): byte

Returns this value with its bytes in reverse order: a one-byte value is itself. Each integer type has this method; see int.swap_bytes.

Returns

  • this value

reverse_bits

reverse_bits(): byte

Returns this value with its bits in reverse order: the lowest bit becomes the highest (llvm.bitreverse).

Returns

  • the value with its 8 bits reversed

Example

assert(((1 as byte)).reverse_bits().leading_zeros() == 0, "bottom to top");

rotate_left

rotate_left(count: int): byte

Returns this value's bits rotated left by count: the bits shifted out at the top come back in at the bottom (llvm.fshl). count is taken modulo 8, so a negative count rotates right.

Parameters

  • count — how many places to rotate

Returns

  • the rotated value

Example

assert((9 as byte).rotate_left(7) == (9 as byte).rotate_right(1), "the same rotation");

rotate_right

rotate_right(count: int): byte

Returns this value's bits rotated right by count: the bits shifted out at the bottom come back in at the top (llvm.fshr). count is taken modulo 8, so a negative count rotates left.

Parameters

  • count — how many places to rotate

Returns

  • the rotated value

Example

assert(((1 as byte)).rotate_right(1) == ((1 as byte)).rotate_left(7), "the bottom bit to the top");

min(other: byte): byte

Returns the smaller of this value and other.

Parameters

  • other — the value to compare with

Returns

  • this when it is not greater than other, else other

Example

assert((3 as byte).min(5) == 3, "smaller");

Returns the larger of this value and other.

Returns

static parse(text: String, base: int = 10): int?

Parses text as an int (i32) written in base: an optional + or -, then one or more digits, and nothing else. Digits past 9 are the letters, either case ("ff" in base 16 is 255). No spaces, prefixes (0x) or separators are accepted.

Returns this - other modulo 2^32: on overflow the result wraps around instead of panicking. For hashes, checksums and random number generators, which rely on wrapping.

Parameters

  • other — the value to subtract

Returns

  • the difference, wrapped to a uint

checked_sub

checked_sub(other: uint): uint?

Returns this - other, or none when the difference does not fit a uint.

Parameters

  • other — the value to subtract

Returns

  • the difference, or none on overflow

saturating_sub

saturating_sub(other: uint): uint

Returns this - other, clamped to 0 on overflow.

Parameters

  • other — the value to subtract

Returns

  • the difference, or the nearest uint to it

overflowing_sub

overflowing_sub(other: uint): (uint, bool)

Returns this - other modulo 2^32, and whether the operation overflowed.

Parameters

  • other — the value to subtract

Returns

  • the wrapped difference, and true when it overflowed

wrapping_mul(other: uint): uint

Returns this * other modulo 2^32: on overflow the result wraps around instead of panicking. For hashes, checksums and random number generators, which rely on wrapping.

Parameters

Returns

Returns this * other, or none when the product does not fit a uint.

Parameters

  • other — the value to multiply by

Returns

  • the product, or none on overflow

saturating_mul

saturating_mul(other: uint): uint

Returns this * other, clamped to the highest uint on overflow.

Parameters

  • other — the value to multiply by

Returns

  • the product, or the nearest uint to it

overflowing_mul

overflowing_mul(other: uint): (uint, bool)

Returns this * other modulo 2^32, and whether the operation overflowed.

Parameters

  • other — the value to multiply by

Returns

  • the wrapped product, and true when it overflowed

leading_zeros

leading_zeros(): int

Returns the number of zero bits above the highest set bit: 32 for zero, 0 when the highest bit is set. One instruction on most CPUs (llvm.ctlz).

Returns

  • the count of leading zero bits, from 0 to 32

Example

assert(((1 as uint)).leading_zeros() == 31, "one bit, at the bottom");

trailing_zeros

trailing_zeros(): int

Returns the number of zero bits below the lowest set bit: 32 for zero. One instruction on most CPUs (llvm.cttz), so it finds the first set bit of a mask without a loop.

Returns

  • the count of trailing zero bits, from 0 to 32

Example

assert((8 as uint).trailing_zeros() == 3, "8 is 0b1000");

count_ones

count_ones(): int

Returns the number of bits that are set (the population count, llvm.ctpop).

Returns

  • the count of one bits, from 0 to 32

Example

assert((11 as uint).count_ones() == 3, "three bits set");

count_zeros

count_zeros(): int

Returns the number of bits that are clear.

Returns

  • the count of zero bits, from 0 to 32

Example

assert((11 as uint).count_zeros() == 29, "three bits set");

swap_bytes

swap_bytes(): uint

Returns this value with its bytes in reverse order (llvm.bswap), to convert between little-endian and big-endian byte order.

Returns

  • the value with its 4 bytes reversed

Example

assert((0x12345678 as uint).swap_bytes() == 0x78563412, "bytes reversed");

reverse_bits

reverse_bits(): uint

Returns this value with its bits in reverse order: the lowest bit becomes the highest (llvm.bitreverse).

Returns

  • the value with its 32 bits reversed

Example

assert(((1 as uint)).reverse_bits().leading_zeros() == 0, "bottom to top");

rotate_left

rotate_left(count: int): uint

Returns this value's bits rotated left by count: the bits shifted out at the top come back in at the bottom (llvm.fshl). count is taken modulo 32, so a negative count rotates right.

Parameters

  • count — how many places to rotate

Returns

  • the rotated value

Example

assert((9 as uint).rotate_left(31) == (9 as uint).rotate_right(1), "the same rotation");

rotate_right

rotate_right(count: int): uint

Returns this value's bits rotated right by count: the bits shifted out at the bottom come back in at the top (llvm.fshr). count is taken modulo 32, so a negative count rotates left.

Parameters

  • count — how many places to rotate

Returns

  • the rotated value

Example

assert(((1 as uint)).rotate_right(1) == ((1 as uint)).rotate_left(31), "the bottom bit to the top");

min

min(other: uint): uint

Returns the smaller of this value and other.

Parameters

  • other — the value to compare with

Returns

  • this when it is not greater than other, else other

Example

assert((3 as uint).min(5) == 3, "smaller");

max

max(other: uint): uint

Returns the larger of this value and other.

Parameters

  • other — the value to compare with

Returns

  • this when it is not less than other, else other

Example

assert((3 as uint).max(5) == 5, "larger");

extend long

Static methods

parse

static parse(text: String, base: int = 10): long?

Parses text as a long (i64) written in base: an optional + or -, then one or more digits, and nothing else. Digits past 9 are the letters, either case. No spaces, prefixes (0x) or separators are accepted.

Parameters

  • text — the text to parse
  • base — the base the digits are written in, from 2 to 36; 10 by default

Returns

  • the value, or none when text is not an integer in base or the value does not fit a long

Panics

  • if base is less than 2 or greater than 36

Example

assert(long.parse("-9000000000").value() == -9000000000, "decimal");
assert(long.parse("9223372036854775808").is_empty(), "too big");

abs

abs(): long

Returns the absolute value: this without its sign. The lowest value, -9223372036854775808, has no positive counterpart in a long, so it panics, as its negation does.

Example

extend float

extend float

Static methods

parse

static parse(text: String): float?

Parses text as a float written in decimal notation: an optional + or -, digits with an optional . among them ("1.5", ".5", "2."), then an optional exponent ("1e-3", "2.5E8"), and nothing else. The value is the nearest float. No spaces, inf, nan or hexadecimal are accepted.

Parameters

  • text — the text to parse

Returns

  • the value, or none when text is not decimal notation or its value is too large for a float (one too small rounds to zero)

Example

assert(float.parse("0.25").value() == 0.25, "decimal");
assert(float.parse("1e39").is_empty(), "too big");

Methods

square_root

square_root(): float

Returns the square root (llvm.sqrt, one instruction on most CPUs): NaN for a negative value, and -0.0 for -0.0.

Returns

  • the non-negative square root

Example

assert((2.25 as float).square_root() == 1.5, "exact");

floor

floor(): float

Returns the largest whole number not greater than this value (llvm.floor).

Returns

  • the value rounded toward negative infinity

Example

assert((-1.5 as float).floor() == -2.0, "down");

ceiling

ceiling(): float

Returns the smallest whole number not less than this value (llvm.ceil).

Returns

  • the value rounded toward positive infinity

Example

assert((-1.5 as float).ceiling() == -1.0, "up");

truncate

truncate(): float

Returns this value without its fractional part (llvm.trunc).

Returns

  • the value rounded toward zero

Example

assert((-1.5 as float).truncate() == -1.0, "toward zero");

round

round(): float

Returns the nearest whole number, halfway cases away from zero (llvm.round).

Returns

  • the rounded value

Example

assert((2.5 as float).round() == 3.0, "half away from zero");

abs

abs(): float

Returns the absolute value: this value with its sign bit cleared (llvm.fabs).

Returns

  • the value without its sign

Example

assert((-2.0 as float).abs() == 2.0, "negative");

copy_sign

copy_sign(sign: float): float

Returns this value's magnitude with the sign of sign (llvm.copysign).

Parameters

  • sign — the value whose sign the result takes

Returns

  • abs() of this value, negated when sign is negative

Example

assert((3.0 as float).copy_sign(-0.0) == -3.0, "negative zero is negative");

multiply_add

multiply_add(factor: float, addend: float): float

Returns this * factor + addend with a single rounding, as one fused multiply-add (llvm.fma): more precise than the two operations, and one instruction where the CPU has it.

Parameters

  • factor — the value to multiply by
  • addend — the value to add to the product

Returns

  • the fused product and sum

Example

assert((2.0 as float).multiply_add(3.0, 1.0) == 7.0, "2 * 3 + 1");

min

min(other: float): float

Returns the smaller of this value and other; when one of them is NaN, the other (llvm.minnum).

Parameters

  • other — the value to compare with

Returns

  • the smaller value

Example

assert((1.5 as float).min(-2.0) == -2.0, "smaller");

max

max(other: float): float

Returns the larger of this value and other; when one of them is NaN, the other (llvm.maxnum).

Parameters

  • other — the value to compare with

Returns

  • the larger value

Example

assert((1.5 as float).max(-2.0) == 1.5, "larger");

sine

sine(): float

Returns the sine of this angle, in radians (llvm.sin).

Returns

  • the sine, from -1 to 1; NaN for an infinity or NaN

Example

assert((0.0 as float).sine() == 0.0, "sine of zero");

cosine

cosine(): float

Returns the cosine of this angle, in radians (llvm.cos).

Returns

  • the cosine, from -1 to 1; NaN for an infinity or NaN

Example

assert((0.0 as float).cosine() == 1.0, "cosine of zero");

tangent

tangent(): float

Returns the tangent of this angle, in radians (llvm.tan).

Returns

  • the tangent; NaN for an infinity or NaN

Example

arc_sine

arc_sine(): float

Returns the angle, in radians, whose sine is this value (llvm.asin).

Returns

  • the angle, from -π/2 to π/2; NaN when this value is outside -1 to 1

Example

arc_cosine

Returns the angle, in radians, whose cosine is this value (llvm.acos).

Returns

  • the angle, from 0 to π; NaN when this value is outside -1 to 1

Example

arc_tangent

arc_tangent(): float

Returns the angle, in radians, whose tangent is this value (llvm.atan).

Returns

  • the angle, from -π/2 to π/2

Example

assert((0.0 as float).arc_tangent() == 0.0, "arc tangent of zero");

arc_tangent2

arc_tangent2(x: float): float

Returns the angle, in radians, from the positive x axis to the point (x, this value), using both signs to pick the quadrant: C's atan2(y, x) with this value as y (llvm.atan2).

Parameters

  • x — the x coordinate of the point

Returns

  • the angle, from -π to π

Example

assert((0.0 as float).arc_tangent2(1.0) == 0.0, "along the positive x axis");
assert((1.0 as float).arc_tangent2(0.0) == (1.0 as float).arc_sine(), "straight up is π/2");

hyperbolic_sine

hyperbolic_sine(): float

Returns the hyperbolic sine of this value (llvm.sinh).

Returns

  • the hyperbolic sine; an infinity when it is too large

Example

assert((0.0 as float).hyperbolic_sine() == 0.0, "hyperbolic sine of zero");

hyperbolic_cosine

hyperbolic_cosine(): float

Returns the hyperbolic cosine of this value (llvm.cosh).

Returns

  • the hyperbolic cosine, at least 1; an infinity when it is too large

Example

hyperbolic_tangent

hyperbolic_tangent(): float

Returns the hyperbolic tangent of this value (llvm.tanh).

Returns

  • the hyperbolic tangent, from -1 to 1

Example

assert((0.0 as float).hyperbolic_tangent() == 0.0, "hyperbolic tangent of zero");

arc_hyperbolic_sine

arc_hyperbolic_sine(): float

Returns the value whose hyperbolic sine is this value (C's asinh).

Returns

  • the inverse hyperbolic sine

Example

assert((0.0 as float).arc_hyperbolic_sine() == 0.0, "inverse of zero");

arc_hyperbolic_cosine

arc_hyperbolic_cosine(): float

Returns the non-negative value whose hyperbolic cosine is this value (C's acosh).

Returns

  • the inverse hyperbolic cosine; NaN when this value is less than 1

Example

assert((1.0 as float).arc_hyperbolic_cosine() == 0.0, "inverse of one");

arc_hyperbolic_tangent

arc_hyperbolic_tangent(): float

Returns the value whose hyperbolic tangent is this value (C's atanh).

Returns

  • the inverse hyperbolic tangent; an infinity for -1 or 1, and NaN outside

Example

assert((0.0 as float).arc_hyperbolic_tangent() == 0.0, "inverse of zero");

exponential

exponential(): float

Returns e raised to this value (llvm.exp).

Returns

  • e to the power of this value; an infinity when it is too large

Example

assert((0.0 as float).exponential() == 1.0, "e to the zero");

exponential2

exponential2(): float

Returns 2 raised to this value (llvm.exp2).

Returns

  • 2 to the power of this value

Example

assert((3.0 as float).exponential2() == 8.0, "2 cubed");

exponential_minus_one(): float

Returns e raised to this value, minus 1 (C's expm1): precise even when this value is near zero, where exponential() - 1 loses its digits.

Returns

  • exponential() - 1, computed without the loss

Example

assert((0.0 as float).exponential_minus_one() == 0.0, "e to the zero, minus one");

logarithm

logarithm(): float

Returns the natural logarithm (base e) of this value (llvm.log).

Returns

  • the logarithm; negative infinity for zero, and NaN for a negative value

Example

parse

static parse(text: String): double?

Parses text as a double written in decimal notation: an optional + or -, digits with an optional . among them ("1.5", ".5", "2."), then an optional exponent ("1e-3", "2.5E8"), and nothing else. The value is the nearest double. No spaces, inf, nan or hexadecimal are accepted.

Parameters

Returns

  • the value, or none when text is not decimal notation or its value is too large for a double (one too small rounds to zero)

Example

assert(double.parse("1.5.2").is_empty(), "not a number");

Comparable

Ordering: Comparable, the trait of types whose values sort in one order, which every number type, char and String declare.

Source: runtime/compare.pep

Comparable

trait Comparable

A type whose values have one order: compare says whether a value sorts before, with or after another.

Declaring it (extend Version with Comparable;) gives the type <, <=, > and >= and the methods min, max and clamp, each written in terms of compare, unless the type declares its own. A generic function asks for an order with T: Comparable.

compare returns a negative number when this value sorts before other, zero when the two sort together, and a positive number when it sorts after. The order must be total and consistent: two calls with the same values give the same answer, and a.compare(b) has the opposite sign of b.compare(a). Array.sort(), Map and Set rely on that.

float and double are Comparable with a total order: NaN sorts after every number and with every other NaN, and -0.0 with 0.0. Their < and > keep IEEE behavior (false whenever NaN takes part), while compare, clamp, Array.sort() and Map keys follow the total order.

Example

struct Version {
    var major: int;
    var minor: int;

    construct(this.major = 0, this.minor = 0) {}

    compare(other: Version): int {
        var order = major.compare(other.major);
        if (order != 0) {
            return order;
        }
        return minor.compare(other.minor);
    }
}

extend Version with Comparable;

assert(Version(1, 2) < Version(1, 10), "by minor");
assert(Version(2, 0).max(Version(1, 9)).major == 2, "max");

sort()

Sorts the elements in place into their own order, compare: by value for numbers (NaN last), by content for String. The sort is stable and otherwise behaves like sort(compare).

Panics

  • if comparing modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var numbers = [3, 1, 2];

Ranges

Ranges of numbers: a..b and a..>b.

a..b (half-open) holds a up to but not including b; a..>b (closed) includes b. Both make a Range<T>, a value that a for loop steps through without allocating:

for (var i in 0..count) { ... }   # 0, 1, ..., count - 1
for (var i in 1..>10) { ... }     # 1, 2, ..., 10

Source: runtime/range.pep

Range

[Value] struct Range<T>

A run of consecutive numbers, from start up to end, as a..b and a..>b make it.

A range is an iterator: next() steps from start up by one, and a for loop over a range is a counting loop. A range whose start is past its end yields nothing. A closed range ending at the largest value of its type (0..>255 as byte) stops there without overflowing.

Ranges are value structs: copying one copies its position, and looping over a range stored in a variable advances that variable.

Type parameters

  • T — the number type, inferred from the bounds (0..n with a ulong n is a Range<ulong>)

Example

var total = 0;
for (var i in 1..>4) {
    total += i;   # 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
}
var r = 0..10;
assert(r.contains(9) && !r.contains(10), "half-open");

Fields

start

T start

The first number of the range.

end

T end

The bound the range stops at: the last number when inclusive, else one past it.

inclusive

bool inclusive

Whether end is part of the range: true for a..>b, false for a..b.

Array

Source: runtime/array.pep

Array

[__Lazy] struct Array<T>

A growable, contiguous, zero-indexed sequence of T values.

Elements live in one heap buffer that doubles when full (starting at 4 slots), so append is amortized O(1) and indexing is O(1). When T is a struct type, each slot holds a counted reference, exactly like a std::vector<std::shared_ptr<T>>: storing an element acquires it, overwriting or removing one releases the old occupant, and destroying the Array releases every element it still holds. Moving elements within the Array (insert, remove_at, swap, reverse) does not change their reference counts.

Array is itself a struct, so assigning it or passing it to a function shares the same Array rather than copying its elements; use clone() for an independent copy.

An empty Array allocates nothing: Array<T>() makes no object until the Array is first written (append, insert, reserve, ...) or shared (assigned, stored, passed or returned), and reading it (count, is_empty, capacity, find, contains, iterating) allocates nothing. Sharing allocates first, so every name for an Array sees the same elements.

An Array is Iterable<T>: for (var x in a) visits each element in index order. Every mutating operation (an element store through [], append, insert, remove_at, pop, clear, a shrinking truncate, swap, fill, retain, remove_if, resize, split_off, drain, extend_from, rotate, select_nth, partial_sort, and reverse, sort, sort_unstable or dedup of two or more elements) invalidates running iterators and slices (slice), and the next step of such a loop panics with "Array modified during iteration".

Type parameters

  • T — the element type

See also

  • ArrayIterator

Example

main(): int {
    var a = Array<int>();
    a.append(1);
    a.append(2);
    a[0] = 5;
    var total = 0;
    for (var x in a) {
        total = total + x;
    }
    return total;   # 7
}

Properties

count

var count: ulong { get; }

The number of elements in the Array.

capacity

var capacity: ulong { get; }

The number of elements the Array can hold before its buffer must be reallocated.

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the Array has no elements.

Constructor

Array()

construct(capacity: ulong = 0)

Creates an empty Array, optionally preallocating room for capacity elements.

With the default capacity of 0, nothing is allocated, not even the Array itself, until the Array is first written or shared (see Array). Preallocating avoids the reallocations append would otherwise perform while the Array grows to a known size.

Parameters

  • capacity — the number of element slots to allocate up front; count is still 0

Example

var a = Array<int>(16);   # a.count == 0, a.capacity == 16

Methods

iterate

[__Reads] iterate(): ArrayIterator<T>

Returns an iterator over the elements in index order; this is what for (var x in array) calls (the Iterable<T> protocol).

The iterator holds a reference to the Array, so iterating a temporary keeps it alive for the whole loop. Modifying the Array while the iterator is in use makes the iterator's next next() or current() panic, except when the Array was empty when the iterator was made: the iterator then sees no elements and ends.

Returns

  • a new iterator positioned before the first element

Example

for (var x in a) {
    total = total + x;
}

data

[__Reads] data(): __ptr<T>

Returns a pointer to the first element, for passing the elements to C, as String.c_str() does for text.

The pointer is owned by the Array. It is valid until the Array is destroyed or its buffer reallocates (append, insert, reserve, or anything else that grows it); writes through it change the elements. For an empty Array it is __null, even when capacity is reserved.

Returns

  • the address of element 0, or __null when the Array is empty

See also

  • append_from

Example

var a = Array<int>();
a.append(7);
var p = a.data();   # p[0] == 7

reserve

reserve(capacity: ulong)

Ensures the buffer has room for at least capacity elements, reallocating it when it is smaller.

Never shrinks the buffer: a capacity at or below the current one does nothing. Elements, their order, and their reference counts are unchanged, and running iterators stay valid. Growing copies the existing elements, which costs O(count).

Parameters

  • capacity — the minimum number of element slots required

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

var a = Array<int>();
a.reserve(8);   # a.capacity >= 8
a.reserve(2);   # no effect: capacity never shrinks

grow

grow()

Makes room for one more element: when the buffer is full, doubles its capacity (to at least 4); otherwise does nothing.

append and insert call this themselves; callers rarely need it. Does not change the elements or invalidate iterators.

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

operator []

[__Reads] [](idx: ulong): T

Returns the element at idx; this is the indexer read a[idx].

Runs in O(1). For a struct T the result is the stored reference itself; binding it to a variable acquires it like any shared copy.

Parameters

  • idx — the zero-based position to read

Returns

  • the element at idx

Panics

  • if idx < count does not hold ("Array index read out of bounds")

Example

var first = a[0];

operator []

[](idx: ulong, value: T): T

Replaces the element at idx with value; this is the indexer write a[idx] = value.

For a struct T the slot acquires value and releases its previous occupant; assigning an element to its own slot (a[i] = a[i]) leaves counts unchanged. Only replaces an existing element: use append to add one. Invalidates running iterators, even when the value is unchanged.

Parameters

  • idx — the zero-based position to overwrite
  • value — the new element

Returns

  • the element now stored at idx (that is, value)

Panics

  • if idx < count does not hold ("Array index write out of bounds")

Example

a[0] = 42;

append

append(item: T)

Adds item to the end of the Array.

Amortized O(1): when the buffer is full it doubles (O(count) for that call). For a struct T the Array acquires a reference to item. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • item — the element to add

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

var a = Array<int>();
a.append(1);
a.append(2);   # a holds [1, 2]

append_from

append_from(source: __ptr<T>, count: ulong)

Appends the count elements at source, in order: the way to fill an Array from a C buffer, as String(data, size) does for text.

Runs in O(count), with one copy of the whole range for a POD T. For a struct T the Array acquires a reference to each element. source must point at count valid elements, and not into this Array, which may reallocate. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • source — the first element to copy; may be __null when count is 0
  • count — the number of elements to copy

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

See also

  • data

Example

var a = Array<u8>();
a.append(1);
a.append(2);
var b = Array<u8>();
b.append_from(a.data(), a.count);   # b holds [1, 2]

insert

insert(idx: ulong, item: T)

Inserts item at position idx, shifting the element there and every later element up by one.

Runs in O(count - idx), plus a reallocation when the buffer is full. idx == count appends. For a struct T the Array acquires a reference to item; shifted elements keep their reference counts. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • idx — the position item will occupy; from 0 through count
  • item — the element to insert

Panics

  • if idx <= count does not hold ("Array insert index out of bounds")
  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

var a = Array<int>();
a.append(1);
a.append(3);
a.insert(1, 2);   # a holds [1, 2, 3]

remove_at

remove_at(idx: ulong): T

Removes and returns the element at idx, shifting every later element down by one.

Runs in O(count - idx). For a struct T the Array's reference is transferred to the caller, so the element stays alive as long as the result is held; shifted elements keep their reference counts. The capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • idx — the position of the element to remove

Returns

  • the removed element

Panics

  • if idx < count does not hold ("Array remove index out of bounds")

Example

var a = Array<int>();
a.append(1);
a.append(2);
var x = a.remove_at(0);   # x == 1; a holds [2]

pop

pop(): T

Removes and returns the last element.

Runs in O(1). For a struct T the Array's reference is transferred to the caller. The capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators.

Returns

  • the element that was last

Panics

  • if the Array is empty ("Array pop on empty Array")

Example

var top = a.pop();

first

[__Reads] first(): T

Returns the first element without removing it; the same as a[0].

Returns

  • the element at index 0

Panics

  • if the Array is empty ("Array first on empty Array")

last

[__Reads] last(): T

Returns the last element without removing it; the same as a[a.count - 1].

Returns

  • the element at index count - 1

Panics

  • if the Array is empty ("Array last on empty Array")

clear

clear()

Removes every element, leaving the Array empty.

Runs in O(count) for a T holding references, each of which is released, and in O(1) for a plain value T (int, u8, a tuple of numbers). The capacity is kept, so refilling the Array does not reallocate. Always invalidates running iterators, even on an empty Array.

truncate

truncate(count: ulong)

Shortens the Array to its first count elements, removing the rest.

Runs in O(removed elements). For a struct T each removed element's reference is released. A count at or above the current count does nothing (the Array never grows) and leaves iterators valid; an actual shrink invalidates them. The capacity is kept.

Parameters

  • count — the number of leading elements to keep

Example

a.truncate(1);   # keeps only a[0]
a.truncate(5);   # no effect when a has fewer than 5 elements

swap

swap(a: ulong, b: ulong)

Exchanges the elements at positions a and b.

Runs in O(1). Reference counts are unchanged: the two references just trade slots. Swapping a position with itself is allowed and changes no element, but still invalidates running iterators like every swap.

Parameters

  • a — the position of the first element
  • b — the position of the second element

Panics

  • if a < count does not hold ("Array swap index out of bounds")
  • if b < count does not hold ("Array swap index out of bounds")

reverse

reverse()

Reverses the order of the elements in place.

Runs in O(count), exchanging elements pairwise, so reference counts are unchanged. An Array of fewer than two elements is left untouched and its iterators stay valid; otherwise running iterators are invalidated.

Example

a.reverse();   # [1, 2, 3] becomes [3, 2, 1]

rotate

rotate(count: ulong)

Moves the first count elements to the end, keeping the order within each part: the element at count becomes the first.

Runs in O(count of the Array), exchanging elements, so reference counts are unchanged. Rotating by 0 or by the Array's count changes nothing and leaves iterators valid; any other rotation invalidates them.

Parameters

  • count — the number of leading elements to move; from 0 through the Array's count

Panics

  • if count is more than the Array's count ("Array rotate count out of bounds")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
a.rotate(2);   # [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]

sort

sort(compare: (T, T) => int)

Sorts the elements in place into the order compare defines. The sort is stable: elements that compare equal keep their relative order.

compare(a, b) returns a negative number when a belongs before b, 0 when their order does not matter, and a positive number when a belongs after b, the convention String.compare follows. It is a merge sort: O(count log count) calls to compare, plus a scratch buffer of count slots. Elements move between the two buffers without changing any reference count. Invalidates running iterators when there are two or more elements.

compare must not modify the Array: its elements are spread over the two buffers while the sort runs.

Parameters

  • compare — returns the order of its two arguments, as above

Panics

  • if compare modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var names = Array<String>();
names.append("pear");
names.append("apple");
names.sort((a, b) => a.compare(b));   # ["apple", "pear"]
var numbers = Array<int>();
numbers.append(3);
numbers.append(1);
numbers.sort((a, b) => b - a);        # descending: [3, 1]

sort_unstable

sort_unstable(compare: (T, T) => int)

Sorts the elements in place into the order compare defines, without keeping equal elements in their original order.

compare follows the convention of sort(compare). It is pattern-defeating quicksort (pdqsort): O(count log count) calls to compare in the worst case, O(count) on an Array that is already sorted or all equal, and no scratch buffer, so it is the faster sort when stability does not matter. Elements only trade slots, so no reference count changes. Invalidates running iterators when there are two or more elements.

Parameters

  • compare — returns the order of its two arguments, as for sort

Panics

  • if compare modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var a = [5, 1, 4, 2, 3];
a.sort_unstable((x, y) => x - y);   # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

select_nth

select_nth(nth: ulong, compare: (T, T) => int)

Reorders the elements so that the one at nth is the element a full sort would put there, every element before it sorts before or with it, and every element after it sorts after or with it (C++'s nth_element). Each side is otherwise in no particular order.

compare follows the convention of sort(compare). Runs in O(count) calls to compare on average and O(count log count) in the worst case, with no scratch buffer. Elements only trade slots, so no reference count changes. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • nth — the position to settle; less than count
  • compare — returns the order of its two arguments, as for sort

Panics

  • if nth < count does not hold ("Array select_nth index out of bounds")
  • if compare modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var a = [9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3];
a.select_nth(2, (x, y) => x - y);   # a[2] == 3, the third smallest

partial_sort

partial_sort(count: ulong, compare: (T, T) => int)

Puts the count elements that sort first into the first count positions, in order, and leaves the rest after them in no particular order: the start of a full sort, found faster.

compare follows the convention of sort(compare). Runs in O(count of the Array + count log count) calls to compare on average, with no scratch buffer; it is not stable. Elements only trade slots, so no reference count changes. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • count — the number of leading elements to sort; from 0 through the Array's count
  • compare — returns the order of its two arguments, as for sort

Panics

  • if count is more than the Array's count ("Array partial_sort count out of bounds")
  • if compare modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var scores = [40, 95, 12, 77, 63];
scores.partial_sort(3, (x, y) => y - x);   # starts [95, 77, 63]

find

[__Reads] find(item: T): ulong?

Returns the position of the first element equal to item, or none when no element matches.

Runs in O(count), scanning from the front. Elements are compared with ==: when T declares an == operator (as String does) that operator decides; for any other struct T it compares references, so only the very same object matches.

Breaking change: find used to return a long that was -1 when nothing matched. It now returns ulong?: test it with is_some() (or as a condition) and read the index with value().

Parameters

  • item — the value to look for

Returns

  • the index of the first match, or none when no element matches (always none for an empty Array)

Example

var a = [3, 9, 4];
var i = a.find(9);         # i.value() == 1
var missing = a.find(7);   # missing.is_empty() == true

contains

[__Reads] contains(item: T): bool

Reports whether any element equals item, compared as find does.

Runs in O(count).

Parameters

  • item — the value to look for

Returns

  • true when find(item) finds a match

slice

[__Reads] slice(start: ulong, end: ulong): ArrayView<T>

Returns a read-only view of the elements from start up to but not including end, without copying them.

The slice holds a reference to this Array, so it cannot outlive it, and it is fail-fast like an iterator: once the Array is modified (see Array for which operations count), every later use of the slice panics, so it never reads elements that moved or were freed.

Parameters

  • start — the position of the first element in the slice
  • end — the position one past the last element; from start through count

Returns

  • a view of end - start elements

Panics

  • if start <= end and end <= count do not both hold ("Array slice out of bounds")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
var middle = a.slice(1, 4);   # views [2, 3, 4]
var second = middle[1];       # 3

chunks

[__Reads] chunks<TElement=T>(size: ulong): ArrayChunks<TElement>

Returns an iterator over the Array in runs of size elements, as slices; the last run is shorter when size does not divide count. The same as slice(0, count).chunks(size).

Type parameters

  • TElement — the element type, T by default

Parameters

  • size — the number of elements in each run

Returns

  • an iterator over count / size runs, rounded up

Panics

  • if size is 0 ("ArrayView chunk size is 0")

Example

var rows = Array<int>();
for (var row in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].chunks(3)) {
    rows.append(row[0]);   # 1, then 4
}

windows

[__Reads] windows<TElement=T>(size: ulong): ArrayChunks<TElement>

Returns an iterator over every run of size consecutive elements, as slices, each starting one element after the one before. The same as slice(0, count).windows(size).

Type parameters

  • TElement — the element type, T by default

Parameters

  • size — the number of elements in each run

Returns

  • an iterator over count - size + 1 runs, or none when the Array is shorter than size

Panics

  • if size is 0 ("ArrayView chunk size is 0")

Example

var rises = 0;
for (var pair in [1, 3, 2, 5].windows(2)) {
    if (pair[1] > pair[0]) {
        rises = rises + 1;   # 2 in all
    }
}

binary_search_by

[__Reads] binary_search_by(order: (T) => int): ulong?

Returns the position of the element that order reports equal to the target, searching an Array sorted in the order order follows, or none when there is none.

Runs in O(log count) calls to order, which must not modify the Array. When several elements match, the first of them is found.

Parameters

  • order — returns a negative number when its argument sorts before the target, 0 when it matches, and a positive number when it sorts after

Returns

  • the index of the first matching element, or none

Panics

  • if order modifies the Array ("Array modified while a slice of it is in use")

Example

var a = [10, 20, 30];
var i = a.binary_search_by((x) => x.compare(20));   # i.value() == 1

fill

fill(value: T)

Replaces every element with value.

Runs in O(count). For a struct T every slot acquires value and releases its previous occupant. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • value — the value each element becomes

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3];
a.fill(0);   # [0, 0, 0]

retain

retain(keep: (T) => bool)

Removes every element for which keep returns false, keeping the order of the rest.

Runs in O(count) calls to keep, which sees each element once, in index order, and must not modify the Array. For a struct T each removed element is released and kept elements keep their counts. The capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • keep — returns true for an element to keep

Panics

  • if keep modifies the Array ("Array modified during retain")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
a.retain((x) => x % 2 == 0);   # [2, 4]

remove_if

remove_if(remove: (T) => bool)

Removes every element for which remove returns true, keeping the order of the rest; the opposite of retain.

Runs in O(count) calls to remove, which sees each element once, in index order, and must not modify the Array. For a struct T each removed element is released. Invalidates running iterators.

Parameters

  • remove — returns true for an element to remove

Panics

  • if remove modifies the Array ("Array modified during retain")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
a.remove_if((x) => x > 2);   # [1, 2]

dedup

dedup()

Removes each element equal (==) to the one before it, so a run of equal elements keeps only its first. On a sorted Array this removes every duplicate.

Runs in O(count). Elements are compared as find does. For a struct T each removed element is released. Invalidates running iterators when there are two or more elements.

Example

var a = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 1];
a.dedup();   # [1, 2, 3, 1]

resize

resize(count: ulong, value: T)

Changes the count to count: removes elements past it, as truncate does, or appends copies of value until there are count elements.

Runs in O(difference in count), plus at most one reallocation. Invalidates running iterators when the count changes.

Parameters

  • count — the number of elements the Array will hold
  • value — the element to append when the Array grows

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

var a = [1, 2];
a.resize(4, 0);   # [1, 2, 0, 0]
a.resize(1, 0);   # [1]

split_off

split_off(index: ulong): Array<T>

Removes the elements from index on and returns them as a new Array, leaving this Array with its first index elements.

Runs in O(count - index). The elements move without changing their reference counts. This Array's capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators when any element moves.

Parameters

  • index — the position of the first element to move; from 0 through count

Returns

  • a new Array holding the elements that were at index and after

Panics

  • if index <= count does not hold ("Array split_off index out of bounds")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
var tail = a.split_off(1);   # a holds [1]; tail holds [2, 3, 4]

drain

drain(start: ulong, end: ulong): Array<T>

Removes the elements from start up to but not including end and returns them as a new Array, shifting the later elements down.

Runs in O(count - start). The elements move without changing their reference counts. This Array's capacity is unchanged. Invalidates running iterators when any element is removed.

Parameters

  • start — the position of the first element to remove
  • end — the position one past the last element to remove; from start through count

Returns

  • a new Array holding the removed elements, in order

Panics

  • if start <= end and end <= count do not both hold ("Array drain range out of bounds")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
var middle = a.drain(1, 3);   # a holds [1, 4, 5]; middle holds [2, 3]

append_all

append_all(rhs: Array<T>)

Appends every element of rhs, in order, to the end of this Array.

Runs in O(count of rhs), growing the buffer at most once and copying the elements in one block. rhs is unchanged, and it may be this same Array (a.append_all(a) doubles a). For a struct T each appended element is acquired once more, since both Arrays now hold it. Invalidates this Array's running iterators when rhs is not empty.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array whose elements are copied

Panics

  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

See also

  • +=

extend_from

extend_from(items: ArrayView<T>)

Appends every element of items, in order, to the end of this Array.

Runs in O(count of items), growing the buffer at most once. items may view this same Array. For a struct T each appended element is acquired once more. Invalidates this Array's running iterators and slices (items among them, when it views this Array) when items is not empty.

Parameters

  • items — the elements to copy

Panics

  • if the Array items views was modified since items was made ("Array modified while a slice of it is in use")
  • if the buffer must grow while an I/O operation in a task is using it

Example

var a = [1, 2];
var b = [7, 8, 9];
a.extend_from(b.slice(1, 3));   # [1, 2, 8, 9]

clone

[__Reads] clone(): Array<T>

Returns a new Array holding the same elements in the same order.

Runs in O(count). The copy is shallow: for a struct T both Arrays refer to the same element objects (each acquired once more), but adding or removing elements in one does not affect the other. The new Array's capacity equals this Array's count.

Returns

  • an independent Array with the same elements

Example

var b = a.clone();
b.append(7);   # a is unchanged

copy

copy(): Array<T>

Returns a deep copy: a new Array holding a copy of each element, made with copy. This is how copy(value) copies an Array (the Copyable<Array<T>> implementation); call copy(array) rather than this method.

Unlike clone(), which shares struct elements, the result shares no element that is not thread-safe with this Array. An element that appears twice is copied once. Runs in O(count) plus the cost of copying the elements.

Returns

  • the copy

Example

var names = Array<String>();
names.append("ada");
var copied = copy(names);   # calls this method

operator ==

[__Reads] ==(rhs: Array<T>): bool

Reports whether both Arrays have the same count and pairwise equal elements, compared with == as find does.

Runs in O(count); stops at the first difference. Two empty Arrays are equal. capacity is not compared.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array to compare with

Returns

  • true when the Arrays are element-wise equal

operator !=

[__Reads] !=(rhs: Array<T>): bool

Reports whether the Arrays differ in count or in any element; the negation of ==.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array to compare with

Returns

  • true when the Arrays are not element-wise equal

operator +=

+=(rhs: Array<T>): Array<T>

Appends every element of rhs to this Array in place (a += b); the same as append_all.

a += a is allowed and doubles a.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array whose elements are appended

Returns

  • this Array, after the append

See also

  • append_all

Example

a += b;   # a now ends with b's elements

operator +

[__Reads] +(rhs: Array<T>): Array<T>

Returns a new Array holding this Array's elements followed by those of rhs (a + b).

Runs in O(count + count of rhs). Neither operand is modified; like clone, the result shares struct elements with its operands.

Parameters

  • rhs — the Array whose elements come second

Returns

  • the concatenation of this Array and rhs

Example

var c = a + b;

extend Array

extend Array<T: Comparable>

The searches of a sorted Array, for an element type with an order (see Comparable).

Type parameters

  • T — the element type, Comparable

Methods

binary_search

[__Reads] binary_search(item: T): ulong?

Returns the position of an element equal to item in this Array, which must be sorted in compare order, or none when there is none.

Runs in O(log count). When several elements equal item, the first of them is found. On an Array that is not sorted the result is unspecified (but never out of bounds).

Parameters

  • item — the value to look for

Returns

  • the index of the first element equal to item, or none

Example

var a = [1, 3, 5, 7];
var i = a.binary_search(5);   # i.value() == 2

lower_bound

[__Reads] lower_bound(item: T): ulong

Returns the first position at which item could be inserted while keeping this sorted Array sorted: the index of the first element that does not sort before item (in compare order), or count when every element does.

Runs in O(log count).

Parameters

  • item — the value to place

Returns

  • the index of the first element at or after item

Example

var a = [1, 3, 3, 5];
var i = a.lower_bound(3);   # 1

upper_bound

[__Reads] upper_bound(item: T): ulong

Returns the last position at which item could be inserted while keeping this sorted Array sorted: the index of the first element that sorts after item (in compare order), or count when none does.

Runs in O(log count). upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x) is the number of elements equal to x.

Parameters

  • item — the value to place

Returns

  • the index of the first element after item

Example

var a = [1, 3, 3, 5];
var i = a.upper_bound(3);   # 3

is_sorted

[__Reads] is_sorted(): bool

Reports whether the elements are in compare order: no element sorts after the one that follows it.

Runs in O(count). An Array of fewer than two elements is sorted.

Returns

  • true when the Array is sorted

sort_unstable

sort_unstable()

Sorts the elements in place into their own order, compare, without keeping equal elements in their original order; otherwise behaves like sort_unstable(compare).

Panics

  • if comparing modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var a = [3, 1, 2];
a.sort_unstable();   # [1, 2, 3]

select_nth

select_nth(nth: ulong)

Reorders the elements so that the one at nth is the one sorting would put there, with the elements before it sorting before or with it and those after it after or with it; see select_nth(nth, compare).

Parameters

  • nth — the position to settle; less than count

Panics

  • if nth < count does not hold ("Array select_nth index out of bounds")
  • if comparing modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var a = [9, 1, 8, 2, 7];
a.select_nth(2);   # a[2] == 7, the median

partial_sort

partial_sort(count: ulong)

Puts the count smallest elements into the first count positions, in order; see partial_sort(count, compare).

Parameters

  • count — the number of leading elements to sort; from 0 through the Array's count

Panics

  • if count is more than the Array's count ("Array partial_sort count out of bounds")
  • if comparing modifies the Array ("Array modified during sort")

Example

var a = [5, 3, 9, 1, 7];
a.partial_sort(2);   # starts [1, 3]

compare

[__Reads] compare(other: Array<T>): int

Returns the lexicographic order of this Array and other: the order of the first pair of elements that differ (by their compare), or, when one Array is the start of the other, the shorter first.

Runs in O(count); stops at the first difference. Two empty Arrays sort together. It follows Comparable's convention, so an Array of Arrays sorts with sort((a, b) => a.compare(b)).

Parameters

  • other — the Array to compare with

Returns

  • a negative number, zero or a positive number as this Array sorts before, with or after other

Example

assert([1, 2, 3].compare([1, 3]) < 0, "2 sorts before 3");
assert([1, 2].compare([1, 2, 0]) < 0, "the shorter first");

ArrayIterator

[Value] struct ArrayIterator<T>

An Iterator<T> over the elements of an Array, in index order; returned by Array.iterate() and driven by for (var x in array).

Holds a reference to the Array, so iterating a temporary keeps it alive for the whole loop. The iterator is fail-fast: if the Array is modified after the iterator was created (see Array for which operations count), its next next() or current() panics instead of skipping or repeating elements (an iterator over an Array that was empty when it was made just ends).

Type parameters

  • T — the element type of the source Array

See also

  • Array.iterate

Example

var it = a.iterate();
while (it.next()) {
    var x = it.current();
}

Methods

next

next(): bool

Advances to the next element.

The first call moves to index 0. Once it returns false it keeps returning false.

Returns

  • true when there is a current element, false once past the end

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the iterator was created ("Array modified during iteration")

current

current(): T

Returns the element the last successful next() moved to.

Returns

  • the current element

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the iterator was created ("Array modified during iteration")
  • if next() was never called ("ArrayIterator.current() before next()")
  • if next() already returned false ("ArrayIterator.current() past the end")

ArrayView

[Value] struct ArrayView<T>

A read-only view of a run of an Array's elements, made by Array.slice, that lets a function take "some of the elements" without copying them.

A slice holds a reference to its Array, so the Array lives at least as long as the slice. It is fail-fast like ArrayIterator: once the Array is modified (see Array for which operations count), every later use of the slice panics with "Array modified while a slice of it is in use" instead of reading elements that moved or were freed. Make a new slice after changing the Array.

A slice is Iterable<T>: for (var x in slice) visits its elements in order.

Type parameters

  • T — the element type of the Array

See also

  • Array.slice

Example

total(values: ArrayView<int>): int {
    var sum = 0;
    for (var x in values) {
        sum = sum + x;
    }
    return sum;
}

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4];
var tail_sum = total(a.slice(2, 4));   # 7

Properties

count

var count: ulong { get; }

The number of elements in the slice.

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the slice has no elements.

Methods

operator []

[](index: ulong): T

Returns the element at index in the slice, index 0 being the slice's first element; this is the indexer read slice[index].

Parameters

  • index — the zero-based position in the slice

Returns

  • the element at index

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the slice was made ("Array modified while a slice of it is in use")
  • if index < count does not hold ("ArrayView index out of bounds")

slice

slice(start: ulong, end: ulong): ArrayView<T>

Returns a view of this slice's elements from start up to but not including end, positions counted within this slice.

Parameters

  • start — the position of the first element
  • end — the position one past the last element; from start through count

Returns

  • a view of end - start elements of the same Array

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the slice was made ("Array modified while a slice of it is in use")
  • if start <= end and end <= count do not both hold ("ArrayView slice out of bounds")

iterate

iterate(): ArrayViewIterator<T>

Returns an iterator over the slice's elements in order; this is what for (var x in slice) calls.

Returns

  • a new iterator positioned before the first element

split_at

split_at(index: ulong): (ArrayView<T>, ArrayView<T>)

Splits the slice in two at index: the elements before it, and the elements from it on.

Parameters

  • index — the position the second slice starts at; from 0 through count

Returns

  • the slices slice(0, index) and slice(index, count)

Panics

  • if the Array was modified since the slice was made ("Array modified while a slice of it is in use")
  • if index <= count does not hold ("ArrayView slice out of bounds")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
var (head, tail) = a.slice(0, 5).split_at(2);   # [1, 2] and [3, 4, 5]

chunks

chunks<TElement=T>(size: ulong): ArrayChunks<TElement>

Returns an iterator over the slice in runs of size elements, as slices, from the start; the last run is shorter when size does not divide count.

Type parameters

  • TElement — the element type, T by default

Parameters

Returns

Panics

  • if size is 0 ("ArrayView chunk size is 0")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
for (var run in a.slice(0, 5).chunks(2)) {
    # [1, 2], then [3, 4], then [5]
}

windows

windows<TElement=T>(size: ulong): ArrayChunks<TElement>

Returns an iterator over every run of size consecutive elements, as slices, each starting one element after the one before; none when the slice is shorter than size.

Type parameters

  • TElement — the element type, T by default

Parameters

Returns

Panics

  • if size is 0 ("ArrayView chunk size is 0")

Example

var a = [1, 2, 3];
for (var pair in a.slice(0, 3).windows(2)) {
    # [1, 2], then [2, 3]

Reports whether both slices have the same count and pairwise equal elements, compared with == as Array.find does. Where the slices are is not compared.
