HashMap and HashSet

Hashing: hash<T>(value), the 64-bit hash HashMap and HashSet use for their keys, and the hash maps and sets themselves.

Source: runtime/hash.pep

hash

hash<T>(value: T): u64

Returns a 64-bit hash of value, the hash HashMap and HashSet use for their keys.

  • POD types (integers, floats, pointers, bool) mix the value's own bits, so equal values hash equally.
  • Struct types hash by identity: the object's address, mixed so that aligned addresses spread across buckets. Two distinct objects with equal fields therefore hash differently and are distinct keys. A null reference hashes to the FNV-1a offset basis (0xcbf29ce484222325).

Every input bit reaches the low bits of the result, which a power-of-two table masks with. The hash is not keyed, so it does not resist inputs chosen to collide.

  • String hashes by content through the concrete hash<String> override, so equal strings at different addresses collide.

A struct whose keys should match by content is marked [Equatable], which derives its == and its hash from its fields, or declares an == operator and overrides this function for itself, hashing the fields == compares: hash<Point>(value: Point): u64. Keys that are == must hash equally (see the "Hashing and equality" chapter of the book).

The result is deterministic within and across runs of a program for POD values and strings; for other struct types it depends on where the object was allocated. Reading the address does no refcount work, and a temporary argument is released afterwards.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value to hash

Parameters

  • value — the value to hash

Returns

  • the 64-bit hash of value

See also

  • hash<String>

Example

var a = hash<int>(5);
var b = hash<int>(5);   # a == b

hash

hash<String>(value: String): u64

Returns a 64-bit hash of a String's bytes, so equal strings hash equally wherever they are stored. Keeps equal String keys of a HashMap or HashSet in one bucket.

Hashes the size bytes of the String (not the NUL terminator) 8 bytes at a time, in O(size). An empty String hashes to the FNV-1a offset basis (0xcbf29ce484222325).

Parameters

  • value — the String to hash; it must not be a null reference

Returns

  • the 64-bit hash of the String's content

Example

assert(hash<String>("hello") == hash<String>("hello"), "content hash");

hash

hash<StringConstant>(value: StringConstant): u64

Returns a 64-bit hash of a StringConstant's bytes, the same hash hash<String> gives a String with the same content, so StringConstant keys work in a HashMap or HashSet. Runs in O(size).

Parameters

  • value — the text to hash

Returns

  • the 64-bit hash of the text's content

HashMap

struct HashMap<K, V>

A hash table that maps keys of type K to values of type V.

Keys are hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==: POD keys by value, String keys by content, and other struct keys by identity (two distinct objects with equal fields are different keys) unless the struct declares an == operator and a matching hash<K> override. Any type can be a key.

The map holds one reference to each stored key and value. It acquires them when they are stored and releases them when they are overwritten, removed, cleared, or when the map is destroyed.

Lookups, inserts, and removals take expected O(1) time. Before an insert of a new key would fill half the table (live entries plus removed-slot tombstones), the table is rebuilt: at double the size, or at the same size when tombstones make up at least half of that load, so churn (many inserts and removals of different keys) does not keep growing it. It never shrinks.

iterate() visits the entries as (key, value) tuples, in no defined order.

Type parameters

  • K — the key type; hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==
  • V — the value type

Example

var ages = HashMap<String, int>();
ages["ada"] = 36;
ages.insert("alan", 41);
assert(ages["ada"] == 36, "lookup");
assert(ages.get("grace") == 0, "a missing key reads as the default");
assert(ages.remove("alan"), "removed");
assert(ages.count == 1, "one entry left");

Properties

count

var count: int { get; }

The number of entries in the map. O(1).

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the map has no entries. O(1).

capacity

var capacity: ulong { get; }

The number of slots in the table, a power of two and at least 8. The map grows before its entries and tombstones reach half of it. O(1).

Constructor

HashMap()

construct(initial_capacity: ulong = 8)

Creates an empty map whose table has room for at least initial_capacity slots.

The slot count is rounded up to a power of two, with a minimum of 8. The map holds up to half its slot count before the first grow, so pass about twice the expected number of entries to avoid regrowing. Allocates three arrays of that many slots.

Parameters

  • initial_capacity — the minimum number of slots in the table

Example

var m = HashMap<int, int>(64);   # 64 slots, 32 entries before growing

Methods

grow

grow()

Doubles the table and reinserts every entry, dropping all tombstones.

insert calls it automatically. Calling it directly is safe but only costs memory. Runs in O(capacity). It replaces the table's arrays and moves entries to new slots. Reference counts are unchanged overall: each entry is acquired by the new arrays and released by the old ones.

cap

[Deprecated("use the 'capacity' property instead")] cap(): ulong

Deprecated: use capacity instead. Returns the number of slots in the table.

Returns

  • the same as capacity

clear

clear()

Removes every entry and releases the map's references to their keys and values. The table keeps its capacity. Runs in O(capacity).

copy

copy(): HashMap<K, V>

Returns a deep copy: a new map holding a copy of each key and value, made with copy. This is how copy(value) copies a HashMap (the Copyable<HashMap<K, V>> implementation); call copy(map) rather than this method.

The copied keys are hashed again, so a map keyed by struct identity finds its entries under the copied keys. Runs in O(capacity) plus the cost of copying the entries.

Returns

  • the copy

contains

contains(key: K): bool

Returns whether the map has an entry for key. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • true when key is present

insert

insert(key: K, value: V): bool

Maps key to value, adding a new entry or overwriting the value of an existing one.

When the key is already present, only the value is replaced: the map keeps the key object it already stores and releases the old value. A new entry acquires both key and value, and may first grow the table (see grow). Expected O(1); a grow costs O(capacity).

Parameters

  • key — the key to add or update
  • value — the value to store for key

Returns

  • true when a new key was added, false when an existing key's value was overwritten

Example

var m = HashMap<int, int>();
m.insert(1, 10);   # true: added
m.insert(1, 20);   # false: overwritten; m.get(1) == 20

get

get(key: K): V

Returns the value stored for key, or the default of V when key is absent.

The default is 0 for numbers and a null reference for struct types, including String. A missing key is not an error and is not inserted. When V is a struct type, call contains first rather than using a null result. The caller gets its own reference to the stored value. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • the value for key, or the default of V when absent

try_get

try_get(key: K): V?

Returns the value stored for key, or none when key is absent. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • the value for key, or none when absent

Example

if (ages.try_get("ada") is Value(age)) {
    print($"{age}");
}

remove

remove(key: K): bool

Removes the entry for key, releasing the map's references to its key and value. Does nothing when key is absent.

The slot becomes a tombstone: occupied for probing, empty for lookup. It counts toward the grow threshold until an insert reuses it or the table grows. Expected O(1).

Parameters

  • key — the key to remove

Returns

  • true when key was present and removed, false when absent

operator []

[](key: K): V

Reads m[key]: returns the value for key, or the default of V (0, or a null reference for struct types) when key is absent. The same as get. A missing key is not inserted.

Parameters

  • key — the key to look up

Returns

  • the value for key, or the default of V when absent

Example

var m = HashMap<String, int>();
var n = m["missing"];   # 0; m is still empty

operator []

[](key: K, value: V): V

Writes m[key] = value: inserts key or overwrites its value, the same as insert.

Parameters

  • key — the key to add or update
  • value — the value to store for key

Returns

  • value, the value of the assignment expression

Example

var m = HashMap<String, int>();
m["hello"] = 5;

iterate

iterate(): HashMapIterator<K, V>

Returns an iterator over the entries as (key, value) tuples, in no defined order; for (var (key, value) in map) drives it.

The iterator holds a reference to the map. Changing a value through an existing key while iterating is allowed; adding or removing an entry makes the iterator's next next() or current() panic.

Returns

  • an iterator positioned before the first entry

Example

var total = 0;
for (var (name, age) in ages) {
    total += age;
}

HashSet

struct HashSet<K>

A hash set of distinct elements of type K, built on the same table as HashMap but without values.

Elements are hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==: POD elements by value, String elements by content, and other struct elements by identity (two distinct objects with equal fields are both members) unless the struct declares an == operator and a matching hash<K> override. The set holds one reference to each member. It acquires the reference on insert and releases it on remove, on clear, or when the set is destroyed.

Membership tests, inserts, and removals take expected O(1) time. Before an insert of a new element would fill half the table (members plus tombstones), the table is rebuilt: at double the size, or at the same size when tombstones make up at least half of that load. It never shrinks. iterate() visits the members, in no defined order. The lowercase fields and the _find_slot and grow methods are the table's internal state: they are public but may change, and writing to them breaks the set.

Type parameters

  • K — the element type; hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==

Example

var seen = HashSet<String>();
seen.insert("a");
seen["b"] = "b";   # the same as seen.insert("b")
assert(seen.contains("a"), "member");
assert(!seen.insert("a"), "already a member");
assert(seen.count == 2, "two members");

Properties

count

var count: int { get; }

The number of members in the set. O(1).

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the set has no members. O(1).

capacity

var capacity: ulong { get; }

The number of slots in the table, a power of two and at least 8. O(1).

Constructors

HashSet()

construct(initial_capacity: ulong = 8)

Creates an empty set whose table has room for at least initial_capacity slots.

The slot count is rounded up to a power of two, with a minimum of 8. The set holds up to half its slot count before the first grow.

Parameters

  • initial_capacity — the minimum number of slots in the table

HashSet()

[Implicit] construct(items: Array<K>)

Creates a set holding each element of items once.

The constructor is [Implicit]: an array converts to a set wherever a set is expected, so an array literal can initialize one.

Parameters

  • items — the elements to insert; duplicates are kept once

Example

HashSet<String> keywords = ["if", "else", "while"];
assert(keywords.contains("else"), "a member");

Methods

grow

grow()

Doubles the table and reinserts every member, dropping all tombstones.

insert calls it automatically. Calling it directly is safe but only costs memory. Runs in O(capacity). It replaces the table's arrays and moves members to new slots.

cap

[Deprecated("use the 'capacity' property instead")] cap(): ulong

Deprecated: use capacity instead. Returns the number of slots in the table.

Returns

  • the same as capacity

clear

clear()

Removes every member and releases the set's references to them. The table keeps its capacity. Runs in O(capacity).

Returns

Adds key to the set if it is not already a member.

A new member is acquired, and the insert may first grow the table (see grow). When an equal member already exists, the set keeps the member it has and does not store key. Expected O(1); a grow costs O(capacity).

Returns

operator []

[](key: K): K

Reads s[key]: returns the stored member equal to key, or the default of K (0, or a null reference for struct types) when key is not a member.

For String elements this returns the instance the set stores, which may be a different object than key with the same content. A missing element is not inserted.

Parameters

Returns

operator []

Writes s[key] = value: makes key a member, the same as insert(key).

A set stores only keys, so value is ignored.

Parameters

  • value — ignored

Returns

  • key (the argument, not an existing equal member), the value of the assignment expression

iterate

iterate(): HashSetIterator<K>

Returns an iterator over the members, in no defined order; for (var x in set) drives it.

The iterator holds a reference to the set. Adding or removing a member while iterating makes the iterator's next next() or current() panic.

Returns

  • an iterator positioned before the first member

Example

for (var name in seen) {
    print(name);

Map and Set

Sorted collections: Map<K, V> and Set<K>, kept in key order on a red-black tree, and compare<T>, the ordering they sort keys by.

Source: runtime/map.pep

compare

compare<T>(a: T, b: T): int

Returns a negative number when a sorts before b, zero when they are equal, and a positive number when a sorts after b: the order Map and Set keep their keys in.

The generic version compares with <, so it works for every Comparable type (see Comparable), every integer type, char, and any struct that declares a < operator. Two values neither of which is < the other are equal keys. String, float and double go through concrete overrides that call their compare, so a NaN key sorts after every number instead of breaking the order.

A struct with no < operator declares Comparable, or overrides this function for itself, to be a Map key or Set element: compare<Point>(a: Point, b: Point): int. The order must be a strict weak order (consistent across calls), or the tree loses track of its keys.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the values to compare

Parameters

  • a — the first value
  • b — the second value

Returns

  • a negative number, zero or a positive number as a sorts before, equal to or after b

See also

  • compare<String>

Example

assert(compare<int>(1, 2) < 0, "1 sorts first");
assert(compare<int>(2, 2) == 0, "equal");

compare

compare<String>(a: String, b: String): int

Compares two Strings by content, the order Map and Set keep String keys in: the same as a.compare(b).

Parameters

  • a — the first String
  • b — the second String

Returns

  • a negative number, zero or a positive number as a sorts before, equal to or after b

Example

assert(compare<String>("apple", "pear") < 0, "apple sorts first");

compare

compare<float>(a: float, b: float): int

Compares two floats in float.compare's total order: by value, with NaN after every number.

Parameters

  • a — the first value
  • b — the second value

Returns

  • -1, 0 or 1 as a sorts before, with or after b

compare

compare<double>(a: double, b: double): int

Compares two doubles in double.compare's total order: by value, with NaN after every number.

Parameters

  • a — the first value
  • b — the second value

Returns

  • -1, 0 or 1 as a sorts before, with or after b

Map

struct Map<K, V>

A map from keys of type K to values of type V that keeps its keys sorted.

Keys are ordered by compare<K>: numbers by value, String by content, and other structs by their < operator or a compare<K> override. Two keys that compare equal are the same key. Lookups, inserts and removals take O(log count) time on a red-black tree.

iterate() visits the entries as (key, value) tuples in ascending key order, reversed() in descending order, and range(from, to) the keys from from up to (not including) to. first, last, lower_bound and upper_bound find single entries by order.

The map holds one reference to each stored key and value. It acquires them when they are stored and releases them when they are overwritten, removed, cleared, or when the map is destroyed.

For keys kept in the order they were inserted, use OrderedMap; for expected O(1) lookups in no order, HashMap.

Type parameters

  • K — the key type; ordered by compare<K>
  • V — the value type

Example

var scores = Map<String, int>();
scores["carol"] = 91;
scores["alice"] = 84;
scores["bob"] = 77;
for (var (name, score) in scores) {
    print($"{name}: {score}");   # alice, bob, carol
}

Set

struct Set<K>

A set of distinct elements of type K kept in sorted order, on the same red-black tree as Map but without values.

Elements are ordered by compare<K> (see Map); two elements that compare equal are the same member. Membership tests, inserts and removals take O(log count) time. iterate() visits the members in ascending order, reversed() in descending order, and range(from, to) the members from from up to (not including) to.

The set holds one reference to each member, acquired on insert and released on remove, on clear, or when the set is destroyed.

Type parameters

  • K — the element type; ordered by compare<K>

Example

Set<int> primes = [7, 2, 5, 3];
for (var p in primes) {
    print($"{p}");   # 2, 3, 5, 7
}

OrderedMap

OrderedMap<K, V>: a hash map that keeps its keys in the order they were first inserted.

Source: runtime/ordered_map.pep

OrderedMap

struct OrderedMap<K, V>

A hash map that iterates its entries in the order their keys were first inserted, like Python's dict.

Keys are hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==, as in HashMap. Lookups, inserts and removals take expected O(1) time. Setting the value of a key that is already present keeps its position; removing a key and inserting it again moves it to the end.

iterate() visits the entries as (key, value) tuples in insertion order. The map holds one reference to each stored key and value, acquired when they are stored and released when they are overwritten, removed, cleared, or when the map is destroyed.

Type parameters

  • K — the key type; hashed with hash<K> and compared with ==
  • V — the value type

Example

var config = OrderedMap<String, String>();
config["name"] = "pepper";
config["version"] = "0.2";
config["license"] = "MIT";
for (var (key, value) in config) {
    print($"{key} = {value}");   # name, version, license
}

BitSet

BitSet: a set of small non-negative integers, stored one bit each.

Source: runtime/bitset.pep

BitSet

struct BitSet

A growable set of non-negative integers, one bit per possible member.

Member n is bit n % 64 of word n / 64, so a set whose largest member is m takes about m / 8 bytes whatever its count: a good fit for visited flags, masks, and sieve or liveness tables over small integers. For sparse or large integers use a HashSet<int>.

insert grows the set as needed and reserve grows it ahead of time; the set never shrinks. contains and remove take O(1); count, is_empty, ==, hash, iteration and the set operations take O(capacity / 64).

Two sets are == when they hold the same members, whatever their capacity, and equal sets hash equally, so a BitSet works as a HashMap or HashSet key. A BitSet is not [Shared]: keep each one on one thread.

Example

BitSet primes = [2, 3, 5, 7];
primes.insert(11);
assert(primes.contains(5), "a member");
assert(primes.count == 5, "five members");
for (var p in primes) {
    print($"{p}");   # 2, 3, 5, 7, 11
}

The number of members the set holds without growing, a multiple of 64.

Deque

Deque: a double-ended queue over a growable ring buffer.

Source: runtime/deque.pep

Deque

struct Deque<T>

A double-ended queue: a sequence that grows and shrinks at both ends in amortized O(1).

Elements live in a ring buffer that doubles when full (starting at 4 slots), so push_front, push_back, pop_front and pop_back are amortized O(1), and indexing is O(1) with index 0 at the front. Use it for first-in first-out queues, breadth-first search, sliding windows and undo history; an Array takes O(count) to remove its first element.

For a struct T the deque holds a counted reference to each element, as an Array does: pushing acquires it, and popping hands the deque's reference to the caller. Deque is itself a struct, so assigning it shares the same deque. A Deque is not [Shared]: keep each one on one thread.

A Deque is Iterable<T>: for (var x in d) visits the elements from front to back. Every change (a push, a pop, an element store, clear) invalidates running iterators, and the next step of such a loop panics with "Deque modified during iteration". An array converts to a deque, so an array literal can initialize one.

Type parameters

  • T — the element type

Example

Deque<int> queue = [1, 2];
queue.push_back(3);
queue.push_front(0);
assert(queue.pop_front() == 0, "front first");
assert(queue.pop_back() == 3, "then the back");
assert(queue[0] == 1 and queue.count == 2, "1 and 2 remain");

Properties

The number of elements.

The constructor is [Implicit]: an array converts to a deque wherever a deque is expected, so an array literal can initialize one.

Parameters

  • items — the elements, the first at the front

Example

Deque<String> names = ["ada", "grace"];
assert(names.front() == "ada", "the first element is the front");

PriorityQueue

PriorityQueue: a binary heap that hands out its greatest element first.

Source: runtime/priority_queue.pep

PriorityQueue

struct PriorityQueue<T>

A priority queue: push adds elements in any order and pop removes the greatest one.

A binary heap over an Array: push and pop take O(log count), peek takes O(1), and building a queue from an array takes O(count). Use it for Dijkstra's and A* searches, schedulers, timers and top-k selection.

Elements are ordered by compare<T> (numbers by value, String by content, a Comparable struct by its compare), or by a comparer given to the constructor, which returns a negative number, zero or a positive number as its first argument sorts before, with or after its second. The greatest element comes out first; reverse the comparer for the smallest first. Elements that sort together come out in no particular order.

For a struct T the queue holds a counted reference to each element: pushing acquires it, and popping hands the queue's reference to the caller. A PriorityQueue is not [Shared]: keep each one on one thread.

Type parameters

  • T — the element type

Example

PriorityQueue<int> queue = [3, 1, 4];
queue.push(5);
assert(queue.pop() == 5, "the greatest first");
assert(queue.peek() == 4, "then 4");

# The smallest first, through a reversed comparer.
var earliest = PriorityQueue<int>((a, b) => b.compare(a));
earliest.push(30);
earliest.push(10);
assert(earliest.pop() == 10, "the smallest first");

The number of elements.

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the queue has no elements.

The constructor is [Implicit]: an array converts to a queue wherever a queue is expected, so an array literal can initialize one.

Iterators

Source: runtime/iterator.pep

Iterator

trait Iterator<T>

Something a for loop can step through, one element at a time.

for (var x in source) drives a source that declares next() and current() directly: it calls next() before each pass and binds current() to the loop variable while next() returns true. A type whose for loop should go through a separate iterator implements Iterable<T> instead. A type with neither protocol is a compile error in a for loop.

The loop goes by the methods a type has, so declaring the trait is optional. Declaring it (extend Foo with Iterator<int>;) checks that the methods match and lets the type be used as an Iterator<int> value, which a for loop drives through the trait.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the elements produced

See also

  • Iterable

Example

struct Countdown {
    int remaining;
    int now;

    construct(this.remaining = 0) {}

    bool next() {
        if (remaining == 0) {
            return false;
        }
        now = remaining;
        remaining = remaining - 1;
        return true;
    }

    int current() {
        return now;
    }
}

extend Countdown with Iterator<int>;

main(): int {
    var total = 0;
    for (int n in Countdown(3)) {
        total = total + n;   # visits 3, 2, 1
    }
    return total;
}

Methods

next

next(): bool

Advances to the next element.

The first call moves to the first element, if any. Once it returns false it must keep returning false.

Returns

  • true if there is a current element, false when the elements are exhausted

current

current(): T

Returns the element the last successful next() moved to.

Calling it before the first next(), or after next() returned false, is an error; the runtime's iterators panic in that case.

Returns

  • the current element

Returns an iterator over transform applied to each element, in order.

Lazy: transform runs once per element, as the result is advanced, and the result advances this iterator. Every type that declares Iterator<T> gets this method.

Type parameters

Parameters

Returns

  • a MapIterator<T, U> over the transformed elements

Example

var names = Array<String>();
for (var size in names.iterate().map((name) => name.size)) {
    print(size);
}

Lazy: keep runs once per element, as the result is advanced, and the result advances this iterator. Every type that declares Iterator<T> gets this method.

Returns

Scoped

The scope protocol behind with (var x = scope) { ... } else { ... }.

A with block holds scope in a hidden local, binds x to scope.enter(), and runs the body. When enter() returns a struct reference that is null, the body is skipped and the optional else block runs instead. Both locals are released on every path out of the block (falling off the end, return, break, continue), the binding first. Cleanup is the scope object's destructor, which calls exit().

Source: runtime/scoped.pep

Scoped

trait Scoped<T>

Something a with block can enter.

enter() runs once when the block is entered, and its result is what the header binds. exit() is the cleanup: implementations call it from their destructor (destruct { this.exit(); }), so it runs when the scope object's last reference is released. For a scope object created in the with header that is the end of the block; for one that is also held elsewhere, it is when that last owner lets go.

A with block with no binding (with (scope) { ... }) still holds the result of enter() until the block ends. An enter() that returns void has nothing to bind.

Type parameters

  • T — the type enter() returns

Example

var open = 0;

struct Session {
    construct() {
        open = open + 1;
    }

    destruct {
        this.exit();
    }

    Session enter() {
        return this;
    }

    exit() {
        open = open - 1;
    }
}

extend Session with Scoped<Session>;

main(): int {
    with (var session = Session()) {
        # open == 1 here
    }
    return open;   # 0: the session was destroyed at the end of the block
}

Methods

enter

enter(): T

Enters the scope.

A null struct reference means there is nothing to use: the with body is skipped and its else block runs instead.

Returns

  • the value the with header binds

exit

exit()

Leaves the scope. Implementations call it from their destructor.

Weak

Weak references: Weak<T> points at an object without keeping it alive.

Source: runtime/weak.pep

Weak

struct Weak<T>

A reference to a struct object, or to the struct behind a trait value (Weak<Shape>), that does not keep it alive, for back pointers (a child's parent, an observer's subject) that would otherwise form a reference cycle and leak.

The object is reached only through a with block, which upgrades the weak reference to an ordinary strong one for the length of the block. Once the object has been destroyed the upgrade fails: the body is skipped and the else block runs instead.

A Weak<T> never changes what it points at, so copies of it can be shared freely.

Type parameters

  • T — the struct or trait type pointed at

See also

  • Scoped

Example

struct Child {
    Weak<Parent> owner;

    construct(Parent owner) {
        this.owner = Weak<Parent>(owner);
    }

    String owner_name() {
        with (var parent = this.owner) {
            return parent.name;
        } else {
            return "(gone)";
        }
        return "";
    }
}

Creates a weak reference to target's object.

Parameters

  • target — the object to point at; a null reference makes a weak reference that is always expired

Returns

Leaves the scope. The strong reference enter() returned is released by the with block itself, so there is nothing to do.

Handle

Handle<T>: owns a resource that Pepper's reference counting does not know about, such as a C library's object, and releases it when the last reference to the handle goes away, like C#'s SafeHandle.

Source: runtime/handle.pep

Handle

struct Handle<T>

Owns a raw resource and calls a release function on it once, when the handle is destroyed or release() is called, whichever comes first.

Use it to tie a C library's object (a __ptr<void> from an extern, a file descriptor) to Pepper's lifetimes: hold a Handle in a struct field, and the resource is freed when the struct is. A handle is a reference like any struct, so copies share one resource, and it is released when the last copy goes away. detach() takes the resource back without releasing it.

release is an ordinary function value, so a closure may capture what the release needs (such as an owner that must outlive the resource: holding it in the closure keeps it alive until the release runs).

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the raw resource, usually __ptr<void> or an integer

Example

extern void* malloc(ulong size);
extern void free(void* p);

main(): int {
    var buffer = Handle<__ptr<void>>(malloc(16), (p) => free(p));
    # use buffer.value; free runs when `buffer` goes out of scope
    return 0;
}

The resource. It stays readable after the handle is released or detached, but it no longer refers to anything the handle owns.

Source: runtime/result.pep

var r = Result<int>.err(Error("boom"));
var n = r.error().message.length;   # 4

The description of what went wrong; empty when none was given.

The constructor is [Implicit]: a String converts to an Error wherever an Error is expected, as in Result<int>.err("bad input").

Parameters

Result

[Value] enum Result<TValue, TError=Error>

The outcome of an operation that can fail: either Ok, holding a TValue, or Err, holding a TError, like Rust's Result<T, E>.

An enum with the cases Ok(value) and Err(error). Build one with a case (Result<int>.Ok(42)) or the static ok or err functions, and read it with match or is (if (r is Err(e)) { ... }), or with is_ok(), is_err(), value() and error(); value() and error() panic on the wrong kind of result. TError defaults to Error, so Result<int> is Result<int, Error>.

Result<void> is the result of an operation that returns nothing on success, like Rust's Result<(), E>. A void type argument erases what it types: that instance's Ok carries nothing (Result<void>.Ok, and the pattern Ok), ok() takes no argument, and value() returns nothing, so it only checks that the result is Ok.

Type parameters

  • TValue — the type of the value an Ok result carries; void when there is none
  • TError — the type of the error an Err result carries; defaults to Error

Example

main(): int {
    var a = Result<int>.ok(42);
    if (a.value() != 42) { return 1; }
    var b = Result<int>.err(Error("boom"));
    if (!b.is_err()) { return 2; }
    var n = match (b) { Ok(v) => v, Err(e) => e.message.length };   # 4
    return b.ok_or(0);   # 0
}

Optional

Source: runtime/optional.pep

Optional

[Value] enum Optional<T>

A value of type T that may be absent: either Value, holding a T, or Empty, holding nothing, like Rust's Option<T> and Swift's Optional.

Use it instead of a null reference or a sentinel (-1, "") wherever a value may be missing: the type says so, and reading the value goes through value(), which checks, or value_or(), which cannot fail. It works for every type, including those that have no null, such as int.

T? is shorthand for Optional<T>, and a variable or field of an optional type that is not given a value starts as Empty.

Build one with its cases (Optional<int>.Value(1), Optional<int>.Empty). Test it with is_value() or is_empty(), as a condition by itself (if (found)), or with match and is on its cases (if (found is Value(v))).

An optional is a value enum: it is stored inline in whatever holds it, with no allocation, and copying one gives an independent optional. It is never null, and has no identity, so compare optionals with ==, not ===.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value a Value optional holds

Example

find_even(values: Array<int>): int? {
    for (var v in values) {
        if (v % 2 == 0) { return Optional<int>.Value(v); }
    }
    return Optional<int>.Empty;
}

main(): int {
    var values = Array<int>();
    values.append(3);
    values.append(4);
    var found = find_even(values);
    if (!found) { return 1; }
    return found.value() - 4;   # 0
}

Cases

Empty

Empty

Holds no value. It is the first case, so an optional that is never given a value is Empty.
