Copying

Deep copies: copy(value) makes a copy that shares no object that is not thread-safe with the original, so it can be handed to another thread; Copyable<T> lets a type say how it is copied.

Source: runtime/copy.pep

copy

copy<T>(value: T): T

Returns a copy of value that shares no non-thread-safe object with it, so the copy can be handed to another thread.

Every struct reachable from value whose type is not thread-safe is copied once. Objects referenced twice stay shared inside the copy, and cycles are preserved. Thread-safe objects ([Shared] structs, shared function values) are not copied: the copy references the same ones. A weak reference to a copied object points at its copy; a weak reference to an object outside the copied value becomes null.

A struct is copied field by field, without running its constructor, unless it implements Copyable<T>. A struct with a destructor or a raw pointer field must implement Copyable<T> to be copied, since copying its fields would share what it owns; String, Array, HashMap and HashSet do. Copying such a struct that does not, or a plain function value, is a compile error.

Called inside a Copyable<T>.copy() implementation while a copy is running, copy continues that copy: an object it already copied is not copied again.

A trait value is copied by copying the struct behind it, which is known only at run time: when that struct cannot be copied, copy panics.

Runs in O(size of the value) and allocates each copied object.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value

Parameters

  • value — the value to copy

Returns

  • a copy that shares no non-thread-safe object with value; value itself when T is thread-safe

Panics

  • if value reaches a trait value holding a struct that cannot be copied

Example

var names = Array<String>();
names.append("ada");
var copied = copy(names);
copied[0].append(" lovelace");   # names[0] is still "ada"

register_copy

register_copy<T>(original: T, made: T)

Records made as the copy of original in the running copy, so that copying original again returns made. A Copyable<T>.copy() implementation calls it before copying the values it holds when one of them may lead back to it; outside a copy it does nothing.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value, a struct

Parameters

  • original — the object being copied
  • made — its copy

Example

copy(): Node {
    var made = Node(value);
    register_copy(this, made);   # a cycle back to this finds made
    made.next = copy(next);
    return made;
}

move

move<T>([MoveSource] value: T): T

Hands over the reference value holds and leaves it null, with no copy and no change to any count: the result is the same object.

value must be a local variable (or a [Move] parameter) that holds the only reference to its value: nothing else may refer to it or to anything it reaches. The compiler checks that, and that the variable is not used again until it is assigned a new value. Use it to pass a value you built to a parameter that takes a new value, such as Channel.send or Mutex.replace, without the cost of copy.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value

Parameters

  • value — the variable to move from

Returns

  • the value value held, which nothing else references

Example

var lines = Array<String>();
lines.append("first");
var log = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(move(lines));   # lines is null now

Copyable

trait Copyable<T>

A type that says how copy copies it, for a struct that copy cannot copy field by field: one with a destructor or a raw pointer field, such as a container that owns a buffer.

Declare it with extend Buffer with Copyable<Buffer>; and give the struct a copy(): Buffer method. The method builds the copy and copies each struct value it holds with copy(value), which, called while a copy is running, reuses a copy already made, so objects referenced twice stay shared.

Type parameters

  • T — the implementing type

Example

struct Buffer {
    __ptr<u8> data;
    ulong size;

    construct(ulong size = 0) {
        data = _pep_malloc(size);
        this.size = size;
    }

    destruct {
        _pep_free(data);
    }

    copy(): Buffer {
        var made = Buffer(size);
        var i: ulong = 0;
        while (i < size) {
            made.data[i] = data[i];
            i = i + 1;
        }
        return made;
    }
}

extend Buffer with Copyable<Buffer>;

Methods

copy

copy(): T

Returns a copy of this value, for copy.

Copy each struct value this one holds with copy(value). A value that can hold a reference back to itself calls register_copy(this, made) before copying what it holds, so the cycle leads back to the copy. Call copy(x), not x.copy(), to copy a Copyable value: copy(x) keeps objects shared inside one copy.

Returns

  • the copy

Copies

[Deprecated("implement 'Copyable<T>' as 'copy(): T', which copies what it holds with 'copy(value)'")] type Copies = _Copies

Deprecated: implement Copyable<T> as copy(): T, which copies what it holds with copy(value) and register_copy(original, made).

The context of a running copy, which a Copyable<T> implementation once took as copy(copies: Copies): T. Such an implementation still works for this release.

URI

URI references (RFC 3986): parse any URI, such as https://example.com/a?b#c, mailto:someone@example.com or /items?page=2, into its parts.

Source: runtime/uri.pep

Uri

struct Uri

A URI reference split into its RFC 3986 components: scheme, authority (user information, host and port), path, query and fragment.

Uri.parse accepts any scheme, and a reference with no scheme (a relative reference, such as /items?page=2, which is what an HTTP server sees as a request's target). The components keep their percent-escapes as written; Uri.decode turns an escaped component into text. The scheme is lowercased, since schemes are case-insensitive; nothing else is changed. to_string() puts the parts back together.

A component that can be absent is optional, so an empty one (http://h/? has an empty query) differs from a missing one (http://h/ has none).

Example

var uri = Uri.parse("HTTPS://user@example.com:8443/a%20b?x=1#top").value();
assert(uri.scheme == "https", "the scheme is lowercased");
assert(uri.user_info.value() == "user", "user information");
assert(uri.host.value() == "example.com", "host");
assert(uri.port.value() == 8443, "port");
assert(uri.path == "/a%20b", "the path keeps its escapes");
assert(Uri.decode(uri.path).value() == "/a b", "decoded");
assert(uri.query.value() == "x=1" && uri.fragment.value() == "top", "query and fragment");

Fields

scheme

var scheme: String

The scheme, lowercased, such as https; empty for a relative reference.

user_info

var user_info: String?

The user information before @ in the authority, if any.

host

var host: String?

The host, without the brackets of an IPv6 address; Empty when the URI has no authority (no //), and empty for one such as file:///tmp. An IPv6 scope keeps its escaped % (RFC 6874): the host of http://[fe80::1%25eth0]/ is fe80::1%25eth0, which Uri.decode turns into the fe80::1%eth0 that io.IpAddress.parse reads.

port

var port: u16?

The port after the host, if the authority gives one.

path

var path: String

The path, possibly empty, with its percent-escapes.

query

var query: String?

The query after ?, without the ?, if any.

fragment

var fragment: String?

The fragment after #, without the #, if any.

Constructor

Uri()

construct()

Creates an empty relative reference: no scheme, no authority, and an empty path.

Static methods

parse

static parse(text: String): Result<Uri>

Parses text as a URI reference: an absolute URI with any scheme, or a relative reference.

Characters outside printable ASCII (spaces, controls, and every non-ASCII byte) must be percent-encoded, and each % must be followed by two hexadecimal digits.

Parameters

  • text — the URI reference

Returns

  • the parsed URI, or an error saying what is wrong: an invalid scheme, a character that must be encoded, a bad escape, an IPv6 host with no ], or a port that is not a number from 0 to 65535

Example

var mail = Uri.parse("mailto:someone@example.com").value();
assert(mail.scheme == "mailto" && mail.host.is_empty(), "no authority");
assert(mail.path == "someone@example.com", "the path holds the address");
assert(Uri.parse("a b").is_err(), "a space must be encoded");

decode

static decode(text: String): Result<String>

Returns text with each percent-escape (%20) replaced by the byte it stands for, decoded as UTF-8. A + is kept as it is; a query that uses + for a space needs that replaced first.

Parameters

  • text — a component with percent-escapes, such as path

Returns

  • the decoded text, where each byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD, the replacement character, or an error when a % is not followed by two hexadecimal digits

Example

assert(Uri.decode("caf%C3%A9%21").value() == "café!", "decoded");
assert(Uri.decode("100%").is_err(), "a lone '%'");

encode

static encode(text: String): String

Returns text with each byte outside RFC 3986's unreserved set (A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~) written as a percent-escape, so the result is safe as one path segment or one query value: /, ?, &, = and % are escaped too. decode reverses it.

Parameters

  • text — the component to escape, such as a file name or a search term

Returns

  • the escaped text, with uppercase hexadecimal digits

Example

assert(Uri.encode("a b/c&d") == "a%20b%2Fc%26d", "escaped");
assert(Uri.encode("café") == "caf%C3%A9", "UTF-8 bytes");

encode_form

static encode_form(pairs: Array<(String, String)>): String

Returns pairs as an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body or query, the way an HTML form sends them: name=value joined with &, each side escaped like encode except that a space is +.

Parameters

  • pairs — the names and values, in order; a name may repeat

Returns

  • the encoded text, such as q=pepper+lang&page=2

Example

assert(Uri.encode_form([("q", "pepper lang"), ("page", "2")]) == "q=pepper+lang&page=2", "a query");

decode_form

static decode_form(text: String): Result<Array<(String, String)>>

Returns the names and values of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body or query, such as a request's query, in order. Each + is a space and percent-escapes are decoded; a pair with no = has an empty value, and empty pairs (a=1&&b=2) are skipped.

Parameters

  • text — the encoded pairs, such as q=pepper+lang&page=2

Returns

  • the decoded pairs, or an error when a % is not followed by two hexadecimal digits

Example

var pairs = Uri.decode_form("q=pepper+lang&page=2").value();
assert(pairs.count == 2 && pairs[0].1 == "pepper lang", "decoded");

Methods

is_absolute

is_absolute(): bool

Returns whether this URI has a scheme (an absolute URI rather than a relative reference).

Returns

  • true when scheme is not empty

authority

authority(): String?

Returns the authority as it appears after //: user information, host (in brackets when it is an IPv6 address) and port.

Returns

  • the authority, such as user@example.com:8443, or Empty when host is Empty

path_and_query

path_and_query(): String

Returns the path and query, as an HTTP request line names its target: the path (/ when it is empty), then ? and the query if there is one. The fragment is left out.

Returns

  • the path and query, such as /items?page=2

resolve

resolve(reference: Uri): Uri

Resolves reference against this URI, its base, as RFC 3986 (section 5.2) describes and as a browser resolves a link on a page: an absolute reference stands as it is, //host/path keeps only the base's scheme, /path keeps its authority too, and a relative path replaces the base's last segment. . and .. segments are removed. The fragment is always the reference's.

Parameters

  • reference — the reference to resolve, such as an HTTP Location

Returns

  • the resolved URI

Example

var base = Uri.parse("https://example.com/docs/guide/intro?x=1").value();
assert(base.resolve(Uri.parse("next").value()).to_string() == "https://example.com/docs/guide/next", "a sibling");
assert(base.resolve(Uri.parse("../api").value()).to_string() == "https://example.com/docs/api", "up one");
assert(base.resolve(Uri.parse("/").value()).to_string() == "https://example.com/", "the root");
assert(base.resolve(Uri.parse("?y=2").value()).to_string() == "https://example.com/docs/guide/intro?y=2", "a new query");

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the URI as text, putting its components back together. For a parsed URI this is the text it was parsed from, except that the scheme is lowercased.

Returns

  • the URI reference as a String

Test checks

Checks for tests: expect_equal, expect_not_equal, expect_true and expect_false, which every program can call without an import. Each panics when its check fails, as assert does, but reports the values it compared, at the line of the call:

math_test.pep:12:5: panic: expect_equal failed
  actual:   3
  expected: 4

A [Test] function fails on that panic (see the testing chapter).

Source: runtime/expect.pep

expect_equal

expect_equal<T>(actual: T, expected: T)

Panics unless actual == expected, reporting both values.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the values; it needs == and a text form (see to_string)

Parameters

  • actual — the value the code under test produced
  • expected — the value it should have produced

Panics

  • if the values differ: prints the location of the call and both values, and aborts (see panic)

Example

var numbers = Array<int>();
numbers.append(1);
expect_equal(numbers.count, 1);

expect_not_equal

expect_not_equal<T>(actual: T, unexpected: T)

Panics if actual == unexpected, reporting the value.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the values; it needs == and a text form (see to_string)

Parameters

  • actual — the value the code under test produced
  • unexpected — the value it must not be

Panics

  • if the values are equal: prints the location of the call and the value, and aborts (see panic)

Example

expect_not_equal("a".repeat(2), "a");

expect_true

expect_true(condition: bool)

Panics unless condition holds. Unlike assert, it needs no message: the location names the check.

Parameters

  • condition — the condition that must hold

Panics

  • if condition is false: prints the location of the call, and aborts (see panic)

Example

expect_true("pepper".starts_with("pep"));

expect_false

expect_false(condition: bool)

Panics if condition holds.

Parameters

  • condition — the condition that must not hold

Panics

  • if condition is true: prints the location of the call, and aborts (see panic)

Example

expect_false("pepper".is_empty);

The io module

Files, directories, paths, and sockets, modeled on Rust's std::fs, std::path and std::net.

Unlike the rest of the standard library, io is a module: bring it in with import io (and write io.File, io.Path) or import names directly with import [File, Path] from io. Every fallible operation returns an IoResult<T>, a Result whose error is an IoError.

  • Path: building, splitting, and inspecting paths
  • File: opening, reading, writing, and locking files, whole-file helpers, and FileTransfer
  • Directory: listing, creating, and removing directories
  • Glob: glob and glob_matches, finding paths by pattern
  • Watch: Watcher, FileChange, and ChangeKind, changes in a directory tree
  • Network addresses: IpAddress, SocketAddress, and resolve
  • Sockets: TcpListener, Incoming, SharedTcpListener, TcpStream, SocketTransfer, and UdpSocket
  • Unix domain sockets: UnixListener, SharedUnixListener, UnixStream, and UnixDatagram
  • Streams: the Reader and Writer traits, lines() and chunks()
  • Streams in memory: ByteReader and ByteWriter
  • Print: deprecated; use Writer
  • Errors and platform types: IoError, ErrorKind, IoResult, and handle types

Example

import io;

main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("greeting.txt");
    assert(io.File.write_text(path, "hello").is_ok(), "write");
    assert(io.File.read_to_string(path).value() == "hello", "read back");
    io.File.remove(path);
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/io/module.pep

Errors and platform types

Source: runtime/io/types.pep

FileHandle

[Target(!OS(Windows))] type FileHandle = int

The raw operating-system handle of an open file: a POSIX file descriptor.

File.Handle holds one. A valid descriptor is >= 0; a File that is closed (or was never opened) holds -1. The standard streams are descriptors 0, 1 and 2. On Windows this is a HANDLE instead.

See also

  • File

Note

  • code that must build for every target should not rely on this being an int

SocketHandle

[Target(!OS(Windows))] type SocketHandle = int

The raw operating-system handle of a socket: a POSIX file descriptor.

TcpListener, TcpStream and UdpSocket hold one. A valid descriptor is >= 0; a closed socket holds -1. On Windows this is a SOCKET instead.

See also

  • TcpStream

Note

  • code that must build for every target should not rely on this being an int

ErrorCode

[Target(!OS(Windows))] type ErrorCode = int

The raw platform error code carried by IoError.code: a POSIX errno value such as ENOENT (2). On Windows this is a DWORD from GetLastError() instead.

The numbers differ between platforms (and a few between Linux and macOS), so portable code classifies an error with IoError.kind() or its predicates (is_not_found(), ...) rather than comparing codes.

See also

  • IoError

Mode

[Target(!OS(Windows))] type Mode = uint

File mode bits as reported in Metadata.Permissions: on POSIX the mode_t permission bits mode & 07777 (the rwx bits for owner, group and others plus setuid, setgid and sticky; the file-type bits are removed). On Windows the same field holds FILE_ATTRIBUTE_* bits instead.

See also

  • Metadata

FileHandle

[Target(OS(Windows))] type FileHandle = __ptr<void>

The raw operating-system handle of an open file: a Windows HANDLE.

File.Handle holds one. A File that is closed (or was never opened) holds null; neither null nor INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE (-1) is a valid handle. The standard streams are the handles from GetStdHandle. On POSIX this is an int file descriptor instead.

See also

  • File

Note

  • code that must build for every target should not rely on this being a __ptr<void>

SocketHandle

[Target(OS(Windows))] type SocketHandle = ulong

The raw operating-system handle of a socket: a Winsock SOCKET, an unsigned pointer-sized integer.

TcpListener, TcpStream and UdpSocket hold one. A closed socket holds INVALID_SOCKET (all bits set). On POSIX this is an int file descriptor instead.

See also

  • TcpStream

Note

  • code that must build for every target should not rely on this being a ulong

ErrorCode

[Target(OS(Windows))] type ErrorCode = uint

The raw platform error code carried by IoError.code: a Windows DWORD error code from GetLastError(), such as ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (2). On POSIX this is an errno value instead.

The numbers differ between platforms, so portable code classifies an error with IoError.kind() or its predicates (is_not_found(), ...) rather than comparing codes.

See also

  • IoError

Mode

[Target(OS(Windows))] type Mode = uint

File attribute bits as reported in Metadata.Permissions: on Windows the whole FILE_ATTRIBUTE_* word of the file (FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY is 1, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_DIRECTORY 16, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT 1024, ...). On POSIX the same field holds mode_t permission bits instead.

See also

  • Metadata

Offset

type Offset = long

A byte position or distance within a file, as taken and returned by the File.seek* methods: a signed 64-bit integer on every target (off_t on POSIX, LARGE_INTEGER on Windows), so files larger than 4 GiB work everywhere.

ErrorKind

enum ErrorKind

The portable kind of an IoError, as IoError.kind() returns it: the platform's error code sorted into the cases a program usually handles.

Each case except Other has a matching IoError predicate (NotFound and is_not_found(), ...), whose documentation lists the codes it covers on each platform. A code that fits none of them, such as the EIO of a short write or the EBADF of a closed File, is Other.

See also

  • IoError.kind

Example

import io;

var r = io.File.open(io.Path("settings.txt"));
if (r.is_err()) {
    match (r.error().kind()) {
        NotFound => { print("no settings file"); }
        PermissionDenied => { print("settings file is not readable"); }
        else => { print(r.error().message); }
    }
}

Cases

NotFound

NotFound

The file, directory or host name does not exist (is_not_found()).

PermissionDenied

PermissionDenied

Access was denied (is_permission_denied()).

AlreadyExists

AlreadyExists

The target already exists (is_already_exists()).

NotADirectory

NotADirectory

A directory was expected but something else was found (is_not_a_directory()).

IsADirectory

IsADirectory

A file was expected but a directory was found (is_is_a_directory()).

DirectoryNotEmpty

DirectoryNotEmpty

A directory to remove still has entries (is_directory_not_empty()).

InvalidInput

InvalidInput

An argument or the data was invalid (is_invalid_input()).

Interrupted

Interrupted

The operation was interrupted before it finished (is_interrupted()).

ConnectionRefused

ConnectionRefused

Nothing accepted the connection (is_connection_refused()).

ConnectionReset

ConnectionReset

The peer reset, aborted or closed the connection (is_connection_reset()).

AddressInUse

AddressInUse

Another socket already uses the address (is_address_in_use()).

AddressNotAvailable

AddressNotAvailable

The address cannot be used on this machine (is_address_not_available()).

TimedOut

TimedOut

The operation timed out (is_timed_out()).

Cancelled

Cancelled

Cancelling the task ended the operation (is_cancelled()).

Other

Other

Any other code, including 0 (no error).

IoError

struct IoError

An I/O failure: the raw platform error code plus a human-readable message.

kind() sorts the code into an ErrorKind, and a predicate per kind (is_not_found(), is_permission_denied(), ...) tests for one of them; each knows the matching codes on the current platform. Test with those rather than comparing code against numbers. Failures that Pepper detects itself (invalid UTF-8, an empty path, a short write, a closed File) use the platform's own code for the kind they are (EINVAL / ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER for invalid input, ENOENT / ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND for an empty path, ...), so the kinds hold for them too. A short write uses EIO / ERROR_WRITE_FAULT and a closed File uses EBADF / ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE; those are ErrorKind.Other.

See also

  • IoResult
  • ErrorKind

Example

import io;

var r = io.File.open(io.Path("settings.txt"));
if (r.is_err()) {
    if (r.error().is_not_found()) {
        print("no settings file");
    } else {
        print(r.error().message);
    }
}

Fields

code

ErrorCode code

The raw platform error code: an errno value on POSIX, a GetLastError() code on Windows; 0 means no error.

message

String message

A human-readable description: the platform's text for code (strerror on POSIX, FormatMessageW on Windows, without its trailing period and line break), or Pepper's own text such as "empty path" for errors it detects itself.

Constructor

IoError()

construct(code: ErrorCode = 0, message: String = "")

Creates an error from a platform code and a message.

The default, IoError(), has code 0 and an empty message; no predicate holds for it.

Parameters

  • code — the raw platform error code (errno on POSIX, GetLastError() on Windows)
  • message — the human-readable description

Static methods

last

static last(): IoError

Captures the calling thread's last platform error now: errno on POSIX, GetLastError() on Windows, with the platform's message for it.

Call it immediately after the failing system call; any call in between (including one that allocates) may overwrite the code.

Returns

  • an error holding the current errno / GetLastError() code and its message

invalid_input

static invalid_input(message: String): IoError

Makes an error for data or an argument that is not valid, such as a damaged file a library parses, with the platform's code for invalid input, so is_invalid_input() holds.

Parameters

  • message — what is wrong

Returns

  • the error

Example

import io;

var error = io.IoError.invalid_input("data.bin: bad header");
assert(error.is_invalid_input(), "the kind");

Methods

kind

kind(): ErrorKind

Returns the portable kind of the error: code sorted by the codes the current platform uses for each kind. Each predicate below is kind() == ErrorKind.X for its kind.

Returns

  • the kind of code; ErrorKind.Other for a code that fits no kind, and for 0

Example

import io;

var r = io.File.open(io.Path("missing.txt"));
if (r.is_err() && r.error().kind() == io.ErrorKind.NotFound) {
    print("no such file");
}

is_not_found

is_not_found(): bool

Returns whether the error means the file or directory does not exist.

Matches ENOENT on POSIX, and ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND or ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND on Windows. An empty path fails with this kind on POSIX (with the message "empty path"), and in File.open_with on every platform.

resolve and TcpStream.connect_host fail with this kind too when a host name has no address.

Returns

  • true when a path, or a directory on the way to it, is missing, or a host name has no address

is_permission_denied

is_permission_denied(): bool

Returns whether the operation was refused for lack of permission.

Matches EACCES or EPERM on POSIX, and ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED on Windows (which Windows also reports for, among others, deleting a read-only file).

Returns

  • true when access was denied

is_already_exists

is_already_exists(): bool

Returns whether the operation failed because its target already exists, such as Directory.create on an existing path or opening with create_new.

Matches EEXIST on POSIX, and ERROR_FILE_EXISTS or ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the target already exists

is_not_a_directory

is_not_a_directory(): bool

Returns whether a path that had to name a directory names something else, such as Directory.open or Directory.remove on a file (or, on POSIX, a file used as a directory in the middle of a path).

Matches ENOTDIR on POSIX, and ERROR_DIRECTORY (267, "the directory name is invalid") on Windows.

Returns

  • true when a directory was expected

is_is_a_directory

is_is_a_directory(): bool

Returns whether an operation that needs a file was given a directory, such as reading from a directory opened as a File.

Matches EISDIR on POSIX, and ERROR_DIRECTORY_NOT_SUPPORTED on Windows (which File reads report for a directory handle).

Returns

  • true when a directory was given where a file was expected

is_directory_not_empty

is_directory_not_empty(): bool

Returns whether a directory could not be removed because it still has entries (Directory.remove on a non-empty directory).

Matches ENOTEMPTY on POSIX (39 on Linux, 66 on macOS) and ERROR_DIR_NOT_EMPTY on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the directory is not empty

is_invalid_input

is_invalid_input(): bool

Returns whether an argument was invalid: bad options (such as opening with no access mode), data that is not valid UTF-8 where text was expected, or a malformed path.

Matches EINVAL on POSIX, and ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER or ERROR_INVALID_NAME on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the input was invalid

is_interrupted

is_interrupted(): bool

Returns whether the operation was interrupted before it finished.

Matches EINTR on POSIX and WSAEINTR on Windows. An aborted Windows operation (ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED) is is_cancelled() instead. The io functions retry interrupted POSIX opens, reads and writes themselves, so callers rarely see this.

Returns

  • true when the operation was interrupted

is_connection_refused

is_connection_refused(): bool

Returns whether a connection attempt was refused: nothing listens on that port (the peer answered with a reset).

Matches ECONNREFUSED on POSIX and WSAECONNREFUSED on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the connection was refused

is_connection_reset

is_connection_reset(): bool

Returns whether an established connection was broken by the peer: reset, aborted, or (when writing) already closed.

Matches ECONNRESET, ECONNABORTED or EPIPE on POSIX, and WSAECONNRESET or WSAECONNABORTED on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the connection was reset or closed by the peer

is_address_in_use

is_address_in_use(): bool

Returns whether binding failed because another socket already uses the address and port.

Matches EADDRINUSE on POSIX and WSAEADDRINUSE on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the address is in use

is_address_not_available

is_address_not_available(): bool

Returns whether an address cannot be used here: binding to an IP address that is not one of this machine's, or connecting to port 0.

Matches EADDRNOTAVAIL on POSIX and WSAEADDRNOTAVAIL on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the address is not available

is_timed_out

is_timed_out(): bool

Returns whether an operation gave up because the peer did not answer in time, such as a connection attempt to an unreachable host, or because an async.timeout scope around it expired.

Matches ETIMEDOUT on POSIX and WSAETIMEDOUT on Windows.

Returns

  • true when the operation timed out

is_cancelled

is_cancelled(): bool

Returns whether an operation stopped because the task waiting for it was cancelled (see async.Task.cancel).

Matches ECANCELED on POSIX, and ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED or ERROR_CANCELLED on Windows.

Returns

  • true when cancellation ended the operation

IoResult

type IoResult<T> = Result<T, IoError>

The result of an io operation: a value on success, an IoError on failure. Check is_ok() / is_err() before calling value() or error(); operations that produce nothing return IoResult<void>.

Type parameters

  • T — the value an operation produces on success

See also

  • IoError

Example

import io;

var cwd = io.Directory.current();
if (cwd.is_ok()) {
    print(cwd.value().to_string());
} else {
    print(cwd.error().message);
}

Reader and Writer

Reader and Writer: the traits of byte streams, such as a File, a TcpStream, a UnixStream or a tls.TlsStream, so code can read from or write to any of them.

Source: runtime/io/stream.pep

Reader

trait Reader

A stream of bytes that can be read: a File, TcpStream, UnixStream or tls.TlsStream, or any type with read(buffer, max).

A type has the trait by providing read; it then gets lines() and chunks(size), which read the stream as a for loop asks for more. Take a Reader (or <R: Reader>) to accept any stream.

Example

import io;

count_lines(source: io.Reader): int {
    var count = 0;
    for (var line in source.lines()) {
        if (line.is_err()) {
            break;
        }
        count += 1;
    }
    return count;
}

Methods

read

read(buffer: u8[], max: ulong): IoResult<ulong>

Waits until some bytes are available, then appends up to max of them to buffer.

Parameters

  • buffer — the array the bytes are appended to
  • max — the most bytes to read

Returns

  • the number of bytes appended, 0 at the end of the stream; an error when the stream fails

lines

lines(): Lines

Returns an iterator over the rest of the stream's lines, read as it goes, so a for loop handles a large file without reading it all.

Each element is an IoResult<String>: a line without its line ending (\n, or \r\n). The last line counts even without a final line ending, and a stream that ends with one has no empty line after it. A read error, or a line that is not valid UTF-8 (is_invalid_input()), is yielded as an error and ends the lines. The stream is read in 64 KiB chunks, so a file's position after the loop is not the end of the last line returned.

Returns

  • a new Lines positioned before the first line

Example

var f = File.open(Path("notes.txt")).value();
for (var line in f.lines()) {
    print(line.value());
}

chunks

chunks(size: ulong): Chunks

Returns an iterator over the rest of the stream in chunks of at most size bytes, each read as the loop asks for it.

Each element is an IoResult<u8[]>: a new array of what one read returned, which may be fewer than size bytes (a socket returns what has arrived). The iteration ends at the end of the stream; a read error is yielded and ends it.

Parameters

  • size — the most bytes in one chunk

Returns

  • a new Chunks positioned before the first chunk

Panics

  • if size is 0 ("Reader.chunks() needs a size above 0")

Example

var total = 0;
for (var chunk in stream.chunks(4096)) {
    total += chunk.value().count;
}

Writer

trait Writer

A stream of bytes that can be written: a File, TcpStream, UnixStream or tls.TlsStream, or any type with write and write_all.

A type has the trait by providing write and write_all(data: u8[]); it then gets print and print_line, which write the text to_string makes of a value (the text $"{value}" would hold).

Example

import io;

main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("report.txt");
    var file = io.File.create(path).value();
    file.print("total: ");
    file.print_line(42);
    file.close();
    assert(io.File.read_to_string(path).value() == "total: 42\n", "printed");
    io.File.remove(path);
    return 0;
}

Methods

write

write(data: u8[]): IoResult<ulong>

Writes what the stream takes in one call, which may be less than all of data.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to write

Returns

  • the number of bytes written; an error when the stream fails

write_all

write_all(data: u8[]): IoResult<void>

Writes all of data.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to write

Returns

  • an Ok result once every byte is written; an error when the stream fails

print

print<T>(value: T): IoResult<void>

Writes the text of value, with no line break after it: a String as it is, anything else through to_string.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value

Parameters

  • value — the value to print

Returns

  • an Ok result once the text is written; an error as for write_all

Example

file.print("n = ");
file.print(3);   # the file now holds "n = 3"

print_line

print_line<T>(value: T): IoResult<void>

Writes the text of value and a line break (\n), as the global print does on standard output.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value

Parameters

  • value — the value to print

Returns

  • an Ok result once the line is written; an error as for write_all

Example

file.print_line($"total: {total}");
file.print_line((1, "two"));   # (1, two)

Lines

struct Lines

The iterator Reader.lines() returns: the lines of a stream, read in chunks as the loop asks for them, each as an IoResult<String>.

See also

  • Reader.lines

Example

var f = File.open(Path("notes.txt")).value();
var it = f.lines();
while (it.next()) {
    var line = it.current();
}

Constructor

Lines()

construct(source: Reader)

Makes an iterator over the lines of source, from what it reads next.

Parameters

  • source — the open stream to read

Methods

next

next(): bool

Reads the next line.

Once it returns false it keeps returning false.

Returns

  • true if there is a current element (a line, or the error that ends the lines), false at the end of the stream

current

current(): IoResult<String>

Returns the element the last successful next() moved to.

Returns

  • the current line, or the error that ended the lines

Panics

  • if next() was never called, or already returned false ("Lines.current() without a line")

Chunks

struct Chunks

The iterator Reader.chunks(size) returns: the rest of a stream, one read of at most size bytes at a time, each as an IoResult<u8[]>.

See also

  • Reader.chunks

Constructor

Chunks()

construct(source: Reader, size: ulong)

Makes an iterator over source in chunks of at most size bytes.

Parameters

  • source — the open stream to read
  • size — the most bytes in one chunk

Methods

next

next(): bool

Reads the next chunk.

Once it returns false it keeps returning false.

Returns

  • true if there is a current element (a chunk, or the error that ends the chunks), false at the end of the stream

current

current(): IoResult<u8[]>

Returns the element the last successful next() moved to.

Returns

  • the current chunk, or the error that ended the chunks

Panics

  • if next() was never called, or already returned false ("Chunks.current() without a chunk")

Path

Source: runtime/io/path.pep

Path

struct Path

An owned file-system path: the text of the path plus operations on it (Rust's Path and PathBuf in one type).

Every method except exists, is_file, is_dir, metadata, symlink_metadata and canonicalize is pure text manipulation: it never touches the file system, so .. is not resolved against symlinks and nothing needs to exist. A part that may be missing comes back as an optional, as in Rust: parent() of a root is none.

Breaking change: parent(), file_name(), file_stem(), extension() and dot_index() used to return an empty Path or String (or name.size) for "none"; they now return Path?, String? and ulong?.

Separators: on POSIX only / separates components (\ is an ordinary byte of a name). On Windows both / and \ separate, and a path may start with a prefix: a drive (C:) or a UNC share (\\server\share). Methods that build a path (join, normalize, with_extension) insert the platform separator (separator()), but the rest of the text is kept as written. Paths are UTF-8 Strings, scanned byte by byte; separators and dots are ASCII, so splitting at them never cuts a character in two.

Example

import io;

var p = io.Path("docs").join("guide.md");   # "docs/guide.md"
var name = p.file_name().value();               # "guide.md"
var ext = p.extension().value_or("");           # "md"
var dir = p.parent();                           # some io.Path("docs")
if (p.is_file()) {
    print(p.to_string());
}

Properties

is_empty

var is_empty: bool { get; }

Whether the path has no text at all. File-system operations on the empty path fail.

Constructor

Path()

[Implicit] construct(value: String = "")

Creates a path holding value as is: no validation, normalization or separator conversion.

The constructor is [Implicit]: a String (or a string literal) converts to a Path wherever a Path is expected, so every API that takes a Path also accepts text.

Parameters

  • value — the path's text; the default, "", is the empty path

Example

import io;

var p = io.Path("/usr/lib");
var empty = io.Path();   # is_empty is true
var q: io.Path = "docs";   # converted implicitly

Static methods

separator

static separator(): String

Returns the separator this platform inserts when it builds a path.

Returns

  • "/" on POSIX, "\" on Windows (where / is also accepted as a separator on input)

dot_index

static dot_index(name: String): ulong?

Returns the byte offset of the dot that starts the extension in the file name name: the last . that is not the first byte. A leading dot (.bashrc) starts the name, not an extension.

Breaking change: this used to return name.size for "no extension"; it now returns none.

Parameters

  • name — a file name (one component, as file_name() returns)

Returns

  • the index of the extension's dot, or none when the name has no such dot (noext, .bashrc, the empty name)

Methods

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the path's text, the same String the Path holds, not a copy.

Returns

  • the path as a String

is_absolute

is_absolute(): bool

Returns whether the path is absolute, meaning it does not depend on the current directory. Pure text: the path need not exist.

On POSIX a path is absolute when it starts with /. On Windows it is absolute when it has a drive followed by a root separator (C:\x, C:/x) or is a UNC path (\\server\share\x); a root without a drive (\x) and a drive without a root (C:x) are both relative. The empty path is relative.

Returns

  • true when the path is absolute

is_relative

is_relative(): bool

Returns whether the path is relative: the opposite of is_absolute(). The empty path is relative.

Returns

  • true when the path is not absolute

join

join(other: Path): Path

Returns this path with other appended as further components.

A platform separator is inserted between the two unless this path already ends in one. If other is absolute, or (on Windows) starts with a root separator or a drive or UNC prefix, it replaces this path instead, as in Rust. Joining an empty other returns a copy of this path; joining onto the empty path returns other. Nothing is normalized: a joined with ../b is a/../b.

Parameters

  • other — the path to append

Returns

  • a new Path; this path is not changed

Example

import io;

var p = io.Path("usr").join(io.Path("lib"));   # "usr/lib" ("usr\lib" on Windows)
var q = io.Path("a/").join(io.Path("b"));      # "a/b"
var r = io.Path("a").join(io.Path("/abs"));    # "/abs"
var so = io.Path("usr").join("lib").join("x.so");   # a String converts to a Path

join_str

[Deprecated("use 'join', which accepts a String", "join")] join_str(other: String): Path

Returns this path with the String other appended, exactly like join(Path(other)). Deprecated: join accepts a String directly, since a String converts to a Path implicitly.

Parameters

  • other — the path text to append

Returns

  • a new Path; this path is not changed

See also

  • join

Example

import io;

var so = io.Path("usr").join("lib").join("x.so");   # "usr/lib/x.so"

has_root_or_prefix

has_root_or_prefix(): bool

Returns whether the path starts with a root separator or, on Windows, a drive or UNC prefix. This is what makes join replace instead of append; unlike is_absolute() it is also true for Windows paths such as \x and C:x. On POSIX it equals is_absolute().

Returns

  • true when the path has a root separator or a prefix

parent

parent(): Path?

Returns the path without its last component. Pure text: .. is not resolved, so the parent of a/.. is a.

Trailing and repeated separators before the last component are dropped (a/b/ and a//b both give a). The parent of a top-level name keeps the root and prefix (/a gives /, C:\x gives C:\, C:x gives C:).

Breaking change: this used to return the empty path for "no parent"; it now returns none.

Returns

  • the parent path, or none for a root (/, C:\, a bare prefix such as C:), a bare name with no root (a, ., ..), or the empty path

Example

import io;

var p = io.Path("/a/b/c.txt").parent().value();   # "/a/b"
var root = io.Path("/a").parent().value();        # "/"
var none = io.Path("/").parent();                 # none

file_name

file_name(): String?

Returns the last component of the path, ignoring trailing separators (a/b/ gives b).

Breaking change: this used to return "" for "no file name"; it now returns none.

Returns

  • the last component, or none for a root (/, C:\), the empty path, or a path whose last component is . or ..

Example

import io;

var name = io.Path("/a/b/c.txt").file_name().value();   # "c.txt"
var none = io.Path("a/..").file_name();                 # none

file_stem

file_stem(): String?

Returns the file name without its extension: everything before the last dot, unless that dot is the first character.

Breaking change: this used to return "" for "no file name"; it now returns none.

Returns

  • the stem (c.tar for c.tar.gz, .bashrc for .bashrc, foo for foo., noext for noext), or none when there is no file name (see file_name())

extension

extension(): String?

Returns the file name's extension, without its dot: the text after the last dot, unless that dot is the first character. Only the file name counts; a dot in a directory name (a.b/c) is not an extension.

Breaking change: this used to return "" for "no extension"; it now returns none. As in Rust, a name ending in a dot (foo.) has the empty extension, which is not none.

Returns

  • the extension (gz for c.tar.gz, "" for foo.), or none when the file name has no dot after its first character (noext, .bashrc) or there is no file name

with_extension

with_extension(ext: String): Path

Returns this path with its file name's extension replaced by ext, added when it has none, or removed when ext is empty. Trailing separators after the file name are dropped.

Parameters

  • ext — the new extension without a leading dot (a dot is inserted; ".md" would give b..md), or "" to remove the extension

Returns

  • the new path, or a copy of this path unchanged when it has no file name (a root, ., .., or the empty path)

Example

import io;

var md = io.Path("a/b.txt").with_extension("md");   # "a/b.md"
var rs = io.Path("a/b").with_extension("rs");       # "a/b.rs"
var bare = io.Path("a/b.txt").with_extension("");   # "a/b"

components

components(): Array<String>

Returns the path split into its components: the prefix (Windows drive or UNC share, such as C:), then the root separator (one character, as written), then each non-empty part between separators.

Repeated and trailing separators produce no empty parts. . parts are dropped, except a leading one in a path with no prefix or root (./a gives . and a). .. parts are kept as they are.

Returns

  • the components in order; empty for the empty path

Example

import io;

var c = io.Path("/usr//lib/./x/").components();   # ["/", "usr", "lib", "x"]
var d = io.Path("./a/b").components();            # [".", "a", "b"]

normalize

normalize(): Path

Returns the path cleaned up lexically, without touching the file system: . parts and repeated or trailing separators are dropped, and each .. removes the part before it.

A .. cannot climb above a root (/../x gives /x) and is kept at the start of a relative path (../a/.. gives ..). The prefix is kept, and every separator becomes the platform separator. Because symlinks are not consulted, link/.. becomes . even when link points elsewhere; use canonicalize() for the path the file system resolves.

Returns

  • the normalized path; . when the path cleans to nothing (a/.., ./), and the empty path for the empty path

See also

  • canonicalize

Example

import io;

var p = io.Path("a/./b/../c").normalize();   # "a/c" ("a\c" on Windows)
var q = io.Path("a/..").normalize();         # "."

exists

exists(): bool

Returns whether something exists at this path, following symlinks. A relative path is resolved against the current directory.

Any error counts as not existing: a dangling symlink, a path under a directory that cannot be read, and the empty path all give false. Use metadata() to tell those apart.

Returns

  • true when the path (or a symlink's target) can be stat'ed

is_file

is_file(): bool

Returns whether the path names a regular file, following symlinks.

Returns

  • true for a regular file or a symlink to one; false for anything else, and on any error (including a missing path)

is_directory

is_directory(): bool

Returns whether the path names a directory, following symlinks.

Returns

  • true for a directory or a symlink to one; false for anything else, and on any error (including a missing path)

is_dir

[Deprecated("use 'is_directory' instead", "is_directory")] is_dir(): bool

Deprecated: use is_directory instead. Returns whether the path names a directory, following symlinks.

Returns

  • the same as is_directory()

metadata

metadata(): IoResult<Metadata>

Returns the metadata of the file or directory at this path, following symlinks: the result describes the target (so on POSIX is_symlink is always false). stat / statx on POSIX; on Windows the path is opened for attributes only.

Returns

  • the Metadata of the path (or of a symlink's target); an error when the path cannot be stat'ed: is_not_found() when it (or a symlink's target) is missing or the path is empty, is_permission_denied() when a directory on the way cannot be searched, and on POSIX is_not_a_directory() when a file is used as a directory in the middle of the path

See also

  • symlink_metadata

Example

import io;

var m = io.Path("data.bin").metadata();
if (m.is_ok()) {
    var size = m.value().size;
}

symlink_metadata

symlink_metadata(): IoResult<Metadata>

Returns the metadata of the path itself without following a symlink at the end of it, so for a symlink is_symlink is true and the rest describes the link rather than its target. lstat / statx with AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW on POSIX; on Windows the path is opened with FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT, and any reparse point (junctions included) reports is_symlink, together with is_directory for a directory link. For anything that is not a symlink it equals metadata().

Returns

  • the Metadata of the path itself; an error as for metadata(), except that a dangling symlink succeeds

See also

  • metadata

canonicalize

canonicalize(): IoResult<Path>

Returns the absolute path the file system resolves this path to: relative to the current directory, with every symlink, . and .. resolved. Unlike normalize(), the path must exist.

POSIX uses realpath. Windows opens the path and asks for its final name; the result uses \, and the \\?\ prefix Windows reports is removed (\\?\UNC\server\share becomes \\server\share).

Returns

  • the canonical absolute path; an error when the path cannot be resolved: is_not_found() when it (or a symlink's target) is missing or the path is empty, is_permission_denied() when a directory on the way cannot be searched

See also

  • normalize

Example

import io;

var real = io.Path("a/../b.txt").canonicalize();
if (real.is_ok()) {
    print(real.value().to_string());
}

read_link

read_link(): IoResult<Path>

Returns the target a symbolic link points to, as stored in the link (readlink on POSIX; on Windows the reparse point's target, junctions included). Only the link itself is read: a relative target stays relative to the directory holding the link, and the target need not exist.

On Windows the \??\ prefix of an absolute target is removed (\??\UNC\server\share becomes \\server\share).

Returns

  • the link's target; an error with is_invalid_input() when the path is not a symlink, is_not_found() when it is missing or empty, or another platform error

See also

  • File.symlink
  • Directory.symlink

Example

import io;

var target = io.Path("current").read_link();
if (target.is_ok()) {
    print(target.value().to_string());
}

set_permissions

set_permissions(mode: Mode): IoResult<void>

Sets the permission bits of the file or directory at this path, following symlinks (chmod on POSIX).

mode holds the raw platform bits, as Metadata.permissions reports them: on POSIX the mode_t bits mode & 07777 (493, octal 755, for rwxr-xr-x). A directory's bits control listing it (r), creating and removing entries in it (w) and reaching anything inside it (x). On Windows mode is the FILE_ATTRIBUTE_* word, and only FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY (1) is applied. WASI has no permission bits, and this fails. set_read_only and set_executable change one property portably.

Parameters

  • mode — the new permission bits

Returns

  • an Ok result once they are set; an error with is_not_found() when the path is missing or empty, is_permission_denied() when the caller does not own it, or another platform error

See also

  • File.set_permissions

Example

import io;

io.Path("deploy.sh").set_permissions(493);   # octal 755: rwxr-xr-x

set_read_only

set_read_only(read_only: bool): IoResult<void>

Makes the file or directory at this path read-only, or writable again, following symlinks: the portable part of set_permissions.

On POSIX, read-only clears every write bit (octal 222), and writable sets only the owner's (octal 200), so nothing becomes writable by group or others this way. On Windows it sets or clears FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY, which Windows ignores on a directory. Fails on WASI, which has no permission bits.

Parameters

  • read_only — true to make it read-only, false to make it writable by its owner

Returns

  • an Ok result once it is changed; an error as for metadata() or set_permissions

See also

  • Metadata.read_only

Example

import io;

var config = io.Path("settings.toml");
config.set_read_only(true);
var ro = config.metadata().value().read_only;   # true

set_executable

set_executable(executable: bool): IoResult<void>

Makes the file at this path executable, or not, following symlinks, without raw permission bits.

On POSIX, executable adds an execute bit for each class (owner, group, others) that may read the file, as chmod +x does with the usual umask; not executable clears all three. Windows has no execute bit (an extension such as .exe decides) and WASI no permission bits, so there this does nothing and succeeds.

Parameters

  • executable — true to make the file executable, false to stop it

Returns

  • an Ok result once it is changed; an error as for metadata() or set_permissions

Example

import io;

io.File.write_text(io.Path("hello.sh"), "#!/bin/sh\necho hello\n");
io.Path("hello.sh").set_executable(true);

set_modified

set_modified(time: long): IoResult<void>

Sets the modification time of the file or directory at this path, following symlinks and leaving its access time alone (utimensat on POSIX, SetFileTime on Windows, where the time is kept to 100 ns).

A directory's modification time changes whenever an entry is added or removed, so set it after its contents are final.

Parameters

Returns

See also

import io;

var source = io.Path("a.txt").metadata().value();
io.Path("b.txt").set_modified(source.modified);

==(rhs: Path): bool

Returns whether two paths have exactly the same text. The comparison is byte by byte, with no normalization and case-sensitive on every platform: a/b differs from a//b, from a/b/, and (on Windows) from a\b and A/b. Compare normalize() or canonicalize() results to ignore spelling differences.

Parameters

Returns

Returns whether two paths differ in their text: the opposite of ==, with the same byte-by-byte comparison.

Returns

File

Source: runtime/io/file.pep

OpenOptions

struct OpenOptions

Describes how File.open_with (or OpenOptions.open) opens a file: which access it asks for, and whether the file is created or truncated.

A builder in the style of Rust's std::fs::OpenOptions. A new OpenOptions has every option off; each setter stores its flag and returns this same OpenOptions, so calls chain. The rules, checked when the file is opened:

  • At least one of read, write or append must be set, or opening fails with is_invalid_input().
  • create, create_new and truncate need write or append, or opening fails with is_invalid_input().
  • append implies write access, and every write goes to the current end of the file whatever the position; it wins over write.
  • create opens an existing file as it is (combine with truncate to empty it) and creates a missing one.
  • create_new creates the file and fails with is_already_exists() when it already exists, atomically (O_EXCL on POSIX, CREATE_NEW on Windows); create is then irrelevant.
  • truncate empties an existing file on open.
  • Without create or create_new, a missing file fails with is_not_found().

On POSIX a created file gets mode 0666 (or the mode set) less the process umask, and the descriptor is opened close-on-exec. On Windows every file is opened sharing read, write and delete access with other openers.

See also

  • File.open_with

Example

var r = OpenOptions().read(true).write(true).create(true).open(Path("data.bin"));
if (r.is_err()) {
    return 1;
}
var f = r.value();

Creates an OpenOptions with every option off. Set at least one of read, write or append before opening.

Sets append mode: the file is opened for writing and every write goes to the current end of the file, whatever the position (seeking still moves the position for reads). Implies write access, and takes precedence over write.

An existing file keeps its mode. Ignored on Windows and WASI; use File.set_read_only there.

Opens path with these options. The same as File.open_with(path, this).

Parameters

Returns

See also

Example

var log = OpenOptions().append(true).create(true).open(Path("log.txt")).value();

FileType

enum FileType

The kind of a file system object, as Metadata.file_type and DirEntry.file_type report it.

A symlink is reported as Symlink only where links are not followed (Path.symlink_metadata() and directory listings); on Windows that is any reparse point, junctions included, even one that points to a directory.

See also

Example

import io;

var m = io.Path("notes.txt").metadata();
if (m.is_ok()) {
    match (m.value().file_type) {
        File => { print("a file"); }
        Directory => { print("a directory"); }
        Symlink, Other => { print("something else"); }
    }
}

Metadata

struct Metadata

Describes a file system object: its kind, size, read-only flag, permission bits and timestamps, as a snapshot taken when it was queried.

Returned by File.metadata(), Path.metadata() (which follows symlinks), Path.symlink_metadata() (which does not) and DirEntry.metadata(). The timestamps are nanoseconds since the Unix epoch (1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC). On POSIX the metadata comes from statx (Linux) or stat (macOS); on Windows from GetFileInformationByHandle.

Example

var m = Path("notes.txt").metadata();
if (m.is_ok() && m.value().is_file) {
    var bytes = m.value().size;
}

ulong size

The file's length in bytes.

file_type

FileType file_type

The kind of object: File, Directory, Symlink or Other. It agrees with is_file, is_directory and is_symlink, except that a Windows reparse point to a directory is Symlink with both is_directory and is_symlink set.

is_file

Whether this is a regular file. On Windows, anything that is neither a directory nor a reparse point (symlink) counts as a file.

Whether this is a directory.

Whether this is a symbolic link itself. Only metadata that does not follow links (Path.symlink_metadata()) can report one. On Windows this is any reparse point (FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT), which includes junctions.

read_only

bool read_only

Whether the file is read-only: on POSIX, no write permission bit (0222) is set for anyone; on Windows, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY is set.

created

The creation (birth) time, in nanoseconds since the Unix epoch; none where the platform does not report one, such as on Linux file systems that do not record it.

The raw permission bits: on POSIX the mode_t permission bits (mode & 07777, for example 256 for owner read); on Windows the FILE_ATTRIBUTE_* bits.

Metadata()

construct()

Creates a Metadata with every number zero, every flag false, file_type Other and created none. Metadata is normally obtained from a query such as File.metadata().

File

[NotCopyable( "owns an operating-system handle and cannot be copied; send its path, and open the file again on the receiving thread" )] struct File

An open file, or a standard stream, read and written through its platform handle (a file descriptor on POSIX, a HANDLE on Windows).

Open one with File.open (read-only), File.create (write-only, created or truncated), or File.open_with / OpenOptions.open for anything else. The static conveniences read_bytes, read_to_string, write_bytes, write_text, copy, rename and remove work on a whole file by path.

I/O is unbuffered: each read and write is one system call. Reads and writes start at the current position and move it forward; the seek_* methods move it explicitly. A write to a standard stream first flushes the output print has buffered, so the two never come out of order.

Closing: the File's destructor closes an owned handle when the last reference to the File is released, and ignores any error. Call close() to close earlier or to observe the error. The standard streams (stdin(), stdout(), stderr()) are never closed by a File. Every operation on a closed File fails with an error that none of the IoError predicates identify (EBADF on POSIX, ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE on Windows).

Errors are IoError values carrying the platform's code; use its predicates (is_not_found(), is_permission_denied(), ...) to tell kinds apart portably.

Example

var f = File.create(Path("out.txt")).value();
f.write_all("hello");
f.close();
var text = File.read_to_string(Path("out.txt")).value();   # "hello"

Fields

path

Path path

The path the File was opened with; <stdin>, <stdout> or <stderr> for a standard stream, and empty for a File() never opened.

Constructor

File()

construct()

Creates a closed File that owns nothing yet: is_open() is false and every I/O method fails. Use File.open, File.create or File.open_with to get an open one.

Static methods

open

static open(path: Path): IoResult<File>

Opens an existing file for reading only. The position starts at 0.

A directory can be opened this way too, but reading it fails with is_is_a_directory().

Parameters

  • path — the file to open

Returns

  • the open File; an error with is_not_found() when the path is empty or does not exist, is_permission_denied() when access is refused, or another platform error

Example

var r = File.open(Path("config.txt"));
if (r.is_err() && r.error().is_not_found()) {
    return 0;
}
var text = r.value().read_string();

create

static create(path: Path): IoResult<File>

Opens a file for writing only, creating it if it is missing and truncating it to 0 bytes if it exists.

On POSIX a created file gets mode 0666 less the process umask.

Parameters

  • path — the file to create or truncate

Returns

  • the open File, empty and positioned at 0; an error with is_not_found() when the path is empty or its parent directory does not exist, is_permission_denied() when access is refused, or another platform error (on POSIX, is_is_a_directory() when the path is a directory)

Example

var f = File.create(Path("report.txt")).value();
f.write_all("done");

open_with

static open_with(path: Path, options: OpenOptions): IoResult<File>

Opens path as options describe. OpenOptions.open is the same call written as a builder.

The options are checked first, as in Rust: at least one of read, write or append is required, and create, create_new or truncate require write or append. The position starts at 0 (append mode still writes at the end).

Parameters

  • path — the file to open
  • options — the access mode and creation behavior

Returns

  • the open File; an error with is_invalid_input() when no access mode is set or create, create_new or truncate is set without write or append; is_not_found() when the path is empty, or the file (or a parent directory) is missing and neither create nor create_new is set; is_already_exists() when create_new is set and the path exists; is_permission_denied() when access is refused; or another platform error

Example

var opts = OpenOptions().write(true).create_new(true);
var r = File.open_with(Path("lock"), opts);
if (r.is_err() && r.error().is_already_exists()) {
    return 1;
}

std_file

static std_file(stream: StdStream, name: String): File

Returns a File for one of the process's standard streams. The File does not own the handle, so neither close() nor the destructor closes the stream. stdin(), stdout() and stderr() are the usual way to call this.

On Windows a process without a console or redirection may get a null handle, and the File is then not open.

Parameters

  • stream — the stream
  • name — the display name stored in the File's path, such as <stdout>

Returns

  • a File on that stream, that does not close the stream when released

Example

var err = File.std_file(StdStream.Error, "<stderr>");
err.write_all("warning");

Returns

stdin

static stdin(): File

Returns a File reading the process's standard input. Each call returns a new File on the same stream; the stream is never closed by a File. A read returns 0 at end of input (on Windows, also when the writing end of a pipe has closed).

Returns

stdout

static stdout(): File

Returns a File writing to the process's standard output. Each call returns a new File on the same stream, and close() only marks that File closed: the stream stays usable. Writes are unbuffered, and each one first flushes what print has buffered, so output from print and from this File comes out in program order.

Returns

Example

var out = File.stdout();
out.write_all("hello");

Returns a File writing to the process's standard error. Each call returns a new File on the same stream, and close() only marks that File closed: the stream stays usable. Writes are unbuffered, and each one first flushes what print has buffered.

Returns

Writes s as UTF-8 as the whole contents of the file at path, creating it or replacing what it held, then closes it. No newline is added.

Returns

static copy(from: Path, to: Path): IoResult<ulong>

Only the contents are copied: to keeps its own permissions and timestamps (a new file gets the defaults of File.create). A failure part way leaves to partly written.

Renames or moves from to to, replacing an existing file at to (rename on POSIX, MoveFileExW with MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING on Windows).

Returns

static hard_link(from: Path, to: Path): IoResult<void>

Creates a hard link at to to the file from (link on POSIX, CreateHardLinkW on Windows): a second name for the same file, which keeps its contents when from is renamed or removed.

Both names must be on one file system (volume); across two it fails rather than copying, and so do directories.

Parameters

  • to — the new name

Returns

static symlink(target: Path, link: Path): IoResult<void>

Creates a symbolic link at link that points to the file target (symlink on POSIX, CreateSymbolicLinkW on Windows). Use Directory.symlink for a link to a directory: Windows makes the two kinds differently, and a file link to a directory does not open there. POSIX makes the same link either way.

target is stored as given and need not exist; a relative target is resolved against the directory that holds the link, not the current directory. On Windows, making a symlink needs Developer Mode or an administrator, and fails with is_permission_denied() otherwise.

Returns

See also

Example

static remove(path: Path): IoResult<void>

Deletes the file at path. A symlink is removed itself, not its target. Directories are not removed: use Directory.remove or Directory.remove_all.

Parameters

  • path — the file to delete

Returns

  • an Ok result on success; an error with is_not_found() when the path does not exist (on POSIX, also when it is empty); when it is a directory, is_is_a_directory() on Linux and is_permission_denied() on macOS and Windows; is_permission_denied() when access is refused (on Windows also for a read-only file); or another platform error

Example

}

is_open

is_open(): bool

Returns whether the File holds a valid handle: true after a successful open, false after close() and for a File() never opened.

Returns

  • true while the File is open

check_open

check_open(): IoResult<void>

Checks that the File is open, for use before an operation.

Returns

  • an Ok result when the File is open; an error with the message "file is closed" otherwise (code EBADF on POSIX, ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE on Windows; no IoError predicate holds)

read

read(buffer: u8[], max: ulong): IoResult<ulong>

Reads up to max bytes from the current position and appends them to buf, growing it; the bytes already in buf are kept. Advances the position by the count read.

One system call: the read may be partial, returning fewer than max bytes before the end of the file (always so for pipes and terminals), and a single call moves at most about 2 GiB on POSIX or 1 GiB on Windows. Loop until it returns 0 to read everything, or use read_all. On POSIX an interrupted read (EINTR) is retried. On failure buffer keeps its previous contents.

Parameters

  • buffer — the array the bytes are appended to
  • max — the most bytes to read; 0 reads nothing and returns 0

Returns

  • the number of bytes appended, 0 at end of file; an error when the File is closed, or is_is_a_directory() when it is a directory, or another platform error

Example

var buf = Array<u8>();
while (true) {
    var r = f.read(buf, 4096);
    if (r.is_err() || r.value() == 0) {
        break;
    }
}

read_all

read_all(): IoResult<u8[]>

Reads everything from the current position to the end of the file, in 64 KiB chunks, leaving the position at the end.

Returns

  • a new array of the bytes read (empty at end of file); an error when the File is closed, is_is_a_directory() when it is a directory, or another platform error, in which case the bytes read so far are discarded

read_string

read_string(): IoResult<String>

Reads everything from the current position to the end of the file, as read_all does, and returns it as UTF-8 text.

The bytes must be strictly valid UTF-8 (RFC 3629: no overlong forms, surrogates, or code points past U+10FFFF). A byte-order mark is kept as part of the text.

Returns

  • the text read (empty at end of file); an error with is_invalid_input() when the bytes are not valid UTF-8, or any error read_all returns

write

write(data: u8[]): IoResult<ulong>

Writes bytes from data at the current position (or at the end, in append mode) with a single system call, and advances the position.

The write may be partial: it can write fewer than data.count bytes, and one call moves at most about 2 GiB on POSIX or 1 GiB on Windows. Use write_all to write everything. On POSIX an interrupted write (EINTR) is retried.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to write

Returns

  • the number of bytes written, which may be less than data.count; an error when the File is closed or was not opened for writing, or another platform error

write_all

write_all(data: u8[]): IoResult<void>

Writes all of data, repeating the write until every byte is written. Advances the position by data.count.

If an error occurs part of data may already have been written.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to write

Returns

  • an Ok result once every byte is written; an error when the File is closed or was not opened for writing, when a write makes no progress ("failed to write the whole buffer", with code EIO on POSIX or ERROR_WRITE_FAULT on Windows), or another platform error

write_all

Writes all of the UTF-8 bytes of s, as write_all does for bytes. No newline or terminator is added.

Parameters

Returns

var f = File.create(Path("greeting.txt")).value();
var r = f.write_all("hello, world");
