write_all(data: u8[]): IoResult<void>

Appends all of data to bytes.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to write

Returns

  • an Ok result; writing to memory does not fail

Print

Print, deprecated: Writer gives print and print_line to every stream.

Source: runtime/io/print.pep

Print

[Deprecated("use 'Writer' instead", "Writer")] trait Print

Deprecated: use Writer instead.

A byte stream that values can be printed to, as the global print prints to standard output.

A type has the trait by providing write_all(data: u8[]); it then gets print and print_line, which write the text to_string makes of a value (the text $"{value}" would hold).

Example

import io;

main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("report.txt");
    var file = io.File.create(path).value();
    file.print("total: ");
    file.print_line(42);
    file.close();
    assert(io.File.read_to_string(path).value() == "total: 42\n", "printed");
    io.File.remove(path);
    return 0;
}

Methods

write_all

write_all(data: u8[]): IoResult<void>

Writes all of data.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to write

Returns

  • an Ok result once every byte is written; an error when the stream fails

print

print<T>(value: T): IoResult<void>

Writes the text of value, with no line break after it: a String as it is, anything else through to_string.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value

Parameters

  • value — the value to print

Returns

  • an Ok result once the text is written; an error as for write_all

Example

file.print("n = ");
file.print(3);   # the file now holds "n = 3"

print_line

print_line<T>(value: T): IoResult<void>

Writes the text of value and a line break (\n), as the global print does on standard output.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of value

Parameters

  • value — the value to print

Returns

  • an Ok result once the line is written; an error as for write_all

Example

file.print_line($"total: {total}");
file.print_line((1, "two"));   # (1, two)

The async module

Threads and concurrency, modeled on Rust's std::thread and C++ std::thread, and tasks: green threads that take turns on a few worker threads.

Like io, async is a module: bring it in with import async (and write async.Thread, async.logical_cpus()) or import names directly with import [Thread, ThreadLocal] from async.

  • Atomic: Atomic<T>, a value threads read and update without a lock
  • Thread: starting, naming and joining threads, ThreadId and ThreadBody
  • ThreadLocal: a variable with a separate value on every thread, and its ThreadLocalGuard<T>
  • Processor counts: logical_cpus() and physical_cpus()
  • Channel: Channel<T>, a queue that carries values between threads, and its ChannelIterator<T>
  • Mutex: Mutex<T>, the MutexGuard<T> a with block holds, and Condition<T>
  • Once: Once, which runs a function once, and Lazy<T>, a value built on first use
  • Tasks: run, Task<T>, spawn, spawn_on_each_worker, run_blocking, sleep, yield_now, timeout and cancellation, for many tasks taking turns on a few worker threads and parking on sockets
  • TaskLocal: a variable with a separate value in every task, and its TaskLocalGuard<T>
  • I/O backends: Backend, how a runtime waits for sockets

Only thread-safe values can be shared between threads: numbers, shared function values (such as a thread's body), and [Shared] structs such as Atomic<T>, Thread, ThreadLocal<T>, Channel<T> and Mutex<T>. Any other value crosses threads only as a new value that nothing else references (Channel.send(move(x)), or send(copy(x))), or stays inside a Mutex, whose with blocks the compiler keeps apart from the rest of the program. Lazy<T> holds thread-safe values only. See the language guide's Threads chapter.

Example

import async;

const hits = async.Atomic<long>(0);

work() {
    hits.fetch_add(1);
}

main(): int {
    var workers = Array<async.Thread>();
    var n = async.logical_cpus();
    var i: ulong = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        workers.append(async.Thread.spawn(work));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    for (var worker in workers) {
        worker.join();
    }
    assert(hits.load() == n as long, "every worker ran");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/async/module.pep

Atomic

Source: runtime/async/atomic.pep

Atomic

[Shared] struct Atomic<T: Shared>

A value of type T that threads can read and update without data races, like C++ std::atomic<T>.

T may be a numeric type, a pointer, or a struct type. For a struct T the Atomic holds a counted reference and every operation follows std::shared_ptr rules: store and a successful compare_exchange acquire the new reference and release the one they replace, and load hands the caller its own reference. Memory ordering: load is an acquire, store a release, and compare_exchange and the fetch_* operations are acquire-release.

Atomic is a [Shared] struct, so copies of it share one slot and may be used from several threads at once: pass the Atomic around (or keep it in a const global) to share the value between threads, so T is constrained Shared: a number, bool, an enum, a [Shared] struct, or another thread-safe type. async.Atomic<String> is a compile error at String.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the stored value, which must be thread-safe (T: Shared)

Example

main(): int {
    var counter = async.Atomic<long>(0);
    var before = counter.fetch_add(5);   # before == 0
    if (counter.load() != 5) { return 1; }
    return 0;
}

Constructor

Atomic()

construct(value: T = __default<T>())

Creates an Atomic holding value.

For a struct T the Atomic acquires a reference to value.

Parameters

  • value — the initial value; defaults to zero for a POD T and null for a struct T

Example

var a = async.Atomic<int>(41);
var p = async.Atomic<Point>();   # holds null until a store

Methods

load

load(): T

Atomically reads the current value, with acquire ordering.

For a struct T the returned reference is acquired for the caller, so it stays valid even if another thread stores a new value afterwards.

Returns

  • the value currently stored

store

store(v: T)

Atomically replaces the stored value with v, with release ordering.

For a struct T this is a shared_ptr assignment: the slot acquires v and releases its previous occupant, and the swap is a single atomic exchange, so concurrent stores never leak or double-release.

Parameters

  • v — the new value

compare_exchange

compare_exchange(expected: T, desired: T): bool

Atomically replaces the stored value with desired if and only if it currently equals expected (a compare-and-swap).

Equality is bitwise: a struct T compares references (the same object, not equal contents), and a floating-point T compares bit patterns, so 0.0 and -0.0 differ. Unlike C++ compare_exchange_strong, expected is not updated on failure; call load() to retry. On success a struct slot acquires desired and releases the old occupant; on failure no reference count changes.

Parameters

  • expected — the value the slot must hold for the exchange to happen
  • desired — the value to store when it does

Returns

  • true if the slot held expected and now holds desired, false if it was left unchanged

Example

var cur = counter.load();
while (!counter.compare_exchange(cur, cur + 1)) {
    cur = counter.load();
}

exchange

exchange(v: T): T

Atomically replaces the stored value with v and returns the value it replaced.

Implemented as a compare_exchange retry loop, so under heavy contention it may retry several times. For a struct T the slot acquires v, and the caller owns the returned reference.

Parameters

  • v — the new value

Returns

  • the value stored immediately before the exchange

Example

var e = async.Atomic<int>(1);
var old = e.exchange(2);   # old == 1, e.load() == 2

is_lock_free

is_lock_free(): bool

Reports whether this Atomic's slot fits a native atomic instruction, so its operations never need a lock or an atomic library call.

True for every POD T of 8 bytes or less and for every struct T (whose slot is one pointer). The answer depends only on T, never on the stored value.

Returns

  • true when the operations are lock-free

fetch_add

fetch_add(v: T): T

Atomically adds v to the stored value and returns the value before the addition, like std::atomic<T>::fetch_add.

Integer T only. Overflow wraps around. For a non-integer T (a floating-point or struct type) the call compiles but aborts the program when it runs.

Parameters

  • v — the amount to add

Returns

  • the value stored immediately before the addition

Example

var c = async.Atomic<long>(10);
var old = c.fetch_add(5);   # old == 10, c.load() == 15

fetch_sub

fetch_sub(v: T): T

Atomically subtracts v from the stored value and returns the value before the subtraction, like std::atomic<T>::fetch_sub.

Integer T only. Overflow wraps around. For a non-integer T the call compiles but aborts the program when it runs.

Parameters

  • v — the amount to subtract

Returns

  • the value stored immediately before the subtraction

fetch_and

fetch_and(v: T): T

Atomically replaces the stored value with its bitwise AND with v and returns the value before the operation, like std::atomic<T>::fetch_and.

Integer T only. For a non-integer T the call compiles but aborts the program when it runs.

Parameters

  • v — the mask to AND with

Returns

  • the value stored immediately before the operation

fetch_or

fetch_or(v: T): T

Atomically replaces the stored value with its bitwise OR with v and returns the value before the operation, like std::atomic<T>::fetch_or.

Integer T only. For a non-integer T the call compiles but aborts the program when it runs.

Parameters

  • v — the bits to OR in

Returns

  • the value stored immediately before the operation

fetch_xor

fetch_xor(v: T): T

Atomically replaces the stored value with its bitwise XOR with v and returns the value before the operation, like std::atomic<T>::fetch_xor.

Integer T only. For a non-integer T the call compiles but aborts the program when it runs.

Parameters

  • v — the bits to XOR with

Returns

  • the value stored immediately before the operation

Thread

Threads: starting, naming, identifying and joining operating-system threads.

Source: runtime/async/thread.pep

ThreadId

type ThreadId = ulong

Identifies a thread for as long as the program runs: every thread, whether started with Thread.spawn or not, gets a distinct id the first time it is asked for one, and ids are never reused.

Ids are assigned by the runtime in the order threads ask for them, starting at 1; they are not the operating system's thread ids. A ThreadId is a number, so it can be compared, hashed and used as a HashMap key.

See also

  • Thread.id

ThreadBody

type ThreadBody = shared () => void

The type of a thread's body: a function that takes no arguments and returns nothing. Thread.spawn runs one on a new thread.

It is a shared function type, because the body runs on another thread: a named function, or a closure that captures only thread-safe values (numbers, Atomic<T>, [Shared] structs, other shared function values). A closure capturing a String, say, is a compile error.

See also

  • Thread.spawn

Thread

[Shared] struct Thread

An operating-system thread.

Start one with Thread.spawn, which runs a function on a new thread and returns its Thread, and wait for it to finish with join(). Every thread, including the main thread, can get its own Thread with Thread.current().

A Thread is [Shared]: the thread that started it and the thread itself can both hold it. Dropping every reference without joining detaches the thread: it keeps running, and its resources are freed when it finishes.

The body runs until it returns; there is no way to stop a thread from the outside. A panic or failed assert on any thread ends the whole program.

Example

import async;

const total = Atomic<long>(0);

add_ten() {
    total.fetch_add(10);
}

main(): int {
    var a = async.Thread.spawn(add_ten, "adder a");
    var b = async.Thread.spawn(add_ten, "adder b");
    a.join();
    b.join();
    assert(total.load() == 20, "both threads ran");
    return 0;
}

Constructor

Thread()

construct(name: String, body: ThreadBody)

Creates a Thread value for a thread that is already running. Programs get threads from spawn and current() instead; a Thread made directly is not attached to any thread and cannot be joined.

Parameters

  • name — the thread's name; empty for an unnamed thread
  • body — the function the thread runs

Static methods

spawn

static spawn(body: ThreadBody, name: String = "", stack_size: ulong = 0): Thread

Starts a new thread that runs body.

The new thread starts right away and runs until body returns. Its Thread.current() is the Thread returned here.

The stack the operating system gives a thread by default differs: usually 8 MiB on Linux (ulimit -s), 1 MiB on Windows, and 512 KiB on macOS. A thread that recurses deeply, such as one walking a deeply nested tree, passes stack_size to get the same stack everywhere. The stack is reserved address space; memory is used only as the thread reaches it.

Parameters

  • body — the function to run on the new thread
  • name — a name for the thread, returned by name(); empty by default
  • stack_size — the bytes of stack the thread gets, rounded up to 64 KiB; 0, the default, for the system's default

Returns

  • the new thread, to join() or query

Panics

  • if the operating system cannot create another thread, or refuses stack_size

Example

var worker = Thread.spawn(do_work, "worker");
worker.join();
var deep = Thread.spawn(walk_tree, "walker", 8388608);   # 8 MiB
deep.join();

current

static current(): Thread

Returns the Thread of the thread that calls it.

For a thread started with spawn this is the Thread that spawn returned. Any other thread (the main thread, or one started by C code) gets a Thread the first time it asks and the same one afterwards; the main thread's is named main, the others are unnamed. Such a Thread cannot be joined.

Returns

  • the calling thread

Example

var me = Thread.current();
print(me.name(), "\n");   # "main" on the main thread

sleep

static sleep(milliseconds: ulong)

Pauses the calling thread for at least milliseconds milliseconds.

The operating system may sleep longer, but never shorter. In a task (see run), it is async.sleep: the task waits and its worker thread runs other tasks, and a cancel or the task's timeout ends the wait early.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — how long to sleep; 0 returns right away

Methods

id

id(): ThreadId

Returns the thread's id, which no other thread in the program has.

Returns

  • the thread's id

name

name(): String

Returns the name the thread was given.

Returns

  • the name passed to spawn, main for the main thread, or an empty String for an unnamed thread

is_finished

is_finished(): bool

Reports whether the thread's body has returned.

A thread that is not finished may finish at any moment, so a false result can be out of date by the time it is used. Always false for a Thread that was not started by spawn.

Returns

  • true once the body has returned

is_joinable

is_joinable(): bool

Reports whether join() can be called: the thread was started by spawn and has not been joined yet.

Returns

  • true if the thread can be joined

join

join()

Waits for the thread's body to return.

Returns right away if it already has. A thread can be joined once; a Thread from current() for a thread not started by spawn cannot be joined at all. Everything the thread did before it finished is visible to the caller after join() returns.

Panics

  • if the thread cannot be joined (see is_joinable()), or if a thread tries to join itself

ThreadLocal

Per-thread values: ThreadLocal<T> gives every thread its own copy of a variable.

Source: runtime/async/thread_local.pep

ThreadLocal

[Shared] struct ThreadLocal<T>

A variable with a separate value on every thread, like C++ thread_local or Rust's thread_local!.

Each thread that calls set stores its own value. When a thread exits, its value is released.

For a thread-safe T (a number, a [Shared] struct), get returns the calling thread's value (the default of T, zero or null, until that thread sets one). For any other T, such as a String, the value is reached through a with block, with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }, and get is a compile error; set then takes a new value (a constructor call, a string literal, copy(x)). Inside the block the value is kept apart from the rest of the program, as for a Mutex.

A ThreadLocal is [Shared], so one object can be used from every thread; it is usually a module-scope variable. T does not have to be thread-safe, because each value stays on the thread that stored it.

Destroying a ThreadLocal releases the calling thread's value; values that other threads still hold are released when those threads exit.

A thread's values are released when it exits if Thread.spawn started it (the async runtime's workers too). The main thread's are released only by clear(), and a thread started by C code leaks the values it did not clear.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the per-thread value

Example

import async;

const calls = async.ThreadLocal<int>();

count_call() {
    calls.set(calls.get() + 1);
}

main(): int {
    count_call();
    count_call();
    assert(calls.get() == 2, "two calls on this thread");
    return 0;
}

Constructor

ThreadLocal()

construct()

Creates a thread-local variable. No thread has a value yet.

Methods

get

get(): T

Returns the calling thread's value.

For a struct T the caller gets its own reference. Only for a thread-safe T: for any other T, use with (var value = local.enter()).

Returns

  • the value this thread last stored, or the default of T (zero or null) if it has not stored one

set

set([Move] value: T)

Stores value as the calling thread's value, replacing (and, for a struct T, releasing) the one it held. Other threads' values are not affected.

For a T that is not thread-safe, value must be a new value (a constructor call, a string literal, copy(x)), which the compiler checks.

Parameters

  • value — the new value for this thread

enter

enter(): ThreadLocalGuard<T>

Returns the guard that a with block enters to reach the calling thread's value: with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }. The body runs with the value bound; the else block runs when this thread has no value (for a struct T).

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns this thread's value

Example

const names = async.ThreadLocal<Array<String>>();

remember(String name) {
    if (!names.is_set()) {
        names.set(Array<String>());
    }
    with (var list = names.enter()) {
        list.append(name.copy());
    }
}

is_set

is_set(): bool

Reports whether the calling thread has stored a value since it started or last called clear().

Returns

  • true if this thread has a value

clear

clear()

Removes the calling thread's value, releasing it for a struct T. get() returns the default of T afterwards.

ThreadLocalGuard

[Isolated] struct ThreadLocalGuard<T>

The access to a thread's ThreadLocal<T> value that a with block holds: enter() returns the value. Get one from ThreadLocal.enter().

A guard is [Isolated]: it can only be the scope of a with header, and the compiler checks the block with the confinement rule (see Mutex).

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the per-thread value

Constructor

ThreadLocalGuard()

construct(local: ThreadLocal<T>)

Creates the guard for the calling thread's value of local; the same as local.enter().

Parameters

  • local — the thread-local variable

Methods

enter

enter(): T

Returns the calling thread's value, for the with header to bind.

Returns

  • this thread's value, or the default of T (null for a struct) when it has none

exit

exit()

Does nothing: the value stays with the thread.

Mutex and Condition

Mutual exclusion: Mutex<T> owns a value that one thread at a time can use, MutexGuard<T> is the lock a with block holds, and Condition<T> lets a thread holding a Mutex sleep until another thread changes its value.

Source: runtime/async/mutex.pep

Mutex

[Shared] struct Mutex<T>

A value that one thread at a time can use, like Rust's Mutex<T> or a C++ std::mutex paired with the data it protects.

The Mutex owns its value, and the way to reach it is a with block: with (var value = mutex.lock()) { ... } waits until no other thread holds the lock, binds the value, and unlocks when the block ends by any path (falling off the end, return, break, continue). Everything a thread did while holding the lock is visible to the next thread that takes it.

T is a struct type, such as Array<String> or a struct of your own. Inside the with block the compiler keeps the locked value and the rest of the program apart: a value that is not thread-safe (a String, an Array) cannot move from one to the other, and no part of the locked value can be returned from the block or stored outside it. Pass copy(x) to move a value either way; new values (a constructor call, a string literal, a call the compiler infers returns a fresh value) and thread-safe values such as numbers pass freely. Mutex<int> is a compile error: use Atomic<int>.

A Mutex is [Shared]: keep it in a module-scope variable or pass it to threads. It is not re-entrant: locking it again on the thread that holds it panics instead of deadlocking. A panic while it is held ends the program, so a Mutex is never left "poisoned".

In a task (see run), waiting for the lock parks the task, not its worker thread, so the other tasks there keep running, including one that holds the lock. Each task counts as its own holder, and a task may hold the lock across a wait of its own (a sleep, a socket call). A cancel does not end the wait for the lock.

Type parameters

  • T — the protected value's type, a struct type

Example

import async;

[Shared]
struct Account {
    const checking: Atomic<long>;
    const savings: Atomic<long>;
    construct(long checking = 0, long savings = 0) {
        this.checking = Atomic<long>(checking);
        this.savings = Atomic<long>(savings);
    }
}

const account = async.Mutex<Account>(Account(100, 0));

save(long amount) {
    with (var a = account.lock()) {
        # No other thread sees the money in neither account.
        a.checking.fetch_sub(amount);
        a.savings.fetch_add(amount);
    }
}

Constructor

Mutex()

construct([Move] value: T)

Creates an unlocked Mutex that owns value.

value must be a new value, such as a constructor call, copy(x) or move(x): nothing outside the Mutex may reference it. The caller hands its reference over, so nothing is copied.

Parameters

  • value — the value to protect; a new value, which the compiler checks

Example

const names = async.Mutex<Array<String>>(Array<String>());

Methods

lock

lock(): MutexGuard<T>

Waits until the calling thread holds the lock, and returns the guard that a with block enters to reach the value.

Use it as the scope of a with header: with (var v = mutex.lock()). The lock is released when the guard is destroyed, which for a guard created in the header is the end of the block. A guard kept anywhere else holds the lock until its last reference is released.

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns the value, and destroying it unlocks

Panics

  • if the calling thread already holds the lock

Example

with (var account = accounts.lock()) {
    account.balance.fetch_add(10);
}

try_lock

try_lock(): MutexGuard<T>

Takes the lock only if no thread holds it right now, without waiting.

In with (var v = mutex.try_lock()) { ... } else { ... }, the body runs when the lock was taken and the else block runs when it was not. The calling thread already holding the lock counts as busy.

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns the value, or null when the lock was busy

Example

with (var account = accounts.try_lock()) {
    account.balance.fetch_add(10);
} else {
    print("busy; try later\n");
}

replace

replace([Move] value: T): T

Replaces the whole value and returns the one the Mutex held, which the caller then owns outright: nothing else references it any more.

Waits for the lock like lock(). value must be a new value, as for the constructor, and is handed over without a copy.

Parameters

  • value — the new value; a new value, which the compiler checks

Returns

  • the value the Mutex held

Panics

  • if the calling thread already holds the lock

Example

var done = pending.replace(Array<Job>());   # take every job at once

is_held

is_held(): bool

Reports whether the caller holds the lock: the calling task, in a task, or else the calling thread.

Returns

  • true between a lock() (or a successful try_lock()) by the caller and the guard's destruction

condition

condition(): Condition<T>

Returns a new condition variable that waits on this Mutex.

Create it once and share it, as the Mutex is shared: every thread that waits or notifies must use the same Condition.

Returns

  • a new Condition bound to this Mutex

Example

const queue = async.Mutex<Jobs>(Jobs());
const not_empty = queue.condition();

MutexGuard

[Isolated] struct MutexGuard<T>

The lock on a Mutex<T> that a with block holds: enter() returns the Mutex's value, and destroying the guard unlocks.

Get one from Mutex.lock() or Mutex.try_lock() in a with header. The block releases the guard on every path out, so the lock cannot be left held by mistake. A guard belongs to the thread that locked it; do not pass it to another thread.

A guard is [Isolated]: it can only be the scope of a with header, so the lock cannot be kept past the block, and the compiler checks the block with the confinement rule (see Mutex).

Type parameters

  • T — the protected value's type

Example

with (var totals = stats.lock()) {
    totals.requests.fetch_add(1);
}   # unlocked here

Fields

locked

bool locked

Whether the guard holds the lock: false once exit() has run, and for a try_lock() that found the lock busy.

Constructor

MutexGuard()

construct(source: Mutex<T>, wait: bool = true)

Locks source and creates the guard that holds it; the same as source.lock() (or source.try_lock() when wait is false).

Parameters

  • source — the Mutex to lock
  • wait — true to wait for the lock; false to take it only if it is free right now

Panics

  • if wait is true and the calling thread already holds the lock

Methods

enter

enter(): T

Returns the Mutex's value, for the with header to bind.

For a struct T the caller gets its own reference.

Returns

  • the protected value, or the default of T (null for a struct) when the guard does not hold the lock

exit

exit()

Unlocks the Mutex if the guard holds it. The destructor calls it; calling it again does nothing.

Condition

[Shared] struct Condition<T>

Lets threads that hold a Mutex sleep until another thread changes the Mutex's value, like C++ std::condition_variable. Get one from Mutex.condition().

wait() must run while the calling thread holds the Mutex, normally inside with (var v = mutex.lock()). It unlocks, sleeps until notified, and locks again before returning. A waiter can also wake without a notification (a spurious wakeup), so always wait in a loop that re-checks the value.

A thread that changes the value calls notify_one() or notify_all(), usually while it still holds the lock.

A Condition is [Shared], like its Mutex.

In a task (see run), wait() parks the task, not its worker thread. A cancel does not end it, since the caller's loop would only wait again; wait_for() still returns when its time runs out.

Type parameters

  • T — the Mutex's value type

Example

import async;

[Shared]
struct Jobs {
    const waiting: Atomic<long>;
    construct() { waiting = Atomic<long>(0); }
}

const jobs = async.Mutex<Jobs>(Jobs());
const has_work = jobs.condition();

take_job() {
    with (var j = jobs.lock()) {
        while (j.waiting.load() == 0) {
            has_work.wait();
        }
        j.waiting.fetch_sub(1);
    }
}

add_job() {
    with (var j = jobs.lock()) {
        j.waiting.fetch_add(1);
        has_work.notify_one();
    }
}

Constructor

Condition()

construct(mutex: Mutex<T>)

Creates a condition variable that waits on mutex. mutex.condition() does the same.

Parameters

  • mutex — the Mutex that waiters hold

Methods

wait

wait()

Unlocks the Mutex, sleeps until another thread calls notify_one() or notify_all(), and locks the Mutex again before returning.

The thread may also wake without being notified, so call it in a loop that re-checks what it waits for.

Panics

  • if the calling thread does not hold the Mutex

Example

with (var q = queue.lock()) {
    while (q.waiting.load() == 0) {
        not_empty.wait();
    }
}

wait_for

wait_for(milliseconds: ulong): bool

Like wait(), but gives up after about milliseconds milliseconds. The Mutex is locked again before it returns either way.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — the longest time to sleep

Returns

  • true if the thread was woken (by a notification or spuriously), false if the time ran out

Panics

  • if the calling thread does not hold the Mutex

wait_while

wait_while([Locked] predicate: (T) => bool)

Waits while predicate holds for the Mutex's value: calls it with the value, and while it returns true, waits as wait() does and asks again. Returns once it returns false, with the Mutex still locked.

Wakeups without a notification are handled here: the predicate is asked again after every wake.

predicate is written at the call, as a closure: the compiler checks its body as it checks a with block's, with its parameter as the locked value, so it cannot keep any part of the value or bring in a value from outside.

Parameters

  • predicate — called with the locked value; true to keep waiting

Panics

  • if the caller does not hold the Mutex

Example

with (var queue = jobs.lock()) {
    not_empty.wait_while((queue: Array<Job>): bool => queue.count == 0);
    var job = queue.remove_at(0);
}

wait_while_for

wait_while_for(milliseconds: ulong, [Locked] predicate: (T) => bool): bool

Like wait_while(), but gives up after about milliseconds milliseconds. The Mutex is locked when it returns either way.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — the longest time to wait
  • predicate — called with the locked value; true to keep waiting

Returns

  • true once predicate returned false, false if the time ran out first

Panics

  • if the caller does not hold the Mutex

notify_one

notify_one()

Wakes one thread or task waiting on this condition, if any. The caller does not need to hold the Mutex, but usually does, having just changed the value.

notify_all

notify_all()

Wakes every thread and task waiting on this condition. Each locks the Mutex in turn before its wait() returns.

Semaphore, Barrier and Latch

Coordination between threads: Semaphore bounds how many threads do something at once, Barrier makes a group of threads meet before any goes on, and Latch lets threads wait until a count of events has happened.

Source: runtime/async/coordination.pep

Semaphore

[Shared] struct Semaphore

A count of permits that threads take and give back, like Java's Semaphore or C++20 std::counting_semaphore: at most permits threads hold one at a time.

acquire() waits until a permit is free and takes it; release() gives one back. The usual form is a with block, which gives the permit back on every path out: with (semaphore.permit()) { ... }.

A Semaphore is [Shared]: keep it in a module-scope variable or pass it to threads. Permits are not tied to a thread: any thread may release a permit that another acquired, and release() may raise the count above where it started.

In a task (see run), waiting for a permit parks the task, not its worker thread.

Example

import async;

# At most two downloads at once.
const downloads = async.Semaphore(2);

download(url: String) {
    with (downloads.permit()) {
        # ... fetch url ...
    }
}

Constructor

Semaphore()

construct(permits: ulong)

Creates a Semaphore with permits free permits.

Parameters

  • permits — how many permits are free at first; 0 makes every acquire() wait for a release()

Methods

acquire

acquire()

Waits until a permit is free, and takes it.

Give it back with release(), or use permit() in a with block, which gives it back for you.

try_acquire

try_acquire(): bool

Takes a permit only if one is free right now, without waiting.

Returns

  • true if the caller now holds a permit, false if none was free

release

release()

Gives a permit back, waking one thread waiting in acquire() if any.

permit

permit(): SemaphorePermit

Waits until a permit is free, takes it, and returns a guard that gives it back when destroyed: at the end of with (semaphore.permit()) { ... } by any path.

Returns

  • the guard holding the permit

Example

with (connections.permit()) {
    serve(client);
}   # the permit is given back here

SemaphorePermit

struct SemaphorePermit

A permit taken from a Semaphore, given back when the guard is destroyed. Get one from Semaphore.permit() in a with header.

Example

with (var permit = pool.permit()) {
    # holds one of the pool's permits
}

Constructor

SemaphorePermit()

construct(semaphore: Semaphore)

Waits for a permit from semaphore and holds it; the same as semaphore.permit().

Parameters

  • semaphore — the Semaphore to take a permit from

Methods

enter

enter(): SemaphorePermit

Returns this guard, for the with header.

Returns

  • this permit

exit

exit()

Gives the permit back if it is still held. The destructor calls it; calling it again does nothing.

Barrier

[Shared] struct Barrier

A meeting point for a fixed number of threads, like Rust's std::sync::Barrier: each thread that calls wait() sleeps until count threads have called it, then all of them go on together.

Exactly one thread of each group, the leader, gets true from wait(), so it can do the work that must happen once per round. The barrier then resets, and the next count calls make the next round.

A Barrier is [Shared]. In a task (see run), wait() parks the task, not its worker thread; the other tasks of a round must then run on other workers or later on the same one.

Example

import async;

const step_done = async.Barrier(4);

work(id: long) {
    var step = 0;
    while (step < 10) {
        # ... this thread's share of the step ...
        if (step_done.wait()) {
            print($"step {step} done\n");   # once per step
        }
        step = step + 1;
    }
}

Constructor

Barrier()

construct(count: ulong)

Creates a barrier for groups of count threads.

Parameters

  • count — how many threads each round waits for; 0 counts as 1, so every wait() returns at once as the leader

Methods

wait

wait(): bool

Waits until count threads, this one included, have called wait() in this round.

Returns

  • true on exactly one thread of each round, the last to arrive; false on the others

Latch

[Shared] struct Latch

A one-shot countdown, like C++20 std::latch: threads wait until count_down() has been called count times. Once open it stays open.

Unlike a Barrier, the threads that count down need not wait, and the threads that wait need not count down: a typical use is a thread that starts workers and waits for each to report that it is ready.

A Latch is [Shared]. In a task (see run), wait() parks the task, not its worker thread.

Example

import async;

const ready = async.Latch(3);

worker() {
    # ... set up ...
    ready.count_down();
    # ... work ...
}

main(): int {
    var threads = Array<async.Thread>();
    var i = 0;
    while (i < 3) {
        threads.append(async.Thread.spawn(worker));
        i = i + 1;
    }
    ready.wait();   # every worker has set up
    for (var t in threads) {
        t.join();
    }
    return 0;
}

Constructor

Latch()

construct(count: ulong)

Creates a latch that opens after count calls to count_down().

Parameters

  • count — how many calls open it; 0 makes a latch that is open from the start

Methods

count_down

count_down()

Counts one event, and opens the latch, waking every waiter, if it was the last one.

Panics

  • if the latch is already open

wait

wait()

Waits until the latch is open. Returns at once if it already is.

is_ready

is_ready(): bool

Reports whether the latch is open, without waiting.

Returns

  • true once count_down() has been called count times

RwLock

Reader/writer locking: RwLock<T> owns a thread-safe value that many threads may read at once or one thread may write, with RwLockReadGuard<T> and RwLockWriteGuard<T> as the locks a with block holds.

Source: runtime/async/rwlock.pep

RwLock

[Shared] struct RwLock<T: Shared>

A thread-safe value that many threads may read at once or one thread may write, like Rust's RwLock<T> or C++ std::shared_mutex.

with (var v = lock.read()) { ... } waits until no writer holds or is waiting for the lock, then binds the value; any number of threads may be reading at once. with (var v = lock.write()) { ... } waits until no other thread holds the lock at all. Both unlock when the block ends by any path, and everything a writer did is visible to the threads that lock after it.

T must be thread-safe, as for Atomic<T>: typically a [Shared] struct whose Atomic fields a writer changes together, so readers never see them half changed. A value that is not thread-safe, such as an Array<String>, is a compile error: readers holding it at once would race on its reference counts. Use a Mutex<T> for such a value.

Writers come first: while a writer waits, new readers wait too, so readers cannot keep a writer out forever. A thread that already reads must not ask to read again, since a writer may be waiting between the two. Asking to write while holding the lock in either mode panics instead of deadlocking.

In a task (see run), waiting for the lock parks the task, not its worker thread.

Type parameters

  • T — the protected value's type, which must be thread-safe (T: Shared)

Example

import async;

[Shared]
struct Range {
    const low: Atomic<long>;
    const high: Atomic<long>;
    construct() {
        low = Atomic<long>(0);
        high = Atomic<long>(0);
    }
}

const range = async.RwLock<Range>(Range());

widen(by: long) {
    with (var r = range.write()) {
        r.low.fetch_sub(by);
        r.high.fetch_add(by);
    }
}

width(): long {
    with (var r = range.read()) {
        return r.high.load() - r.low.load();   # never half widened
    }
    return 0;
}

Constructor

RwLock()

construct(value: T)

Creates an unlocked RwLock holding value.

Parameters

  • value — the value to protect

Methods

read

read(): RwLockReadGuard<T>

Waits until no writer holds or waits for the lock, takes it for reading, and returns the guard that a with block enters to reach the value. Other threads may read at the same time.

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns the value, and destroying it unlocks

Panics

  • if the calling thread holds the lock for writing

Example

with (var config = settings.read()) {
    print($"{config.port.load()}\n");
}

try_read

try_read(): RwLockReadGuard<T>

Takes the lock for reading only if that needs no wait: no writer holds it or waits for it.

In with (var v = lock.try_read()) { ... } else { ... }, the body runs when the lock was taken and the else block runs when it was not.

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns the value, or null when the lock was not free for reading

write

write(): RwLockWriteGuard<T>

Waits until no other thread holds the lock, takes it for writing, and returns the guard that a with block enters to reach the value.

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns the value, and destroying it unlocks

Panics

  • if the calling thread already holds the lock for writing

Example

with (var config = settings.write()) {
    config.port.store(8080);
}

try_write

try_write(): RwLockWriteGuard<T>

Takes the lock for writing only if no thread holds it right now, without waiting.

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns the value, or null when the lock was busy

replace

replace(value: T): T

Replaces the whole value under the write lock and returns the one the RwLock held.

Parameters

  • value — the new value

Returns

  • the value the RwLock held

Panics

  • if the calling thread already holds the lock for writing

RwLockReadGuard

struct RwLockReadGuard<T: Shared>

The read lock on an RwLock<T> that a with block holds: enter() returns the value, and destroying the guard unlocks. Get one from RwLock.read() or RwLock.try_read() in a with header.

Type parameters

  • T — the protected value's type

Example

with (var stats = counters.read()) {
    total = stats.hits.load() + stats.misses.load();
}   # unlocked here

Fields

locked

bool locked

Whether the guard holds the lock: false once exit() has run, and for a try_read() that could not take it.

Constructor

RwLockReadGuard()

construct(source: RwLock<T>, wait: bool = true)

Takes source for reading and creates the guard that holds it; the same as source.read() (or source.try_read() when wait is false).

Parameters

  • source — the RwLock to lock
  • wait — true to wait for the lock; false to take it only if that needs no wait

Panics

  • if wait is true and the calling thread holds the lock for writing

Methods

enter

enter(): T

Returns the RwLock's value, for the with header to bind.

Returns

  • the protected value, or the default of T (null for a struct) when the guard does not hold the lock

exit

exit()

Unlocks if the guard holds the lock. The destructor calls it; calling it again does nothing.

RwLockWriteGuard

struct RwLockWriteGuard<T: Shared>

The write lock on an RwLock<T> that a with block holds: enter() returns the value, and destroying the guard unlocks. Get one from RwLock.write() or RwLock.try_write() in a with header.

Type parameters

  • T — the protected value's type

Example

with (var stats = counters.write()) {
    stats.hits.store(0);
    stats.misses.store(0);
}   # unlocked here

Fields

locked

bool locked

Whether the guard holds the lock: false once exit() has run, and for a try_write() that found the lock busy.

Constructor

RwLockWriteGuard()

construct(source: RwLock<T>, wait: bool = true)

Takes source for writing and creates the guard that holds it; the same as source.write() (or source.try_write() when wait is false).

Parameters

  • source — the RwLock to lock
  • wait — true to wait for the lock; false to take it only if it is free right now

Panics

  • if wait is true and the calling thread already holds the lock for writing

Methods

enter

enter(): T

Returns the RwLock's value, for the with header to bind.

Returns

  • the protected value, or the default of T (null for a struct) when the guard does not hold the lock

exit

exit()

Unlocks if the guard holds the lock. The destructor calls it; calling it again does nothing.

Once and Lazy

One-time initialization: Once runs a function exactly once however many threads ask, and Lazy<T> builds a value on first use.

Source: runtime/async/once.pep

Once

[Shared] struct Once

Runs a function exactly once, however many threads ask, like C++ std::call_once or Rust's std::sync::Once.

The first call runs its body. Callers that arrive while it runs wait for it to finish, and later callers return right away. Every caller sees everything the body did once call returns.

A Once is [Shared]: keep it in a module-scope variable or pass it to threads.

Example

import async;

const setup = async.Once();
const setups = Atomic<long>(0);

initialize() {
    setups.fetch_add(1);
}

work() {
    setup.call(initialize);   # only the first caller runs it
}

Constructor

Once()

construct()

Creates a Once whose body has not run.

Methods

call

call(body: ThreadBody)

Runs body if no call has run a body yet; otherwise waits until that run has finished. Everything the body did is visible to the caller when this returns.

Only one body ever runs, even if later calls pass different ones.

Parameters

  • body — the function to run once

Panics

  • if body itself calls call on the same Once (it would wait for itself forever)

Example

config_once.call(load_config);

is_done

is_done(): bool

Reports whether a body has finished running.

Returns

  • true once a call has completed its body on some thread

Lazy

[Shared] struct Lazy<T: Shared>

A value built on first use by whichever thread asks first, like Rust's LazyLock. The usual way to give a module-scope variable a value that is expensive to build, or that cannot be built before main runs.

The first get() runs the initializer; threads that call get() while it runs wait for it, and every later call returns the same value.

T is constrained Shared (a thread-safe type such as a number, a [Shared] struct, or a shared function type), because every thread gets the same value; Lazy<String> is a compile error.

Type parameters

  • T — the value's type, which must be thread-safe (T: Shared)

Example

import async;

[Shared]
struct Settings {
    const workers: long;
    construct(this.workers = 1) {}
}

load_settings(): Settings {
    return Settings(async.logical_cpus() as long);
}

const settings = async.Lazy<Settings>(load_settings);

main(): int {
    var workers = settings.get().workers;   # built here, on first use
    return 0;
}

Constructor

Lazy()

construct(initializer: shared () => T)

Creates a Lazy whose value initializer builds on the first get(). Nothing runs yet.

Parameters

  • initializer — builds the value; runs at most once, on the thread that first calls get()

Methods

get

get(): T

Returns the value, building it with the initializer on the first call.

For a struct T the caller gets its own reference.

Returns

  • the value the initializer built

Panics

  • if the initializer itself calls get() on the same Lazy

is_built

is_built(): bool

Reports whether the value has been built.

Returns

  • true once a get() has finished running the initializer

Channel

Channels: Channel<T> carries values from threads that send to threads that receive, and ChannelIterator<T> receives in a for loop.

Source: runtime/async/channel.pep

Channel

[Shared] struct Channel<T>

A queue that carries values from threads that send to threads that receive, like Go channels or Rust's mpsc, with any number of each.

Values arrive in the order they were sent (from any one sender). A bounded channel holds at most capacity values, and send waits while it is full; Channel<T>(0), the default, is unbounded and send never waits.

close() ends the stream: later sends fail, and receivers take what is left and then get an error. Only close() closes a channel; dropping it or the threads that use it does not. for (var v in channel) receives until the channel is closed and empty.

send takes a new value, which nothing on the sending thread references, and hands it to the receiver without copying it: a constructor call, a literal, a call that returns a fresh value, move(x) (a variable that holds the only reference) or copy(x) (a copy, when the sender keeps using x). Sending a variable that something else still references is a compile error. A thread-safe value (a number, a [Shared] struct, a shared function value such as a ThreadBody) passes freely.

A Channel is [Shared]: keep it in a module-scope variable or pass it to threads.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the values carried

Example

import async;

const jobs = async.Channel<long>(64);
const total = Atomic<long>(0);

worker() {
    for (var job in jobs) {
        total.fetch_add(job);
    }
}

main(): int {
    var thread = async.Thread.spawn(worker);
    jobs.send(20);
    jobs.send(22);
    jobs.close();
    thread.join();
    assert(total.load() == 42, "the worker received both jobs");
    return 0;
}

Properties

count

var count: ulong { get; }

The number of values waiting to be received. Other threads may change it as soon as it returns.

Constructor

Channel()

construct(capacity: ulong = 0)

Creates an open, empty channel.

Parameters

  • capacity — how many values may wait before send blocks; 0 (the default) for no limit

Example

var bounded = async.Channel<long>(16);
var unbounded = async.Channel<long>();

Methods

send

send([Move] value: T): bool

Queues value, first waiting while a bounded channel is full.

value must be a new value: nothing else may reference it. The caller hands its reference over and the value itself is queued, with no copy. Pass move(x) to send a variable's value, or copy(x) to keep using x.

In a task (see run), waiting parks the task and its worker runs other tasks; a cancel or the task's timeout ends the wait.

Parameters

  • value — the value to send; a new value, which the compiler checks

Returns

  • true if the value was queued, false if the channel is closed or the task's wait was cancelled or timed out (the value is dropped)

Example

var line = "hello";
lines.send(copy(line));
line.append(" again");   # the receiver still gets "hello"
lines.send(move(line));   # line is null now

try_send

try_send([Move] value: T): bool

Queues value only if there is room right now, without waiting. The value is dropped when it is not queued.

Parameters

  • value — the value to send; a new value, as for send

Returns

  • true if the value was queued, false if the channel is full or closed

receive

receive(): Result<T>

Takes the next value, waiting until one arrives.

In a task (see run), waiting parks the task and its worker runs other tasks; a cancel or the task's timeout ends the wait.

Returns

  • the value, or an error once the channel is closed and empty, or when the task's wait was cancelled or timed out

Example

var job = jobs.receive();
if (job.is_ok()) {
    run(job.value());
}

try_receive

try_receive(): Result<T>

Takes the next value if one is waiting, without waiting.

Returns

  • the value, or an error if none is waiting (see is_closed() to tell an empty channel from a closed one)

receive_for

receive_for(milliseconds: ulong): Result<T>

Like receive(), but gives up after about milliseconds milliseconds.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — the longest time to wait

Returns

  • the value, or an error if the time ran out, once the channel is closed and empty, or when the task's wait was cancelled

close

close()

Closes the channel and wakes every waiting sender and receiver.

Later sends fail. Values already queued stay, and receivers still get them; after the last one, receive() returns an error and for loops end. Closing a closed channel does nothing.

is_closed

is_closed(): bool

Reports whether close() has been called.

Returns

  • true once the channel is closed, even while values are still queued

iterate

iterate(): ChannelIterator<T>

Returns an iterator that receives until the channel is closed and empty. A for loop over the channel calls it.

Several threads may loop over one channel at once; each value goes to exactly one of them.

Returns

  • the iterator a for loop drives

Example

for (var line in lines) {
    print(line, "\n");
}   # ends once `lines` is closed and empty

ChannelIterator

[Value] struct ChannelIterator<T>

Receives from a Channel<T> in a for loop: next() waits for the next value and returns false once the channel is closed and empty.

Channel.iterate() returns one; a for loop over a channel uses it without naming it. It belongs to the thread that runs the loop.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the values carried

Example

var values = jobs.iterate();
while (values.next()) {
    total = total + values.current();
}

Constructor

ChannelIterator()

construct(source: Channel<T>)

Creates an iterator that receives from source. source.iterate() does the same.

Parameters

  • source — the channel to receive from

Methods

next

next(): bool

Waits for the next value.

Returns

  • true if a value arrived (read it with current()), false once the channel is closed and empty

current

current(): T

Returns the value the last successful next() received.

Returns

  • the current value

Select

Waiting on several channels at once: Select<E> takes the first value any of them receives, or sends a value to the first that has room, and turns what happened into a case of your own enum, which a match then handles.

Source: runtime/async/select.pep

Select

struct Select<E>

Waits on several channels at once and takes the first value any of them receives, or sends to the first that has room, like Go's select.

Each channel to receive from is added with receive(channel, wrap), where wrap turns one of its values into an E, usually a case of an enum of your own that carries it. A value to send is added with send(channel, value, sent), where sent returns the E that says it was sent. wait() then fires whichever arm is ready first and returns its E, for a match to handle. The channels may carry different types.

  • The value is taken under the channel's own lock, so no other receiver can take it between "ready" and "take".
  • A send arm's value goes into its channel only when that arm fires; until then the select holds it. Once sent, the arm leaves the select, so the next wait() does not send it again. A value never sent is dropped with the select.
  • When several channels have values, each wait starts after the channel that fired last, so a busy channel cannot starve the others.
  • A channel that is closed and empty is skipped, and so is a send arm whose channel is closed. Once every arm is, wait() returns an error.
  • In a task (see run), waiting parks the task and its worker runs other tasks; a cancel or the task's timeout ends the wait.

A Select is not [Shared]: use it from the thread (or task) that made it.

Type parameters

  • E — the type every channel's values are turned into

Example

enum Event {
    Job(job: Job),
    Tick(count: long),
    Stop,
}

var select = async.Select<Event>();
select.receive(jobs, (job: Job): Event => Event.Job(job));
select.receive(ticks, (count: long): Event => Event.Tick(count));
select.receive(quit, (stop: bool): Event => Event.Stop);
var running = true;
while (running) {
    match (select.wait()) {
        Ok(event) => {
            match (event) {
                Job(job) => { run(job); }
                Tick(count) => { report(count); }
                Stop => { running = false; }
            }
        }
        Err(error) => { running = false; }   # every channel closed
    }
}

Constructor

Select()

construct()

Creates a select with no channels yet.

Methods

receive

receive<T>(channel: Channel<T>, wrap: (T) => E)

Adds channel: its values, turned into an E by wrap, are among those wait() returns.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the channel's values

Parameters

  • channel — the channel to receive from
  • wrap — turns a value received from channel into an E; it runs on the waiting thread

Example

select.receive(lines, (line: String): Event => Event.Line(line));

send

send<T>(channel: Channel<T>, [Move] value: T, sent: () => E)

Adds a send arm: wait() sends value to channel once the channel has room (a bounded channel that is full waits), and returns what sent returns.

value must be a new value, as for Channel.send: the select holds it and moves it into the channel only when this arm fires, so it is never sent if another arm fires first. Once sent, the arm leaves the select. A send arm whose channel is closed never fires, and its value is dropped with the select.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the channel's values

Parameters

  • channel — the channel to send to
  • value — the value to send; a new value, which the compiler checks
  • sent — returns the E that wait() returns once the value is sent; it runs on the waiting thread

Example

select.send(results, copy(line), (): Event => Event.Sent);

wait

wait(): Result<E>

Fires the first arm that is ready, waiting until one is: takes the next value any of the channels receives, or sends a send arm's value to a channel with room.

Returns

  • the arm's E (the value received, turned into an E, or what a send arm's sent returned); or an error once every channel is closed (and empty, for a receive arm), when the select has no arms, or when the task's wait was cancelled or timed out

wait_for

wait_for(milliseconds: ulong): Result<E>

Like wait(), but gives up after about milliseconds milliseconds.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — the longest time to wait

Returns

  • the arm's E, as for wait(); or an error if the time ran out, once every channel is closed (and empty, for a receive arm), or when the task's wait was cancelled

try_wait

try_wait(): Result<E>

Fires an arm if one is ready now, without waiting: takes a value if a channel has one waiting, or sends a send arm's value if its channel has room.

Returns

  • the arm's E, as for wait(); or an error if no arm is ready, or once every channel is closed (and empty, for a receive arm)

Processor counts

Processor counts.

Source: runtime/async/cpus.pep

logical_cpus

logical_cpus(): ulong

Returns the number of logical processors the operating system can run threads on: every hardware thread, so a core with hyperthreading (SMT) counts two or more times.

This is the upper bound on how many threads can run at the same moment, and a sensible default size for a pool of CPU-bound worker threads. Inside a virtual machine it counts the processors the guest sees. On Linux, a CPU quota on the process's cgroup or any cgroup above it (cgroup v2's cpu.max, or v1's cpu.cfs_quota_us over cpu.cfs_period_us, as docker run --cpus sets) caps the count, rounded up to whole processors, as Go and the JVM do: a quota of 1.5 processors counts as 2.

Returns

  • the number of logical processors, at least 1

See also

  • physical_cpus

Example

import async;

main(): int {
    print(async.logical_cpus(), " logical processors\n");
    return 0;
}

physical_cpus

physical_cpus(): ulong

Returns the number of physical processor cores: hardware threads that share a core through hyperthreading (SMT) count once.

On Linux the count comes from the kernel's CPU topology (/sys/devices/system/cpu), on macOS from hw.physicalcpu, and on Windows from GetLogicalProcessorInformationEx. Inside a virtual machine the guest cannot see the host's hardware, so this counts the cores the hypervisor presents. Where the topology is not available, it returns logical_cpus().

Returns

  • the number of physical cores, at least 1 and at most logical_cpus()

See also

  • logical_cpus

Tasks

Tasks: functions that run concurrently on a few worker threads, each on its own small stack, switching only where they wait.

run(body) turns the calling thread into the first worker, starts the others, and runs body as the first task. A task starts others with Task<T>.spawn_local (on its own worker) or spawn (on any worker), and gives its worker to the other tasks there whenever it waits: sleep, yield_now, and Task.join, whenever a socket call would block, and whenever it waits on a Mutex, Condition or Channel. Nothing preempts a task, so a task that computes for a long time without waiting keeps every other task on its worker waiting too.

A task is a green thread (a fiber): an ordinary function with its own stack, so code that waits looks the same as code that does not, and a function called in a task can wait without being marked in any way.

Source: runtime/async/task.pep

RuntimeOptions

struct RuntimeOptions

Settings for run_with, built by chaining: RuntimeOptions().stack_size(65536).

Constructor

RuntimeOptions()

construct()

Creates the default options: one worker per logical CPU, 256 KiB of stack per task, the system's best I/O backend, and up to 64 threads for run_blocking.

Methods

workers

workers(count: ulong): RuntimeOptions

Sets how many workers (threads that run tasks) the runtime has. The thread that calls run_with is the first; the rest are new threads. Tasks from spawn_local run on the worker that started them; tasks from spawn run on whichever worker is free. The default is logical_cpus().

Parameters

Returns

Panics

blocking_threads

blocking_threads(count: ulong): RuntimeOptions

Sets how many threads run_blocking may start. The runtime starts them one at a time, when a blocking call finds none idle, and keeps them until run_with returns. Once there are count, further calls wait for one of them to be free. The default is 64.

Parameters

Returns

Panics

backend

Sets which I/O backend the runtime waits on sockets with. The default, Backend.Automatic, picks the system's best (or the one the PEPPER_IO_BACKEND environment variable names).

Parameters

Returns

  • these options

Note

  • run_with panics if the system does not have the backend

stack_size

stack_size(bytes: ulong): RuntimeOptions

Sets how much stack each task reserves. Only the pages a task touches use memory; the rest is address space. A task that uses more than this crashes the program, as a thread that overflows its stack does.

Parameters

Returns

Panics

Task

struct Task<T>

A task started with spawn_local or spawn, and the value its body returns.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the body's result; void when there is none

Example

import async;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var a = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => { return 20; });
        var b = async.Task<int>.spawn_local(() => { return 22; });
        print(a.join().value() + b.join().value());   # 42
    });
    return 0;
}

Constructor

Task()

construct(core: _TaskCore)

Wraps the scheduler's record of a task. Only spawn_local and spawn have one; start tasks with those.

Parameters

  • core — the scheduler's record of the task

Static methods

spawn_local

static spawn_local(body: () => T): Task<T>

Starts a task on the current worker that runs body. It runs the next time the running task waits, and may use anything the running task can, since it stays on this thread.

Parameters

  • body — the task's code

Returns

  • the task

Panics

  • outside run

Methods

join

join(): Result<T, TaskError>

Waits for the task to finish and returns its value. Other tasks run meanwhile.

Returns

  • the body's result, or a TaskError if the task was cancelled before it finished, the task calling join was cancelled while it waited, or a timeout around the join expired first

Panics

  • if a task joins itself, or if called outside run on a task that has not finished

cancel

cancel()

Asks the task to stop: from now on is_cancelled() is true inside it, sleep returns at once, and its join calls fail. A task is never stopped by force; it finishes when its body returns.

is_finished

is_finished(): bool

Returns whether the task's body has returned.

Returns

  • true once the task has finished

run

run(body: () => void)

Runs body as the first task of a new runtime, and returns once body has returned and every task it started has finished. The calling thread is the first worker; the runtime starts one more thread per logical CPU after it (see RuntimeOptions.workers). When body returns, the tasks still running are cancelled (see Task.cancel), on every worker, and run waits for them to finish.

Parameters

  • body — the first task

Panics

  • if called inside a task, or if every remaining task is waiting on another and none can continue

Example

import async;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var t = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            async.sleep(10);
            print("second");
        });
        print("first");
        t.join();
    });
    return 0;
}

run_with

run_with(options: RuntimeOptions, body: () => void)

Runs body like run, with the given settings.

Parameters

  • options — the runtime's settings
  • body — the first task

Panics

  • if called inside a task, if every remaining task is waiting on another and none can continue, or if the system does not have the backend options asks for

spawn

spawn<T: Shared>(body: shared () => T): Task<T>

Starts a task that runs body on whichever worker is free first, and returns it. Unlike Task<T>.spawn_local, the task may run on another thread, in parallel with the calling task, so the body must be a shared function (it may capture only thread-safe values) and its result crosses threads, so T is constrained Shared: a thread-safe type such as a number, a [Shared] struct, or a shared function type (spawn<String> is a compile error at String).

A task, once started, stays on the worker that started it. Joining and cancelling work as for spawn_local.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the body's result, which must be thread-safe (T: Shared); void when there is none

Parameters

  • body — the task's code

Returns

  • the task

Panics

  • outside run

Example

import async;

sum(from: long, to: long): long {
    var total: long = 0;
    var i = from;
    while (i < to) {
        total = total + i;
        i = i + 1;
    }
    return total;
}

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var low = async.spawn<long>(() => { return sum(0, 500000); });
        var high = async.spawn<long>(() => { return sum(500000, 1000000); });
        print(low.join().value() + high.join().value());   # 499999500000
    });
    return 0;
}

spawn_on_each_worker

spawn_on_each_worker(body: shared () => void): Array<Task<void>>

Starts one task on every worker, each running body, and returns them in worker order. Use it to give each worker its own copy of a loop, such as a server's accept loop on an io.SharedTcpListener, so that every worker takes part. Each task runs on its own worker, the calling task's worker included; they are otherwise like tasks from spawn, and body must be a shared function.

Parameters

  • body — the code each worker runs

Returns

  • one task per worker, the first on the first worker

Panics

  • outside run

Example

import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.SharedTcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("0.0.0.0:7000").value()).value();
        var loops = async.spawn_on_each_worker(() => {
            while (true) {
                var accepted = listener.accept();
                if (accepted.is_err()) {
                    return;
                }
                var (stream, peer) = accepted.value();
                async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
                    stream.write_all("hello");
                });
            }
        });
        for (var loop in loops) {
            loop.join();
        }
    });
    return 0;
}

run_blocking

run_blocking<T: Shared>(body: shared () => T): T

Runs body on a separate thread and returns what it returns, parking the calling task meanwhile so the worker keeps running other tasks. Use it for work that would otherwise hold the worker up: a call that blocks in the operating system (reading a file, resolving a host name, a C library that waits) or a long computation.

The runtime keeps a pool of threads for these calls, started as needed up to RuntimeOptions.blocking_threads. body runs on one of them, so it must be a shared function and T is constrained Shared, as for spawn. On a pool thread, sockets block the thread, and sleep and the other task functions behave as outside run.

body always runs to the end: cancelling the calling task, or a timeout around the call expiring, takes effect once run_blocking has returned. Outside a task, run_blocking just calls body.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the body's result, which must be thread-safe (T: Shared); void when there is none

Parameters

  • body — the blocking code

Returns

  • what body returns

Example

import async;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var ticker = async.Task<void>.spawn_local(() => {
            async.sleep(10);
            print("the worker kept running");
        });
        var answer = async.run_blocking<int>(() => {
            async.Thread.sleep(50);   # blocks a pool thread, not the worker
            return 42;
        });
        print(answer);
        ticker.join();
    });
    return 0;
}

yield_now

yield_now()

Lets every other ready task run before the calling task continues. Does nothing outside a task.

sleep

sleep(milliseconds: ulong)

Waits at least milliseconds. In a task, other tasks run meanwhile, and a cancelled task returns at once, as does one whose timeout expires first; outside a task, the thread sleeps.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — how long to wait

sleep

sleep(duration: os.Duration)

Waits at least duration, the same as sleep(milliseconds). A duration that is not a whole number of milliseconds rounds up, so the wait is never shorter than asked.

Parameters

  • duration — how long to wait

Example

async.sleep(os.Duration.from_seconds(1));

is_cancelled

is_cancelled(): bool

Returns whether the running task has been cancelled (see Task.cancel), so a long computation can stop early. False outside a task.

Returns

  • true when the running task was asked to stop

Deadline

struct Deadline

A time limit on the waits inside a with block, made by timeout.

While the block runs, a socket call that has to wait fails with an IoError for which is_timed_out() holds once the limit passes, Task.join fails with a TaskError for which is_timed_out() holds, and sleep returns early. Code that does not wait is never interrupted. Timeouts nest: an inner one cannot extend an outer one.

Constructor

Deadline()

construct(milliseconds: ulong)

Creates a limit milliseconds from now. Use timeout instead.

Parameters

  • milliseconds — how long from now the limit passes

Methods

enter

enter(): Deadline

Starts applying the limit to the running task; a with block calls it.

Returns

  • this deadline

Panics

  • outside a task

exit

exit()

Stops applying the limit; the end of the with block calls it.

is_expired

is_expired(): bool

Returns whether the limit has passed.

Returns

  • true once the time is up

timeout

timeout(milliseconds: ulong): Deadline

Returns a time limit for a with block: the waits inside it give up milliseconds from now (see Deadline).

Parameters

  • milliseconds — how long the block's waits may take in all

Returns

  • the limit, for a with header

Example

import async;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        with (var deadline = async.timeout(50)) {
            var accepted = listener.accept();   # nobody connects
            assert(accepted.error().is_timed_out(), "timed out");
        }
    });
    return 0;
}

current_backend

current_backend(): Backend

Returns the I/O backend the running runtime waits on sockets with (see RuntimeOptions.backend).

Returns

  • the backend; never Backend.Automatic

Panics

  • outside run

TaskLocal

Per-task values: TaskLocal<T> gives every task its own copy of a variable.

Source: runtime/async/task_local.pep

TaskLocal

[Shared] struct TaskLocal<T>

A variable with a separate value in every task, the task counterpart of ThreadLocal<T>.

Each task that calls set stores its own value, which is released when the task finishes. A task starts with no value, including one started by a task that has one: values are not inherited. Tasks that take turns on one worker thread each see their own value, which a ThreadLocal cannot give them.

Code that does not run in a task (before async.run, or on a plain Thread) has one value per thread, as with a ThreadLocal.

For a thread-safe T (a number, a [Shared] struct), get returns the calling task's value (the default of T, zero or null, until it sets one). For any other T, such as a String, the value is reached through a with block, with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }, and get is a compile error; set then takes a new value (a constructor call, a string literal, copy(x)).

A TaskLocal is [Shared], so one object can be used from every task and thread; it is usually a module-scope variable. Destroying one releases only the caller's value, so destroy it only after the tasks that used it have finished.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the per-task value

See also

  • ThreadLocal

Example

import async;

const request_id = async.TaskLocal<long>();

handle(id: long) {
    request_id.set(id);
    async.yield_now();   # the other tasks run meanwhile
    assert(request_id.get() == id, "still this task's id");
}

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var tasks = Array<async.Task<void>>();
        for (var id in [1, 2, 3]) {
            tasks.append(async.spawn<void>(() => {
                handle(id);
            }));
        }
        for (var task in tasks) {
            task.join();
        }
    });
    return 0;
}

Constructor

TaskLocal()

construct()

Creates a task-local variable. No task has a value yet.

Panics

  • if the operating system has no thread-local keys left

Methods

get

get(): T

Returns the calling task's value.

For a struct T the caller gets its own reference. Only for a thread-safe T: for any other T, use with (var value = local.enter()).

Returns

  • the value this task last stored, or the default of T (zero or null) if it has not stored one

set

set([Move] value: T)

Stores value as the calling task's value, replacing (and, for a struct T, releasing) the one it held. Other tasks' values are not affected.

For a T that is not thread-safe, value must be a new value (a constructor call, a string literal, copy(x)), which the compiler checks.

Parameters

  • value — the new value for this task

enter

enter(): TaskLocalGuard<T>

Returns the guard that a with block enters to reach the calling task's value: with (var value = local.enter()) { ... }. The body runs with the value bound; the else block runs when this task has no value (for a struct T).

Returns

  • the guard; its enter() returns this task's value

Example

const trail = async.TaskLocal<Array<String>>();

note(step: String) {
    if (!trail.is_set()) {
        trail.set(Array<String>());
    }
    with (var steps = trail.enter()) {
        steps.append(step.copy());
    }
}

is_set

is_set(): bool

Reports whether the calling task has stored a value since it started or last called clear().

Returns

  • true if this task has a value

clear

clear()

Removes the calling task's value, releasing it for a struct T. get() returns the default of T afterwards.

TaskLocalGuard

[Isolated] struct TaskLocalGuard<T>

The access to a task's TaskLocal<T> value that a with block holds: enter() returns the value. Get one from TaskLocal.enter().

A guard is [Isolated]: it can only be the scope of a with header, and the compiler checks the block with the confinement rule (see Mutex).

Type parameters

Constructor

Creates the guard for the calling task's value of local; the same as local.enter().

Parameters

Methods

enter(): T

Returns the calling task's value, for the with header to bind.

Returns

  • this task's value, or the default of T (null for a struct) when it has none

exit

exit()

Does nothing: the value stays with the task.

I/O backends

I/O backends: how a task runtime waits for sockets.

Source: runtime/async/driver.pep

Backend

enum Backend

The I/O backend a runtime waits on sockets with (see RuntimeOptions.backend).

Cases

Automatic

Automatic

The best one the system has: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows. The PEPPER_IO_BACKEND environment variable (epoll, io_uring, kqueue, iocp or poll) picks another.

Epoll

Epoll

Linux's epoll, edge-triggered.

IoUring

IoUring

Linux's io_uring (kernel 5.11 or later), waiting for sockets with one multishot poll request each. Not the default: container seccomp profiles and hardened kernels often refuse it.

Kqueue

Kqueue

The BSD and macOS kqueue, edge-triggered.

Iocp

Iocp

A Windows I/O completion port, fed readiness by AFD poll requests.

Poll

Poll

poll() (WSAPoll on Windows): available everywhere, but each wait passes every waiting socket to the system, so it suits few connections. The reference the others are tested against.

The process module

Child processes, and what belongs to the running one, modeled on Rust's std::process.

process is a module: bring it in with import process (and write process.Command) or import names directly with import [Command, Stream] from process. arguments() and exit() stay in the prelude, and the module passes them on as well.

  • Command: Command describes a program to start; run() waits for it and collects its output, spawn() starts it and returns a Child, and exec() runs it in place of the running program
  • Child: a running child process, its piped streams, and its ExitStatus
  • The running process: id(), executable_path(), and fork(), which starts a copy of it
  • Finding programs: find_executable() looks a program up on the PATH, find_companion() looks beside the running program first, and is_executable() checks a file
  • Signals: signals() returns a channel that receives Ctrl-C, a request to terminate or a hangup, for a clean shutdown

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var output = process.Command("git").argument("--version").run();
    if (output.is_err()) {
        print("git is not installed");
        return 1;
    }
    print(output.value().stdout);
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/process/module.pep

Command

Starting a program: Command names it and its arguments, environment, working directory and standard streams; spawn() starts it and run() also waits for it and collects what it wrote.

Source: runtime/process/command.pep

Stream

enum Stream

Where a child's standard input, output or error goes (see Command.stdin, Command.stdout and Command.stderr).

Cases

Inherit

Inherit

The child shares the parent's stream: it reads the parent's input, or writes where the parent writes.

Pipe

Pipe

A pipe connects the stream to the parent, which reaches it through Child.stdin(), Child.stdout() or Child.stderr().

Null

Null

The stream is the null device: reading it finds the end at once, and what is written to it is thrown away.

Output

struct Output

What a program Command.run() waited for left behind: how it ended and what it wrote.

Fields

status

var status: ExitStatus

How the program ended.

stdout

var stdout: String

Everything the program wrote to standard output, decoded as UTF-8 (each byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD); empty when standard output was not piped.

stderr

var stderr: String

Everything the program wrote to standard error, decoded the same way; empty when standard error was not piped.

Constructor

Output()

construct(status: ExitStatus, stdout: String, stderr: String)

Creates an Output from its parts.

Parameters

  • status — how the program ended
  • stdout — what it wrote to standard output
  • stderr — what it wrote to standard error

Command

struct Command

Describes a program to start: the program, its arguments, its environment, its working directory, and where its standard streams go.

A builder in the style of Rust's std::process::Command: each setter stores its value and returns this same Command, so calls chain, and one Command can start the program any number of times.

The program is found the way a shell finds it: a name with no path separator is searched for on the PATH (on Windows, also in the directory of the running program and the system directories, and .exe is added when the name has no extension); anything else is a path, relative to the parent's current directory.

The child inherits the parent's environment, changed by environment, remove_environment and clear_environment. By default it also inherits the parent's current directory and its three standard streams; run() instead pipes standard output and error, and gives standard input the null device, unless they were set.

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var output = process.Command("clang").arguments(["--version"]).run().value();
    if (!output.status.success()) {
        print(output.stderr);
        return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

Fields

program

var program: String

The program to start, as given to the constructor.
