Adds one argument after those already added. It reaches the program as one element of its arguments, whatever it holds: no shell splits or expands it. On Windows, where a program receives one command line, it is quoted so that the C runtime splits it back out as it was.

spawn

spawn(): io.IoResult<Child>

Starts the program and returns at once, without waiting for it.

Each stream that was not set is inherited. A piped stream is reached through the Child; close a piped standard input when done writing, or a child that reads to the end never finishes. Wait for the child with Child.wait(): a child that is never waited for stays in the process table until the parent ends.

Returns

  • the running child; an error when the program cannot be started: is_not_found() when it is not found, is_permission_denied() when it is not executable, or another platform error

Example

var child = process.Command("sort").stdin(process.Stream.Pipe).stdout(process.Stream.Pipe).spawn().value();
child.stdin().write_all("pear\napple\n");
child.stdin().close();
var sorted = child.stdout().read_string().value();   # "apple\npear\n"
child.wait();

run

run(): io.IoResult<Output>

Starts the program, waits for it to end, and returns how it ended with what it wrote.

Standard output and error are piped and collected unless they were set, and standard input is the null device unless it was set. Both outputs are read at once, so a child that fills one pipe while the parent reads the other does not stall. In a task, the reads and the wait park the task rather than blocking its worker.

Returns

  • the exit status and output; an error when the program cannot be started (as for spawn()) or its output cannot be read

Example

var output = process.Command("echo").argument("hello").run().value();
assert(output.status.success(), "echo succeeds");
assert(output.stdout == "hello\n", "and prints its argument");

exec

exec(): io.IoError

Replaces the running program with this one, as a shell's exec does: the program receives this process's signals, and its exit status becomes this process's own. A launcher that only hands its command line on to another program, such as pepper, ends this way.

On POSIX the program takes over this process (execvp): it keeps the process id, the standard streams and every other descriptor not marked close-on-exec, and nothing after the call runs. Windows cannot replace a process, so there the program is started with the standard streams inherited and waited for, and this process then ends with its exit status, running no atexit handler, as a replaced process does not. While it waits, this process ignores Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break, which the program, sharing the console, receives and handles itself.

Output print has buffered is flushed first. The standard streams must be left inherited: no process remains to hold a pipe's other end. When the call fails, the process carries on unchanged, in its own working directory.

Returns

  • only when the program cannot be started: why, as for spawn(), or an error with is_invalid_input() when a standard stream was set to something other than Stream.Inherit

Example

import process;

main(args: String[]): int {
    # Run git with this program's arguments, as if it were git.
    var git = process.Command("git");
    ulong index = 1;
    while (index < args.count) {
        git.argument(args[index]);
        index += 1;
    }
    var error = git.exec();
    print($"cannot run git: {error.message}");
    return 1;
}

Child

A running child process (Child), the pipes to it, and how it ended (ExitStatus).

Source: runtime/process/child.pep

ExitStatus

struct ExitStatus

How a child process ended: with an exit code, or (on POSIX) killed by a signal.

Example

var status = process.Command("false").run().value().status;
assert(!status.success(), "false fails");
assert(status.code().value() == 1, "with code 1");

Constructor

ExitStatus()

construct(code: int = 0, signal: int = 0)

Creates an ExitStatus.

Parameters

  • code — the exit code, when the process exited
  • signal — the signal that ended the process, or 0 when it exited

Methods

success

success(): bool

Returns whether the process exited with code 0.

Returns

  • true for exit code 0

code

code(): int?

Returns the exit code: the value the process passed to exit or returned from main. On POSIX only its low 8 bits reach the parent, so it is from 0 to 255; on Windows it is the whole 32-bit code (an unhandled exception gives an NTSTATUS such as 0xC0000005, a negative number here).

Returns

  • the exit code, or none when a signal ended the process

signal

signal(): int?

Returns the signal that ended the process (POSIX only; a Windows process always has an exit code).

Returns

  • the signal number, such as 9 for SIGKILL, or none when the process exited

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns how the process ended as text.

Returns

  • exit code N or signal N

Child

[NotCopyable("owns a child process handle and cannot be copied")] struct Child

A child process started by Command.spawn(): its id, the pipes to the streams that were piped, and its exit status once it ends.

Wait for every child with wait() (or until try_wait() returns a status): on POSIX a child that ended but was never waited for stays in the process table until the parent ends. Releasing the last reference to a Child neither waits for it nor kills it; the process runs on.

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var child = process.Command("sleep").argument("10").spawn().value();
    child.kill();
    var status = child.wait().value();
    assert(!status.success(), "killed");
    return 0;
}

Constructor

Child()

construct()

Creates a Child that stands for no process: id() is 0, its streams are closed, and wait(), try_wait() and kill() fail. Use Command.spawn() to start one.

Methods

id

id(): ulong

Returns the child's process id, as the operating system knows it. After the child has been waited for, the system may give the id to a new process.

Returns

  • the process id

stdin

stdin(): io.File

Returns the pipe to the child's standard input, for writing. Close it when done (close()), so that a child reading to the end sees the end.

Returns

  • the pipe, or a closed File when standard input was not Stream.Pipe

stdout

stdout(): io.File

Returns the pipe from the child's standard output, for reading. A read returns 0 once the child has ended (or closed its standard output) and everything it wrote has been read.

Returns

  • the pipe, or a closed File when standard output was not Stream.Pipe

stderr

stderr(): io.File

Returns the pipe from the child's standard error, for reading.

Returns

  • the pipe, or a closed File when standard error was not Stream.Pipe

wait

wait(): io.IoResult<ExitStatus>

Waits for the child to end and returns how it ended. Standard input, when piped, is closed first, so a child reading it to the end can finish. Waiting again returns the same status.

In a task, the wait parks the task (it runs on a run_blocking thread) rather than blocking its worker. Read piped output before waiting: a child stalls when a pipe it writes to is full.

Returns

  • the exit status, or an error from the system

try_wait

try_wait(): io.IoResult<ExitStatus?>

Returns how the child ended if it has, without waiting.

Returns

  • the exit status, or none while the child runs; or an error from the system

kill

kill(): io.IoResult<void>

Ends the child at once: SIGKILL on POSIX, TerminateProcess (with exit code 1) on Windows. The child still has to be waited for. Killing a child that has already been waited for does nothing.

Returns

  • Ok, or an error from the system

The running process

The running process: its arguments, id, executable and working directory, and how it ends.

Two functions are listed only here, since the module exports them under names the deprecated prelude functions still hold:

  • arguments(): Array<String> returns the program's command-line arguments: element 0 is the program as it was started, and the arguments typed after it follow in order. main receives the same array when it is declared main(args: String[]): int. On Windows they are read as UTF-16 and converted to valid UTF-8.
  • exit(code: int) ends the program at once with status code (only its low 8 bits reach a POSIX parent), as C's exit does: the handlers registered with C's atexit run, then standard output and the other C output streams are flushed. Locals are not released and destructors do not run; other threads keep running while the handlers run. In a copy fork() started, the handlers, which are the parent's, are skipped.

Source: runtime/process/current.pep

fork

fork(): io.IoResult<Child?>

Starts a copy of the running process (POSIX fork): the copy has the same memory, open files and code, and both go on from here. In the parent, returns the copy as a Child to wait for; in the copy, returns none. The copy has only the calling thread, so fork before starting threads or tasks, and end the copy with exit(), which there skips the parent's atexit handlers.

The C standard streams are flushed first, so what print buffered is written once. Not on Windows or WASI, which start processes only from a program: there it returns an error.

Returns

  • the child in the parent, none in the copy, or an error

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var forked = process.fork();
    if (forked.is_err()) {
        return 0;
    }
    if (!forked.value().is_value()) {
        process.exit(3);
    }
    var status = forked.value().value().wait().value();
    return status.code().value() == 3 ? 0 : 1;
}

id

id(): ulong

Returns the running process's id, as the operating system knows it.

Returns

  • the process id (getpid on POSIX, GetCurrentProcessId on Windows)

executable_path

executable_path(): io.IoResult<io.Path>

Returns the path of the running program's executable file, as an absolute path with symbolic links resolved (on Linux the target of /proc/self/exe; on macOS _NSGetExecutablePath, resolved; on Windows GetModuleFileNameW). A tool installed alongside others finds them next to it with executable_path().value().parent().

Returns

  • the executable's path, or an error when the system cannot report it

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var path = process.executable_path().value();
    print(path.to_string());
    return 0;
}

working_directory

working_directory(): io.IoResult<io.Path>

Returns the process's current directory, against which relative paths are resolved. The same as io.Directory.current().

Returns

  • the current directory as an absolute path; an error when it cannot be determined, such as is_not_found() on POSIX when the directory has been removed

change_working_directory

change_working_directory(path: io.Path): io.IoResult<void>

Changes the process's current directory. This affects the whole process, every thread included. The same as io.Directory.set_current.

Parameters

  • path — the new current directory; a relative path is resolved against the old one

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when the directory cannot be entered: is_not_found() when it is missing, is_not_a_directory() when it is a file, or is_permission_denied()

Finding programs

Finding programs: find_executable looks a program up on the PATH, as a shell does before running it, find_companion looks beside the running program first, and is_executable tells whether a file can be run.

Source: runtime/process/find.pep

find_executable

find_executable(name: String): io.Path?

Returns the program name would run as a command: the first file named name in the directories PATH lists, in order, that this process may run. A name that holds a path separator is not looked up: it is returned when it names such a file itself. On Windows, a name with no extension also matches name.exe.

Parameters

  • name — the program's file name, such as "perf"

Returns

  • the program's path, or none when no directory on the PATH holds it

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var git = process.find_executable("git");
    print(git.is_value() ? git.value().to_string() : "git is not installed");
    return 0;
}

is_executable

is_executable(path: io.Path): bool

Returns whether path is a file this process may run: on Linux and macOS, a file with an execute permission bit set; on Windows, any file.

Parameters

  • path — the file to check

Returns

  • true when path names a file that may be run

find_companion

find_companion(name: String): io.Path?

Returns the program name installed beside the running one, else the one find_executable finds on the PATH: how a tool finds the other tools of its suite, as pep-test finds pep-build. On Windows, .exe is added to name when looking beside the running program.

Parameters

  • name — the program's file name, such as "pep-build"

Returns

  • the program's path, or none when neither place holds it

Example

import process;

main(): int {
    var compiler = process.find_companion("pep-build");
    print(compiler.is_value() ? compiler.value().to_string() : "pep-build is not installed");
    return 0;
}

Signals

Signals: Ctrl-C, a request to terminate and a hangup, received as values on a Channel so a program can shut down cleanly.

signals() returns a channel that receives each signal it names. No program code runs inside an operating-system signal handler: on POSIX the handler only writes a byte to a pipe, and a runtime thread turns that byte into a channel message; on Windows the console control handler already runs on a thread of its own and sends the message itself.

Source: runtime/process/signals.pep

Signal

enum Signal

A signal a program can receive from signals().

Cases

Interrupt

Interrupt

Ctrl-C: POSIX SIGINT, or Windows CTRL_C_EVENT and CTRL_BREAK_EVENT.

Terminate

Terminate

A request to end: POSIX SIGTERM, or Windows CTRL_CLOSE_EVENT, CTRL_LOGOFF_EVENT and CTRL_SHUTDOWN_EVENT.

Hangup

Hangup

The terminal closed: POSIX SIGHUP. Windows never sends it.

signals

signals(wanted: Array<Signal>): async.Channel<Signal>

Returns a new channel that receives each of wanted when the process gets it, instead of the signal's default action (ending the program).

Receive from it like any channel: receive() waits outside a task and suspends inside one, and a task can select on it. Every channel that names a signal receives it. Closing the channel stops it receiving (the runtime lets go of it at the next signal or signals() call); once no open channel names a signal, the signal's default action returns.

Nothing runs inside an operating-system signal handler, so the program reacts to a signal only by receiving from the channel. On Windows, the system ends the program a few seconds after Terminate (the console closing, a log-off or a shutdown) whatever it does, so clean up quickly. WASI has no signals: the channel never receives.

Parameters

  • wanted — the signals the channel receives

Returns

  • the channel

Example

import process;
import [Signal] from process;

main(): int {
    var stop = process.signals([Signal.Interrupt, Signal.Terminate]);
    start_serving();
    stop.receive();
    print("shutting down");
    stop_serving();
    return 0;
}

The os module

What the operating system provides beyond the running process: environment variables, clocks and time, and the machine and user.

os is a module: bring it in with import os (and write os.environment("HOME")) or import names directly with import [Instant, Duration] from os.

  • Environment: environment(name), environment_flag(name), environment_variables(), set_environment(name, value) and remove_environment(name)
  • Time: Duration, Instant (a monotonic clock, for measuring) and SystemTime (the wall clock)
  • Machine: system_os(), system_name(), system_version(), architecture(), hostname(), processor counts, total_memory(), page_size()
  • User: user_name(), home_directory(), temp_directory(), is_elevated()

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    var start = os.Instant.now();
    var runtime = os.environment("PEPPER_RUNTIME").value_or("runtime");
    print($"runtime at {runtime} on {os.hostname()}");
    print($"took {os.Instant.now() - start}");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/os/module.pep

Environment

The running process's environment variables: reading them, and setting and removing them for the process itself.

Every read and change the runtime makes goes through one lock, so Pepper code never races with itself over the environment, on any thread. C code that calls getenv itself is outside that lock: on POSIX setenv races with such a call on another thread, as in every language. To give only a child process a different environment, use process.Command's environment, remove_environment and clear_environment instead.

Source: runtime/os/environment.pep

environment

environment(name: String): String?

Returns the value of the environment variable name, or none when it is not set.

A variable set to the empty string is some empty String, not none. On Windows names are not case-sensitive (Path finds PATH), and values are read as UTF-16 and converted to UTF-8, so text outside the ANSI code page survives.

Parameters

  • name — the variable's name

Returns

  • its value, or none when it is not set

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    var home = os.environment("HOME");
    if (home) {
        print(home.value());
    }
    return 0;
}

environment_flag

environment_flag(name: String): bool

Returns whether the environment variable name turns a switch on: it is set to anything but the empty string or 0, as PEPPER_LOCKED=1 does.

Parameters

  • name — the variable's name

Returns

  • true when it is set to a value other than empty or 0

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    if (os.environment_flag("VERBOSE")) {
        print("verbose");
    }
    return 0;
}

set_environment

set_environment(name: String, value: String)

Sets the environment variable name to value for the running process, replacing any value it had.

The process's own later reads see the change, and so do the children it starts afterwards. Safe from any thread for Pepper code; C code that calls getenv on another thread at the same time can race with it on POSIX (see this page's introduction). On Windows names are not case-sensitive. WASI keeps the change inside the program.

Parameters

  • name — the variable's name
  • value — its new value; may be empty

Panics

  • if name is empty or contains = or a NUL byte, or value contains a NUL byte

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    os.set_environment("GREETING", "hello");
    print(os.environment("GREETING").value());   # hello
    return 0;
}

remove_environment

remove_environment(name: String)

Removes the environment variable name from the running process.

Removing a variable that is not set does nothing. The same thread-safety note as set_environment's applies.

Parameters

  • name — the variable's name

Panics

  • if name is empty or contains = or a NUL byte

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    os.remove_environment("GREETING");
    print(os.environment("GREETING").is_empty());   # true
    return 0;
}

environment_variables

environment_variables(): HashMap<String, String>

Returns every environment variable of the running process, by name.

The map has no order. On Windows it includes the variables whose names start with =, such as =C:, which cmd.exe uses for each drive's current directory; its keys keep the case the system reports, so look a name up with environment(name) to ignore case. When a POSIX environment holds one name twice, the first value wins, as getenv returns it.

Returns

  • a new map from each variable's name to its value

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    for (var (name, value) in os.environment_variables()) {
        print($"{name}={value}");
    }
    return 0;
}

Time

Clocks and spans of time: Duration, Instant for measuring, and SystemTime for the wall clock.

Source: runtime/os/time.pep

Duration

[Value] struct Duration

A span of time, counted in nanoseconds, like Rust's std::time::Duration. It is never negative and reaches about 584 years.

Make one with from_seconds, from_milliseconds, from_microseconds or from_nanoseconds, or by subtracting two Instants. A value struct: it is copied, compared with ==, and allocates nothing.

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    var timeout = os.Duration.from_seconds(2) + os.Duration.from_milliseconds(500);
    print(timeout.milliseconds());   # 2500
    print(timeout);                  # 2.5s
    return 0;
}

Instant

[Value] struct Instant

A moment on a monotonic clock, for measuring how long something takes, like Rust's std::time::Instant.

The clock only moves forward: setting the system's date and time does not change it. Its readings mean nothing by themselves, only the Duration between two of them, and they cannot be compared across processes or reboots. Use SystemTime for the date and time.

The clock is CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Linux and macOS and QueryPerformanceCounter on Windows, read to the nanosecond.

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    var start = os.Instant.now();
    var total = 0;
    for (var i in 0..1000000) {
        total = total + i;
    }
    var elapsed = os.Instant.now() - start;
    print($"summed in {elapsed.milliseconds()} ms");
    return 0;
}

SystemTime

[Value] struct SystemTime

A date and time on the system's wall clock, counted in nanoseconds from the Unix epoch (1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC), like Rust's std::time::SystemTime. It reaches from the year 1677 to 2262.

The wall clock can jump, backwards too, when the system's time is set, so measure how long something takes with Instant instead. The time module turns it into dates, times of day and time zones, and back.

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    var now = os.SystemTime.now();
    print($"{now.unix_seconds()} seconds since 1970");
    return 0;
}

Returns the processor architecture the program was built for: "x64", "aarch64" or "wasm32", the names [Target(Arch(...))] uses.

Returns

[Target(Arch(aarch64))] architecture(): String

Returns the processor architecture the program was built for: "x64", "aarch64" or "wasm32", the names [Target(Arch(...))] uses.

architecture

[Target(Arch(wasm32))] architecture(): String

Returns the processor architecture the program was built for: "x64", "aarch64" or "wasm32", the names [Target(Arch(...))] uses.

Returns

  • the architecture's name

hostname

hostname(): String

Returns the machine's host name, as hostname prints it (on Windows its DNS host name). WASI does not report one.

Returns

  • the host name, or an empty String when the system does not report it

logical_cpus

logical_cpus(): ulong

Returns the number of logical processors: every hardware thread, so a core with hyperthreading counts two or more times. On Linux a cgroup CPU quota (docker run --cpus) caps it, rounded up. The same as async.logical_cpus().

Returns

  • the number of logical processors, at least 1

See also

  • physical_cpus

physical_cpus

physical_cpus(): ulong

Returns the number of physical processor cores: hardware threads that share a core count once. The same as async.physical_cpus().

Returns

  • the number of physical cores, at least 1 and at most logical_cpus()

See also

  • logical_cpus

total_memory

total_memory(): ulong

Returns the machine's physical memory in bytes. Inside a virtual machine this is what the guest sees. On Linux, a lower memory limit on the process's cgroup or any cgroup above it (cgroup v2's memory.max or v1's memory.limit_in_bytes, as docker run --memory sets) is returned instead, as the JVM does. WASI does not report it.

Returns

  • the total physical memory, or the container's memory limit when that is lower, in bytes; 0 when the system does not report it

peak_memory

peak_memory(): ulong

Returns the most physical memory this process has held at once since it started: its peak resident set size (ru_maxrss on Linux and macOS, the peak working set on Windows). WASI does not report it.

Returns

  • the peak resident set size in bytes; 0 when the system does not report it

Example

var megabytes = os.peak_memory() / 1048576;

page_size

page_size(): ulong

Returns the size of a page of virtual memory in bytes: the unit the operating system maps memory in, usually 4096 (16384 on Apple silicon; 65536, WebAssembly's page, on WASI).

Returns

  • the page size in bytes

User

The user the program runs as: their name, directories, and whether they have administrator rights.

Source: runtime/os/user.pep

user_name

user_name(): String?

Returns the name of the user the program runs as: on POSIX the login name of the effective user id (from the user database, else USER), on Windows GetUserNameW's answer (else USERNAME), and on WASI USER.

Returns

  • the user name, or none when it cannot be found

is_elevated

is_elevated(): bool

Returns whether the program runs with administrator rights: on POSIX, as root (effective user id 0); on Windows, from an elevated ("Run as administrator") process of a member of Administrators (IsUserAnAdmin); never on WASI. Tools that need them, such as a profiler that reads kernel events, check this to say so up front.

Returns

  • true when the program runs as root or elevated

home_directory

home_directory(): io.Path?

Returns the user's home directory: on POSIX HOME, or the user database's entry when HOME is unset or empty; on Windows USERPROFILE; on WASI HOME.

Returns

  • the home directory, or none when it cannot be found

Example

import os;

main(): int {
    var home = os.home_directory();
    if (home) {
        print(home.value().join(".config").to_string());
    }
    return 0;
}

temp_directory

temp_directory(): io.Path

Returns the directory for temporary files: TMPDIR or /tmp on POSIX (/data/local/tmp on Android), GetTempPathW on Windows. The same as io.Directory.temp().

Returns

  • the temporary directory

The time module

Calendar time: dates, times of day, offsets from UTC, time zones, and formatting and parsing them, on the proleptic Gregorian calendar. Leap seconds are ignored, as in Unix time. os.SystemTime is the instant this module turns into dates and back.

time is a module: bring it in with import time (and write time.Date(2024, 2, 29)) or import names directly with import [Date, TimeZone] from time.

  • Dates and times: Date, Time, DateTime, Weekday, is_leap_year and days_in_month, with no time zone
  • Offsets: Offset, a fixed offset from UTC, and OffsetDateTime, an RFC 3339 timestamp, with HTTP dates
  • Time zones: TimeZone (UTC, fixed, local, or named from the system's database), now() and now_utc()

Every type's format(pattern) lays it out with C strftime codes:

CodeGivesCodeGives
%Yyear, at least four digits (2024)%Hhour, 00 to 23
%Ccentury (20)%Ihour, 01 to 12
%yyear in the century, 00 to 99%pAM or PM
%mmonth, 01 to 12%Mminute, 00 to 59
%dday, 01 to 31%Ssecond, 00 to 59
%eday, space-padded ( 1)%Nnanoseconds, nine digits; %3N milliseconds
%jday of the year, 001 to 366%T%H:%M:%S
%F%Y-%m-%d%R%H:%M
%aweekday, Mon%zoffset, +0100
%Aweekday, Monday%:zoffset, +01:00
%b, %hmonth, Jan%sUnix seconds
%Bmonth, January%uISO weekday, 1 (Monday) to 7
%GISO 8601 week-numbering year%wweekday, 0 (Sunday) to 6
%VISO 8601 week, 01 to 53%n, %t, %%newline, tab, %

Names are English, whatever the locale. %z, %:z and %s need an offset, so only OffsetDateTime.format takes them.

Example

import os;
import time;

main(): int {
    var now = time.now();
    print(now);                                  # 2024-03-01T09:00:00.25+01:00
    print(now.format("%A %e %B %Y, %H:%M"));     # Friday  1 March 2024, 09:00
    print(now.to_http_date());                   # Fri, 01 Mar 2024 08:00:00 GMT
    var date = time.Date.parse("2024-02-29").value();
    print(date.add_years(1));                    # 2025-02-28
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/time/module.pep

Dates and times

Calendar dates and times of day with no time zone: Date, Time, DateTime and Weekday, on the proleptic Gregorian calendar, plus is_leap_year and days_in_month.

Source: runtime/time/civil.pep

is_leap_year

is_leap_year(year: int): bool

Returns whether year is a leap year on the Gregorian calendar: divisible by 4, except centuries not divisible by 400. Year 0 (1 BC) is one.

Parameters

Returns

Example

assert(time.is_leap_year(2024) && !time.is_leap_year(1900), "leap years");

Date

[Value] struct Date

A date on the proleptic Gregorian calendar, which extends the calendar's rules to years before it was adopted: a year, a month (1 to 12) and a day of the month (1 to 31), with no time of day or time zone.

A value struct: copied, compared with ==, < and the other comparisons, and never allocated. Years run from -999999 to 999999; year 0 is 1 BC. Its text is ISO 8601's 2024-02-29.

Example

import time;

main(): int {
    var day = time.Date(2024, 2, 28).add_days(1);
    print(day);               # 2024-02-29
    print(day.weekday());     # Thursday
    return 0;
}

Time

[Value] struct Time

A time of day with no date or time zone: an hour (0 to 23), a minute, a second and a nanosecond. Leap seconds are not represented, as in Unix time.

A value struct: copied, compared with ==, < and the other comparisons, and never allocated. Its text is ISO 8601's 08:30:00, with a fraction of a second when there is one (08:30:00.25).

Example

import time;

main(): int {
    var lunch = time.Time(12, 30);
    print(lunch);   # 12:30:00
    return 0;
}

DateTime

[Value] struct DateTime

A date and a time of day with no time zone, such as a meeting's 2024-03-01 09:00 written down without saying where. TOML calls it a local date-time. Attach an offset with OffsetDateTime, or a zone's rules with TimeZone.at_local, to name an instant.

A value struct: copied, compared with ==, < and the other comparisons, and never allocated. Its text is ISO 8601's 2024-03-01T09:00:00.

Example

import time;

main(): int {
    var start = time.DateTime(2024, 3, 1, 9, 0);
    var end = start + os.Duration.from_seconds(90 * 60);
    print(end);   # 2024-03-01T10:30:00
    return 0;
}

Offsets

Fixed offsets from UTC, Offset, and the date and time at one, OffsetDateTime: an instant written the way RFC 3339 and TOML write it.

Source: runtime/time/offset.pep

Offset

[Value] struct Offset

A fixed offset from UTC, east positive: +02:00 for Central European Summer Time, -05:00 for US Eastern Standard Time, +00:00 for UTC.

A value struct: copied, compared with ==, and never allocated. It is less than a day either way, to the second. Its text is +02:00, with the seconds when there are any (+00:19:32).

Example

import time;

main(): int {
    var india = time.Offset.from_hours(5, 30);
    print(india);            # +05:30
    print(india.seconds);    # 19800
    return 0;
}

OffsetDateTime

[Value] struct OffsetDateTime

A date and time at a fixed offset from UTC, such as 2024-03-01T09:00:00+01:00: an instant, together with the local date and time it was written in. This is RFC 3339's timestamp and TOML's offset date-time.

A value struct: copied and never allocated. == compares the date, time and offset, so the same instant at two offsets is not ==; compare instants with to_system_time(), or with < and the other comparisons, which compare instants. Its text is RFC 3339's, with Z for UTC.

Example

import time;

main(): int {
    var meeting = time.OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-03-01T09:00:00+01:00").value();
    print(meeting.to_utc());   # 2024-03-01T08:00:00Z
    print(meeting.to_http_date());   # Fri, 01 Mar 2024 08:00:00 GMT
    return 0;
}

parse

static parse(text: String): Result<OffsetDateTime>

Returns the RFC 3339 timestamp in text, such as 2024-03-01T09:00:00+01:00 or 2024-03-01T08:00:00.5Z, or an error when it is not one. A space or a lowercase t may stand for the T and a lowercase z for the Z, and the seconds may be left out, as TOML allows.

parse_http_date

static parse_http_date(text: String): Result<OffsetDateTime>

Returns the HTTP date in text, as RFC 9110 defines it, or an error when it is not one. It reads the preferred IMF-fixdate (Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT) and the two obsolete forms that servers must still accept: RFC 850's (Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT, where a two-digit year from 70 is in the 1900s and below 70 in the 2000s) and C's asctime (Sun Nov 6 08:49:37 1994). The weekday must match the date.

Parameters

  • text — the text to read

Returns

  • the date and time in UTC, or an error saying what is wrong with text

Time zones

Time zones: TimeZone, the rules that give an instant's offset from UTC, for UTC, a fixed offset, the system's local zone, or a named zone such as Europe/Paris from the system's time zone database; and now().

Source: runtime/time/zone.pep

TimeZone

struct TimeZone

The rules that give the offset from UTC at each instant in one place: UTC, a fixed offset, the system's local time zone, or a named zone from the IANA time zone database, such as Europe/Paris or America/New_York, with its daylight saving time and its history.

Named zones come from the system's database, nothing is bundled: the files under /usr/share/zoneinfo on Linux and macOS, and ICU's (icu.dll, Windows 10 version 1903 and later) on Windows. On every system, a folder of database files that the TZDIR environment variable names takes their place. Leap seconds are ignored, as in Unix time.

A zone is a reference, and it does not change once made, so copies share it.

Example

import os;
import time;

main(): int {
    var paris = time.TimeZone.named("Europe/Paris").value();
    var instant = time.OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-07-14T10:00:00Z").value();
    print(paris.at(instant.to_system_time()));   # 2024-07-14T12:00:00+02:00
    var local = paris.at_local(time.DateTime(2024, 12, 25, 18, 0));
    print(local.offset);                         # +01:00
    return 0;
}

Example

at_local

at_local(local: DateTime): OffsetDateTime

Returns the instant that a local date and time names in this zone, with its offset.

Where the clocks go back, a local time happens twice; this returns the earlier, at the offset from before the change. Where they go forward, a local time never happens; this moves it forward by the length of the gap, so 02:30 on a night that skips from 02:00 to 03:00 is 03:30. This is what Java's ZonedDateTime.of does.

Parameters

  • local — the date and time on the zone's clocks

Returns

  • the date and time with the zone's offset at that instant

Returns the current date and time in the system's local time zone.

print(time.now());   # such as 2024-03-01T09:00:00.123456789+01:00

The math module

Numbers beyond the operators: the math library as it grows.

Bring it in with import math. The floating-point functions (sine, logarithm, cube_root, is_nan, ...) are methods of float and double, which every program has without an import; this module holds the constants and the integer functions.

  • Constants: PI, TAU, E, INFINITY, NAN, and the epsilon and limits of float and double
  • Integers: gcd and lcm
  • Parsing: parse_int, deprecated: every number type has a static parse (long.parse(text, base)) without an import

Example

import math;
var radius = 2.0;
var area = math.PI * radius ** 2;
assert((math.PI / 2).sine() == 1.0, "a quarter turn");

Source: runtime/math/module.pep

The hint module

Hints to the optimizer about memory a loop will soon read or write.

Bring it in with import hint. A hint never changes what a program computes, only how fast: a prefetch starts loading a cache line early. Where the CPU has no prefetch instruction it does nothing.

To say which way a branch usually goes, write [Likely] or [Unlikely] above the if or match arm; likely and unlikely here are deprecated.

Example

import hint;

main(): int {
    var text = "a long text that a loop will read";
    hint.prefetch_read(text.c_str());
    assert(text.length > 0, "a prefetch changes nothing");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/hint/module.pep

likely

[Deprecated("write '[Likely]' above the 'if' instead")] likely(condition: bool): bool

Deprecated: write [Likely] above the if instead.

Returns condition, telling the optimizer it is usually true (llvm.expect).

Parameters

Returns

  • condition

unlikely

Deprecated: write [Unlikely] above the if instead.

Parameters

Returns

prefetch_read

prefetch_read(address: __ptr<void>)

Starts loading the cache line holding address for reading, so a read of it soon after does not wait on memory (llvm.prefetch). It never faults, even for an address that is not mapped, and does nothing where the CPU has no prefetch instruction.

Parameters

Example

hint.prefetch_read(text.c_str());

prefetch_write

prefetch_write(address: __ptr<void>)

Starts loading the cache line holding address for writing, so a store to it soon after does not wait on memory (llvm.prefetch). It never faults, even for an address that is not mapped, and does nothing where the CPU has no prefetch instruction.

Parameters

The simd module

SIMD vectors: Vector<T, N> holds N numbers of type T and computes on all of them at once, in the CPU's vector registers.

Bring it in with import simd. T is an integer or floating-point type (byte, char, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float, double) and N, the lane count, is a power of two from 1 to 64, written as a number: simd.Vector<byte, 16>. A vector is a value ([Value]): it is stored inline, copied like a number, and safe to share between threads.

The operations compile to the target's vector instructions: SSE2 on x86-64 (AVX2 with -march=x86-64-v3), NEON on arm64, and simd128 on WebAssembly with -msimd128. A target without vector registers gets the same results from scalar code. Sixteen bytes (Vector<byte, 16>, Vector<int, 4>, Vector<double, 2>) is the width every target handles well; wider vectors use several registers where the target has no wider ones.

Lane-wise comparisons (less, equal, ...) give a Mask<N>, which selects lanes (select), answers any and all, and packs into a bit mask with to_bits, whose trailing_zeros finds the first match.

Example

import simd;

main(): int {
    var a = simd.Vector<int, 4>(10);
    var b = a + simd.Vector<int, 4>(5);
    assert(b[0] == 15 && b.sum() == 60, "lane-wise add");
    var over = b.greater(12);
    assert(over.all() && over.to_bits() == 0xF, "a mask per lane");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/simd/module.pep

Lane

trait Lane

The number types a Vector holds: every integer and floating-point type. The runtime declares the conformances; another type cannot be a lane.

IntegerLane

trait IntegerLane

The integer lane types, whose vectors have checked division, the bitwise operators, shifts and rotates.

FloatLane

trait FloatLane

The floating-point lane types, whose vectors have floating-point division, square_root, floor and ceiling.

Vector

[Value] struct Vector<T: Lane, N>

N lanes of the number type T, computed on together.

Integer +, - and * wrap around on overflow in each lane, as vector instructions do, where scalar arithmetic panics. Integer / and % panic on a zero divisor lane; shifts panic on a count outside the lane's width. Every other operation is defined for every input.

Type parameters

  • T — the lane type: an integer or floating-point type
  • N — the lane count: a power of two from 1 to 64

The debug module

Stack walking, panic backtraces, and talking to a debugger.

debug is a module: bring it in with import debug (and write debug.capture()).

  • Backtraces: capture() records the calls that led to the current point, cheaply; Backtrace.frames() resolves each return address to its function and, in a -g build, its source line. print_backtrace() writes the current stack to standard error.
  • The debugger: output() writes to the platform's debugger channel, is_debugger_attached() asks whether a debugger is watching, and breakpoint() stops in it.

A panic prints a backtrace after its message in a build without -O; the PEPPER_BACKTRACE environment variable turns that on (1) or off (0) in any build (see print_backtrace).

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    var trace = debug.capture();
    var frames = trace.frames();
    assert(frames.count > 0, "main is on the stack");
    debug.output("captured a backtrace");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/debug/module.pep

Backtraces

Capturing the call stack (capture, Backtrace) and resolving it to functions and source lines (StackFrame).

Capturing only records return addresses, so it is cheap enough to do whenever something might need reporting later. The addresses are resolved, from the program's symbol table and its debug info, only when Backtrace.frames() or to_string() asks for them.

A function name needs the program's symbol table, which every build keeps unless the executable is stripped. A file, line and column need the debug info a -g build carries:

  • Linux: the executable's ELF symbol table and DWARF line table.
  • macOS: the executable's symbol table, and the DWARF line table of the .dSYM bundle a -g build writes beside it.
  • Windows: DbgHelp, which reads the .pdb every build writes beside the executable: function names only, or with -g source lines too (no columns).
  • WASI: a WebAssembly program cannot walk its stack, so a backtrace is empty.

A function the optimizer inlined into its caller has no frame of its own, so each address is expanded into its chain of inlined calls, from the debug info of a -g build: one StackFrame per call, marked inlined.

Frames inside the runtime's own capture and panic code are left out, and so are the runtime's operator methods (Array<int>.__index_get, what a[i] calls) between a panic and the code that caused it, and the C runtime's frames below main. frames(full = true), or PEPPER_BACKTRACE=full for a panic's backtrace, keeps them all.

Source: runtime/debug/backtrace.pep

StackFrame

struct StackFrame

One call on the stack: where it returns to, and the function and source position that address belongs to.

A call the optimizer inlined is a frame too, with inlined set: it shares its address with the frames of its callers, up to the first frame that is not inlined, which is the real one.

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    var frame = debug.capture().frames()[0];
    assert(frame.function == "main", "the innermost frame is main");
    print(frame.to_string());   # main at main.pep:4:21 in a -g build
    return 0;
}

Fields

address

var address: ulong

The return address: the instruction the call returns to.

function

var function: String

The function's name, such as main or Point.length; empty when the program has no symbol for the address.

file

var file: String

The source file, as it was named to the compiler; empty without debug info.

line

var line: int

The 1-based source line of the call; 0 without debug info.

column

var column: int

The 1-based source column of the call; 0 when unknown.

inlined

var inlined: bool

Whether the optimizer inlined this call into its caller, the next frame: the function has no frame of its own on the stack.

Constructor

StackFrame()

construct(address: ulong = 0)

Creates a StackFrame for address, with no function or source position yet.

Parameters

  • address — the return address

Methods

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the frame as text: function at file:line:column, with the parts that are unknown left out, the address in hexadecimal when the function is unknown, and (inlined) after an inlined call.

Returns

  • the frame as text

Backtrace

struct Backtrace

The call stack at the point capture() ran, as return addresses, innermost first.

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    var trace = debug.capture();
    for (var frame in trace.frames()) {
        print(frame.to_string());
    }
    return 0;
}

Fields

addresses

var addresses: Array<ulong>

The return address of each call, innermost first, as captured: it includes the frames of capture itself, which frames() leaves out.

Constructor

Backtrace()

construct()

Creates an empty Backtrace. Use capture() to record the stack.

Methods

frames

frames(full: bool = false): Array<StackFrame>

Resolves each return address to its function and source position. Runs in time proportional to the program's symbol table and debug info, which it reads each call.

In a -g build, an address inside code the optimizer inlined becomes a frame for each inlined call, innermost first, each marked inlined, followed by the real frame (Linux and macOS read the DWARF, Windows asks DbgHelp).

Unless full, leaves out, at the top, the frames of capture and of the runtime's panic code and the runtime's operator methods (Array<int>.__index_get for a[i]) a panic came through; and at the bottom, the C runtime's frames below main.

Parameters

  • full — whether to keep every frame

Returns

  • the frames, innermost first

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the frames as text, one per line, each numbered and indented ( 0: main at main.pep:4:5), with a newline after the last.

Returns

  • the frames as text

capture

capture(): Backtrace

Records the call stack: the return address of every call that led here. Cheap: the addresses are resolved only when Backtrace.frames() or to_string() asks for them.

Records at most 128 calls, the innermost ones. On WASI the Backtrace is empty.

Returns

  • the stack, innermost call first

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    var trace = debug.capture();
    print(trace.to_string());
    return 0;
}

print_backtrace

print_backtrace()

Writes the current call stack to standard error, a line per frame, after a backtrace: line: what a panic prints after its message.

A panic prints it in a build without -O. Set the PEPPER_BACKTRACE environment variable to 1 to print it in an optimized build too, to full to also print the runtime frames it leaves out (see Backtrace.frames), or to 0 to never print it.

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    debug.print_backtrace();
    return 0;
}

The debugger

Talking to a debugger: output() writes to the platform's debugger channel, is_debugger_attached() asks whether a debugger is watching, and breakpoint() stops in it.

Source: runtime/debug/debugger.pep

output

output(text: String)

Writes text to the platform's debugger channel, followed by a newline when it does not end in one.

  • Windows: OutputDebugStringW, which Visual Studio's Output window and WinDbg show (and DebugView, with no debugger attached). Nothing is written anywhere else.
  • Linux, macOS and WASI: standard error, which debuggers show; these systems have no separate channel.

Parameters

  • text — the text to write

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    debug.output("starting");
    return 0;
}

is_debugger_attached

is_debugger_attached(): bool

Returns whether a debugger is attached to the program: the TracerPid of /proc/self/status on Linux, P_TRACED on macOS, and IsDebuggerPresent on Windows. Always false on WASI.

Returns

  • true while a debugger is attached

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    if (debug.is_debugger_attached()) {
        debug.output("hello, debugger");
    }
    return 0;
}

breakpoint

breakpoint()

Stops in the debugger, as a breakpoint set on this line would: the processor's debug trap (int3 on x64, brk on AArch64), through llvm.debugtrap. The debugger can then continue the program.

With no debugger attached the trap ends the program: SIGTRAP on Linux and macOS, a breakpoint exception on Windows. Guard it with is_debugger_attached() to stop only under a debugger. Does nothing on WASI.

Example

import debug;

main(): int {
    if (debug.is_debugger_attached()) {
        debug.breakpoint();
    }
    return 0;
}

The log module

Leveled, structured logging: lines with a level, a message, key/value fields and the place of the call, written whole to standard error or to a Writer of your choice, from any thread or task.

log is a module: bring it in with import log (and write log.info("started")).

  • error, warning, info, debug and trace write a line at their Level. Each takes optional fields (made with field) and a target, the part of the program the line is about.
  • set_level picks the least important level shown, for every target or for one; enabled asks whether a line would be written.
  • set_output sends lines to a Writer (a file, a socket) in a Format: readable text or JSON Lines.

By default lines go to standard error as text, in color when it is a terminal (unless NO_COLOR is set), and info and above are shown. The PEPPER_LOG environment variable sets the levels when the program first logs: comma-separated items, each a level for every target or target=level for one, such as PEPPER_LOG=warning,http=debug. The levels are off, error, warning (or warn), info, debug and trace.

A text line reads:

2026-10-17T23:40:01.123Z INFO  [http] request done status=200 path="/" (main.pep:5:5)

Example

import log;

main(): int {
    log.info("started");
    log.warning("disk almost full", [log.field("free_mb", 120)], target = "storage");
    log.debug("not shown unless PEPPER_LOG=debug");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/log/module.pep

Logging

Levels, fields, the output, and the functions that write a line.

Source: runtime/log/log.pep

Level

enum Level

How much a line matters, most important first.

As the level a target shows (set_level, PEPPER_LOG), each level also shows the ones above it: Info shows errors, warnings and info lines.

Cases

Off

Off

Nothing: as the level a target shows, turns its lines off.

Error

Error

Something failed (error).

Warning

Warning

Something looks wrong but the program carries on (warning).

Info

Info

What the program is doing, at the level of whole operations (info).

Debug

Debug

Detail for finding a bug (debug).

Trace

Trace

Step-by-step detail (trace).

Format

enum Format

How each line is written.

Cases

Text

Text

One readable line: the UTC time, the level, the target in brackets, the message, key=value fields, and the call's location in parentheses.

Json

Json

One JSON object per line (JSON Lines), with the keys time, level, target (when there is one), message and location, then each field.

Field

struct Field

A key and value attached to a line. Make one with field.

Fields

key

var key: String = ""

The key.

value

var value: String = ""

The value as JSON text: 200, "ann", true.

Constructor

Field()

construct(key: String, value: String)

Creates a field from a key and the JSON text of its value; field makes the text from any value.

Parameters

  • key — the key
  • value — the value's JSON text

field

field<T>(key: String, value: T): Field

Makes a field for a line: log.info("done", [log.field("ms", 12)]).

The value is turned into JSON (see json.encode) when the field is made, whether or not the line is written; guard costly fields with enabled.

Parameters

Returns

Example

import log;

main(): int {
    log.info("request done", [log.field("status", 200), log.field("path", "/")]);
    return 0;
}

set_level

set_level(level: Level, target: String = "")

Sets the level a target shows, or with no target the level every target without its own shows. The default is Level.Info, unless the PEPPER_LOG environment variable says otherwise.

Parameters

  • level — the least important level to show; Level.Off shows nothing
  • target — the target, as the logging functions' target; empty for the global level

Example

import log;

main(): int {
    log.set_level(log.Level.Debug);
    log.set_level(log.Level.Warning, "http");
    log.debug("shown");
    log.info("not shown", target = "http");
    return 0;
}

set_output

set_output([Move] writer: io.Writer, format: Format = Format.Text)

Sends every line from now on to writer in format, instead of to standard error. Lines are written whole, one write_all each, under a lock, so lines from many threads and tasks never interleave. A failed write is ignored. Colors are off.

Parameters

  • writer — where lines go: a new value, or one handed over with move(x), since the log keeps it
  • format — how each line is written

Example

import io;
import log;

main(): int {
    var path = io.Directory.temp().join("app.log");
    var file = io.File.create(path).value();
    log.set_output(move(file), log.Format.Json);
    log.info("started");
    return 0;
}

enabled

enabled(level: Level, target: String = ""): bool

Reports whether a line at level for target would be written, so a caller can skip building a costly message or field.

Cheap when no target shows level: two atomic loads, with no lock.

Parameters

  • level — the line's level
  • target — the line's target; empty for none

Returns

  • true when target shows level; false for Level.Off

Example

import log;

main(): int {
    if (log.enabled(log.Level.Debug)) {
        log.debug($"state: {[1, 2, 3]}");
    }
    return 0;
}

error

Example

log.error("cannot open the database", [log.field("path", path)]);

warning

warning( message: String, fields: Array<Field> = Array<Field>(), target: String = "" )

Parameters

  • fields — keys and values to add to the line (see field)
  • target — the part of the program the line is about; empty for none

info

info( message: String, fields: Array<Field> = Array<Field>(), target: String = "" )

  • target — the part of the program the line is about; empty for none

log.info("listening", [log.field("port", 8080)]);

The text module

Converting text to and from bytes in a given encoding.

Bring it in with import text. A String always holds UTF-8; these types encode one into the bytes of an encoding (u8[]) and decode bytes back. Each decode is strict and gives none when the bytes are not valid in the encoding (code page 437's always succeeds, since every byte is a character); each decode_lossy replaces what is invalid with U+FFFD and always succeeds.

  • UTF-8: Utf8
  • UTF-16: Utf16
  • ASCII: Ascii
  • Code page 437: CodePage437

Example

import text;

main(): int {
    var bytes = text.Utf8.encode("héllo");
    assert(bytes.count == 6, "é takes two bytes");
    assert(text.Utf8.decode(bytes).value() == "héllo", "round trip");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/text/module.pep

UTF-8

UTF-8, the encoding a String holds.

Source: runtime/text/utf8.pep

Utf8

struct Utf8

Encodes a String to UTF-8 bytes and decodes them back. A String already holds UTF-8, so encoding copies its bytes; decoding checks them.

Example

import text;

var bytes = text.Utf8.encode("hi");
assert(text.Utf8.decode(bytes).value() == "hi", "round trip");

Static methods

encode

static encode(value: String): u8[]

Returns the UTF-8 bytes of value, without a terminating NUL.

Parameters

  • value — the text to encode

Returns

  • a new array of value.size bytes

is_valid

static is_valid(bytes: u8[]): bool

Returns whether bytes is valid UTF-8: no stray continuation bytes, no truncated, overlong or surrogate sequences, and nothing past U+10FFFF.

Parameters

  • bytes — the bytes to check

Returns

  • true when every byte is part of a valid sequence

decode

static decode(bytes: u8[]): String?

Decodes bytes as UTF-8, or gives none when they are not valid UTF-8 (see is_valid). A byte-order mark is kept as part of the text.

Parameters

  • bytes — the bytes to decode

Returns

  • the text, or none when bytes is not valid UTF-8

Example

import text;

var bad = Array<u8>();
bad.append(255);
assert(text.Utf8.decode(bad).is_empty(), "0xFF is never UTF-8");

decode_lossy

static decode_lossy(bytes: u8[]): String

Decodes bytes as UTF-8, replacing each byte that does not start a valid sequence with U+FFFD, so it always succeeds. Valid input gives the same text as decode.

Parameters

  • bytes — the bytes to decode

Returns

  • the text

Example

import text;

var data = Array<u8>();
data.append(104);
data.append(255);
data.append(105);
assert(text.Utf8.decode_lossy(data) == "h\u{FFFD}i", "255 is replaced");

find_invalid

static find_invalid(value: String): ulong?

Returns the byte offset of the first byte of value that does not start a valid UTF-8 sequence (see is_valid), or none when all of it is valid. A String made from checked bytes is always valid; one made from C memory may not be.

Parameters

  • value — the text to check

Returns

  • the offset of the first invalid byte, or none

Example

import text;

assert(text.Utf8.find_invalid("héllo").is_empty(), "valid");

code_point_at

static code_point_at(value: String, offset: ulong): (uint, ulong)

Decodes the code point whose UTF-8 sequence starts at byte offset of value.

Parameters

  • value — the text to read
  • offset — the byte offset where the sequence starts

Returns

  • the code point and the number of bytes its sequence takes, from 1 to 4, so offset plus that is where the next one starts

Panics

  • if offset is not less than value.size ("Utf8.code_point_at offset out of bounds")
  • if no valid sequence starts at offset ("Utf8.code_point_at found invalid UTF-8")

Example

import text;

var (point, run) = text.Utf8.code_point_at("é!", 0);
assert(point == 233 and run == 2, "U+00E9 takes two bytes");

append_code_point

static append_code_point(out: u8[], code_point: uint)

Appends the UTF-8 encoding of code_point, from 1 to 4 bytes, to out.

Parameters

  • out — the bytes to append to
  • code_point — the code point to encode

Panics

  • if code_point is a surrogate (U+D800 to U+DFFF) or above U+10FFFF ("Utf8.append_code_point needs a Unicode scalar value")

Example

import text;

var out = Array<u8>();
text.Utf8.append_code_point(out, 8364);
assert(text.Utf8.decode(out).value() == "€", "U+20AC");

UTF-16

UTF-16, as Windows and Java hold text.

Source: runtime/text/utf16.pep

Utf16

struct Utf16

Encodes a String to UTF-16 bytes and decodes them back. Each code unit takes two bytes, little-endian unless big_endian is set; a code point past U+FFFF takes two units (a surrogate pair). No byte-order mark is written, and one read is kept as part of the text.

Example

import text;

var bytes = text.Utf16.encode("hi");
assert(bytes.count == 4 && bytes[0] == 104 && bytes[1] == 0, "little-endian");
assert(text.Utf16.decode(bytes).value() == "hi", "round trip");

Static methods

encode

static encode(value: String, big_endian: bool = false): u8[]

Returns the UTF-16 bytes of value.

A String holds UTF-8, but one made from C memory may not be valid: each byte that does not start a valid UTF-8 sequence (see Utf8.is_valid) is encoded as U+FFFD, as Utf8.decode_lossy reads it, so the result is always valid UTF-16.

Parameters

  • value — the text to encode
  • big_endian — whether each code unit's high byte comes first; false (little-endian) by default

Returns

Code page 437

Code page 437, the character set of the original IBM PC, which old zip archives use for entry names.

Source: runtime/text/code_page_437.pep

CodePage437

struct CodePage437

Encodes a String to code page 437 bytes and decodes them back. Bytes below 128 are ASCII; each of the 128 above stands for one character (accented letters, Greek letters, box-drawing and math symbols), so every byte decodes and decode always succeeds. Bytes below 32 decode as the ASCII control characters, not the PC's graphical glyphs, as zip readers do.

import text;

assert(bytes.count == 4 && bytes[3] == 0x82, "é is 0x82");
assert(text.CodePage437.decode(bytes) == "café", "round trip");

The regex module

Regular expressions: test whether text matches a pattern, find the matches and their capture groups, and replace or split by a pattern.

Bring it in with import regex. The syntax is RE2's, and matching takes time linear in the size of the text whatever the pattern.

  • Regex and Match: Regex, Match, Matches

Example

import regex;

main(): int {
    var word = regex.Regex("\\b(\\w)(\\w*)\\b");
    assert(word.replace_all("hello big world", "${1}.") == "h. b. w.", "initials");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/regex/module.pep

Regex and Match

Regex, Match and the iterator over every match.

Source: runtime/regex/regex.pep

Regex

[Shared] struct Regex

A compiled regular expression: compile a pattern once, then test, find, replace or split text with it.

The syntax is RE2's, the one Go and Rust's regex use. Matching runs in time linear in the text whatever the pattern, because the engine never backtracks; in return there are no backreferences (\1) and no lookaround ((?=...)), and a pattern using them fails to compile.

  • Positions (Match.start(), Match.end(), find_at) are byte offsets, like String.find, so they work with substr_bytes.
  • . and a negated class ([^a]) match one code point, never part of one.
  • \d, \w, \s, \b and case-insensitive matching are ASCII-only.

A Regex never changes once compiled and is [Shared], so one compiled at module scope (const word = regex.Regex("\\w+");) serves every thread.

Example

import regex;

main(): int {
    var date = regex.Regex("(\\d{4})-(\\d{2})-(\\d{2})");
    var found = date.find("due 2026-10-01").value();
    assert(found.group(1).value() == "2026", "the year");
    assert(found.start() == 4, "a byte offset");
    return 0;
}

The json module

JSON: parse text into a JsonValue, look values up and change them, and write them back as compact or indented text.

Bring it in with import json. Parsing follows RFC 8259 strictly, and accepts JSONC (comments and trailing commas) on request. Objects keep their keys in the order they were written, so a document round-trips unchanged. encode and decode convert structs to JSON text and back.

  • JsonValue: JsonValue
  • Parsing: parse, JsonError
  • Documents with comments: parse_document, JsonDocument
  • Struct conversion: encode, decode, to_json, from_json, UnknownKeys, with the attributes of the serialize module

Example

import json;

main(): int {
    var parsed = json.parse("{\"name\": \"pepper\", \"port\": 8080}");
    if (parsed.is_err()) {
        print(parsed.error().to_string());
        return 1;
    }
    var root = parsed.value();
    assert(root["name"].as_string().value() == "pepper", "a string");
    assert(root["port"].as_int().value_or(80) == 8080, "a number");
    root["debug"] = json.JsonValue.Bool(true);
    assert(root.to_string() == "{\"name\":\"pepper\",\"port\":8080,\"debug\":true}", "compact");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/json/module.pep

JsonValue

JsonValue: a JSON value of any kind, and how it is written as text.

Source: runtime/json/value.pep

JsonValue

enum JsonValue

A JSON value: null, a boolean, a number, a string, an array or an object. json.parse makes one from text and to_string writes it back.

Look values up with value["key"] and value[index]. A lookup that finds nothing (a missing key, an index past the end, or a lookup on a value of another kind) gives Null rather than panicking, so lookups chain: root["server"]["port"]. Then read the value with an as_ method, which gives none when the value is of another kind, or match on its case.

Numbers keep the form they were written in: an integer within ±(2^53 − 1), the range every JSON implementation agrees on (RFC 7493), is an Integer; any other number is a Number, a double.

An Array or Object case holds its array or map by reference, so changing them through value[key] = ..., append or the map from as_object() changes every holder of the value.

Example

import json;

var reply = json.JsonValue.object();
reply["id"] = json.JsonValue.Integer(42);
reply["tags"] = json.JsonValue.array([json.JsonValue.String("a")]);
assert(reply.to_string() == "{\"id\":42,\"tags\":[\"a\"]}", "compact");
assert(reply["id"].as_int().value() == 42, "a lookup");
assert(reply["missing"]["deeper"].is_null(), "lookups chain");

to_string() renders it like a compiler error: config.json:3:17: error: expected ',' or '}'.

The path given to parse, which names the text in to_string(); empty when none was given.

JsonError()

Creates an error.

Parameters

  • message — what is wrong
  • path — the name of the text, or empty
  • line — the line of the error, from 1
  • column — the column of the error, from 1
  • offset — the byte offset of the error, from 0

Methods

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the error as a compiler prints one: path:line:column: error: message, without the path: when there is no path and without line:column: when line is 0.

Returns

  • the rendered error

parse

parse( text: String, comments: bool = false, path: String = "", max_depth: ulong = 1000 ): Result<JsonValue, JsonError>

Parses JSON text into a JsonValue.

Parsing is strict RFC 8259: one value, surrounded only by spaces, tabs and line breaks. A byte-order mark at the start is skipped. The text must be valid UTF-8, and a string cannot hold a raw control character or a \u escape of an unpaired surrogate ("\uD800"). When an object repeats a key, the last value wins, in the place of the first.

With comments = true the text may be JSONC, as VS Code's settings files are: // line comments, /* */ block comments, and a trailing comma after the last element or member. The comments are skipped.

Nesting comes from the text, so the parser keeps its own stack rather than recursing, and max_depth bounds it.

Parameters

  • text — the JSON text
  • comments — whether to accept comments and trailing commas
  • path — the name of the text (a file name, say), which the error's to_string() puts first
  • max_depth — how deeply arrays and objects may nest

Returns

  • the value, or an error naming the first problem and its line and column

Example

import json;

var parsed = json.parse("{\"server\": {\"port\": 8080}}");
assert(parsed.value()["server"]["port"].as_int().value() == 8080, "a lookup");
var bad = json.parse("[1 2]", path = "list.json");
assert(bad.error().to_string() == "list.json:1:4: error: expected ',' or ']'", "where");

Documents with comments

JsonDocument: a JSONC document that keeps its comments, so a settings file can be read, changed and written back with them.

Source: runtime/json/document.pep

JsonDocument

struct JsonDocument

A JSON value with the comments of the JSONC text it was read from, as parse_document makes it.

Each comment belongs to a value, by the value's path from the root $ ($.editor.tab_size, $.files[0]): the comments on the lines before a value, or on the line it ends (after its comma), stay with it, and those before a closing bracket stay at the end of their array or object. to_string() writes them back in those places, so text read and written unchanged keeps every comment, in the indented layout to_pretty_string uses.

Change root freely. A comment whose value is gone (a removed key, an array shortened past it) is not written; one whose path names another value afterwards (an element shifted into its index) goes with that value.

Example

import json;

var text = "{\n  // The editor.\n  \"tab_size\": 4, // spaces\n  \"wrap\": true\n}";
var document = json.parse_document(text).value();
document.root["wrap"] = json.JsonValue.Bool(false);
assert(
    document.to_string() == "{\n  // The editor.\n  \"tab_size\": 4, // spaces\n  \"wrap\": false\n}",
    "the comments stay"
);
assert(document.comments("$.tab_size")[0] == "// The editor.", "by path");

Replaces the comments on the lines before the value at path. Each must be a whole comment, // ... (one line) or /* ... */.

  • path — the value's path from the root, as for comments
  • comments — the comments to write before the value; empty removes them

Panics

  • if a comment does not start with // or /* ("a JSONC comment starts with '//' or '/*'")

to_string

to_string(indent: int = 2, ascii_only: bool = false): String

Returns the document as indented JSONC text with its comments, each element and member on its own line, as to_pretty_string writes it.

Parameters

  • indent — the number of spaces per level of nesting
  • ascii_only — whether to escape every non-ASCII character as \u

Returns

  • the text, without a final line break

Panics

  • if indent is negative ("JsonDocument.to_string needs a non-negative indent")

parse_document

parse_document(text: String, path: String = "", max_depth: ulong = 1000): Result<JsonDocument, JsonError>

Parses JSONC text into a JsonDocument, keeping its comments.

The text is read as parse reads it with comments = true: // and /* */ comments, and a trailing comma after the last element or member. Use it to change a file people edit, such as a settings file, and write it back with its comments; use parse when the comments do not matter.

Parameters

  • text — the JSONC text
  • path — the name of the text (a file name, say), which the error's to_string() puts first
  • max_depth — how deeply arrays and objects may nest

Returns

  • the document, or an error naming the first problem and its line and column

Struct conversion

Struct conversion: encode and decode turn Pepper values into JSON text and back, through reflection, with no per-type code to write.

Source: runtime/json/convert.pep

UnknownKeys

enum UnknownKeys

What decode does with an object key that names no property of the struct it is read into.

Cases

Ignore

Ignore

Skips the key and its value.

Reject

Reject

Fails with an error naming the key and its path.

to_json

to_json<T>(value: T): JsonValue

Converts value to a JsonValue.

T may be a number type, bool, String, an enum (a case that carries no values as its name, "Point"; one that carries values as {"Circle": {"radius": 2}}; [Tag] and [Untagged] choose other forms), Optional<U> (the value, or null), Array<U>, a map with String keys (HashMap, OrderedMap or Map) as an object, JsonValue itself, or a struct, whose public properties become an object's members in declaration order. Element and property types follow the same rules, so structs nest.

A struct property takes its key from [Name("key")] when it has one, and is left out when marked [Ignore] (the attributes of the serialize module, which json exports). A property of a struct type that holds no object (a struct field never assigned) is written as null. An empty Array, even one never assigned, is written as [].

The conversion is generated while compiling, by a static block per type. A type it cannot convert, such as a Result or an io.File, is a compile error naming the property: 'encode' cannot convert property 'outcome' of type 'Result<int>' to JSON.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value

Parameters

  • value — the value to convert

Returns

  • the value as JSON

Example

import json;

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 1;
    p.y = 2;
    assert(json.to_json(p)["y"].as_int().value() == 2, "a member");
    return 0;
}

encode

encode<T>(value: T, indent: int = 0, ascii_only: bool = false): String

Writes value as JSON text, converting it as to_json does.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value

Parameters

  • value — the value to write
  • indent — spaces per nesting level; 0, the default, writes compact text on one line
  • ascii_only — whether to escape every character outside ASCII as \u

Returns

  • the JSON text

Example

import json;

struct ServerConfig {
    var host: String;
    var port: int;
    [Name("max-connections")]
    var max_connections: int;
    [Ignore]
    var started_at: long;
}

main(): int {
    var config = ServerConfig();
    config.host = "localhost";
    config.port = 8080;
    config.max_connections = 16;
    var text = json.encode(config);
    assert(text == "{\"host\":\"localhost\",\"port\":8080,\"max-connections\":16}", "compact");
    return 0;
}

from_json

from_json<T>(value: JsonValue, unknown_keys: UnknownKeys = UnknownKeys.Ignore): Result<T, JsonError>

Converts a JsonValue to a T, the reverse of to_json.

A struct is made with its constructor that takes no arguments, then each property found in the object is read in. A missing key leaves its property at its default, unless the property is marked [Required], which makes it an error; a property marked [Ignore] is never read. A key that names no property is skipped, or with unknown_keys = UnknownKeys.Reject is an error.

A number converts to an integer type when it has no fraction and fits the type, and to float or double always. null converts only to an Optional (as none) and to JsonValue.

An error names where in the document it is, as a path from the root $ in its value_path and at the start of its message, and has no line or column, since there is no text: $.server.port: expected a number, found a string.

Type parameters

  • T — the type to convert to

Parameters

  • value — the JSON value
  • unknown_keys — what to do with an object key that names no property

Returns

  • the converted value, or the first error

Example

import json;

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var parsed = json.parse("{\"x\": 1, \"y\": 2}");
    var p = json.from_json<Point>(parsed.value());
    assert(p.value().y == 2, "a property");
    return 0;
}

decode

decode<T>( text: String, unknown_keys: UnknownKeys = UnknownKeys.Ignore, comments: bool = false, path: String = "" ): Result<T, JsonError>

Parses JSON text and converts it to a T: parse, then from_json.

Type parameters

  • T — the type to convert to

Parameters

  • text — the JSON text
  • unknown_keys — what to do with an object key that names no property
  • comments — whether to accept JSONC: comments and trailing commas
  • path — the name of the text (a file name, say), which the error's to_string() puts first

Returns

  • the value, or the first error: a syntax error, or a conversion error with its path in the document; either has its line and column

Example

import json;

struct ServerConfig {
    var host: String;
    [Required]
    var port: int;
    var tags: Array<String>;
    var timeout: int?;
}

main(): int {
    var config = json.decode<ServerConfig>("{\"host\": \"a\", \"port\": 80, \"tags\": [\"x\"]}");
    assert(config.value().port == 80, "a number");
    assert(config.value().tags[0] == "x", "an array");
    assert(config.value().timeout.is_empty(), "a missing optional");

    var bad = json.decode<ServerConfig>("{\"port\": \"80\"}", path = "server.json");
    assert(bad.error().to_string() == "server.json:1:10: error: $.port: expected a number, found a string", "a path");
    return 0;
}

The serialize module

Serialization attributes: how a struct's properties are written to and read from text formats.

json reads these attributes when it converts a struct (json.encode, json.decode), and other formats will share them, so one set of attributes describes a type for every format. Write them above a property (or an enum or one of its cases: Tag, Untagged, Name); import serialize brings them in, and import json alone is enough too, since json exports them.

Example

import json;

struct ServerConfig {
    var host: String;
    [Name("max-connections")]
    var max_connections: int;
    [Required]
    var port: int;
    [Ignore]
    var started_at: long;
}

Source: runtime/serialize/module.pep

Name

[Attribute] struct Name

Writes a property, or an enum case, under value rather than under its own name.

Example

import json;

struct Limits {
    [Name("max-connections")]
    var max_connections: int;
}

Fields

value

const value: String

The key the property is written under, or the name the case is written as.

Ignore

[Attribute] struct Ignore

Leaves a property out: it is not written, and reading leaves it as it was.

Required

[Attribute] struct Required

Makes a missing key an error when reading. Without it, a missing key leaves the property at its default.

Tag

[Attribute] struct Tag

Writes an enum's cases as objects that name their case under key, rather than as {"Case": {...}}.

Without content, a case's values sit beside the tag: {"kind": "Circle", "radius": 2}. With content, they go in an object under that key: {"kind": "Circle", "data": {"radius": 2}}. A case that carries no values is {"kind": "Point"} either way. Write it above an enum.

Example

import json;

[Tag("kind")]
enum Shape {
    Circle(radius: int),
    Point,
}

Fields

key

const key: String

The key that holds the case's name.

content

const content: String = ""

The key that holds the case's values, or empty to put them beside the tag.

Untagged

[Attribute] struct Untagged

Writes an enum's cases with no tag at all: a case that carries values as the object of its values ({"radius": 2}), and one that carries none as its name ("Point").

Reading tries each case in order and takes the first that reads without an error, so list a case whose values are a superset of another's first. Write it above an enum.

Example

import json;

[Untagged]
enum Size {
    Fixed(px: int),
    Auto,
}

The toml module

TOML: parse a document into a TomlValue, look values up and change them, write tables back as documents, edit a document in place keeping its comments and layout, and convert structs to TOML and back.

Bring it in with import toml. Parsing follows TOML 1.0 and checks all of its rules; errors carry a line and column, like a compiler's. Tables keep their keys in the order they were written.

  • TomlValue: TomlValue, TomlDateTime
  • Parsing: parse, TomlError
  • Writing: to_string, to_document
  • Documents with comments: parse_document, TomlDocument, for changing a file people edit, such as pep.toml, without reformatting it
  • Struct conversion: encode, decode, to_toml, from_toml, UnknownKeys, with the attributes of the serialize module

Example

import toml;

main(): int {
    var parsed = toml.parse("[package]\nname = \"demo\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\n");
    if (parsed.is_err()) {
        print(parsed.error().to_string());
        return 1;
    }
    var root = parsed.value();
    assert(root.lookup("package.name").value().as_string().value() == "demo", "a string");
    var package = root["package"];
    package["edition"] = toml.TomlValue.Integer(2026);
    print(root.to_document());
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/toml/module.pep

TomlValue

TomlValue: a TOML value of any kind, and TomlDateTime, TOML's dates and times.

Source: runtime/toml/value.pep

TomlDateTime

struct TomlDateTime

A TOML date, time, or date and time: an offset date-time (1979-05-27T07:32:00Z), a local date-time (1979-05-27T07:32:00), a local date (1979-05-27) or a local time (07:32:00.5).

has_date, has_time and has_offset say which of the four it is; the fields of a part it does not have are 0. to_string() writes it in the RFC 3339 form TOML uses, with as many fraction digits as it was read with.

Example

import toml;

var when = toml.TomlDateTime.offset(1979, 5, 27, 7, 32, 0, -420);
assert(when.to_string() == "1979-05-27T07:32:00-07:00", "an offset");
assert(toml.TomlDateTime.date(2024, 2, 29).to_string() == "2024-02-29", "a date");

The year, 0 to 9999; 0 without a date.

hour

The hour, 0 to 23.

minute

The minute, 0 to 59.

second

The second, 0 to 59.

nanosecond

The fraction of the second, in nanoseconds.

fraction_digits

var fraction_digits: int

How many digits of the fraction to_string() writes, 0 to 9; 0 writes none.

offset_minutes

var offset_minutes: int

The offset from UTC in minutes (-07:00 is -420); 0 for Z.

has_date

Whether it has a date.

has_time

Whether it has a time of day.

has_offset

Whether it has an offset from UTC, which only a date and time has.
