TomlValue

enum TomlValue

A TOML value: a string, an integer, a float, a boolean, a date-time, an array or a table. toml.parse makes a table from a document, and to_document writes one back.

Look members up with value["key"] and elements with value[index], which panic when there is none; try_get and lookup give none instead, and lookup follows a dotted key ("package.name"). Then read the value with an as_ method, which gives none when the value is of another kind, or match on its case.

A Table keeps its keys in the order they were written. An Array or Table case holds its array or map by reference, so changing them through value[key] = ... or append changes every holder of the value.

Example

import toml;

var package = toml.TomlValue.table();
package["name"] = toml.TomlValue.String("demo");
package["authors"] = toml.TomlValue.array([toml.TomlValue.String("Ada")]);
assert(package.to_string() == "{ name = \"demo\", authors = [\"Ada\"] }", "inline");
assert(package["name"].as_string().value() == "demo", "a lookup");

Source: runtime/toml/parse.pep

TomlError

struct TomlError

What parse reports when the text is not TOML, and what decode reports when a value does not fit its property: what is wrong, and the line and column where it is.

to_string() renders it like a compiler error: pep.toml:4:12: error: expected '='.

Fields

var message: String

What is wrong, worded like a compiler error (expected '=').

path

var path: String

The path given to parse, which names the text in to_string(); empty when none was given.

line

var line: ulong

The line of the error, from 1; 0 for an error with no text to point into, such as one from from_toml.

column

var column: ulong

The column of the error, from 1, counting bytes as clang does; 0 when line is.

offset

var offset: ulong

The byte offset of the error in the text, from 0.

value_path

var value_path: String

Where in the document the value an error is about is, as a path from the root $ ($.package.version, $.bin[0].name); empty for an error in the text's syntax. decode and from_toml set it, and start message with it.

Constructor

TomlError()

construct(message: String = "", path: String = "", line: ulong = 1, column: ulong = 1, offset: ulong = 0)

Creates an error.

Parameters

  • message — what is wrong
  • path — the name of the text, or empty
  • line — the line of the error, from 1
  • column — the column of the error, from 1
  • offset — the byte offset of the error, from 0

Methods

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the error as a compiler prints one: path:line:column: error: message, without the path: when there is no path and without line:column: when line is 0.

Returns

  • the rendered error

parse

parse(text: String, path: String = "", max_depth: ulong = 1000): Result<TomlValue, TomlError>

Parses a TOML 1.0 document into a TomlValue, a Table.

Every rule of TOML 1.0 is checked: a key or table defined twice, a table extended after it was closed (an inline table, or one written with dotted keys in another section), strings, numbers and dates as the specification spells them. The text must be valid UTF-8; a byte-order mark at the start is skipped. Tables keep their keys in the order they were written. A line break in a multi-line string reads as \n, also when the text has \r\n.

Arrays and inline tables nest as deeply as the text says, so the parser keeps its own stack rather than recursing, and max_depth bounds it.

Parameters

  • text — the TOML text
  • path — the name of the text (a file name, say), which the error's to_string() puts first
  • max_depth — how deeply arrays and inline tables may nest

Returns

  • the document's table, or an error naming the first problem and its line and column

Example

import toml;

var parsed = toml.parse("[server]\nport = 8080\n");
assert(parsed.value()["server"]["port"].as_int().value() == 8080, "a lookup");
var bad = toml.parse("name \"demo\"", path = "pep.toml");
assert(bad.error().to_string() == "pep.toml:1:6: error: expected '=' after the key", "where");

Writing

Writing TOML: values on one line, and tables as documents.

Source: runtime/toml/write.pep

Documents with comments

TomlDocument: a TOML document changed in place, keeping its comments, blank lines and layout, as pepper package add changes pep.toml.

Source: runtime/toml/document.pep

TomlDocument

struct TomlDocument

A TOML document that keeps the text it was read from, so a file people edit can be changed and written back without reformatting it.

set and remove change only the text they must: a changed value is rewritten where it stands, a new key goes after the last key of its table, a new table goes at the end, and a removed key or table takes its lines with it, along with the comment lines right above them. Every other byte, comments included, stays as it was. Each edit parses the result again, so root() and get always see the current text.

Keys are given as arrays, outermost first (["dependencies", "json5"]), so a key holding a dot needs no quoting. An edit cannot reach inside an array of tables ([[bin]]); set or remove the whole array instead.

Example

import toml;

var text = "[package]\nname = \"demo\"  # the name\n\n[dependencies]\njson5 = \"1.0\"\n";
var document = toml.parse_document(text).value();
document.set(["package", "version"], toml.TomlValue.String("0.2.0")).value();
document.set(["dependencies", "yaml"], toml.TomlValue.String("0.3")).value();
document.remove(["dependencies", "json5"]).value();
assert(
    document.to_string()
        == "[package]\nname = \"demo\"  # the name\nversion = \"0.2.0\"\n\n[dependencies]\nyaml = \"0.3\"\n",
    "only the edits change"
);

Constructor

TomlDocument()

construct()

Creates an empty document.

Methods

root

root(): TomlValue

Returns the document's table, as parse reads the current text. Changing it does not change the document; use set and remove.

Returns

  • the root table

get

get(keys: Array<String>): TomlValue?

Returns the value at keys.

Parameters

  • keys — the keys, outermost first

Returns

  • the value, or none when a part is missing or is not a table

lookup

lookup(key: String): TomlValue?

Returns the value at a dotted key, read as TOML reads a key: package.name, dependencies."my.package".

Parameters

  • key — the dotted key

Returns

  • the value, or none when it is missing or key is not a valid TOML key

set

set(keys: Array<String>, value: TomlValue, inline: bool = false): Result<void, TomlError>

Sets the value at keys, adding the key, and any tables above it, when it is missing.

A key that is there has its value rewritten in place, on one line; a key inside an inline table rewrites that inline table. A new key goes after the last key of the table it belongs to, indented like it, or under a new [header] at the end when that table has no section to put it in. A new table value (or array of tables) is written as its own [header] section at the end, unless inline is true, which writes it { ... } on the key's line instead, as cargo add writes a dependency.

Parameters

  • keys — the keys, outermost first
  • value — the value to store
  • inline — whether a new table value is written as an inline table rather than a section

Returns

  • nothing, or an error when a part of keys holds a value that is not a table, or lies inside an array of tables

Panics

  • if keys is empty ("TomlDocument.set needs a key")

remove

remove(keys: Array<String>): Result<bool, TomlError>

Removes the key or table at keys, with its lines and the comment lines right above them. Removing a table removes its sections, the tables below it, and any dotted keys that define it.

Parameters

  • keys — the keys, outermost first

Returns

  • whether something was removed, or an error when a part of keys lies inside an array of tables

Panics

  • if keys is empty ("TomlDocument.remove needs a key")

to_string

to_string(): String

Returns the document's text, with every edit made.

Returns

  • the TOML text

parse_document

parse_document(text: String, path: String = ""): Result<TomlDocument, TomlError>

Parses a TOML document into a TomlDocument, to change it in place.

The text is read as parse reads it. Use it to change a file people edit, such as pep.toml, and write it back with its comments and layout; use parse when only the values matter.

Parameters

  • text — the TOML text
  • path — the name of the text (a file name, say), which an error's to_string() puts first

Returns

  • the document, or an error naming the first problem and its line and column

Struct conversion

Struct conversion: encode and decode turn Pepper values into TOML documents and back, through reflection, with no per-type code to write. They read the same serialize attributes json does, so one set of attributes describes a type for both formats.

Source: runtime/toml/convert.pep

UnknownKeys

enum UnknownKeys

What decode does with a table key that names no property of the struct it is read into.

Cases

Ignore

Ignore

Skips the key and its value.

Reject

Reject

Fails with an error naming the key and its path.

to_toml

to_toml<T>(value: T): TomlValue?

Converts value to a TomlValue.

T may be a number type, bool, String, TomlDateTime, an enum (a case that carries no values as its name, "Point"; one that carries values as { Circle = { radius = 2 } }), Optional<U>, Array<U>, a map with String keys (HashMap, OrderedMap or Map) as a table, TomlValue itself, or a struct, whose public properties become a table's members in declaration order. Element and property types follow the same rules, so structs nest.

TOML has no null, so what JSON writes as null is left out: an empty Optional, a String or struct property that holds no object, and such an element of an array or map. A ulong past the largest TOML integer, 2^63 - 1, is written as a float.

A struct property takes its key from [Name("key")] when it has one, and is left out when marked [Ignore] (the attributes of the serialize module, which toml shares with json).

The conversion is generated while compiling, by a static block per type. A type it cannot convert, such as a Result, is a compile error naming the property: 'encode' cannot convert property 'outcome' of type 'Result<int>' to TOML.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value

Parameters

  • value — the value to convert

Returns

  • the value as TOML, or none when there is nothing to write

Example

import toml;

struct Point {
    var x: int;
    var y: int;
}

main(): int {
    var p = Point();
    p.x = 1;
    p.y = 2;
    assert(toml.to_toml(p).value()["y"].as_int().value() == 2, "a member");
    return 0;
}

encode

encode<T>(value: T): String

Writes value, a struct or a map, as a TOML document, converting it as to_toml does.

Type parameters

  • T — the type of the value

Parameters

  • value — the value to write

Returns

  • the document text

Panics

  • if value does not convert to a table, as a number or an array does ("toml.encode needs a value that converts to a table")

Example

import toml;

struct Package {
    var name: String;
    var version: String;
    var authors: Array<String>;
}

struct Manifest {
    var package: Package;
    [Name("build-script")]
    var build_script: String?;
}

main(): int {
    var manifest = Manifest();
    manifest.package = Package();
    manifest.package.name = "demo";
    manifest.package.version = "0.1.0";
    manifest.package.authors = ["Ada"];
    var text = toml.encode(manifest);
    assert(text == "[package]\nname = \"demo\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nauthors = [\"Ada\"]\n", "a document");
    return 0;
}

from_toml

from_toml<T>(value: TomlValue, unknown_keys: UnknownKeys = UnknownKeys.Ignore): Result<T, TomlError>

Converts a TomlValue to a T, the reverse of to_toml.

A struct is made with its constructor that takes no arguments, then each property found in the table is read in. A missing key leaves its property at its default (an empty Optional, for one), unless the property is marked [Required], which makes it an error; a property marked [Ignore] is never read. A key that names no property is skipped, or with unknown_keys = UnknownKeys.Reject is an error.

An integer converts to an integer type it fits, and to float or double; a float converts only to float or double.

An error names where in the document it is, as a path from the root $ in its value_path and at the start of its message, and has no line or column, since there is no text: $.package.version: expected a string, found an integer.

Type parameters

  • T — the type to convert to

Parameters

  • value — the TOML value
  • unknown_keys — what to do with a key that names no property

Returns

  • the converted value, or the first error

decode

decode<T>( text: String, unknown_keys: UnknownKeys = UnknownKeys.Ignore, path: String = "" ): Result<T, TomlError>

Parses a TOML document and converts it to a T: parse, then from_toml.

Type parameters

  • T — the type to convert to

Parameters

  • text — the TOML text
  • unknown_keys — what to do with a key that names no property
  • path — the name of the text (a file name, say), which the error's to_string() puts first

Returns

  • the value, or the first error: a syntax error, or a conversion error with its path in the document; either has its line and column when the value it is about is written in the text

Example

import toml;

struct Package {
    [Required]
    var name: String;
    var version: String;
    var authors: Array<String>;
    var edition: int?;
}

struct Manifest {
    [Required]
    var package: Package;
}

main(): int {
    var text = "[package]\nname = \"demo\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nauthors = [\"Ada\"]\n";
    var manifest = toml.decode<Manifest>(text);
    assert(manifest.value().package.name == "demo", "a string");
    assert(manifest.value().package.authors[0] == "Ada", "an array");
    assert(manifest.value().package.edition.is_empty(), "a missing optional");

    var bad = toml.decode<Manifest>("[package]\nname = 7\n", path = "pep.toml");
    assert(
        bad.error().to_string() == "pep.toml:2:8: error: $.package.name: expected a string, found an integer",
        "where"
    );
    return 0;
}

The compress module

Compression: DEFLATE (RFC 1951) with its zlib and gzip framings, in one call or as streams, and the CRC-32 and Adler-32 checksums.

Bring it in with import compress. It is written in Pepper, so it needs no zlib, unless the program is built with -D USE_ZLIB, which makes it use zlib with the same API. Corrupt data is an io.IoError whose is_invalid_input() holds.

  • Formats and streams: Format, Deflate, Zlib, Gzip, DecompressReader, CompressWriter
  • Checksums: Crc32, Adler32

Example

import compress;

main(): int {
    var data = "to be or not to be, that is the question".bytes();
    var packed = compress.Gzip.compress(data);
    assert(compress.Gzip.decompress(packed).value() == data, "round trip");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/compress/module.pep

Formats and streams

Format, the one-call Deflate, Zlib and Gzip functions, and the streaming DecompressReader and CompressWriter.

Source: runtime/compress/format.pep

Format

enum Format

The framing around DEFLATE-compressed data.

Example

import compress;

var packed = compress.Gzip.compress("hi".bytes());
var reader = compress.DecompressReader(io.ByteReader(packed), compress.Format.Gzip);

Cases

Raw

Raw

Raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951) with no header or checksum, as zip archives and HTTP's Content-Encoding: deflate from some servers carry it.

Zlib

Zlib

zlib (RFC 1950): a two-byte header, DEFLATE, then an Adler-32 checksum. PNG images and HTTP's deflate encoding use it.

Gzip

Gzip

gzip (RFC 1952): a header, DEFLATE, then a CRC-32 and the length. .gz files and HTTP's gzip encoding use it. Reading accepts several members one after another, as cat a.gz b.gz makes.

Deflate

struct Deflate

Raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951) data, compressed or decompressed in one call.

Example

import compress;

var data = "abcabcabcabc".bytes();
var packed = compress.Deflate.compress(data);
assert(compress.Deflate.decompress(packed).value() == data, "round trip");

Static methods

compress

static compress(data: u8[], level: int = 6): u8[]

Compresses data into raw DEFLATE data.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to compress
  • level — from 0 (store without compressing) through 9 (smallest output, slowest); 6 balances the two, as zlib's default does

Returns

  • the compressed bytes

Panics

  • if level is not 0 through 9 ("compression level must be 0 through 9")

decompress

static decompress(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<u8[]>

Decompresses raw DEFLATE data. Bytes after the end of the compressed data are ignored.

Parameters

  • data — the compressed bytes

Returns

  • the decompressed bytes; an is_invalid_input() error when data is not valid DEFLATE data or ends too soon

Zlib

struct Zlib

zlib (RFC 1950) data, compressed or decompressed in one call.

Example

import compress;

var packed = compress.Zlib.compress("hello".bytes());
assert(packed[0] == 0x78, "the zlib header");
assert(compress.Zlib.decompress(packed).value() == "hello".bytes(), "round trip");

Static methods

compress

static compress(data: u8[], level: int = 6): u8[]

Compresses data into a zlib stream.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to compress
  • level — from 0 (store without compressing) through 9 (smallest output, slowest); 6 balances the two

Returns

  • the compressed bytes

Panics

  • if level is not 0 through 9 ("compression level must be 0 through 9")

compress

static compress(data: u8[], dictionary: u8[], level: int = 6): u8[]

Compresses data into a zlib stream that starts from a preset dictionary: bytes the data is likely to repeat, such as the common keys of small JSON messages, which the stream can then refer back to without carrying them. The header names the dictionary by its Adler-32, and decompressing needs the same dictionary. Only its last 32 KiB are used.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to compress
  • dictionary — the preset dictionary
  • level — from 0 (store without compressing) through 9 (smallest output, slowest); 6 balances the two

Returns

  • the compressed bytes

Panics

  • if level is not 0 through 9 ("compression level must be 0 through 9")

Example

import compress;

var dictionary = "{\"name\": \"\", \"email\": \"\"}".bytes();
var data = "{\"name\": \"Ada\", \"email\": \"ada@example.com\"}".bytes();
var packed = compress.Zlib.compress(data, dictionary);
assert(compress.Zlib.decompress(packed, dictionary).value() == data, "round trip");

decompress

static decompress(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<u8[]>

Decompresses a zlib stream and checks its Adler-32 checksum. Bytes after the stream are ignored. A stream made with a preset dictionary needs the overload that takes one.

Parameters

  • data — the compressed bytes

Returns

  • the decompressed bytes; an is_invalid_input() error when data is not a valid zlib stream, ends too soon, fails its checksum, or needs a preset dictionary

decompress

static decompress(data: u8[], dictionary: u8[]): io.IoResult<u8[]>

Decompresses a zlib stream that may need a preset dictionary, and checks its Adler-32 checksum. A stream that does not ask for a dictionary decompresses as without one.

Parameters

  • data — the compressed bytes
  • dictionary — the preset dictionary the stream was compressed with

Returns

  • the decompressed bytes; an is_invalid_input() error when data is not a valid zlib stream, ends too soon, fails its checksum, or names a dictionary whose Adler-32 is not that of dictionary

Gzip

struct Gzip

gzip (RFC 1952) data, as in .gz files, compressed or decompressed in one call.

Example

import compress;
import io;

var packed = compress.Gzip.compress("hello".bytes());
io.File.write_bytes(io.Path("hello.txt.gz"), packed);
assert(compress.Gzip.decompress(packed).value() == "hello".bytes(), "round trip");

Static methods

compress

static compress(data: u8[], level: int = 6): u8[]

Compresses data into one gzip member with no file name and no modification time.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to compress
  • level — from 0 (store without compressing) through 9 (smallest output, slowest); 6 balances the two

Returns

  • the compressed bytes

Panics

  • if level is not 0 through 9 ("compression level must be 0 through 9")

decompress

static decompress(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<u8[]>

Decompresses gzip data, checking each member's CRC-32 and length. Several members one after another decompress to their contents joined. The header's file name, comment and extra field are skipped.

Parameters

  • data — the compressed bytes

Returns

  • the decompressed bytes; an is_invalid_input() error when data is not valid gzip data, ends too soon, fails a check, or has bytes after the last member

DecompressReader

struct DecompressReader

A Reader that decompresses another stream as it is read, such as a .gz file or an HTTP response body, without holding all of it in memory.

It reads its source in chunks of up to 64 KiB and keeps at most about 160 KiB of output, however large the data. Corrupt or truncated data is an is_invalid_input() error from read, after the bytes decoded before the problem; an error from the source is passed on.

Example

import compress;
import io;

var file = io.File.open(io.Path("notes.txt.gz")).value();
var reader = compress.DecompressReader(file, compress.Format.Gzip);
for (var line in reader.lines()) {
    print(line.value());
}

Constructors

DecompressReader()

construct(source: io.Reader, format: Format)

Makes a reader of the decompressed contents of source.

Parameters

  • source — the stream of compressed bytes
  • format — the framing of the compressed data

DecompressReader()

construct(source: io.Reader, format: Format, dictionary: u8[])

Makes a reader of the decompressed contents of source, which was compressed with a preset dictionary (see Zlib.compress). A zlib stream uses it when its header asks for it; raw DEFLATE data always starts from it.

Parameters

  • source — the stream of compressed bytes
  • format — Format.Zlib or Format.Raw
  • dictionary — the preset dictionary

Panics

  • if format is Format.Gzip ("gzip data has no preset dictionary")

Methods

read

read(buffer: u8[], max: ulong): io.IoResult<ulong>

Decompresses up to max more bytes and appends them to buffer.

Parameters

  • buffer — the array the bytes are appended to
  • max — the most bytes to read

Returns

  • the number of bytes appended, 0 at the end of the compressed data; an error when the data is invalid or the source fails

read_all

read_all(): io.IoResult<u8[]>

Decompresses the rest of the stream.

Returns

  • the decompressed bytes not read yet; an error as for read

CompressWriter

struct CompressWriter

A Writer that compresses what is written to it and writes the result to another stream, such as a .gz file.

Compressed bytes reach the sink in pieces as blocks fill; finish() writes the rest and the format's trailer, and must be called once at the end, since dropping the writer does not. It does not close the sink.

Example

import compress;
import io;

var file = io.File.create(io.Path("log.txt.gz")).value();
var writer = compress.CompressWriter(file, compress.Format.Gzip);
writer.print_line("first line");
writer.print_line("second line");
writer.finish();
file.close();

Constructors

CompressWriter()

construct(sink: io.Writer, format: Format, level: int = 6)

Makes a writer that compresses into sink.

Parameters

  • sink — the stream the compressed bytes are written to
  • format — the framing to write
  • level — from 0 (store without compressing) through 9 (smallest output, slowest); 6 balances the two

Panics

  • if level is not 0 through 9 ("compression level must be 0 through 9")

CompressWriter()

construct(sink: io.Writer, format: Format, dictionary: u8[], level: int = 6)

Makes a writer that compresses into sink, starting from a preset dictionary (see Zlib.compress). A zlib header names the dictionary by its Adler-32; raw DEFLATE data carries no sign of it.

Parameters

  • sink — the stream the compressed bytes are written to
  • format — Format.Zlib or Format.Raw
  • dictionary — the preset dictionary; only its last 32 KiB are used
  • level — from 0 (store without compressing) through 9 (smallest output, slowest); 6 balances the two

Panics

  • if level is not 0 through 9 ("compression level must be 0 through 9"), or if format is Format.Gzip ("gzip data has no preset dictionary")

Methods

write

write(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<ulong>

Compresses all of data.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to compress

Returns

  • data.count; an error when writing to the sink fails

Panics

  • if finish() was called ("CompressWriter used after finish()")

write_all

write_all(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<void>

Compresses all of data.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to compress

Returns

Panics

finish

finish(): io.IoResult<void>

Compresses what is still buffered, writes the format's trailer, and ends the stream. Later calls do nothing.

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when writing to the sink fails

Checksums

Crc32 and Adler32: the checksums gzip and zlib streams carry, for checking data as it is read or written.

Source: runtime/compress/checksum.pep

Crc32

struct Crc32

The CRC-32 checksum (IEEE 802.3, the polynomial gzip, zip and PNG use), computed over data given in one or more pieces.

Example

import compress;

var crc = compress.Crc32();
crc.update("hello ".bytes());
crc.update("world".bytes());
assert(crc.value == compress.Crc32.of("hello world".bytes()), "same in pieces");
assert(compress.Crc32.of("123456789".bytes()) == 0xCBF43926, "the check value");

The archive module

Archives: tar files, read entry by entry, extracted safely into a directory, or written.

Bring it in with import archive. Combine it with compress for .tar.gz: wrap the file in a compress.DecompressReader to read one, or in a compress.CompressWriter to write one. A damaged archive is an io.IoError whose is_invalid_input() holds.

  • Tar archives: TarReader, TarWriter, TarEntry, EntryKind
  • Entry paths: safe_components

Example

import archive;
import io;

main(): int {
    var out = io.ByteWriter();
    var writer = archive.TarWriter(out);
    writer.append_file("hello.txt", "hi\n".bytes());
    writer.finish();

    var reader = archive.TarReader(io.ByteReader(out.bytes));
    var entry = reader.next_entry().value().value();
    assert(entry.path == "hello.txt" && entry.size == 3, "the header");
    assert(reader.read_all().value() == "hi\n".bytes(), "the contents");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/archive/module.pep

Tar archives

TarReader and TarWriter: tar archives (POSIX ustar, with the pax and GNU extensions for long names), read entry by entry from a stream, extracted safely into a directory, or written.

Source: runtime/archive/tar.pep

EntryKind

enum EntryKind

What a tar entry is.

Cases

File

File

A regular file, whose contents follow the entry's header.

Directory

Directory

A directory.

Symlink

Symlink

A symbolic link to TarEntry.link_target.

HardLink

HardLink

A hard link to the earlier entry named TarEntry.link_target.

Other

Other

Anything else: a device, a FIFO, or a type this reader does not know.

TarEntry

struct TarEntry

One entry of a tar archive: its header, without its contents.

Example

import archive;

var entry = archive.TarEntry("bin/run.sh", archive.EntryKind.File);
entry.mode = 493;   # octal 755: rwxr-xr-x

Fields

path

var path: String

The path in the archive, with / between components, as stored (a directory's may end with /).

kind

var kind: EntryKind

What the entry is.

size

var size: ulong

The length of the contents in bytes; 0 for anything but a file.

mode

var mode: uint

The permission bits, such as 420 (octal 644, rw-r--r--).

modified

var modified: long

The modification time, in seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC.

link_target

var link_target: String

The target of a symlink or hard link; empty otherwise.

Constructor

TarEntry()

construct(path: String = "", kind: EntryKind = EntryKind.File)

Makes an entry with the given path and kind, mode 420 (octal 644) for a file and 493 (octal 755) otherwise, size 0 and modification time 0.

Parameters

  • path — the path in the archive
  • kind — what the entry is

TarReader

struct TarReader

Reads a tar archive from a stream, one entry at a time: next_entry() moves to the next entry and returns its header, then read (it is an io.Reader) reads that entry's contents. Contents not read are skipped.

It reads POSIX ustar archives and the pax (x) and GNU (L, K) extensions for long paths, link targets and sizes, which is what GNU tar, bsdtar and Git (git archive, and the .tar.gz snapshots GitHub, GitLab and Codeberg serve) write. Global pax headers (g) are skipped. Wrap the source in a compress.DecompressReader to read a .tar.gz.

Example

import archive;
import compress;
import io;

var file = io.File.open(io.Path("release.tar.gz")).value();
var tar = archive.TarReader(compress.DecompressReader(file, compress.Format.Gzip));
while (true) {
    var entry = tar.next_entry().value();
    if (entry.is_empty()) {
        break;
    }
    print(entry.value().path);
}

Constructor

TarReader()

construct(source: io.Reader)

Makes a reader of the archive in source, before its first entry.

Parameters

  • source — the stream of the archive

Methods

next_entry

next_entry(): io.IoResult<TarEntry?>

Moves to the next entry, skipping what is left of the current one's contents, and returns its header.

The archive ends at two zero blocks, as tar writes, or at the end of the stream between entries.

Returns

  • the next entry, or none at the end of the archive; an is_invalid_input() error for a damaged or truncated archive, or the source's error

read

read(buffer: u8[], max: ulong): io.IoResult<ulong>

Reads up to max more bytes of the current entry's contents and appends them to buffer.

Parameters

  • buffer — the array the bytes are appended to
  • max — the most bytes to read

Returns

  • the number of bytes appended, 0 at the end of the entry's contents (or before the first next_entry()); an error when the archive is truncated or the source fails

read_all

read_all(): io.IoResult<u8[]>

Reads the rest of the current entry's contents.

Returns

  • the bytes not read yet; an error as for read

extract

extract(target: io.Path, strip_components: ulong = 0): io.IoResult<void>

Extracts the rest of the archive into the directory target, creating it and any directories the entries need.

Each entry's path is checked first, so that no archive can write outside target: an absolute path, a .. component, a \ or a : (which Windows would read as a separator or a drive) is an is_invalid_input() error. Files are written (replacing a file already there) and directories created; a hard link becomes a copy of the file it names, which must be an earlier entry. Devices and FIFOs are skipped.

Each file and directory gets the entry's modification time and, on Linux and macOS, its permission bits less the process umask, as tar gives them by default, so a script keeps its executable bit; the setuid, setgid and sticky bits are never applied. A directory's mode and time are set once everything inside it is written, so a read-only directory can still be filled. A directory that already exists keeps its own. On Windows and WASI permission bits are not applied.

Symlinks are made after every other entry, so no file is ever written through one, and only when they stay inside target: a link whose target is absolute or climbs out of target with .., or that would be made inside another symlink, is skipped. Windows, where making a symlink needs Developer Mode or an administrator, skips them all.

Parameters

  • target — the directory to extract into
  • strip_components — how many leading path components to drop from each entry, as tar's --strip-components does: 1 drops the name-version/ directory that GitHub's snapshots put everything in. An entry with no components left is skipped.

Returns

  • an Ok result once every entry is extracted; an is_invalid_input() error for an unsafe path or a damaged archive, or the error of a file that could not be written

Example

import archive;
import compress;
import io;

var file = io.File.open(io.Path("pepper-main.tar.gz")).value();
var tar = archive.TarReader(compress.DecompressReader(file, compress.Format.Gzip));
tar.extract(io.Path(".pep/deps/pepper"), strip_components = 1).value();

TarWriter

struct TarWriter

Writes a tar archive to a stream: each append writes one entry's header and contents, and finish() writes the end-of-archive marker.

It writes POSIX ustar headers, and a pax header before an entry whose path or link target does not fit one (a path over 100 bytes that cannot be split at a / into 155 and 100), so every path is kept whole. Owner ids are 0 and owner names empty. Wrap the sink in a compress.CompressWriter to write a .tar.gz.

Example

import archive;
import io;

var out = io.ByteWriter();
var tar = archive.TarWriter(out);
tar.append_directory("docs");
tar.append_file("docs/readme.txt", "hello\n".bytes());
tar.finish();
assert(out.bytes.count == 4 * 512 + 2 * 512, "headers, contents, end marker");

append

Appends an entry with the given header and contents. The size written is data.count for a file and 0 for anything else, whatever entry.size holds.

append_stream

append_stream(entry: TarEntry, source: io.Reader): io.IoResult<void>

Appends a file entry whose contents are read from source: exactly entry.size bytes, so a large file need not be in memory.

Parameters

  • entry — the entry's header; its kind must be File
  • source — the stream holding the contents

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when reading or writing fails, or an is_invalid_input() error when source ends before entry.size bytes (the archive is then incomplete)

Panics

  • if finish() was called ("TarWriter used after finish()")
  • if entry.kind is not File ("append_stream needs a file entry")

Example

var file = io.File.open(io.Path("big.bin")).value();
var entry = archive.TarEntry("big.bin");
entry.size = file.metadata().value().size;
tar.append_stream(entry, file);

finish

finish(): io.IoResult<void>

Writes the end-of-archive marker (two zero blocks). Later calls do nothing. It does not close the sink.

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when writing to the sink fails

Entry paths

safe_components: checking an entry's path before extracting it, so an archive cannot write outside the directory it is extracted into.

Source: runtime/archive/path.pep

safe_components

safe_components(path: String): String[]?

Splits the path of an archive entry into its components, or gives none when extracting it could write outside the target directory ("zip slip"): an absolute path, a .. component, a \ or a : (which Windows would read as a separator or a drive letter). Empty and . components are left out, so a//./b/ gives a and b.

TarReader.extract checks every entry with it, and so does the zip package; a reader of another archive format should too.

Parameters

  • path — the entry's path as stored, with / between components

Returns

  • the components to join onto the target directory, or none for an unsafe path

Example

import archive;

assert(archive.safe_components("docs/./readme.md").value().count == 2, "safe");
assert(archive.safe_components("../etc/passwd").is_empty(), "climbs out");
assert(archive.safe_components("C:/Windows").is_empty(), "a drive");

The digest module

Cryptographic hashes: SHA-256, SHA-1 and BLAKE3, and HMAC.

Bring it in with import digest. Each hash has an incremental hasher (update any number of times, then finish) and a one-shot function, and both take bytes (u8[]) or a String (its UTF-8 bytes). A digest is a u8[]; to_hex writes it as text.

  • SHA-256: Sha256, sha256
  • SHA-1: Sha1, sha1, for formats that need it, such as git object ids
  • BLAKE3: Blake3, blake3, with keyed hashing, key derivation and output of any length
  • HMAC: Hmac, hmac_sha256, hmac_sha1, and equal_constant_time to check a MAC, and pbkdf2_sha256, PBKDF2 over HMAC-SHA-256
  • Hexadecimal: to_hex and from_hex

The implementations are portable Pepper with no link dependency, unless the program is built with -D USE_LIBCRYPTO: then SHA-256 and SHA-1 call OpenSSL's libcrypto (CNG on Windows), which uses the CPU's SHA instructions. They are not hardened against timing side channels, which matters only when hashing secrets.

For the hash tables of HashMap and HashSet, use hash<T> instead: it is much faster, but neither cryptographic nor stable between versions.

Example

import digest;

main(): int {
    var id = digest.to_hex(digest.sha256("hello"));
    assert(id == "2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824", "SHA-256");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/digest/module.pep

SHA-256

SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4): 32-byte digests, as used to check downloads and sign data.

Source: runtime/digest/sha256.pep

Sha256

struct Sha256

An incremental SHA-256 hasher: feed it bytes with update, any number of times and in pieces of any size, then read the 32-byte digest with finish.

The digest of the input is the same however it was split between update calls. finish resets the hasher, so it can hash a new input.

Example

import digest;

var hasher = digest.Sha256();
hasher.update("hello ");
hasher.update("world");
assert(hasher.finish_hex() == digest.to_hex(digest.sha256("hello world")), "same digest");

SHA-1

SHA-1 (FIPS 180-4): 20-byte digests, as git uses for object ids. SHA-1 is broken for collision resistance; use it to read existing formats, and SHA-256 or BLAKE3 for anything new.

Source: runtime/digest/sha1.pep

Sha1

struct Sha1

An incremental SHA-1 hasher: feed it bytes with update, any number of times and in pieces of any size, then read the 20-byte digest with finish.

SHA-1 is not collision resistant: someone can make two inputs with the same digest. Use it only where a format requires it, such as git object ids. finish resets the hasher, so it can hash a new input.

Example

import digest;

# The id git gives an empty file ("blob 0" and a NUL byte).
u8[] nul = [0];
var hasher = digest.Sha1();
hasher.update("blob 0");
hasher.update(nul);
assert(hasher.finish_hex() == "e69de29bb2d1d6434b8b29ae775ad8c2e48c5391", "git blob id");

BLAKE3

BLAKE3: 32-byte digests, faster than SHA-256 in hardware without SHA instructions, and the hash the compiler's build cache keys objects with. Also a keyed hash (a MAC), key derivation, and output of any length.

Source: runtime/digest/blake3.pep

Blake3

struct Blake3

An incremental BLAKE3 hasher: feed it bytes with update, any number of times and in pieces of any size, then read the 32-byte digest with finish.

Blake3() is the default hash mode; Blake3.keyed and Blake3.derive_key make hashers for the other two modes, and finish(length) reads output of any length in each.

This is a portable implementation, one block at a time; it does not use SIMD or threads, so it runs well below the speed of the official C and Rust implementations. The digests are the same. finish resets the hasher, so it can hash a new input.

Example

import digest;

var hasher = digest.Blake3();
hasher.update("hello ");
hasher.update("world");
assert(hasher.finish_hex() == digest.to_hex(digest.blake3("hello world")), "same digest");

Constructor

Blake3()

construct()

Creates a hasher in the initial state, with no input.

Static methods

keyed

static keyed(key: u8[]): Blake3

Returns a hasher for BLAKE3's keyed mode, a MAC: only someone with key can compute or check the digest of an input.

Parameters

  • key — the 32-byte secret key

Returns

  • a hasher with no input, keyed with key

Panics

  • if key is not 32 bytes

Example

import digest;

var key = digest.blake3("a key made some other way");
var mac = digest.Blake3.keyed(key);
mac.update("message");
assert(mac.finish().count == 32, "a 32-byte MAC");

derive_key

static derive_key(context: String): Blake3

Returns a hasher for BLAKE3's key derivation mode: the digest of its input (the key material, such as a shared secret or a password hash) is a key for the purpose that context names.

context should be a hard-coded string, unique to the application and the purpose, such as "example.com 2026-10-16 session tokens v1"; different contexts give unrelated keys from the same material. Read the key with finish, or finish(length) for one of another length.

Parameters

  • context — the application and purpose the key is for

Returns

  • a hasher with no input, for keys in context

Example

import digest;

var hasher = digest.Blake3.derive_key("example.com 2026-10-16 session tokens v1");
hasher.update("the shared secret");
var key = hasher.finish();

HMAC

HMAC (RFC 2104): a message authentication code from a hash and a secret key, as webhook signatures, JWTs (HS256) and S3-style request signing use, and a constant-time comparison to check one. Also PBKDF2, the password-based key derivation built on HMAC-SHA-256.

Source: runtime/digest/hmac.pep

Hmac

struct Hmac<T>

An incremental HMAC hasher over the hash T: feed it the message with update, any number of times and in pieces of any size, then read the MAC with finish.

Only someone with the key can compute the MAC of a message, so a receiver that shares the key can check that the message is authentic. Compare a MAC you receive with equal_constant_time, not ==. finish resets the hasher to the same key, so it can sign a new message.

Type parameters

  • T — the hash: Sha256 or Sha1, or another hasher with a 64-byte block, a constructor taking no arguments, and update and finish methods

Example

import digest;

var mac = digest.Hmac<digest.Sha256>("key");
mac.update("The quick brown fox ");
mac.update("jumps over the lazy dog");
var expected = "f7bc83f430538424b13298e6aa6fb143ef4d59a14946175997479dbc2d1a3cd8";
assert(mac.finish_hex() == expected, "HMAC-SHA-256");

A key longer than 64 bytes is hashed with T first, as RFC 2104 says; one as long as T's digest is the usual choice.

pbkdf2_sha256

pbkdf2_sha256(password: u8[], salt: u8[], rounds: ulong, length: ulong): u8[]

Derives length bytes from password and salt with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (RFC 8018), running rounds iterations of HMAC-SHA-256 for each 32-byte block of the output.

This is SCRAM's Hi() (PostgreSQL, MongoDB and SASL logins), and it derives keys from passphrases for formats that specify it. To store new passwords, use Argon2id (crypto.hash_password in pepper-crypto) instead: PBKDF2 needs almost no memory, so GPUs and ASICs test guesses against it cheaply. Where PBKDF2 is required, give each password its own random salt of 16 bytes or more, and as many rounds as the login can afford (OWASP suggests 600,000).

The time grows with rounds times the number of 32-byte blocks, so a length above 32 costs the caller more but an attacker, who needs only the first block, no more.

Parameters

  • password — the password or passphrase
  • salt — the salt
  • rounds — the iteration count, at least 1
  • length — the number of bytes to derive; 0 returns none

Returns

  • the length-byte derived key

Panics

  • if rounds is 0, or length is over (2^32 - 1) * 32 bytes, RFC 8018's limit; under -D USE_LIBCRYPTO, also if a size or rounds is over what the platform takes (2^31 - 1 for libcrypto, 2^32 - 1 bytes for CNG), or the platform's PBKDF2 fails

Example

import digest;

var key = digest.pbkdf2_sha256("passwd".bytes(), "salt".bytes(), 1, 16);
assert(digest.to_hex(key) == "55ac046e56e3089fec1691c22544b605", "RFC 7914 section 11");

pbkdf2_sha256

pbkdf2_sha256(password: String, salt: u8[], rounds: ulong, length: ulong): u8[]

Derives length bytes from the UTF-8 bytes of password and salt with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, as the u8[] overload does.

Parameters

  • password — the password or passphrase
  • salt — the salt
  • rounds — the iteration count, at least 1
  • length — the number of bytes to derive; 0 returns none

Returns

  • the length-byte derived key

Panics

  • if rounds is 0, or length is over (2^32 - 1) * 32 bytes, RFC 8018's limit; under -D USE_LIBCRYPTO, also if a size or rounds is over what the platform takes (2^31 - 1 for libcrypto, 2^32 - 1 bytes for CNG), or the platform's PBKDF2 fails

Example

import digest;

var key = digest.pbkdf2_sha256("passwd", "salt".bytes(), 1, 16);
assert(digest.to_hex(key) == "55ac046e56e3089fec1691c22544b605", "RFC 7914 section 11");

equal_constant_time

equal_constant_time(a: u8[], b: u8[]): bool

Returns whether a and b hold the same bytes, taking the same time wherever they first differ.

Check a MAC with this rather than ==, which stops at the first difference: timing it would let an attacker find a valid MAC a byte at a time. The lengths are not secret, so arrays of different lengths return false at once.

Parameters

  • a — the first bytes, such as the MAC computed
  • b — the second bytes, such as the MAC received

Returns

  • true if a and b have the same length and bytes

Example

import digest;

var mac = digest.hmac_sha256("key", "message");
assert(digest.equal_constant_time(mac, digest.hmac_sha256("key", "message")), "a valid MAC");

Hexadecimal

Hexadecimal text for digests, and back.

Source: runtime/digest/hex.pep

to_hex

to_hex(bytes: u8[]): String

Returns bytes as lowercase hexadecimal text, two digits per byte, the way checksums and git object ids are usually written.

Parameters

  • bytes — the bytes to write, such as a digest from finish

Returns

  • a String of 2 * bytes.count characters from 0-9a-f

Example

import digest;

assert(digest.to_hex([0, 15, 255]) == "000fff", "two digits per byte");

from_hex

from_hex(text: String): Result<u8[]>

Returns the bytes that hexadecimal text stands for, two digits per byte, the reverse of to_hex. Upper- and lowercase digits are both accepted.

Parameters

  • text — hexadecimal text, such as a checksum

Returns

  • the bytes, or an error when text has an odd length or a character that is not a hexadecimal digit

Example

import digest;

var bytes = digest.from_hex("000fFF").value();
assert(bytes.count == 3 && bytes[2] == 255, "two digits per byte");
assert(digest.from_hex("abc").is_err(), "an odd length");

The random module

Random numbers: bytes from the operating system's secure source, and Generator, a fast seedable generator for everything else.

random is a module: bring it in with import random (and write random.next_int(1..>6)) or import names directly with import [Generator, shuffle] from random.

  • Entropy: bytes, fill and secure_ulong, from the operating system, for keys, tokens and identifiers
  • Generators: Generator, seeded from entropy or from a fixed seed, and next_int, next_double, next_bool, choose and shuffle on this thread's own generator

Example

import random;

main(): int {
    var die = random.next_int(1..>6);            # 1 to 6
    var names = ["ada", "grace", "edsger"];
    random.shuffle(names);
    var key = random.bytes(32);                   # 32 secure bytes
    var replay = random.Generator(42);            # the same numbers every run
    print(replay.next_double());
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/random/module.pep

Entropy

Secure random bytes from the operating system: getentropy on Linux, Android, macOS, iOS and WASI, and BCryptGenRandom on Windows. They are unpredictable, so they suit keys, tokens and identifiers, but each call asks the kernel; a Generator is much faster for everything else.

Source: runtime/random/entropy.pep

Generators

Generator, a fast pseudo-random generator, and functions that use this thread's own generator, so code that only needs a random number need not pass one around.

The algorithm is xoshiro256** (Blackman and Vigna): 256 bits of state, a period of 2^256 - 1, and statistically strong output. It is not secure: anyone who sees enough output can predict the rest, so keys and tokens come from random.bytes instead.

Source: runtime/random/generator.pep

The base64 module

Base64 (RFC 4648): bytes written as text, for HTTP basic authentication, data URIs, JSON Web Tokens, PEM files and WebSocket handshakes.

Bring it in with import base64. encode writes the standard alphabet (A-Z a-z 0-9 + /) with = padding; pass url_safe for the URL and file name alphabet (- and _ in place of + and /), and padded = false to leave the padding off, as JSON Web Tokens do. decode takes text with or without padding, and rejects anything else that is not base64, including whitespace.

Example

import base64;

main(): int {
    var text = base64.encode("user:secret".bytes());
    assert(text == "dXNlcjpzZWNyZXQ=", "standard, padded");
    var bytes = base64.decode(text).value();
    assert(bytes.count == 11 && bytes[0] == 'u', "round trip");
    assert(base64.encode([251, 255], true, false) == "-_8", "URL-safe, unpadded");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/base64/module.pep

encode

encode(bytes: u8[], url_safe: bool = false, padded: bool = true): String

Returns bytes as base64 text: four characters for each three bytes.

Parameters

  • bytes — the bytes to write
  • url_safe — true for the URL and file name alphabet, with - and _ in place of + and /
  • padded — false to leave off the = that pads the text to a multiple of four characters

Returns

  • the base64 text, empty when bytes is

Example

assert(base64.encode("hi".bytes()) == "aGk=", "padded");
assert(base64.encode("hi".bytes(), false, false) == "aGk", "unpadded");

decode

decode(text: String, url_safe: bool = false): Result<u8[]>

Returns the bytes that base64 text stands for.

The padding is optional, but when present it must complete the last group of four. The decoding is strict, so each text has one meaning: a character outside the alphabet (whitespace included), a length no encoding gives, or unused bits that are not zero is an error.

Parameters

  • text — base64 text, such as aGk= or aGk
  • url_safe — true for the URL and file name alphabet, with - and _ in place of + and /

Returns

  • the decoded bytes, or an error naming what is not base64

Example

var bytes = base64.decode("aGk").value();
assert(bytes.count == 2 && bytes[1] == 'i', "unpadded");
assert(base64.decode("a b=").is_err(), "a space");

The uuid module

UUIDs (RFC 9562): 128-bit identifiers, written as 0190163d-8694-739b-aea5-966c26f8ad91.

Bring it in with import uuid (or import [Uuid] from uuid). Uuid.v4() makes a random one; Uuid.v7() puts the time first, so ids made later sort later, which keeps database indexes compact. Both draw their random bits from the operating system's secure source (random.bytes).

Example

import uuid;

main(): int {
    var id = uuid.Uuid.v4();
    var text = id.to_string();                       # such as 9b2c3c1e-...
    assert(uuid.Uuid.parse(text).value() == id, "round trip");
    assert(id.version() == 4, "random");
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/uuid/module.pep

Uuid

[Value] struct Uuid

A UUID, as a value struct of two 64-bit halves: == compares them and hash hashes them, so a Uuid works as a map key.

Example

var id = Uuid.parse("0190163D-8694-739B-AEA5-966C26F8AD91").value();
assert(id.version() == 7, "the version digit");
assert(id.to_string() == "0190163d-8694-739b-aea5-966c26f8ad91", "lowercase");

The first 8 bytes, the first byte in the top bits.

low

The last 8 bytes, the first of them in the top bits.

v7

static v7(): Uuid

Returns a new time-ordered UUID (version 7): the wall clock's Unix time in milliseconds in the first 48 bits, then 74 random bits. Ids made in different milliseconds sort by time, both as values and as text; ids made in the same millisecond are in no particular order.

Returns the UUID that text writes: 32 hexadecimal digits, either case, in groups of 8, 4, 4, 4 and 12 separated by -.

Parameters

Returns

The cli module

Command-line parsing: declare a program's options and arguments, then parse them, with the help, version and error messages generated from the declarations.

Bring it in with import cli. The raw arguments stay where they are, in main(args: String[]) and process.arguments().

  • Parser: Parser, and the handles its declarations return: Flag, Argument, ArgumentList; and closest, which picks the name a misspelled one most likely meant
  • Completions: Shell, the shells Parser.completions writes a completion script for
  • Options: Option and Positional, the attributes that shape what Parser.add_options declares from a struct's fields

Example

import cli;

main(args: String[]): int {
    var parser = cli.Parser("greet", "Greets someone");
    var loud = parser.flag("loud", "l", "shout the greeting");
    var name = parser.positional("name", "who to greet", required = false, default_value = "world");
    if (!parser.parse(args)) {
        return 2;
    }
    var greeting = $"hello, {name.value()}";
    print(loud.is_set ? greeting.upper() : greeting);
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/cli/module.pep

Parser

Parser and the handles its declarations return: Flag, Argument and ArgumentList.

Source: runtime/cli/parser.pep

Parser

struct Parser

Declares a program's command-line interface and parses its arguments.

Declare each option and positional argument with flag, option, multiple, positional and positionals; each returns a handle that reads its value once parse has run. parse also writes the help (--help), the version (--version) and clang-style errors, all from the declarations.

Options have a long name (--output), a one-letter short name (-o), or both. A value follows as --output a.out, --output=a.out, -o a.out or -oa.out; short flags combine (-vq is -v -q), and -- ends the options, so every argument after it is positional. A value is taken as it is, even when it starts with -. An option declared with an implicit_value takes a value only when it is attached (--emit-ast=json, -O3), and the implicit one when it is not. When an option that takes one value is given twice, the last value wins.

Subcommands (git add, pep-package update) are parsers of their own, made with command. Options before the command's name belong to this parser, and everything after it to the command's.

Example

import cli;

main(args: String[]): int {
    var parser = cli.Parser("pepper", "Compiles a Pepper program", version = "0.2.1");
    var output = parser.option("output", "o", "the executable to write", default_value = "a.out");
    var imports = parser.multiple("import-path", "I", "a directory to search for modules");
    var verbose = parser.flag("verbose", "v", "say what is happening");
    var source = parser.positional("source", "the program's entry file");
    if (!parser.parse(args)) {
        return 2;
    }
    print($"{source.value()} -> {output.value()}");
    return 0;
}

Properties

is_selected

var is_selected: bool { get; }

Whether the last parse reached this parser: whether this command was given. The top-level parser is selected whenever its arguments were parsed.

Parameters

  • name — the program's name, as the help and errors show it

Declares an option that takes one String value, such as --output a.out. option<T> declares one whose value is a number, a path or an enum case.

option

option<T>( name: String, short_name: String = "", help: String = "", value_name: String = "", default_value: String = "", required: bool = false, global: bool = false, implicit_value: String = "" ): Argument<T>

Declares an option that takes one value of type T, such as --jobs 4 for option<int>. A value that does not read as a T fails the parse: invalid value 'x' for '--jobs': expected an integer.

T may be String, an integer type, float, double, io.Path, or an enum whose cases carry no values; a case is written in kebab case (DebugInfo is debug-info), and the help lists them.

  • required — whether leaving the option out is an error
  • global — whether the option may also be given after the name of a command, at any depth
  • implicit_value — the value when the option is given without one, written as on the command line (-O alone as -O2); when not empty, a value must be attached (--name=value, -xvalue) and the next argument is never taken as one

  • help — what the values are, for the help

command

command(name: String, about: String = ""): Parser

Declares a subcommand, such as add in pep-package add NAME, and returns its parser, on which to declare its own options and arguments.

A parser with commands requires one: the first argument that is not an option names it, and the arguments after it go to its parser. After parse, is_selected on the command's parser tells whether it was the one given.

Parameters

  • name — the command's name
  • about — what the command does, for the help

Returns

  • the command's parser

Panics

  • if name is empty, starts with - or is already declared, or if this parser has positional arguments

add_options

add_options<T>(options: T)

Declares an option or positional argument for each public field of options, and has every successful parse store the values in those fields.

A field's type picks what it declares: bool is a flag, String an option with one value, String? one that may be left out, and String[] one that may be given many times. An option is named after its field, with each _ written - (import_path is --import-path); [cli.Option] on a field gives it a short name, help, another name, or makes it required. [cli.Positional] makes a field the next positional argument instead.

A String field that holds a value when this is called keeps it as the default; an empty one has no default, so leaving the option out leaves it empty, or is an error for a positional argument. Every parse sets every field: a flag to whether it was given, a list to the values given.

The declarations are the same as the builder methods make, so the help and errors read the same, and the two styles mix on one parser.

Type parameters

  • T — the options struct

Parameters

  • options — the struct whose fields to declare and fill in

Example

import cli;

struct Options {
    [cli.Option("o", "the executable to write")]
    var output: String = "a.out";
    [cli.Option("v", "say what is happening")]
    var verbose: bool;
    [cli.Positional("the program's entry file")]
    var source: String;
}

main(args: String[]): int {
    var options = Options();
    var parser = cli.Parser("pepper", "Compiles a Pepper program");
    parser.add_options(options);
    if (!parser.parse(args)) {
        return 2;
    }
    print($"{options.source} -> {options.output}");
    return 0;
}

usage

usage(): String

Returns the one-line usage, such as usage: pepper [OPTIONS] <source>.

Returns

  • the usage line, without a line break

help

help(): String

Returns the help that --help prints: what the program does, the usage, and a line for each argument, option and command.

Returns

  • the help text, ending in a line break

completions

completions(shell: Shell): String

Returns a script that completes this program's command line in shell: its options, commands and enum choices, and file names where a value is a String or an io.Path. A program usually prints it from a command of its own (pkg completions bash), for the user to install where Shell's cases say.

Call it on the program's parser, after the declarations.

Parameters

  • shell — the shell the script is for

Returns

  • the script, ending in a line break

Example

var parser = cli.Parser("pkg");
var shell = parser.option<cli.Shell>("completions", help = "print a completion script");
if (!parser.parse(args)) {
    return 2;
}
if (shell.is_set) {
    print(parser.completions(shell.value()));
}

try_parse

try_parse(args: String[]): Result<String?>

Parses args and fills in every handle, or reports the problem.

Writes nothing. Use it to handle errors, help and the version yourself; parse does it the usual way.

Parameters

  • args — the arguments as main receives them: the program's name, then its arguments

Returns

  • some text when --help or --version was given (the program should print it and exit with 0), none when the arguments were parsed, or an error when they are wrong, with a clang-style message such as missing value for '-o'

parse

parse(args: String[]): bool

Parses args and fills in every handle.

For --help or --version it prints the text to standard output and ends the program with status 0. When the arguments are wrong it writes the error, the usage and a hint to standard error, such as

pepper: error: missing value for '-o'
usage: pepper [OPTIONS] <source>
Run 'pepper --help' for more information.

and returns false; exit with status 2, as the example does.

Parameters

  • args — the arguments as main receives them: the program's name, then its arguments

Returns

  • true when the arguments were parsed, false after an error

usage_error

usage_error(message: String): int

Writes a usage error found after parse, such as two options that cannot be used together, as parse writes one: the error, this parser's usage and a hint, to standard error.

Parameters

Returns

  • 2, the status a program exits with after a usage error

Example

if (test.is_set and library.is_set) {
    return parser.usage_error("'--test' cannot be used with '--lib'");
}

closest

closest(name: String, candidates: Array<String>): String?

Returns the candidate closest to a misspelled name, for a "did you mean" suggestion: the one the fewest single-byte insertions, deletions and substitutions turn name into, when that is at most 2. Of equally close candidates the first wins.

Parameters

  • candidates — the names it could have meant

Returns

Example

var names = Array<String>();
names.append("build");
names.append("fmt");
var best = cli.closest("buidl", names);   # some("build")

import cli;

Declares a field of an options struct as the next positional argument instead of an option. Shell

enum Shell

A shell that Parser.completions writes a completion script for.

Cases

Bash

Bash

GNU Bash: source the script, or put it in ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/NAME.

Zsh

Zsh

Zsh: put the script in a directory on $fpath as _NAME.

Fish

Fish

Powershell

Powershell

PowerShell (powershell on a command line): dot-source the script from your profile.

The http module

HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 clients and servers, over TCP or TLS.

Bring it in with import http. A Client sends a Request to an http:// or https:// URL and returns the Response; a Server accepts connections on every worker of async.run and answers each request with a handler function. Bodies are read into memory, or streamed through an io.Reader (Client.open, set_reader). Over TLS the client and server choose HTTP/2 through ALPN when both have it, with the same Request and Response types.

  • Messages: Headers, Request, and Response
  • Client: Client, Session and BodyReader
  • Server: Server, Connection and reason_phrase

Example

import async;
import http;
import io;

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("127.0.0.1:0").value()).value();
        var port = server.local_address().value().port();
        async.spawn<void>(() => {
            server.serve((request) => {
                return http.Response(200).set_text("hello");
            });
        });
        var response = http.Client().get("http://127.0.0.1:" + to_string(port) + "/").value();
        assert(response.text() == "hello", "served");
    });
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/http/module.pep

Requests and responses

HTTP messages: Headers, Request and Response, the values a Client sends and receives and a Server handler takes and returns.

Source: runtime/http/message.pep

Headers

struct Headers

HTTP header fields, by name. Names ignore ASCII case: they are stored lowercased, so Content-Type and content-type are the same field. A name may hold several values, kept in the order added. Different names have no defined order, as HTTP allows.

Headers takes any name and value, but a Client refuses to send a field name that is not an RFC 9110 token or a value with CR, LF or NUL, and a Server answers 500 instead of sending one.

Example

var headers = http.Headers();
headers.add("Accept", "text/html");

struct Response

An HTTP response.

Client.send returns one with the body read in full; Client.open returns one whose body is read as it arrives, through reader(). upgrade

upgrade(protocol: String, takeover: (Connection) => void): Response

Makes this a 101 Switching Protocols response that hands the connection to takeover, for a protocol that starts as HTTP/1.1, such as WebSocket. The server sends the status, Upgrade: protocol, Connection: Upgrade and the other headers (no Content-Length, no body), then calls takeover in the connection's task with the connection, and serves no more HTTP on it. The connection closes when takeover returns, or earlier at Connection.close().

Only a request whose can_upgrade() is true can be upgraded: for any other (HTTP/1.0, or an HTTP/2 stream) the server sends 501 Not Implemented instead and never calls takeover.

Parameters

  • protocol — the Upgrade field: the protocol the connection switches to, such as websocket
  • takeover — speaks the new protocol on the connection; bytes the client sent right after the request are the first it reads

Returns

  • this response

Example

echo(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    return http.Response().upgrade("echo", (connection) => {
        for (var chunk in connection.chunks(4096)) {
            connection.write_all(chunk.value());
        }
    });
}

The HTTP client: Client sends a Request over HTTP or HTTPS and returns the Response.

Client

[Shared] struct Client

Sends HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests and reads their responses.

Each request opens a new connection (plain TCP for http://, TLS for https://), sends the request with Connection: close, and reads the response: send reads the whole body into memory, and open returns once the header fields arrive, with the body to read as a stream. To send requests on connections kept open between them, use a Session (client.session()).

For https:// the client offers HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 through ALPN and speaks the one the server chooses; the request and response are the same either way. Over HTTP/2 the response's reason is the standard phrase for its status. Plain http:// uses HTTP/1.1.

Redirects (301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 with a Location) are followed, up to max_redirects of them, as RFC 9110 describes: 303, and 301 or 302 after a POST, become a GET without the body; 307 and 308 repeat the method and body. A request whose body comes from Request.set_reader cannot be repeated, so its 307 or 308 is returned as it is. When a redirect leaves the origin (scheme, host and port), Authorization, Proxy-Authorization and Cookie are dropped. Make a client with max_redirects 0 to get every redirect back as it is.

A client is [Shared]: make one and use it from every thread and task. In a task, a request parks only the task while it waits.

Example

import http;

main(): int {
    var client = http.Client();
    var response = client.get("https://example.com/").value();
    print(to_string(response.status));   # 200
    print(response.text());
    return 0;
}

open

open(request: Request): io.IoResult<Response>

Sends request and returns the response as soon as its header fields arrive, with the body still to read: response.reader() returns it as a BodyReader, which reads it from the connection as it arrives, with no limit on its size. Use it for a large download, writing each chunk to a file or through a compress.DecompressReader.

The connection closes when the body has been read to its end, when the BodyReader is closed, or when the last reference to it goes. The request goes out, and redirects are followed, as for send.

Parameters

Returns

Example

var response = client.open(http.Request("GET", "https://example.com/large.tar.gz")).value();
var archive = compress.DecompressReader(response.reader(), compress.Format.Gzip);
var file = io.File.create(io.Path("large.tar")).value();
for (var chunk in archive.chunks(65536)) {
    file.write_all(chunk.value());
}

Returns a new Session that sends requests with this client's settings and keeps their connections open for the requests after them.

Returns

  • the session, with no connections yet

Session

struct Session

A run of requests that share connections: each connection stays open after its response (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive) and the next request to the same scheme, host and port uses it again, saving the TCP and TLS handshakes. Make one with client.session(); it sends requests and follows redirects with that client's settings.

A connection goes back to the session once its response body has been read to its end (which send does), unless the server asked to close it. Up to max_idle_per_host connections wait for each scheme, host and port; one idle for longer than idle_timeout is closed instead of used. A request that finds its reused connection closed by the server is sent again on a new one, unless its body came from Request.set_reader.

Over HTTP/2 the session keeps one connection per origin, which every request to that origin shares at once on a stream of its own, so tasks started with spawn_local can send through one session concurrently.

A session is not [Shared]: use it from one thread or task. Its connections close when the last reference to it (and to the BodyReaders it returned) goes, or at close().

Example

var session = http.Client().session();
for (var page in 1..>3) {
    var response = session.get($"https://example.com/items?page={page}").value();
    print(response.text());
}
# One connection carried all three requests.

The body of a response from Client.open, read from the connection as it arrives. It is an io.Reader: read it with read, chunks or lines, or hand it to anything that takes a stream. Server

The HTTP server: Server accepts HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 connections on every worker of async.run and answers each request with a handler function.

Source: runtime/http/server.pep

MAX_REQUEST_BODY

const MAX_REQUEST_BODY: ulong = 16777216

The largest request body a Server reads: 16 MiB. A larger one gets 413 Content Too Large.

Server

[Shared] struct Server

An HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 server.

Server.bind listens on an address (Server.bind_tls serves HTTPS); serve then accepts connections on every worker of the running async.run and serves each connection in a task of its own, calling the handler for every request. Connections are kept open between requests unless the client asks to close (or speaks HTTP/1.0).

The handler gets the Request with its body read in full and returns the Response; the server adds Content-Length (and Connection: close when it will close). A request the server cannot parse gets 400 Bad Request, one with header fields over 64 KiB 431 Request Header Fields Too Large, and one with a body over MAX_REQUEST_BODY 413 Content Too Large; the connection then closes. A response whose reason phrase or field value holds CR, LF or NUL, or whose field name is not an RFC 9110 token, is sent as 500 Internal Server Error instead, since those characters would split the response; the 500's text body names the field (or the reason phrase) at fault.

HTTP/2 is served to a client that chooses it through ALPN (see bind_tls) or that starts a plain TCP connection with the HTTP/2 preface (prior knowledge): each stream is a request, answered by the same handler in a task of its own.

Example

import async;
import http;
import io;

hello(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    var response = http.Response(200).set_text("hello from " + request.path());
    response.headers["Content-Type"] = "text/plain";
    return response;
}

main(): int {
    async.run(() => {
        var server = http.Server.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("0.0.0.0:8080").value()).value();
        server.serve(hello);
    });
    return 0;
}

Connection

struct Connection

A connection a Server handler took over by answering with Response.upgrade: the raw stream after the 101 Switching Protocols head, TCP or (under Server.bind_tls) TLS, as an io.Reader and an io.Writer.

Reads return first the bytes the server had already read past the request (a client may send its first message right after the request), then what arrives. Like the handler, it belongs to the connection's task.

Example

upgraded(request: http.Request): http.Response {
    return http.Response().upgrade("echo", (connection) => {
        var data = Array<u8>();
        while (connection.read(data, 4096).value() > 0) {
            connection.write_all(data);
            data.clear();
        }
    });
}
