The tls module

Encrypted connections: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 over TCP, for clients and servers.

Bring it in with import tls. A TlsConnector opens client connections and checks each server's certificate; a TlsAcceptor accepts connections with a certificate and key from PEM files; a TlsStream reads and writes like an io.TcpStream. In a task, a call that has to wait parks only the task.

On Linux and macOS the module uses OpenSSL 3, loaded when the first connector or acceptor is made; on Windows it uses SChannel. On Android the program links a static OpenSSL 3 that the toolchain carries, and a connector trusts the system's certificate store. On iOS it uses the system's Security.framework (Secure Transport, TLS 1.2), for clients only: there TlsAcceptor.create and TlsConnector.set_identity return an error.

  • Streams: TlsConnector, TlsAcceptor, and TlsStream

Example

import tls;

main(): int {
    var connector = tls.TlsConnector.create().value();
    var stream = connector.connect_host("localhost", 8443).value();
    stream.write_all("ping");
    var reply = Array<u8>();
    while (stream.read(reply, 4096).value() > 0) {
    }
    return 0;
}

Source: runtime/tls/module.pep

Connectors and streams

TLS connections: TlsConnector opens client connections, TlsAcceptor accepts server connections, and TlsStream is one encrypted connection over a TcpStream.

Source: runtime/tls/stream.pep

TlsConnector

[Shared] struct TlsConnector

Opens TLS client connections, checking each server's certificate.

A connector trusts the system's root certificates; add_root_certificate trusts more, such as a test certificate authority. Each connect runs the TLS handshake over a connected TcpStream and checks that the server's certificate is valid and issued for the host name given. Only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are offered (on iOS, only TLS 1.2).

A server that asks for a client certificate (mutual TLS) gets the one set with set_identity; without one, the connector presents none.

A connector is [Shared]: make one and use it from every thread and task. Configure it (add_root_certificate, set_identity) before the first connect.

See also

  • TlsStream

Example

import tls;

var connector = tls.TlsConnector.create().value();
var stream = connector.connect_host("localhost", 8443).value();
stream.write_all("ping");

Constructor

TlsConnector()

construct(context: __ptr<void>)

Wraps a platform context. Use TlsConnector.create.

Parameters

  • context — the platform's client context, or null for none

Static methods

create

static create(): io.IoResult<TlsConnector>

Creates a connector that trusts the system's root certificates (on Android, the system's certificate store less those the user turned off, plus those the user installed where the process may read them).

Returns

  • the connector; an error when no TLS library is available (on Linux and macOS, OpenSSL 3: libssl.so.3, or Homebrew's or MacPorts' libssl.3.dylib; on iOS, Security.framework; on Android the program links its own OpenSSL)

Methods

add_root_certificate

add_root_certificate(path: io.Path): io.IoResult<void>

Also trusts the certificates in the PEM file at path, for servers whose certificates the system does not trust, such as a private or test certificate authority.

Parameters

  • path — a file of one or more PEM certificates

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when the file cannot be read or holds no certificate

set_identity

set_identity(certificate_chain: io.Path, private_key: io.Path): io.IoResult<void>

Presents the certificate chain in certificate_chain, with the private key in private_key, to servers that ask for a client certificate (mutual TLS, as a TlsAcceptor does after require_client_certificate). A later call replaces the identity.

Parameters

  • certificate_chain — a PEM file: the client's certificate first, then any intermediate certificates
  • private_key — a PEM file with the certificate's private key (on Windows, PKCS #8: BEGIN PRIVATE KEY)

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when a file cannot be read or the key does not match the certificate, and always on iOS, which does not support client certificates yet

Example

var connector = tls.TlsConnector.create().value();
connector.set_identity(io.Path("client.pem"), io.Path("client-key.pem")).value();
var stream = connector.connect_host("internal.example.com", 443).value();

set_protocols

set_protocols(protocols: String[]): io.IoResult<void>

Offers protocols to every server through ALPN (RFC 7301), most preferred first, such as ["h2", "http/1.1"]. After connect, TlsStream.protocol names the one the server chose, if it chose one. Call it before the first connect; a later call replaces the list.

Parameters

  • protocols — the protocol names, each 1 to 255 bytes

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when the list is empty or a name is empty or longer than 255 bytes

Example

var connector = tls.TlsConnector.create().value();
connector.set_protocols(["h2", "http/1.1"]).value();
var stream = connector.connect_host("example.com", 443).value();
var http2 = stream.protocol() == Optional<String>.Value("h2");

connect

connect(stream: io.TcpStream, host: String): io.IoResult<TlsStream>

Runs the TLS handshake as the client over stream and checks the server's certificate.

Parameters

  • stream — a connected TCP stream; the TlsStream keeps it, and nothing else should read or write it afterwards
  • host — the name the certificate must be for, also sent to the server as the requested name (SNI); an IP address is checked against the certificate's addresses instead

Returns

  • the encrypted stream; an error when the handshake fails or the certificate is not trusted ("certificate verify failed: ..."), or an io error from the socket

connect_host

connect_host(host: String, port: u16): io.IoResult<TlsStream>

Connects to host on port with TcpStream.connect_host, then runs the handshake as connect does.

Parameters

  • host — a host name or an IP address
  • port — the port, usually 443

Returns

  • the encrypted stream; the errors of TcpStream.connect_host and of connect

TlsAcceptor

[Shared] struct TlsAcceptor

Accepts TLS server connections with one certificate.

An acceptor presents a certificate chain and its private key, read from PEM files. Each accept runs the TLS handshake over a TcpStream that a TcpListener accepted. Clients are not asked for certificates unless require_client_certificate is called (mutual TLS).

An acceptor is [Shared], so the accept loops of every worker can share one.

See also

  • TlsStream

Example

import io;
import tls;

var acceptor = tls.TlsAcceptor.create(io.Path("cert.pem"), io.Path("key.pem")).value();
var listener = io.TcpListener.bind(io.SocketAddress.parse("0.0.0.0:8443").value()).value();
while (true) {
    var (tcp, peer) = listener.accept().value();
    var accepted = acceptor.accept(tcp);
    if (accepted.is_ok()) {
        accepted.value().write_all("hello over TLS");
    }
}

Constructor

TlsAcceptor()

construct(context: __ptr<void>)

Wraps a platform context. Use TlsAcceptor.create.

Parameters

  • context — the platform's server context, or null for none

Static methods

create

static create(certificate_chain: io.Path, private_key: io.Path): io.IoResult<TlsAcceptor>

Creates an acceptor that presents the certificate chain in certificate_chain with the private key in private_key.

Parameters

  • certificate_chain — a PEM file: the server's certificate first, then any intermediate certificates
  • private_key — a PEM file with the certificate's private key (on Windows, PKCS #8: BEGIN PRIVATE KEY)

Returns

  • the acceptor; an error when a file cannot be read, the key does not match the certificate, or no TLS library is available (see TlsConnector.create), and always on iOS, which does not support TLS servers yet

Methods

require_client_certificate

require_client_certificate(roots: io.Path): io.IoResult<void>

Asks every client for a certificate and accepts only clients whose certificate is issued by one of the certificates in the PEM file at roots (directly or through intermediates the client sends) and is valid for client authentication. A handshake with a client that sends no certificate, or an untrusted one, fails. Call it before the first accept.

Parameters

  • roots — a file of one or more PEM certificates: the authorities that issue client certificates

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when the file cannot be read or holds no certificate

Example

var acceptor = tls.TlsAcceptor.create(io.Path("cert.pem"), io.Path("key.pem")).value();
acceptor.require_client_certificate(io.Path("clients-ca.pem")).value();

set_protocols

set_protocols(protocols: String[]): io.IoResult<void>

Accepts protocols through ALPN (RFC 7301), most preferred first: the handshake chooses the first of them that the client offers, and TlsStream.protocol names it. A client that offers no protocols connects with none chosen; one that offers only protocols not in the list fails the handshake with the no_application_protocol alert (RFC 7301). Call it before the first accept.

Parameters

  • protocols — the protocol names, each 1 to 255 bytes

Returns

  • an Ok result; an error when the list is empty or a name is empty or longer than 255 bytes

accept

accept(stream: io.TcpStream): io.IoResult<TlsStream>

Runs the TLS handshake as the server over stream.

Parameters

  • stream — a connection a TcpListener accepted; the TlsStream keeps it, and nothing else should read or write it afterwards

Returns

  • the encrypted stream; an error when the handshake fails (including, after require_client_certificate, a client with no trusted certificate), or an io error from the socket

TlsStream

[NotCopyable("owns a TLS connection and cannot be copied")] struct TlsStream

An encrypted connection: TLS over a TcpStream.

Get one from TlsConnector.connect or TlsAcceptor.accept. Reading and writing work as on a TcpStream, on the decrypted bytes: read appends what has arrived and returns 0 once the peer has closed the connection, write may send part of the data, and read_exact and write_all loop until done. In a task, a call that has to wait parks only the task.

shutdown() tells the peer that nothing more is coming (a TLS close_notify). A peer that closes the TCP connection without one also ends the stream: read returns 0.

Closing: the destructor closes the connection when the last reference goes; close() closes it earlier. Neither sends close_notify; call shutdown() first for that.

See also

  • TlsConnector
  • TlsAcceptor

Example

var stream = connector.connect_host("localhost", 8443).value();
stream.write_all("ping");
var reply = Array<u8>();
while (stream.read(reply, 4096).value() > 0) {
}

Constructor

TlsStream()

construct(tcp: io.TcpStream, session: __ptr<void>)

Wraps a finished handshake. Use TlsConnector.connect or TlsAcceptor.accept.

Parameters

  • tcp — the TCP connection
  • session — the platform's session, or null for a closed stream

Methods

is_open

is_open(): bool

Returns whether the stream is open.

Returns

  • false after close()

protocol

protocol(): String?

Returns the protocol the handshake chose through ALPN, from the lists TlsConnector.set_protocols and TlsAcceptor.set_protocols set.

Returns

  • the protocol name, such as h2; none when no protocol was chosen or the stream is closed

read

read(buffer: u8[], max: ulong): io.IoResult<ulong>

Waits until data arrives, then appends up to max decrypted bytes of it to buffer.

Parameters

  • buffer — the array the bytes are appended to
  • max — the most bytes to read; 0 reads nothing and returns 0

Returns

  • the number of bytes appended, 0 once the peer has closed the connection; an error when the stream is closed, a TLS error, or an io error from the socket

read_exact

read_exact(buffer: u8[], count: ulong): io.IoResult<void>

Reads until exactly count more bytes are appended to buffer.

Parameters

  • buffer — the array the bytes are appended to
  • count — the number of bytes to read

Returns

  • an Ok result once count bytes are appended; an error when the connection ends first, or an error as for read. The bytes read before an error stay in buffer.

write

write(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<ulong>

Encrypts and sends bytes from data. The send may be partial; use write_all to send everything.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to send

Returns

  • the number of bytes sent; an error when the stream is closed, a TLS error, or an io error from the socket

write_all

write_all(data: u8[]): io.IoResult<void>

Sends all of data, repeating the send until every byte is sent.

Parameters

  • data — the bytes to send

Returns

  • an Ok result once every byte is sent; an error as for write

write_all

write_all(text: String): io.IoResult<void>

Sends all of the UTF-8 bytes of text, as write_all(u8[]) does. No newline or terminator is added.

Parameters

  • text — the text to send

Returns

  • an Ok result once every byte is sent; an error as for write

Example

stream.write_all("ping");

write_string

[Deprecated("use 'write_all' instead", "write_all")] write_string(text: String): io.IoResult<void>

Deprecated: use write_all instead. Sends all of the UTF-8 bytes of text, exactly like write_all(text).

Parameters

  • text — the text to send

Returns

  • an Ok result once every byte is sent; an error as for write_all

See also

  • write_all

shutdown

shutdown(): io.IoResult<void>

Tells the peer that nothing more is coming (sends a TLS close_notify). The peer's reads return 0 after the data sent before.

Returns

  • an Ok result on success; an error when the stream is closed, or an io error from the socket

close

close(): io.IoResult<void>

Closes the connection now, without a close_notify (see shutdown). Closing a closed stream does nothing.

Returns

  • an Ok result on success or when already closed; the platform error when closing the socket fails

The testing module

The test program pep-build --test builds: a main that lists the entry file's [Test] functions or runs one of them.

A test build loads testing into every file, as --import testing would, and adds to the entry file a main (marked [TestMain], which replaces the file's own) that registers each [Test] function with a TestRunner and calls run. Test files do not import it themselves: the checks they call, such as expect_equal, are in the prelude, and the fixture TempFolder (a scratch folder removed when released) is here.

pep-test (pepper test) drives the program: it lists the tests with --list and runs each in a child process of its own with --run NAME (see the testing chapter).

Source: runtime/testing/module.pep

TestRunner

The main of a test program: TestRunner holds the tests of the files it was built from and answers pep-test's --list and --run NAME.

Source: runtime/testing/runner.pep

keep_for_the_program

keep_for_the_program(body: () => void)

Runs body and lets what it leaves allocated stay without failing the test's leak check: for what a program makes once, on first use, and keeps until it ends, such as a lazily made global (async.Lazy), when a test is the first to use it.

Call it at the start of the test, with the first use alone, so the rest of the test is still checked.

Parameters

  • body — the code that makes what the program keeps

Example

import tls;

[Test]
connects() {
    # The first connector loads the TLS library, which stays loaded.
    keep_for_the_program(() => {
        tls.TlsConnector.create();
    });
    # ... the checks, under the leak check as usual
}

TestMain

[Attribute] struct TestMain

Marks the main that pep-build --test generates: in a test build it replaces the entry file's own main.

TestRunner

struct TestRunner

The tests of one test program, which its generated main registers and then runs with the program's arguments.

The program answers two requests, both made by pep-test:

  • --list prints one line per test, its fields separated by tabs: the name, file:line, returns or panics (for [ShouldPanic]), and the text the panic must contain (empty for any panic or none).
  • --run NAME [--timeout SECONDS] runs the test NAME (or file::NAME, which tells apart tests of one name in two files) and exits with 0 when it returns, or with 1 when it left an allocation behind (or released one too many); a panic aborts the program. With a timeout above 0, a test still running after that many seconds ends the program with exit status 124 and a message on standard error. However the program ends (the test returns, panics, crashes or times out), every process the test started ends with it (a job object on Windows, a process group elsewhere), so none holds pep-test's pipes to its output open.

With PEPPER_TEST_DIRECTORY set and not empty, the program first makes that folder its current one: pep-test sets it where a program cannot start in the folder the tests run from (the iOS simulator).

Constructor

Creates a runner for the tests of file.

Parameters

Makes file the file of the tests registered after this call.

Parameters

TempFolder

TempFolder, a test fixture: a fresh folder that is removed with everything in it when the fixture is released.

Source: runtime/testing/temp_folder.pep

TempFolder

struct TempFolder

A fresh, empty folder under the system's temporary folder, for a test that writes files. The folder and everything in it are removed when the last reference to the fixture is released, so a test that holds it in a local cleans up when it returns.

Its name joins the name the test gives with the process id, so tests running at once, each in a process of its own, never share a folder. When a folder of that name is left from an earlier run (whose process had the same id) and cannot be removed, a number is added to the name, so the folder is always new and empty.

Example

[Test]
writes_a_file() {
    var folder = TempFolder("writes_a_file");
    var path = folder.path.join("notes.txt");
    io.File.write_text(path, "hello");
    expect_equal(io.File.read_to_string(path).value(), "hello");
}

Fields

path

const path: io.Path

The folder's path.

Constructor

construct(name: String)

Makes the folder, removing what a crashed run left at its path, or taking a numbered name when that cannot be removed.

Parameters

  • name — a name for the folder, such as the test's

Panics

  • if the folder cannot be made

Building Pepper from source

Pepper is written in Pepper. The compiler, pep-build, is the Pepper program in tools/compiler (also called pepc), and every other tool is a Pepper program under tools/. Building them takes a Pepper compiler, so the first one comes from a published toolchain, the build of main (stage 0), the same way CI and the release build get theirs. The Rust compiler that once bootstrapped Pepper plays no part.

You need this to work on Pepper itself, or on a platform with no prebuilt binaries. To use Pepper, install it instead.

Setting up

Four steps, on every platform:

  1. The build of main. Every merge into main that changes the compiler, the runtime or the tools publishes it as a prerelease named x.y.z-dev, which pepper install list --available lists. Install it and make it the default, with the install script on a new machine or with pepper install:

    sh scripts/install.sh --version 0.4.0-dev    # the -dev version listed
pepper install add 0.4.0-dev && pepper install use 0.4.0-dev

    A prerelease is picked only by its exact name, never by update or latest. pepper install add --force <version> refreshes it.

  2. Platform prerequisites, for linking:

    • Windows: Visual Studio 2022 or newer with the C++ workload (or the standalone Build Tools), which clang links through; PowerShell (pwsh 7.x is what the setup script is tested with; Windows PowerShell 5.1 also works); and 7-Zip, only for -DevTools, which extracts lldb from the llvm.org installer rather than running it.
    • macOS: the Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install), for the SDK, system headers and ld. The clang that drives the link comes from the LLVM prefix when it has one, which it does on macOS.
    • Linux (Debian/Ubuntu names): sudo apt install build-essential clang curl xz-utils. clang is the link driver, and on Linux nothing else provides one: llvm-20-dev installs no bin/clang into its prefix.

  3. LLVM 20. The compiler links LLVM through the pepper-llvm package, which binds LLVM 20, so building it needs an LLVM 20 development install. One command provisions it (every option is in Setting up LLVM):

    ./scripts/setup-llvm.sh --devtools            # macOS / Linux
pwsh -File scripts/setup-llvm.ps1 -DevTools   # Windows

  4. The packages. tools/compiler depends on pep-lang/pepper-llvm, tools/pep-lsp on pep-lang/pepper-lsp, and tools/pep-package on pep-lang/pepper-semver. The first build of each fetches its package into the tool's .pep/deps, with the pep-package beside the compiler or on the PATH, or with git at the commit pep.lock records when there is none. So pep-package itself builds before any pep-package exists; the release build fetches all three with stage 0's.

Where LLVM comes from

On macOS and Linux your package manager has an LLVM 20 and the script uses it:

platformwhere LLVM comes fromcost
Linuxapt install llvm-20-dev (plus libpolly-20-dev)4–8s, 400–750 MB
macOSbrew install llvm@2013–17s
Windowsthe official release archive896 MB download

Windows needs the archive because nothing else on the platform works: the llvm.org installer and the winget, scoop and chocolatey packages ship neither llvm-config nor the component libraries. The script falls back to the archive on Linux and macOS too, but only when the package manager has no LLVM 20.

That fallback is sound on Linux but usually unusable on macOS: the release tarballs are LTO builds, so their static libraries are LLVM bitcode, and Apple's linker rejects bitcode produced by a newer LLVM than its own (could not parse bitcode object file … Unknown attribute kind). Homebrew's llvm@20 is not LTO-built and works, so on macOS install it with brew and re-run the script. It warns about this when it takes the archive path there.

The script records the prefix it settled on in .pep/llvm-prefix (gitignored), which the test, release and CI scripts read (a git worktree reads its main checkout's). Re-run it on a new machine rather than copying that file. With a valid install present it only rewrites the file, and ./scripts/setup-llvm.sh --check reports what it would use, changing nothing.

CI provisions LLVM with scripts/ci-provision-llvm.sh, through .github/actions/provision-llvm. On Linux, apt's 89 MB of packages come from the runner's Ubuntu mirror, which on a slow day took longer than the step's 15 minutes, so the action caches the .deb files apt downloaded (keyed on scripts/setup-llvm.sh and the Ubuntu release) and the script puts them in apt's archive, so apt downloads none it already has. A miss, or a set the image has moved past, downloads from the mirror, retrying a download that stalls for 30 seconds, and refills the cache; only main's runs save it, under a new key, so the newest set is the one restored.

Only the Windows archive path is large: budget roughly 5 GB of disk for the tree plus its cached archive, and a few minutes for the first run. Everything lands outside the repository, under %LOCALAPPDATA%\pepper or ~/.local/share/pepper, except a package-manager prefix, which stays wherever apt or brew put it.

The debugger

--devtools sets up the lldb debugger, and is worth it: a compiler that generates and links native code fails in native ways, an access violation or SIGSEGV from inside LLVM or the code it generated, and lldb turns that into a symbolized stack. On Windows it installs lldb, lldb-dap and lldb-server into the LLVM prefix (an extra 335–434 MB), extracting them from the llvm.org installer with 7-Zip and placing the embeddable Python that liblldb.dll needs beside them. On macOS and Linux it checks for a usable lldb and says how to install one if there is none. PEPPER_SETUP_DEVTOOLS=1 turns it on for every run.

Build the compiler with -g for its own frames, then:

lldb --batch -o run -k "thread backtrace" -- target/bin/pep-build tests/hello.pep

On Windows the setup script leaves the PATH alone, so run "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\pepper\llvm\20.1.8\bin\lldb.exe" by its full path. Debugging covers debugging Pepper programs.

Building

Build the compiler from tools/compiler with the installed toolchain, against this checkout's runtime, then every tool with the compiler you built. Each tool is a project: its tools/<tool>/pep.toml adds tools/ to the import search path, for the modules the tools share, and names the packages it depends on. On macOS and Windows the compiler's link needs LLVM's library folder (-L), and on Windows its LLVM-C.dll beside it:

export PEPPER_RUNTIME="$PWD/runtime"
llvm="$(head -1 .pep/llvm-prefix)"
mkdir -p target/bin
pepper build -O tools/compiler/main.pep -o target/bin/pep-build    # + -L "$llvm/lib" on macOS and Windows
# Windows: cp "$llvm/bin/LLVM-C.dll" target/bin/
for tool in pepper pep-fmt pep-test pep-package pep-profile pep-run pep-new pep-init pep-install pep-doc pep-lsp; do
  target/bin/pep-build -O "tools/$tool/main.pep" -o "target/bin/$tool"
done

(.exe names on Windows.) The release build (scripts/release-build.sh) does the same, then builds the compiler once more with itself, and ships that one. A cold build of the compiler takes several minutes; the build cache makes a rebuild after an edit take seconds.

Testing

The tests are Pepper [Test] functions, run by scripts/pepper-tests.sh as CI runs them; there is no cargo test.

scripts/pepper-tests.sh                      # with the installed build of main
scripts/pepper-tests.sh target/bin           # with the compiler you built
PEPPER_OPT_LEVEL=2 scripts/pepper-tests.sh   # every build the tests make at -O2
WASI_SDK_PATH=/opt/wasi-sdk WASMTIME=/opt/wasmtime/wasmtime scripts/pepper-tests.sh

The last also builds the docs examples and the corpus for wasm32-wasip1 and runs them under wasmtime, except those that need threads, tasks, sockets or processes; without a wasi-sdk those tests say they skipped and pass, except under CI on Linux, which provisions both. Testing the runtime and the compiler says what runs and where new tests go. Before a pull request, also run what CI checks:

target/pepper-tests/bin/pep-doc check        # the reference and the tools' pages are current
target/pepper-tests/bin/pep-fmt --check runtime tools

AGENTS.md, at the repository's root, holds the rules every change follows, for people and agents alike: the reference-counting model, how errors are reported, naming, formatting, and which docs a change must update. INTERNALS.md is the map of the compiler: where each stage lives and the patterns it follows. .agents/skills/ holds step-by-step workflows (build, test, finish a PR, test another platform), and its build and test skills carry the failure signatures this project has hit, such as LLVM discovery and link failures and the packages' fetch. Start there before diagnosing a failure from scratch.

The VS Code extension

The extension lives in pep-lang/vscode-pepper and runs the toolchain's pep-lsp. scripts/install-vscode-extension.ps1 installs its newest release. To try a server built from a branch, set pepper.lspPath to the pep-lsp you build (see The language server: pep-lsp); the extension restarts the server whenever that file changes.

Platforms

  • Windows x64, Linux x64 and macOS arm64 build and pass the suite; CI runs it on all three.
  • Cross-compiling (--target): CI links from each of Linux x64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 for the other two with lld and their system roots and runs the programs on their own OS. Other pairs emit their objects; their links are untested.
  • WebAssembly (--target wasm32-wasip1) and iOS and Android: see Platform selection and iOS and Android.
  • macOS x86_64 is untested. LLVM 20 publishes no macOS-X64 archive, so it needs Homebrew's llvm@20.

To exercise another platform from the machine you are on, run the platform-test workflow (gh workflow run platform-test.yml -f platforms=linux); the platform-test skill in .agents/skills/ describes it.

Setting up LLVM: setup-llvm.sh

The compiler, pep-build (tools/compiler), links LLVM 20 through the pepper-llvm package, so building it from source needs an LLVM 20 development install. The setup scripts provision one:

./scripts/setup-llvm.sh --devtools            # Linux and macOS
pwsh -File scripts/setup-llvm.ps1 -DevTools   # Windows

They record the LLVM they settled on in .pep/llvm-prefix (gitignored), which scripts/pepper-tests.sh, the release scripts and the workflows read. Run them again on each new machine rather than copying that file. Building Pepper from source says what each platform needs first.

scripts/setup-llvm.sh [options]
pwsh -File scripts/setup-llvm.ps1 [-DevTools] [-Force]

What it does

  • provisions LLVM 20, the one LLVM major Pepper builds with, cheapest source first: an LLVM 20 that is already installed, else the platform's package manager (apt llvm-20-dev or Homebrew llvm@20), else the LLVM release archive (cached, so a second run is free). Windows always uses the archive: no Windows package ships llvm-config and the component libraries;
  • on macOS, installs Homebrew lld@20 when LLVM's ld64.lld is not in the prefix: iOS links need it, and Homebrew's llvm@20 no longer ships it. Homebrew keeps both off the PATH, so to link for iOS, put them first: export PATH="$(brew --prefix lld@20)/bin:$(brew --prefix llvm@20)/bin:$PATH". In GitHub Actions the script does that itself, through $GITHUB_PATH, for the job's later steps;
  • writes the prefix, one line, to .pep/llvm-prefix in the checkout;
  • does nothing more when a valid install is already there.

Options

scripts/setup-llvm.sh takes these; --help prints them.

OptionWhat it does
--devtoolsAlso check for the lldb debugger, with instructions when it is missing
--no-devtoolsSkip the debugger, even when PEPPER_SETUP_DEVTOOLS is set
--no-packagesDo not use apt or Homebrew: use an LLVM already installed, or the release archive
--checkReport the LLVM it would use and what .pep/llvm-prefix records, changing nothing; the status is 0 only when they agree
-h, --helpPrint the options

Of --devtools and --no-devtools, the last one given wins. An unknown argument is an error that exits with status 2.

scripts/setup-llvm.ps1 takes -DevTools, which installs lldb, lldb-dap and lldb-server into the same prefix, and -Force, which downloads and extracts the archive again even when a valid install is there.

Environment variables

VariableWhat it does
PEPPER_SETUP_DEVTOOLS1 sets up the debugger on every run, as --devtools does, so it can be turned on once per machine
PEPPER_LLVM_VERSIONProvisions that LLVM (such as 20.1.8) instead of the one the scripts pin; llvm-package.yml sets it to package another release

Building this documentation

This book lives in docs/ and is rendered with mdBook. The standard library reference (docs/src/reference/) is generated from the runtime's doc comments by pep-doc, a Pepper tool in this repository (tools/pep-doc), which scripts/pepper-tests.sh builds beside pep-build.

Install mdBook once, from its releases (a single binary to put on the PATH), then:


pep-doc serve                                 # live preview while writing
pep-doc reference                             # regenerate the reference after changing runtime docs
pep-doc build                                 # render into target/docs-site/dev/
pep-doc build --version 0.2.0 --site <dir>

Run it as target/pepper-tests/bin/pep-doc after scripts/pepper-tests.sh, or as pepper doc.

pep-doc's commands and options are described in The documentation builder: pep-doc.

Keeping the book current

Documentation changes land in the same PR as the code they describe. The checklist of what to update for each kind of change is in AGENTS.md, under "Keep the documentation current".

Examples are tested

Every runnable example lives in docs/examples/: a single name.pep, or a folder name/ whose entry point is main.pep. Chapters pull them in with mdBook's include syntax, so the text on the page is the file that was tested:

```pepper
{{#include ../../examples/structs.pep}}
```

tools/pep-doc/examples_test.pep, which scripts/pepper-tests.sh runs, builds and runs every example; each must return 0 from main and uses assert to check what it shows. An example that prints ends with an # Output: block, a # line for each line it prints (# alone for an empty one), and must print exactly that; leave it out where the output differs between runs or platforms. A failure is printed as it happens. PEPPER_DOCS_EXAMPLE=structs limits it to the examples whose name starts with structs, and PEPPER_DOCS_EXAMPLES=platform to those marked per platform, which is all a pull request's macOS and Windows jobs run (see Testing). An example whose code differs per platform marks it with [Target(OS(...))] or [Target(Arch(...))]. A sample of the examples is also built at -O2 -g, where LLVM checks the debug info. Short fragments that are not whole programs can stay inline in the chapter.

Versions

Documentation is versioned with the compiler's semantic version (the one line of the root VERSION file). pep-doc build --version X.Y.Z renders the book into <site>/X.Y.Z/ and leaves every other version in the site alone; versions.json lists them for the version picker, and the site's index.html opens the newest release. Builds from main publish as dev.

The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) publishes to the gh-pages branch: pushing to main updates dev, and pushing a tag vX.Y.Z adds the X.Y.Z docs. Published versions are never deleted.

The reference stays current

pep-doc check fails when docs/src/reference/ does not match the runtime, and CI runs it.

What the compiler provides rather than the runtime declares is still declared in the runtime, marked [__BuiltIn]: runtime/reflect.pep declares the reflect functions of static blocks and the values they return, and runtime/builtins.pep the raw pointer and weak reference types, __null, sizeof, unsafe_cast and the __ intrinsics. The compiler ignores such a declaration (its functions and methods end in ;, with no body), so it costs nothing and cannot clash with the built-in; the reference, the doc comment check and the language server read it like any other. A string argument names the built-in when it is not the declaration's own name: [__BuiltIn("reflect.name")] titles the entry and its signature reflect.name, and hover and go-to-definition on a use of reflect.name lead to it. Only the runtime may use the attribute.

Each reference page's title and place in the table of contents come from pages() in tools/pep-doc/reference.pep. A new runtime file with public declarations must be added there, under its module's module.pep; until it is, reference and check fail and name the file.

check also fails on chapter Markdown that renders broken without an mdBook error. An include indented inside a list item is one: mdBook pastes the file's lines at column 0, which ends the list and the code block, so the rest of the example shows as prose and its # comments as headings. Put an included example at column 0, after the list or in its own ### section. The runtime itself must meet the doc comment standard in AGENTS.md, which pep-doc check enforces.

Tool options stay documented

Every command-line option of every tool has its place in the book: docs/src/tools/<tool>.md for pep-build, pepper, pep-fmt, pep-lsp and pep-doc, and Setting up LLVM for scripts/setup-llvm.sh. pep-doc check takes each tool's options from the tool itself (its --help text, from the tools that scripts/pepper-tests.sh builds beside pep-build) and fails, naming the tool, the option and the page, when a page does not mention one. It also checks pep-build's option values, trace channels and environment variables, and pep-lsp's initialization options and VS Code settings. A new option goes in the tool's --help (or the usage text at the top of setup-llvm.sh) and on its page in the same PR.

Testing the runtime and the compiler

The tests are written in Pepper: [Test] functions (see Unit tests) that pepper test (pep-test) builds and runs. They cover the runtime and the Pepper tools, the compiler written in Pepper (tools/compiler) among them.

They are the whole suite: Pepper is written in Pepper, and so are its tests.

Where runtime tests live

Code under testIts tests
A module, runtime/<module>/runtime/<module>/test/<topic>_test.pep, which imports the module
A prelude file, runtime/<name>.pepruntime/test/<topic>_test.pep
A file's private functions[Test] functions in that file itself
A Pepper tool, tools/<tool>/tools/<tool>/<topic>_test.pep, which imports the tool's files (import "format";), or runs the built tool (see Tests that run the tools)

A test/ folder holds no module.pep, so no program that imports the module loads it. Its files are still files of the module, though: a test file that imports one of the module's files (import "../atomic"; in runtime/async/test/) sees its unexported names. pep-test builds each folder's tests into one program, so a helper (or test name) that two test files of one folder declare collides; mark it private in each (as runtime/async/test/ does). Prefer it to tests inside a source file, which only a test of private internals needs. The reference generator and the doc-comment check skip test/ folders, so a test file needs no ## comments.

Running them

scripts/pepper-tests.sh runs them all:

sh scripts/install.sh --version 0.4.0-dev        # the build of main; see below
scripts/pepper-tests.sh                          # every runtime and tool test
scripts/pepper-tests.sh -f parses                # by name, in each run
scripts/pepper-tests.sh target/bin               # with a pep-build you built

The tests build with the installed toolchain's pep-build, the one pepper install which names. Every merge into main that changes the compiler, the runtime or the tools publishes the build of main as a prerelease named x.y.z-dev (pepper install list --available shows it), replacing the one before; CI and the workers install it with the install scripts rather than building the compiler, and so can you (run the install again to refresh it). The compiler's own tests (tools/compiler/*_test.pep) build the compiler's sources into their test programs, so they test a change to it. To run the whole suite with the changed compiler too, build it from tools/compiler (see Building Pepper from source) and pass its folder as the first argument.

The script builds the Pepper tools (pepper, pep-test, pep-doc and the others) from the checkout with that pep-build, against the checkout's runtime, into target/pepper-tests/bin beside a copy of the pep-build, and runs pepper test:

  • in runtime/, every runtime test;
  • in runtime/, the compress tests again with -D USE_ZLIB and the digest tests with -D USE_LIBCRYPTO, which link the system's zlib and libcrypto (on Windows the zlib run needs PEPPER_TEST_ZLIB_DIR, a folder holding zlib.lib, and is skipped without it);
  • in tools/, the tools' tests, each under its tool's pep.toml.

PEPPER_TESTS_PART runs part of them: compiler the compiler's tests (tools/compiler/), others everything else; unset or all, both.

The tools' run, the longest, starts as soon as the tools its tests run (pepper, pep-test, pep-fmt, pep-profile, pep-package, pep-run, pep-new and pep-init) are built, and runs beside the runtime's runs. Its output is interleaved with theirs as it comes, each line starting tools| , so a slow test shows while it runs.

Once pepper is built, run any part of them by hand:

cd runtime
pepper test                       # every runtime test
pepper test json/test             # one module's
pepper test -f parses test        # by name

Further arguments to scripts/pepper-tests.sh go to each of its pepper test runs. --shard I/N splits every run into N parts and takes the Ith, so the N runs from 1/N to N/N, on as many machines, run the whole suite between them:

scripts/pepper-tests.sh target/compiler --shard 2/4

Tests run with runtime/ as the current folder, so a test reads data files kept beside it by a path from there (archive/test/gnu.tar.gz). The builds go to runtime/.pep/, which git ignores. A test that writes files uses a fresh folder under the system's temporary folder (TempFolder in the testing module makes and removes one).

CI runs scripts/pepper-tests.sh with the installed build of main on Linux, macOS and Windows, in two jobs on each: one runs the compiler's tests (PEPPER_TESTS_PART=compiler), the other everything else (PEPPER_TESTS_PART=others), and every build in a job shares one build cache. A PR that changes the compiler (tools/compiler/) or stage 0's pin (.github/stage0) is tested with that compiler instead: CI builds it with stage 0 first (scripts/ci-build-compiler.sh, from a build cache CI keeps between runs, keyed on stage 0's contents) and runs the suite with it.

On a pull request, the docs examples (tools/pep-doc/examples_test.pep) build and run in full only on Linux. The macOS and Windows jobs set PEPPER_DOCS_EXAMPLES=platform, which keeps only the examples that select code per platform: those with a line holding a [Target(...)] that names an OS(...) or an Arch(...). On main, and on every other event, every OS runs every example. To run only those examples by hand:

PEPPER_DOCS_EXAMPLES=platform scripts/pepper-tests.sh target/compiler

Each job has a time limit a little above its slowest passing runs, and prints the runner's memory, swap, disk and biggest processes every minute beside the tests (scripts/ci-monitor.sh). A job that fails, is cancelled or runs out of time ends with a Diagnostics step (scripts/ci-monitor.sh --report): the samples with the least memory free, every process still running with its age and size (a hung build or test is the old one), the disks, and on Linux the kernel's out-of-memory kills.

CI also builds the compiler for a commit that leaves tools/compiler/ alone when the published build of main is stale. The build of main publishes only after main's CI passes, so a run cancelled by the next push leaves it behind main's newest compiler change, and main's new tests would run with the old compiler. scripts/ci-published-compiler.sh decides: the published compiler is used only when the commit the v<VERSION> tag is on is on the commit's history and its tools/compiler/ is the commit's. Otherwise, or when VERSION is not published, CI builds the commit's compiler with stage 0. CI's changes job runs it on pull requests, on pushes to main and on dispatches on main. It prints the decision and its reason in its log and in the run's summary, under "Compiler". To check a commit by hand:

scripts/ci-published-compiler.sh [<commit>]   # exit 0: the published compiler will do

On iOS and Android

scripts/mobile-test.sh runs the runtime's tests in the iOS simulator and the Android emulator, with pep-test --target (see Testing on iOS and Android), from runtime/ as above, then every docs example and the prototype apps (see iOS and Android). By hand, on a Mac with Xcode, or on Linux for Android:

bash scripts/openssl-android.sh fetch runtime     # once: the tls module's OpenSSL for Android
PEPPER_RUNTIME=$PWD/runtime bash scripts/mobile-test.sh target/compiler/pep-build /tmp/mobile android

Or only the tests, in a simulator or emulator already running:

cd runtime
pepper test --target x86_64-linux-android

CI's mobile workflow (.github/workflows/mobile.yml) runs the script on GitHub-hosted runners, iOS on macOS and Android on Linux (where scripts/ci-provision-android.sh sets up the emulator, with KVM), on every push to main and nightly, but not on pull requests: the iOS job takes about 40 minutes on a 3-core macOS runner and holds one of the few macOS runners CI's own test jobs wait for. Each job builds the commit's compiler with stage 0, from the build cache the test jobs keep, and the Android job fetches the OpenSSL itself, so gh workflow run mobile.yml --ref <branch> checks a branch with nothing else to set up. A test that cannot run there (the runtime's need a Unix socket file or a hard link, which adb shell may not make) leaves that part out with [Target(!OS(Android))].

Two Pepper tools depend on packages in other repositories. The compiler written in Pepper, tools/compiler, depends on pep-lang/pepper-llvm, and the language server tools/pep-lsp depends on pep-lang/pepper-lsp. Both are public, so the build clones them over HTTPS with no credentials.

Stage 0

Stage 0 is the published compiler that builds the compiler: in CI, in the release build and in scripts/stage0-check.sh. It is a pinned build of main, named in .github/stage0: its version, the commit it is the build of, and the SHA-256 sum of each archive. The build of main replaces its archives on every merge, so the pinned ones are copies on the repository's stage0 release, named <commit>-<asset> with the commit's first 12 hex digits. scripts/ci-install-toolchain.sh installs stage 0 by default (--newest installs the newest published toolchain, --version a release). A stage 0 that stays the same from run to run keeps the compiler's build cache, which is keyed on it.

The Stage 0 workflow (.github/workflows/stage0.yml) moves the pin. Every night, and when dispatched, it takes the newest build of main once its publish has passed, copies it onto the stage0 release, and pushes the branch stage0/bump that pins it. GitHub Actions may not open pull requests in this repository, so the run's summary and a warning link to open one. Its CI runs as any pull request's, building the compiler with the new stage 0 and running the whole suite with it, so it may auto-merge. While that pull request is open the branch stays put (a push with the workflow's token would start no CI on it); the run after it merges pins the next build. The stage0 release keeps the newest 20 builds and the one main pins, so an older branch whose pin is gone (a patch release made from it, say) copies main's .github/stage0 first.

gh workflow run stage0.yml                                  # pin the newest build of main now
git fetch origin stage0/bump:stage0/bump                    # then open its pull request
gh pr create --base main --head stage0/bump --fill

So runtime code may only use what stage 0 accepts. A runtime change that needs a newer compiler than stage 0 dispatches the workflow and merges its pull request first.

The branch's compiler can hide a runtime change that needs a compiler fix stage 0 does not have, which breaks main's CI and the release, since both build the compiler with stage 0. So a PR that changes tools/compiler/ or runtime/ also runs, before it merges:

scripts/stage0-check.sh                    # with stage 0
scripts/stage0-check.sh --version 0.10.0   # with a release

It installs stage 0 with scripts/ci-install-toolchain.sh into target/pepper-home, builds tools/compiler with it (scripts/ci-build-compiler.sh, into target/compiler), then runs the runtime's tests with stage 0's own pepper test. Further arguments go to that pepper test. It needs GH_TOKEN while the repository is private, and on macOS and Windows LLVM's prefix, as scripts/pepper-tests.sh does (PEPPER_LLVM_PREFIX, or this checkout's .pep/llvm-prefix).

Tests that run the tools

Some tests run programs rather than call functions: pep-build on programs, and the Pepper tools on files and folders, checking their output and exit status as a user would see them.

TestWhat it runs
tools/compiler/corpus_test.peppep-build -I tests on each tests/<Name>/test.pep, then the program from the repository's root, which must exit with 0. With WASI_SDK_PATH set and wasmtime on the PATH (or WASMTIME naming it), each again for wasm32-wasip1 under wasmtime; it says it skipped otherwise, except under CI on Linux, which provisions both (scripts/ci-provision-wasi.sh) and where it fails without them. A new tests/<Name>/test.pep joins the run.
tools/compiler/programs_test.peppep-build on the programs of tools/compiler/testdata/, each run with the arguments and environment it needs: cli's parse and an add_options error, os's environment and host, time's zones (TZif files under TZDIR, TZ, the system's database), and process's arguments, exit and the atexit handlers it runs, main's arguments, children that are copies of the program, and exec; and a build with a runtime copied into a package's folder, which leaves that package's files out.
tools/pep-doc/examples_test.peppep-build on every example of the book, then the example (see Building this documentation).
tools/pep-fmt/repository_test.pepformat_source in the test itself on every .pep file under runtime/, tools/, tests/ and docs/examples/: each formats, formatting it again changes nothing, the syntax tree stays the same, and the files of runtime/ and tools/ are already formatted (pep-fmt -w fixes one that is not).
tools/pep-fmt/cli_test.peppep-fmt on standard input and on files and folders (--check, -w), its syntax errors and usage errors.
tools/pepper/pepper_test.peppepper, copied beside stand-in tools built from tools/pepper/testdata/; and every tool's --version against the version in each tools/*/main.pep (and pep-lsp's tools/pep-lsp/arguments.pep).
tools/pep-test/pep_test_test.peppep-test on test files it writes (tests that pass, fail, time out, leak an allocation or release one too many), from tools/pep-test/testdata/ (named .pep.txt so that the suite's own run skips them).
tools/pep-package/package_test.peppep-package and pep-build on projects whose dependencies are bare git repositories in a test folder, and archives on a loopback server, including builds of one project side by side, which fetch once under .pep/fetch.lock; skipped without git.
tools/pep-run/pep_run_test.peppep-run building and running the programs in tools/pep-run/testdata/ with a Pepper home of its own: arguments, exit status, working folder, the up-to-date rerun, compile errors and the options it refuses.
tools/pep-new/pep_new_test.peppep-new and pep-init scaffolding programs and packages into temporary folders, which pepper build and pepper test then build and test (a package with itself on the import path, as its tests/run.sh puts it); the refusal to overwrite, and the name and license errors.
tools/pep-profile/profile_test.peppep-profile on the recordings in tools/pep-profile/testdata/, and on a real program when samply or a working perf is installed (skipped otherwise).

They find pep-build and the tools beside the test program or on the PATH (process.find_companion), where scripts/pepper-tests.sh puts the ones it builds from the checkout, so they test this checkout's tools. To run one by hand, put that folder first on the PATH (after a run of the script, or with the tools built there as the script builds them):

export PATH="$PWD/target/pepper-tests/bin:$PATH"
cd tools && pepper test pep-fmt/cli_test.pep

The tool_testing module (tools/tool_testing/) holds what they share: tool(name) finds a tool, run and run_with_input run a process.Command and read its output with Windows' line ends made \n, build_program builds a program with pep-build, and expect_exit, expect_contains, expect_starts_with and expect_ends_with show the program's output when they fail. tool_testing.server's serve_folder serves a folder over HTTP on loopback, for a test that downloads (pep-install, pep-package).

Leaks fail a test

Each test counts the runtime's live allocations before and after it runs, and fails when they differ:

error: test 'parses_components' left 2 allocations behind

So a test needs no census of its own: every object it made must be released by the time it returns. What the program keeps for good, such as a global made on first use (async.Lazy), is made inside keep_for_the_program(() => { ... }) at the start of the test, which leaves it out of the count.
